As to why the Law declares the mouse an unclean animal, besides the reasons that occur to anyone, these too are offered: that it is useless and harmful, and a type of those who say,
We are mere numbers, born to consume the fruits of the earth.

In Cyril, Against Julian, book 9: γαλῆ καὶ μῦς γράφουσί πως ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφώδη τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [galē kai mys graphousi pōs eph᾽ heautois ta deila, kai ananda, kai psophōdē tōn kleptōn genē], the weasel and the mouse represent the timid, unwarlike and noisy kinds of thieves. Since noisy is here entirely beside the point, I maintain that for ψοφώδη [psophōdē] we should read ψοφοδεῆ [psophodeē], that is, afraid of every noise. This word is used by Lucian in the Scythian, and by Plutarch in the book On Preserving Health; and the same author in the book Utra anim. says of the chameleon: Ὑπὸ δέους ἄλλως τρέπεται, φύσει ψοφοδεὴς ὢν, καὶ δειλός [Hypo deous allōs trepetai, physei psophodeēs ōn, kai deilos]· From fear it changes into another colour, being by nature fearful and timid. Hence in Hesychius ψοφοδεὴς [psophodeēs] is δειλὸς, κενοφόβος, ὁ καὶ τοὺς ψόφους καὶ τὰ ἐλάχιστα φοβούμενος [deilos, kenophobos, ho kai tous psophous kai ta elachista phoboumenos]. How well this suits the mouse the excellent Poet shows in his fable of the country mouse and the town mouse, Satire 6, book 2:
The clatter of the doors shook both from their couches: in panic they ran through the whole room, and trembled the more, half dead, as soon as the lofty house rang with Molossian hounds. — — — —

The Hebrews offer another reason, namely that eating mouse flesh induces forgetfulness. The most learned Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] proves this from Avoda Zera ch. 3 (where, however, I do not find it) and from Beth Iacob fol. 181, where to the question why a dog recognizes its master but a cat does not, the answer is given that cats are forgetful because they eat mice, whose flesh, and indeed whatever they have gnawed, if eaten, disturbs the brain and the memory. Hence this conclusion is drawn: האוכל ממה שהעכבר אוכל משכח תלמודו האוכל עכבר עצמו לא כ״ש He who eats of what a mouse has eaten forgets his learning: how much more, then, he who eats the mouse itself?

The defeat of Sennacherib, which the sacred writers ascribe to an angel , and Josephus , following Berosus, to a plague sent by God, the Egyptians in Herodotus strangely refer to field mice. They relate that these, τοῖσι ἐναντίοισι αὐτοῖσι ἐπιχυθέντας νυκτὸς, κατὰ μὲν φαγέειν τοὺς φαρετρεῶνας αὐτέων, κατὰ δὲ τὰ τόξα, πρὸς δὲ τῶν ἀσπίδων τὰ ὄχανα· ὥς τε τῇ ὑστεραίῃ φευγόντων σφέων, γυμνῶν ὅπλων, πεσέειν πολλούς· [toisi enantioisi autoisi epichythentas nyktos, kata men phagein tous pharetreōnas auteōn, kata de ta toxa, pros de tōn aspidōn ta ochana; hōs te tē hysteraiē pheugontōn spheōn, gymnōn hoplōn, peseein pollous] poured over the enemy themselves by night, gnawed through their quivers, their bows, and the handles of their shields, so that the next day, stripped of their arms and with many lost, they took to flight. Is it relevant here that λοιμὸς [loimos] plague and λαμὰς [lamas] mouse in Hesychius are words so close that one could have been used for the other, and thus a defeat brought about by plague was ascribed to mice? However that may be, something of the kind is recorded to have happened to those Cretans who founded Hamaxitus, a city of the Troad. For when Apollo , consulted about where to found their city, had answered that it must be founded ἔνθα ἂν αὐτοῖς οἱ γηγενεῖς πολεμήσωσι [entha an autois hoi gēgeneis polemēsōsi], where the earth-born should make war on them, they understood that Hamaxitus was meant; because, when they had pitched camp there, μυῶν ἄφατόν τι πλῆθος ἐφερπύσαν τά τε ὄχανα αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀσπίδων διέτραγε, καὶ τὰς τῶν τόξων νευρὰς διέφαγεν [myōn aphaton ti plēthos epherpysan ta te ochana autois tōn aspidōn dietrage, kai tas tōn toxōn neuras diephagen], an immense host of mice, bursting forth, gnawed the handles of their shields and ate through the strings of their bows. So Aelian, History, book 12, chapter 5. Not very differently the old Scholiast of Homer on book 1 of the Iliad: Νυκτὸς ἐπιγενομένης, μῦες ἔκοψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς τελαμῶνας τῶν ὅπλων [Nyktos epigenomenēs, myes ekopsan autōn tous telamōnas tōn hoplōn], When night had come, mice cut through the straps of their arms. Accordingly, in Aristotle, Rhetoric, book 2, chapter 24, Polycrates praises mice ὅτι ἐβοήθησαν διατραγόντες τὰς νευρὰς [hoti eboēthēsan diatragontes tas neuras], because they brought help (to his countrymen) when they gnawed through the strings of the enemy's bows. And in Clement's Protrepticus, Polemo reports that the peoples neighbouring the Troad τοὺς ἐπιχωρίους μῦς, οὓς σμίνθους καλοῦσι θρησβεύειν, ὅτι τὰς νευρὰς τῶν πολεμίων διέτρωγον τῶν τόξων· [tous epichōrious mys, hous sminthous kalousi thrēsbeuein, hoti tas neuras tōn polemiōn dietrōgon tōn toxōn] worship the mice of that place, which they call sminthoi, because they had gnawed the strings of the enemy's bows. Since these accounts are very similar to what the Egyptians relate of the Assyrians, I would think that they worked this Cretan, or if you prefer Trojan, story into their own.

Simonis, in his Lexicon and in the Arcanum Formarum p. 660, thinks the word עכבר is compounded from the verb עכר, which he supposes has the same meaning as the Arabic عرك [ʿarak] he rubbed, and from the word בר, so that it denotes the animal rubbing grain. How frigid this is, anyone will feel at once. Nor do I like any better what Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] put forward in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 5, p. 1908, referring the Hebrew עכבר to the Arabic عُكَبٌ [ʿukabun] nimble, brisk.

The singular جُرَذٌ [juradhun] is explained in the lexicons as: a species of field mouse. Under the name جِرْذ [jirdh], Dschird, Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] described this animal in Travels p. 156 of the German trans., from which it is clear that it is the mus Glis with a hairy tail, the body dark ash-grey above, whitish below, or the sciurus canus subtus albidus of Linnaeus, p. 155, ed. 13, the μυωξον [myōxon] of Oppian, Cyneg. 2, 574.

Bochart passed over the Syriac translator, who put ܥܘܟܒܪܐ [עוכברא], a word that signifies both a mouse and a creeping disease, one that twists itself like a serpent, on the testimony of the lexicographer Bar Bahlul. To this belongs the view of Hensler too, chief physician to the king of Denmark, that by the word עכברים in 1 Sam 6:5 not mice are meant but carbuncles, perhaps venereal buboes. Michaelis reports this conjecture, from a letter Hensler sent him, in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1909, and not without approval: “There is,” he says, “something in the whole narrative that urges us to understand buboes or piles of this kind. Among the evils that had afflicted the Philistines, 1 Sam. V makes no mention of mice, which so troubled the translators that the LXX and the Vulgate translator added mice at 1 Sam 5:6; Houbigant approved this, but no manuscript has confirmed it. We are freed from all doubt if the mice of Chapter VI are much the same as עפלים, carbuncles, or a kind of tumour or ulcer.” But he soon adds: “Yet verse five of chapter VI seems to stand in the way and to favour mice that lay waste the field: עכבריכם המשחיתים את הארץ.”

“It is certain that female mice gnaw metals and other hard bodies which they cannot eat, namely at the time when they are pregnant. Nor do only mice act so then, but also the females of the other animals that belong to the family of the Glires. — It may be that the teeth of pregnant females are severely affected, and the animals ease this pain by gnawing or biting.” So Beckmann on Aristotle, On Marvellous Things Heard ch. 24, p. 57.

Examples of fields laid waste by mice in the West Indies, from travel accounts, will be given by Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], Vermischte Sammlungen fasc. 2, ch. 3, p. 45.

Oedmann, loc. cit., thinks that both glires [rats] (Ratzen) and sorices [shrews] are comprised under the Hebrew name עכבר, led chiefly by the fact that some of those who have visited Eretz Yisrael report that the fields there are laid waste by both these kinds of animals. This argument would hardly satisfy others. I would think the Hebrew names שפן and עכבר differ thus: the former signifies the Syrian sorex, Arab. وَبْر [wabr] (cf. note 3 to the preceding Chapter), the other, עכבר, the mus jaculus, on the authority of the Arabic dialect, in which عَكْبَر [ʿakbar] and يربوع [yarbūʿ] are nearly synonyms; see Bochart above and p. 1015.
2 Reg. XIX, 35. Isa 37:36. Sir 48:24 (var. 21.). Tob 1:21 (var. 24.). 1 Macc 7:41 and 2 Macc 8:19.
It is proved that חולד choled is not the weasel, as they hold, but the mole. Other names of the mole.

Lev 11:29. The Hebrew חלד choled the Greeks render γαλῆν [galēn], and Jerome mustela [weasel] ; Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] renders it כרכושתא carcoustha, and the Syriac ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא] cacaustho, which is the very same thing . In Hesychius, indeed, κέρκος [kerkos] is ἀρουραῖος μῦς [arouraios mys], field mouse. And I once suspected that כרכושתא carcoustha was derived from κέρκος [kerkos], with the same meaning. But that כרכושתא carcoustha is an animal somewhat like the cat is proved by the Talmudic proverb in Sanhedrin ch. 2, fol. 85. 1: כרכושתא ושונרא עבדו הלולא מחרבא דבישא גדא, "When the carcoustha and the cat make a wedding, he who had been unfortunate lifts himself up." And that it is the weasel is clear from the fact that in Ps 113:9 the Hebrew words עקרת הבית, the barren woman of the house, are rendered thus, on the testimony of Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi], in some copies of the Chaldee Paraphrase: דיתבא מוריקא לאינשי ביתה היך כרכושתא דיתבא מדורא בעקרי ביתא, "She who sits pale before the men of her house, like the carcoustha, which sets its dwelling in the foundations of the house." As if עקרת in that place did not mean barren, but she who out of grief dwells בעקרי in the foundations, that is, in the lowest part of the house, as the carcoustha is wont to do. That this fits the description of the κατοικιδίου [katoikidiou] [domestic] weasel will be evident from what follows. Therefore, since חולד choled in Moses is the weasel, according to the opinion of so many ancients, all the Hebrews will seem to follow this with good reason: Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh], R. Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]; and the more recent interpreters of Scripture, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Castellio, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], etc.; also the vernacular ones, as many as I have been able to see, namely the French, Italian, English, Dutch, German. Not to mention the lexicographers, of whom there is none, as far as I know, who renders חולד choled otherwise than as weasel, or martes [marten], which is a species of weasel. And the Hebrew paraphrast of Aristeas, who renders these Greek words, Κακοποιητικὸς γὰρ ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ, καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos gar ho tropos esti, kai galēs, kai myōn], into Hebrew thus:

כי הנה החולד והעכבר הם בטבעם דורכים אל ההשחתה ומועדים תמיד להרע, "For behold, the choled and the achbar (that is, the weasel and the mouse) by their nature tend toward destruction, and are always inclined to evil."

Yet I have reasons to doubt whether this is the true rendering. The first of them is that the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chuldo, plainly formed from it, means the mole, not the weasel. So Giovanni Battista Ferrari and Thomas a Novaria determine in their Lexicons, or Syriac Nomenclators, published at Rome in the years 1622 and 1636 . And this is confirmed by the most learned of the Maronites, Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)], who rendered the words of the Syriac translator in Proverb. XXIV, 31., ܘܚܦܝܘ ܐܦܘܗܝ ܚܘܠܕܐ [וחפיו אפוהי חולדא], into Latin thus: And moles covered its surface. Nor indeed does the passage allow weasels to be understood. For it concerns the field of a lazy man, which is so neglected that nettles cover it. Nettles, that is, חרלים, is what stands in the Hebrew. But the Syriac read חלדים, the letter Resh being moved from its place and changed into Daleth, because the letters are similar; and accordingly he rendered ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] . That this word signifies not weasels but moles the matter itself shows. For a neglected field does not swarm with weasels, but it can swarm with moles, as the greatest Poet teaches in book 1 of the Georgics:
— — — — often the tiny mouse has set up its home beneath the ground and built its granaries; or blinded moles have dug their chambers.

This is the greatest bane of a field. Hence Simocatta in his Epistles: Τί δῆτα περὶ τῶν ἀσπαλάκων λέξαιμι, φοβερὸν γὰρ τῷ γεωργῷ τὸ κακὸν, καὶ δυσανταγώνιστον τὸ πολέμιον [Ti dēta peri tōn aspalakōn lexaimi, phoberon gar tō geōrgō to kakon, kai dysantagōniston to polemion]. What then shall I say about moles? For to the ploughman this evil is terrible, and the enemy not easily overcome. Accordingly Stesimbrotus fabled that this animal ὑπὸ τῆς Γῆς τυφλωθῆναι, διὰ τὸ φθείρειν τοὺς καρποὺς [hypo tēs Gēs typhlōthēnai, dia to phtheirein tous karpous], had been blinded by Earth, because it ruined the crops. So Suidas and Apostolius under Τυφλότερος ἀσπάλακος [Typhloteros aspalakos].

Moreover, not only for the Syrians but also for the Arabs خلد [khuld] chuld, or chold, is the mole. This is plainly shown, to say nothing of the rest, by the descriptions of it. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] : الخلد الغارة العميا [al-khuld al-ghāra al-ʿamyā] Alchold, the blind mouse. The book entitled الفلاحة الفارسية [al-Filāḥa al-Fārisiyya] Persian Agriculture, cited by Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār]: الخلد دابة عميا تحت الارض تاكل عروق الشجر ويحب رايحة البصل والكراث وتخرج من حجرتها في طلب الرايحتها [al-khuld dābba ʿamyā taḥt al-arḍ taʾkul ʿurūq al-shajar wa-yuḥibb rāyiḥat al-baṣal wa-l-kurrāth wa-takhruj min ḥujratihā fī ṭalab al-rāyiḥatihā] Alchold, a blind animal that eats the roots of trees under the ground, and that takes such delight in the smell of onion and leek that, lured by it, it comes out of its hiding-place . And Giahid: الخلد دويبة عميا صما لا تعرف ما بين يديها الا بالشم تخرج من حجرها وهي تعلم انها لا سمع لها ولا بصر فتنفتح فاها وتقف عند حجرها فياتي الذباب فيسقط علي شدقيها ويمر بين لحييها فيستد خله جوفها بنفسها وهي تعرض لذلك في الساعات التي يكون فيها الذباب اكثر [al-khuld duwaybba ʿamyā ṣammāʾ lā taʿrif mā bayn yadayhā illā bi-l-shamm takhruj min ḥujrihā wa-hiya taʿlam annahā lā samʿ lahā wa-lā baṣar fa-tanfatiḥ fāhā wa-taqif ʿind ḥujrihā fa-yaʾtī al-dhubāb fa-yasquṭ ʿalā shidqayhā wa-yamurr bayn laḥyayhā fa-yastad khalahu jawfahā bi-nafsihā wa-hiya taʿriḍ li-dhālika fī al-sāʿāt allatī yakūn fīhā al-dhubāb akthar] Alchold is a small animal, blind and deaf, which does not recognize what is in front of it except by smell. When it comes out of its hiding-place, well aware that it lacks hearing and sight, it stands with open mouth near its hiding-place; and flies that come fall into its mouth and walk between its jaws, and are drawn by its breath into its belly. And so it opens its mouth wide at those hours when flies are most numerous. So he, who deprives الخلد [al-khuld] alchold, that is, the mole, not only of sight but also of hearing. But Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] judges otherwise; his words are: كل حيوان له عينان الا الخلد وانما خلق كذلك لانه ترابي جعل الله له الارض كالما للسمك وغذاوه في بطنها وليس له في ظاهرها قوة ولا نشاط ولما لم يكن له بصر عوضه الله حدة حاسة الشمع فيدرك الوطي [kull ḥayawān lahu ʿaynān illā al-khuld wa-innamā khuliqa ka-dhālika li-annahu turābī jaʿala Allāh lahu al-arḍ ka-l-māʾ li-l-samak wa-ghidhāʾuhu fī baṭnihā wa-laysa lahu fī ẓāhirihā quwwa wa-lā nashāṭ wa-lammā lam yakun lahu baṣar ʿawwaḍahu Allāh ḥiddat ḥāssat al-shamʿ fa-yudrik al-waṭʾ] الخفي من مسافة بعيدة فانا احس بذلك جعل يحفر الارض [al-khafī min masāfa baʿīda fa-anā aḥass bi-dhālika jaʿala yaḥfur al-arḍ] Every animal has eyes except alchold, which was created without eyes, because it lives in the earth, which God assigned to it as water to the fishes, so that its food is in the belly of the earth, and outside it it lacks strength and vigour. But God compensated for the lack of sight by the keenness of the sense of hearing, by which it perceives even from a great distance those who walk with stealthy step; and as soon as it perceives them, it hides itself in the earth. With this agrees the statement of Pliny: Moles, though buried in the earth, so dense and deaf an element of Nature, hear more clearly. But in the opinion of some there are two kinds of mole, namely خلد [khuld] chold and زباب [zabāb] zebab, of which the former lacks sight, the latter hearing. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār], that is, On the mouse: ومنها اليرابوع والزباب والخلد فالزباب صم والخلد اعمي [wa-minhā al-yarābūʿ wa-l-zabāb wa-l-khuld fa-l-zabāb ṣumm wa-l-khuld aʿmā] Among the species of mice there are also aljarbuo (or choerogryllius), zebab, and chold; of which zebab is deaf and chold blind. I could add much more, but from this it is more than sufficiently clear that for the Arabs as well as the Syrians, chold or chuld is the mole.

Third, in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Moëd Katon, ch. 1, fol. 6b, in the words of the Mishnah צדין את האישות ואת העכברים, One may lawfully hunt moles and mice, in these words (I say) האישות, that is, the mole or moles (as all acknowledge, and as we shall show at greater length below), is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. I have not, indeed, read this in it myself, since the book is not at hand; but so the Gloss asserts on the passage of Moëd Katon just cited: אישות מפירש בירושלמי חולדה The word אישות is rendered in the Jerusalem Talmud as חולדה chulda. There, therefore, חולדה chulda is the mole, not the weasel.

Fourth, in Lev 11:29. חולד choled heads the list of those animals which are comprised under the name שרץ. Two things, moreover, are characteristic of these. One, that because of the shortness of their feet they seem to creep rather than walk. The other, that they multiply beyond measure. For this is what the verb שרץ properly signifies, and accordingly it is applied to fishes in Gen 1:20, to frogs in Exod 8:3 and Ps 105:30, and, καθ' ὑπερβολὴν [kath' hyperbolēn], to the Israelites in Egypt, Exod 1:7, because in that servitude God's blessing increased their number, I might almost say, beyond all belief. Everyone knows that these marks suit weasels less than moles, whose legs are very short and whose multitude (on the authority of Pliny somewhere) is so great that they undermine whole fields.

Fifth, if חולד choled is the mole, then חולד choled and עכבר achbar, that is, the mole and the mouse, are rightly joined in Moses, since the mole is akin to the mouse, and indeed a species of mouse, if we believe the Arabs; and Hesychius, for whom Λὼτ [Lōt] is ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax], the mole, or μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Acharnians, where he defines σκάλοπας [skalopas] as μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas], certain mice, which we call moles; and Oecumenius on 2 Petri I, 9., where he holds that μυωπάζειν [myōpazein] is the same as τυφλώττειν [typhlōttein], to be blind, ἀπὸ τῶν ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν μυῶν τυφλῶν εἰς ἅπαν διατελούντων [apo tōn hypo tēn gēn myōn typhlōn eis hapan diatelountōn], from the mice which live under the earth entirely blind, that is, from moles. Accordingly, according to Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] , the mole belongs to the genus of mice. For others the mole is merely an animal similar to the mouse. Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὁ ἀσπάλαξ ζῶον μυῒ ἐμφερὲς, ὑπὸ γῆν διάγον, τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἐστερημένον [Esti de ho aspalax zōon myi empheres, hypo gēn diagon, tō ophthalmō esterēmenon]; The mole is an animal similar to the mouse, living under the earth, deprived of eyes. Accordingly they are joined in the passage of the Talmud that we cited, צדין אישות ועכברים, They hunt moles and mice. But the weasel is a quite different animal, larger and stronger than the mouse, and as hostile to it as the cat. Hence Theophrastus, in the little book On the animals that appear in multitudes [?], in the passage where he treats of mice: Φθείρουσι δ' αὐτοὺς καὶ αἱ ἄγριαι γαλαῖ [Phtheirousi d' autous kai hai agriai galai]; Wild weasels kill them. And the author of the Batrachomyomachia, whoever he is, line 9[?]:
Μῦς ποτε διψαλέος, γαλέης κίνδυνον ἀλύξας, [Mys pote dipsaleos, galeēs kindynon alyxas,]

A mouse once, thirsty, having escaped the danger of a weasel. And in Athenaeus the poet Carcinus wrote a play entitled Μῦες [Myes], in which a weasel strangles mice by night. Plautus too, in the Stichus, Act 3:
A weasel snatched a mouse away from right before my feet. It did its shopping briskly. — — —

Likewise Pliny, book 8, chapter 27: The weasel (restores its strength) with rue when hunting mice, once it has joined battle with them. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3: The weasel also pursues serpents and mice. Abdollatif of Baghdad : ربما عادي الفار وقتله لكن الخوف الفار من السنور اشد خوفه منه [rubbamā ʿādā al-fār wa-qatalahu lākin al-khawf al-fār min al-sinnawr ashadd khawfihi minhu] It (the weasel) sometimes pursues mice and kills them. Yet the mouse fears the cat more gravely than the weasel.

Sixth, the verb חלד chalad (from which חולד choled is derived) means to penetrate and to dig under. It is properly said of the earth, as these examples show. The Jerusalem Talmud, in Kilayim, last chapter, as the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] cites it: מחליד הקב״ה לפניהם את הארץ God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, digging under the earth before them. And the Babylonian Talmud, in Bava Batra fol. 19b, of vines: מפני שמחלידין את הקרקע ומעלין עפר תיחוח Because they dig under the ground and loosen the soil. And the Syriac translator of the hedgehog in Es. XXXIV, 15.: ܘܢܚܠܕ ܘܢܥܘܠ ܒܛܠܠܗ [ונחלד ונעול בטללה] And it will dig out, and penetrate into its shade. From this it is transferred metaphorically to other things. Thus חלד, of metals, is to contract rust; and חלודה, rust, in Jonathan חלדות, Num 31:22, because it penetrates metals and eats into them to their innermost parts. Likewise gangrene is called ܡܣܟܝܢܘܬܐ [מסכינותא] in the Syriac paraphrase, 2 Tim. II, 17., because it is a disease that is ὑπόνομος [hyponomos], penetrating deeper into the flesh. Again, in slaughtering a victim, חלדה was the name for the deep plunging of the knife into the victim, which rendered the slaughter illegitimate, as is found in the Talmudic tractate Chullin, ch. 2, fol. 20b, and in Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah]' treatise On Slaughtering, ch. 3, §§ 9 and 10. To the same belongs the fact that in 2 Tim. III, 6., for Paul's words οἱ ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας [hoi endynontes eis tas oikias], that is, who penetrate into houses, the Syriac has ܕܡܣܟܝܢ ܒܒܝܬ ܒܬܐ [דמסכין בבית בתא]. For it speaks there of those who, as if making for the depths of houses, search and scrutinize everything most hidden. Accordingly the Arabic version published at Paris rendered it with a not dissimilar metaphor: الذين يغوصون في المنازل [alladhīna yaghūṣūna fī al-manāzil] who plunge themselves into houses. Nor does the conjecture of the most learned Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanies, book 3, chapter 14, lack plausibility: that the Chalybes near Trapezus and Pharnacia were called Chaldaeans by the Phoenicians not because they had anything in common with the Babylonian Chaldaeans, but as חלדיא, or καταδύτας [katadytas], because they searched the bowels of the earth to dig metals out of it. They are thought to have been the first of all to devote effort to this. Callimachus, in the elegy On the Lock of Berenice:
— — Χαλύβων ὡς ἀπόλοιτο γένος, [Chalybōn hōs apoloito genos,] Γειόθεν ἀντέλλον τι κακὸν φυτὸν οἵ μιν ἔφηναν. [Geiothen antellon ti kakon phyton hoi min ephēnan.]
— — May the whole race of the Chalybes perish, And he who first began to seek veins beneath the earth, etc.
Valerius too, in book 5 of the Argonautica, says elegantly of the same people:

The sleepless toil of the Chalybes is heard; the country-dwellers wear out arms for you, Gradivus; there sounds that hand, the first creator of war, cruel against all lands. For before they dug out the hard beds of unknown iron and supplied swords, sick hatreds wandered without arms, and wraths lacked means, and Erinys was sluggish.

And Arrian in the Alexander: Χάλυβες πρῶτοι ἀνθρώπων αἰτίαν ἔχουσι χαλκεύσασθαι σίδηρον [Chalybes prōtoi anthrōpōn aitian echousi chalkeusasthai sidēron]; the Chalybes are charged with having been the first to forge iron. And Ammianus, book 22: the Chalybes, by whom iron was first dug out and worked. Yet others attribute the same invention to the Cyclopes. Pliny, book 7, chapter 56: Some think that the Chalybes, others that the Cyclopes first showed the craft of working bronze. However that may be, from the frequent digging of metals the land of the Chalybes could be called Chaldia, and its inhabitants Chaldi, Chaldii and Chaldaei. For that the ancients wrote it in all these ways is attested by Eustathius in his Notes on Dionysius Periegetes, page 101 b. And these names clearly allude to the verb חלד chalad, which, when said of the earth, means to dig, as was proved at length above . Now who does not see that the name חולד choled can fittingly be referred to the same root, for the mole, which seems born and designed for this very purpose: to undermine and dig beneath the earth with unceasing labour? That is why no one defines the mole without making this part of the definition. Thus in Hesychius, under the words Λὼτ [Lōt] and Σκάλοψ [Skalops], we read that it is μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn], a blind mouse that bores through the earth; and ζῶον γεώρυχον τυφλὸν [zōon geōrychon typhlon], a blind animal that digs the earth. Epiphanius, on the Adamites, right at the beginning: Ἀσπάλακα καλοῦσί τι ζῶον ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω ἐμφωλεῦον, τετράπουν, ὅπερ ὀρύττει τὴν γῆν [Aspalaka kalousi ti zōon en tē gē katō emphōleuon, tetrapoun, hoper oryttei tēn gēn], etc. They call mole a certain four-footed animal that has its lairs in the depths of the earth, which it digs out, etc. In Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 2: It is an animal without eyes, which is always digging the earth and throwing up the soil. In R. Solomon on the same passage: חפרפרות מיני שרצים שחופרין הארץ שקורין טלפא בלעז, Chaphorpheroth are kinds of creeping things that dig the earth, and in the vernacular are called talpae [moles]. And in Moed Katan fol. 6b: בריה שאין לה עיניים חופרת בקרקע It is a creature that lacks eyes and digs in the earth. Accordingly, naturalists note that its very sharp snout serves this purpose. And the forward part of its forelegs has this peculiarity, that it consists of paired and very short bones, which are inserted directly into the humerus, so that they may dig more powerfully. For the same reason the forefeet and toes point not downward but sideways; and they have a quite broad palm and very strong claws, far larger in proportion to the size of the body than in other animals. Hence they dig the earth so easily and so swiftly as almost to pass belief, as we experience daily to the damage of our property. Therefore the other name for moles, חפרפרות, Isa 2:20, is also taken from digging. For, like חלד chalad, חפר chaphar also means to dig, as everyone knows. Hence the reduplicated חפרפרות intensifies the meaning, so that the name designates an animal wholly given over to digging the earth. But the Greek σπάλαξ [spalax] or ἀσπάλαξ [aspalax] must also be referred to the same idea; its true origin has so far escaped the learned. For those who derive it παρὰ τὸ σπᾶν [para to span], that is, from drawing, talk nonsense. Rather, σπάλαξ [spalax] was formed by metathesis from σκάλοψ [skalops], which was the old word for the mole among the Athenians, as we know from Nicocles: Σκάλοψ, ὁ σπάλαξ λέγεται παρὰ Ἀττικοῖς, ὡς λέγει Νικοκλῆς [Skalops, ho spalax legetai para Attikois, hōs legei Nikoklēs]. So the Etymologicum. And Aristotle confirms it in the Acharnians, where he has σκάλοπας [skalopas] for moles. On this passage the Scholiast: Σκάλοπας] μύας τινὰς, οὓς φαμεν σπάλακας [Skalopas] myas tinas, hous phamen spalakas]. It is called σκάλοψ [skalops], however, not as if κεκαλυμμένους ἔχων τοὺς ὦπας [kekalymmenous echōn tous ōpas], as the Etymologicum idly claims, but ἀπὸ τοῦ σκάλλειν, ἢ σκαλεύειν [apo tou skallein, ē skaleuein], from digging; and by the compound word σκαλόπεζα [skalopeza], as if having digging feet, as in the Poet ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], silver-footed Thetis. Hesychius: Σκάλοψ· σκαλόπεζα, ἀσπάλαξ [Skalops; skalopeza, aspalax]. So it should be read, not σκαλόπετα [skalopeta], as our editions have it. Again, from σκάλοψ [skalops], mole, comes σκαλοπιὰ [skalopia] for a mole's lair, or a heap of earth thrown up by moles. And it must certainly be taken so in these words of Theophrastus, History, book 7, chapter 11, on the roots of the phasganon (or gladiolus): Πολλὰς δὲ εὑρίσκουσι παρὰ ταῖς σκαλοπιαῖς· χαίρει γὰρ, καὶ συλλέγεται τὸ ζῶον [Pollas de heuriskousi para tais skalopiais; chairei gar, kai syllegetai to zōon]. They find many near the scalopiae, or mole-holes; for this animal seeks them and gathers them. Very badly, then, do the translators render it: They find a great many scolopendras near it. Nor is it true, as others hold, that τὴν σκαλοπιὰν [tēn skalopian] is the same as τὴν σκάλοπα [tēn skalopa]. As if someone held that τὴν μυρμηκιὰν [tēn myrmēkian], the ants' nest, were the same as τὴν μύρμηκα [tēn myrmēka], the ant. What I had nearly omitted: in a certain part of France too the mole is called foyon, as fovir is French for to dig, as the late Cappel (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]) observes in the Critica Sacra, page 382. And Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], under Talpa, page 932, records several German names for the mole that belong to the same idea. Thus it is common to the Hebrews, the Greeks, the Germans and some of the French to name the mole from digging.

From what has been said I think it is clear that the חולד choled of Moses was the mole, just like the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chulda and the Arabic خلد [khuld] chuld or chold. Yet it must not be concealed that among the Talmudic doctors חולדה chulda is for the most part the weasel. The following passages make this plain. In the tractate Cholin, cited above: חלדה הר בחלדה הדרה בעיקרי בתים דמכסי הכא, "The thrusting in of the knife in slaughtering is called Chalada, an expression borrowed from chulda, which lives in the foundations of houses so as to lie hidden there." This does not fit the mole, which lives only in the field, but it fits the house-dwelling weasel, κατοικίδιον [katoikidion]. To this is regularly opposed חולדת סנאים or חולדת הסניים, the weasel of the brambles, that is, the wild weasel: as in Kilaim ch. 8, fol. 32a b., הקופד וחולדת הסניים, "the hedgehog and the weasel of the brambles." There the Gloss of Maimonides says: וחולדת הסניים חיה דומה לחולדה ממיני השועלים, that is, "The weasel of the brambles is a wild animal similar to the common weasel, among the species of foxes." And in Bava kama ch. 4, fol. 80. 1: מגדלין כלבין כופרין וחתולין וקופין וחולדות סנאים מפני שעושין לנקראת הבית, "One may raise village dogs, and cats, and monkeys, and weasels of the brambles (which are called חולדות), because they are made for digging through houses." And shortly after: אמר ר׳ יהודה שרצא חרצא ואיכא דאמר חרזא דקטני שקי דרעיא ביני וורדיני, "R. Iuda said: It is a creeping thing (CHARTSA) that cuts. And there are those who say (CHARZA) that bores, because it has slender legs and feeds among thickets." So too Pliny, book 29, chapter 4: "There are two kinds of weasels: one is wild. They differ in size. The Greeks call them ictidas, etc. But this one, which roams about in our houses," etc. That the Talmudists generally take חולדה chulda to be the weasel, not the mole, as we have said, also follows from their claim that this animal strangles children, which no one would say of the mole. To this end a passage is cited from the tractate Thaanith ch. 1, fol. 8. 1: בא וראה כמה גדולים בעלי אמנה מניין מחולדה ובור ומה המאמין בחולדה ובור כך המאמין בהקב״ה על אחת כמה וכמה, "Come and see how the chulda and the pit are reckoned among the great witnesses of faith. And who trusts the chulda and the pit, and would not trust much more the Holy One, Blessed be He?" On this passage the Talmudic Glossator relates this tale: מחולדה ובור שהמיתו שני בני אדם מצוי הוא באגדה מעשה בבחור אחד שנתן אמונתו לריבה אחת שישאנה אמרה מי העיד והיה שם בור א׳ וחולדה אמר הבחור בור וחולדה עדים בדבר לימים עבר על אמונתו ונשא אחרת והוליד שני בנים אחד נפל לבור ומת ואחד נשכתו חולדה ומת אמרה לו אשתו מה מעשה הוא זה שבנינו מתים במיתה משונה ואמר לה כך וכך היה מעשה, "The chulda and the pit, by which two people were put to death. The story is found in the Aggada about a certain young man who pledged his faith to a girl that he would marry her. 'Who will be witness?' she said. Now there were there a pit and a chulda (weasel). And the young man said: 'The pit and the chulda will be witnesses of the matter.' But some days later he broke his pledge and married another, who bore him two sons. One of these fell into the pit and died; the other also died, bitten by a chulda, or weasel. Then, when his wife asked him why both sons had died a violent death, he told her how the matter stood." Baal Aruch relates many more details of the same story, among them that the child was a boy, already three months old, strangled by the chulda. The words are: וילדה בן זכר כשהגיע לג׳ חרשים חנקתו חולדה, "And she bore a male son, whom the chulda strangled when he had already reached the third month." Likewise, of the الزبزب [al-zabzab] zebzeb, a kind of larger weasel or ferret, caught at Baghdad in the year 304 of the Hegira, the Arabs related above انه ياكل اطفالهم [annahu yaʾkul aṭfālahum], that it devoured their infants, and bit men's hands and women's breasts. To this must be added what the Talmudists adduce in comparing the words חולדה chulda or חולד choled and חלד cheled. The latter means the world in Ps. XLIX, 2., where men are called יושבי חלד, inhabitants of cheled, that is, of the earthly world. And the doctors dispute among themselves why the earth is called חלד cheled, and ask what it has in common with חולד choled, the animal. In the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin ch. 9, fol. 127a, someone answers: כל שיש ביבשה יש בים חוץ מן החולדה, "Whatever animal is on land is also in the sea, except only the chulda." Lest this be thought said without grounds, here is a pretty story which the most learned Buxtorf brings from the writings of the Rabbis in his Lexicon Talmudicum under the word חלד: "The princes of the world held an assembly on right government. The prince of the sea complained that he did not have enough subjects. He was therefore permitted to seek more from the land, provided he made provision for their food. He cast all the land animals into the sea, with the command that they should propagate their kind there too. So it was done; hence it is said that all land animals are also in the sea, except that some have been changed into monstrous form. When he came to the weasel, she, standing on the shore, said to the prince of the sea: 'Why will you throw me into the sea again? Do you not see that I am already in the sea?' She said this showing her image in the sea. The prince was satisfied and let the weasel go. Hence the Talmudists say that all land creatures are in the sea except the weasel, which escaped by her cunning. And the earth is called חלד cheled because it remained the property of the weasel, which is called חולדה chulda or חולד choled." In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of the chapter On the eight creeping things, the same question is treated, and some answer the very thing we have just said, that the earth and earthly men are compared with the chulda: לפי שכל מה שיש ביבשה יש בים והרבה מינין יש בים מה שאין כן ביבשה ואין חולדה בים, "because, although everything that is on land is also in the sea, and there are many species in the sea that are not on land, yet the chulda is not in the sea." The other answer is this: חולדה זו גוררת ומנחת ואינה וודעת למי מנחת כך כל באי העולם גוררין ומניחין ואינן יודעין למי מניחין כמו שנאמר יצבור ולא ידע מי אספם, "The chulda drags in many things and leaves them behind, not knowing for whom she leaves them. So also all worldly people drag in many things and leave them behind, not knowing for whom they will leave them. As it is said Ps 139:2: 'He will heap up, and will not know who will gather them'." So the Aruch cites these things, which, however utterly trifling, nevertheless serve our purpose. For they show that by the word chulda most Talmudists do not mean the mole. For the mole, which is blind, would not be said to have seen its image in the sea and shown it to others. Nor is it read to store up and hide anything in its burrows. But this is the disposition of the weasel, of which Abdollatiph of Baghdad writes, in the place cited above: في طبعه انه يسرق ما وجد من فضة او ذهب كما يفعل الغار [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yasriq mā wajada min fiḍḍa aw dhahab kamā yafʿal al-ghār], "It is in its nature to steal whatever silver (or gold) it finds, as mice do." And so in the same place this story is told of the weasel: رجل صاد فرخا منها وحبسه في قفص بحيث تراه امه فلما اراته ذهبت ثم جات وفي فمها دينار فالقته بين يديه كانها تفدي ولدها فلم يتركه لها فذهبت وعادت بدينار اخر حتي بلغت من العدد خمسا فلما ان لا يطلق لها ذهبت وعادت بخرقة كانها تشير الي فراغ حاصلها فلم يكترث بها فلما رات ذلك عادت الي دينار فاخذته منه فخشي الرجل من ذلك فاطلق لها ولدها [rajul ṣāda farkhan minhā wa-ḥabasahu fī qafaṣ bi-ḥaythu tarāhu ummuhu fa-lammā arāthu dhahabat thumma jāʾat wa-fī famihā dīnār fa-alqathu bayna yadayhi kaʾannahā tafdī waladahā fa-lam yatrukhu lahā fa-dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-dīnār ākhar ḥattā balaghat min al-ʿadad khamsan fa-lammā an lā yuṭliq lahā dhahabat wa-ʿādat bi-khirqa kaʾannahā tushīr ilā farāgh ḥāṣilihā fa-lam yaktarith bihā fa-lammā raʾat dhālika ʿādat ilā dīnār fa-akhadhathu minhu fa-khashiya al-rajul min dhālika fa-aṭlaqa lahā waladahā] "A certain man caught a weasel's young and shut it in a cage, so that the mother could see it. When she had seen it, she went away and came back with a denarius in her mouth, which she threw down before him, as though to ransom her young. But when he did not release it, she went off again and brought more denarii, until she reached the number five. And when she saw that her young was still not released, she also brought a cloth (in which the coins had been), to show that she had exhausted her whole store. And when she noticed that no heed was paid to her, she went back to the coins to take them back. But the man, struck with fear, returned her young to her." It is clear, then, that by the word חולדה chulda the Talmudists mostly mean the weasel. But their authority in this matter moves us little, since they are not consistent with themselves, and among the Arabs and Syrians chuld or chulda is the mole; and both the origin of the word and the circumstances of the Mosaic text plainly show that the word is to be taken in this way.

Note in passing that not only the Hebrews but also the most learned of our own scholars labour to reconcile the words חולד choled and חלד cheled, of which the former means, as they would have it, weasel, the latter earth or age, and to show how it came about that the senses of such different words were derived from one origin. There are some who understand by the word חלד cheled nothing but a short time, so that the weasel would hence be called חולד choled as a βραχύβιον [brachybion] animal. So Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs]. For others חלד is a verb meaning to pass away gradually and to creep in; and accordingly, as they would have it, not only is the weasel called חולד choled from its stealthy movement, but time too is called חלד cheled, because it runs by silently and its motion is not perceived.
The times glide by, and we grow old with the silent years.

This is the opinion of Schindler. But for Fuller, just as חלד chalad is a verb meaning καταδῦναι [katadynai], that is, to penetrate into deep places, so the weasel is called חולד choled as a ζῶον καταδυτικὸν [zōon katadytikon], and both the earth itself and the time during which we live on earth are called חלד cheled, as it were κατάδυσις [katadysis], as Aquila renders it, that is, a hiding-place or a submersion: because here all things are full of thick darkness and are not to be compared with the light of supercelestial things. These things are indeed attractively said, but with too little solidity, as I at least think. For it is certain that the verb חלד chalad has two very different meanings, of which one prevailed among the Syrians, the other among the Arabs. For the Syrians, namely, ܚܠܕ [חלד] chalad properly means to dig deep places and to penetrate, as was amply proved above. But for the Arabs خلد [khalada] chalada means something quite different, namely to remain, to endure, to last for ever, to be eternal. And just as from the former meaning came חולד choled for the mole, so from the latter came חלד cheled, which first means duration, as in Ps 39:6. וחלדי, And my duration is as nothing before thee; and Ps 89:48. זכור אני מה חלד, Remember of what duration I am, that is, of how brief a span. Then חלד cheled also means the world, as in Ps 49:2 Hear, all ye inhabitants of חלד, the world: because the world and the things in it consist of a fixed duration. So also עולם olam, its synonym, first means age and eternity, and then also the world, as everyone knows.

In place of the true name of the mole, namely חולד choled, Lev 11:29, the interpreters substitute another: namely תנשמת thinsemeth in the following verse, which is rendered mole by Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], the Greeks, Jerome, Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], Kimchi, Pomarius, Pagninus, Arias, the Italians, the English, the Genevans, and nearly all the new versions there are. But although
Their number defends them, and phalanxes joined boss to boss,

I nevertheless see nothing certain in this rendering. Indeed, if חולד choled truly is the mole, which we consider now established, then תנשמת thinsemeth is something else. For in the list of creeping things rejected as unclean, Moses names these two separately, as different animals. And since there are eight in all, the first in that list is חולד choled and the last is תנשמת thinsemeth, so that they could not have been placed further apart from each other. But in the following book we shall show what תנשמת thinsemeth is.

They also hold that אשת eseth is the mole in these words of David, Ps 58:9, כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, which many of the Hebrews render thus: Like the abortive and the mole, they have not seen the sun. Among them are R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], R. Obadias Gaon on the Psalms, Pomarius in his Lexicon, and Elias in the Methurgeman, having no doubt been so taught by their forebears. For in the very Mishnah of the Talmud, than which the Jews have nothing, after the Bible, either more sacred or more ancient, the mole is called אישות esuth, a word derived from אשת eseth. So in the tractate Kelim, ch. 11, fol. 34a: מצודת האשות טהורה The net for the mole is clean. And in Moëd Katon, cited above: צדין את האשות ואת העכברים משדה האילן ומשדה הלבן כדרכו במועד ובשביעית It is permitted to hunt the mole and mice, both in a planted field and in an arable field, during the minor festival and in the seventh year. And there the Gemara: מאי אישות אמר רב יהודה בריה שאין לה עיניים What is esuth? Rabbi Judah said: It is an animal lacking eyes. And a little later: מאי קרא כמו שבלול תמס יהלך כפל אשת בל חזו שמש, Why is it so called? (because it is said in Ps 58:9) as a snail that melts away, as the abortive and the eseth (or mole) have not seen the sun. And in the same place, in the Gloss, אשות esuth is defined as בריה שאין לה עיניים וחופרת בקרקע, an animal deprived of sight, and digging in the earth. Accordingly the Chaldee translator paraphrases [παραφράζει, paraphrazei] the passage of the Psalm thus: היך נפול ואישותא די סמין ולא חמין שמשא Like an abortive fetus, and the esutha (mole), which are blind and do not see the sun. It is certain, however, that this version has nothing sound in it. For the Hebrew words נפל אשת, which they render the abortive and the mole, mean nothing other than ἔκτρωμα γυναικὸς [ektrōma gynaikos], the miscarriage of a woman, as among the ancients Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion and Jerome explained them very well. נפל nephel, for an abortive, takes its name from falling, like the Arabic سقط [saqṭ] sikt, or sukt. Nor does it occur only here, but also in Job 3:16 and Eccl 6:3. And אשת eseth, for woman, occurs more often in the construct state, but also in the absolute. So Deut 21:11. And if you see among the captives אשת יפת תאר an eseth (that is, a woman) beautiful in form. And 1 Sam 28:7. Seek me אשת בעלת אוב an eseth (or woman), a Pythoness. And Jer 13:21. Pains will seize you כמו אשת לדה, as labour seizes an eseth (or woman). So here נפל אשת is the abortive fetus of an eseth (or woman). Thus in these words there is nothing difficult, nothing ambiguous, nothing that could be drawn in different directions. And the sense too is perfectly plain. Those who are soon to lose the light of life are compared with the abortive fetus of a woman, whose enjoyment of life was so brief, and in so dark a place, that it never saw the sun. So there was no need to imagine a mole here, especially since it is customary in Scripture to assert of abortive fetuses the very thing the Psalmist asserts here, namely that they have not seen the light. So Job 3:16. Like a hidden abortive, I would no longer be; like infants who have not seen the light, which is added by way of explanation [ἐπεξηγητικῶς, epexēgētikōs]. And Eccl 6:3–4. 5. The abortive is happier than he, though it came in vain, and went into darkness, and its name was covered with darkness, and it neither saw the sun nor knew, etc. Accordingly there seems to be an antithesis [ἀντίθετον, antitheton] in the words of Paul, 1 Cor 15:8 Ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί· [Hōsperei tō ektrōmati ōphthē kamoi], as if he were saying: “Christ was seen even by me, though in matters pertaining to salvation I was once as blind as an abortive is to the light of the sun.” Yet granted, though not conceded, that אשת eseth in the passage of the Psalm means the mole, even so they would not have what they want. For the words נפל אשת would mean the abortive of a mole, not the abortive and the mole, as they render it, supplying the conjunction AND, which does not appear in the text. Yet lest they seem to do this without precedent, R. Selomo here cites a similar passage from Jer 11:19, where he would have the Hebrew words ככבש אלוף rendered like a lamb and an ox, likewise adding the conjunction. But we have shown in its place that nothing is to be supplied there, and that in Hebrew כבש אלוף is a tame lamb, and that الوف [alūf] aluph is still taken in this sense among the Arabs today.

There is more reason in those who hold that חפרפרות chapharpheroth are moles in this passage, Isa 2:20. In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which he had made for himself to worship, לחפרפרות ולעטלפים, to the chaphorpheroth (or moles) and the bats. But much must be noted about this word. Let the first point be this: although it is a single word, it is nevertheless written separately, לחפר פרות, as if there were two words, as happens with some others. Thus at 2 Chr 34:6 in most editions בחר בתיהם is written for בחרבותיהם, with their hammers. Jer 46:20. יפה פיה for יפהפיה, most beautiful. Lam 4:3. כי ענים for כיענים, like ostriches; Ezek 27:6. בת אשורים for בתאשורים, of boxwood. The same happened with this word, so that it was split in two. Hence some explain it as though the words were separate: for instance, to the digger of fruits, as if it were a kind of bird so called because it pierces and bores through the fruits of trees; or to the digging of pits, as if פירות stood for חפירות, which is what the Hebrews call pits. But it is certain that the ancient interpreters, namely the Septuagint, the Elders, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Jerome, the Chaldee, the Syriac and the Arabic, read לחפרפרות as one word, since they rendered it by one word. Iarchius and Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] also hold that it is a single word. But this single word is explained in various ways. The Elders render τὰ μάταια [ta mataia], vain things; Aquila ὄρυγας [orygas], diggings; Symmachus ἄκαρπα [akarpa], fruitless things; Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, ἀφαρφερώθ [apharpherōth]; the Chaldee טעותא, idols; the Syriac ܣܪܝܩܘܬܐ [סריקותא], vanities; Aben Ezra thinks it is שם עוף יעוף בלילה כעטלף ומביא עצמו ביום במקום סתר, the name of a bird which flies by night like a bat and by day withdraws into a hidden place. To weigh each of these is not for our present leisure . It will suffice to point out that, deservedly, all of these are surpassed by Jerome among our writers, and among the Hebrews by R. Selomo, who understand moles here. For from the verb חפר chaphar, which means to dig, animals that are supremely ὀρυκτικὰ [oryktika], and that spend their whole life digging, are most fittingly named. And, as we already touched on in passing above , in חפרפרות chaphorpheroth the radicals are doubled so that the meaning may be intensified. So too אדמדם adamdem for intensely red; ירקרק jerakrak for intensely yellow; שחרחר secharchor for very dark; עקלקל akalkal for exceedingly winding; הפכפך haphachphach for exceedingly changeable; פתלתל pethalthol for exceedingly twisted; יפהפיה jephephija for exceedingly beautiful. Moreover, this same rendering joins moles with bats, which are animals alike in many respects, although the one creeps beneath the earth and the other rises into the air in flight. First, both are lowly and unclean little animals. Second, both are in some way referred to the mouse kind. This has already been proved of the mole , and in the case of the bat it is known to everyone. Hence in Nonius, Varro says in the Agathon: I have become a bat; I am neither wholly among the mice nor among the birds. In Aesop a bat, caught by a weasel as a bird, in order to escape ἔλεγεν, ὀυκ ὄρνις, ἀλλὰ μῦς εἶναι [elegen, ouk ornis, alla mys einai], said that it was not a bird but a mouse. Scaliger maintains that it has a nature midway between the shrew and the swallow. Accordingly in Eustathius τρισμὸς [trismos] is common to the mouse and the bat. And Victorinus in his book De orthographia calls the bat sorex avis [bird-shrew]; Kimchi calls it העטלף בעל כנפים, a winged mouse; the Lombards ratto penago, that is, feathered mouse; the Spaniards morcego, that is, blind mouse; the French chauve-souris, that is, bald shrew. Third, the mole is blind, and the bat sees little. Hence in Arabic it is خغاش [khughāsh] chuphas. For خغش [khaghash] chaphas among them denotes smallness and weakness of the eyes, and اخغش [akhghash] achphaso is μύωψ [myōps]. Accordingly, as moles live beneath the earth, so bats spend the day in caves and dark places.
— — — and, hating the light, they fly by night, and take their name from the late evening .

This is very much to the point. For idols are said to be cast to the moles and the bats when they are thrust down, as it were into darkness, from the lofty place in which they stood out, so that they may no longer deceive superstitious people with their splendour. And among the Hebrews there seems to have been a proverbial expression by which something utterly despised and held in the greatest contempt was said to be cast to the moles and the bats. Accordingly Kimchi rightly holds that this is said דרך בזיון, that is, by way of contempt. Although the Patriarch Jacob also fulfilled it literally when he buried the idols of his household under the terebinth, Gen. XXXV, 4. Jerome renders it otherwise: In that day a man shall cast away the idols, etc. which he had made for himself to worship, moles and bats. So also, among the Hebrews, Rabbi Solomon. This pleases me less, although the Hebrew could bear it, because I have nowhere read that moles and bats were worshipped as gods by the ancients.
Who does not know, Bithynian Volusius, what monsters mad Egypt worships? — — —

Yet not even in Egypt did the insane frenzy of the idolaters descend so far. Though the nearest thing to it is that the Athribites worshipped the μυγάλην [mygalēn], that is, the shrew-mouse, as Strabo testifies in book 7. Not to mention the Musorites, heretical Christians, by whom shrews are read in Philastrius to have been worshipped .

Among the works of Jerome there is extant a Book of Names, begun by Philo, enlarged by Origen, and completed by Jerome, in which are explained all the proper names that occur in the books of the Prophets. Among these you may see פרפר Farfar, the name of a river of Damascus, 2 Reg. V, 12., explained as mole; the author of this explanation, whoever he is, thought that פרפר had been shortened from the preceding חפרפר. In the same way in the Talmud a ditch is called פירה by aphaeresis for חפירא.

The mole is deservedly counted among the unclean animals in the Law, since it neither divides the hoof nor chews the cud. Moreover, by its blindness it is a type of those whose minds the god of this world has blinded, lest the splendour of the Gospel should dawn upon them, 2 Cor 4:4. And while it is continually busy digging in the earth, it represents those men who care for nothing but earthly things, Philipp. III, 19. and whose wisdom is earthly, sensual, devilish, Iacobi III, 15. But the weasel (mustela), which the interpreters have hitherto wanted to be designated by the word חולד choled, signifies, as Cyril taught us above (as emended by us), τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφοδεῆ τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [ta deila, kai ananda, kai psophodeē tōn kleptōn genē]. Of the same sort is that in Aristeas: Κακοποιητικὸς ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ καὶ γαλῆς, καὶ μυῶν [Kakopoiētikos ho tropos esti kai galēs, kai myōn]; Mischievous are the habits both of the weasel and of mice. And a little later: Τότε τῆς γαλῆς γένος ἰδιάζον ἐστί. χωρὶς γὰρ τοῦ προειρημένου, ἔχει λυμαντικὸν κατάστημα· διὰ γὰρ τῶν ὤτων συλλαμβάνει, τεκνοποιεῖ δὲ τῷ στόματι [Tote tēs galēs genos idiazon esti. chōris gar tou proeirēmenou, echei lymantikon katastēma; dia gar tōn ōtōn syllambanei, teknopoiei de tō stomati]. Which in the Hebrew runs thus: הנה עוד בסגולת טבעו התועבה הזאת שהנקבה תהר מאזנה ותלד מפיה, Behold, moreover, among the peculiarities of its nature is this abomination, that the female conceives through the ear and gives birth through the mouth. And Algiahid, inverting this, pretends that Aristotle taught, in the books On the Nature and Properties of Animals, ان الانثي من بنات عرس تلقح من افواهها وتلد من اذانها [inna al-unthī min banāt ʿirs tulqaḥ min afwāhihā wa-talid min ādhānihā] that the females among weasels conceive through the mouth and give birth through the ear. Yet nothing similar occurs in the writings of Aristotle. Indeed, those who idly claim that the weasel gives birth through the mouth he not only refutes but also reveals the origin of the tale, in book 3 On the Generation of Animals, chapter 6. There, after saying that the womb of the weasel is arranged in the same way as that of other quadrupeds, and that the foetus cannot pass from it to the mouth, he adds that this opinion arose διὰ τὸ τίκτειν πάμπαν τὴν γαλῆν σμικρὰ, τῷ δὲ στόματι πολλάκις μεταφέρειν τοὺς νεοττοὺς [dia to tiktein pampan tēn galēn smikra, tō de stomati pollakis metapherein tous neottous], from the fact that the weasel bears very small young, and often carries them about in its mouth. But another explanation presents itself to me, which seems closer to the truth. I think that what the ancients observed in the fish called mustelus [dogfish] was transferred to the weasel. For ὁ γαλεὸς [ho galeos], or the fish mustelus, is also believed to give birth through the mouth. Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 55: Ὁ γαλεὸς ὠδίνει διὰ τοῦ στόματος ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ [Ho galeos ōdinei dia tou stomatos en tē thalattē], The mustelus gives birth in the sea through the mouth. And in book 9, chapter 65: Οἱ μυούμενοι τοῖν Θεοῖν οὐκ ἂν πάσαιντο γαλεοῦ φασιν· οὐ γὰρ εἶναι αὐτὸν καθαρὸν ὄψον ἐπεὶ τῷ στόματι τίκτει [Hoi myoumenoi toin Theoin ouk an pasainto galeou phasin; ou gar einai auton katharon opson epei tō stomati tiktei]. They say that the priests of the Goddesses (namely Ceres and Proserpina) never eat the mustelus fish, for it is not clean food, since it gives birth through the mouth. And it is believed to give birth through the mouth because it sometimes takes its little ones into its mouth, and those who see them coming out imagine this to be a birth. The Philosopher himself touches on this in passing when he says of the mustelus or galeus fishes, in History, book 6, chapter 10: Ἐξαφιᾶσι καὶ δέχονται εἰς ἑαυτοὺς τοὺς νεοττούς [Exaphiasi kai dechontai eis heautous tous neottous]; They take their young back into themselves after letting them out. But others say it much more explicitly. Antigonus, History 25: Τῶν δὲ γαλεῶν τὰ ἔμβρυα, ἐξιόντα ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας, νέμεται· καὶ πάλιν ἐκδύεται (read εἰσδύεται [eisdyetai]) κατὰ τὸ στόμα [Tōn de galeōn ta embrya, exionta ek tēs koilias, nemetai; kai palin ekdyetai … kata to stoma]. The foetuses of the galei, coming out of the womb, feed, and enter again through the mouth. Athenaeus, book 7, chapter 12: Τίκτει δὲ ὁ γαλεὸς τὰ πλεῖστα τρία, καὶ εἰσδέχεται τὰ γεννηθέντα εἰς τὸ στόμα,. καὶ πάλιν ἀφίησι [Tiktei de ho galeos ta pleista tria, kai eisdechetai ta gennēthenta eis to stoma, kai palin aphiēsi]; The mustelus usually bears three young, and takes them into its mouth, and lets them out again. Plutarch says that the young are formed from an egg within the mother's womb itself, and then let out through the mouth as if by a second generation. The words are in the book Utra anim.: Τίκτουσι μὲν γὰρ ὠὸν, εἶτα ζῶον, οὐκ ἐκτὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐντὸς ἐν ἑαυτοῖς. καὶ τρέφουσιν οὕτως, καὶ φέρουσιν, ὥσπερ ἐκ δευτέρας γενέσεως [Tiktousi men gar ōon, eita zōon, ouk ektos, alla entos en heautois. kai trephousin houtōs, kai pherousin, hōsper ek deuteras geneseōs]. And in Περὶ Φιλοστοργίας [Peri Philostorgias] he says that they take back those they have let out, and wrap them, as they sleep, in their own entrails: Οἱ γαλεοὶ ζωογονοῦσι μὲν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐκβαίνειν δὲ παρέχουσιν ἐκτὸς, καὶ νέμεσθαι τοῖς σκύμνοις, εἶτα πάλιν ἀναλαμβάνουσι, καὶ περιπτύσσουσιν ἐγκοιμώμενοι τοῖς σπλάγχνοις [Hoi galeoi zōogonousi men en heautois, ekbainein de parechousin ektos, kai nemesthai tois skymnois, eita palin analambanousi, kai periptyssousin enkoimōmenoi tois splanchnois]. Aelian too, book 2, chapter 55: Πάλιν τε εἰσδέχεται τὰ βρέφη, κἀνεμεῖ ταῖς αὐταῖς ὁδοῖς ζῶντα, καὶ ἀπαθῆ [Palin te eisdechetai ta brephē, kanemei tais autais hodois zōnta, kai apathē]; It takes its young back (through the mouth) and by the same way vomits them up again alive and unharmed. That is, it protects them in this way in sudden fear. The same Aelian, book 9, chapter 65: Οὐ τίκτειν δὲ αὐτὸν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν· ἀλλὰ, δείσαντά τι τῶν ἐπιβουλευόντων, τὰ σκυλάκια καταπίνειν, καὶ ἀποκρύπτειν. εἶτα τοῦ φοβήσαντος παραδραμόντος, ζῶντα αὖθις ἀνεμεῖν [Ou tiktein de auton enioi legousin; alla, deisanta ti tōn epibouleuontōn, ta skylakia katapinein, kai apokryptein. eita tou phobēsantos paradramontos, zōnta authis anemein]. Some say that it does not give birth through the mouth, but that, struck with fear of some attacker, it swallows its young and hides them; then, when the fear is removed, it vomits them up again alive. Many report the same of the glaucus fish, as the same Aelian, book 1, chapter 16; Oppian, Halieutica, book 1, line 749; Phile, chapter 69. Tzetzes too, Chiliad 4, History 126, writes that the glaucus, the dogfish and the galeus hide their young in fear, the glaucus and the dogfish in the mouth, the galeus in the belly, καὶ πάλιν ταῦτα γεννᾷν, τοῦ φόβου [kai palin tauta gennan, tou phobou] παρελθόντος [parelthontos], and bring them forth again when the fear has passed. Thus from this cloud of witnesses it appears that it is not τὴν γαλῆν [tēn galēn], that is, the four-footed weasel, but τὸν γαλεὸν [ton galeon], that is, the mustelus fish, that emits its young from the mouth; and that this was believed either to be a true birth or to be like a birth. Rightly, therefore, Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 3, refutes those who say that the weasel conceives through the ear and pours forth its offspring through the mouth (so it must be read, not, as commonly, conceives through the mouth and through the ear, etc., although the Arabs follow the latter). And many indeed said that the weasel gives birth through the mouth, as we know from the Philosopher. But whether anyone said that it conceives through the ear before Aristeas, I do not know; he seems to have embellished the tale in this way so that the weasel might be a type of informers and slanderers. For these, he says, entangle others in evils, ὅσα διὰ ἀκοῆς λαβόντες, ταῦτα τῷ λόγῳ σωματοποιήσαντες [hosa dia akoēs labontes, tauta tō logō sōmatopoiēsantes], as it were embodying in words what they had received through their ears, that is, exaggerating and magnifying them: which is a new and wholly unusual sense of the verb σωματοποιεῖν [sōmatopoiein]. Barnabas too is mistaken when, in order to fasten on the weasel the horrible crime of fellators, he says not that it gives birth through the mouth but κύειν [kyein], conceives. Ἀλλὰ, he says, καὶ τὴν γαλῆν ἐμίσησε καλῶς. οὐ μὴ γάρ φησιν, ὁμοιωθήσῃ τοῖς τοιούτοις, οἵους ἀκούομεν ἀνομίαν ποιοῦντας τῷ στόματι, διὰ ἀκαθαρσίαν, etc. Τὸ γὰρ ζῶον τοῦτο τῷ στόματι κύει [Alla … kai tēn galēn emisēse kalōs. ou mē gar phēsin, homoiōthēsē tois toioutois, hoious akouomen anomian poiountas tō stomati, dia akatharsian … To gar zōon touto tō stomati kyei]. Therefore we do not think anything should be changed in that passage; nor in this respect do we agree with the opinion of a most excellent and most learned man, and a very dear friend of ours, who in his Notes on this Epistle (how learned they are!) holds that this passage is corrupt and must be restored from Aristeas. The Egyptians also wanted the weasels to be an example of the lewdness of tribades, as Horapollo teaches, Hieroglyphica, book 2, chapter 34; but others, more decent, in Plutarch's Isis, hold that τὴν γαλῆν κατὰ τὸ οὖς ὀχευομένην, τῷ δὲ στόματι τίκτουσαν, εἴκασμα τῆς τοῦ λόγου γενέσεως εἶναι [tēn galēn kata to ous ocheuomenēn, tō de stomati tiktousan, eikasma tēs tou logou geneseōs einai], the weasel, since it is covered through the ear and gives birth through the mouth, represents the generation of speech. Thus sometimes
A very great history is born from nothing.

That the Syriac word means cat, and not weasel, was recently argued by Geo. Guil. Kirsch in the Preface to the Chronicle of Gregory Barhebraeus translated into Latin, p. VIII. He was moved by two passages of Barhebraeus in which he judges that no meaning other than cat fits the word ܟܟܘܣܬܐ [ככוסתא]. One of these passages is on p. 216, line 16 of the Syriac text, where Barhebraeus speaks of a great famine that arose in the region of Khorasan: So great was the famine that a litra of bread was sold for one gold denarius, and people ate dogs and ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא]. On these words Kirsch remarks: "Since the meaning weasel hardly fits, it is not difficult to guess what ܟܟܘܫܬܐ [ככושתא] was. Yet this passage, which would not settle the matter, should be compared with another, much clearer one, which leaves no room for doubt. On p. 268, line 4, he describes a famine that afflicted above all the city of Damascus, of whose inhabitants, who numbered 300,000 before the famine, he reports that only 3,000 survived it. He then continues: Because of this failure of the grain supply the mice, troublesome to people, increased beyond measure, because the ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] were lacking, having long since been eaten by the people. Since ܥܘܟܒܪ̈ܐ [עוכברא] are by general agreement mice, it is evident without my pointing it out that ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] means cat, the animal more hostile to mice than any other. Although I do not deny that weasels also hunt mice, everyone will think of the cat as soon as the question arises which kind of animal, when lacking, lets mice multiply." So Kirsch. Against this, however, Lorsbach rightly objected, in the book entitled Archiv für die morgenländische Litteratur, vol. 1, p. 204, first, the corresponding Chaldee word כרכושתא, which Bochart has amply proved on this very page to mean weasel, not cat. The name was aptly given to the weasel from its agile and swift movement, for כרכש, كركس [karkas], means he moved, drove to and fro. As to the point on which Kirsch's view chiefly rests, that mice multiplied when the animals called ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ [כרכושתא] were lacking, Lorsbach answers well that weasels hunt mice no less than cats do, indeed better, because the slenderness of their bodies lets them get into mouse-holes more easily.

But J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], on the Syriac Lexicon of Castell [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] which he edited, p. 297, argues that the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] means a kind of lizard. His only argument is that at Lev 11:30 the Syriac translator put this word for the Hebrew כח, which means lizard. Others, however, will hardly accept this. For the Arabic dialect stands in favour of the mole: that خُلْدٌ [khuld] is the mole is perfectly clear from what Bochart will next adduce from the Arabs.

In the passage of Proverbs, however, Michaelis thinks this word was put, by an error either of a scribe or of an editor, for ܚܘܪܓܐ [חורגא], "as the Chaldee too, which in Proverbs is almost identical with the Syriac and derived from it, has חורלי."

The same features are observed in the kind of mole peculiar to Asia, which Guldenstaedt described in the Act. Academ. Petropol. vol. 14, p. 409, under the name Spalax Microphtalmus. Cf. Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 2, ch. 4, p. 51. 52.

What Bochart cites from Abdollatif is taken from his great work on Egyptian matters, divided into 13 books. Its Compendium, made by Abdollatif himself, was recently edited in Arabic from a Bodleian manuscript by Jos. White, Professor of Arabic at Oxford.
The reasoning of the ancient versions was carefully examined by J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 876, and vol. 6, p. 2042. Cf. our note on Isa 2:20.

Koppe held (in his notes on Lowth's Commentary on Isaiah) that the word חפרפר means two-legged jumping mice, without adequate reason; for this he was also criticized by Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 876, who himself attempted other explanations, though no more certain ones. Oedmann, in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 3, p. 82. 83, interpreting the Hebrew word as spy of the cows, argues that it means a certain night-roving bird which, according to the fable, sucks the udders of cows: in Linnaeus it is called Caprimulgus (Europaeus), in German Nachtrabe. This seems more learned than probable or suited to the passage of Isaiah. More satisfying is what Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] offered in the Clavis Philolog. in Iesaiam. He thinks it should be written as two words, לחפר פרות, which he renders into the holes of field mice (חפר, something dug out, a hole, Arab. حُفْرٌ [ḥufr], and פר, a field mouse or mountain mouse, after the Arabic فَأْر [faʾr]). In favour of this interpretation is the fact that לחפר פרות is found written together as one word in only a few manuscripts.
It is proved that קפוד kippod is the hedgehog and the porcupine.

Three elements contend over the animal קפוד kippod: some assign it to the earth, others to the water, others to the air along with the birds. In the first rank I place the Greeks and Jerome, for whom קפוד kippod is ἐχῖνος [echinos], the hedgehog, namely the land hedgehog, which lives in hedges in summer and in winter in tree trunks or in holes in the ground. Others infer that it is an aquatic animal from Isa 14:23, on Babylon: I will make it a hereditary possession of the kippod and pools of water. But the ranks of these are divided in two, or even in three. Some hold it to be the tortoise, some the beaver, some the otter. All rely on the etymology of the word. For in Isa 38:12. קפד means to cut off, where the weaver cuts off the warp when the whole web has been woven. And these animals have a remarkable power of cutting. With the beaver the matter is very well known. It is an animal with a fearsome bite (says Pliny, book 8, chapter 30); it cuts down trees by rivers as if with iron. But Varro too, in book 4 On the Latin Language, would have the otter [lutra] named from λύειν [lyein], because it is said to undercut the roots of trees on the bank and to loosen them. The same power in the tortoise is all the more remarkable because, though it has no teeth, it nevertheless crushes everything with the edge of its beak. That is, the edges of the beak are sharp, the upper part closing over the lower in the manner of a box. So Pliny, book 11, ch. 37, and book 9, ch. 10. Similar to this is what is read of the sea turtle in Porta coeli, fol. 34a: ויש לה כח גדול בפיה ובשיניה ואם תקח אבן בפיה תשבור אותה בחוק גדול לחלקים קטנים, It has enormous strength in its mouth and teeth. And if it takes a stone into its mouth, it crushes it with great force into the tiniest pieces. Add to this that in Arabic, if both Kimchis are to be believed, the name of the tortoise is קנפאר, which does not differ much from the Hebrew קפוד. But those who hold the third opinion, namely that קפוד kippod is a species of bird, object that elsewhere kippod is named by Isaiah and Zephaniah together with birds. The passage of Isaiah, chapter 34, verse 11, reads thus: The pelican and the kippod shall possess it. And Zephaniah, chapter 2, verse 14, not very differently: Both the pelican and the kippod shall lodge on its lintels. Again, these are in doubt as to what kind of bird kippod is: some explain it as the owl; others as the vulture; others as the blackbird; others as the bittern, or starry heron; others as the cypselus, which is also the apus; others as the plancus, or duck-eagle[?]; and what not? And the most learned Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], in his Miscellanea, book 1, chapter 18, compares most of those interpretations with one another in such a way that he rejects none except the one which alone is true. I mean that most ancient one, by which קפוד kippod is explained as the hedgehog; and many things serve to confirm it.

First, the authority of the Greeks and of Jerome, who consistently explain it so. I do not think it safe to depart from them unless there are weighty reasons, and here I see none. 2. To the Greeks I add the Hebrews, among whose most learned men this opinion has long prevailed, that קפוד is the hedgehog. R. Nathan explains it with the Spanish word ריצ"ו rizo, or erizo; Poniarius with the Italian ריצ"יו riccio; Rabbi Selomo with the French הריצ"ון herisson; Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] with the German איג"יל Igel. And in the Talmud קפוד kippod, or קופד kuphad, which is the same in the Chaldee inflection, is often placed among land quadrupeds. Thus in Berachoth, chapter 9, folio 57b: כל מיני חיות יפות לחלום חוץ מן הפיל והקוף והקפוד, All species of wild beasts are good for a dream (that is, of good omen when seen in sleep), except the elephant, the ape and the kippod, that is, the hedgehog. For R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] talks nonsense when he explains it as the long-tailed monkey. And in the tractate Kelaim, ch. 8, folio 32a: והקופד וחולדת הסניים, And the kuphad (hedgehog) and the bramble weasel. And in Bava Kama, chapter 7: אין מגדלין חתולים וקופדים, They do not raise cats and kuphadim (hedgehogs). And in Sabbath, chapter 5, folio 57b: ואין העגל יוצא בגימון ולא פרא בעור הקופד, A calf may not go out (on the Sabbath) with a gemon, nor a cow with the skin of a kuphad. I think the Hebrew גימון gemon is κημὸν [kēmon], a muzzle, and that the word is derived from it; although by this term they do not mean any muzzle whatever, but the one by which a calf is prevented from sucking. The Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] defines it: לוח בפיו שלא יוכל לשתות החלב, A board that is put in its mouth so that it cannot suck the milk. In Greek you would call it πύσσαχον [pyssachon]. Hesychius: Πύσσαχος· ξύλον καμπύλον τοῖς μόσχοις περὶ τοὺς μυκτῆρας τιθέμενον, ὃ κωλύει θηλάζειν· [Pyssachos; xylon kampylon tois moschois peri tous myktēras tithemenon, ho kōlyei thēlazein] A curved piece of wood placed around the nostrils of calves, by which they are prevented from sucking. And the skin of a kuphad (that is, of a hedgehog) was tied to the cow's udder for the same purpose, that is, so that neither the calf nor any other animal might suck it. Rabbi Selomo on this passage: קופד שרץ הוא שנימיו חדים כמחט וקורין לו הריצון וקושרין עורו בדדי הפרה שלא יניקוה שרצים, Kuphad is a creeping thing (so the Hebrews call the smallest quadrupeds) whose hairs are sharp like needles; it is commonly called herisson. Its skin is tied to the cow's udder so that creeping things may not suck it. For the milk had to be guarded not from the calf alone, but also from serpents, among which boas are fed at first on the juice of cow's milk, whence they took their name. So Pliny, book 8, chapter 14. And Solinus, who follows him: It (the boa) lies in wait for herds of cattle, and fastens itself to the udder of whichever cow is most abundant in milk, and fattened by continual sucking, etc. 4. Finally, in Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, plural قنافذ [qanāfidh] kanaphido, is the hedgehog. Barbarous translators write caused, ceufud, ceufund, etc. The matter is too well known to need proof. I will only advise the reader that the name قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud includes, besides the hedgehog, also the porcupine. This is clear from Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], who says that among the species of kunphud one is the mountain kind, having spines that can be shot, whose proper name is دلدل [duldul] duldul, that is, the porcupine. Hence in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] the female hedgehog is called أم دلدل [umm duldul] mother τοῦ [tou] duldul, that is, of the porcupine. And duldul, or porcupine, is defined in the same place as عظيم القنافد [ʿaẓīm al-qanāfid], the larger hedgehog. And according to Algiahid: الفرق بين الدلدل والقنافد كالفرق بين البقر والجوامس والبخاتي من الابل العراب [al-farq bayna al-duldul wa-al-qanāfid ka-al-farq bayna al-baqar wa-al-jawāmis wa-al-bakhātī min al-ibil al-ʿirāb] Duldul and kanaphido (that is, the porcupine and hedgehogs properly so called) differ no otherwise than oxen from buffaloes, and Bactrian camels from Arabian ones. Finally Elmacinus, in the Saracen History, book 1, chapter 5, seems to have meant by القنفد [al-qunfud] alkunphud the porcupine rather than the hedgehog, when he writes of Aisha's camel: صار كالقنفد من السهام [ṣāra ka-al-qunfud min al-sihām] It became like an alkunphud from the darts, that is, from the multitude of darts with which it was pierced. But in this the Arabs had Pliny and Oppian to follow: the former, in book 8, chapter 35, expressly places porcupines in the hedgehog kind; the latter, in book 2 of the Cynegetica, line 603, making two kinds of land hedgehogs, some small and unwarlike, others μεγέθει πολὺ μείζονας [megethei poly meizonas], far larger, and bristling all round — ἀρειοτέρῃσιν ἀκωκαῖς [areioterēsin akōkais], with stronger points, seems to understand porcupines by those larger hedgehogs. And for Suidas too ἡ ὕστριξ [hē hystrix], the porcupine, is ὁ ἀκανθόχοιρος, ὁ χερσαῖος ἐχῖνος [ho akanthochoiros, ho chersaios echinos], the spiny pig, the land hedgehog.

Now, lest anyone object, on the authority of both Kimchis, that the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the tortoise, I say that they are gravely mistaken on this point. For in Arabic the tortoise is not called kunphud but سلخفاة [sulaḥfāh] sulachpha, or سلخفية [sulaḥfiya] sulachphia, as if you were to say hiding in a shell or husk: for خفا [khafā] chapha means to hide, and سلخ [salkh] silch, or sulch, is φολὶς [pholis], a covering, properly of a serpent, but also of a tortoise; just as γῆρας [gēras], a word most use for the leberis, or slough of a serpent, but some also for χελωνίω [chelōniō], as Aelian, History book 2, ch. 37, and Suidas under Φολίδωτον [Pholidōton]. But that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog no one will deny who has read Damiri, where قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is surnamed ابو الشوك [abū al-shawk] abussuchi, that is, father of thorns; and انقد [anqad] ankado, that is, the stripper of bark; and ابو سفين [abū safīn] abusaphin, that is, the father who scrapes or polishes, because garments are polished with its skin; and العساعس [al-ʿasāʿis] alasaiso, because it roams at night. For that is properly عس [ʿassa] assa, as also سري [sarā] sara; hence the proverb in use among them, اسري من قنفذ [asrā min qunfudh], More night-roaming than the kunphud. In the same place you may find many things pertaining to its description, among which these are remarkable: القنفذ ان جاع صعد الكرم منكسا فيقطع العناقيد ويرمي بها ثم ينزل فياكل منها ما اطاق واذا كان له فراخ تمرغ في العناقيد لتشتبك في شوكه ويذهب به الي فراخه وهو لا يظهر الا ليلا وهو مولع باكل الافاع ولا يتالم لها وانا لذعته الحية اكل الصعتر البري فيبري وله خمسة اسنان في فيه والبرية منها تسفد قايمة وظهر الذكر لاصق بظهر الانثي [al-qunfudh in jāʿa ṣaʿida al-karm munakkasan fa-yaqṭaʿu al-ʿanāqīd wa-yarmī bihā thumma yanzilu fa-yaʾkulu minhā mā aṭāqa wa-idhā kāna lahu firākh tamarragha fī al-ʿanāqīd li-tashtabika fī shawkihi wa-yadhhabu bihi ilā firākhihi wa-huwa lā yaẓharu illā laylan wa-huwa mūlaʿ bi-akl al-afāʿ wa-lā yataʾallamu lahā wa-anā ladhaʿathu al-ḥayya akala al-ṣaʿtar al-barrī fa-yabraʾ wa-lahu khamsat asnān fī fīhi wa-al-barriyya minhā tusfadu qāʾima wa-ẓahr al-dhakar lāṣiq bi-ẓahr al-unthā] Alkunphud, when it is hungry, climbs a vine upside down and plucks off the clusters, which it throws down.
