Then, coming down from there, it eats of them as much as it can. If it has young, it rolls about in the clusters so that they become entangled in its spines, and with them it hurries to its young. It does not appear except at night. It has a wonderful appetite for eating vipers, and is not harmed by them. When bitten by a serpent, it is healed by eating wild marjoram. It has five teeth in its mouth. The land kunphud copulates upright, so that the back of the male clings to the back of the female. Everyone sees that these things pertain to the hedgehog, although among them there are some that you would seek in vain in the Greeks. Now, if we consult the physicians, say Avicenna, Ibn al-Baitar and that same Damiri mentioned above, we shall find not only that they attribute to the kunphud the same virtues that the Greek writers attribute to the ἐχίνῳ [echinō], but also that, in rendering the passages of Dioscorides and Galen on the land and sea hedgehog, they consistently call the former القنفذ البري [al-qunfudh al-barrī] alkunphud albarri, or land hedgehog, the latter القنفذ البحري [al-qunfudh al-baḥrī] alkunphud albahari, or sea hedgehog. Not to mention that the translators of the Prophets, who made the Arabic version from the Greek, everywhere rendered the Greek ἐχίνους [echinous] by القنافذ [al-qanāfidh] alkanaphido, which is the plural of kunphud. For examples see Isa 14:23 and XXXIV, 11. and Zeph 2:14. Accordingly, among the Hebrews, R. Nathan, far more learned in Arabic than Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], readily acknowledges that قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is the hedgehog. Further, that the Hebrews' קפוד kippod, the Chaldeans' קופד kuphad, and the Arabs' قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud are the same animal, anyone who has some taste of these languages will at once recognize. The long vowel in קופד kuphad makes up for the lack of the Daghesh point found in קפוד kippod. And that very Daghesh is replaced by the letter Nun, which shows itself in the Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, as also in the Ethiopic ቀንፈዝ፡ [qanəfaz] konphoz of the same meaning. Thus חטה chitta, that is, wheat, stands for חנטה chinta, as the Arabs write it. The wood of which the ark of the testimony was made is called שטה sitta, for שנטה sinta; as in Arabic سنط [sanṭ] sent. The spider is עכביש accabis, for ancabis; as in Arabic عنكبوث [ʿankabūth] ancabuths. And עז ez, that is, goat, plural עזים izzim, is in Arabic عنز [ʿanz] enz. This is to be noted here against those who trace the word קפוד kippod to the root קפד kaphad, so that it would signify an animal endowed with some peculiar power of cutting. But the true root is not קפד kaphad, but the unused קנפד kanphad; unless someone thinks that the word is a compound, with the gutturals elided (as happens), of קנה kana, which is a dart, and אפד aphad, which is to clothe, because this animal is clothed and fenced about with spines and prickles as with darts. Or, if you prefer that the Nun in قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud is epenthetic, even the root קפד kaphad has certain meanings which you could refer here. As when קפדן kaphdan is used of a harsh and irascible man. In this sense, in Sanhedrin, chapter 11, the prophet Elijah is said to have been קפדן. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 30b: לעולם יהא אדם ענותן כהלל ואל יהא קפדן כשמאי, Let a man always be gentle like Hillel, and not kaphdan (or irascible) like Shammai. Because, as the Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] says, a harsh and irascible man is כמו הקפוד עם קוצים, like a hedgehog with spines. So these Greek proverbs, Ἐχῖνου τραχύτερος [Echinou trachyteros] and Ἅπας ἐχῖνος τραχὺς [Hapas echinos trachys], signify a morose and intractable man. To the same point belongs the fact that קפד kaphad, or הקפיד hikphid, means to be attentive and anxious, and הקפדה hakkephada means attention and anxiety; because, as is in the Pomarius, when the hedgehog קורץ כל גופו, covers its whole body with spines, its face hiding between its feet, and raises its prickles, with which it defends itself as with a shield and wounds those who wish to lay violent hands on it, פעולת הזאת היא השגחה והרגשה נמרצת, this action is one of providence and the keenest attention. Moreover, ܩܦܕ [קפד] for the Syrians is to shudder, or to bristle, as when the hairs stand on end from fear, as in hedgehogs. So in the Syriac Psalm 119, verse 120: ܩܦܕ ܒܣܪܝ ܡܢ ܕܚܠܬܟ [קפד בסרי מן דחלתך], My flesh shuddered for fear of you, that is, the hairs of my flesh stood on end, as is found in Iob. IV, 15. In French you would say herisser by the same metaphor. For herisser, that is, ὀρθοτριχεῖν [orthotrichein], to bristle, and herisson are cognates.

Now, to reply to the objections: Fuller denies that there is anything in the nature of the hedgehog that suits the kippod. This I cannot sufficiently wonder at, since Isaiah and Zephaniah always describe the kippod as a solitary animal and φιλέρημον [phileremon], dwelling in the desolate cities of Babylon, Bozrah and Nineveh. That the hedgehog is such, there is no one who does not know: ζῶον χῆρον, ἤτοι ἔρημον [zōon chēron, ētoi erēmon], an animal which its spines, which no one touches with impunity, keep from all society with other animals. Hence it came about that in Greek it was called χὴρ [chēr]. Hesychius: χήρ· ἐχῖνος [chēr: echinos], namely from χηρώσις [chērōsis], that is, ἐρημώσις [erēmōsis]. Hence also the Latin name; not ab haerendo [from clinging] or horrendo [from bristling], as some would have it. For just as hir for vola manus [the palm of the hand] in Probus and Charisius was made from the Greek χεὶρ [cheir], so her for hericius [hedgehog] comes entirely from the Greek χήρ [chēr]. The animal which a later age, as the word grew longer, called herix, hericius, herinacius, the ancients called her. Nemesianus in the Cynegetica:
And the hedgehog wrapped up in the fold of its spiny body.
And long before, Plautus in the Captivi, Act 1, as emended by the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes]:
Go now, hunt a hare: now you hold a hedgehog.
Or, if by the name kippod in the Prophets we understand the porcupine (which [?] we have proved from the ancients to be included in the same genus as the hedgehog), the matter will seem[?]

all the more fitted to inspire horror, if the Prophets threaten that populous cities, such as Babylon among the Chaldeans, Nineveh among the Assyrians, and Bozrah among the Idumaeans, will pass as an inheritance to porcupines. For the porcupine is both larger and fiercer than the hedgehog, and, because of the missile spines which it hurls at dogs and hunters with a sure and well-aimed stroke, far more terrible . Accordingly the excellent Poet, after vividly describing the porcupine bristling with hairs sharp like arrows, teaches in these words how far the porcupine surpasses the echinus, that is, the hedgehog:

But this array does not stay fixed, in the manner of the woodland hedgehog. It fights on the offensive with frequent volleys, and guards its limbs from afar, and, whirled through the air, its native missile flies out from its shaken back.
And whereas Ion in the Phoenix mocks the οἰζυρὰς τέχνας [oizyras technas], the wretched arts, of the hedgehog, which, when attacked by other beasts,

Στρόβιλον ἀμφ' ἄκανθαν εἰλίξας δέμας, Κεῖται δακεῖν τε καὶ θιγεῖν ἀμήχανος· [Strobilon amph' akanthan eilixas demas, keitai dakein te kai thigein amēchanos] Keeping its body under a dense ball of thorns, it lies there, unable to bite or to touch in return:
the porcupine's courage and skill in fighting so carried the most illustrious Poet away in admiration that it drew these verses from him:

Sometimes, fleeing in the manner of the Parthians, it wounds its pursuer: sometimes, as if pitching camp in order, it lashes out its terrifying point in a dense wave, and roughens its shoulders with kindred shafts. The whole body of the beast does battle, and its back, shaken, resounds with a harsh crash; you would think columns roused by the goad of trumpets were clashing with standards joined. So great a din rages in so small a space. To its arms is added cunning, and a fear sparing of itself, and an anger never prodigal of its darts, cautiously content to threaten, and spending its shots only to save its life. Error is absent; skill directs a sure stroke, the distance never deceiving its measure; and the mute skin keeps its course and guides the efforts of a practised eye.

Behold, a small beast is armed with its own weapons, and seeks no outside help; it carries everything with it; it is its own quiver, its own javelin, its own bow. One animal possesses all the arts of war.
Finally he concludes that we learned the art of shooting from this beast. And of the same the emperor Hadrian:
With missile spines it kept dogs and men far off, and put them all to flight.

Ὕστριξ δὲ τὰς ἄνωθεν ἐκπέμπει τρίχας, Ἃς ἡ φύσις γ᾽ ἔθηξε καὶ πρὸ τῆς μάχης. Φρίξασα γὰρ τὰ νῶτα βάλλει τοὺς πέλους Οἷον ἀπὸ νευρᾶς εὐτυχῶν τις τοξότης. [Hystrix de tas anōthen ekpempei trichas, has hē physis g' ethēxe kai pro tēs machēs. Phrixasa gar ta nōta ballei tous pelous hoion apo neuras eutychōn tis toxotēs.] As the rough porcupine hurls its hairs like darts, which shrewd nature has sharpened for battle, for when it draws in its back, as with a bowstring drawn taut, it hurls darts at its enemies from afar.
And Oppian, book 3 of the Cynegetica, v. 398:

— — — Θοὰς δ᾽ ἔφριξεν ἐθείρας Καί τ᾽ ὀπίσω νώτοισιν ἀκαχμένον ὠκυπέτῃσιν Ἰθὺς ἀκοντίζει μαλερὸν βέλος. — — [Thoas d' ephrixen etheiras kai t' opisō nōtoisin akachmenon ōkypetēisin ithys akontizei maleron belos.]
It raises its sharp spines, and shoots straight backwards the deadly dart fixed on its swift-flying back. And a little later,
Δηθάκις ἔκτεινεν κύνα κάρχαρον, [Dēthakis ekteinen kyna karcharon,]

it has often killed a dog rough with teeth. Accordingly hunters, since they do not dare to set dogs on the porcupine, take it by a certain stratagem, which the same Oppian professed he would describe in what follows, but, prevented by death, he did not keep his promise. Nor is there reason for anyone to think that these things are said on poetic authority, since all who have written on the nature of animals report the same. Thus the Philosopher, History, book 9, chapter 39, mentions certain animals τὰ βάλλοντα ταῖς θριξὶν, οἷον αἱ ὕστριχες [ta ballonta tais thrixin, hoion hai hystriches], which shoot their hairs, like porcupines. And Pliny, book 8, chapter 35: The porcupine has longer quills, and, when it stretches its skin, they can be shot. It pierces the mouths of dogs pressing on it, and shoots a little farther off. Solinus also: Bristling on its back with spines (the porcupine), which, often loosened, it discharges by voluntary shooting, so as to wound attacking dogs with continual showers of quills. And Aelian, book 1, chapter 31: Τὰς ἄνωθεν τρίχας οἱονεὶ βέλη ἐκπέμπει, καὶ εὐστόχως βάλλει πολλάκις, τὰ νῶτα φρίξασα, καὶ ἐκεῖναί γε πηδῶσιν. ὥσπερ οὖν ἔκ τινος ἀφειμέναι νευρᾶς· [Tas anōthen trichas hoionei belē ekpempei, kai eustochōs ballei pollakis, ta nōta phrixasa, kai ekeinai ge pēdōsin. hōsper oun ek tinos apheimenai neuras] It sends forth its upper hairs like arrows, and often aims them straight as at a target, contracting its back as it bristles. And they leap out as if shot from a bowstring. The Scholiast on Aristophanes on the Peace, and from him Suidas: Ἔστι δὲ ὕστριξ θηρίον τρίχας ἔχον ὑὸς, ἂν ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι ἐπακοντίζει κατὰ τῶν διωκόντων· [Esti de hystrix thērion trichas echon hyos, an en tō diōkesthai epakontizei kata tōn diōkontōn] The porcupine is a wild beast bristling with swine's bristles (whence its name), which, when someone pursues it, it shoots out at its pursuers. Porta coeli p. 19 d: גם יש מין מחוירי הבר שיש להם שערות גסים כמו חצים וזה לסבת גסות העור, There is a species of wild swine whose hairs are thick like arrows, namely because of the thickness and hardness of the skin. Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter قنفذ [qunfudh] Kunphud, والجبلي هو الدلدل ذو الشوك السهمي [wa-l-jabalī huwa al-duldul dhū al-shawk al-sahmī] And the mountain one (kunphud) is the duldul (porcupine), which has arrow-like spines, that is, missiles. Damir in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul: واذا راي ما يكرهه انقبض فيخرج منه شوك كالمسال يخرج من اصابه والشوك الذي علي ظهره بحو الذراع [wa-idhā rāy mā yakrahuhu inqabaḍa fa-yakhruju minhu shawk ka-l-masāl yakhruju min aṣābahu wa-l-shawk alladhī ʿalī ẓahrihi bḥw al-dhirāʿ] And when it sees anything hostile, it contracts itself. And spines like needles come out of it, by which those pressing on it are wounded. And the spines that are on its back are about a cubit long. Marco Polo, book 1, chapter 33, on Scassem, a city of Tartary: In that region there are many spiny swine (porcupines), which, when they are caught, often injure men and dogs with their spines. For the dogs, set on the swine by the hunters, so provoke and stir up those beasts that, running together (contracting) their backs, on which the spines rest, they shake them violently, and with a certain violence discharge the very quills and hurl them at the nearer men and dogs. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: It strikes whomever it wishes with a sure and aimed blow, with a wound sometimes almost incurable, being narrow and deep, dangerous indeed if a nerve is pierced. So that Oppian not without reason sings,
Ὑστρίγγων οὔπω τι πέλει κατὰ δάσκιον ὕλην Ῥίγιον εἰσιδέειν, ὅτ' ἀργαλεώτερον ἄλλο, [Hystringōn oupō ti pelei kata daskion hylēn Rhigion eisideein, hot' argaleōteron allo]
Which Stephanus condensed thus in his Notes on Callimachus:
Nothing in the shady woods is more dreadful to behold than the porcupine.

That the Prophets spoke of this animal may be the more probable because I learn from the Arabs something hitherto unknown, that the porcupine is an animal common in Syria. Damir, in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul, or On the Porcupine: هو كثير ببلاد الشام والعراق وبلاد المغارب [huwa kathīr bi-bilād al-Shām wa-l-ʿIrāq wa-bilād al-Maghārib] It abounds in the region of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), and in the region of Megareb, that is, western Africa. He teaches the same about the hedgehog, thus: وهو صنفان قنفد يكون بارض مصر قدر الفار وقنفد يكون بارض الشام وعراق في قدر الكلب القلطي والفرق بينهما كالفرق بين الفار والجرذ [wa-huwa ṣinfān qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ Miṣr qadr al-fār wa-qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ al-Shām wa-ʿIrāq fī qadr al-kalb al-qalṭī wa-l-farq baynahumā ka-l-farq bayn al-fār wa-l-jurdh] The hedgehog is of two species. One is in the land of Egypt, of the size of a shrew; the other in the lands of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), of the size of a Maltese dog, so that they differ as much as the shrew and the mouse differ. Those who infer that the kippod kippod קפוד is an aquatic animal from these words of Isaiah about Babylon, I will make it a possession of the kippod, and pools of water, do not even so adduce anything that stands in the way of our view. For among aquatic creatures too there is a species of hedgehog, which by Avicenna, Damir and Ibn al-Baitar is called قنفد بحري [qunfud baḥrī], by others ἐχῖνος θαλάσσιος [echinos thalassios], sea hedgehog, or else ποτάμιος [potamios], river hedgehog. For Paul of Aegina reported that there are also river hedgehogs. The Euphrates near Babylon could have teemed with them. At least we learn from Nearchus that hedgehogs of remarkable size are found near the islands lying off the mouth of the Euphrates. Strabo: Λέγει δὲ (ὁ Νέαρχος) ἐν ταῖς πρὸ τοῦ Εὐφράτου νήσοις φύεσθαι παγούρων καὶ ἐχίνων μεγέθη· [Legei de (ho Nearchos) en tais pro tou Euphratou nēsois phyesthai pagourōn kai echinōn megethē]. But we interpret the passage of Isaiah very differently, namely in this way: I will make it a possession of the kippod (that is, of the land hedgehog), even the pools of water. That is, not only will the city be laid waste, but the neighbouring pools too will dry up, so that they will be as fit a dwelling as the city for the land hedgehog, which delights above all in dry places. Thus in Zeph 2:13 Nineveh is said to be made לשממה וציה, a desolation and dryness, and only then does it come about that the kippod lodges in it. And in Isa 34:11, before Idumaea is handed over as a possession of the kippod, the streams are turned into pitch and the dust into brimstone.

To prove that the kippod kippod קפוד is a bird, it carries little weight that in Es. XXXIV, 11. it is named together with birds. For right in verse thirteen dragons and ostriches are joined together, although they are animals of entirely different kinds. And Zephaniah gathers flocks, beasts, the pelican and the kippod together into one bundle. This affects the reader all the more, since in a description of devastation the things that inspire horror are set forth in such a jumbled order. When Sophocles, in this line of the satyr play Amycus, mentions hares among many birds,
Γέρανοι, κορῶναι, γλαῦκες ἴκτινοι, λαγοὶ, [Geranoi, korōnai, glaukes iktinoi, lagoi,]

Cranes, crows, owls, kites, hares: who would conclude from this that the hare is a kind of bird? I know that someone has substituted λάροι [laroi], a kind of water bird, for λαγοὶ [lagoi]. But in vain. For Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 14, cites this line to prove that λαγοὶ [lagoi] is as much Attic as λαγώ [lagō]. So λαγοί [lagoi] must be retained. Conversely, in Lucian's Syrian Goddess you may see eagles named among many quadrupeds thus: Ἐν δὲ τῇ αὐλῇ ἄφετοι νέμονται βόες μεγάλοι, καὶ ἵπποι, καὶ αἐτοὶ, καὶ ἄρκτοι, καὶ λέοντες· [En de tē aulē aphetoi nemontai boes megaloi, kai hippoi, kai aetoi, kai arktoi, kai leontes] In the court, moreover, there graze freely great oxen, and horses, and eagles, and bears, and lions. From which it would be absurd to infer that the eagles there are not birds but a kind of quadruped.
The story of quills shot out to a distance like a javelin is a fable; when irritated, the animal merely bristles over its whole body; see BUFFON Hist.Nat. vol. 6, p. 4.
ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE BOOK FOUR ON THE OVIPAROUS QUADRUPEDS.
It is proved that צב tsab in Lev 11:29 is the land crocodile, concerning which much is brought forward from the records of the Arabs that has not yet been published.

After the viviparous quadrupeds follow the oviparous, which are few in nature and fewer still in Scripture. Moses lists six species of them in Lev 11:29–30., namely צב tsab, אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. It will seem that a seventh can be added, שממית semamith, from Prov 30:28. But we shall show in its place that semamith differs from anaka in name only. And an eighth, לויתן leviathan, which is plainly the crocodile, Iob. XL et XLI. But we have preferred to describe the crocodile among the aquatic animals, because it is an ἀμφίβιον [amphibion] animal. Finally, the tortoise will have a place here, if we follow the Elders at Hos 12:12. The oviparous quadrupeds that we have listed from Moses belong in some way to the species of lizards, and are so similar to one another that it is not for just anyone to distinguish them from each other by definite marks. For us it was certainly very laborious, because here the Hebrews leave us entirely destitute. Nor was there much more help from the other interpreters of Scripture, most of whom grope in the dark when they come to these minutiae. But far more light has shone from the records of the Arabs, in whose soil these pests are born and reared. What follows will make this plain. In it we shall try to explain the individual words in the very order in which Moses sets them out.

Lev 11:29. For Jerome the Hebrew צב tsab is the crocodile; for the Greeks ὁ κροκόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος [ho krokodeilos ho chersaios]. But among more recent interpreters some render it toad or bramble-toad [rubeta], others tortoise; Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], however, "kinds of shellfish." The first group, if I am not mistaken, is led by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], a French Jew, who wrote about 550 years ago. For he was the first, so far as I know, to write that צב tsab is an animal similar to a frog, called פויוט. But one should read פרוט frot, the German name for the toad, then in use in France. To this I refer the fact that Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] renders צב tsab in Spanish as גריישנט graissant. At that time, namely, graissant was for the Spaniards the bramble-toad, as graisset and croisset for the French, and Grasfrosch for the Germans, literally "grass frog." Following these, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], Munster, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], and Robert Olivetan interpret צב tsab as toad, or bramble-toad, or frog, or שרץ שדומה לצפרדע, "a creeping thing similar to a frog." They thought, namely, that this animal was so called from swelling, because צבה means to swell; just as from bufo [toad] the vernacular word bouffi was formed, which means swollen. Add that in Illyrian zaba is frog, as if the word were derived from צב tsab. But Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi], easily the most learned of the Jews in Germany, explains צב tsab in his language as שלטפרוט schildfrot, that is, tortoise, because the shells of tortoises seem to resemble the roofs of covered wagons, which in Hebrew are called צבים tsabbim. So slight a reason had such force that it drew to assent Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Schindler, and the English, Italian and Genevan translators. Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], in his Lexicon, not quite knowing which side to join, renders צב tsab both as toad and as tortoise.

Amid this hesitation of such great men, I will add also this hallucination, if I may say so with their leave, I hope I shall do the learned reader a most welcome service if I establish the true and genuine meaning of the word, not now from conjecture, but by certain and solid reasons. Indeed, even if I said nothing, anyone who weighs what the Arabs write about this animal will accomplish this without any trouble. To them it cannot but be very well known, because it is more common in Arabia than anywhere else on earth. But as well known as the animal is to them, so unknown is it to us. Therefore I find it necessary to pursue these matters more carefully.

To begin with the name: it should be known that, like the Hebrew צב, the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] is written with the same letters. But, as the dialects vary, the Arabic Tsade at the beginning of a word is pronounced as d or dh, because of the dot added to it. Thus this little word is pronounced ضب [ḍabb] dhab among the Arabs. The plural is ضباب [ḍibāb] dhibab, or أضب [aḍubb] adhab, and the feminine ضبة [ḍabba] dhabba. Hence ضبب [ḍabab] dhabab, and مضب [maḍabb] mudhab, and مضبب [muḍbib] mudhbib denote a place full of these animals; and مضبب [muḍabbib] mudhabbib their hunter. Further, ضب [ḍabb] dhab is defined by Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] as حيوان بري معروف من الحشرات يشبه الورل [ḥayawān barrī maʿrūf min al-ḥasharāt yushbih al-waral] a well-known wild animal among the reptiles, similar to the guaril, or greater stellio: just as Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] writes that it differs from the guaril, وان كان [wa-in kāna] يشبهه وكان قريب الاحوال والقوي منه [yushbihuhu wa-kāna qarīb al-aḥwāl wa-al-quwā minhu] although it is similar to it, and very close to it both in constitution and in powers. So he writes in the second book of the Canon, in the chapter ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or tsab, if you prefer. And in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, which was entirely omitted by the Latin translator: هو الضب وطبعه قريب من طبع الورل وهو اشبه الوزغ بما يتعزي به [huwa al-ḍabb wa-ṭabʿuhu qarīb min ṭabʿ al-waral wa-huwa ashbah al-wazagh bi-mā yataʿazzī bihi] Chardaun is the same as dhab: its nature comes close to the guaril, and its attributes are the same as those of the guezga. And in the chapter ورل [waral] guaril, هو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف من الورل وربما قريب في طبايعه [huwa ghayr al-ḍabb wa-al-ḍabb lā yakūn aw qalla mā yakūn illā fī al-bādiya wa-raʾsuhu wa-badanuhu wa-dhanabuhu khālif min al-waral wa-rubbamā qarīb fī ṭabāyiʿihi] The guaril is different from the dhab. For the dhab is not found, or only rarely, anywhere but in the desert. And it differs from the guaril in head, trunk and tail, although it is close to it in nature. And Abdollatif of Baghdad: الورل والضب والحربا وشحمة الارض والوزغ كلها متناسبة في الخلق [al-waral wa-al-ḍabb wa-al-ḥirbā wa-shaḥmat al-arḍ wa-al-wazagh kulluhā mutanāsiba fī al-khalq] The guaril, and the dhab, and the hirba, and the fat of the earth, and the guezga all share the same nature. These, namely, are so many species of lizards, of which we shall speak below. Therefore ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, which is the same, is neither a toad, nor a bramble-toad, nor a tortoise, nor a shelled animal, but belongs to the lizard kind. Now, so that it may be known more fully, we shall say what the Critics, Philosophers, Theologians, Magicians and Physicians of the Arabs have written about it, most of which has not yet been published.

The Critics, then, teach that it is an animal πολυώνυμον [polyōnymon], with many names. For besides ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, the common name, it is also called حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun (the Chaldeans write חרדונא chara[?], the Syrians ܚܕܪܘܢܐ [חדרונא] chadrona, and the Samaritans [?] adrona, as will be shown below). It is likewise called برق [barq] bork, and علين [ʿlyn] alin, and هيقل [hayqal] haikal. And, if it is fat, سبحل [?] or سحبل [siḥbal] sichbal: if old, قرسم [qirsim] kirsem; if of bad disposition, ضغطار [ḍighṭār] dhiphtar: just as the female is commonly ضبة [ḍabba] dhabba; but, when fat, حيكانا [ḥaykānā] chaicana; when with young, مكون [makūn] machun, and ممكن [mumkin] mamchin. From the verb مكن [makina] machina, proper to this animal and to the locust when they lay eggs, the egg is مكين [makīn] machin, and شلقة [shalqa] silka. The young in general, حضرم [ḥiḍrim] chidhrim; the first, مطبح [muṭbiḥ] mutbich; when just hatched from the egg, حسل [ḥisl] chisel; when already more grown, غيداق [ghaydāq] chaidak. The fat which it has around the belly and the root of the tail, كشية [kushya] chusia. And حلم [ḥalama] halama properly means to take out that fat, just as عكد [ʿakida] achada, to be fat, is used of the dhab ضب [ḍabb] alone. The male member, in the dual, نزكان [nazkān] nazachani; because it is forked. Hence the animal itself is also called سديم [sadīm] sadim, that is, well furnished in that part. Its hiding-place is عكدة [ʿukda] ochda, and عرن [ʿirn] arin, and لغز [lughz] logoz, but more commonly جحر [juḥr] giochar, whence جحر الضب [jaḥara al-ḍabb] the dhab has entered its hiding-place. And اجحر فلان [ajḥara fulān] someone drove it into its hiding-place. But ادلق [adlaqa] adlaka he poured water into it, so that the dhab would come out. And دلق الضب [dalaqa al-ḍabb] dalaka dhab, that is, it came out of its hiding-place because of the water poured in. And اهوي يده الي الضب [ahwā yadahu ilā al-ḍabb] he put in his hand to catch the dhab. And حرش [ḥarasha] charasa, he hunted, used properly of this animal. These things have been gathered and excerpted here and there from Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] and other books of the Critics.

But the philosophers report a good many notable things about the nature of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. That its penis is forked, as we said, Damir teaches in these words: للضب نكران وللانثي فرجان كما للورل وللحردون [li-l-ḍabb nakrān wa-li-l-unthā farjān kamā li-l-waral wa-li-l-ḥardūn] The male dhab has two penises, and its female two vulvas, like the guaril and the chardaun. And Alcamus: للنزك نكر الضب والورل ولهم نزكان [li-l-nazk nakr al-ḍabb wa-l-waral wa-lahum nazkān] Nazach is the penis of the dhab and of the guaril, which have a double one (the lexicographers, not understanding these words, twisted them to another sense). Accordingly the priest Abuchanipha writes that the penis of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is كلسان الحية اصل واحد له فرعان [ka-lisān al-ḥayya aṣl wāḥid lahu farʿān] like the tongue of a serpent, which, though born from one root, is nevertheless forked. It has a remarkably knotty tail, whence the proverb in Damir, اعقد من ذنب الضب [aʿqad min dhanab al-ḍabb] Knottier than the tail of the dhab. For they say there are حد وعشرون عقدة [ḥd wa-ʿishrūn ʿuqda] 21 knots in it, whereas the scorpion's tail, which is itself very knotty, has at most seven knots [?] joints. It is added that the same animal [?] has continuous [teeth], which therefore never fall out. [?] يقال ان اسنانه قطعة واحدة [yuqāl anna asnānahu qiṭʿa wāḥida]: [?] its teeth cohere into one. Alcamus: لا اتيك سن الحسل اي ابدا لان سنه لا تسقط [lā ātīka sinn al-ḥisl ay abadan li-anna sinnahu lā tasquṭ] The tooth of the chisel (that is, of the young of the dhab) will not come to you: that is, it will never come to you, because its teeth do not fall out. Here is another similar proverb about the same animal in Damir! لا افعله حتي يرد الضب لان الضب لا يرد [lā afʿaluhu ḥattā yarida al-ḍabb li-anna al-ḍabb lā yarid] I will not do this until the dhab goes down to the water (that is, I will never do it), because the dhab never goes down to the water. For it does not drink at all, and so it rarely urinates. The same: الضب لا يشرب الما [al-ḍabb lā yashrab al-mā] The dhab abstains entirely from drinking water. And a little later: يقال انه يبول في كل اربعين يوما مرة [yuqāl annahu yabūl fī kull arbaʿīn yawman marra] It is said to urinate only once every forty days, or قطرة [qaṭra] one little drop, as another copy has it. On its eyes, in the same place: الضب يخرج من حجره كليل البصر فيجلوه بالتحدق في الشمس [al-ḍabb yakhruj min juḥrihi kalīl al-baṣar fa-yajlūhu bi-l-taḥadduq fī al-shams] The dhab comes out of its hiding place with rather dim sight; but when its pupil has been cleansed against the sun, it sees more clearly. Epiphanius, in the Sampsaeans, asserts that the σαῦραν ἡλιακὴν [sauran hēliakēn], the solar lizard, recovers its sight in the same way when it begins to grow dim: Ἐκείνη, he says, ἀμβλυωπήσασα χρόνῳ ἀναβλέπει, διὰ ἡλιακῆς στροφάλιγγος ἐν φωλεῷ πρὸς ἀνατολὴν προσέχοντι ἑαυτὴν προσθλίψασα, καὶ νηστεύσασα πρὸς ἀνατολὴν κατανοοῦσα· [Ekeinē amblyōpēsasa chronō anablepei, dia hēliakēs strophalingos en phōleō pros anatolēn prosechonti heautēn prosthlipsasa, kai nēsteusasa pros anatolēn katanoousa] When it has dulled sight, it recovers it some time later by turning toward the sun, pressing itself into a den facing the east, and, fasting, looking toward the East. Again Damir on the dhab: ويتغذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبره الهوا وذلك عند الهرم وفنا الرطوبات ونقص الحرارت [wa-yataghadhdhā bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-barh al-hawā wa-dhālika ʿind al-haram wa-fanā al-ruṭūbāt wa-naqṣ al-ḥarārāt] And it is nourished by breath and lives on cold air, and this until decrepit old age, and until the (radical) moisture is consumed and the heat fails. And below: وهو طويل العمر ومن هذه الجهة يناسب الحيات والافاعي [wa-huwa ṭawīl al-ʿumr wa-min hādhihi al-jiha yunāsib al-ḥayyāt wa-l-afāʿī] It is a long-lived animal, which it has in common with serpents and vipers. And Ibno-chalvia: يعيش سبع ماية فصاعدا [yaʿīsh sabʿ māya fa-ṣāʿidan] It lives seven hundred years and more. This I think was invented by those who say greater things about great matters. But it is also altogether false, and wrongly transferred here from the account of the chameleon, that it is said to be fed by its own breath and to live on cold air. For it is an almost παμφάγον [pamphagon] animal, feeding chiefly on roots and fruits. Hence Alcamus, after writing that خبلة [khabla] chobla is the name for the roots of the vine and the fruits of thorny trees, adds: ضب خابل ياكلها [ḍabb khābil yaʾkuluhā] dhab chabil is a dhab that feeds on them. And the female, when stung by a scorpion, اكلت من حشيشة تسمي اذان الفار يزول عنها الم اللسع [akalat min ḥashīsha tusammā ādhān al-fār yazūl ʿanhā alam al-lasʿ] eats a herb called mouse-ear, and the pain of the sting abates. So it is in Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]. Moreover, on the authority of Damir himself (as will be said more fully below), the dhab returns to its vomit like a dog, and devours its own young. That it lives on air alone is therefore a mere fiction. It has this in common with the jarboa, or choerogryllius, that it chooses its hiding place in rocky and steep places. Alkazuinius: من كيسه انه لا يتخذ البيت الا في موضع صلب ليلا ينهدر عليه في حوافر الدواب ولما علم انه نساء لا يتخذ البيت الي عند الاكمته او صخرة عظيمة او شجرة ليستدل بها علي بيته اذا عاب ويتباعد عن بيته [min kaysihi annahu lā yattakhidh al-bayt illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb laylā yanhadir ʿalayhi fī ḥawāfir al-dawābb wa-lammā ʿalima annahu nassāʾ lā yattakhidh al-bayt ilā ʿind al-akamatih aw ṣakhra ʿaẓīma aw shajara li-yastadill bihā ʿalā baytihi idhā ʿāb wa-yatabāʿad ʿan baytihi] It is part of its shrewdness that it does not take a home except in hard ground, lest, trampled by the hooves of beasts of burden, it collapse upon it. And since it knows itself to be very forgetful, it chooses it on a high hill or a lofty rock, or by a tree, which it may have as a marker when it is away from it or goes far off. Damir also: لا يتخذ حجره الا في كدية حجر خوفا من السيل والحافر ولذلك براثنه ناقصة كليلة لحفره بها في الاماكن الصلبة [lā yattakhidh juḥrahu illā fī kudyat ḥajar khawfan min al-sayl wa-l-ḥāfir wa-li-dhālika barāthinuhu nāqiṣa kalīla li-ḥafrihi bihā fī al-amākin al-ṣulba] Nor does it have a hiding place anywhere but in the hardest rocks, because it fears floods and diggers. And accordingly its claws are worn and blunt, since it digs stony places with them. Likewise: وفي طبعه النسيان وعدم الهداية وبه يضرب المثل في الحيرة ولذلك يحفر جحره عند الاكمة او صخرة ليلا يضل عنه اذا خرج لطلب والطعم [wa-fī ṭabʿihi al-nisyān wa-ʿadam al-hidāya wa-bihi yuḍrab al-mathal fī al-ḥayra wa-li-dhālika yaḥfir juḥrahu ʿind al-akama aw ṣakhra laylā yaḍill ʿanhu idhā kharaja li-ṭalab wa-l-ṭuʿm] Forgetfulness and ἀβλεψία [ablepsia] are natural to them. So its bewilderment has become proverbial. Accordingly it digs its den on a hill or in a rock, so as not to stray from it when it goes out to seek its food. The proverb Damir mentions is cited by him thus under the heading On Proverbs: اضل من الضب [aḍall min al-ḍabb] More apt to stray from the way than the dhab. Because the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a wicked animal, whence it is called ضغطار [ḍghṭār] dhiphtar, as already observed, here is another proverb in use among the Arabs, which Alcamus taught me: اطعم اخاك كشية الضب حشة على المواسات [aṭʿim akhāka kushyat al-ḍabb ḥashsha ʿalā al-muwāsāt] He fed your brother the fat of the dhab, that is, he incited him to commit evil! As for breeding: اذا ارادت الضبة ان تخرج بيضها حفرت في الارض حفرة ورمت فيها البيض وطمته بالتراب وتعاهده كل يوم حتي يخرج وذلك في اربعين يوما [idhā arādat al-ḍabba an tukhrija bayḍahā ḥafarat fī al-arḍ ḥufra wa-ramat fīhā al-bayḍ wa-ṭammathu bi-l-turāb wa-taʿāhadathu kull yawm ḥattā yakhruj wa-dhālika fī arbaʿīn yawman] When the dhabba (that is, the female of the dhab) is about to lay her eggs, she digs a pit in the ground, into which she throws the eggs and covers them with dust, and visits them daily until they hatch, that is, until the fortieth day. So Damir, following Alkazuinius in part, whose words are: فاذا اراد ان يبيض حفر مثل ادحي النعام ويرمي فيها ثمانين بيضة ويدفنها في التراب وبيضها مثل بيض الحمام ويدعها اربعين يوما ثم ياتي وحسول قد خرجت منها فيتعدون فياكل منها ما قدرت [fa-idhā arāda an yabīḍa ḥafara mithl udḥī al-naʿām wa-yarmī fīhā thamānīn bayḍa wa-yadfinuhā fī al-turāb wa-bayḍuhā mithl bayḍ al-ḥamām wa-yadaʿuhā arbaʿīn yawman thumma yaʾtī wa-ḥusūl qad kharajat minhā fa-yataʿaddawn fa-yaʾkul minhā mā qadarat] When it is about to lay, it digs something like an ostrich's nest, into which it throws eighty eggs, like pigeons' eggs, and buries them in the dust. When it returns to them after leaving them forty days, the young, coming out of them, run about. Of these it eats as many as it can. Indeed, as Damir says, يوصف العقوق لانه ياكل حسوله [yūṣaf al-ʿuqūq li-annahu yaʾkul ḥusūlahu] it is described as notable for cruelty, because it devours its own young. Hence the poet: اكلت بنيك كاكل الضب حتي تركت بنيك ليس لهم غذي [akalta banīka ka-akl al-ḍabb ḥattā tarakta banīka laysa lahum ghidhā]

You have eaten your children, as the dhab eats its young, so that they have perished for lack of food. The Arabs attribute the same thing to it that Peter attributes to the dog ). Again Damir: من طبعه انه يرجع في قيه كالكلب وياكل رجيعه [min ṭabʿihi annahu yarjiʿu fī qayʾihi ka-l-kalb wa-yaʾkulu rajīʿahu] It is also in its nature that, like a dog, it returns to its vomit, and devours again that to which it has returned. And this too: في الشتا لا يخرج من حجره [fī al-shitā lā yakhruju min juḥrihi] through the whole winter it does not come out of its burrow. Yet it lives and grows fat, and God so provides for it that it does not perish from hunger. Hence the poet Chatimolasem:

وكيف اخاف الفقر والله رازقن [wa-kayfa akhāfu al-faqra wa-llāhu rāziqun] ورازق هذا الخلق في العسر واليسر [wa-rāziqu hādhā al-khalqi fī al-ʿusri wa-l-yusri] تكفل بالارزاقي للخلق كلهم [takaffala bi-l-arzāqi li-l-khalqi kullihim] وللضب في البيداء وللحوت في البحر [wa-li-l-ḍabbi fī al-baydāʾi wa-li-l-ḥūti fī al-baḥri]

Why should I fear poverty, when God provides for me? He provides for His creatures in hardship and want. He bestows sustenance on all creatures, even on the dhab in the desert and on the fish in the sea. The Arabs have also observed with which animals the dhab has sympathy and antipathy. Damir: بينه وبين العقارب مودة فلذلك يويها في حجره لتلسع المتحرش به اذا ادخل يده لاخذه [baynahu wa-bayna al-ʿaqārib mawadda fa-li-dhālika yuwīhā fī juḥrihi li-talsaʿa al-mutaḥarrish bihi idhā adkhala yadahu li-akhdhihi] There is mutual love between it and scorpions. It therefore receives them into its hiding place, so that they may sting the hunter when he puts his hand in to catch it. The same author, in the chapter on فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī], as if you were to say searcher of vipers, asserts that this name is given to ضرب من الخنافس رقط تالف العقارب في حجرة الضب لانها اذا اخرجت يعلم ان الضب خارج لا محالة واذا زويت في الحجر علم ان وراها العقارب والحيات [ḍarb min al-khanāfis ruqṭ taʾlafu al-ʿaqārib fī ḥujrat al-ḍabb li-annahā idhā kharajat yuʿlamu anna al-ḍabba khārij lā maḥāla wa-idhā zuwiyat fī al-juḥr ʿulima anna warāhā al-ʿaqārib wa-l-ḥayyāt] a species of beetle of varied colour, which lives together with scorpions in the hiding places of the dhab. That is, when this little creature comes out of the hiding place, it signifies that the dhab has certainly gone out too. But when it goes back in, it signifies that serpents and scorpions lurk behind it. But the dhab is most hostile to الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or the greater stellio, which barbarous writers call guaril. Abdollatif of Baghdad, on the guaril: بينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحية وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفشه ولا يحفر حجر بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا يستولي عليه [baynahu wa-bayna al-ḍabb ʿadāwa fa-yaghlibu al-waral al-ḍabba wa-yaqtuluhu lākinnahu lā yaʾkuluhu kamā yafʿalu bi-l-ḥayya wa-huwa lā yattakhidhu baytan li-nafshihi wa-lā yaḥfiru juḥr bal yukhriju al-ḍabba min juḥrihi ṣāriʿan yastawlī ʿalayhi], Between the guaril and the dhab there is grave enmity. The guaril overcomes it and kills it. Yet it does not eat it, as it usually does serpents; but, since it builds no home for itself nor digs a hiding place, it drives the dhab out of its lair by fighting and prevails over it. It also has a second enemy, a black serpent, which in Arabic is called اسود سالخ [aswad sālikh] asvvad-salich. Alcamus: الحراش الاسود السالخ لانه يحرش الضباب [al-ḥarrāsh al-aswad al-sālikh li-annahu yaḥrushu al-ḍibāb]. The sense is that this serpent is called by another name charras, that is, hunter, because it hunts the dhab. For حرش [ḥarasha] charrasa is a verb meaning to hunt, not in general, but specifically to hunt the dhab, as we noted earlier . To these let a third enemy be added, ظربان [ẓarbān] dhorban, that is, the putorius [polecat], as they call it, a most fetid animal of the weasel kind, by which it is vanquished not by strength but by blasts from its hind parts turned toward its burrow. الظربان يقصد حجر الضب وفيه حسوله وبيضه فياتي اضيق موضع فيه فيسده بذنبه فيحول دبره ويفسوا ثلاث فسوات حتي يغشي علي الضب فياكله ويقيم في حجره حتي ياتي علي اخر حسولة [al-ẓarbān yaqṣidu juḥr al-ḍabb wa-fīhi ḥusūluhu wa-bayḍuhu fa-yaʾtī aḍyaqa mawḍiʿ fīhi fa-yasudduhu bi-dhanabihi fa-yuḥawwilu duburahu wa-yafsū thalāth faswāt ḥattā yughshā ʿalā al-ḍabb fa-yaʾkuluhu wa-yuqīmu fī juḥrihi ḥattā yaʾtī ʿalā ākhir ḥusūlih] The dhorban (or putorius) approaches the burrow of the dhab when it has its young and its eggs there, and occupies its narrowest spot, which it blocks with its tail; and, turning its rear toward it, it emits three blasts of wind, until the dhab falls into a swoon. Having devoured it, it stays in the burrow until it has finished off its young, down to the last one . So much from the philosophers about the species of lizard with which we are dealing.

This same animal has also given the theologians ample matter for dispute. For it is asked why it is permitted to eat it, since it is one of الحشرات [al-ḥasharāt], the reptiles, which are forbidden as food. Some reply that this one alone is excepted. For so says الوسيط [al-Wasīṭ], that is, the book entitled The Mediator, in which these questions are fully settled: لا يوكل من الحشرات الا الضب [lā yūkal min al-ḥasharāt illā al-ḍabb] No reptile may be eaten except τὸν [ton] dhab. Others join to the dhab اليربوع والقنفد [al-yarbūʿ wa-l-qunfud] jarbuo and kunphud, that is, the choerogryllus and the hedgehog, which are themselves reptiles too and yet are permitted as food. Others leave the matter undecided, after arguing at length on both sides, although they admit that in Arabia this food is in frequent use. These same pseudo-theologians heap up great absurdities about this animal, of which it will be enough, indeed more than enough, to relate one here. A certain man had sworn concerning Muhammad that he would never believe unless هذا الضب [hādhā al-ḍabb] this dhab, which by chance had appeared at the mouth of its burrow, believed first. Then the dhab came out of the burrow, approached the Prophet, and said to him بلسان طلق فصيح عربي مبين يفهمه القوم جميعا لبيك وسعديك يا رسول رب العالمين [bi-lisān ṭalq faṣīḥ ʿarabī mubīn yafhamuhu al-qawm jamīʿan labbayka wa-saʿdayka yā rasūl rabb al-ʿālamīn] in eloquent and clear speech, in plain Arabic language, which all understood: I am devoted to you, and may you be blessed, O Apostle of the Lord of the worlds. And when the Prophet had said من تعبد [man taʿbud] Whom do you worship?, the dhab answered: I worship Him whose throne is in heaven, and His dominion on earth, and His path in the sea, and His wrath and punishment in the underworld. Then the Prophet said to it: Who am I? And the dhab replied: You are the Apostle of the Lord of the worlds, and the seal of the Prophets. Well be it for him who believes in you and obeys you; and may whoever turns away from you or accuses you of falsehood perish miserably.

The magicians also play their part here. For to them I attribute those superstitions which I read in Damir and Alkazuini. If a ضب [ḍabb] dhab comes out from between a man's feet, the man to whom this happens will be unable to have intercourse with any woman. If anyone carries its testicles, his slaves will love him greatly. A horse that has the ankle-bone of the dhab tied to its forehead will not be outrun by any other in a race. Whoever makes for his sword a قرابا [qirāban] scabbard, or rather a sheath, from its skin will be valiant. Others prefer that only the نصاب السيف [niṣāb al-sayf] hilt of the sword be wrapped in this skin, as though that mattered much. In the most frivolous writers you may find more of this sort, which one is ashamed and loath to relate.

The physicians have less, but more reliable. Avicenna, in the chapter ضب [ḍabb] dhab: يطلي بعره علي الكلف والنمش فينفع ۞ زبله نافع لبياض العين ونزول الما ۞ [yuṭlī baʿruhu ʿalā al-kalaf wa-l-namash fa-yanfaʿ ۞ zibluhu nāfiʿ li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn wa-nuzūl al-mā ۞] Its dung, smeared on, helps freckles and spots of the face; likewise white specks of the eye and cataracts. And in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, after noting that the chardaun is the same as the dhab: زبله للبياض والحكة ويحد البصر [zibluhu li-l-bayāḍ wa-l-ḥikka wa-yuḥidd al-baṣar] Its dung (helps) white specks and itching of the eyes, and sharpens the sight. And in the chapter دم [dam] Dam, or On the blood of animals: دم الورل والحردون يقوي البصر [dam al-waral wa-l-ḥardūn yuqawwī al-baṣar] The blood of the guaril and the chardaun strengthens the sight. And in the chapter زبل [zibl] Zebel, or On dung: The dung of locusts removes spots and vitiligo from the face; as does the dung of thrushes fed on rice. وكذلك زبل الحردون والورل ويحسن اللون [wa-ka-dhālika zibl al-ḥardūn wa-l-waral wa-yuḥassin al-lawn] The dung of the chardaun and the guaril does the same, and makes a good complexion. And below: بعر الضب يجلو الكلف مجرب [baʿr al-ḍabb yajlū al-kalaf mujarrab] The dung of the dhab cleanses spots from the face: this has been tested. Likewise: زبل الورل والضب والتمساح لبياض العين [zibl al-waral wa-l-ḍabb wa-l-timsāḥ li-bayāḍ al-ʿayn] The dung of the guaril, the dhab and the crocodile for white specks of the eyes; supply is to be applied. And in the chapter بعر الحيوان [baʿr al-ḥayawān], that is, On the dung of animals: بعر الضب ينفع من البرص والكلف بجلايه [baʿr al-ḍabb yanfaʿ min al-baraṣ wa-l-kalaf bi-jalāyih] The dung of the dhab by its cleansing power heals elephantiasis and spots on the face. And shortly after: بعر الضب يجلو بياض العين [baʿr al-ḍabb yajlū bayāḍ al-ʿayn] The dung of the dhab cleanses white specks of the eyes. So too Damir: بعرة ينفع من البرص والكلف طلا ومن البياض ونزول الما في العين اكتحالا [baʿra yanfaʿ min al-baraṣ wa-l-kalaf ṭilā wa-min al-bayāḍ wa-nuzūl al-mā fī al-ʿayn iktiḥālan] Its dung, smeared on, heals leprosy and spots of the face; and eye-salves made from it remove white specks and the flux of humours into the eyes. This is taken from Alkazuini, where it is found in almost the same words. You may also read similar things in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], and in other anonymous writers that I have .

Now, that the animal which the Arabs have described to us under the names ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun is the very same as the צב tsab of Moses is shown by so many considerations that to doubt it would be wrong. First, it is supported by the similarity of the Hebrew name to the Arabic. For although the Hebrew צב tsab and the Arabic ضب [ḍabb] dhab differ in sound, in both the initial letter is Tsade, which among the Arabs sounds differently because of the dot added to it. Nothing is more frequent than this change. Thus sheep, צאן tson to the Hebrews, is ضان [ḍān] dhan to the Arabs. Hyena is צבוע tsebua to the former, ضبع [ḍabuʿ] dhebu to the latter. Frog is צפרדע tsephardea to the former, ضفدع [ḍifdaʿ] dhephda to the latter. Rib is צלע tsela to the former, ضلع [ḍilʿ] dhila to the latter. Diadem, or braid of hair, is צפירה tsephira to the former, ضفيرة [ḍafīra] dhephira to the latter. Dung is צפיע tsephia to the former, ضفع [ḍfʿ] dhepha to the latter. Distress is צוק tsuk to the former, ضيق [ḍīq] dhik to the latter. To laugh is צחק tsachak to the former, ضحق [ḍḥq] dhachika to the latter. 2. Secondly, that צב tsab is what we have said is made plain by the series of related animals in the same context. For in the following verse mention is made of the lizard, the stellio, the chameleon, the salamander, etc., as will be shown in its place. And there was equal reason why this species of lizard should be rejected as unclean. Nor ought it to have been omitted, since it is native to Arabia, which borders on Judaea, and is eaten among the Arabs. 3. To this is added the authority of the ancients, none of whom, I assert, took it otherwise. Certainly the four Arabic versions I was able to consult, two printed and two in manuscript, though they differ greatly among themselves elsewhere, here consistently have الضب [al-ḍabb] aldhab; and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has צבא tsaba, which is the Hebrew word itself, with only its ending adapted to Chaldee usage. In Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], for צב tsab you read חרדונא chardona; in the Syriac ܚܕܪܘܢܐ [חדרונא] chadrona; and in the Samaritan [?] adrona: all three come to the same thing. What is meant, namely, is the حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun of the Arabs, which Avicenna asserted above to be the same as the ضب [ḍabb] dhab. Some hold it to be similar to it, others its male. Damir: الحردون دويبة شبيه بالضب وقيل هو ذكر الضب لان له ذكرين مثله [al-ḥardūn duwaybba shabīh bi-l-ḍabb wa-qīla huwa dhakar al-ḍabb li-anna lahu dhakarayn mithlahu] Alchardaun (or rather alchirdaun, for he directs it to be written so) is a small animal, similar to τῷ [tō] dhab: indeed it is said to be its male, because like it it has two penises. Alcamus: الحردون لذكر الضب ودويبة احري [al-ḥardūn li-dhakar al-ḍabb wa-duwaybba aḥrī] Alchardaun is said of the male τοῦ [tou] dhab. There is also another (similar) small animal .

To the Arabs and Chaldeans I add the ancient Hebrews, who openly place צב tsab, or חרדון chardon, among the species of lizards. This will be made plain by two passages which I shall cite; many have already noticed them, but they have not yet been explained. The first is in the Talmudic tractate Cholin, ch. 9, fol. 127a, where the Hebrews hold that similar species are included under the name צב tsab, forbidden in the Law, because the words after its kind are added. For the words of the Law run thus: These shall be unclean to you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth: the mole and the mouse, והצב למינהו, and the tsab after its kind. They say: להביא העריד ובן־נפילים וסלמנדרא, to include the arod and the ben-nephilim and the salamander, as species close to the dhab. Now the more recent writers do not know what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. But it is at least known that the salamander belongs to the lizard kind. Therefore צב tsab must necessarily be assigned to the same kind. The matter will be clearer if we show what ערוד arod and בן־נפילים ben-nephilim are here. Elsewhere the former means wild ass, the latter son of giants. These seem beside the point. Here, therefore, the interpreters are at a loss, and neither the Glossators of the Talmud nor the Lexicographers offer anything with the appearance of truth. But the first word is corrupt, and instead of ערוד arod, or iruad, one should write עסוד isvvad. This is a white kind of lizard, living in the sands, to which the Arab poets compare the fingers of girls. Some call it عذفوط [ʿadhfūṭ] odphut, and عضرفوط [ʿaḍrafūṭ] adhraphut. Alcamus: العذفوط دويبة بيضا ناعمة يشبة بها اصابع الجواري [al-ʿadhfūṭ duwaybba bayḍā nāʿima yushbih bihā aṣābiʿ al-jawārī] Alodphut, a small animal, white and pleasing, to which the fingers of girls are compared. And elsewhere: العضرفوط العذفوط او ذكر العظا [al-ʿaḍrafūṭ al-ʿadhfūṭ aw dhakar al-ʿaẓā] Aladhraphut, the same as alodphut, or the male lizard. And again: العسود للعضرفوط من العظاء [al-ʿaswad li-l-ʿaḍrafūṭ min al-ʿaẓāʾ] Aliswad is said of the adraphut, a kind of lizard. Likewise: العسودة دويبة بضا يشبه بها بنان العذاري وتكني بنة النقا [al-ʿaswada duwaybba baḍā yushbah bihā banān al-ʿadhārī wa-tukannā binat al-naqā] Aliswada, a small white animal, to which the fingertips of virgins are compared; it is surnamed Binth-onnakai, that is, daughter of the sand. Therefore, since ערוד is reckoned by the Talmudists among the species of lizards, by a slight change we should read עסוד instead of ערוד, so that the lizard we have described is meant. Unskilled scribes changed עסוד, a little-used word and perhaps not known from elsewhere, into ערוד, which means something quite different, namely wild ass. It remains for us to say what animal the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is, of the same kind as these. A man outstanding in these studies, who today has no equal, rightly infers that this animal is aquatic, because we read in Semoth rabba, sect. 15: וזיע את הימים והראהו את בן־הנפילים שנאמר קול יי על המים He (God) moved the seas and showed him (Moses) the Ben-nephilim, as it is said Ps 29:3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters.“ But the same man errs very gravely when, from the affinity of the words and the similarity of the animals (as he asserts), he infers that בן־נפילים ben-nephilim is the nauplius, or nautilus. For even if we grant that nephilim alludes in some way to nauplius, in the things themselves there is no similarity. For the nauplius, or nautilus, has nothing in common with the tsab, whether this word signifies, as he holds, a toad or a tortoise, or some species of lizard, which with me is most firmly established. For lizards, toads and tortoises differ in their whole kind from the nauplius or nautilus fish. Nor is it at all likely that the Hebrews derived their נפילים nephilim from the name nauplius, which is little used, and occurs nowhere, so far as I remember, except in one passage of Pliny. Nor, conversely, was nauplius made from נפילים nephilim. For it is evident that this name was taken from the thing itself, and that the nautilus is called nauplius because it sails as in a ship, from the noun ναῦς [naus] and the verb πλεῖν [plein]. What, then, is the בן־נפילים ben-nephilim? It seems altogether to be the Egyptian skink, of which Avicenna says in book 2, in the chapter اسقنقور [isqanqūr] Iscancur, as the Arabs call the skink: هو ورل الماي يصاد من نيل مصر ويقولون انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما ونشا خارجا [huwa waral al-māy yuṣād min Nīl Miṣr wa-yaqūlūn innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā wa-nashaʾa khārijan] It is the aquatic guaril, which is caught in Egypt on the bank of the Nile. They say that it is born from the seed of the crocodile when it sheds it outside the water, and that it grows up outside the water . And again in the chapter سقنقور [saqanqūr] Scancur: ورل نيلي يصاد بمصر ويزعمون انه من نتاج التمساح في البر [waral nīlī yuṣād bi-Miṣr wa-yazʿumūn annahu min nitāj al-timsāḥ fī al-barr] It is the Nile guaril, which they catch in Egypt, and they say it is born on land from the seed of the crocodile. And Alkazuinius, after citing Avicenna: وقال غيره انه من نسل التمساح اذا وضعه خارج الما فما قصد الما صار تمساحا وما قصد البر صار سقنقورا [wa-qāla ghayruhu innahu min nasl al-timsāḥ idhā waḍaʿahu khārij al-mā fa-mā qaṣada al-mā ṣāra timsāḥan wa-mā qaṣada al-barr ṣāra saqanqūran] Others, he says, have said that it comes from the seed of the crocodile when it has cast it out of the waters; and that whatever reaches the waters becomes a crocodile, and whatever stays on land a skink. And Damir: الاسقنقور نوعان هندي ومصري فالمصري منه ما يتولد ببحر القلزم وهو يغتذي بالسمك في الما وفي البر بالقطا يسرطه كالحيات [al-isqanqūr nawʿān hindī wa-miṣrī fa-l-miṣrī minhu mā yatawallad bi-baḥr al-Qulzum wa-huwa yaghtadhī bi-l-samak fī al-mā wa-fī al-barr bi-l-qaṭā yasruṭuhu ka-l-ḥayyāt] The skink is of two species, the Indian and the Egyptian. Among the Egyptian ones is one that is born in the sea of Kelzem (that is, the Red Sea), and feeds on fish in the water, and on land on doves, which it swallows like snakes. Since this is absurd, instead of بالقطا [bi-l-qaṭā], that is, on doves, one should read بالعظا [bi-l-ʿaẓā] on lizards. And further on, inquiring how the guaril and the skink differ from each other, he places the chief difference in this: أن ورل لا ياوي الا البراري الاسقنقور لا ياوي الا بالقرب من الما او فيه [anna waral lā yaʾwī illā al-barārī al-isqanqūr lā yaʾwī illā bi-l-qurb min al-mā aw fīhi] that the guaril lives only on land, but the skink only near the waters, or even in the waters themselves. And further on: لا نعرف اليوم في عصرنا الاسقنقور في ديار المصرية الا ببلاد الفيوم ومنها يجلب الي القاهرة لمن اعتني بطلبه ولا يصاد الا في ايام الشتا لانه اذا اشتد حليه البرد خرج الي البر فيصاد [lā naʿrif al-yawm fī ʿaṣrinā al-isqanqūr fī diyār al-miṣriyya illā bi-bilād al-Fayyūm wa-minhā yujlab ilā al-Qāhira li-man iʿtanā bi-ṭalabihi wa-lā yuṣād illā fī ayyām al-shitā li-annahu idhā ishtadda ḥlyh al-bard kharaja ilā al-barr fa-yuṣād] Today, in our age, we know of the skink in the Egyptian territory nowhere but in the province of Phium, from which it is brought to Cairo for whoever takes the trouble to seek it. It is caught only in winter; for, driven by the force of the cold, it comes out onto land, and is caught there. And shortly after: يحل اكل الاسقنقور الهندي لانه سمك ويحتمل ان ياتي فيه وجه الحرمة لان له شبهين في البر احدهما احرام وهو الورل واخر حلال وهو الضب واما الاسقنقور المصري فهو حرام لانه متولد من التمساح فهو حرام كاصله [yaḥill akl al-isqanqūr al-hindī li-annahu samak wa-yuḥtamal an yaʾtī fīhi wajh al-ḥurma li-anna lahu shibhayn fī al-barr aḥaduhumā aḥrām wa-huwa al-waral wa-ākhar ḥalāl wa-huwa al-ḍabb wa-ammā al-isqanqūr al-miṣrī fa-huwa ḥarām li-annahu mutawallid min al-timsāḥ fa-huwa ḥarām ka-aṣlihi] It is lawful to eat the Indian skink, because it is a fish , although an aspect of something forbidden may be attributed to it, because on land the guaril and the dhab resemble it, of which one is forbidden and the other permitted. But the Egyptian skink is forbidden, because it is born from the crocodile; it is therefore forbidden like its root. Of the many things the Arabs say about the skink, we have excerpted these few, because they serve our purpose. For three things are inferred from them. First, that the skink is contained under the same kind as the dhab and the guaril, since it is similar to them in appearance. Second, that it is amphibious, and lives mostly in the waters of the Nile, and so also in the sea, so that God can rightly be said to have moved את הימים, the seas, in order to show the skink to Moses. Though there is an error in that word, and instead of הימים, that is, seas, one should read המים, waters, with one small letter fewer, as what follows shows: As it is said, „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. Third, since the skink is believed (how truly, we do not now ask) to be born from the seed of the crocodile, as the Arabs consistently write, it is clear why it was called by the Hebrews בן-נפילים, that is, son of giants. For by the name of giants the Orientals denote not only men but also any beasts of greater bulk. Thus an Arab writer in Damir: في جرادة خلق عشرة من جبابرة من الحيوان [fī jarāda khalq ʿashara min jabābira min al-ḥayawān] In the locust is the nature of ten giants among animals; so it reads word for word, that is, of ten larger animals. For, as follows, the locust has the face of a horse, the eyes of an elephant, the neck of a bull, the horns of a stag, etc. On the same pattern the skink is called by the Hebrews son of giants, that is, of crocodiles, compared with which it is nothing but a very tiny animal. These things being thus explained, the truth will shine out more and more if the whole passage is read, of which we have cited only a part. It runs thus: God stirred the waters, to show him (Moses) the son of giants, as it is said Ps 29:3: „The voice of the Lord is upon the waters“. He stirred the earth, to show him the צב tsab, as it is written Ps 29:8: „The voice of the Lord makes the desert bring forth“. He stirred fire, to show him the salamander, as it is said Ps 29:7: „The voice of the Lord cuts out flames of fire“. Thus from three elements are drawn three animals of different species but of the same kind: the son of giants, or of crocodiles, the skink, from the waters, in which it mostly lives; the צב tsab from the earth, to which it is so attached, as if to the soil, that it never goes down to the waters, as we proved above ; and finally the salamander from fire, in which many wrongly suppose it is born and on which it feeds.

The other passage is from Bereshit Rabbah, section 83, and it is no better understood than the former: הביא חכינא וזיוג לה חרדון ויצאת מהם חברבר, He brought a chacina and coupled it with the chardon, and from them was born the chabarber. The subject is Anah, who is read to have found הימים jemim in the desert, that is, to have come upon the Emim, as we have shown elsewhere . But the Hebrews understand mules, of which Anah was supposedly the first inventor, by bringing a she-ass to a horse or a wild ass. Since such a coupling of different species is forbidden by the Law of Moses, God, they say, in punishment for this crime, chose himself also to mix animals of different species, so that something harmful to man would be born from them. So he coupled the חרדון chardon with the חכינה chacina; from these was born a third species, worse than either, namely the חברבר chabarber , whose bite is so harmful that מעולם לא נשך אדם חברבר וחיה, a man whom the chabarber has bitten never recovers. Hence the Jerusalem Talmud, in Berakhot, fol. 12b: מימיו לא יאמר לך אדם שעקצו חברבר וחיה שנשכו כלב שיטה וחיה שבעטתו פרדה וחיה No one will ever tell you that he recovered after being stung by a chabarber, or recovered after being bitten by a rabid dog, or recovered after being kicked by a she-mule. And on fol. 9a a little story is told of R. Chanina, son of Dosa, who, while he was praying, was bitten by a chabarber and did not stop praying. Yet he himself did not die; rather the chabarber that had bitten him died. And so it was said: אי לו לאדם שנשכו חברבר ואי לו לחברבר שנשך את רבי חנינה Woe to the man whom the chabarber has bitten! But woe to the chabarber that has bitten Rabbi Chanina! Now if you consult the lexicographers to learn what the חרדון chardon is, what the חכינא chacina is, and what the חברבר chabarber is, they will teach you that the chardon is a toad or a tortoise, and the chacina a kind of serpent, and that from their union the chabarber was born, that is, a beast sharing the nature of both. Since this is utterly absurd, why should we not say here with the Poet,
Shall griffins now be mated with horses? — — —

For the toad, or the tortoise, has nothing in common with serpents. Such different animals cannot copulate, nor, if they did mate, could some third thing be born from them. Accordingly no one has so far shown what that third species, born of a snake and a toad (or a tortoise), might be. Therefore, however inept the masters of the Hebrews may be, far be it from me to think that they reached such a degree of folly as to invent these monsters. These three words, then, חרדון chardon, חכינא chacina, and חברבר chabarber, certainly designate three animals which, though different in species, nevertheless agree in genus. Nor is it so very difficult to show what they are. For we have already learned that חרדון chardon is the same as צב tsab, or ضب [ḍabb] dhab, a kind of lizard about which the Arabs have taught us so much. And for חכינא chacina we must most certainly read חבינא chabina, with Beth and Caph interchanged; these letters are very similar and are not rarely confused through the carelessness of copyists. Accordingly Buxtorf observes that in the Ialkut this word is read with Beth, חבנא chabna, or chabina, and this spelling is entirely correct. For in Arabic حبن [ḥabana] chabna means to suffer from dropsy. No word is more frequent in the books of the physicians. And hence ام حبين [umm ḥubayn] ummo chubaini, as it were mother of dropsy, and حبينة [ḥubayna] chubaina, or chabina, as it were the dropsical one, is the name of the female chameleon, or of a certain species of lizard very like it, because it has a swollen belly, as if it suffered from dropsy . Both names are in Alcamus. And the former is explained thus in Damir: واغا سميت بذلك من الحبن لكبر بطنها وهي علي خلقة الحربا غير صدر [wāghā summiyat bi-dhālika min al-ḥabn li-kibar baṭnihā wa-hiya ʿalī khilqat al-ḥirbā ghayr ṣadr] It is so called from dropsy, because of the size of its belly, and it is of the nature of the chameleon, the chest alone excepted. And Ibnossachith: هي اعرض العظاة وراسها عرض [hiya aʿraḍ al-ʿaẓāh wa-raʾsuhā ʿarḍ] This is broader than the common lizard, and has a broad head. And Ibnokatiba: ام حبين تستقبل للشمس وتدور معها كيف دارت وهذه صفة الحربا [umm ḥubayn tastaqbil lil-shams wa-tadūr maʿahā kayfa dārat wa-hādhihi ṣifat al-ḥirbā] Ummo chubain turns itself toward the sun and turns round with it, which is the property of the chameleon. And the author of المرصع [al-Muraṣṣaʿ], that is, the Inlaid Work: اختلف في ام حبين فقيل هي ضرب من العظا وقيل هي اعرض منها وقيل هي انثي الحرابي يتحاماها الاعراب فلا ياكلونها لنتنها [ukhtulifa fī umm ḥubayn fa-qīla hiya ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā wa-qīla hiya aʿraḍ minhā wa-qīla hiya unthā al-ḥarābī yataḥāmāhā al-aʿrāb fa-lā yaʾkulūnahā li-natnihā] There is disagreement about it. Some say it is a kind of common lizard, others that it is broader, others that it is the female of the chameleon. Because of its stench the Arabs shun it and do not take it as food. This, then, is the chabina, from whose coupling with the chardon the chabarber is imagined to arise, that is, the salamander, if I am not mistaken. How potent its venom is, namely in warmer places, these words of Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, may show: Among all venomous creatures the salamander's wickedness is the greatest. For the others strike individuals and do not kill many at once. The salamander can kill whole peoples unawares. For if it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison and kills those who eat it, with a cold force no different from aconite. Indeed, if a crust of bread is baked on wood it has touched, or with its foot, the same poisoning results, or if it falls into a well. For when its saliva is sprinkled on any part of the body, even the sole of the foot, all the hair on the whole body falls out. And book 10, chapter 67: By its fluid, which it vomits milky from its mouth, whatever part of the human body is touched, all the hair falls out; and the part touched changes its colour into a leprous blotch. And these words of Aelian, book 9, chapter 28, about a pig that has eaten a salamander: Τοὺς γε μὲν αὐτῆς γευσαμένους ἀποκτείνει [Tous ge men autēs geusamenous apokteinei]. It kills those who eat its flesh. And these of Theophrastus: It makes waters with which it has been mixed deadly; likewise fruits, especially when it is dead. And these of Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], page 89: Certain Frenchmen once told me that it is commonly said among them that if a Blanda (so the people of Narbonne call the salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much so that even hens feeding on it die. And further on: In certain places of France they call this lizard arressada; they think its bite so deadly that no hope of life remains (which is the very thing the Hebrews say of the chabarber). So they commonly repeat these verses:
Si mordu tá une arressade, Pren ton linceul, et ta flessade.

If a salamander bites you, take your linen and your blanket: that is, lie down in bed as one about to die. And the Rhaetians say that one bitten by a salamander needs as many physicians as the spots with which it is marked. This too should be noted: the animal is spotted, and is therefore called varius [variegated] by Dioscorides and stellatus [starred] by Pliny. This it has in common with the stellio. Hence, then, it was called חברבר chabarber by the Hebrews. For in Jer 13:23. חברברות chabarburoth are the spots of leopards. So Gesner conjectures that it is called Maal in German from the spots and dots with which its whole body is painted and marked. For (he says) our people say Maal for a spot, and maalen for to paint.

It remains for us to say why in the Greek version ὁ κροκόδειλος ὁ χερσαῖος [ho krokodeilos ho chersaios] is read for צב tsab, and in the Vulgate crocodilus [crocodile], without an epithet. The reason for this rendering cannot be fully grasped unless we go further back, for the sake of the less learned, who understand by the name crocodile nothing other than the Egyptian beast of great bulk. But for the Ionians, the first of mortals to use this word, the crocodile was a kind of lizard that usually lives in hedges and dry-stone walls. Ridiculous, therefore, is the invention of the grammarians, who dream that the crocodile is so called either from its saffron colour, or because it fears saffron, or from τὰς κρόκας [tas krokas], that is, the shores. For there was no other reason for the name than its likeness in form to the Ionian crocodiles, that is, the lizards of the hedges. Herodotus, book 2: Κροκοδείλους δὲ Ἴωνες ὠνόμασαν, εἰκάζοντες αὐτῶν τὰ εἴδεα τοῖσι παρὰ σφίσι γινομένοισι κροκοδείλοισι, τοῖσιν ἐν τῇσιν αἱμασίῃσι [Krokodeilous de Iōnes ōnomasan, eikazontes autōn ta eidea toisi para sphisi ginomenoisi krokodeiloisi, toisin en tēisin haimasiēisi]. To such crocodiles must be referred what Pliny excerpted from Democritus, that the chameleon is similar in size to the crocodile. For elsewhere he ascribes to the chameleon the size of a lizard. Nor did the old grammarian, whoever he is, from whom the Etymologicum and Phavorinus copied these words, have anything else in mind: Ὁ δὲ κροκόδειλος ζωΰφιόν ἐστι μικρόν [Ho de krokodeilos zōyphion esti mikron] (unless, with Eustathius, we read κροκύδειλος [krokydeilos] for κροκόδειλος [krokodeilos]). And this may have been taken from the account of the spring Zareta, or Azaritia, near Chalcedon, in which the ancients described small crocodiles, that is, water lizards. Antigonus, Mirabilia, chapter 162: Εὔδοξον δ’ ἱστορεῖν τὴν μὲν ἐν Καρχηδόνι [Eudoxon d’ historein tēn men en Karchēdoni] (read Χαλκηδόνι [Chalkēdoni]) κρήνην κροκοδείλους ἐν αὐτῇ μικροὺς (ἔχουσαν) ὁμοίους τοῖς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ [krēnēn krokodeilous en autēi mikrous (echousan) homoious tois en Aigyptōi]. Strabo, book 12, on Chalcedon: Ἔχει δ’ ἡ χώρα μὲν μικρὰν ὑπὲρ τῆς θαλάττης κρήνην Ἀζαριτίαν, τρέφουσαν κροκοδείλους μικρούς [Echei d’ hē chōra men mikran hyper tēs thalattēs krēnēn Azaritian, trephousan krokodeilous mikrous]. Stephanus: Ζάρητα· κρήνη ὑπὲρ τῆς Καλχηδονίας θαλάσσης, μικροὺς τρέφουσα κροκοδείλους, οἱ καλοῦνται Ζαρήτιοι [Zarēta; krēnē hyper tēs Kalchēdonias thalassēs, mikrous trephousa krokodeilous, hoi kalountai Zarētioi]. In his Saturnalian jest Statius calls these crocodiles Byzantine lizards, when he writes of a book sent to him:
You [sent] one gnawed by moths and rotten with mould, such as those that are soaked with Libyan olives, or keep Nilotic incense or pepper, or house Byzantine lizards.

This was the use of the word crocodile among the most ancient Greeks. But the same Greeks, having transferred the name to the beasts of the Nile, gradually took it away from lizards. Except that they did not cease to call by this name certain foreign species of that kind which seemed remarkable above the rest in use, shape or size, or to come closer to the form of the larger crocodile. Yet the epithet land was generally added, to distinguish them from the river crocodile. Thus Aristotle, History, book 2, chapter 17, on the belly of animals, says that the belly is of the same structure τοῖς κροκοδείλοις ἀμφοῖν [tois krokodeilois amphoin], in both crocodiles, that is, the land as well as the aquatic. And in book 5, chapter 33: Τίκτουσι δὲ καὶ σαῦροι, καὶ κροκόδειλοι οἱ χερσαῖοι, καὶ οἱ ποταμιοὶ, εἰς τὴν γῆν [Tiktousi de kai sauroi, kai krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi, kai hoi potamioi, eis tēn gēn]. Apollonius, Marvels, chapter 39, from Aristotle's Extracts τῶν ἀνατομῶν [tōn anatomōn]: Ὄφις ὤφθη ἐν Πάφῳ πόδας ἔχων δύο, ὁμοίους χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Ophis ōphthē en Paphō podas echōn dyo, homoious chersaiō krokodeilō]. Aelian, History, book 1, chapter 58: Καὶ αἱ σαῦραι δὲ ἐπιβουλεύουσι ταῖς μελίτταις, καὶ οἱ κροκόδειλοι οἱ χερσαῖοι [Kai hai saurai de epibouleuousi tais melittais, kai hoi krokodeiloi hoi chersaioi]. And in book 16, chapter 6, on the Indian phattages: Ἐν Ἰνδοῖς γίνεται ζῶον κροκοδείλῳ χερσαίῳ παραπλήσιον ἰδεῖν [En Indois ginetai zōon krokodeilō chersaiō paraplēsion idein], etc. The Scholiast on Nicander, on the salamander: Ἔοικε δὲ τῷ χερσαίῳ κροκοδείλῳ [Eoike de tō chersaiō krokodeilō]. Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 2, chapter 6: Although the Syrians used to eat land crocodiles too, and the Africans even green lizards. Accordingly Hesychius, to show that the name crocodile is a homonym applying to both, says: Κροκόδειλος, τὸ ζῶον· καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ Νείλῳ, καὶ τὸ χερσαῖον [Krokodeilos, to zōon; kai to en tō Neilō, kai to chersaion]. Meanwhile it is not sufficiently established which species of lizards, exactly, are given the name land crocodile. In his Corinthiaca Pausanias writes as though there were no other lizards of this name than those large ones two cubits long in Mauretania in Libya. For these are his words: Λιβύη μέν γε μόνη κροκοδείλους τρέφει χερσαίους διπήχεων οὐκ ἐλάσσονας [Libyē men ge monē krokodeilous trephei chersaious dipēcheōn ouk elassonas]. In Herodotus the same are said to be κροκόδειλοι, ὅσον τε τριπήχεες χερσαῖοι, τῇσι σαυρῇσι ἐμφερέστατοι [krokodeiloi, hoson te tripēchees chersaioi, tēsi saurēsi empherestatoi], crocodiles about three cubits long, living on land, very like lizards. Strabo calls them σαύρας, διπήχεις [sauras, dipēcheis]. And Aristotle describes similar ones in Arabia, if these words of Aelian, book 16, chapter 41, are true: Σαύρους δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης ἐν τῇ τῶν Ἀράβων γῇ τίκτεσθαί φησι, καὶ δύο πήχεις ἔχειν αὐτούς [Saurous de Aristotelēs en tē tōn Arabōn gē tiktesthai phēsi, kai dyo pēcheis echein autous]. But in the passage of Aristotle from which Aelian drew this, they are said only to be πηχυαῖοι [pēchyaioi], a cubit long, nowhere διπήχεις [dipēcheis], two cubits long. The words are in the History, book 8, chapter 28: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ σαῦροι μείζους πηχυαίων [En de tē Arabia sauroi meizous pēchyaiōn]. Hence Pliny, book 8, chapter 39: The lizards of Arabia are a cubit long. In Dioscorides the skink and the land crocodile differ only as species and genus. For he defines the skink as κροκόδειλον χερσαῖον ἰδιογενῆ [krokodeilon chersaion idiogenē], a land crocodile of its own kind. But Pliny rebukes those who hold this view and assigns to the skink definite marks by which it may be distinguished from the land crocodile, though how truly, I do not quite know: Of the same likeness, he says, is the skink, which some have said is a land crocodile, only with a whiter and thinner skin. Its chief difference from the crocodile, however, is recognized in that the set of its scales is turned toward the head. Some of the moderns use skink and land crocodile indiscriminately, as if they were the same animal. So Gesner, Rondeletius and Marcellus Vergilius on Dioscorides. Others imagine the land crocodile to be a huge beast, almost equal to the river crocodile. See Bellonius, and Cardano, book 9, On Subtlety.

But here let everyone believe what he will. I, however, am fully persuaded that the land crocodile among most of the ancients was neither the skink nor a huge beast, but that very animal which, as we have said, is called צב tsab by the Hebrews, ܚܪܕܘܢܐ [חרדונא] chardona by the Chaldeans and Syrians, and ضب [ḍabb] dhab and حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun by the Arabs . How it differs from the skink, these same writers teach us abundantly. That the matter is so will at once be noticed by anyone who compares the nature and powers of the two. 1. The blood of the dhab strengthens the sight. So in Pliny, book 28, chapter 8: the blood of the land crocodile, applied as an ointment, gives clearness of sight and remedies scars of the eyes. Hence Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 6: Εἰ δὲ τὸ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου (αἷμα) ποιητικὸν ὀξυδερκίας ἐστὶν, οὐ δε πειράζειν ἔμελλον, ἔχων ὀξυδερκῆ φάρμακα δόκιμα· [Ei de to tou chersaiou krokodeilou (haima) poiētikon oxyderkias estin, ou de peirazein emellon, echōn oxyderkē pharmaka dokima] Whether the blood of the land crocodile sharpens the sight I had no need to test, since I had other proven drugs for that purpose. 2. But the ضب [ḍabb] dhab has more potency in its dung, by which white spots and cataracts are removed from the eyes. See this very thing in Pliny concerning crocodilea, that is, the dung of the land crocodile! It lives only on land and among the most fragrant flowers. For this reason its intestines are diligently sought out, stuffed with a pleasant scent. They call it crocodilea; it is most useful for defects of the eyes, applied with leek juice, and against cataracts or dimness. Alexander of Tralles too, book 2, chapter 5, wants the dung of the land crocodile mixed into an eye-salve for scars of the eyes and for wiping away λευκώματα [leukōmata]. 3. The dung of the ضب [ḍabb] dhab gives brightness to the face, removing spots, warts, scurf and freckles. The same is the power of crocodilea; Pliny: Smeared on with Cyprus oil, it also removes blemishes growing on the face; with water, all diseases whose nature is to spread over the face, and it restores brightness. It removes freckles and pimples and all spots. Dioscorides, book 2, in the chapter On the dung of animals: Ἡ δὲ τοῦ χερσαίου κροκοδείλου ἄφοδος ἁρμώζει ἐπὶ τῶν γυναικῶν πρὸς εὔχροιαν, καὶ στίλβωσιν τῶν προσώπων. [Hē de tou chersaiou krokodeilou aphodos harmōzei epi tōn gynaikōn pros euchroian, kai stilbōsin tōn prosōpōn.] Galen, On Simples, book 10, chapter 29: Τὴν δὲ τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων τούτων, τῶν μικρῶν τε, καὶ χαμαιρεπῶν, κόπρον ἔντιμον αἱ τρυφῶσαι πεποιήκασι, γυναῖκες· αἷς οὐκ ἀρκεῖ τοῖς ἄλλοις φαρμάκοις, τοσούτοις οὖσι, λαμπρόν τε καὶ τετανὸν ἐργάζεσθαι τὸ περὶ τὸ πρόσωπον δέρμα. προστιθέασι δὲ αὐταῖς καὶ τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρον. [Tēn de tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn toutōn, tōn mikrōn te, kai chamairepōn, kopron entimon hai tryphōsai pepoiēkasi, gynaikes· hais ouk arkei tois allois pharmakois, tosoutois ousi, lampron te kai tetanon ergazesthai to peri to prosōpon derma. prostitheasi de autais kai tōn krokodeilōn kopron.] On this account Clement of Alexandria, in book 3 of the Paedagogus, declares the women of his time deserving to perish not once but three times. Τρὶς γὰρ, he says, οὐχ ἅπαξ ἀπολωλέναι δίκαιαι κροκοδείλων ἀποπάτοις χρώμεναι. [Tris gar … ouch hapax apolōlenai dikaiai krokodeilōn apopatois chrōmenai.] Note especially that the words of Dioscorides just cited are rendered thus in the Arabic version in Ibn al-Baitar: خرو الحردون يصلح للغمرة ولتحسين اللون وصقال الوجه والبشرة [khurū al-ḥardūn yaṣluḥu li-l-ghumra wa-li-taḥsīn al-lawn wa-ṣiqāl al-wajh wa-l-bashara] The dung of alchardaun is useful for a liniment by which brightness is given to women, and the colour becomes more beautiful, and the face and skin more shining. Thus in place of the land crocodile there stands chardaun. And that chardaun is the same as ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or צב tsab, has been abundantly proved above ). 4. The Arabs prescribe the dung of the dhab against alphoi, vitiligo and elephantiasis. So, on the authority of Paul of Aegina, ἡ τῶν χερσαίων κροκοδείλων κόπρος, ἀλφοὺς ἀποῤῥύπτει· [hē tōn chersaiōn krokodeilōn kopros, alphous aporrhyptei] And Aetius describes at length how the Indians use the land crocodile against elephantiasis.
