And Galen, in the place cited: Ἡ δέ γε τῶν κροκοδείλων κόπρος ὥσπερ τῶν προσώπων τὴν ἔφηλιν ἀφαιρεῖν πέφυκεν, οὕτω καὶ ἑλεῖν ἀλφοὺς, καὶ λειχῆνας. [Hē de ge tōn krokodeilōn kopros hōsper tōn prosōpōn tēn ephēlin aphairein pephyken, houtō kai helein alphous, kai leichēnas.] 5. Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)], chapter 446, says word for word about the dung of the stellio the same things that Dioscorides and Galen say about the dung of the land crocodile. But there stellio in Arabic is ضب [ḍabb] dhab, or حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun. So too the old translators of Galen and Dioscorides everywhere use the name stellio for the land crocodile. By the same error the late Erpenius renders حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun in Luqman's Fables as stellio. 6. In Avicenna the ضب [ḍabb] dhab is a rare animal, almost peculiar to Arabia. So is the land crocodile, whose dung in Galen is ἔντιμον [entimon]; in Aetius, hard to find; in Pliny, diligently sought out. But Dioscorides states that skinks are found in Mauretania, Egypt, India and Arabia; Solinus says they are very numerous around the Nile. 7. Finally, there is no reason why the skink should be called the land crocodile, since it is an animal just as ἀμφίβιον [amphibion] as the larger crocodile, and lives mostly in the water. Nor are the same powers attributed to the skink and the land crocodile: of the latter no one, as far as I know, has written what all report of the skink, that its use rouses torpor of the nerves and extinguishes the force of poison. So that from this too it appears that they are different animals.
For land crocodile the Vulgate translator has simply crocodile. So Horace in Epode 12,
— — — — — and her complexion painted with crocodile dung, — —

namely the land crocodile. The same must be supplied in Vegetius, when he wants crocodile dung to be applied to clean away the white defect in horses' eyes. Meanwhile this abbreviated expression has given many people occasion for error, who thought that the crocodile, the great beast, was meant. Among them is the poet Ovid, when he says in book 3 of the Art,
The pale woman tints her body with purple strokes; the darker one should flee to the aid of the Pharian fish:

that is, to the larger Egyptian crocodile, from whose dung he believed crocodilea was made, by which the face is given its sheen. Avicenna likewise errs when he writes that the dung of the تمساح [timsāḥ] thimsach, that is, of the larger crocodile, removes albugo. For this is proper to the smaller one. So too Radulphus, who holds that by the name crocodile in Leviticus public robbers are signified. And Cornelius a Lapide, who decides that the crocodile is unclean in the Law because it is amphibious, hard and rapacious. For it is evident that these things are said of the larger crocodile, whereas Moses dealt with the smaller. Nor, I think, are the more recent geographers of Eretz Yisrael, Breidenbach and Ziegler, less mistaken when they describe to us marshes near Caesarea and Ptolemais teeming with a multitude of larger crocodiles, because Pliny and Strabo mention a Town of the Crocodiles around these places. Certainly, if such monstrous beasts had infested the shores or lakes of the Phoenicians, there would not be so deep a silence about them in the records of the ancients. And at least from present-day pilgrimages to Jerusalem the matter would be thoroughly known. I therefore think that the Syrians named that town not after the larger crocodile, ܟܦܪ ܬܡܣܚ [כפר תמסח] Caphar-timsach, but after the smaller, ܟܦܪ ܨܒܐ [כפר צבא] Caphar-tsaba. Another town of this name lay on that very coast, not far from Caesarea. My witness is Josephus, who writes the old name of Antipatris sometimes Καφαρσαβᾶ [Kapharsaba] , sometimes Καφαρζαβά [Kapharzaba] , because the Greeks render the Hebrew Tsade either by σ or by ζ. And this very fact is evidence that the land crocodile is also found in Phoenicia.

I shall add here some names of the land crocodile that are less commonly known. One is from Hesychius: Κίκερος· ὁ χερσαῖος κροκόδειλος [Kikeros; ho chersaios krokodeilos]. But I would think this fits the skink rather. For κίκερος [kikeros] seems to be a name shortened from the Egyptian and Arabic سقنقور [saqanqūr] skankur, or skinkur, in Avicenna and others. Yet κίκερος [kikeros] also echoes the Coptic name ΧΑΡΟΥΚῚ, by which الضب [al-ḍabb], or the land crocodile, is called in the Lexicon. What if it was called κίκερος [kikeros] from its smallness, because it is far smaller than the other? For in Hesychius κύκερος [kykeros] is rendered τὸ ἐλάχιστον [to elachiston]. And the Hebrew רקיק rekik has the same meaning, if we believe Pomis and Boderianus [=Guy Le Fèvre de la Boderie], who explain it as קטן, small, as if from the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], where, however, I do not find it. Accordingly רקיק rekic seems to be wrongly written for דקיק dekik, Res for Daleth. Two barbarous names of the same little animal are found in the Arabic Pandectarius: Dhab (he says) is a certain animal like a large lizard, big-bellied; and in Latin it is called ballecola. It is a species of Arabian stellio. In Spanish it is called botrax. What ballecola is, I do not know. I think the word is corrupt, since elsewhere it is written balleccara. But botrax appears in Isidore among the species of lizard. There are several kinds of lizards, he says, such as the botrax, the salamander, the saura, the stellio. The botrax is so called because it has the appearance of a frog. Perhaps it is a skink-like frog. Hence the borax stone (read botrax), crapaudine, in the Pandectarius.

We hope we shall do our readers a welcome service if, to what Bochart has so far adduced from the Arabs on the lizard ضب [ḍabb], we add what experts in these matters among our own writers report about it. Among these let the first be LEO AFRICANUS, who in Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 52, p. [?], Zurich ed. 1559, has this: The Dub (otherwise Dab) is an animal living in the deserts; in form it resembles the stellio, though it is somewhat thicker; in length it fills a forearm, in breadth four fingers. It does not drink water, and if anyone pours water on them, it dies on the spot. It hatches eggs in the manner of the tortoise, and it lacks venom. They are caught by the Arabs in the deserts; indeed I myself cut the throat of one I had caught, yet it gives out little blood. It is eaten roasted, with the skin removed, and has the flavour and taste of a small frog. In speed it resembles the lizard, and if during the hunt it is driven into an underground hole, with its tail remaining outside, it cannot be pulled out by any force; but when the opening has been widened with mattocks, it is taken by the hunters. When, three days after being killed, it is put on the fire, it moves no differently than if it had been freshly killed. But far more accurately HASSELQUIST described this animal in his Itiner. p. 353, German trans., under the name Lacerta Aegyptia cauda verticillata squamis denticulatis, pedibus pentadactylis [Egyptian lizard with whorled tail, denticulate scales, five-toed feet]. — Head roughly triangular, elongated, continuous with the neck and a little higher than it. — Snout blunt, very short, scarcely distinguishable from the head, flattened above, uneven, ending behind at the sides in two prominences, one on each side. — Eyes behind the snout, at the sides of the head, nearer the upper part of the head than the throat. Pupil black. Iris dark. Two small pits, one on each side, oblong, immediately above the eyes, behind the prominences of the snout. The area of the eyes deeper [relative to the prominences of the head and snout], oblong, sprinkled with very small tubercles. The space between the eyes oblong, slightly raised, slightly narrowed. Crown in the middle of the head, behind the said space, a little higher than it, transversely oblong, very short. The space behind the crown [the base of the head] slightly sloping, rather broad towards the rear, flat. Two small pits, oblong, rather broad, one on each side of this space, set obliquely. The sides of the head protuberant, uneven. — Two hollows, one on each side, behind these protuberances, at the base of the sides of the head, crescent-shaped, fairly deep, smooth, even, with a membranous floor; ears? — Nostrils 2, one on each side, fairly large, round, surrounded by a membranous margin, near the tip of the snout, immediately above the upper jaw. — Jaws equal, rather broad. Lips mobile, covering the jaws; the upper one ends on each side at the edges in scaly tubercles, which surround its margin and imitate small teeth. Each jaw is composed of bones. These tubercles number 12 on each side, of which the 4 rear ones are pointed, the rest convex and very blunt. The tip of this lip smooth. The lower lip is covered at its margin with simple, oblong scales. — The small teeth are serrations of the jawbones; in the upper jaw about 43: three in front, and 20 at the sides on each side; of the front ones the middle is the broadest, slightly convex, with a semicircular margin, longer than all the others. The other two slightly pointed, slightly convex, shorter than the middle one, one on each side of it, set against its side. The front lateral ones, 8, very minute, close together, with a nearly linear tip; the rear ones, 12, larger, with distinct tips, somewhat pointed, the last ones blunter. Small teeth in the lower jaw about 20 on each side. The front ones very short, scarcely distinguishable; the rest very blunt, close together, longer. — Neck cylindrical, continuous with the head, of its thickness and twice as long, rather broad at the base. — Body strongly flattened on both sides, narrowed towards each end, more so behind but over a shorter space; less in front, but over a somewhat longer space; broad in the middle. — Sides convex, slightly protuberant, bellied. — Tail cylindrical, continuous with the body and of the same length, elongated, gradually narrower up to the tip, covered above with spiny scales arranged vertically, but below with oblong, smooth scales. The rings of scales are 22, the larger composed of about 10 scales, and successively of fewer. Each scale oblong, forming a parallelogram with truncated corners, ending behind in a spine which projects at an obtuse angle from the body of the scale. — Feet 4, two at each end of the body. The front ones immediately below the neck, at the sides of the body, cylindrical, shorter than the hind ones by about half; thighs short, not thicker than the shanks; shanks twice as long as the thighs, continuous with them and distinguished from them only by the joint. The hind ones immediately above the tail, at the sides of the head, almost twice as long as the front ones. Thighs as long as the shanks, much thicker than them, slightly narrower below. Shanks slightly compressed in the lower half, cylindrical in the upper. Toes of each foot 5, a little smaller on the front feet, on all compressed, scaly, unequal; the two outer ones shorter than the rest, equal; of the rest, the one next to the inner is a little longer than it, the one following it longer, and the one after that, the fourth from the inner, the longest of all. Lobes of the feet several. Claws end all the toes, compressed, sloping, pointed, slightly hooked. — Scales cover the head, feet and whole body: on the head hexagonal and octagonal, mixed, large, raised, smooth; on the feet rhomboidal and roundish, the front ones flat, smooth; the hind ones in some cases furnished with a pointed spine rising from their middle; on the toes oblong, convex, blunt at the tip, imbricate, arranged in three lines on each toe. Scales of the back slightly imbricate, very minute, roundish. A line runs through the middle of the whole back, composed of indistinct scales, yet perceptible to the eye. Scales of the abdomen four-sided, imbricate, smooth, three times as long as the dorsal ones, more raised. — Tubercles, scaly, fragile, raised, roundish, are seen 1) scattered here and there over the upper part of the head and neck; 2) over the sides of the head, especially towards the tail, where some are irregularly scattered. 3) A line of these tubercles runs underneath along the middle of the thighs; these are a little larger, whitish, marked with a dark dot in the middle. — Cuticle thin, easily stripped off. — Colour: head, back and feet dark. Abdomen, toes and tail whitish-brown. Throat variegated with dark and yellowish. — Total length from the tip of the snout to the tip of the tail 3¼ spans. Of the head with snout 2 inches. Of the neck 3 inches. Of the body 1 span 2 inches. Of the tail 1 span 2 inches. — Breadth of the head above the crown and of the neck 1½ inches. Of the body near the neck 1 palm, near the tail 2 inches. Of the body near the middle 1½ palms. — Height of the front foot 1 palm 1 inch, of the hind 2 palms. Thickness of the neck and head 5 inches. Of the snout 3 inches. Of the tail at the base 5 inches, near the middle 4 inches, towards the end 1 inch. At the tip of the smallest toe. Of the front shanks and thighs 3 inches, of the hind thighs 4½ inches. Of the hind shanks 3 inches. — Breadth of the lobes of the foot 1 inch. — Length of the smallest toe 2½ inches. — Habitat: Egypt, plain and mountainous. So far Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)]. To be added is FORSKAL in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: „Lacerta Aegyptia. To the Arabs Dabb. Thighs terete, without warts. Tail whorled, not long. Scales spreading, subconical, mucronate. Body naked, wrinkled.“

It is the Lacerta Stellio of Hasselquist (Travels p. 351), who writes the Arabic name as Hardun. Snout very short, blunt, sloping. Jaws equal. — Nostrils in front of the eyes, at the sides of the head, near the snout, round. — Eyes at the sides of the head, in the middle. Orbit protruding at its upper margin, keeled. Brows crenate-tuberculate, pupil small, black, eyelids mobile, smooth. Crown depressed, scaly, slightly concave, raised beside the eyes. — Neck folded and wrinkled, as are the sides of the head behind the eyes. Throat with a pouch; the pouch longitudinal, compressed, keeled. Ear area hollowed out. Body depressed, ovate; sides of the abdomen protruding. Back furrowed, scaly, the scales ending in a point. Three lines of spiny tubercles on each side of the abdomen, each tubercle composed of about 7 raised, prickly scales. — Tail cylindrical, longer than the body, covered with spiny-angular scales in whorls. — Loins and legs scaly-spiny. Toes 5 on each foot, the middle ones longer. Claws curved. — Colour dusky with black and whitish spots, but it sometimes also takes on bright greenish spots and admits them on the sides of the abdomen and head, by which it comes somewhat close to the nature of the chameleon, which is thus not the only one to enjoy this faculty of changing colours. — Length of body under a span; of tail 1 span. — Habitat: ruins of Natolia, Syria and Eretz Yisrael.

Lacerta Nilotica cauda tereti longa, corpore toto glabro, squamis angulo obtuso notatis of Hasselquist, p. 361–363. "Habitat: the marshy places of Egypt near the Nile. — It is a fable of the Egyptians that this animal is generated from crocodile eggs laid on land, whereas from those laid in water come crocodiles." Hasselquist, ibid.

The Indian skink of the Arabs is without doubt the Lacerta Stincus cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus pentadactylis; digitis lobato-squamosis, squamis laevibus nitidis of Hasselquist, p. 359. "It is an error," he says on p. 361, "of almost all authors that they have believed the sea skink to be a fish."
Whoever wants more should consult ABDOLLATIF, Compendium Memorabilium Aegypti, book 1, Chapter 3, p. 42 ff.
It only swells up when it is provoked, according to Hasselquist, who carefully observed this animal himself and describes it accurately in his Travels p. 348–351, German trans.
Pliny, book 28, ch. 8, and book 8, ch. 33.
It is proved that אנקה anaka of Lev 11:30 is a kind of stellio, so called from its harsh shrill cry.

Next, in Lev 11:30, follow five species of creeping things whose names are not easy to ex- plain, since they are found nowhere else. They are אנקה anaka, כח coach, לטאה letaa, חמט chomet, תנשמת thinsemeth. Of these, אנקה anaka is for the Greeks and for Jerome μυγάλη [mygalē] mygale, that is, the mus araneus [shrew]. They hold that it is called Μυγάλην [Mygalēn] because it is born ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς [ek myos kai galēs], from a mouse and a weasel. The scholiast on Nicander says: Ἀμύντας δή φησι τὴν μυγάλην ἐκ μύος καὶ γαλῆς γίνεσθαι [Amyntas dē phēsi tēn mygalēn ek myos kai galēs ginesthai]. This is utterly absurd, since the weasel is much larger than the mouse and as hostile to it as the cat, as we observed above . That a weasel should mate with a mouse and a shrew be born of it is therefore wholly improbable. Aetius puts it better in the Tetrabiblos, book 4, sermon 1, chapter 14: The shrew is like the weasel in colour, but like the mouse in size; hence it also obtained the name mygale. Yet the shrew has the appearance of a mouse rather than its size, for it is altogether smaller than a mouse. The Romans seem to call it mus araneus [spider mouse] from its venom, which it shares with the spider. And in Hebrew it has been thought to be called אנקה anaka by reason of its voice, which is extremely shrill, so that it can be taken for a groan and a wail; for otherwise אנקה anaka means groaning or outcry to the Hebrews. If Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] understood the same, then in his Paraphrase, instead of ילא jala (the word by which אנקה anaka is rendered there), one must read פלא pala, or phala. For the Arabs call the shrew so. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], book 4, Fen 6, tract. 3, last chapter, in the title: فصل في عضة موغالي وهو الغلا [faṣl fī ʿaḍḍat mūghālī wa-huwa al-ghalā] Chapter on the bite of the mygale, which (for the Arabs) is alphala. In the Latin version one reads alcale, which would be الغلا [al-ghalā]. I should think that half-learned men changed one or the other into ילא jala. Under this name two very different animals occur in the Talmudic books, namely the leech and the hedgehog. But neither of them has a place here. For neither is called אנקה anaka in Hebrew; rather the hedgehog is called קפוד kippod, and the leech עלוקה aluka, or rather עלקה alka. Moreover, the subject here is those creeping things that creep upon the earth, and the leech is not of that number. So much for the first and most ancient interpretation of the word אנקה anaka.

The second is that of Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and of the Jerusalem Targum: the one of them has here מינקת חויא, and the other פלית חויא, or פיילת חויא. So it should be read, not חיוא, in the Lexicon of Baal-Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome]. The lexicographers understand neither. For it is beside the point that they take פליית here for a locust, as in פליא ביארי in chapter 9 of the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath. For פליא ביארי is one thing, פליית חויא another. Namely, the very thing that the Arabs call فالية الافاعي [fāliyat al-afāʿī] phaliath alaphai, that is, the searcher of serpents, or of vipers (they taught us above that this name is given to a painted kind of beetle which usually lives with scorpions and serpents in the lair of the land crocodile), that very thing, I say, is the Chaldee פליית חויא. For to them חויא is serpent, and פליית paljath, or phaljath, is plainly derived from the Arabic فالية [fāliya] phaliath, which we render searcher, because فلي [falā] phala means to search. Thus فلي الراس [falā al-raʾs] he searched the head, to look for lice in it; فلي الشعر [falā al-shiʿr] he searched the poem, that is, he explored and examined it in order to penetrate the poet's mind. And this kind of beetle is rightly said to search the serpents, since it lives continually with them in the same lair, and so constantly accompanies the serpents, whether coming or going, in such a way that by its arrival or its departure it signals whether they are near or away. Hence the proverb current among the Arabs: اتكلم فالية الافاعي [a-takallama fāliyat al-afāʿī] Have you spoken to the phaliath alaphai, the searcher of serpents? It is used لاول شر ينتظر بعده شر منه [li-awwal sharr yuntaẓar baʿdahu sharr minhu] of a first evil after which another is expected to arise from it. But since the verb فلي [falā] phala means not only to search but also to nourish and to rear, Jonathan has, instead of פליית חויא, מינקת חויא, i.e. the nurse of the serpent. Further, why the two Chaldee translators wished this kind of beetle to be designated by the word אנקה anaka, I see no reason except the very order of the words. Namely, as the word צב tsab signifies the land crocodile, as we have proved at length , so the following אנקה anaka seemed to signify פליית חויא, that is, the searcher of the serpent, which is the constant companion of the land crocodile and usually lives in the same lair with it. But this reason, such as it is, carries little weight with me, as does the version itself, which seems to rest on it. Something I had almost omitted: for some of the Arabs these little creatures are not beetles but بنات وردان [banāt wardān] benath vvardan, which is what Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] calls the σίλφας [silphas] of Dioscorides, or blattae [cockroaches].

In third place I count those for whom אנקה anaka is a kind of lizard; they are neither few nor to be despised. For in the Syriac we read ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, which the most learned of the Maronites, the late Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)] (ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs]), rendered lacerta [lizard]. In the Samaritan it is [?] semamitha, that is, stellio, as will become clear in its proper place. In Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] it is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, that is, a species of lizard which the barbarous writers call guaril. In the Arabic edition published at Paris it is الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which is the same thing . For by what chance I do not know, in Avicenna and others الورك [al-warak] alvvarco is written far more often, although the true spelling is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo. This is taught by all the Arabic lexicographers, and the barbarous name guaril is derived from it. Not to mention the critical observation which is found in Damiri, in the chapter ورل [waral] Guaril: لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة [lā taltaqī al-rāʾ maʿa al-lām illā fī arbaʿ mawāḍiʿ al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥayawān al-madhkūr wa-aral ism jabal wa-al-ghurla wa-hiya al-qulfa wa-ḥaral wa-huwa ḍarb min al-ḥijāra]. Re does not meet with Lam (that is, R with L) except in four places. 1. In alvvarlo, the name of the animal discussed above. 2. In Aral, the name of a mountain discussed above. 3. In alghorla, which means foreskin (like the Hebrew ערלה). 4. In charal, which is a kind of stone. These, then, are the four ancient versions, the Syriac, the Samaritan and the two Arabic, for which anaka is a species of lizard. I have weighty reasons for casting my vote with them. 1. צב tsab, that is, the land crocodile, had preceded, and four other species of lizards are added immediately afterwards , as will be evident from what follows. Accordingly anaka seems to belong to the same genus. For the mygale, or any other animal, would be inserted rather inappropriately among so many species of lizards. 2. The Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, plainly arose from the Hebrew אנקה anaka. For these two words (apart from the ending, which is Hebrew in the one and Syriac in the other) differ in no respect, except that the Syrians changed the Hebrew NUN into MEM, a change than which nothing is more frequent in those languages. Thus among the Chaldeans or Syrians strong is ܚܣܝܢ [חסין] chasin and ܚܣܝܡ [חסים] chasim; reason, ܛܥܢܐ [טענא] taana and ܛܥܡܐ [טעמא] taama; nymph, ܢܝܢܦܐ [נינפא] ninphe and ܢܝܡܦܐ [נימפא] nimphe; cudgel, ܩܘܪܢܣܐ [קורנסא] kurnesa and ܩܘܪܡܙܐ [קורמזא] kurmeza; the terebinth, or the tree that bears the pistachio, ܒܘܛܡܐ [בוטמא] butem, as in Hebrew בוטן boten. And in Arabic thumb is ابهام [ibhām] ibham for the Hebrew בהן bohen; likewise to grow fat, دسم [dasama] dasama, for the Hebrew דשן dasen; and to sing, رنم [ranima] ranima, for the Hebrew רנן ranan. In Ethiopic ዘመወ፡ [zamawa] zamavva, he committed fornication, for the Hebrew זנה zana; እድሜ፡ [ʾədəmē] edem, time, for the Chaldee עדן iddan; አደመ፡ [ʾadama] adam, pleasant, sweet, from the Hebrew עדן adan, to take delight. Of the same kind is the Egyptian ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ [metōpon], a kind of ointment, from the Hebrew נטף nataph or the Chaldee נטופא netopha; and ΜΕΙΣΙ [meisi], serpent, from the Hebrew נחש naas. So too the Egyptian city of Memphis is called by the Prophets now נוף Noph, now מוף Moph. By a like example the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha is here derived from the Hebrew אנקה anaka, with N and M interchanged. Therefore, whatever the Syriac amaktha may be, it is highly probable that the Hebrew anaka is the very same. Now it is certain that ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] is a kind of lizard, and indeed the stellio, Prov. XXX, 28, where it stands in the Syriac Paraphrase for the Hebrew שממית semamith; just as in the Chaldee, by metathesis (μετάθεσιν [metathesin]) of the letters, אקמתא akmetha, which is the same. Therefore, as the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, and the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha is the stellio, so also is the Hebrew אנקה anaka. Hence it is that the Samaritan too renders אנקה anaka by * [?] semamitha, that is, stellio; and both Arabic versions by الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, a kind of lizard close to the stellio, which many therefore take for the stellio, because it is similar in form. Accordingly Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says of it: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sawām abraṣ] It is a large one, of the same form as the guezga and savvamabras, that is, as the smaller and larger stellios. This is taken from Avicenna. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh] Alvvarlo (commonly guaril), an animal like the dhab (or land crocodile). And it is the large one among those which have the form of the guezga, or stellio. 3. In Hebrew אנקה anaka means a groan and a shrill cry, such as is uttered in great mourning. If anyone should deny that the stellio can be so called, as though it were a mute animal, he will be refuted by these words of Pliny on the stellio of Greece, book 29, chapter 4: The Greeks call it colotes, and ascalabotes, and galeotes. It does not occur in Italy. For it is covered with spots, has a harsh shriek, and feeds on *. All of which is foreign to our stellios. Note: a harsh shriek. In Greek you would say τρισμοῦ τραχέος [trismou tracheos], whence it is rightly called אנקה anaka. And as among the Hebrews a masculine plural is often formed from a feminine singular, as יעלים from יעלה, and יענים from יענה, so from אנקה anaka the plural could be אנקים. And in the second Targum of Esther, chapter 1, verse 2, where among the various animals which each utter their own cry before Solomon are described אנקין בכיין anakin weeping, or wailing, this should perhaps be understood not (as it is commonly taken) of the screaming of eagles, but of the cry and harsh shriek of stellios, which the very word אנקה anaka attests approaches wailing. And for this very reason the Arabs, since they knew at least this much, that the anaka is a kind of lizard, rendered it الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, which itself also has a voice, though perhaps less resonant. Hence Alcamus: ضغث الورل صوت [ḍaghatha al-waral ṣawt] Dhagathsa alvvarlo, that is, it cried out. This those of our scholars who have published Arabic lexicons did not sufficiently understand. For one rendered it The thigh made a cracking noise; another, The hip sounded. For they read الورك [al-warak] alvvarco, which means ירך, i.e. hip. But they ought to have remembered that this very الورك [al-warak] occurs everywhere for الورل [al-waral], as we noted above . Not to mention that in the copy of Alcamus which I used, الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo is quite correctly written. Therefore, what has hitherto escaped our scholars, let this stand as established: that among the lizards some are vocal, and among them is the stellio, which shrieks very shrilly. But we shall say more about the stellio in the explanation of the word שממית semamith.

To the three interpretations of this word that we have adduced, three others may be added, in which not even a drop of good sense appears. The first is that of the Arabic paraphrasts, whom I have read in manuscript, where אנקה anaka is عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, that is, aranea [spider]. This aranea perhaps arose from the mygale of the Greeks and of Jerome, or mus araneus [shrew-mouse]: as though the shrew-mouse were the same as the spider, which would be the height of ignorance; or from the Syriac ܐܡܟܬܐ [אמכתא] amkatha, since most of the Hebrews take the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, which is synonymous with it, for the spider. But for the Hebrews the spider is not אנקה anaka but עכביש accabis. Nor is it at all likely that the Prophet mentions the spider here among the species of lizards.

The second interpretation is that of R. Mardochai in the Hebrew Concordance, where he defines this animal as שרץ העוף, a flying creeping thing, although Moses expressly places it among the creeping things that creep upon the earth, Lev 11:29–30.

The third is that of R. Solomon, who rendered it with the French word בברא bieure, that is, fiber or castor [beaver], as it is in the Pomarium: an animal so amphibious that it is rather aquatic. For it has the tail of a fish, and feet fitted for swimming rather than for walking, and it lives on the banks of rivers, from which it seeks its food. Dioscorides: Ζῶόν ἐστιν ἀμφίβιον, τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν ὕδασι σὺν ἰχθύσι, καὶ καρκίνοις τρεφόμενον [Zōon estin amphibion, to pleiston en hydasi syn ichthysi, kai karkinois trephomenon]; It is an amphibious animal, mostly feeding in the waters on fish and crabs. Alkazuini: القندر بري بحري يكون في الانهار العظيمة من بلاد ايسو يتخذ في البر بيتا الي جانب النهر [al-qundur barrī baḥrī yakūn fī al-anhār al-ʿaẓīma min bilād Īsū yattakhidh fī al-barr baytan ilā jānib al-nahr] Alkundur (that is, the beaver) is an amphibious animal. It is found in the great rivers of the region of Aisu, and chooses a home for itself on the river bank. Accordingly Varro and Festus hold that it is called fiber from the outermost edges of rivers. For the ancients said fibrum for extremum [outermost]. Hence the fibrae [lobes] of the liver and the fimbriae [fringes] of garments were so named. Who then would believe that Moses listed such an animal among the creeping things of the earth? Especially since the proportion is very unequal. For here Moses calls moles, mice and kinds of lizards creeping things. Moreover, there is no reason why the beaver should be called אנקה anaka from crying and wailing, since the voice of the beaver has nothing remarkable about it, so far as I know. But the first author of this opinion, whoever he was, seems to have confused castores and castorides: these are said to be marine animals of so horrible a wailing that whoever hears it soon dies. Aelian, History, book 9, chapter 50: Αἱ καστορίδες ζῶόν εἰσι θαλάττιον, καὶ ἐπὶ ταῖς ἀκταῖς, καὶ ταῖς πέτραις ταῖς προβεβλημέναις, ἀπόΦημόν τινα κωκυτὸν μεθιᾶσι, καὶ ὠρύονται βαρύτατα. Τούτου τοίνυν τοῦ ἤχου ὅστις ἂν ὑπακούσῃ, ἄφυκτα οἵ ἐστι, καὶ οὐ μετὰ μικρὸν ἀποθνήσκει [Hai kastorides zōon eisi thalattion, kai epi tais aktais, kai tais petrais tais probeblēmenais, apophēmon tina kōkyton methiasi, kai ōryontai barytata. Toutou toinyn tou ēchou hostis an hypakousē, aphykta hoi esti, kai ou meta mikron apothnēskei]; The castorides, a marine animal, utter an ill-omened wail on the shores and the jutting rocks, and roar most heavily. So that whoever hears their cry cannot escape departing from life shortly afterwards. Oppian, Halieutica, book 1, v. 398 ff.

Καστορίδες τ᾽ ὀλοαὶ δυσπενθέες, αἵ τ᾽ ἀλεγεινὴν Ὅσσαν ἐπὶ κροκαλοίσιον ἀπαίσιον ὠρύονται Ἀνδράσιν· ὃς δέ κε γῆρυν ἐν οὔασιν ἀλγινόεσσαν Δέξηται, στυγερῆς τ᾽ ἐνοπῆς κωκυτὸν ἀκούσῃ, Οὐ τηλοῦ θανάτοιο τάχ᾽ ἔσσεται· ἀλλὰ οἱ ἄτην Καὶ μόρον αἰνοτάτη κείνη μαντεύεται αὐδή. [Kastorides t᾽ oloai dyspenthees, hai t᾽ alegeinēn Ossan epi krokaloision apaision ōryontai Andrasin; hos de ke gēryn en ousin alginoessan Dexētai, stygerēs t᾽ enopēs kōkyton akousē, Ou tēlou thanatoio tach᾽ essetai; alla hoi atēn Kai moron ainotatē keinē manteuetai audē.]

And the deadly castorides of grievous mourning, which on the shores utter a sad voice, ill-omened for men. Whoever receives the doleful cry in his ears and hears the wailing of the plaintive voice will not be far from death: that most grievous voice foretells ruin and death for him. Tzetzes, Chiliad 6, History 47:
Ἡ καστορὶς δ᾽ ὠρύεται, ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἀκούσῃ ταύτης Χρόνῳ βραχεῖ παρέρχεται τοῦ ταλαιπώρου βίου· [Hē kastoris d᾽ ōryetai, hos d᾽ an akousē tautēs Chronō brachei parerchetai tou talaipōrou biou;]

And the castoris roars, and whoever hears it will shortly depart from this wretched life. This is what I find about the wailing and roaring of the castorides. But those are mistaken who take the castoris for the fiber or castor [beaver], among them the most learned Rittershusius in his Notes on Oppian. For the castor is one thing, the castoris another. The former is an amphibious quadruped, the latter is a fish. Tzetzes, in the place cited above:
Πάντες δ᾽ ἰχθύες ἄφωνοι, πλὴν σκάρου, καὶ καστορίδος· [Pantes d᾽ ichthyes aphōnoi, plēn skarou, kai kastoridos;]

But all fishes are mute, except the scarus and the castoris. The former is described on the banks of rivers, the latter around the shores of the sea, and it is counted by Oppian among those sea monsters that sometimes come out of the sea onto dry land; whereas the beaver, on the contrary, goes from land into rivers. Finally, the beaver is a real animal; the castoris is fabulous, as I at least think, since I know of no animal in the sea to which this description fits.

Among the more recent writers, אנקה anaka is, for Pagnino, who followed the Greeks and Jerome, the mygale; for Deodati the mus araneus [shrew-mouse]; for Münster and the Genevans the ericius [hedgehog], as if on the authority of Onkelos, whose Paraphrase is corrupt here; for Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] the attelabus, as if on the authority of the Jerusalem translator, whom they had not sufficiently understood; for Castellio the fiber [beaver], on the authority of Rabbi Solomon; for Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] the viverra [ferret], as if from the same source. But Solomon's ב״ברא should not have been read as viverra, since viverra is a Roman word, whereas ב״ברא is purely French. For Rabbi Solomon was a Frenchman, and he interprets Hebrew words only by French ones. Yet from the same source the English too have here a ferret, that is, furo, an animal similar to the viverra. But it is no wonder that so many translators went astray, since they had seen neither the Syriac nor the Samaritan paraphrase, nor those two Arabic ones, from which we have extracted the true meaning of the word אנקה anaka.
It is proved that כח coach is the ورل [waral] guaril, the largest and strongest of the lizards in Arabia.

Next comes כח coach, which almost all the ancients, as many as there are, place in the lizard family. The Greeks and Jerome render it chameleon. Both printed Arabic versions have حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, that is, the land crocodile, or a species of it. So also R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] and David Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. R. Solomon has lizard. The Chaldee versions and the Samaritan keep the Hebrew word, with only the ending changed. But the Syriac, by a great error, has ܚܘܠܕܐ [חולדא] chulda here, and the manuscript Arabic versions الخلد [al-khuld] alchuld, that is, mole. Among the more recent translators, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Münster, Castellio, the English and the Italians render it chameleon; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] and Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] lizard; Petrus Robertus tortoise; Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] slug; certain Jews (in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]) squirrel; the Genevans crocodile. We side with those who understand a kind of lizard, because lizards are the subject here, and this is how most of the ancients take it, and the most ancient of them. Once this is granted, it will be easy to establish that the Hebrew name כח coach signifies الورل [al-waral], that is, the guaril of the Arabs, as the barbarous writers call it. This is clear from the name itself, which is taken from strength. For in more than a hundred other passages of Scripture כח coach is used for strength. And in Arabic كوح [kawḥ], with the same letters, means to be superior in a fight. It is therefore entirely fitting that, within the lizard family, the one called כח coach should be the one that is most powerful in strength and surpasses the rest in fighting. And that is undoubtedly الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or guaril, whose strength stands out above all in fighting against serpents and the land crocodile. Lest anyone call this into doubt, here are the most explicit testimonies of the Arabic writers on the matter! Alkazuini: هو عدو للضب وللحية يدخل بيتها وياكلها وليس شي من الحيوان اقوي علي قتل الحيات منه ولا يحتفر لنفسه بل يغتصب كل شي بيته لان اي بيت دخله هرب ساكنه وبغتصب بيت الحية كما يغتصب الحية بيت ساير الاجناس [huwa ʿaduww li-l-ḍabb wa-li-l-ḥayya yadkhulu baytahā wa-yaʾkuluhā wa-laysa shayʾ min al-ḥayawān aqwā ʿalā qatl al-ḥayyāt minhu wa-lā yaḥtafiru li-nafsihi bal yaghtaṣibu kull shayʾ baytahu li-anna ayy bayt dakhalahu haraba sākinuhu wa-byaghtaṣibu bayt al-ḥayya kamā yaghtaṣibu al-ḥayya bayt sāyir al-ajnās] It is hostile to the land crocodile and to the serpent, whose hiding place it enters in order to devour it. And no animal is stronger than it at killing serpents. Nor does it dig a hiding place for itself, but it invades the hiding places of all others. For whatever hiding place it approaches, its occupant takes flight. Indeed, it invades the serpent's den, just as the serpent invades the dens of other kinds (I would prefer الاحناش ساير [sāyir al-aḥnāsh], of other reptiles). Algiahid on the same animal: وهو يقوي علي الحيات وياكلها اكلا ذريعا ويخرجها من حجرها ويسكن فيه فهو اظلم من ظالم [wa-huwa yaqwā ʿalā al-ḥayyāt wa-yaʾkuluhā aklan dharīʿan wa-yukhrijuhā min juḥrihā wa-yaskunu fīhi fa-huwa aẓlam min ẓālim] It prevails over serpents and eats them greedily, and drives them out of their hiding places in order to occupy them, and it is more violent than the violent. Abdollatif, followed by Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وبينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحيه وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفسه ولا يحفر حجرا بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا ويستولي عليه وانه كان اكثر براثن منه واقوي لكن الظلم يمنعه ولهذا يضرب به المثل في الظلم ويكفي في ظلمه انه يغصب الحية حجرها ويبلعها وربما قتل فوجد في بطنه الحية العظيمة وهو لا يتبلعها حتي يشدخ راسها [wa-baynahu wa-bayna al-ḍabb ʿadāwa fa-yaghlibu al-waral al-ḍabb wa-yaqtuluhu lākinnahu lā yaʾkuluhu kamā yafʿalu bi-l-ḥayya wa-huwa lā yattakhidhu baytan li-nafsihi wa-lā yaḥfiru juḥran bal yukhriju al-ḍabb min juḥrihi ṣāriʿan wa-yastawlī ʿalayhi wa-innahu kāna akthar barāthin minhu wa-aqwā lākin al-ẓulm yamnaʿuhu wa-li-hādhā yuḍrabu bihi al-mathal fī al-ẓulm wa-yakfī fī ẓulmihi annahu yaghṣibu al-ḥayya juḥrahā wa-yablaʿuhā wa-rubbamā qutila fa-wujida fī baṭnihi al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma wa-huwa lā yatabalaʿuhā ḥattā yashdakha raʾsahā] Between it and the τὸν [ton] dhab (or land crocodile) there is fierce enmity. But the guaril is superior and kills it. Yet it does not eat it, as it does with serpents. Nor does it choose a dwelling for itself or dig a hiding place. Rather, it thrusts the land crocodile out of its own home by wrestling, and prevails over it. Although the crocodile excels in the strength of its claws, this one is superior in violence. Hence its violence has become proverbial. It is so great in it that it suffices to thrust a serpent out of its den and devour it. Accordingly, a large serpent is sometimes found in the belly of one that has been killed; it does not swallow it without first crushing its head. There are many proverbs about it among the Arabs, of which these are worth noting: اجبر من الورل [ajbar min al-waral] Fiercer (or prouder) than the τῷ [tō] guaril. And اظلم من الورل [aẓlam min al-waral] More unjust (or more violent) than the τῷ [tō] guaril, to which Abdollatif alluded above. And اسرع من تلظم الورل [asraʿ min talaẓẓum al-waral] Quicker than the guaril turns food over in its mouth. To this belongs what Algiahid writes, that it eats the serpent greedily, or اكلا نريعا [aklan narīʿan], that is, literally, with a swift and headlong eating . From this description it appears that the name כח coach, taken from strength, suits this lizard exceedingly well .

If anyone wishes to know more about this kind of lizard, unknown in these lands, Ibno-saida describes it: دابة علي خلق الضب الا انه اعظم منه [dābba ʿalā khalq al-ḍabb illā annahu aʿẓam minhu] an animal of the nature of the dhab, except that it is larger. And Abdollatif: فاما الورل وهو الحردون [fa-ammā al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥardūn] Guaril is indeed the same as chardaun. But on the contrary Algiahid, in Damir, reports ان الحردون غير الورل ووصفه دابة تكون غالبا بارض مصر موشاة بالوان كثير ولها كف ككف الانسان مقسومة اصابعها الي الانامل [anna al-ḥardūn ghayr al-waral wa-waṣafahu dābba takūn ghāliban bi-arḍ Miṣr muwashshāh bi-alwān kathīr wa-lahā kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūma aṣābiʿuhā ilā al-anāmil] that chardaun is different from guaril; he describes it as an animal common in Egypt, marked with many colours, having hands like those of a man, and fingers divided into joints. And Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسام ابرص الطويل الذنب الصغير الراس وهو سريع السير خفيف الحركة [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sāmm abraṣ al-ṭawīl al-dhanab al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs wa-huwa sarīʿ al-sayr khafīf al-ḥaraka] It is the largest of the lizards that have the form of the guezga and the sam-mabras (these are species of stellio, the former smaller, the latter larger), with a long tail, a small head, a swift gait and nimble movement. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] too, after comparing it with the stellios and describing its tail and head in the same way as Alkazuinius, says: وهو غير الضب والضب لا يكون او قل ما يكون الا في البادية وراسه وبدنه وذنبه خالف الورل وربما قاربة في طبايعه [wa-huwa ghayr al-ḍabb wa-al-ḍabb lā yakūn aw qall mā yakūn illā fī al-bādiya wa-raʾsuhu wa-badanuhu wa-dhanabuhu khālaf al-waral wa-rubbamā qārabahu fī ṭabāʾiʿihi] And it is different from the dhab (or land crocodile).

For the dhab is never, or very rarely, found anywhere but in the desert. And in head, body and tail it differs from the guaril. Yet it is close to it in nature. Hence Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ طويل الذنب صغير الراس [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh ṭawīl al-dhanab ṣaghīr al-raʾs] Guaril is an animal like the dhab, large among those which have the form of the guezga, with a long tail and a small head. Some think it is born from the seed of the crocodile, like the skink; but Damir refutes them, both because they differ much in skin and hide, and because their size is very unequal: والورل لا يزيد قدره علي ذراعين او ذراع ونصف والتمساح عشرة اذرع واكثر [wa-al-waral lā yazīd qadruhu ʿalā dhirāʿayn aw dhirāʿ wa-niṣf wa-al-timsāḥ ʿashara adhruʿ wa-akthar] For the guaril does not grow beyond two cubits, or one and a half, whereas the crocodile grows beyond ten cubits and more. The same animal is described as very lustful. Abdollatif: فليس في الحيوان اكثر سفاد منه [fa-laysa fī al-ḥayawān akthar sifādan minhu] There is no animal that copulates more often. And, if Alcamus is to be believed, شحمه يعظم الذكر دلكا [shaḥmuhu yuʿaẓẓim al-dhakar dalkan]. Let him understand this who can. He says the same about eating its flesh: لحمه حار جدا يسمن بقوة [laḥmuhu ḥārr jiddan yusamminu bi-quwwa] Its flesh is very hot and fattens greatly. And Alkazuinius: لحمه وشحمه سمن طبقات الناس [laḥmuhu wa-shaḥmuhu samman ṭabaqāt al-nās] Its flesh and fat fatten women above all. So also Avicenna and Damir. They add that the same flesh has a power by which it draws out of the body السلي والشوك [al-salā wa-al-shawk] splinters and thorns; that its hairs, tied to a woman's arm, prevent conception; that numb limbs are revived if smeared with the ash of its burnt skin mixed with the dregs of oil; that its dung removes white spots of the eye, freckles and warts; and finally that its blood strengthens and sharpens the sight. They write the same of the land crocodile.

It may be asked whether this lizard is the same as the green lizard, which many things will seem to suggest. 1. The green lizard is the largest of those found among us. Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia] in the Dialogue On Friendship: Italy has large lizards, and green ones. Gesner: They are almost twice as large as common lizards. 2. Green lizards are ὀφιομάχοι [ophiomachoi]. Erasmus in the same place: This animal is by nature both friendly to man and hostile to serpents. And a little later: One day I saw a very large and wonderfully green one fighting with a serpent at the mouth of a hole. At first we wondered what was going on, for the serpent was not visible to us. An Italian told us that the enemy was in the cave. A little later the lizard came to us, as if showing its wounds and begging for a remedy, etc. The serpent had gnawed away almost the whole of one side and had turned it from green to red. So what we read in Pliny, that lizards fight with serpents, should be referred to these lizards. Hence the more recent writers gave it the name ὀφιονίκος [ophionikos].

The Pandectarius: OFIONICOS in Greek, that is, lizard. 3. Just as the Arabs write that they grow fat by eating the guaril, so Pliny and Marcellus report that the green lizard is most useful for consumptives and benefits them incredibly. 4. The dung of both, smeared on the face, is said to remove blemishes. Yet colour distinguishes the guaril from the green lizard, for Algiahid describes it as variegated. Moreover the guaril, as the Arabs describe it, seems far to surpass the green lizard in strength and fierceness of spirit. I therefore think that the guaril is a kind of lizard peculiar to Arabia, and that the green lizard is so similar to it that it is
Next to it, but next by a long interval.

In Leo Africanus, Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 53, this lizard is called Guaral. An animal, he says, similar to the aforementioned [Dub, ضبّ [ḍabb]] but somewhat larger; it likewise carries venom in its head and tail, and when these parts have been cut off the Arabs are accustomed to eat it; otherwise it is ugly and of a foul colour. But ورل [waral] must not be confused with وَرَنٌ [waranun], which in Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] is rendered a species of reptile, but which, on Forskål's testimony, is the name of the Nile lizard; see Descriptiones Animalium, quae in itinere Orientali observavit Petrus Forskal, p. 13.

But Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] rightly points out in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1221, that several further etymologies present themselves, not considered by Bochart, to which the name of that lizard could be referred. We have already noted quite often that this method, fishing out the meanings of the names that denote animals by etymologies alone, is wholly uncertain. The name כח seems to be one of those whose meaning we must utterly despair of determining, since we lack the aid both of the other dialects and of passages from which the nature and character of this animal might be known well enough for anything certain to be established about it.
It is proved that the word לטאה letaa signifies a lizard, similar to the stellio, extremely venomous and clinging to the ground, which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] vvachara.

Some of the more recent writers try to interpret the Hebrew לטאה letaa from the Greek language, in which λὼτ [lōt] is the mole. Hesychius: Λώτ· ἀσπάλαξ, μῦς τυφλὸς ὁ τὴν γῆν τρυπῶν [Lōt· aspalax, mys typhlos ho tēn gēn trypōn]. And λάταξ [latax] is an amphibious animal, akin to the beaver and the otter, of which the Philosopher speaks in History, book 8, chapter 5. Thus in their view לטאה letaa would be either the mole or the latax. Others prefer the shrew-mouse, into which Λητὼ [Lētō], that is, Latona, is fabled to have been changed, on account of the allusion between the words Λητὼ [Lētō] and letaa, which would be the μυγάλη [mygalē]. And it is indeed true that Latona is fabled to have been changed into a shrew-mouse for fear of Typhon. Antoninus Liberalis, Metam. 28: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις· Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθύς· Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis; Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys; Artemis de ailouros] (not σίλουρος [silouros], as our editions wrongly have it). Τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος· ἔλλῳ δ᾽ Ἡρακλῆς· βοῒ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος· μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [Tragō de eikazetai Dionysos; ellō d᾽ Hēraklēs; boi d᾽ Hēphaistos; mygalē de Lētō]. But it does not follow from this that the word letaa signifies the shrew-mouse, any more than the mole or the latax because λὼτ [lōt] and λάταξ [latax] sound alike. For the mole has already been dealt with in the preceding verse. And the latax cannot be counted among the reptiles of the earth (any more than the beaver, discussed above) , since it lives rather in the water and has hair partly like that of the seal. It is better, therefore, to follow the ancients, who also number this animal among the species of lizards. Thus for the Greeks it is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] or ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs], and for Jerome the stellio; for Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] שממיתא semamitha, which is the very same thing; for the Syrian ܨܪܘܪܝܬܐ [צרוריתא] tseruritha, that is, the salamander, as they claim; and for the Arabs العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] aladha or العظاية [al-ʿaẓāya] aladhaja, the lizard. So also Solomon [Rashi], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and the Pomarium. That the Talmudists also took it so is clear from the tractate Oholoth (ch. 1, fol. 45b), where certain beasts and birds are said to quiver after the head has been cut off, כגון הזנב של הלטאה שהיא מפרכסת, like the tail of the letaa, which (when cut off) still keeps moving. To this the words in the Porta coeli allude: ויש מב״ח אם יכרתו מזנבותיהם יתנועעו זמן רב אחר כן כזנב הלטאה וזנבות השרצים, There are certain animals whose tails, if cut off, move for some time, like the tail of the letaa and of other reptiles. Of the same kind is what Aelian, History, book 2, chapter 23, and Phile, chapter 53, assert: that when a lizard is cut in two by the blow of a rod, each part lives and crawls on two feet, and sometimes they grow together again. I would not, however, lightly believe what is said in the Porta coeli about tails so cut off, כי הן יגדלו אחרי כריתותם, that they grow after being cut off, since it is held as established that once divided they live only a very short time.

So far, then, it is established that the letaa belongs to the lizard kind, since the ancients so determine with great agreement. But to define the species is not for just anyone. The Syrian explains it as the salamander. Of the more recent writers some prefer the stellio, others the lizard. The former is followed by Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)]; the latter by Munster, Schindler, the Genevans, the English, the Italians. I understand a species of lizard which in Arabic is called وحرة [waḥra] wachra or wachara. Concerning it the Arabs note chiefly three things: 1. That it is similar to the stellio. 2. That it clings very closely to the ground. 3. That whatever food it treads on is infected with its venom. These three settle the matter, as we shall show later. But first the Arabs must be heard. Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ]: الوحرة دويبة حمرا تلتصق بالارض كالعظا [al-waḥra duwaybba ḥamrā taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ ka-l-ʿaẓā] Alvvachra, a small red animal, clinging to the ground, like a lizard. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: هي دويبة شبيهة بسام ابرص تلتصق بالارض او ضرب من العظا لا تطا طعاما ولا سرابا الا سميته [hiya duwaybba shabīha bi-sām abraṣ taltaṣiqu bi-l-arḍ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ ṭaʿāman wa-lā sarāban illā sammathu] It is a small animal, similar to the sammabras (or greater stellio), clinging to the ground, or a species of lizard, infecting with its venom whatever food or drink it treads on. In the same place others say: وقيل هي علي شكل سام ابرص [wa-qīla hiya ʿalī shakl sām abraṣ] It is said to be of the form of the sammabras. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الوحرة وزغة كسام ابرص او ضرب من العظا لا تطا شي لا سميته [al-waḥra wazagha ka-sām abraṣ aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā lā taṭaʾ shay lā sammathu] Alvvachara is a guezga, like the sammabras, or a species of lizard, which treads on nothing that it does not infect. Hence وحر [waḥira] vvachara is a verb meaning to infect with venom. Accordingly they say: وحر الصدر عشه ووسواسه [waḥira al-ṣadr ʿishshuhu wa-waswāsuhu] His deceit and his insinuation infected the breast. Likewise: الغل اللازق به كما تلزق الوحرة بالارض [al-ghill al-lāziq bihi kamā talzaqu al-waḥra bi-l-arḍ] Deceit clings to him, as the alvvachara clings to the ground.

Now I shall prove without any difficulty that this, whatever it is, fits the letaa. 1. That this kind of lizard is similar to the stellio, or even a species of it, is suggested by the fact that the most ancient of the interpreters, the Greek, the Chaldee and the Roman, render it stellio. 2. That it clings to the ground is gathered from the name itself. For in Arabic the verb لطا [laṭā] lataa, or لطئ [laṭiʾa] latia, properly means to cling, not to anything at all, but to the ground. It is never taken otherwise. Hence Damir, in the chapter قبرة [qubbara] Kobbara, or On the Lark: It is its nature that noise does not frighten it; and sometimes it is crushed by a millstone, ولطي بالارض حتي يتجاوزها الحجر [wa-laṭiya bi-l-arḍ ḥattā yatajāwazahā al-ḥajar] and it clings to the ground until the stone has passed over it. And in the chapter عنكبوت [ʿankabūt], or On the Spider, فانا اراد صيد الذباب لطي بالارض [fa-nā arāda ṣayd al-dhubāb laṭiya bi-l-arḍ] And when it wants to hunt flies, it clings to the ground. Thus לטאה letaa, derived from it, properly signifies the animal that clings to the ground. This is what Giauhari and Damir note in the definition of the vvachara. 3. Finally, that the letaa is a venomous animal, and one to be guarded against above all, is taught by the enlarged Lamed at the beginning of the name. For it is not written לטאה, but לטאה. Hence Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] in the Commentarius Masorethicus, ch. 14: The small Masora notes an enlarged La- med in the word והלטאה, Lev 11:30, which some render lizard, others stellio. The enlarged letter indicates that among the other reptiles this reptile is to be guarded against most of all.

As for the rest, what this animal is called in Greek no one could easily say, unless one thinks it to be a species of salamander. For some of the ancients compare the salamander with the stellio, as similar to it, or even a species of it. Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 1, ch. 52: The salamander is an animal similar to the stellio. The Scholiast of Nicander on the Alexipharmaca: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα, εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra, eidos askalabōtou]. 2. The same animal is said to infect whatever it treads on. Pliny, in the place cited above: If it has crept onto a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison. Likewise: If a crust of bread is baked over wood or a foot touched by it, the poisoning is the same. To this belongs what the people of Narbonne keep saying, according to Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: If a Blanda (that is, a salamander) is found in a heap of wheat, the whole is infected, so much that even hens feeding on it die. Accordingly الوحرة [al-waḥara] alvvachara, to which the Arabs attribute these same things, might seem to be the same as the salamander, except that the colour does not agree. For in the wachara it is red, in the salamander variegated. Therefore the wachara is another kind of Arabian lizard, unknown to us, yet similar in many respects to the stellio and the salamander. Hence it is that לטאה letaa, which we take to be the vvachara of the Arabs, is rendered ܣܡܢܕܪܐ [סמנדרא] salamandra by the Syriac, and stellio by most of the other ancients .

What we noted on the preceding chapter, note 2, applies here too in every respect. Nor have I been able to find anything about the lizard which the Arabs call وحرة [waḥra] in the accounts of those who have visited those regions.
It is proved that חומט chomet is a lizard living in the sand, which the Arabs call حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca.

For the more recent Hebrews, Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], חומט chomet is the limax [slug]. Nor do those Spaniards mean anything else who in Kimchi render it in the vernacular as כרבר. For one should read כר״כול caracol, which is what they call the slug. This is followed by Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Münster, Pierre Robert, the Genevans and the English, who here too have limax [slug]. The ancients, however, thought otherwise. For to the Greeks and to Jerome חומט chomet is σαῦρα [saura], a lizard. And in the printed Arabic versions it is حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, the chameleon; in the manuscript ones سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, the stellio. Nor does the Syriac ܚܘܠܡܛܐ [חולמטא] chaulmata mean anything else here, according to Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)], whom I prefer to believe rather than Battista Ferrari, who renders it: a bird having a back marked with black and purple feathers; plainly ἀπροσδιονύσως [aprosdionysōs]. For the subject here is not birds but creeping things of the earth. Therefore, like the preceding ones, חומט chomet also seems to belong to the lizard kind. Nor is the origin of the word obscure. For to the Talmudists חומטון chometon is sand. Hence in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 5, fol. 54a (where the Talmudists discuss why in 1 Reg. IX, 13 Hiram, king of the Tyrians, called ארץ כבול, the land of Chabul, the district which Solomon had given him), R. Nachman, son of Isaac, says: ארץ חומטין היתה אמאי קרו לה כבול דמשתרגה בה כרעא עד כבלא It was a land of chometon; hence they called it the land of chabul, because in it the leg sank down to the ankle. And Kimchi, citing this passage in his Lexicon under the root כבל, though with slightly altered words, explains חומטון chometon as חול chol, that is, sand. So for them land of chometon is land of sand, or sandy land. Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] likewise explains the whole passage thus: פי׳ שרגליו של אדם משתקעות בה מחמת החול כאילו הן כבולין לכן אינה עושה פירות It means that a man's feet sank into it (the land) because of the (abundance of) sand, as if they had been fettered, and that it was therefore unfruitful. In the Gloss on the Talmud, the land of chometon is land מלחה ומתבקעת, salty and cracked. And in ch. 2 of the same tractate, fol. 31a, חומטון for the Glossator is ארץ מלחה ומשמרת את הפירות מהתליע, salty soil, which preserves fruits from worms. But the former interpretation is the truer, and suits both passages exceedingly well. For sand is both troublesome to the feet of those walking, and in hot places has a ἀρτυτικὴν [artytikēn] power, by which it preserves things from corruption for a long time. Thus many assert that in the sands of Africa corpses are embalmed and sold as mummy. Indeed the word חומטון chometon, although it does not occur in the Prophetic books, seems to be very ancient . And I think the Greeks, dropping the aspiration, derived from it ἄμαθον [amathon], and, with a prefix, ψάμαθον [psamathon]. Both are found in the most ancient writers, Homer for instance and others, in the sense of sand. Yet the Grammarians hold that ἄμαθον [amathon] is μεσόγειον [mesogeion], inland sand, and ψάμαθον [psamathon] παραθαλασσίαν [parathalassian], or shore sand. So, roughly, Hesychius, the Suda and others distinguish them.

Therefore, just as חימטון chometon is sand, so חומט chomet is a species of lizard that lives in the sands. And it seems that the Arabs' حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca, or لحكا [lḥkā] lucha, and luchaca, is meant; of which Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] says: الحلكا دويبة تغوص في الرمل او ضرب من العظا كالحلكا [al-ḥlkā duwaybba taghūṣu fī al-raml aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā ka-al-ḥlkā] Alchulaca, a little animal that plunges into the sand; or a species of lizard, which is also called chulaca. The same: اللحكا دويبة زرقا تشبه العظا [al-lḥkā duwaybba zarqā tushbihu al-ʿaẓā] Luchaca, a little blue animal, like a lizard. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: لحلكا دويبة شبيهة بالعغناة تغوص في الرمل [lḥlkā duwaybba shabīha bi-al-ʿghnāt taghūṣu fī al-raml] Alchulaca, a little animal like a lizard, which plunges into the sands. Alazhari: اللحكا دويبة كانها سمكة تكون في الرمل فاذا احست الانسان دارت في الرمل وغاصت فيه [al-lḥkā duwaybba ka-annahā samaka takūnu fī al-raml fa-idhā aḥassat al-insān dārat fī al-raml wa-ghāṣat fīhi] Luchaca, a little animal living in the sand like a fish (in water); which, when it senses a man, rolls about in the sand and plunges into it. And Ibnosacith: اللحكا دوبة شبيهة بالعظاية وقوايم خفيفة [al-lḥkā dwba shabīha bi-al-ʿaẓāya wa-qawāyim khafīfa] Luchaca, a little animal like a lizard, with very light feet. Asseidalanius and Arruvianus: دويبة مثل الاصبع تجري في الرمل ثم تغوص [duwaybba mithl al-iṣbaʿ tajrī fī al-raml thumma taghūṣu] فيه وهذا يقوي قول الجوهري انه مقلوبة من الحلكا [fīhi wa-hādhā yuqawwī qawl al-Jawharī annahu maqlūba min al-ḥlkā] It is a little animal the size of a finger, which runs through the sands and plunges into them. This confirms the statement of Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] that the name luchaca is inverted from chulaca. Again Damir: العرب تسيها بنات النقا لانها تسكن نقيات [al-ʿarab tsyhā banāt al-naqā li-annahā taskunu nqyāt] The Arabs also call them daughters of the sand-hill, because it lives in sand-hills.

But there is also one species of the common lizard that is ἀμμώδης [ammōdēs]. Damir, in the chapter العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] Aladha, or On the Lizard: وهي انواع كثيرة منها الابيض والاحمر والاصغر وكلها منقطه بالسواد والوان بحسب مساكنها فان منها ما يسكن الرمال ومنها ما يسكن قريبا من الما والعشب [wa-hiya anwāʿ kathīra minhā al-abyaḍ wa-al-aḥmar wa-al-aṣghar wa-kulluhā munaqqaṭa bi-al-sawād wa-alwān bi-ḥasab masākinihā fa-inna minhā mā yaskun al-rimāl wa-minhā mā yaskun qarīban min al-mā wa-al-ʿushb] There are many species of them: some white, some red, some yellow; all of them are spotted with black. And their colours correspond to the place they occupy. For some live in the sands, others near waters and in grassy places. And Alazhari: هي دويبة ملسا تعدوا وتترد كثيرا تشبه سام ابرص الا انها احسن منه وتسي العظاه وشحمة الارض وشحمة الرمل [hiya duwaybba malsā taʿdū wa-tataraddad kathīran tushbih sāmm abraṣ illā annahā aḥsan minhu wa-tusī al-ʿaẓāh wa-shaḥmat al-arḍ wa-shaḥmat al-raml] It is a soft animal, running about a great deal and going back and forth, similar to the sammabras, or stellio, except that it is prettier than it. It is called aladha, and Fat of the earth, and fat of the sand. You see, reader, that both this lizard and the other, less common one discussed above take their name from sand, just as the Hebrew חומט chomet does. Therefore חומט chomet signifies either one of the two, or both .

Note in passing that عظاية [ʿaẓāya] or عضاية [ʿaḍāya] is used in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] for the salamander, and in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] sometimes for the salamander, sometimes for the seps or Chalcidian lizard, not without serious error. For both of these are venomous. But العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] lacks venom, as the Arabs explicitly teach. Damir: ومن خرافات العرب قالوا ان السوم لما فرق علي الحيوان احتبست العظاة عند التفرقة حتي نفد السم واخذ كل حيوان قسطه منه علي قدر السبق اليه فلم يكن لها فيه نصيب وفي طبعها انها عتشي مشيا سريعا ثم تقف ويقال ان ذلك يعرض لها من التذكرة والاسف علي ما فاتها من السم [wa-min khurāfāt al-ʿArab qālū anna al-sūm lammā furriqa ʿalā al-ḥayawān iḥtabasat al-ʿaẓāh ʿinda al-tafriqa ḥattā nafida al-summ wa-akhadha kull ḥayawān qisṭahu minhu ʿalā qadr al-sabq ilayhi fa-lam yakun lahā fīhi naṣīb wa-fī ṭabʿihā annahā ʿatmshī mashyan sarīʿan thumma taqif wa-yuqāl anna dhālika yaʿriḍ lahā min al-tadhkira wa-al-asaf ʿalā mā fātahā min al-summ] It is one of the fables of the Arabs that they say that, when venoms were distributed among the animals, the aladha held back while the distribution was taking place, until the venoms ran out, each animal having taken its portion according to the order in which it had come first. And it got no portion. Accordingly, since it is natural to it to move at a rapid pace and then suddenly stop, they say this happens to it because it remembers and grieves that venom was denied it. In the same place Damir: وتمسي بارض مصر السحلية [wa-tumsī bi-arḍ Miṣr al-suḥliyya] In the land of Egypt it is called SUCHLIA, which Azhari asserts is similar to the stellio, الا انها لا تودي وهي احسن منه [illā annahā lā tūdī wa-hiya aḥsan minhu] except that it is not harmful, and is prettier than it. Those, therefore, must be mistaken who confuse this little animal with the salamander or with the Chalcidian lizard, which are extremely harmful.

This is said against Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], who holds that the Talmudists' חוממון was formed from a Greek word (in the Lexicon Chald. p. 782). Certainly the meaning sand is in no common use in any of the other cognate dialects.

But this whole discussion rests on the opinion that חומט means sand; and no foundation could be weaker than that, see above note 1. Among the Chaldeans the verb חמט denotes he bent, curved, bent himself. Hence perhaps the caterpillar is called خُمَّاطٌ [khummāṭ] by the Arabs (see Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], Lexic. p. 652), unless it was rather named from the fact that it gnaws plants; for خَمَطَ [khamaṭa] means he stripped the bark from a tree. But from bending the snail could also have got its name, which some of the learned favoured at Lev 11:30 (see Bochart at the beginning of this Chapter). You are thus taught by a new example how vain a thing it is to derive the meanings of names that designate animals from etymologies alone.
It is proved that תנשמת thinsemeth in Levit. XI, 30. is the chameleon.

In the passage we are dealing with, only תנשמת thinsemeth remains, that is, the mole, if we follow the Greeks and Jerome, and among the Chaldees Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos], and the Hebrews of recent times, Solomon, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]; and the modern translators of the Bible, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Münster, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], the Genevans, the English, the Italians, etc. Although the authority of all these carries great weight with me, two things above all keep it from drawing my assent, which I have already noted elsewhere. The first is that the mole was already dealt with in the preceding verse. For we have proved, with arguments that no one will easily refute , that it is חולד choled. Therefore תנשמת thinsemeth in this verse is something else, unless we wish Moses to have forbidden the same animal twice in one and the same sequence of text, and imagine him to have spoken thus: Among the creeping things that creep upon the earth, these shall be unclean to you: the mole, and the mouse, and the land crocodile, etc. and the mole. Moreover, I do not see at all how the name תנשמת thinsemeth, which is derived from breath and breathing, can fit the mole, whose breathing is so slight that it spends whole days under the earth, as fish do under water. Hence the burrows of the mole and of the underground mouse are distinguished by this mark: when they are buried with earth, the mouse opens them at once so as not to suffocate, whereas the mole often unseals them only on the second or third day. Accordingly many of the ancients saw that תנשמת is not the mole; among them three other, very different, renderings of this word are found.

First, to the Samaritan translator תנשמת is [?], that is, the weasel, which in Chaldee is כרכושתא, and in Syriac ܟܒܟܘܫܬܐ [כבכושתא], with the first radical doubled, whereas the Samaritans double the second.

Second, for the same word תנשמת the Syriac has ܝܘܕܥܝܕܐ [יודעידא] jodaida, the many-footed one; and the Arabic manuscripts have البدال وهو أم اربعة اربعين [al-badāl wa-huwa umm arbaʿa arbaʿīn] Albedal, which is the mother of forty-four, supply feet; that is, which has 44 feet, i.e. the iulus or scolopendra. But for بدال [badāl] bedal, a meaningless word, one should read ندال [nadāl] nedal. For in Chaldee and among the Talmudists נדל nedal or nedel is the scolopendra. Thus below in verse 42, where among the creeping things of the earth כל מרבה רגלים is forbidden, whatever creeping thing has many feet, Gr. ὃ πολυπληθεῖ ποσὶν [ho polyplēthei posin], Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] has נדל דמסגי ריגלין, nedal, which is many-footed, that is, the scolopendra. And the Talmudists in Chullin ch. 3, fol. 67b: מרבה רגלים זה נדל, that which has many feet, that is, nedal. And there the Gloss: נדל מאה רגלים קורין לו, Nedal is commonly called the hundred-footed, a definite number, of course, for an indefinite one. But the Arabs, who usually speak precisely, call it the mother of 44 feet. Thus Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], book 4, Fen 6, tract. 6, where he treats of small animals whose bite is venomous, in chapter 19 describes the animal الاربعة والاربعين [al-arbaʿa wa-l-arbaʿīn], that is, of forty-four feet, as follows: هو الحيوان المعروف بدخال الاذن وربما كان في طول شبر وله في كل جانب اثنان وعشرون قايمة وقد يمشي قدما وقد ينكص بحاله [huwa al-ḥayawān al-maʿrūf bi-dakhkhāl al-udhn wa-rubbamā kāna fī ṭūl shibr wa-lahu fī kull jānib ithnān wa-ʿishrūn qāyima wa-qad yamshī quduman wa-qad yankuṣu bi-ḥālihi] It is a well-known animal, because it enters the ear. Usually it is a span in length. On each side it has twenty-two feet, and it sometimes walks forward, sometimes moves backward. That the scolopendra enters the ear I have read nowhere else. But that it moves ἐπὶ τὴν οὐρὰν [epi tēn ouran], toward the tail, is said by the Philosopher, History, book 4, chapter 7. Hence Nicander, Theriaca verse 812, calls it ἀμφικαρὴς σκολόπενδρα [amphikarēs skolopendra]. On which words the Scholiast: Ἀμφικαρὴς δὲ, ἤγουν δικέφαλος. Ψευδῶς δέ φησιν, οὐ γάρ ἐστιν. Ἀλλ᾽, ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶν, εἰς τοὐπίσω πολλάκις ἕρπει, καὶ παρέχει δόξαν τοῦ δικέφαλος εἶναι [Amphikarēs de, ēgoun dikephalos. Pseudōs de phēsin, ou gar estin. All', hōs Aristotelēs phēsin, eis toupisō pollakis herpei, kai parechei doxan tou dikephalos einai]. As for the number of feet, different authors define it differently, so that it need not be the same in every place. However that may be, that the scolopendra is meant by this name is taught us by Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] on the chapter of Dioscorides Περὶ σκολοπένδρας θαλασσίας [Peri skolopendras thalassias], whose name, after he has rendered it in Arabic letters thus, سقولوفندريا تالاسيا هو حيوان بحري وسمي باسم الحيوان الذي يقال له اربعة واربعون [sqūlūfandriyā tālāsiyā huwa ḥayawān baḥrī wa-summiya bi-ism al-ḥayawān alladhī yuqāl lahu arbaʿa wa-arbaʿūn] This is a sea animal, which they call the 44-footed.

Third, for Jonathan תנשמת thinsemeth is סלמנדרא salamandra. And for Erpenius' Arabic translator it is صنبرص [ṣnbrṣ] senabras, a corruption of سامابرص [sāmābrṣ] sammabras, as the Paris edition has it. I think these have come closest to the truth, and that, as with the five preceding names, this name too denotes some species of lizard, namely the chameleon, which is so called from breathing. For in Hebrew נשם is to breathe, and נשמה means not only spirit but also breath or breathing, as does נשימה. Hence, on these words of Ps 150:6. כל נשמה תהלל יה, Let every spirit praise God, the author of Bereshit Rabba, ch. 14, says: על כל נשימה ונשימה שאדם נישם צריך לקלס לבוראו מה טעם כל נשמה תהלל יה כל הנשימה תהלל יה For every breath that a man breathes he must praise his Creator. For what reason? (Because it is said) „Let every spirit praise the Lord“, that is, Let every breath praise the Lord. Anyone who has a clear understanding of its nature must admit that the chameleon is rightly named from breathing, or from breathing in: for since it keeps its mouth open in a perpetual gape and draws in air with its breath, many believe that it feeds on air alone. Pliny, book 8, chapter 33: It holds itself erect, with its mouth always open, and alone of animals is nourished neither by food nor by drink, nor by any nourishment other than air. Solinus: Its gaping is perpetual and serves no use; for it takes no food, is not nourished by drink, and lives on no other nourishment than the air it draws in. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15:
That too, the animal that is fed on winds and air.

Its lung, namely, is very large. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: The chameleon has a lung very large in proportion, and nothing else inside. Plutarch, in the book Utra anim.: Συνέπεται δὲ καὶ πνεύματος πλῆθος, ὡς Θεόφραστος. Ὀλίγον γὰρ ἀποδεῖ πᾶν τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου πλῆρες εἶναι πνεύμονος, ᾧ τεκμαίρεται τὸ πνευματικὸν αὐτοῦ [synepetai de kai pneumatos plēthos, hōs Theophrastos. Oligon gar apodei pan to sōma tou zōou plēres einai pneumonos, hō tekmairetai to pneumatikon autou]; There is also an abundance of breath in it, as Theophrastus reports. For the whole body is very nearly full of lung, from which he infers how full of air it is. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)]: Since it is furnished with large lungs extending along the sides of the belly, it draws air inward with great force and swells up . Tertullian in the book De pallio: It feeds by gaping, ruminates by puffing like bellows; its food comes from the wind, etc. But, what is more surprising, it is also believed to go on breathing for a long time after being dissected. The Philosopher, in that excellent description of the chameleon in book 2, chapter 11 of the History: Ἐνεργεῖ δὲ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ἀνατετμημένος ὅλος ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον, βραχείας ἰσχυρῶς ἔτι κινήσεως ἐν αὐτῷ περὶ τὴν καρδίαν οὔσης [energei de kai tō pneumati, anatetmēmenos holos epi polyn chronon, bracheias ischyrōs eti kinēseōs en autō peri tēn kardian ousēs]; Even when it has been dissected entirely, it retains the power of breath for a long time, that is, as long as some motion, however slight, remains around the heart. This breath is called in Arabic نسيم [nasīm] nasim, from the very root from which its name תנשמת thinsemeth comes. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: يغتذي بالنسيم ويعيش بالبرد الهوا [yaghtadhī bi-l-nasīm wa-yaʿīsh bi-l-bard al-hawā] It is nourished by τῷ [tō] nasim (that is, by breath) and feeds on cold air. Yet by a very great error he transfers this to the land crocodile, as we noted above , although it is proper to the chameleon. And yet it is not quite truly written that the chameleon lives on air alone. For it has a very long tongue, sticky at the tip, by darting which it catches flies and gnats from the branch of the tree on which it sits. Damir: لسانه طويل جدا مقدار ذراع وذلك دليل علي انه يكون مطوي في حلقه وهو يبلع ما بعد عنه من الذباب [lisānuhu ṭawīl jiddan miqdār dhirāʿ wa-dhālika dalīl ʿalā annahu yakūn maṭwī fī ḥalqihi wa-huwa yablaʿ mā baʿuda ʿanhu min al-dhubāb] Its tongue is very long, namely a cubit in measure. Accordingly it keeps it folded in its throat, and shoots it out in order to (catch and) eat flies that are at a distance from it. Algazel in the Mirabilia: والحربا خلق الله لسانها بخلاف المعتاد لتلحق به ما بعد عنها بثلاث اشبار ونحوه وتصتاد به علي هذه المسافة [wa-l-ḥirbā khalaqa Allāh lisānahā bi-khilāf al-muʿtād li-talḥaqa bihi mā baʿuda ʿanhā bi-thalāth ashbār wa-naḥwihi wa-taṣtād bihi ʿalā hādhihi al-masāfa] God created for the chameleon a tongue quite different from the usual, so that with it it might reach things about three spans away from it, and hunt what lies within this distance. Johannes Landius, cited by Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], supports the Arabs: he says that when he was in farthest Syria he saw one of the five chameleons he had bought pick off, by a sudden, instantaneous dart of its tongue, a fly that was on its breast. And Belon, who had seen them alive in Egypt and Arabia: It has a round tongue, a palm and a half long, which it darts from afar at the insects on which it chiefly feeds; and with the spongy slime it has at the tip it draws flies, beetles, locusts and ants to itself . Hence its name حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, as if one were to say the darter. For حربة [ḥarba] charba is a kind of javelin or short lance. Accordingly the herb lonchitis, whose seed resembles the point of a lance, is called in Arabic حربة [ḥarba] charba . But why it is called χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] in Greek is less clear, since this most sluggish and timid animal seems to have scarcely anything in common with the lion. Tertullian, in the place cited above: When you hear of a chameleon, not knowing it before, you will at once fear something more than a lion. But when you come upon it in a vineyard, almost entirely under a vine leaf, you will immediately laugh at the boldness of the name. Yet by the Arab poets too it is called باقرة [bāqira] bakira, that is, lioness. For with them باقر [bāqir] bakir is lion. And an animalcule similar to the chameleon is called ليث عفرين [layth ʿIfrīn] lion of Iphrin, from the place where it is born.
