Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: ليث عفرين دابة كالحربا يتعرض للراكب ويضربه بذنبه [layth ʿIfrīn dābba ka-l-ḥirbā yataʿarraḍ li-l-rākib wa-yaḍribuhu bi-dhanabihi] The lion of Iphrin, an animal like the chameleon, which attacks a rider and strikes him with its tail. So it is rightly called a lion, since in a chameleon's body it has a lion's spirit. Accordingly, if it were established that this animal was known to the Greeks, I would say that the name chameleon was first given to it and afterwards transferred to the other, similar animal. But since none of the ancients mentions this animalcule, it seems to me more probable that, just as the Arabs call the chameleon جمل [jamal] gemel, or جمل يهود [jamal yahūd] gemel jehoud, that is, the Jewish camel, as Damir and Abenbitar report, so the Phoenicians in Africa called it גמל gamal, or גמליון gamalion, from which the word χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn] was formed, inflected in the Greek manner so that it would seem to be Greek. Nor is it obscure why the Arabs called it a camel. For, just as they attribute to it the head of a calf, the body of a little fish and the feet of a gecko, so too, in Damir, سنام البعير [sanām al-baʿīr] the hump of a camel, because like a camel it has a humped back. There are also those who call it مجوسي [majūsī], that is, a Magian or Magusaean, because it seems to worship the sun, since it is constantly turned towards it. It is said to change hour by hour, according as the sunlight is stronger or its heat more intense: in the morning it is ash-grey, then yellow, and finally green when the sun is hottest . But in fear too, or if something is put in its way, it takes on other colours. Hence the proverb about one who does not remain in the same state: تلون الحرباء [talawwana al-ḥirbāʾ] The chameleon has changed colour. So Alcibiades was once called χαμαιλέοντος εὐμεταβολώτερος [chamaileontos eumetabolōteros], more changeable than a chameleon. The Arabs forbid eating it, because it is venomous and a species of وزغ [wazagh] guezga, or gecko. In Avicenna and Abenbitar, its blood removes the hair of the eyelids. In Damir, its gall removes dimness of sight, and its fat is applied to ulcers and scars. In Alkazuini, remedies from the chameleon are prescribed against epilepsy, hail, locusts and enchantment. But to dwell on these any longer is not a matter for our leisure.

I shall only observe that the Hebrews were so ignorant of what kind of animal the chameleon is that they took it to be a bird. My witness is Kimchi, who, inquiring in his Lexicon what לילית lilith is, Isa 34:14, writes that some assert שהוא עוף גדל מן הרוח כמו סלמנדרא מן האש שקורין לו קמליאן that Lilith is a bird which feeds on air (as the salamander on fire), which they call the chameleon. Of the same kind is the description of the salamander in the Tanchuma, section וישב, fol. 18a, as similar to a spider. The words run thus: When glassmakers, who make glass, have kept the furnace burning for seven days and 7 nights without interruption, from the force of the fire היוצא משם בריה הדומה לעכבית והבריה קורין אותה סלמנדרא there comes forth an animal similar to a spider, which animal is called the salamander. Some would read לעכבר, to a mouse, instead of לעכבית, to a spider; but this is no sounder, since the salamander is no more like a mouse than like a spider. Since, then, the nature of animals was so little understood by the Hebrews, they are not to be trusted rashly in explaining these words.

In the Greek version it is said of Nineveh, Soph. II, 4.: χαμαιλέοντες, καὶ ἐχῖνοι ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν αὐτῆς κοιταθήσονται [chamaileontes, kai echinoi en tois phatnōmasin autēs koitathēsontai]; Chameleons and hedgehogs shall lie in its coffered ceilings. But in the Hebrew text, in place of the chameleon, there is קאת, which the same translators render pelican in Lev 11:18 and Ps. CI, (Hebr. CII,) 7. Why, then, is the same word taken here for the chameleon? If, with the Complutensian editors, we write λέοντες [leontes] for χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes], we shall not cure the fault, because the Hebrew קאת no more means lion than chameleon. I suspect that the Greeks read לטאה in place of קאת, a kind of lizard, which for them in Leviticus is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], stellio [gecko], and here would have been χαμαιλέων [chamaileōn], since these species are not infrequently confused; or else that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or, what is the same, γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], was changed into χαμαιλέοντες [chamaileontes] . In support of this is the fact that the chameleon is nowhere said to lie ἐν τοῖς φατνώμασιν [en tois phatnōmasin], in coffered ceilings. But this is characteristic of the καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], or γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], the stellio. Hence Dioscorides, book 6, chapter 1, directs that food be prepared in the open air; or, if it is prepared ἐν ὑποστέγῳ [en hypostegō], in a covered place, ἐπιμελῶς καταμανθάνειν τὰς ὀροφὰς, πολλάκις γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ὑπερκειμένων πίπτει ζωΰφια φθοροποιὰ, ὥσπερ φαλάγγια, καὶ ἄλλα τινὰ ἑρπετὰ, καὶ ὁ καλούμενος ἀσκαλαβώτης [epimelōs katamanthanein tas orophas, pollakis gar ek tōn hyperkeimenōn piptei zōyphia phthoropoia, hōsper phalangia, kai alla tina herpeta, kai ho kaloumenos askalabōtēs], to examine carefully the vault of the roof, or the coffered ceiling (if you prefer): for deadly little creatures often fall from above, such as spiders and certain other reptiles, and the one called the stellio. And in the Clouds of Aristophanes, Act 1, it is said of Socrates:

Ζητοῦντες αὐτοῦ τῆς σελήνης τὰς ὁδοὺς, Καὶ τὰς περιφορὰς, εἶτ᾽ ἄνω κεχηνότος, Ἀπὸ τῆς ὀροφῆς νύκτωρ γαλεώτης κατέχεσεν· [Zētountes autou tēs selēnēs tas hodous, kai tas periphoras, eit᾽ anō kechēnotos, apo tēs orophēs nyktōr galeōtēs katechesen]

As he was investigating the paths and revolutions of the moon, and gaping upward, a stellio from the ceiling of the roof dropped its excrement on him at night. Some take τὰ φατνώματα [ta phatnōmata] to be mangers. I see that the translators of the Greek text were in this very ridiculous error. Yet even if you follow them, you will gain nothing, because the stellio is accustomed to frequent mangers as much as the coffered ceilings of roofs. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 1: Κωλωτῇ δ᾽ ὄνος πολέμιος. Κοιμᾶται γὰρ ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ αὐτῆς, καὶ κωλύει ἐθίειν, εἰς τοὺς μυκτῆρας ἐνδυόμενος· [Kōlōtē d᾽ onos polemios. Koimatai gar en tē phatnē autēs, kai kōlyei ethiein, eis tous myktēras endyomenos] The ass is an enemy to the stellio. For the stellio sleeps in its manger and, entering its nostrils, prevents it from eating. Whereas the chameleon lives in desert places. But more will be said about the stellio in the following chapter.

On the animal's lung Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] writes thus, p. 348: "The lung is single, below the diaphragm, occupying the left hypochondrium; very large, very thin, made up of a few blood vessels and very many air vesicles, which are very distinct and wide; it ends below in 5 or 6 appendages, which are cylindrical, membranous, tubular and unequal, to each of which an air bladder is attached."

Again Hasselquist, p. 349: "The tongue is triangular at the tip, thinned, rough; then muscular, strong, tubular, narrower at the base, very long, with a tubular longitudinal small bone in the middle, which is continued from the hyoid bone."

J. E. FABER sought to prove that Bochart erred in this explanation of the name حربا [ḥrbā] in his Dissertation de Animalibus, quorum mentio fit Zeph 2:14 (appended by C. F. CRAMER to the book entitled Scythische Denkmäler in Palaestina). After reviewing Bochart's opinion on the word حربا [ḥrbā], he continues thus (p. 305 of the book cited): "But Bochart is quite mistaken. For the name of the spear is rather far from the root, and was derived from it by another route. Rather, [the chameleon] is named from חרב, whose proper force and meaning among the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Syrians lies in drying up, like יבש; for this reason it is said of the drying up of waters, Isa 19:5. LI, 10., and is found joined with יבש, to be dried up. For the chameleon delights in the sun and is, as it were, dried up by its heat." So Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)], who is so far from having corrected Bochart that he has rather himself put forward plain falsehoods. For to the name حِرْباء [ḥirbāʾ], used only in the Arabic dialect, he attributes the notion of drying up, which is entirely foreign to the Arabic verb حَرِبَ [ḥariba]. Next, anyone will feel for himself how unsuitably the chameleon would be thought to be named from drying up because it loves sunny places. Nor is it any more satisfactory that the same Faber holds the Hebrew חרב in Zeph 2:14 to be the name of the chameleon. He did not consider the usage of the Hebrew language, which consistently employs this word now to denote desolation, now dryness. And there appears no need to reject the notion of desolation in the passage of Zephaniah. How we think that passage should be interpreted we have set out above at book 3, ch. 8, note 7, p. 115.

ويتلون الوانا بحر الشمس وهي الظل اخضر [wa-yatalawwan alwānan bi-ḥarr al-shams wa-hiya al-ẓill akhḍar] it changes colour in the heat of the sun, and is now black, now green. So Nahhas the grammarian on verse 29 of the poem of Kaab son of Zuhair, p. 24 of Lette's edition. Moreover, on the change of colour in the chameleon, worth reading are Hasselquist, p. 350 of the Travels in the German translation, and a certain learned man skilled in natural history, on Belon's Travels, translated by the most celebrated Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] in the Sylloge Itinerariorum Orientalium (Sammlung der merkwürdigsten Reisen in den Orient) vol. 2, p. 259. 260.

In the Alexandrian version of the passage of Zephaniah, χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] corresponds to the Hebrew קאת, while κορακα [koraka] corresponds to חרב. But Faber, to add strength and weight to his opinion that חרב means the chameleon, would have the order of those two words disturbed in the manuscripts of the Alexandrian version, so that in place of χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes] κορακες [korakes] should be restored, and in place of κορακες [korakes] χαμαιλεοντες [chamaileontes]. Since this has been devised in favour of a rather flimsy opinion and rests on no authority, we think it needs no refutation.
It is proved that שממית semamith in Prov 30:28 is neither the ape nor the spider, but the stellio.

Of the four animals whose cleverness Solomon extols in XXX, 28., the last is שממית semamith, which he writes takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Over this animal there is a great dispute among the Hebrew doctors. Some explain it as תולעת של מטר, a rain-worm; others as שרץ של כנפים, a winged creeping thing, or שרץ מה מהעופים, some creeping thing of the number of those that fly. R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] explains semamith by the Arabic word خطاف [khaṭṭāf] chottaph, that is, the swallow, as though it were the same as סנונית senunith, as the Chaldeans and the Talmudic doctors call the swallow. This is utterly absurd, since the swallow does not have hands with which to handle and grasp, nor is it one of the small land creatures with which Solomon deals here: There are four, he says, little things of the earth. So this explanation has nothing sound in it. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Emmanuel and Kabuenaki, to avoid these difficulties, preferred that שממית semamith be the ape, a most clever animal, a delight of kings, and furnished with hands like a man. But in my judgement it is too large to be counted בקטני ארץ among the little creatures, such as are the ant, the choerogryllius and the locust; for these are the examples Solomon used before. Some press in vain the resemblance of the word semamith to simia [ape]. For the name simia comes from nowhere else than from the simae [snub] noses. That is why the same animals were once called enares [noseless] , and the Πιθηκοῦσσαι [Pithēkoussai] of the Greeks are the Enariae islands of the Latins, as the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] observes on Solinus. Quite otherwise think R. Levi, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi]: namely, that שממית semamith is the spider, which is accustomed to dwell in the towers of kings as much as in the huts of the poor, and there to weave its web with such skill of its feet that they can take the place of hands. So too the manuscript Arabic translator, who has here العنكبوت [al-ʿankabūt], the spider. To this interpretation Santes, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], the English, Italian and Genevan versions, and any other more recent translators subscribe with complete agreement. But these men, by far the most skilled in the Hebrew language, ought to have observed that nowhere, neither in Scripture nor in the writings of the ancient Hebrews, is the spider called שממית semamith, but everywhere עכביש accabis, whence the Chaldee עכובית accobith and the Arabic عنكبوت [ʿankabūt] ancabuths, still in use today. Moreover, I admit that the feet of spiders are sometimes called fingers, as in the Frogs of Aristophanes, Act 5, Εἰλίσσετε δακτύλοις φάλαγγες ἰσότονα πηνίσματα [Eilissete daktylois phalanges isotona pēnismata],
Twist with your fingers, o spiders, the threads by which the weaver's beam is stretched. And in Ovid's Metamorphoses, book 6, fable 2,
Thin fingers cling to her sides in place of legs.

Τίς τοὺς ἀράχνας λεπτοδακτύλους πλάσας, Νήθειν διδάσκει, καὶ πρὸς ἔργα τοὺς μίτους Ἐκ τῶν παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς ἐντέρων ἀναπτύειν; [Tis tous arachnas leptodaktylous plasas, Nēthein didaskei, kai pros erga tous mitous Ek tōn par' autois enterōn anaptyein?]

Who teaches the spiders, made with slender fingers, to spin, and to spit out threads for their works from their own entrails? But one cannot find anyone who attributes hands to them. For although the spider's feet imitate fingers after a fashion, there is nothing in them that approaches the form of hands. Indeed, in Symphosius, Riddle 17, the spider expressly denies that it has any hands:
I have no hand, yet everything is done by my feet.

But granting, without conceding, that the spider's feet can be taken for hands because they perform the office of hands, the Divine Writer would still not have said that it takes hold with its hands, but that it spins, or weaves, or draws out threads: for that it handles and grasps with its feet is a slight matter, and shared with many animals; that it weaves is peculiar and θαυματῶδες [thaumatōdes]. Nor would he have said that it is in kings' palaces, since the filth of spiders does not well suit the elegance of a royal court. They rather dwell in the house of poor Euclio, in which
— — — there is nothing for thieves to gain, so filled is it with emptiness and spiders.

As Plautus writes in the Aulularia. Everyone knows the fable of the gout and the spider, who, they say, agreed that the former should dwell in the palaces of the rich and the latter in the hovels of the poor. Accordingly, when someone is said to have spiders in his house, or in his chest, or in his vessels, or in his purse, it is the same as saying that he lives in slender circumstances. Hence Afranius in Festus:
Is your little chest so full of spiders?
And Catullus, excusing himself to Fabullus for entertaining him, invited to dinner, less sumptuously:
— — — —, your Catullus's purse is full of cobwebs.

Ἐκ δ᾽ ἀγγέων ἐλάσειας ἀράχνια [Ek d᾽ angeōn elaseias arachnia], But you will drive the spiders out of the vessels, that is, emptiness and want. Accordingly the Scholiast explains it thus: Εἰ καλῶς ἀροτριάσεις, καὶ σπείρεις, ἁδροὺς ἕξεις στάχους (lege στάχυας). Ἐκ δὲ τῶν σιτοφόρων σου κιβωτίων τῶν μέχρι τότε κενῶν ἑστηκότων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἀραχνιέντων, ἐξελάσειας τὰ ἀράχνια, καὶ ἐμπλήσεις δηλονότι ταῦτα τοῦ σίτου [Ei kalōs arotriaseis, kai speireis, hadrous hexeis stachous (lege stachyas). Ek de tōn sitophorōn sou kibōtiōn tōn mechri tote kenōn hestēkotōn, kai dia touto arachnientōn, exelaseias ta arachnia, kai emplēseis dēlonoti tauta tou sitou]; If you plough and sow well, you will have thick ears of grain; and from your grain vessels, which until then had been empty and therefore full of spiders, you will drive out the spiders, namely so that you may fill them with grain. Therefore it is hardly likely that Solomon assigned spiders a home in the palaces of kings.

What, then, will שממית semamith be? Plainly another animal, namely the stellio. This is proved by so many arguments that learned men weary themselves in vain seeking another interpretation, since this one is true and certain, and fits the passage best. As its authorities I have, first, the LXX translators, for whom שממית semamith is καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs], the stellio. For Mercerus, following the Complutensians, is mistaken in asserting that καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] there is a kind of fish. Καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is indeed among the fishes, but also among the lizards. Both are in Hesychius: Καλαβώτης· ἰχθῦς ποῖος, καὶ σαῦρος [Kalabōtēs; ichthys poios, kai sauros]. Clearly καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] is the same as ἀσκαλαβώτης [askalabōtēs]. Hence at Lev 11:30 the Complutensian and Parisian editions have καλαβώτην [kalabōtēn] for the Hebrew הלטאה, where the others have ἀσκαλαβώτην [askalabōtēn]. Nor should anyone believe that the Greeks were so mad as to count a fish among ἐν ἐλαχίστοις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [en elachistois epi tēs gēs]. 2. To the Greeks I add Jerome, in whom שממית semamith here is the stellio. 3. Also the Syriac translator, for whom ܐܡܩܬܐ [אמקתא] amaktha, or amkatha, is the very same thing, as we proved abundantly above in the chapter on אנקה anaka. 4. As also the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha, with the order of the letters changed, as in forma [form] from μόρφη [morphē].

Moreover, that very word שממית semamith, for a kind of lizard, and indeed for the stellio, is known to us from elsewhere as well. For at Lev 11:30 one reads [?] or [?] semamitha in the Samaritan translator and in the two Chaldee ones, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and the other, named after the city: in the former for אנקה anaka, in the latter for לטאה letaa, where the Greek version has καλαβώτης [kalabōtēs] and the Roman stellio. Finally, that the ancient Hebrews used it in this way is evident from what is read in the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 8, p. 77b: אימת שממית על העקרב, The terror of the semamith is upon the scorpion. By these words they indicate that this animal is a terror to the scorpion. Hence it appears that the semamith is not the spider. For no one has written that it carries on enmity with the scorpion or is a terror to it. But concerning the scorpion Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, says thus: The stellio is reported to be especially hostile to scorpions, so that even by its sight it brings them fear and a torpor of cold sweat. And Aelian, History book 6, chapter 22: Ἔχθιστα δὲ τῷ μὲν λέοντι πῦρ, καὶ ἀλεκτρυών· ὕαινα δὲ τῇ παρδάλει· σκορπίος δὲ ἀσκαλαβώτῃ, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει προαχθέντος οἱ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ προειρημένου [Echthista de tō men leonti pyr, kai alektryōn; hyaina de tē pardalei; skorpios de askalabōtē, narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei proachthentos hoi tou zōou tou proeirēmenou]; Most hostile to the lion are fire and the cock; the hyena to the panther; and the scorpion to the stellio, at whose approach it is seized with torpor. And Galen, On Theriac, to Piso, book 1, chapter 9: Ὁ οὖν ἀσκαλαβώτης, ὁραθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν σκορπίων, πήγνυσιν αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὕτως ἀναιρεῖ [Ho oun askalabōtēs, horatheis hypo tōn skorpiōn, pēgnysin autous, kai houtōs anairei]; The stellio, when seen by scorpions, stupefies them and so kills them. And Isidore, book 12, chapter 4: The stellio is reported to be so hostile to scorpions that, when it is seen, it brings them fear and terror. And Phile, chapter 29, from Aelian, wrongly read and understood:
— — — ἡ δ᾽ ὕαινα πάρδαλιν, Καὶ ἀσκαλαβώτην ὁ φθορεὺς κλὼψ σκορπίος, Νάρκη δὲ τοῦτον· — — — — — [hē d᾽ hyaina pardalin, Kai askalabōtēn ho phthoreus klōps skorpios, Narkē de touton]

And the hyena the panther (supply δυσμενῆ κρινεῖ [dysmenē krinei], considers hostile, which is to be repeated from the preceding ) and the thieving destroyer scorpion the stellio, but numbness seizes it. For in Aelian's words, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει [narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei], the word νάρκη [narkē] is not the torpedo [electric ray] fish, but the torpor [numbness] which seizes the scorpion when it sees the stellio. If, with some, you correct it to ναρκοῖ δὲ τοῦτον [narkoi de touton], but it (the scorpion) numbs it (the stellio), Phile would have said something utterly false, namely that the stellio is numbed by the scorpion, whereas on the contrary the stellio numbs the scorpion. Indeed Democritus, Pliny, Galen, Aëtius, Diophanes and others prescribe a stellio cut open, steeped in oil and left to putrefy, as an effective remedy against the stings of scorpions. Nor is it of slight weight that even today in the vulgar tongue of the Greeks the stellio is called σαμιαμίνθη [samiaminthē], a name plainly distorted from the Hebrew שממית semamith. The Glossae: Ἀσκαλαβώτης· τὸ σαμιαμίνθη [Askalabōtēs; to samiaminthē]. By Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] it is written θαμιάμιθος [thamiamithos] and ψαμαμύθη [psamamythē]; by Bellonius SAMIAMITOS, who wrongly takes it for the Chalcidian lizard. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1161.

There are some who write שׁממית schemamith with Shin, as if it came from שמם schamam, that is, to stupefy. This itself fits well the nature of the stellio, which stupefies the scorpion by its mere sight, as we have shown. But in Kimchi and in the purest copies of the Bible it is written שׂממית semamith with Sin Semol, just as סממית with Samech in the Talmudic writings and in the Samaritan paraphrase. Thus it is to be derived from סמם, not from שמם, that is, from poison, not from stupor. So, to understand the true reason for the name, one must know that two species of stellio are reported: one with a harmless bite, the other with a venomous one. The writers, however, do not agree in which places they are born. The Philosopher assigns the venomous ones to Italy and Sicily, the harmless ones to Greece. On the other hand Theophrastus, in Pliny, book 8, chapter 31, states that stellios, deadly in their bite in Greece, are harmless in Sicily. In Thrace too the stellio has a pernicious bite, as is found in Nicander. And Bustamantinus of Complutum asserts that stellios are so pernicious that, mixed by chance with food, they have laid waste entire populations. Hence Aëtius, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] and Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] prescribe so many remedies against the bite of the stellio. And Columella, book 10, chapter 7, wants the openings of beehives to be very narrow, lest the venomous stellio ravage the combs through the wider spaces of the entrance. He added the epithet venomous διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because another kind is harmless. The name stellio suits the venomous one better, if Verrius, in Varro and Festus, truly asserts that the stellio is so called because it drips venom. To the same was given the name סממית semamith, because סם sam among the Hebrews and Syrians is φάρμακον [pharmakon], or poison; and in Arabic سم [samm] samma is the verb to infect with poison. Therefore סממית semamith is properly σαῦρα φαρμακὶς [saura pharmakis], or φαρμακῖτις [pharmakitis]. I see that this very name is used by the Greeks in a sense little different. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 537:
Φαρμακίδος σαύρης πολυμήδεος, ἣν σαλαμάνδρην Κλείουσιν. — — — — — — — [Pharmakidos saurēs polymēdeos, hēn salamandrēn Kleiousin.]

You see that there the σαῦρα φαρμακίς [saura pharmakis] is the salamander, a kind of lizard so similar to the stellio that some take it for a species of stellio. Accordingly the Scholiast there: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα· εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra; eidos askalabōtou]. Yet in Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 4, ch. 52, the salamander, the stellio and the venomous lizard, in Greek σαῦρα φαρμακῖτις [saura pharmakitis], are different little animals, but very similar to one another. The salamander, he says, is an animal similar to the stellio, rougher, and more scaly than the venomous lizard. Perhaps by the name stellio he means only the harmless one, and by the name pharmacitis lizard, or venomous lizard, distinct from the salamander, the stellio with a harmful bite. Thus the pharmacitis lizard will be the same as the סממית semamith.

The same point is supported by the fact that the Arabs record two species of venomous stellio, which differ only in size. The larger is called سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, and the smaller وزغة [wazagha] vvezga. In the name sammabras, compounded of سام [sām] and ابرص [abraṣ], the first part is shortened from semamith and means venomous; the second means leprous, or marked with spots of leprosy. So, literally, sammabras is leprous semamith, or a species of lizard notable for venom and for spots of leprosy. For two things are to be noted in the stellio: first, that it is venomous, which has already been treated; second, that it is leprous, that is, marked with spots as if of leprosy. The Arabic SAMMABRAS contains both of these, the Hebrew SEMAMITH only the first. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وانما سمي هذا النوع سام ابرص لانه سم اي جعل الله فيه السم وجعله ابرص [wa-innamā summiya hādhā al-nawʿ sām abraṣ li-annahu summa ay jaʿala Allāh fīhi al-summ wa-jaʿalahu abraṣ] This species of lizard indeed has the name sammabras, because it is venomous, that is, God put venom in it, and (moreover) made it leprous . The Romans called the stellio's spots by a more honourable name, stellae [stars], whence the animal itself is called stellio. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 5, fable 7:
— — — — and it has a name suited to its colour, its body starred with varied drops.

Salonius on Proverbs: What kind of animal is the stellio? A kind of lizard, very sluggish and of varied colour. ' Hence it got the name stellio, because it is marked and variegated as if with stellae, that is, drops. Here he follows the Poet in such a way that he seems to have taken stellae [stars] for stillae [drops], or guttae [drops]. By the opposite error many explain מרים Marjam, the Syrian name of Mary, as maris stella [star of the sea] instead of maris stilla [drop of the sea]. Pliny also calls them lentigines [freckles], when he writes of the Greek stellio in book 29, chapter 4: This one is full of freckles. Hence a freckled eunuch is called by Menander γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], that is, stellio, because of the spots on his face. Terence in the Eunuch wrongly rendered this colore mustelino [of weasel colour], as if γαλεώτης [galeōtēs] were named ἀπὸ τῆς γαλῆς [apo tēs galēs], that is, from the weasel, as Donatus observes there.

In Alkazuini, sammabras is defined as الوزغ الصغير الراس الطويل الذنب [al-wazagh al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs al-ṭawīl al-dhanab] alvvezgo (or stellio) with a small head and a long tail. In Damir and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author], an animal من كبار الوزغ [min kibār al-wazagh] of the large guezgi, or stellios. The Arabs tell the fable that leprosy was inflicted on it as punishment for a crime it committed, namely because with its breath it kindled the fire into which Abraham was thrown. They add that leprosy is produced by eating salt in which it has rolled, or on which it has discharged slime. Hence this animal is most hateful to the Arabs . And Iahius, son of Iamer, says that he holds dearer one who has killed a hundred stellios than one who has redeemed ماية رقبة [māya raqaba] a hundred necks, that is, a hundred slaves. Many sayings of Muhammad are cited on this matter. Nor was the stellio less hateful to the ancient Greeks. Antoninus Liberalis, in the passage cited above on the stellio: Ὑπὸ Θεῶν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μεμίσηται· ὁ δ' ἀποκτείνας κεχαρισμένος γίνεται Δημῆτρι [Hypo Theōn kai hypo anthrōpōn memisētai; ho d' apokteinas kecharismenos ginetai Dēmētri]. It is hateful to gods and men; and he who kills it does a thing pleasing to Ceres. Yet it is useful for many things, which do not belong here. But I cannot fail to note what Alkazuini has in the chapter On sammabras: لحمه يوضع علي لسع العقرب ينفع نفعا بينا [laḥmuhu yūḍaʿ ʿalī lasʿ al-ʿaqrab yanfaʿ nafʿan bayyinan] Its flesh, when placed on a scorpion's sting, is of evident benefit. So also Damir. It is thus established that it is the same animal as the stellio discussed above, although Avicenna sometimes uses the word for the common lizard.

Now, if what Solomon says of the semamith is examined, everything will be found to fit the stellio. There are four things, he says, little upon the earth (the Greeks ἐλάχιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [elachista epi tēs gēs]), yet wise, as if taught wisdom. Among these the stellio is rightly counted, a small animal and very clever . On its small stature Ovid writes thus:
And it is contracted into a small form, lest it have great power to harm, and its size is less than a small lizard.
Claudian, or whoever is the author of the Sorrows of Ceres:
Spots appear, its form is small, a tail smeared on rises, and it imitates the wandering limbs of a tiny lizard.
Porphyry in Eusebius, book 5 of the Praeparatio, Ζώοισιν λεπτοίσι κατοικιδίοις σκαλαβώταις [Zōoisin leptoisi katoikidiois skalabōtais], To small little animals, domestic stellios.

There are many proofs of the stellio's skill. Hesychius, under Κωλώτης [Kōlōtēs], says that the stellio εὐστόχως ἅλλεσθαι περὶ τὰς μυίας [eustochōs hallesthai peri tas myias], leaps skilfully about flies; that is, in order to catch them. Phavorinus ineptly has περὶ τοὺς μῦς [peri tous mys], about mice: with which the stellio has nothing to do. But Augustine also speaks of flies in book 10 of the Confessions, chapter 35: What of it, when, as I sit at home, a stellio catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into its webs, often holds my attention? Theophrastus, in the book De anim. invid., adduces another proof, but a less certain one: Ὅτι ὁ γαλεώτης, φθονῶν τῆς ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καταπίνει τὸ δέρμα, ὅταν ἐκδύηται· ἔστι γὰρ βοήθημα ἐπιλήπτῳ· [Hoti ho galeōtēs, phthonōn tēs ōpheleias tois anthrōpois, katapinei to derma, hotan ekdyētai; esti gar boēthēma epilēptō;] The stellio, begrudging men the benefit, devours its own skin as soon as it has shed it. For it helps those suffering from epilepsy. Antigonus has the same in the Mirabilia, chapter 24, and Apuleius in his first Apology for himself. And from this Pliny, book 30, chapter 10, concludes that no animal more deceitfully begrudges man. From the same source the names stelliones [swindlers] and stellionatus [fraud] were transferred into terms of abuse. There are also those who think that the Galeotae, the most skilful interpreters of portents in Sicily, took their name from the cleverness of this animal. To this Stephanus refers these words: Γαλεῶται μάντεων εἶδος Σικελῶν· Γαλεὸς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκαλαβώτης [Galeōtai manteōn eidos Sikelōn; Galeos de, ho askalabōtēs] (where for γαλεὸς [galeos] one should read γαλεώτης [galeōtēs]). But since in Hebrew גלה gala means to reveal, which is most characteristic of seers, I suspect that the name of the Galeotae is Hebrew, like a great many others which, as I have proved elsewhere, were carried over into Sicily with the colonies of the Phoenicians.

But Solomon himself amply proves the stellio's skill with these words: It takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Why he attributes hands to it is obscure to no one. Just as lacertus [lizard] is named from lacerti, that is, arms, so the stellio is called in Greek κωλώτης [kōlōtēs] from τοῖς κώλοις [tois kōlois]. Κῶλα [Kōla] are hands and feet. I call the forefeet hands together with Avicenna , who writes that غظاية [ghaẓāya] adhajam, that is, the salamander (in Avicenna's view), is preserved in honey only if it is gutted and يداها ورجلاها [yadāhā wa-rijlāhā] its hands and feet are cut off: where Dioscorides has φυλάσσεται ἐν μέλιτι ἐξεντεριθεῖσα, τῶν ποδῶν ἀφαιρεθέντων [phylassetai en meliti exenteritheisa, tōn podōn aphairethentōn]. If the salamander has hands, why not also the stellio, an animal very like the salamander? Thus Damir, in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, or On the land crocodile: له كف ككف الانسان مقسومة الاصابع الا انامل [lahu kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūmat al-aṣābiʿ illā anāmil] It has a hand like the hand of a man, with fingers divided into joints. Indeed, you may rightly call the feet of any lizard, especially the forefeet, hands, since they are like hands. Gesner, from his own observation: The lacertus is named from its likeness to the lacerti [arms] of a man, because their feet are likewise split into fingers, as if from hollow hands or palms. The same: Very slender fingers, five in front and five behind, with little claws. On the hind feet the longest is the one that occupies the place of the index finger; the thumb is in a lower position, as in the hands of man: but the front feet have the thumb in the same position as the other fingers. You see that the forefeet, or more truly the arms, are in the shape of a human arm and hand, with the same number of fingers, and in the same position. How much better does the name hands suit such arms than the legs of spiders?

Now, the statement that the stellio takes hold with its hands I refer either to its walking or to its hunting. For when it walks upside down, hanging from a ceiling, it must either fix its little claws in small cracks or clasp with its hands whatever projects or is rough. That it walks upside down is asserted in express words by the Philosopher in the History, book 9, chapter 9, where he speaks of the woodpecker thus: Πορεύεται ὕπτιος καθάπερ οἱ ἀσκαλαβῶται [poreuetai hyptios kathaper hoi askalabōtai]; It walks upside down like stellios. And in the Marvels: Τὸν δρυοκολάπτην τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπὶ τῶν δένδρων βαδίζειν φασὶν ὥσπερ τοὺς ἀσκαλαβώτας, καὶ ὕπτιον, καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν γαστέρα [ton dryokolaptēn to orneon epi tōn dendrōn badizein phasin hōsper tous askalabōtas, kai hyption, kai epi tēn gastera]; They say that the woodpecker walks on trees like stellios, upside down as well as face down. It is strange why Pliny renders ἀσκαλαβώτας [askalabōtas] as feles [cats], and ὕπτιον [hyption] as in subrectum [upright] instead of supinum [upside down], when he says in book 10, chapter 18, that the hollowers of trees (that is, δρυοκολάπτας [dryokolaptas], woodpeckers) climb upright in the manner of cats. All the more so since the same author, in book 29, chapter 4, acknowledges that the stellio is called in Greek colotes, ascalabotes and galeotes, so that no one should think Pliny was ignorant of the Greek names of the stellio. Similar is what we read in Plutarch's book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: that what the geographers teach is highly paradoxical, ἀντίποδας οἰκεῖν, ὥσπερ θρίπας, ἢ γαλεώτας, τραπέντα ἄνω τὰ κάτω, τῇ γῇ προϊσχομένους [antipodas oikein, hōsper thripas, ē galeōtas, trapenta anō ta katō, tē gē proischomenous], that antipodes inhabit the earth, who, like woodworms or stellios, with the lower parts of their bodies turned upward, cling to the earth. Here likewise the first translators had written feles [cats] instead of stelliones.

We have also said that the stellio uses its hands for hunting, when it catches flies or spiders. Bustamantinus: It seizes with hands that promise security. Indeed the deceitful feet, which were bound to serve for motion, take the place of hands and carry out the plunder; and to it the feet on which it rests in moving are hands, and the hands with which it seizes its prey are feet. Rightly therefore Solomon says, The stellio takes hold with its hands, whether it walks upside down or throws itself upon its prey. Both are marvellous and most worthy of note in a tiny creature. The Greeks have here Καλαβώτης χερσὶν ἐρειδόμενος [Kalabōtēs chersin ereidomenos], and Jerome The stellio leans on its hands; the Arabic too has يتنسد بيديه [yatanassadu bi-yadayhi] it leans on its hands: as if referring this to walking. But no one could easily say what אקמתא דמסככה בידיה in the Chaldee means. For I do not understand what the Latin version means, The spider makes coverings with its hands. Nor much better is Gabriel, who rendered the same words of the Syriac paraphrase thus: The stellio, which creeps with its hands. I would rather read sepit [fences]; for סכך is to fence. But why the stellio should be said to fence, or to make coverings, I do not understand at all. Here too Drusius was at a loss in the Observations, book 10, chapter 6, and he suspects the passage of corruption. And instead of מסככה, fences or covers, he would sometimes read מסבכה, with Beth, entangling or making an intricate work, which would be said of the spider's web; sometimes מסמכה, leaning, which would be said of the stellio; so that the Chaldee would thus agree with the Greek and the Roman translators. But it is better to reconcile the Chaldee translator with the Hebrew text, in which תפש is to take hold. Accordingly Theodotion had rendered ἐλλαμβανόμενος [ellambanomenos]. I would therefore prefer to read, instead of מסככה mesacceca, מפככה mephacceca, Pe for Samech, letters not entirely dissimilar in shape. For פכך in Chaldee is the same as תפש in Hebrew, to take, to take hold. Thus Prov 5:22 in the Venice edition: With the cords of his sins אתפכך, he is taken, or held fast.

Solomon adds that the semamith is in kings' palaces. This was the one objection that Mercerus had to raise . "Our translator," he says, "renders semamith as stellio, which does not seem to fit, because it does not live in the courts of kings." But that the stellio lives in houses was not, I believe, unknown to this most learned man, since nearly all who have written about the stellio proclaim it with one voice. Thus in Eusebius, Porphyry speaks of κατοικιδίους σκαλαβώτας [katoikidious skalabōtas], domestic stellios. Suidas, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others among the Greeks define it as ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον [zōyphion eoikos saura en tois toichois tōn oikēmatōn anerpon], a little animal like a lizard, creeping along the walls of houses. So also Elluchasem, a physician of Baghdad, in his book On Animals: The stellio is a lizard that inhabits houses. Hence Kiranides calls it τοιχοβάτην [toichobatēn]. And in Spain the Catalans call it dragon de las casas, that is, dragon of the houses. That it lives especially in old buildings is reported by Niphus on Aristotle and by Ponzettus in his book On Poisons. But that it is also seen in new ones is asserted by Marcellinus in Hermolaus. According to the Philosopher it lives in mangers; according to Antoninus Liberalis , παρ᾽ ὀχετὸν [par᾽ ocheton], near drains; according to Pliny , about doors and windows, or in caves or tombs; according to Arnobius , it builds its nests under the hollows of statues. Matthiolus assigns to it the hollows of walls near the ground. But the ancients assign it ceiling panels and the vaults of roofs, where it may walk upside down. Accordingly, besides Aristophanes and Dioscorides, whom I have already cited above , you may also read in Avicenna that the stellio sometimes falls from above into a drink and turns it into poison if it dies in it . These things, if I am not mistaken, amply prove that the stellio is not a wild animal but a domestic one. Further, I see no privilege by which royal houses should be immune from this pest. Indeed, the greater the pile and mass of stones in them, the deeper are the fissures and cracks in the walls. From this you may not unreasonably conclude that such little animals, which live mostly in holes in walls, dwell even more safely in the courts and palaces of kings than in a private house.
Hist. anim. book 8, ch. 29, and in the Mirabil.

This lizard was carefully described by HASSELQUIST, Travels p. 356-358, under this name: Lacerta (Gecko) cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus cristatis, subtus longitudinaliter lamellosis [lizard (gecko) with a moderate, rounded tail, crested feet, lamellate lengthwise underneath]. "The body," he says, "the head and the feet are hairless and smooth. Very small, raised, shining points are scattered over the whole back. Very small pores run along the abdomen. Rather large, soft scales cover the very small space between the loins underneath. The back, head and tail are whitish above, with grey transverse spots scattered irregularly; the throat, abdomen and tail are whitish underneath." From these words it is clear enough that the name leprous was not undeservedly given to this lizard. Now hear the same Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] on the animal's poison, from which it is called سام [sām]. "Most remarkable is this animal's poison, which it exhales from the lobes of its toes. The little animal seeks out places and any things soaked or tinged with sea salt; when it finds such a thing, it runs over it several times, and as it runs it leaves behind it a highly noxious poison. In Cairo, in July 1750, I saw two women and a girl close to death who had eaten fresh salted cheese, bought in the market, on which this little animal had deposited its poison. How acrid the exhalations of its toes are I once saw in Cairo, when the little animal ran over the hand of a certain monk who wanted to catch it: at once, over the whole area the animal had touched, very small pustules arose, with redness, heat and slight pain, exactly as in those who have touched a nettle." FORSKAL also mentions this lizard, in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: "Lacerta Gecko. By the Egyptians it is called ابو برص [abū baraṣ], i.e. father of leprosy, or leprous; by the people of Aleppo Burs." Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in Comment. ad Proverb. Chapter XXX. vs. 28. p. 486 b, interprets سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] as leprous breather, from سُمَام [sumām], which he says means pestilent blast.

Forskal p. 13: "The origin of the name among the Egyptians is amusing: if it lets its saliva drop into salt intended for use at table, it brings leprosy on the person who tastes it. For this reason they carefully cover the salt-cellar, or add garlic, which the lizard abhors. Others think the animal's name arose from the likeness of its colour to leprosy."
Book 2 of the Canon, ch. 2. عظاية [ʿaẓāya], which the Latin translator omitted.

Hasselquist on the gecko: "Locality: Cairo, where it is very common inside and outside houses." To him should be added Forskal, loc. cit.: "Common in houses at Cairo, roaming over the walls in summer. In winter it is not seen, but is said to hide in the roofs and to come out again in the middle of March."
Why the altars of the idols are said to be ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai], like tortoises, in the Greek version of Hos 12:12. And on the chelonis of Holofernes, Jdt 14:13.

No word is better known to the Hebrews than גל gal, for a heap of stones. From it Galaad, a very famous mountain in the land of Canaan, took its name, Gen 31:48. So too Gallim, a town near Accaron, on which see 1 Sam 25:44. Isa 10:30 and Eusebius and Jerome in the Places. When Achan had been stoned because he had taken from the devoted things, a great גל gal of stones (that is, a heap) was piled over him as a memorial of the deed, Josh 7:26. Likewise over the corpse of the rebel Absalom, 2 Sam 18:17. Houses, too, and cities that are demolished are said to be reduced לגל, to a gal (that is, a heap), Isa 25:2 or לגלים, to gallim (that is, heaps), Job 15:28 and Jer 9:11 and LI, 37. And to become גלים נצים gallim nitsim (that is, desolate heaps), 2 Reg. XIX, 25. There is therefore nothing obscure in these words of Hos 12:11 (var. 12.): Their altars are כגלים, like gallim (or heaps of stones) on the furrows of the field. The Prophet is speaking of the altars which the idolaters of Gilgal had built to their gods not only in the city but also in the neighbouring fields; and he compares them with the heaps of stones customarily piled up by those who clear stony fields. The Greek translators, however, for whom גל gal is elsewhere βουνὸς [bounos], a mound, χῶμα [chōma] an embankment, σωρὸς [sōros] a heap, συναγωγὴ λίθων [synagōgē lithōn] a collection of stones, render the plural גלים gallim in this passage of Hosea quite differently, namely as χελώνας [chelōnas], tortoises. Τὰ θυσιαστήρια αὐτῶν [Ta thysiastēria autōn] (they say), ὡς χελῶναι ἐπὶ χέρσον ἀγροῦ [hōs chelōnai epi cherson agrou], Their altars are like tortoises on the waste of the field. And on these words Theodoret observes that the tortoise, when swimming in the water, escapes the hands of fishermen more easily, whereas when walking on land it is πρόχειρος, καὶ εὐάλωτως [procheiros, kai eualōtōs], ready to hand and easily caught; so it would come about that the altars of the Gilgalites would easily be taken and overthrown by their enemies. Jerome preferred to apply what is said of the altars to the heretics, who, like tortoises, are slow of step and move about in one place, etc. Wiser than these, perhaps, will seem Cyril, for whom χελῶναι [chelōnai] in this passage are not animals but αἱ τῶν χωμάτων ἐγέρσεις [hai tōn chōmatōn egerseis], the raising of embankments; just as for Drusius too tortoises signify γεωλόφους [geōlophous], mounds of earth. And I would gladly agree with them if any example of a similar expression were given. But since none is adduced, I have two conjectures. The first is that instead of ὡς χελῶναι [hōs chelōnai] we should read ὡς κολῶναι [hōs kolōnai], a word often used for mounds. As in the Iliad, β΄ [book 2], line 811.
Ἔστι δέ τις προπάροιθε πόλεως αἰπεῖα κολώνη, [Esti de tis propároithe poleōs aipeia kolōnē,]
Now there is near the city a certain lofty mound. And in Apollonius' Argonautica, book 1, line 1114.
Φαίνετο δ᾽ ἠερόεν στόμα Βοσπόρου, ἠδὲ κολῶναι Μύσιαι. — — — — — — [Phaineto d' ēeroen stoma Bosporou, ēde kolōnai Mysiai.]

And the misty mouth of the Bosphorus and the ridges of Mysia appeared. Prose writers also use it: for example Polemo in Athenaeus, book 13, and another in the Suda; and Pausanias in the Laconica, where he speaks of Colona, a place in Sparta. In Hesychius κολώνη [kolōnē] is τόπος ὑψηλὸς, καὶ ἐπανάστημα γῆς βουνοειδὲς [topos hypsēlos, kai epanastēma gēs bounoeides], a lofty place, and an elevation of the ground in the manner of a mound. And in the scholiasts on Homer, τόπος εἰς ὕψος ἀνήκων, καὶ γεώλεφος ἐξοχὴ [topos eis hypsos anēkōn, kai geōlephos exochē], a place rising to a height, and a hilly prominence. The other conjecture is that גלים gallim is rendered here as χελώνας [chelōnas], or tortoises, following the usage of the Syriac language, in which ܓܠܐ [גלא] gala is tortoise. Accordingly the Syriac here has ܐܝܟ ܓܠܐ [איך גלא], that is, like tortoises, according to Gabriel Sionita [=translator of al-Idrīsī's geography into Latin (Geographia Nubiensis, Paris 1619)]. And in the Syriac Lexicon of Giovanni Battista Ferrari, page 107, ܓܠܐ [גלא] gala is rendered tortoise. Yet in the Thesaurus of Thomas of Novara, page 241, the Syriac words ܫܠܘܦܝܬܐ [שלופיתא] seluphita and ܥܓܠܐ [עגלא] gala are distinguished in such a way that the former signifies the tortoise in general, the latter only the male tortoise. This I think is more correct, since the Arabs call the same animal غيلم [ghaylam] gailam, surely in allusion to this word. So testify Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author], Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and others. And the name is formed from lust. For غلم [ghalam] galam means lust, and the verb غلم [ghalima] galima means to burn with lust. That the male tortoise is rightly called غيلم [ghaylam] gailam may be shown by these words of Aelian, Historia, book 15, chapter 19: Χερσαία χελώνη ζῶον λαγνίστατον· ἀλλὰ ὅγε ἄῤῥην. ὁμιλεῖ δὲ ἡ θήλεια ἄκουσα [Chersaia chelōnē zōon lagnistaton; alla hoge arrhēn. homilei de hē thēleia akousa]. The land tortoise is a most lustful animal; that is, its male: for the female mates only unwillingly. And Damostratus writes that she shrinks from mating for this reason: because, when she has been turned on her back by the male, she cannot right herself on account of the excessive weight of her shell, and after mating lies open as prey to the eagle and to other animals. But I think what others write is more correct, that in the very act of mating she suffers severe pain, because the male's member is hard and spiny. I pass over the fable of Damostratus, not omitted by Damir, about a certain unknown herb which the male holds in his mouth and so draws the resisting female to himself. Meanwhile, although not only for the Greeks but also for the Syriac and the Arabic translators גלים gallim in Hosea are tortoises, I nevertheless see no reason why we should depart from the received rendering of that passage. Everyone sees that the altars of the idols, met everywhere in the fields, are rightly compared with those heaps of stones we have mentioned, both on account of their cheapness and on account of their frequency. Not to mention that to those viewing them from afar their appearance is not dissimilar. But whatever is adduced to establish a likeness between these altars and tortoises is forced and far-fetched. Hosea's words can also be taken as spoken prophetically, as if he foretold that the altars of the people of Gilgal would shortly be כגלים, like heaps of stones that are in the fields, that is, would shortly be demolished. Nor should the allusion of the word Galgal to גלים gallim be neglected, so that Galgal and its altars are said to be destined to become like gallim, or heaps of stones. Just as in Zeph 2:4: Aza (or Gaza) shall be עזובה (azuba) forsaken. And Accaron תעקר (theaker) shall be uprooted. As in the Pseudo-Sibyllines,
Καὶ Ῥώμη ῥύμη ἔσεται, καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος· [Kai Rhōmē rhymē esetai, kai Dēlos adēlos;]
and in the history of Susanna σχίσαι [schisai] and πρίσαι [prisai] allude to the names of the trees σχίνον [schinon] and πρίνον [prinon].

When we read that Bagoas found the trunk of Holofernes thrown down ἐπὶ τῆς χετλωνίδος [epi tēs chetlōnidos], Jdt 14:13, others rightly observe that in place of χετλωνίδος [chetlōnidos], a meaningless word, we should read χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], as Hesychius and Suidas read it, and that χελωνίς [chelōnis] is so called ἀπὸ τῆς χελώνης [apo tēs chelōnēs], from the tortoise. But what exactly a χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is, is not sufficiently clear. The Vulgate translator renders it cortina [curtain]. Most of the more recent interpreters render it stratum [couch] or lectus [bed]; they are easily refuted. For Judith had cut off Holofernes' head, καὶ ἐπεκύλισε τὸ σῶμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς στρωμνῆς [kai epekylise to sōma autou apo tēs strōmnēs], and had rolled his body off the couch, ch. 13, v. 10. Therefore the χελωνὶς [chelōnis], in which Bagoas found this body ἐῤῥιμμένον [erhrimmenon], thrown down, is something different from the couch and the bed. Hesychius, under χελωνίδος [chelōnidos], explains it as οὐδὸς τῆς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς [oudos tēs thyras tēs skēnēs], the threshold of the door of the tent. So Suidas too must be corrected from him, since he writes ὅδου [hodou] for οὐδοῦ [oudou]. This is hardly likely, both because the name does not fit, and because Holofernes' body was rolled from the couch into the chelonis. The chelonis, then, was not near the threshold of the door, but in the innermost part of the tent, where the commander's bed itself also stood. Not to detain the reader any longer: to me the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] is קבה kubba. The word occurs once in Scripture and is not well understood, namely Num 25:8, where, while Zimri and Kozbi were fornicating, Phinehas went אל הקבה, into the kubba, and pierced them both through. Different people explain this differently. But among the Arabs قبة [qubba] kubba, or kobba, and with the article القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, is a chamber of vaulted work, by which a bed is enclosed. The Spaniards call it alcoba and alcova, a word which among us too has a similar meaning. The root قب [qabba] kabba in the second conjugation means to vault, or to build vaulted work. So, just as the musical instrument χέλυς [chelys], or testudo [tortoise], is called in Arabic العود [al-ʿūd] alaud, whence the Spanish laud or laut, and our lut, so القبة [al-qubba] alkobba, or the chamber we have described, is called in Arabic by another name ام العود [umm al-ʿūd] ommolaudi, that is, mother of the tortoise, because it is of vaulted, tortoise-shaped work. Among the Arabs the bridal chamber is in such an القبة [al-qubba] alkobba. And leading the bride there is called بنا [banā] bana and زف [zaff] zappha. So Holofernes' bedchamber, when he was about to lie with Judith, as he thought, was in an alcobba of this kind; and why it is called χελωνὶς [chelōnis] in Greek is now clear to anyone. Perhaps the χελωνὶς [chelōnis] was also named from its material. For in former times tortoise shell was much used in the beds and bedsteads of the great. This luxury, first adopted in the East, finally reached the Romans. The date is noted by Pliny, book 9, chapter 11: To cut tortoise shells into plates, he says, and to veneer beds and sideboards with them, was introduced by Carbilius Pollio. And book 16, chapter 43: Tortoise shell is cut for this purpose. And recently, in the principate of Nero, it was devised by monstrous ingenuity that it should destroy itself with paints and sell for more by imitating wood. Thus high prices are sought for beds. Hence Martial, book 12, Epigram 67:
Beds jewelled with the finest tortoise shell gleam.
What kind of tortoise swam in the waves of Ocean, to make a splendid and noble headrest for the Trojan-born.

Where the Scholiast says: That he might have a tortoise-shell bed. For the ancients adorned beds with the tortoise shell of Ocean. Apuleius too, not far from the end of book 10: A bed shining with Indian tortoise shell, swelling with a heap of feathers, etc. But this is more than enough on a matter of no great importance. So here we end, and now pass on to the birds.
ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE PART TWO BOOK ONE ON ON THE CLEAN BIRDS.
On the Hebrew name of the dove.

The sacred writers touch on the clean birds only briefly, with the single exception of the dove, about which they say more than about all the others taken together. It is therefore necessary to treat it more carefully. It is held that the dove is called in Hebrew יונה jona from the verb ינה jana, which means to oppress, as if it lay open to the plundering of all. On this point the poets are cited:
Censure pardons the ravens and harasses the doves.

This seems far-fetched. I shall therefore try to offer something more probable. In Jer 46:16 and L, 16. the Hebrew words מפני חרב היונה are rendered by the Greeks ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας Ἑλληνικῆς [apo prosōpou machairas Hellēnikēs], from the face of the Greek sword; by Jerome, from the face of the sword of the dove; by the Syriac, from the face of the sword ܡܣܝܒܐ [מסיבא] of the tormentor; by R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], האונסת, of the oppressor. But the Chaldee Paraphrast has מן קדם חרב סנאה דהיא כחמר מרויא, from the face of the hostile sword, which is like intoxicating wine, as if היונה were formed from יין, that is, from wine, with Yod and Vav interchanged. From the same source, then, יונה jona for the dove could be derived. If we follow this, יונה jona will properly be the οἰνὰς [oinas], a kind of wild dove so named from wine. 1. Because, on the authority of Eustathius, it is οἰνωπὸς τὸ χρῶμα [oinōpos to chrōma], that is, because it resembles wine, or ripe grapes, in colour. 2. Because it usually appears at the time of the vintage. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3: Οἰνὰς δὲ τοῦ φθινοπώρου καὶ φαίνεται μάλιστα, καὶ ἁλίσκεται· [Oinas de tou phthinopōrou kai phainetai malista, kai halisketai] The oenas (or, as Gaza renders it, vinago) appears and is caught chiefly in autumn. Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11: Ἡ δὲ φὰψ, καὶ ἡ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· ἡ δὲ οἰνὰς φθινοπώρῳ μόνῳ· [Hē de phaps, kai hē peristera aei phainontai; hē de oinas phthinopōrō monō] The smaller wood pigeon and the dove are always to be seen; but the vinago only in autumn. But this etymology is contradicted by the usage of the Hebrews, among whom יונה jona, or יון jon, is not the οἰνὰς [oinas] but the dove in general, and properly the domestic one. Accordingly the οἰνὰς [oinas] dove was called by the Syrians ܟܪܡܝܘܢ [כרמיון] charmion, or ܟܪܡܝܘܢܐ [כרמיונא] charmiona, a word compounded of two, ܟܪܡ [כרם] and ܝܘܢ [יון], or ܝܘܢܐ [יונא], of which the former means vine and the latter dove. This was the very name of one of those famous handmaids of Cleopatra. In Greek it is written Χάρμιον [Charmion], or Χαρμιόνη [Charmionē], or Χαρμιουνώ [Charmiounō]. Plutarch in the Antony: Εἴρας ἡ Κλεοπάτρας κουρεύτρια, καὶ Χάρμιον, ὑφ᾽ ὧν τὰ μέγιστα διοικεῖται τῆς ἡγεμονίας· [Eiras hē Kleopatras koureutria, kai Charmion, hyph᾽ hōn ta megista dioikeitai tēs hēgemonias] Iras, Cleopatra's hairdresser, and Charmion, by whom the most important affairs of the realm were managed. And further on, regarding the death of Cleopatra: Τῶν δὲ γυναικῶν ἡ μὲν Εἴρας λεγομένη πρὸς τοῖς ποσὶν ἀπέθνησκεν· ἡ δὲ Χάρμιον, ἤδη σφαλλομένη, καὶ καρηβαροῦσα, κατεκόσμει τὸ διάδημα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς. [Tōn de gynaikōn hē men Eiras legomenē pros tois posin apethnēsken; hē de Charmion, ēdē sphallomenē, kai karēbarousa, katekosmei to diadēma peri tēn kephalēn autēs] Of her women, the one called Iras had died at her feet; Charmion, however, already tottering and heavy-headed, was adorning her head with the diadem. Galen, On theriac to Piso, book 1, chapter 8: Καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι λεγόμεναι Νάειρα, καὶ Καρμιόνη· ἡ μὲν ἀναπλέκουσα τὰς τρίχας εὐπρεπῶς, ἡ δὲ ἀποτέμνουσα τὰς ὑπεροχὰς τῶν ὀνύχων εὐφυῶς. [Kai tois onomasi legomenai Naeira, kai Karmionē; hē men anaplekousa tas trichas euprepōs, hē de apotemnousa tas hyperochas tōn onychōn euphyōs] And (Cleopatra's handmaids) called Naira and Carmione, of whom the former braided her hair becomingly, the latter skilfully trimmed the tips of her nails. Tzetzes, Chil. 6, Hist. 44:

Τῇ Κλεοπάτρᾳ τῇ σοφῇ, τῇ καὶ ὡραιοτάτῃ, Καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς δὲ σύμπασι πολλῶν ὑπερφερούσῃ, Πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν τριχῶν, καὶ τῶν ὀνύχων, ἦσαν Χαρμιουνὼ, καὶ Τάειρα τί δε δηλοῦσι τάδε; Σύρον τὸν Τζέτζην βλέπε νῦν, Ἰσμαηλίτην ἅμα, Καὶ ταῦτα διαρθροῦντα σοι ταῖς γλώσσαις ταῖς ἐκείνων. Κατὰ Ἑβραίων γλῶσσάν τε, καὶ τὴν τῶν Σύρων ἅμα, Χαρμὶ δηλοῖ τὴν ἀμπελον, Οὐνὼ περιστεράν δε, Τὴν, ἣν φησιν οἱ Ἕλληνες περιστερὰν οἰνάδα, Κατὰ Ἰσμαηλίτας δὲ, τοὺς Ἄγαρ γόνους λέγω, Περιστερὰν τὴν Γάειραν σημαίνουσάν μοι νόει. [Tē Kleopatra tē sophē, tē kai hōraiotatē, / Kai tois loipois de sympasi pollōn hyperpherousē, / Pros epimeleian trichōn, kai tōn onychōn, ēsan / Charmiounō, kai Taeira ti de dēlousi tade? / Syron ton Tzetzēn blepe nyn, Ismaēlitēn hama, / Kai tauta diarthrounta soi tais glōssais tais ekeinōn. / Kata Hebraiōn glōssan te, kai tēn tōn Syrōn hama, / Charmi dēloi tēn ampelon, Ounō peristeran de, / Tēn, hēn phēsin hoi Hellēnes peristeran oinada, / Kata Ismaēlitas de, tous Agar gonous legō, / Peristeran tēn Gaeiran sēmainousan moi noei.]

Cleopatra, wise, most beautiful, and far surpassing all other women, had for the care of her hair and nails Charmiuno and Taïra. But what do these names signify? See now Tzetzes, at once a Syrian and an Ishmaelite, explaining them to you in their languages. In the language of the Hebrews as well as of the Syrians, Charmi signifies the vine, and Uno the dove, which the Greeks call the oenas dove. But among the Ishmaelites, I mean those descended from Hagar, understand that Taïra signifies the dove to me. From this gather that in Plutarch for Εἴρας [Eiras], and in Galen for Νάειρα [Naeira], one must write Τάειρας [Taeiras] or Τάειρα [Taeira], as in Tzetzes, who indeed writes this word correctly but interprets it wrongly. For the Arabic طاير [ṭāyir] taïr, or طايرة [ṭāyira] taira, does not signify a dove, but a bird in general. Hence for the Chaldeans טייר tajer means to take auguries. Nor should Charmiuno have been divided into Charmi and Uno, but into כרם charm and יונא juno. Meanwhile there is no doubt that Charmiuno, or Charmiona, is truly οἰνάς [oinas]. So יונה jona by itself is not οἰνὰς [oinas], but any dove. This being granted, no reason appears why יונה jona should be named from wine. Therefore something else must be sought. Nor perhaps will it be absurd to think that doves were called by their native name יונים jonim, as if Greek ones. For the Greeks were formerly called Ἴωνες [Iōnes] Iones, as we have proved elsewhere; and in Hebrew יונים jonim, with the same letters, although today they pronounce javanim, because that pleased the Masoretes. Two things chiefly suggest that doves were named from this. One, that in Pliny, book 10, chapter 29, Theophrastus reports that doves were imported into Asia. The other, that mythical history amply shows that there were doves in Greece from all time. Thus 1. they say that the Dodonaean dove ἱζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν, αὐδάξασθαι φωνῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ, ὡς χρεὼν εἴη, μαντήϊον αὐτόθι Διὸς γένεσθαι [hizomenēn epi phēgon, audaxasthai phōnē anthrōpinē, hōs chreōn eiē, mantēion autothi Dios genesthai], sitting on a beech tree, said with a human voice that it was fated that an oracle of Jupiter should be founded in that place, which was by far the most ancient of all Greece. 2. As from Noah, so from Deucalion they relate περιστερὰν, ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην, δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ, ἀποπτᾶσαν [peristeran, ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn, dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de, apoptasan], that a dove, sent out from the ark, was a sign of storm when it returned there, and of fair weather when it flew away. 3. Doves are said to have fed Jupiter, crying as an infant in Crete, with ambrosia brought from Ocean, according to Moero of Byzantium in Athenaeus, book 11,

Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἐνὶ Κρήτῃ τρέφετο μέγας, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τίς νιν Ἠήδει μακάρων. ὁ δ᾽ ἀέξετο πᾶσι μέλεσσι Τὸν μὲν ἄρα τρήρωνες ὑπὸ ζαθέῳ τρέφον ἄντρῳ, Ἀμβροσίην φορέουσαι ἀπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων. [Zeus d᾽ ar᾽ eni Krētē trepheto megas, oud᾽ ara tis nin ēēdei makarōn. ho d᾽ aexeto pasi melessi; ton men ara trērōnes hypo zatheō trephon antrō, ambrosiēn phoreousai ap᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn.]

In Crete great Jupiter was nourished, and none of the Blessed knew him. And he grew in all his limbs. Doves, moreover, fed him in the divine cave, bringing ambrosia from the streams of Ocean. This is taken from Odyssey μ´ [12], where doves

— — ἀμβροσίην Διῒ πατρὶ φέρουσιν [ambrosiēn Dii patri pherousin], — — bring ambrosia to father Jupiter. Hence it is that in Plutarch's Symposium Cleodemus says to the poet Chersias: Εἰ τὴν ἀμβροσίαν τῷ Διῒ πελειάδες τινὲς κομίζουσιν, ὡς ὑμεῖς λέγετε [Ei tēn ambrosian tō Dii peleiades tines komizousin, hōs hymeis legete], If certain doves bring ambrosia to Jupiter, as you poets say. 4. At Aegium, a city of Achaea, Jupiter, changed into a dove, is said to have lain with the maiden Phthia. Athenaeus, book 9: Αὐτοκράτης ἐν τοῖς Ἀχαικοῖς καὶ τὸν Διὰ ἱστορεῖ μεταβαλεῖν τὴν μορφὴν εἰς περιστερὰν, ἐρασθέντα παρθένου Φθίας ὄνομα ἐν Αἰγείῳ [Autokratēs en tois Achaikois kai ton Dia historei metabalein tēn morphēn eis peristeran, erasthenta parthenou Phthias onoma en Aigeiō]. Autocrates in his Achaica relates that Jupiter himself, loving a maiden named Phthia in Aegium, changed his form into a dove. So too Aelian, Varia book 1, chapter 15. 5. The Argonauts, about to pass between the clashing Symplegades, were advised by the seer Phineus to send out a dove, and if it passed through them safely, they too should follow; and this they did. This dove is mentioned by Apollonius, book 2 of the Argonautica, Asclepiades, book 2 of the Τραγῳδούμενα [Tragōdoumena], Apollodorus, book 1 of the Bibliotheca, Hyginus, Fable 19, and not a few others. 6. When Ctesylla, daughter of Alcidamas of Ceos, who died in childbirth, was being carried out for burial, ἐκ τῆς στρομνῆς πελειὰς ἐξέπτη, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς Κτησύλλης ἀφανὲς ἐγένετο [ek tēs stromnēs peleias exeptē, kai to sōma tēs Ktēsyllēs aphanes egeneto], a dove flew out of the bier, and the body of Ctesylla vanished. So Nicander, book 3 of the Ἑτεροιούμενα [Heteroioumena]. Hence Ovid, of Medea borne through the air, Metamorphoses book 7, Fable 12,
He passes also the walls of ancient Carthaea on Ceos, where the father Alcidamas was to marvel that a gentle dove could be born from the body of his daughter.
7. In the same author (Metam. book 13, Fable 4), the Oenotropae, daughters of Anius, as their father Anius tells Anchises,
— — — took on wings, and were turned into the snow-white birds of your consort, doves.

That is, into the birds of Venus, who had been the consort of Anchises. These stories, however fabulous, nevertheless serve our purpose. For from them you may at least gather that, in the opinion of those who invented these fables, there had always been doves in Greece. 8. What of the fact that Homer calls Boeotian Thisbe and Laconian Messene πολυτρήρωνας [polytērōnas], from their abundance of doves, Iliad 2? And Pliny, book 5, chapter 31, lists near Smyrna seven islands called Peristerides, that is, Columbariae [Dove Islands]. It is therefore very likely that after the Flood doves first made their way into Greece and the neighbouring places, and from there were gradually dispersed over the rest of the world.

You will say that these things are adduced in vain, since in those most ancient times after the Flood Syria too was πολυτρήρονα [polytērona], as is proved both from sacred and from profane histories. For in the sacred histories Abraham, than whom the Greeks have nothing more ancient, is commanded to offer to God a turtledove and a dove, Gen 15:9. And throughout the Law of Moses sacrifices of turtledoves and young doves are prescribed . For examples see Lev 1:14 and V, 7. 11. and XII, 6. and XIV, 22. and XXV, 14. 29. and Num 6:10. In the profane histories too, Semiramis, believed to be a contemporary of Abraham, is said to have been exposed in desert and rocky places near Ascalon, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος, παραδόξως τροφῆς καὶ σωτηρίας τυχεῖν τὸ βρέφος [en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos, paradoxōs trophēs kai sōtērias tychein to brephos], where, since a great multitude of doves was accustomed to nest, the infant was wondrously fed and preserved. Indeed, the name of Semiramis is derived from the same source, as being κατὰ τὴν τῶν Σύρων διάλεκτον παρωνομασμένον ἀπὸ τῶν περιστερῶν [kata tēn tōn Syrōn dialekton parōnomasmenon apo tōn peristerōn], taken from doves in the language of the Syrians. So Diodorus, from Ctesias, in book 2. And R. Azarias [=Azariah de' Rossi, Meʾor ʿEnayim], in Meor Enajim, chapter 21, derives it from the word זמיר zemir, which denotes the song of birds, and specifically of the turtledove, Song 2:12. His words are as follows: נקראת סמיראמיס אשר לפי דבריו בלשון הארמי יורה על צפצוף העוף ולדעתי הוא מלשון עת הזמיר הגיע בחלוף הזין בסמך וכן בארמי פק דנטין זמרא דמנא זמרא דפומא ולזה אות דגלה היה יונה She is called Semiramis, which, according to his words, (that is, those of Diodorus, whom he had cited) signifies in the Syrian language the song of birds. This seems to be taken from the word זמיר zemir, as it is said in Song 2:12 "The time of zemir, that is, of song, has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land." For also in Syriac, in the Talmudic tractate Gittin, chapter 1, זמרא דמנא zemara demana is instrumental music, and זמרא דפומא zemara dephuma vocal music. And therefore Semiramis had a dove as the emblem of her banner. Indeed, he contends in what follows that not only Semiramis but all the kings of Assyria had a dove as the symbol of their banners. And that this is why, for the wrath and sword of the Assyrians, Jeremiah had said חרון היונה, the wrath of the dove, Jer 25:38 and חרב היונה, the sword of the dove, Jer 46:16, and L, 16. This he confirms from the version of Jerome and from the Commentaries of Thomas Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] on Jeremiah. To the same he also refers the fact that Jerusalem in Zeph 3:1 is called היונה, the dove, as if the Prophet were reproaching her שהיא במעשיו דומה לבבל אשר אות דגלה יונה, that in her deeds she is like Babylon, which had a dove on its banner as its military emblem. And following him, R. David Ganz, in book 2 of his Chronology, at the year 1958: The emblem of the banner of Semiramis was the figure of a dove. This banner emblem all the kings of Assyria imitated. Hence Jeremiah, chapter XXV, verse 28: "Because of the wrath of the dove"; and chapter XLVI, verse 6: "Before the sword of the dove". To this the ancients add that Semiramis was changed into a dove. Diodorus, in the place cited above: Ἔνιοι δὲ μυθολογοῦντές φασιν αὐτὴν γενέσθαι περιστερὰν, καὶ πολλῶν ὀρνέων εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν καταπετασθέντων, μετ᾽ ἐκείνων ἐκπετασθῆναι· [Enioi de mythologountes phasin autēn genesthai peristeran, kai pollōn orneōn eis tēn oikian katapetasthentōn, met᾽ ekeinōn ekpetasthēnai] But others tell the fable that she became a dove, and that when many birds had flown into the house, she flew away with them. Ovid, Metam. book 4, Fable 2, where, concerning her mother Derceto,

Or rather, that, having taken wings from that daughter of hers, she spent her last years in lofty towers? Lucian in De Syria Dea: Τὸ Σεμιράμιος τέλος εἰς περιστερὰν ἀπίκετο [To Semiramios telos eis peristeran apiketo], Semiramis was at last turned into a dove. Athenagoras, in the Legatio, on the same woman: Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, εἰς περιστερὰν μετέβαλεν ἡ γυνή· ὁ μύθος παρὰ Κτησίᾳ [To gar adynaton, eis peristeran metebalen hē gynē; ho mythos para Ktēsia]. For, what is impossible, the woman was changed into a dove. The tale is found in Ctesias. This is why among the Syrians and Assyrians doves were held in great veneration, as Ctesias teaches in Diodorus, after relating that Semiramis was nourished by doves and also took her name from them: Ἃς ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνων τῶν χρόνων, οἱ κατὰ Συρίαν ἅπαντες διετέλεσαν, ὡς Θεὰς τιμῶντες [Has ap᾽ ekeinōn tōn chronōn, hoi kata Syrian hapantes dietelesan, hōs Theas timōntes]; These, from those times on, all the Syrians have never ceased to worship as goddesses. And after the story of her metamorphosis into a dove the same author adds: Διὸ καὶ τοὺς Ἀσσυρίους τὴν περιστερὰν τιμᾷν ὡς Θεὸν, ἀπαθανατίζοντες τὴν Σεμίραμιν [Dio kai tous Assyrious tēn peristeran timan hōs Theon, apathanatizontes tēn Semiramin]; Hence the Assyrians also venerate the dove as a goddess, in order to rescue Semiramis from death. Xenophon too, in book 1 of the Cyrus the Younger, speaking of the fish of the Chalus, a river of Syria: Οὓς οἱ Σύροι Θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, καὶ ἀδικεῖν οὐκ εἴων, οὐδὲ τὰς περιστεράς [Hous hoi Syroi Theous enomizon, kai adikein ouk eiōn, oude tas peristeras]. These the Syrians regarded as gods, and forbade anyone to harm them, as also the doves. Philo in Eusebius, near the end of book 8 of the Praeparatio Evangelica: Ἀμήχανόν τι πελειάδων πλῆθος ἐπὶ τῶν τριόδων, καὶ κατ᾽ οἰκίαν ἑκάστην, ἐθεασάμην. πυνθανομένῳ δέ μοι τὴν αἰτίαν ἔφασαν, οὐ θεμιτὸν εἶναι συλλαμβάνειν. ἀπειρῆσθαι γὰρ ἐκ παλαίου τοῖς οἰκήτορσι τὴν χρῆσιν [Amēchanon ti peleiadōn plēthos epi tōn triodōn, kai kat᾽ oikian hekastēn, etheasamēn. pynthanomenō de moi tēn aitian ephasan, ou themiton einai syllambanein. apeirēsthai gar ek palaiou tois oikētorsi tēn chrēsin]. I saw an immense multitude of doves at the crossroads and in every house (at Ascalon). And when I asked the reason, they answered that it was unlawful to catch them, for their use had long ago been forbidden to the inhabitants. Tibullus, Elegy 8:
The white dove, sacred to the man of Palestine.

Al. Syro, or suo. Hyginus, Fab. 197: the Syrians regard fish and doves as among the gods; they do not eat them. Lucian, in the place cited above, on the Hierapolitans: Ὀρνίθων τε αὐτέοισι περιστερὴ δοκέει χρῆμα ἱρώτατον, καὶ οὐδὲ ψαύειν αὐτέων δικαιεῦσι· [Ornithōn te auteoisi peristerē dokeei chrēma hirōtaton, kai oude psauein auteōn dikaieusi] Among birds the dove seems to them the most sacred, and they do not think it right even to touch it. Likewise: Ὄρνιθας τοὺς μὲν ἄλλους σιτέονται· περιστερὴν δὲ μούνην οὐ σιτέονται, ἀλλὰ σφίσι ἥδε ἱερή. [Ornithas tous men allous siteontai; peristerēn de mounēn ou siteontai, alla sphisi hēde hierē] They eat other birds, but abstain from the dove alone, which is sacred to them. Phornutus [=L. Annaeus Cornutus, De natura deorum], in the book On the Gods, in the chapter on Rhea: Ἔοικε δὲ ἡ αὐτὴ ἡ παρὰ Σύροις Ἄρταγα εἶναι, ἣν διὰ τὸ περιστερὰς καὶ ἰχθύος ἀπέχεσθαι τιμῶσι· [Eoike de hē autē hē para Syrois Artaga einai, hēn dia to peristeras kai ichthyos apechesthai timōsi] She seems to be the same as the one whom the Syrians call Artaga (others Atergatis and Derceto) and whom they worship by abstaining from fish and the dove. Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus: Οὐδέ γε τῶν τὴν Φοινίκην Σύρων κατοικούντων (ἐκλήσομαι) ὧν οἱ μὲν τὰς περιστερὰς, οἱ δὲ τοὺς ἰχθῦς οὕτω σέβουσι περιττῶς, ὡς Ἠλεῖοι τὸν Δία· [Oude ge tōn tēn Phoinikēn Syrōn katoikountōn (eklēsomai) hōn hoi men tas peristeras, hoi de tous ichthys houtō sebousi perittōs, hōs Ēleioi ton Dia] Nor shall I forget the Syrians who live in Phoenicia, some of whom worship doves, others fish, as fervently as the Eleans worship Jupiter. Meor enajim: ונמצאו קצת אמות שבכה אהבו את זכר סמיראמיס ואות דגלה שאסרו על עצמן לאכול את בני היונה And certain nations were found who so revered the memory of Semiramis and the emblem of her banner that they forbade themselves to eat doves. Nor were the Samaritans free from this superstition, if indeed we believe the Jews. The Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 1, fol. 6a, on the Cuthaeans or Samaritans: אמר רב נחמן בר יצחק דמות יונה מצאו להן בראש הר גריזים שהיו עובדין אותה Said Rab Nachman, son of Isaac: they found among them the image of a dove, which they worshipped on Mount Gerizim. The gloss on the Talmudic tractate Avodazera, fol. 26b: אל ימול כותי שמל לשם דמות שנמצאו בראש הר גריזים ועובדין לה עבודה כדאמר בהכל שיחטין ומלו את בניהם לשם יונה זו, A Cuthaean shall not circumcise, for he circumcises in the name of the image which they found on the summit of Mount Gerizim, and they worship it, as is related in the chapter (of Cholin, cited above, which begins) "All slaughter": and they circumcise their sons in the name of this dove. Meor enajim: קרוב בעיני להאמין שהכותיים אשר הושיב מלך אשור ובבל בשומרון לאות ולעד הכנעם באהבה אל מלכם ההוא אשר אות דגלה יונה חבבו אותה והקימוהו ליראתם בראש הר גריזים אשר עם שכם ראש ממלכת שומרון בימים ההם, I am fully persuaded that the Cuthaeans, whom the king of Assyria and Babylonia had deported to Samaria, as a sign and testimony of their love and devotion toward their king, who had the dove as the emblem of his banner, loved the dove, and erected a statue, which they worshipped, on the summit of Mount Gerizim, near the city of Shechem, which was then the capital of the Samaritan kingdom. Tsemach David, in the Chronology of the Second Temple, at the year 881: In the days of R. Meir they found the Cuthaeans' image of a dove on Mount Gerizim, as is stated in the first chapter of Cholin. And he decreed that they should be treated in every respect as gentiles of the land. .

From this it might seem possible to conclude that doves have nested in Syria as well as in Greece from all time. Yet there is an objection to be raised: in the age of Moses, it is true, בני יונה, young of doves, were offered even by common people in Israel, as the Law expressly prescribes; but whether Abraham offered the same can be called into question. For we do not read that he offered תור ובן יונה, a turtledove and a young dove, as is commanded in the Law of Moses, but תור וגוזל, a turtledove and a gozal. This word signifies not only the young of the dove properly so called, but also the young of the turtledove, of the wood pigeon, of the livia, of the vinago, and of any other bird that may be assigned to the dove kind. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On القطا [al-qaṭā] alkata, as the Arabs call a certain kind of wood pigeon, writes: يقال القطا والحمام وانواعها امهات الجوازل والجوازل فراخها الواحد جوزل [yuqāl al-qaṭā wa-l-ḥamām wa-anwāʿuhā ummahāt al-jawāzil wa-l-jawāzil firākhuhā al-wāḥid jawzal] "Alkata and the dove, and birds of the same kind are called the mothers of the algavvazil. And the algavvazil are their young, from the singular gauzal." Now جوزل [jawzal] gauzal is for the Arabs exactly what גוזל gozal is for the Hebrews. Accordingly, since there are various species of gozal, when a pipio [squab] is meant precisely, there is sometimes added, by way of distinction, "gozal, young of the dove." Thus in the Chaldee paraphrast of the Song of Songs, chapter 1, verse 15: "Your eyes are כגוזלין בני יונתא, like gozalin, young of the dove." And Vajikra Rabba [=Leviticus Rabbah], chapter 22, on the emperor Titus: קראו לרופאים ומצאו בו כמו גוזל בן יונה והיה בו משקל שתי לטראות, "They called the physicians, who (when his skull had been cut open) found in it something like a gozal, a young of the dove, weighing two pounds." It is called gozal, or gauzal, from its peeping, just as in Latin pipio. For الجزل [al-jazl] algezel is pipitus [peeping]. In the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] it is rendered صوت الحمام [ṣawt al-ḥamām] the voice of the dove, namely of one still peeping and not yet grown. Therefore those are mistaken who derive גוזל gozal from the verb גזל gazal, that is, to seize, because it is exposed to plunder. The Syrians, by metathesis, say ܙܘܓܠ [זוגל] zogal instead of ܓܘܙܠ [גוזל] gozal. But the Phoenicians of old said gozol. Hence peristereon is in Punic חציר־גוזול azirgozol, that is, herb of the squab, in the Herbarium of Apuleius, chapter 65.

Now, the same objection could be raised regarding the doves of Semiramis. For although the later Syrians also worshipped יונים jonim, that is, domestic doves, those properly so called, out of regard for Semiramis, it nevertheless seems possible to infer, even from Ctesias, that wild doves were attendant on her. For he calls the places in which those doves lived desert and rocky, ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους [erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous]. Accordingly the name of Semiramis, taken from this, is explained by Hesychius as περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], mountain dove. We have shown elsewhere that this word is Arabic, not Syrian as is supposed, and that it was written Serimam, which the Greeks changed διὰ τὴν εὐφωνίαν [dia tēn euphōnian] into Σεμίραμιν [Semiramin].
