For among the Arabs حمام [ḥmām] himam is dove, and سراة [srāh] sera mountain, شعرا [shʿrā] sera forest, صحرا [ṣḥrā] sahra desert; from some one of these words joined with حمام [ḥmām] himam the name Serimam was formed, for dove of the mountain, or of the forest, or of the desert. Such is the composition in the words כרמיון charmion or כרמיונא charmiona, of which we have spoken, and חריונים chirjonim or דביונים dibjonim, of which we shall speak. But the chief point is this: from the history of Semiramis it can in no way be proved that doves were already worshipped in Syria in ancient times, because her date is quite uncertain. For if we follow Ctesias, a highly fabulous writer, Semiramis was the wife of Ninus, whose reign would fall in the times of Abraham. But others make Semiramis the daughter of Belochus, who was more than five hundred years later than Ninus. Hence Eusebius at the number 582, which is the tenth year from the death of Joshua: Eighteenth king of the Assyrians, Belochus, for 25 years; whose daughter Atossa, who is also Semiramis, reigned with her father for 12 years. And Photius, on author 186, concerning the Canon, Hist. 9: Ὅσα οἱ ἄλλοι περὶ Ἀττόσης Ἀσσυρίου ἀναγράφουσι, ταῦθ᾽ οὗτος εἰς Σεμίραμιν ἀναφέρει· [Hosa hoi alloi peri Attosēs Assyriou anagraphousi, tauth᾽ houtos eis Semiramin anapherei] Whatever others write about Atossa the Assyrian, he refers to Semiramis. But, what is more surprising, if we believe Herodotus in his first book, Semiramis was older only by πέντε γενεαῖς [pente geneais], five generations, that is, at most two hundred years, than Nitocris, the mother of that Labonitus whom Cyrus defeated. Yet between Cyrus and Belochus more than a thousand years intervene, and between him and Ninus fifteen or sixteen hundred. Nor can the deeds of Semiramis be referred to the age of Abraham, when, as may be gathered from Gen. XIV, the king of שנער, or Babylonia, was a petty prince. And equally uncertain is what some assert, that the kings of Babylonia had the dove as a military standard, since no ancient author is cited who reports this . And it is most probable that Cyrus, after subjecting the Babylonians to his rule, adopted the same military standards that his predecessors, the Medes and Assyrians, had had. But that he had an eagle as his standard is clear from these words of Xenophon in the seventh book of the Cyropaedia: Ἦν δ᾽ αὐτῷ τὸ σημεῖον ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμένος [Ēn d᾽ autō to sēmeion aetos chrysous epi doratos makrou anatetamenos]. His standard was a golden eagle, stretched out upon a long spear. This all the kings of the Persians thereafter imitated. The same Xenophon: Καὶ νῦν δὲ ἔτι τοῦτο τὸ σημεῖον τῷ Περσῶν βασιλεῖ διαμένει· [Kai nyn de eti touto to sēmeion tō Persōn basilei diamenei] This standard still remains even today for the king of the Persians. Curtius, book 3, on the army of Darius: Among these they had consecrated a golden eagle, resembling one spreading its wings. Philostratus in the Heroica, in the chapter on Themistocles: Μῆδοι ταῦτα, καὶ Βαβυλὼν μέση, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τὸ βασίλειον ὁ χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ τῆς πέλτης ἀετός· [Mēdoi tauta, kai Babylōn mesē, kai to sēmeion to basileion ho chrysous epi tēs peltēs aetos] These things are the Medes, and Babylon in the middle, and the military standard, a golden eagle upon a spear. Therefore in Jeremiah [XXV, 38. XLVI,16. L,16.] חרב היונה is not, as I at least think, the sword of the dove, but the oppressing or devastating sword, such as that of the Babylonians was under King Nebuchadnezzar . Accordingly the prophet says of the same, Jer 46:14: אכלה חרב סביביך, The sword has devoured round about you. But that the Samaritans also worshipped doves is entirely fabulous. What idols they worshipped when they were first transplanted from Assyria into Samaria is related in 2 Reg. XVII, 30. 31.: The men of Babylon made Succoth-Benoth, the Cuthites made Nergal, etc. But there the Sacred History says not a γρῦ [gry] about a dove, or its image, worshipped by them. Nor was this anywhere charged against them by Josephus, who in many places inveighs sharply against them. See the ninth book of the Jewish Antiquities, and the end of the eleventh; and chapters 1 and 7 of book 12; and chapter 6 of book 13; and chapters 3 and 5 of book 18; and chapter 5 of book 20. Nor could the worship of the dove, or of its image, in any way have been consistent with the Law of Moses, which they accepted. For, to say nothing of the fact that all images are forbidden so often and so expressly by Moses, on what pretext could they possibly have worshipped the very animal which they were commanded to slaughter to God in sacrifice? Nevertheless it is undoubtedly true, as Xenophon, Ctesias, Lucian and other eyewitnesses, αὐτόπται [autoptai], assert, that the Syrians and Assyrians either worshipped doves as goddesses, or at least abstained from them as from something sacred. But at what precise time this superstition was introduced into Syria or Assyria, no one could easily say.
Plutarch, in the book Utra anim.

That the dove was given the name יונה because it had been brought from Greece into Asia seems hardly probable. For what Bochart proves with a great display of learning, that doves are mentioned in Greece from all time past, is irrelevant to the matter. Does it follow from this that doves were native to no other region, or that they were brought from Greece into Asia? I am therefore surprised that this opinion pleased Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], so much that he even adorned it with new arguments, in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. 4, p. 1094 ff. I would think that the dove was given its name from its gentleness, a notion present in the Arabic verbs أَانَ [ʾāna] and هَانَ [hāna], whence أون [ʾawn] is mildness, affability, and هون [hawn] gentleness, mildness, so that it corresponds in a way to the Chaldee הון, rest, ease. Other conjectures on the reason for that name will be given by Simonis in the Arcanum Formarum, p. 42.

The emptiness of this opinion has been shown at length by J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1096 ff., and in the Observationes Criticae et Philologicae in Ieremiae Vaticinia, on Chapter XXV, 38., with which compare Schleusner, a most reverend man, on Michaelis' Observationes in Ierem. XLVI, 16, p. 309.
This interpretation has been defended by the two men praised in the preceding note, in the places mentioned there.
On the dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight.

I am pleased to begin the description of the dove with its plumage and feathers, whose beauty the sacred poet commends thus, Ps 68:14: The wings of the dove covered with silver, and its feathers with the paleness of gold. Wings and feathers stand here by συνεκδοχὴν [synekdochēn] for the whole body. Covered with silver, that is, supremely white like silver, and bright with a certain splendour. For silver is called in Greek ἀργύριον [argyrion], from τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν [to argon, to leukon, "the bright, the white"]; and things that are most brilliantly white are called silver. Hence in the poets ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], that is, λευκόπους [leukopous]. So it is in Hesychius, who likewise explains ἀργυροδίνην κρήνην [argyrodinēn krēnēn] as λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν [leuka rheumata echousan]; and in the eighth book of the Aeneid,
is, on the testimony of Servius, an epithet of colour. The raven too was once a silver bird, when it equalled doves in whiteness. Ovid, Metam. book 2, Fable 7:

For this was once a silver bird with snowy feathers, so that it equalled doves wholly without blemish. For among doves some are extremely white . Varro, On Agriculture book 3, ch. 7: The other kind of doves is the tamer, which, content with household food, is usually fed within the threshold of the door. This kind is mostly white in colour. That is, at some times and in some places, not always nor everywhere. For in Greece white doves were seen late, namely when the forces of Xerxes were routed at Mount Athos. This is expressly reported in the Persica by Charon of Lampsacus, who lived at that time and wrote before Herodotus. Athenaeus, book 9: Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περσικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“ [Charōn d᾽ ho Lampsakēnos, en tois Persikois peri Mardoniou historōn, kai tou diaphtharentos stratou Persikou peri ton Athō, graphei tauta: "Kai leukai peristerai tote prōton eis Hellēnas ephanēsan, proteron ou gignomenai"]. Charon of Lampsacus, in the Persica, treating of Mardonius and of the Persian army routed at Mount Athos, writes this: "And white doves were then first seen among the Greeks, there having been none before", namely in Greece, not anywhere, as the translator there wrongly has it. Aelian in the Varia book 1, ch. 15: Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω [Charōn de ho Lampsakēnos peri ton Athō phanēnai peristeras leukas legei, hote entautha apōlonto hai tōn Persōn triereis parakamptousai ton Athō]; But Charon of Lampsacus asserts that white doves were seen around Athos when the triremes of the Persians perished there while sailing past Athos. There follows in the Psalm ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, And its feathers with the paleness of gold; supply covered, which must be repeated from the preceding hemistich. Paleness of gold, that is, gold of paleness, or pale gold. Similar is Hab 2:6. עב טיט, thickness of mud, for mud of thickness, or thick mud. התואר במקום המתואר, the predicate for the subject, as Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] has it here. Gold is called חרוץ charuts, that is, dug out of the earth, here and in Zech 9:3 and frequently in Solomon's Proverbs . From this comes the Greek χρυσός [chrysos]. And the paleness of gold is ירקרק, with doubled letters, so that the meaning is intensified. Accordingly from this very word comes the Ethiopic ወርቅ፡ [warəq] vvark for gold. The Greek translators rightly call the paleness of gold χλωρότητα χρυσίου [chlōrotēta chrysiou]. For this is the true colour of gold. Hence Diogenes, asked Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; [Dia ti to chrysion chlōron estin?] Why is gold pale?, answered Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας [Hoti pollous echei tous epibouleuontas], Because it has many plotting against it. So it is in Laertius; and Catullus in the wedding of Peleus and Thetis,
O how often she grew paler than the sallow hue of gold!
A guest paler than a gilded statue.
And Statius to Maximus Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] in the fourth book of the Silvae,
When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back to sweet Latium, where, having seen Dis, the pale miner returns, of the same colour as the gold he has dug up?

And Lucian in the Cock, to a greedy rich man: Οἴμωζε, καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ ὅμοιος γίγνου τὸ χρῶμα τῷ χρυσῷ, προσετηκὼς αὐτῷ [oimōze, kai agrypnei, kai homoios gignou to chrōma tō chrysō, prosetēkōs autō]; Lament and keep watch, and, wasting away over your gold, become like it in colour. Now, if you ask why this golden colour is attributed to doves, Kimchi answers: שיש בכנפי היונה נוצה שהמצהבת כזהב, In the wings of doves there is plumage yellow like gold: namely in the wings of the younger birds, after they have left the nest. The Talmudists observe the same of turtledoves, and say that from this one learns when they are fit or unfit for sacrifice. For since the Law commands that of doves only the young, and of turtledoves only the adults, be offered, they hold that the former become unfit for sacrifice, and the latter fit, precisely when the feathers begin to turn yellow like gold. The words are in the tractate Cholin, chapter 1, folio 22b: מאימתי התורים כשרים משיצהיבו מאימתי בני יונה פסולים משיצהיבו When are turtledoves (for offering) fit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. When are young doves (for offering) unfit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. And on the word משיצהיבו the Gloss has: שיהא כנפי גופן גדולים ואדומים ומזהיבים כזהב, because the feathers of the body become large and red, and yellow like gold. And somewhat earlier: תחילה הציהב כשמתחילין לצהב כנפים שמסביבות צוארן The beginning of the yellowing is when the feathers they have around the neck begin to turn yellow like gold. So also Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] in Issure Mizbeach ch. 3, §2: והתורים כשרים משיזהבו Turtledoves are fit for offering from the time they have a golden colour. Where the Gloss is the same as in the Talmud above. But the necks of doves too, when facing the sun, shine with a golden colour. The Philosopher, in the book On Colours: Οἱ τῶν περιστερῶν τράχηλοι, καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων οἱ σταλαγμοὶ φαίνονται χρυσοειδεῖς, τοῦ φωτὸς ἀνακλωμένου [Hoi tōn peristerōn trachēloi, kai tōn hydatōn hoi stalagmoi phainontai chrysoeideis, tou phōtos anaklōmenou]. The necks of doves and drops of water appear to be of a golden colour when the light is reflected. Others write only that they gleam with various colours. Lucretius, book 2, line 800:

As the plumage of doves appears in the sun, which, set about the nape, crowns the neck: for at times it comes to be red with bright fire-bronze, at times, by a certain way of seeing, it seems to mingle green emeralds with sky-blue.

Philo, in the book On Drunkenness: Τὸν αὐχένα τῆς περιστερᾶς ἐν ἡλιακαῖς αὐγαῖς οὐ κατενόησας μυρίας χρωμάτων ἀλλάττοντα ἰδέας; ἢ οὐχὶ φοινικοῦν, καὶ κυανοῦν, πυροπόν τε, καὶ ἀνθρακοειδὲς, ἔτι τε ὠχρὸν, καὶ ἐρυθρὸν, καὶ ἄλλα παντόδαπα ἴσχει χρώματα, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς κλήσεις ῥάδιον ἀπομνημονεῦσαι [Ton auchena tēs peristeras en hēliakais augais ou katenoēsas myrias chrōmatōn allattonta ideas? ē ouchi phoinikoun, kai kyanoun, pyropon te, kai anthrakoeides, eti te ōchron, kai erythron, kai alla pantodapa ischei chrōmata, hōn oude tas klēseis rhadion apomnēmoneusai]. Have you never seen a dove's neck in the sun's rays varied into countless colours? Does it not have crimson, and sky-blue, and the colours of fire-bronze and of carbuncle, and pale, and red, and colours of every other kind, whose mere names it would not be easy to recount? This Eustathius copied almost word for word in the Hexaemeron, page 29. Nero, in Seneca, Natural Questions book 1, ch. 5:
The necks of Cytherea's dove shine as it moves.

Pliny, book 10, chapter 26: Doves have a certain sense even of glory. You would think they know their own colours and the ordered variety of them. And book 37, chapter 5: The Carchedonian, etc. uncertain in colour, and like the feathers of the green in peacocks' tails and on the necks of doves. Ausonius, on ducks, Epistle 3:
Whom iridescent plumage has painted with varied colour, rivals of doves in their necks.

But these colours are only apparent. Thus in Martianus, book 2, Arcesilas, gazing at the neck of doves and moved by this uncertainty of variation, began to build up further his doctrine of ἀκαταληψία [akatalēpsia]. And Carneades, to prove that our senses are uncertain, brought forward the necks of doves, which change colour at every turn. So Jerome attests in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. But Oppian, in book 1 of the Cynegetica, taught that the young even in the egg can be marked with various colours, and real ones at that: namely if, when the females are about to mate, there are set before them

— — — — — δαίδαλα πολλὰ Εἵματα πορφύρεα· ταὶ δὲ κλιδὸν ὄσσε βαλοῦσαι, Θυμὸν ἰαινόμεναι τίκτουσ᾽ ἁλιπόρφυρα τέκνα, [— — — — — daidala polla heimata porphyrea; tai de klidon osse balousai, thymon iainomenai tiktous' haliporphyra tekna,]

many richly wrought purple garments: and they, casting sidelong glances at them and delighted in mind, bring forth purple young. I cite this the more gladly because by a similar art Jacob obtained parti-coloured sheep for himself.

The eyes of doves are attributed to the bride in Song 1:15 and IV, 1., and to the bridegroom as well in Song 5:12; that is, eyes that are pure, lovely, simple, and finally chaste. This last is what the Hebrews chiefly understand here, because the dove looks only to its mate and does not cast its eyes on any other. Rabbi Selomo: משמכרת את בן זוגה אונה מניחתו שיזדווג לאחר, After she has been betrothed to her mate, she does not delight in being joined to another. And Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra]: מנהג בני יונה שלא להתחבר אלא עם זוגה שלה, Doves are not accustomed to associate with any other than their own mate. Aelian teaches the same of the wood pigeon in Hist. book 3, ch. 44, and then says: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐποφθαλμιάσωσιν ἑτέροις, περιέρχονται αὐτοὺς οἱ λοιποὶ, καὶ τὸν μὲν ἄῤῥενα οἱ ὁμογενεῖς διασπῶσιν, αἱ θήλειαι δὲ τὸν θῆλυν [Ean de epophthalmiasōsin heterois, perierchontai autous hoi loipoi, kai ton men arrena hoi homogeneis diaspōsin, hai thēleiai de ton thēlyn]; But if they cast lustful eyes on others, the rest surround them, and the males tear the male to pieces, the females the female. Note here that the verb ἐποφθαλμιᾶν [epophthalmian] is used of a lustful look, because the eyes are the leaders in love, and ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται ἐρᾷν [ek tou horan ginetai eran]. Hence John speaks of Ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν [Hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn], and Peter of ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες μεστοὺς μοιχαλίδος [ophthalmous echontes mestous moichalidos]. David , having learned this to his own cost, earnestly asked God to turn his eyes away so that they should not behold vanity. And Job made a covenant with them that they should not look upon a virgin. The interpreters inquire anxiously what these words refer to in Song 5:12: His eyes (the bridegroom's) are like (the eyes) of doves by the streams of waters, washed in milk, dwelling by the fullness. I think the sacred writer had only this in view: that doves have livelier eyes by the waters, because they prefer to live near them. Accordingly Varro (De re rustica, book 3, chapter 7), in his description of the dovecote, τῆς περιστεροφείου [tēs peristeropheiou], says: There should be pure water flowing in, from which they can both drink and bathe; for these birds are very clean. And they are described not only as by the waters but also as by the fullness (supply "of the waters", as Scripture repeatedly speaks of the fullness of the sea), that is, by places where waters gush forth and come up close to the top of the banks, so that they are easy to drink from. The same doves are said to be washed in milk, that is, very white, as if things washed in milk became white, as things washed in ink become black. Compare Job. IX, 30.: If I wash myself with snow water, and cleanse my hands with soap. Far-fetched, and found nowhere else so far as I know, is the view of Gregory on the Canticle, chapter 5, that doves sit beside streams so that they may see in the water the shadow of birds flying overhead, and by throwing themselves upon it may thus escape the talons of birds of prey. But this seems to have been taken in part from the story of a certain bird which in Arabic is called خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi] chatipho-dhillihi, as if to say snatcher of its own shadow, because اذا راي ظله في الما اقبل اليه ليخطفه [idhā rāy ẓillahu fī al-mā aqbala ilayhi li-yakhṭafahu], when it sees its shadow in the water, it approaches it in order to snatch it. So Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]. In Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] it is called otherwise: قرلا [qirlā] koralla, a Persian word; رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph, from the fluttering of its wings; and ملاعب ظله [mulāʿib ẓillihi] mulaibo dhillihi, playing with its shadow. It is asserted to be في جنس العصافير [fī jins al-ʿaṣāfīr] of the kind of sparrows, or small birds. It is therefore not the jackdaw, which I once thought it was, because Tzetzes says of jackdaws in Chiliad 4, Hist. 119:

— εἴπερ χέεις ἔλαιον ἔν τινι λεκανίσκῃ, Πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν τὴν ἑαυτῶν τοὺς κολοιοὺς κρατήσῃς. Ναρκίσσους ἄλλους Λάκωνας ὄντας τῶν φιλοσκίων. [— eiper cheeis elaion en tini lekaniskē, Pros tēn skian tēn heautōn tous koloious kratēsēs. Narkissous allous Lakōnas ontas tōn philoskiōn.]

If you pour oil into a small basin, you will hold the jackdaws fast at their own shadow, as if they were Laconian Narcissi, of those who love their own shadow. Note in passing that Narcissus was not a Laconian but a Boeotian, as Ovid, Metam. book 3, Fab. 5, Conon, Hist. 24, Strabo, book 9, Hyginus, Fab. 271, Pausanias in the Boeotica, Claudian, book 2 de raptu, and countless others attest. Yet Tzetzes makes him a Laconian both here and in Chil. 1, Hist. 9, as if he were a countryman of Hyacinthus, with whom he compares him in Hist. 11. This μνημονικὸν σφάλμα [mnēmonikon sphalma] is not to be tolerated in a man who, in that very passage, boasts thus:
Οὐδὲ γὰρ μνημονέστερον τοῦ Τζέτζου Θεὸς ἄλλον Ἄνδρα τῶν πρίν τε, καὶ τῶν νῦν ἐξέφηνεν ἐν βίῳ. [Oude gar mnēmonesteron tou Tzetzou Theos allon Andra tōn prin te, kai tōn nyn exephēnen en biō.]

For God has not brought into life any other man more mindful than Tzetzes, of those who have been or who now are. And shortly before he had said that he knew all books. But, to return to the point from which we digressed, the Hebrews render the sacred words, which we refer to doves as to the eyes of doves, thus: His eyes are like doves' (eyes) by the courses of waters, washed with milk, set in fullness, that is, filling their place like a gem its setting. This is what in Hebrew is called מלואת אבן, fullness or filling of stone, Exod 28:17. So Aben Ezra and R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], who holds that the eyes are described as לא בולטות יותר מדאי ולא שיקעות אלא יושבות מלאת גומא שלהם, neither more prominent than is fitting, nor sunken, but so placed that they fill their socket. And the recent interpreters follow this. But in this interpretation I find some things lacking. First, that in this way a milky colour seems to be attributed to the eyes, whose principal part, that is, the pupil, is black, or blue, etc. Second, that although stones enclosed in a setting are called in Hebrew אבני מלואים, stones of fillings, that is, which fill the setting, and the setting of a stone in a bezel is called מלואת אבן, filling of stone, yet a stone set in a bezel is nowhere said to be יושב על מלאת, remaining at fullness. Nor indeed can this be said. For who would say that money remains or stands at the fullness of a bag, or wine at the fullness of a cask, when the bag is full of money, or the cask full of wine ?
In the voice of the dove there is something plaintive and moaning. Hence doves are said to moan. The author of the Philomela:
And the chaste turtledove and the dove moan.
Virgil, Eclogue 1: Yet meanwhile neither will the hoarse wood-pigeons, your care, nor the turtledove cease to moan from the airy elm.
Here moans the wood-pigeon, there the wax-coloured turtledove.

Gregory on Job, book 32, ch. 4: We know that the young of doves, or turtledoves, have moaning instead of song. And on the Song, ch. 1: The dove in its love moans instead of singing. For the Greeks too this same thing is στένειν [stenein]. Theocritus, Idyll 7, verse 141:
Ἄειδον κόρυδοι, καὶ ἀκανθίδες, ἔστενε τρυγὼν, [Aeidon korydoi, kai akanthides, estene trygōn,]

The larks and goldfinches were singing, the turtledove was moaning. Hence Chrysostom, in the Homily On the Turtledove: Ἡ τρυγὼν ἡ φιλέρημος, ὅτε ἐν ὕλαις συγκοιταζομένη καλεῖ τὸν ὁμόζυγον, γοεραῖς κολακείαις τὰς κοιλάδας δονήσασα· [Hē trygōn hē philerēmos, hote en hylais synkoitazomenē kalei ton homozygon, goerais kolakeiais tas koilada donēsasa;] The solitary turtledove, when lying in the woods it calls its mate, stirring the valleys with mournful blandishments. Others say that turtledoves τρύζειν [tryzein] and doves γογγύζειν [gongyzein]. Pollux, book 5, chapter 13, §. 2, which is entitled Ὄρνεων φωναὶ [Orneōn phōnai], Voices of Birds: Εἴποις ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. Γογγύζειν [Gongyzein] means to murmur. Hence you may find murmura [murmurs] for the moaning of doves: as when the emperor Gallienus, in Trebellius, says of the bride and groom in an epithalamium,
— — — let not doves surpass your murmurs, nor ivy your arms, nor shells your kisses.

But the Hebrew has הגה, which is rightly rendered by the verb to moan, since it everywhere refers to mourning. So in the song of King Hezekiah about his illness, Isa 38:14 אהגה כיונה, I moaned like a dove. And Isa 59:11, where the afflicted condition of the Jews is treated: We all growl like bears, וכיונים הגה נהגה, and like doves we moan with moaning, that is, with heavy and continuous moaning . But המה too, which properly means to roar, applies to the moaning of doves, when it is said in Ezek 7:16. כיוני הגאות כלם הומות איש בעונו, like doves of the valleys they all roared (that is, moaned), each for his own sin. For כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys, the Septuagint read כיונה הגות. Hence arose that rendering ὡς περιστεραὶ μελετητικαὶ [hōs peristerai meletētikai], like moaning doves. For with them μελετᾷν [meletan], said of doves, means to moan. Accordingly Theodoret on this passage: Ὀδυρόμενοι γὰρ καὶ θρηνοῦντες περιστεραῖς μελετώσαις ἀπεικαθήσονται· στένουσι γὰρ ἔοικε τῶν περιστερῶν ἡ φωνή [Odyromenoi gar kai thrēnountes peristerais meletōsais apeikasthēsontai; stenousi gar eoike tōn peristerōn hē phōnē]. This must certainly be rendered thus: For those who lament and mourn will be compared to moaning doves (not to doves on high, as the translator has it here). For the voice of doves is like that of people moaning. The voice of the dove is also taken for mournful moaning in Nahum II, 7., where the queen of Nineveh, as she is led into captivity, is accompanied by maidservants moaning, as with the voice of doves, and beating their breasts. The Hebrew has מנהגות כקול יונים, leading away as with the voice of doves. Leading away here, as they hold, is the same as accompanying, and moaning must be supplied. For to lead away is put for to lead away and to moan: one for two. So in Prov 25:22, You will take coals of fire upon his head, for you will take and put; and Ps 68:19, You received gifts for men, for you received and gave, or you received things to give. Accordingly Paul renders it he gave gifts to men, Ephes. IV, 8. What if for מנהגות, leading away, one were to read מהגות, moaning, with one small letter less? The sense would thus be plainer; yet I would not dare to change anything, since it is established that the most ancient translators read מנהגות .

Scripture praises the flight of the dove more than once. Thus Isa 60:8: Who are these that fly together like clouds, and like doves to their windows? The Rabbis refer this to the Israelites, who were to return from the Babylonian captivity with the greatest eagerness. Hence the Chaldee paraphrast: Who are these who come openly like swift clouds without delay? The exiles of Israel, who are gathered and return to their land, כיונין דתיבין לגו שובכיהן, like doves that return to their dovecotes. On these words Kimchi: יותר יעופו מהרה בשובם אל קניהם ממה שיעופו בצאתם מהם מפני שהם ממהרות לשוב אל גוזליהם שהניחו להאכילם מאשר בפיהם, They fly faster when they return to their nests than when they go out from them, because they hasten to return to the young they have left, to offer them the food which they have in their mouth. A similar passage is Hos 11:11: They will tremble like a little bird out of Egypt, and like a dove from the land of Assyria. They will tremble, יחרדו, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. So 1 Sam. XVI, 4., when Samuel came to Bethlehem, ויחרדו, And the elders of the city trembled (that is, hurried in agitation) to meet him. And in this same prophet, Ose. III, 5.: They will tremble to the Lord and to his goodness, that is, they will hurry up in agitation. Aben Ezra: ישובו במהרה במרוצא פתע פתאום, They will return hastily, at a run, quickly, swiftly. Yet in the sacred text there is not חרדו but its synonym פחדו. Indeed, verbs of trembling sometimes relate to haste. Virgil, in the ninth book of the Aeneid:
Do not tremble, Teucrians, to defend my ships.

that is, do not hurry. So Servius and Nonius Marcellus. And Livy, book 23: And soon, while each hurries [trepidat] running about to his own duties at the first signals. Trepidat, that is, festinat [hurries]. So certainly in Hosea: They will tremble like a dove (that is, they will flee with the utmost haste) from Assyria . For the flight of the dove is extremely swift. Hence it is that in Psal. LV, 7. David wishes for the wings of a dove, to withdraw by swift flight from imminent danger. Who (he says) will give me a wing like a dove's, with which I might fly away to safety? Behold, I would wander as far away as possible, to stay in the wilderness. And I would hasten my escape, swifter than the most rapid wind and whirlwind. Just as the Chorus in Sophocles' Oedipus at Colonus:

Εἴτ᾽, ἀελλαία ταχύῤ- [Eit', aellaia tachyr-] Would that, like a dove of swift ῥωστος πελειὰς, [rhōstos peleias,] whirlwind onrush, Αἰθερίας νεφέλας [Aitherias nephelas] I might pass through Κύρσαί με, [Kyrsai me,] etc. the ethereal clouds, etc.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in Oration 17, says that David longed for the wings of a dove ὡς κουφοτέρας, καὶ ταχυτέρας [hōs kouphoteras, kai tachyteras], as being lighter and swifter. And Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom] in his Paraphrase: O that wings were given me such as the dove has, which of all birds is the swiftest in flight; so that, as by its most rapid flight, and by that alone, it frees itself from its enemy the hawk, etc. Pliny too, book 10, chapter 36, says that doves in free flight are much swifter than the hawk. And Phaedrus, book 1, Fable 31:
The doves, when they had often fled the kite, And by the swiftness of their wings escaped death.
And Euripides, of the Bacchae hastening to the slaughter of Pentheus:
Ἤιξαν πελέιας ὠκύτητ᾽ οὐκ ἥσσονες, [Ēixan peleias ōkytēt᾽ ouk hēssones,]
They rushed on, not inferior to doves in swiftness. Accordingly Virgil, Aeneid book 5, compares the ship of Mnestheus, which
With the swift stroke of oars, and the winds called up, Makes for the sloping seas, and runs down the open main,
to a dove in flight, at the moment when
It is borne flying into the fields, and gliding through the still air Skims its liquid path, and does not move its swift wings.

And, so that the Argo may be believed to have been a very swift ship, the poets describe it as quick ὅσον πελειάδος [hoson peleiados], like a dove. And they invent the story that a dove was sent by the Argonauts between the Symplegades, and that when it had got through, they concluded from this that the Argo too would get through, as Eustathius teaches on Odyssey μ´. The Arabs and Hebrews agree with this. Thus Damir, after teaching that الشهرمان والشاهين [al-shahramān wa-l-shāhīn], the saharman and the sahin, species of hawk, are most hostile to the dove, says: وهو اطير منهما ومن ساير الطير كلها [wa-huwa aṭyar minhumā wa-min sāyir al-ṭayr kullihā] And it surpasses them in flight, and all birds whatsoever. And on the passage of the Psalm that we have cited, R. Simon, R. Iodan, R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim], and R. Kimchi, to the question why David prefers the wings of the dove to the wings of other birds, answer thus: כל העופות בשעה שיגעים הם נסים על גבי הסלע או על גבי האילן ונתפסין אבל יונה בשעה שיגעה היא קובצת אחת מאגפיה ופורחת באחת והיא נצולת ואינה נתפסת, All other birds, when they are tired from flying, flee onto a rock or onto a tree, and are caught; but the dove, when it is tired, folds one of its wings and flies with the other, and so escapes and is not caught. And Aben Ezra: והזכיר יונה שהיא עם בני אדם ועמה ישגרו המלכים ספריהם, He mentions the dove because it lives with men, and kings send letters by it. Indeed, in the twelfth century after Christ, when Aben Ezra wrote, this was much practised. Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Aemilius, On the Deeds of the Franks, book 4, where he speaks of the governor of Hasarchum, a town of Syria: His envoys (sent to Baldwin to beg for help) tied a letter to the tail of a dove which they had brought with them from home when they set out on their embassy, and sent it back as agreed. Thus informed, the governor defended himself excellently . And where he speaks of Jerusalem besieged by the Christians: It happened that a dove flying over the camp of the Latins, descending as a hawk pressed upon it, was caught by our men. Under its wings was found a letter written in Arabic, both in words and in letters. And in book 5: While they were encamped before the walls (of Tyre), some authors say that a dove flew up. When our men, taught by experience, recognized it as a letter-carrier, so great a shout was raised by the land and naval forces of the Latins that the bird, as if driven by a whirlwind of the disturbed air, fell to the ground. The letter taken from it, written in barbarian characters to the Tyrians, said that help would soon come, that they should be of good courage and endure the siege a few days. Our men, on the other hand, had another letter written in the hand and language of those barbarians whom they held in their power etc. and sent the bird back with the forged and deceitful letter, telling the besieged to take counsel for themselves according to their present need, etc. that no hope of help near at hand could be held out, etc. The Tyrians yielded to the trick. Marmol, in his Africa, book 2, chapter 31, refers this to the year 1123. On the same matter see Jacques de Vitry, Histor. Orient. book 1; Arnold of Lübeck in the History of the Slavs; Vincent in the Doctrinale book 16, ch. 154; and Wildebrand of Oldenburg in the Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, where he wrongly ascribes to the people of Tripoli what others attribute to the Tyrians. But older histories too offer us examples of the same art. For, to pass over fables, such as what the Samaritans write in chapter 20 of their spurious book of Joshua, that after defeating the five kings he informed Eleazar of this victory by a letter tied to the wings of birds, and in chapter 34 that he sent a letter to Nebichus by the service of a dove; and what we read in Aelian, History, book 6, chapter 7, that Mares, king of Egypt, used a crow to carry letters wherever he wished: to pass over these, I say, since they are plainly fabulous, why should we not believe what is found in Aelian's Varia, book 9, chapter 2, that Taurosthenes, the Ὀλυμπιονίκην [Olympionikēn], announced his victory to his father in Aegina from Olympia on the same day by a dove as messenger? They say, namely, περιστερὰν τὸν Ταυροσθένην ἐπάγεσθαι ἀπολιποῦσαν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς νεοσσοὺς ὑγροὺς ἔτι, καὶ ἀπτῆνας, νικήσαντα, καὶ ἀφεῖναι τὴν πελειάδα, προσάψαντα πορφύραν αὐτῇ· τὴν δὲ ἐπειγομένην πρὸς τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ἀπαυθημερῆσαι ἐκ Πίσσης εἰς Αἴγιναν· [peristeran ton Taurosthenēn epagesthai apolipousan tous heautēs neossous hygrous eti, kai aptēnas, nikēsanta, kai apheinai tēn peleiada, prosapsanta porphyran autē; tēn de epeigomenēn pros tous neottous, apauthēmerēsai ek Pissēs eis Aiginan] that Taurosthenes took with him a dove taken away from its chicks, still tender and unfledged; and when he had won, he sent it back with a piece of purple tied to it, and it, hastening with all speed to its chicks, flew on the same day from Pisa to Aegina. Pliny and Frontinus report that something similar happened at the siege of Mutina, although they hardly agree with each other. For the latter, in book 3 of the Stratagems, writes that Hirtius sent letters, tied with a bristle to a dove's neck, to Decimus Brutus, besieged in Mutina by Antony; the former, in book 10, chapter 37, says that doves were messengers in great affairs, with letters attached to their feet, at the siege of Mutina, when D. Brutus sent them to the consuls' camp. But in the same siege the same Brutus could have both received and sent back letters by the service of doves. You may often see the poets allude to this skill of doves. Among them Anacreon, in Ode 9, attributes the following to his dove:

Ἐγὼ δ᾽ Ἀνακρέοντι [Egō d᾽ Anakreonti] And I, for Anacreon, Διακονῶ τοσαῦτα, [Diakonō tosauta,] serve in such matters, Καὶ νῦν οἵας ἐκείνου [Kai nyn hoias ekeinou] And now see Ἐπιστολὰς κομίζω. [Epistolas komizō.] what letters of his I carry.
Pherecrates in the Painters, in Athenaeus, book 9:
Ἀπόπεμψον ἀγγέλλοντα, τὸν περιστερὸν, [Apopempson angellonta, ton peristeron,]
Send back the dove as messenger. Martial, on a dove that flew down into the lap of Aretulla, book 8, Epigram 32:
Perhaps this bird has come to you from the Sardinian shores of the exile, a messenger that your brother will return.
To these I cannot help adding these few lines from the most charming Elegy of the late Heinsius on the doves of Leiden, book 3, Elegy 10:

Here he sends the sacred bird down from the anxious city, to carry back his directions; she flies. And soon, rejoicing to see her home and sweet nest again, she glided back through the midst of the air. She carries in her wings the letters and orders of Boisot, and has now completed the sweet work of her service.

This art, which had nearly died out in our fathers' time, the Dutch revived. So too did the Turks: Linschoten, in his description of Ormuz, chapter 6, writes that their emperor learns within a short time by means of doves what is happening in the most remote parts of his empire. Accordingly, in the book On Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsaphe into Hebrew in the year of Christ 1316, it is said of the dove: היונה המסולסל הוא זה המגביה לעוף נושה כתבים ואגרות מארץ אל ארץ לחבונתו, The dove, raising itself on high, that is, which is exalted in its flight, when by its intelligence it carries letters from place to place. For, as Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says, اذا ارسل من موضع بعيد يصعد نحو الهوا وتكون صعوده مدورا فلا يزال يصعد وينظر حتي يري شيا من علامات بلده فعند ذلك يهبط اليها بادني زمان [idhā ursila min mawḍiʿ baʿīd yaṣʿad naḥwa al-hawā wa-takūn ṣuʿūduhu mudawwaran fa-lā yazāl yaṣʿad wa-yanẓur ḥattī yarī shayan min ʿalāmāt baladihi fa-ʿinda dhālika yahbiṭ ilayhā bi-adnā zamān] When it is sent from a very distant place, it climbs into the highest air, and its ascent is made in a circle. Nor does it stop climbing and looking about until it notices some sign of its own region. Then it descends to it in a short time. And Damir: في طبعه انه يطلب وكره ولو ارسل من الف فرسخ ويحمل الاخبار وياتي بها من المسافة البعيدة في المده القريبة وفيه ما يقطع ثلاثة الاف فرسخ في يوم واحد [fī ṭabʿihi annahu yaṭlub wakrahu wa-law ursila min alf farsakh wa-yaḥmil al-akhbār wa-yātī bihā min al-masāfa al-baʿīda fī al-mudda al-qarība wa-fīhi mā yaqṭaʿ thalāthat ālāf farsakh fī yawm wāḥid] And its nature is to seek its nest again, even if it is sent from a thousand parasangs, and to carry messages from the most remote places in the shortest time, so that some are said to have covered three thousand parasangs in a single day. This exceeds all belief, and I think it was invented by those who tell of great things as still greater. The little letter that is tied to the dove is called in Arabic by a special name, بطاقة [biṭāqa] bittaka, that is, πιττάκιον [pittakion], pittacium [slip]. And زجل [zajala] zagiala means to send out a dove for this purpose; and a dove so sent is called زجال [zijāl] zigial. So it is in Alcamus .

Such as the crested dove, common in India, which HASSELQUIST describes as entirely snow-white, Travels p. 333. The same author has this on the dove of Palestine, p. 553: “The size of a wood pigeon. The neck, head, breast and shoulders are grey. The back grey with dark spots. The tail feathers and flight feathers white at the tip. The eyes and feet are reddish.”

But Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] vol. III, p. 950, note, rightly pointed out that this etymology is far too broad, since absolutely all metals are dug out of the earth. He nevertheless omitted what A. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] discussed concerning this word in Commentar. ad Prov. [=Albert Schultens, Commentarius in Proverbia Salomonis (1748)] XXI, 5, p. 252. Gold seems to have been called חרוץ because in some places of Arabia Felix, where rain pours heavily over ground rich in gold, the gold is laid bare and so is found as if already dug out, not by art but of its own accord. See the passage from Taurizius, the grammarian, cited by Schultens in the place mentioned.

The ancient interpreters also understood the word מלאת, with unanimous agreement, of the fullness of waters, as Bochart explained above. See HUFNAGEL's Observationes in Canticum Canticorum (under the title Auch etwas übers hohe Lied) in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat. edited by Eichhorn, vol. XI, p. 131. Moreover, what Bochart remarks here about the interpretation of the word מלאת devised by some of the Hebrews applies also to Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses], who in his commentary on this passage (Der Schwesternhandel, eine morgenländische Idyllenkette, mit historischkritischen Untersuchungen pp. 425–428) brings forward much from his manifold store of learning to explain the simile used by the Hebrew poet, but little, I suspect, that bears on the matter. By doves washed in milk our poet undoubtedly meant to express the pure and, as it were, radiant whiteness of the eyes around the pupils. That these doves are pictured as sitting by the waters belongs to the ornament of the image; no further simile should be sought in this. It is tedious to report the guesses of other interpreters.

The original sense of the verb הגה, which lies in seething heat, and the series of meanings derived from it, since it is then transferred to all the more agitated and vehement emotions, whether these seethe inwardly in the mind (hence it is also used of meditation, which for an Oriental is a kind of agitation and commotion of the mind) or boil over and burst out into murmurs, moaning, howls, cries (hence also of the roaring of a lion), and into songs, both mournful and satirical: all this ALB. Schultens uncovered and expounded with the help of the Arabic هجى [hajā] in his Commentarius in Prov. p. 320 ff., compare p. 71; further in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1040, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. in Thren. Ierem. Chapter III, v. 62, p. 509.

But everything is plain, and there is no need either to supply some verb or to alter the received reading, if the verb נהג is explained from the Arabic نهج [nahaja] to sigh, to moan, to draw sighs, as ALB. Schultens first showed in Animadverss. Philoll. ad Nah. II, 7, p. 342; to whom add I. D. Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. V, p. 1603.

Compare ALB. Schultens, Animadverss. Philologg. on Esaj. XIX. 17., p. 265 of the Opera minora, Leiden 1769. ED. Pococke [=Edward Pococke, Commentary on Hosea (1685)] shows a similar use of the Arabic verb فزع [fazaʿa] in his Commentar. on Hos. III, 5.

On carrier doves, whose service the Turks still use today for carrying letters, much is reported by DELLA VALLE in his Travels vol. I, letter 12, pp. 128–129 of the German translation (who asserts that a six days' journey is completed by a carrier dove in a single day), and by ALEX. RUSSELL in the Natural History of Aleppo p. 66. The plan of our work does not allow us to transcribe these passages here, since they are too long.
On the dwelling places of doves.

In dovecotes, doves have ארבות arubboth, that is, windows or openings, in which they usually hide and nest. Isa 60:8. Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves אל ארבותיהם, to their windows? That is, לגו שובכיהון, to their dovecotes, as the Chaldee has it. But when afraid they hide anywhere: in pits, in rocks, in mountains, etc. Hence in Jer 48:28 the Moabites, who for fear of the enemy abandon their cities and hide in caves in the cliffs, are said to be כיונה תקנן בעברי פי פחת, like the dove that (in a similar fear, contrary to its nature) nests in the sides of the mouth of a pit. There the Chaldee has כיונא דשבקא פום שובכה ונחתא ושריא בארעית גובא, like a dove that leaves the opening of the dovecote and goes down to dwell at the bottom of a pit . And in Song 2:14 by the dove that hides בחגוי הסלע בסתר המדרגה, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding place of the cliff, the Hebrews understand the Israelites, whom at the exodus from Egypt Pharaoh pursued on one side, while on the other the desert, full of snakes, hemmed them in. Hence the Chaldee translator: הות מתילא כנישתא דישראל ליונתא דסגירא בחגוי טנרא והיוא מעיק לה מגיו וגצא מעיק לה מברא, The Israelite congregation was like a dove shut up in the clefts of the rock. And the serpent besieges it from within, and the hawk from without. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] develops this at greater length. So too in Quintus of Smyrna, book 12:
Ἴρηξ σεῦε πέλειαν· ἐπειγομένη δ᾽ ἄρα κείνη Κηραμον ἐς πέτρης κατεδύσατο· — — [Irēx seue peleian; epeigomenē d' ara keinē Kēramon es petrēs katedysato]
A hawk was pursuing a dove; and she, hard pressed, slipped into a hollow of the rock. This is taken from these lines of Homer, Iliad φ᾽ [phi], line 495:
— — — φύγεν, ὥς τε πέλεια, Ἥ ῥάθ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην· [phygen, hōs te peleia, Hē rhath' hyph' irēkos koilēn eiseptato petrēn]
She fled like a dove that, before a hawk, has flown into a hollow rock, into a cave. Yet these lines of the Poet suggest that doves nest in caves even apart from fear:
As a dove suddenly startled from a cave, whose home and sweet nests are in the hollow rock.

So too we read in Diodorus that Semiramis was exposed εἰς τινας ἐρήμους, καὶ πετρώδεις τόπους, ἐν οἷς πολλοῦ πλήθους περιστερῶν ἐννοσσεύειν εἰωθότος [eis tinas erēmous, kai petrōdeis topous, en hois pollou plēthous peristerōn ennosseuein eiōthotos], in certain desert and rocky places, in which, since a great number of doves used to nest there, etc., if indeed doves in the proper sense are meant there. Also in Ezek 7:16 those who escaped a great slaughter are said to wander on the mountains כיוני הגיאות, like doves of the valleys. These, that is, for fear of the fowler or the hawk, abandon their natural home and are forced to withdraw elsewhere to save their lives. Mountain doves are contrasted with doves of the valleys, as wild animals are with domestic ones. Thus in Hesychius, Semiramis is περιστερὰ ὄρειος [peristera oreios], as has already been explained. And in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] العزف [al-ʿazf] Alozpho is الحمام الطورانية [al-ḥamām al-ṭūrāniyya], mountain dove.

Unless I am mistaken, doves of the trees, or of the groves, are also mentioned in the title of Psal. LVI., in the rendering of which I think interpreters have so far laboured in vain. For, to pass over the ancients, who go off in the most diverse directions, who could tolerate Selomo or Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], who render the Hebrew words על יונת אלם רחוקים as concerning the dove of silence of those far off, so as to refer them to David? For, as Selomo says, David was then among the Philistines, far from the land of Israel. And Kimchi adds that he is called a dove because in Hos 7:11 the dove is called silly, and David was feigning to be a fool; and a dove of silence, that is, mute, because he did not speak in his usual manner but like a madman. Nor do I much more approve of a great man from among our own, who, following the authors of the Midrash, explains the same words thus: Concerning the soul suffering violence from a band of those far off. This interpretation, like the former one we have discussed, does such manifest violence to the Hebrew text that anyone even moderately learned in Hebrew will see why I reject it. Leaving these aside, then, I shall say what the matter is. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] rightly saw that the words יונת אלם רחוקים are the opening of a song to whose melody David composed this Psalm; but he left them ἀνερμήνευτα [anermēneuta]. Here, however, we are asking what those words mean. And it is certain that no suitable sense can be drawn from them as they are read by the Masoretes. Let the experts therefore consider whether, keeping the same letters but changing one vowel point, it would not be wiser to read אלם elim instead of אלם elem, that is, Hirec for Segol. Granted this, the opening of the sacred song whose melody David follows in this Psalm would be: The dove of the distant groves. What misled the interpreters, and even the Masoretes themselves, is that אלם lacks the Iod, the mark of the plural. But, as the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] rightly observes in Thesaurus Grammaticus, book 1, ch. 9, Iod often drops out of the plural, as in תנינם, dragons, Deut 32:33, תמימם, unblemished, Lev 9:2. I add only an example of a similar ellipsis in this very word, though in another sense: באלם, among the mighty gods, for באלים, Exod 15:11. Further, יונת אלים, the dove of the trees, or of the groves, is the wild dove, that is, the wood pigeon (palumbus), which lives in woods and nests in trees. Theocritus, Idyll 5:
Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθω καθελών· τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφίσδει· [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn; tēnei gar ephisdei]
And I will soon give the girl a wood pigeon, taken from the juniper: for there it sits. Nemesianus, Eclogue 2:
Besides, I have sent a tender hare and a pair of wood pigeons, the spoils of the woods, which I lately could.
The wood pigeon claps its wings, calling from the leafy tree.

Accordingly the French call it ramier, from the branches (rami) of the trees on which it perches. The same is written also of the rock doves (liviae), which the Greeks call πελειάδες [peleiades]. Thus Herodotus in Euterpe describes a πελειάδα [peleiada], a rock dove, ἰζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν [izomenēn epi phēgon], perching on a beech. And of the turtledove Origen on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: It always lingers on the ridges of mountains and on the tops of trees. Theodoret also, on Cant. 2, says that the turtledove ἐν δένδροις ἀμφιλαφέσι τὰς καλιὰς πηγνύναι [en dendrois amphilaphesi tas kalias pēgnynai], builds its nests in shady trees. And Chrysostom in the homily On the Turtledove: Ἐπὶ τῶν στερεμνίων πρέμνων τὴν καλίαν αὐτῶν πήξασαι, καὶ ἀφόβως ἐπωάζουσαι, τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἐκεῖθεν πετάζουσι· [Epi tōn steremniōn premnōn tēn kalian autōn pēxasai, kai aphobōs epōazousai, tous neottous heautōn ekeithen petazousi] Fixing their nest on firm tree trunks and brooding securely, they spread out their young there. This is infrequent in doves properly so called, yet not without example. Hence Anacreon, Ode 9, says that a περιστερὰν [peristeran] πέτασθαι ὄρη τε, καὶ κατ᾽ ἄγρους, καὶ δένδρεσιν καθίζειν [petasthai orē te, kai kat' agrous, kai dendresin kathizein], flies over mountains and fields and perches on trees. And Horace, book 1, Ode 2:
And the race of fishes clung to the top of the elm, which had been the familiar seat of doves.
And Virgil in book 6, of the doves sent to Aeneas by Venus:
They settle in the longed-for seat upon the twofold tree.

And Suetonius in the Octavius, ch. 94, on the palm near Munda which the deified Julius had ordered to be preserved as an omen of victory: From it a shoot at once sprang up and in a few days grew so much that it not only equalled the parent tree but even overshadowed it, and was frequented by the nests of doves, although that kind of bird especially avoids hard and rough foliage. From these it is plain what the dove of the trees, or of the distant groves, in the title of the Psalm is: namely, distant from cities and cultivated places .

That the dove is here said to nest in the sides of the mouth of the hole, Gussetius, in his Lexicon p. 573, refers to the fact that doves are not accustomed to place their nest directly opposite the opening, but to one side or the other of the opening; hence those who build dovecotes open the windows of the cells not in their middle but at the outer edge of the face. But I much prefer the opinion of Grotius, who understands the words עברי פי - פחת of the sides of a split rock. The guesses of the ancient interpreters, which contribute nothing to understanding the meaning, have been listed by J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in Observatt. Critt. et Philologg. ad Ierem. p. 256.
Franciscus Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible].

I wholeheartedly agree with Bochart in saying that the words יונה אלם רחוקים are the beginning of a song to whose tune David composed this Psalm (what we noted above, at vol. 1, book 3, ch. 17, note 8, about a similar custom of the Syrians in titling songs should be recalled here); but in explaining the words themselves one would labour in vain today. For who could draw a sound meaning from the words Sey Lob und Ehr, which are found written above many hymns, unless he knew the first line of the song whose tune is prescribed? We may therefore remain ignorant of the sense of those three Hebrew words without loss. Yet no one would readily deny the conjecture put forward by Bochart the praise of acuteness, especially if one compares it with the trifles other interpreters have produced about these much-vexed words, which, if one wishes, can be read gathered together in Pfeiffer's Dubia Vexata p. 605, further in Simonis' Lex. Hebr. under the words אלם and עלם, and in J. B. Koehler's Animadverss. Critt. on Ps 56:1 in the Repertorium für bibl. und morgenl. Litterat., edited by Eichhorn, vol. 8, p. 252 ff.
On the dove's simplicity, gentleness, chastity and timidity.

Now, as we are about to treat of the habits of doves, we shall begin with the famous saying of Christ, Matt 10:16 Γίνεσθε φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις, καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί [Ginesthe phronimoi hōs hoi opheis, kai akeraioi hōs hai peristerai]· Be ye prudent as serpents, and simple as doves. By Tzetzes, Chiliad 9, Hist. 263, φρόνιμοι [phronimoi] and ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are taken as meaning the same thing. For after he has asserted that they are called prudent when, like serpents, they guard their head, that is, their faith in God, he immediately adds:

Ἀκέραιοι δὲ γίνεσθε, ὡς αἱ περιστεραί μοι· Καὶ τοῦτο πάλιν τὸ αὐτὸ δηλοῖ τε, καὶ σημαίνει. Ἀκέραιοι γὰρ λέγονται περιστεραὶ τοιώς δε, Φρόνιμοι, ὥσπερ λέγεται περιστερὰ τοῦ Νῶε. [Akeraioi de ginesthe, hōs hai peristerai moi; Kai touto palin to auto dēloi te, kai sēmainei. Akeraioi gar legontai peristerai toiōs de, Phronimoi, hōsper legetai peristera tou Nōe.]

But be ye simple for me as doves. And this again indicates and signifies the same thing. For doves are called simple, prudent in such a way as Noah's dove is spoken of. That is, the dove which returned to the ark, that is, to the church, from which one must not depart. Nothing more absurd could have been devised. For, like the serpent and the dove, so φρόνιμος [phronimos] and ἀκέραιος [akeraios] are in no way synonyms. Nor did Christ join them as synonyms, but as opposites, in a striking antithesis, such as Martial uses when he says, in book 10, Epigr. 47:
Prudent simplicity, friends who are equals.

For just as prudence without simplicity degenerates into cunning, so simplicity without prudence is nothing but foolishness and stupidity. The prudent in Hebrew are ערומים, and the simple פתיים, or פתאים. Solomon often sets these two against each other. Thus Prov 1:4. לתת לפתאים ערמה, to give prudence to the simple. Prov 8:5 O ye simple, understand prudence. Prov 14:15. פתי, the simple believes every word, וערום, but the prudent considers his step. Prov 19:25. ופתי יערים, And the simple will become prudent. Prov 22:3. ערום, The prudent, when he sees evil, hides himself, ופתיים, but the simple pass on and are punished. And, just as the serpent is called ערום, φρόνιμος [phronimos], Gen 3:1, so the dove is called פתה, simple, Hos 7:11 And Ephraim has become כיונה פתה אין לב, like a simple dove, lacking heart, that is, senseless. To these two passages Christ no doubt alluded. You may object that both are put as vices: that the serpent is called ערום not because it is prudent but because it is crafty and wily, and the dove פתה not because it is simple but because it is foolish, and אין לב, senseless, as immediately follows. I reply, first, that both ערום and פתי or פתה are neutral words, which according to their subject may also turn to praise. Thus ערום means not only crafty and cunning but also prudent, and ערמה prudence, as the passages of Solomon cited above amply show. Conversely פתי signifies not only ἄφρονα [aphrona], foolish, but also ἀκέραιον [akeraion], simple, as in Ps 116:6. שמר פתאים יהוה, the Lord preserves the simple. Christ could therefore use these words in praise as well. Second, neither the serpent's prudence nor the dove's simplicity is praised by Christ on its own and torn from the other; they are praised only when joined together, so that the one supplies what is lacking in the other, or corrects what is excessive. In the same way, from two drugs that are harmful separately a third is compounded that is useful and wholesome, because they temper each other. Hence the ancients so often join these two. Gregory of Nazianzus, on his father, Oration 19: Τὸ γὰρ τοῦ ὄφεως φρόνιμον περὶ τὸ κακὸν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς ἀκεραίῳ περὶ τὸ καλὸν ἀναμίξας, οὐδὲ τὸ φρόνιμον εἴασε κακοῦργον γενέσθαι. οὔτε τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἀνόητον, ἀλλ᾽ ἓν ἀρετῆς εἶδος, ὡς μάλιστα ἐνῆν, ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων ἀπηκριβώσατο. [To gar tou opheōs phronimon peri to kakon tō tēs peristeras akeraiō peri to kalon anamixas, oude to phronimon eiase kakourgon genesthai. oute to haploun anoēton, all᾽ hen aretēs eidos, hōs malista enēn, ex amphoterōn apēkribōsato.] Having joined the serpent's prudence regarding evil with the dove's simplicity regarding good, he so conducted himself that he let neither prudence degenerate into cunning wickedness nor simplicity into stupidity, but from both, as far as was possible, he produced a single form of virtue, perfect and complete in every respect. Jerome, to Paulinus on the training of a monk: Have the simplicity of the dove, so as not to contrive snares against anyone, and the cunning of the serpent, so as not to be tripped up by the plots of others. Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, epist. 175: Ἡ φρόνησις τῇ ἁπλότητι κιρνωμένη θεῖόν τι χρῆμα· φημὶ δὲ ἐντελεστάτην ἀρετὴν ἀποτελεῖ· εἰ δὲ θατέρα θατέρας χωρισθείη, ἡ μὲν εἰς πονηρίαν ἐμπίπτει, ἡ δὲ εἰς μωρίαν τελευτᾷ· [Hē phronēsis tē haplotēti kirnōmenē theion ti chrēma; phēmi de entelestatēn aretēn apotelei; ei de thatera thateras chōristheiē, hē men eis ponērian empiptei, hē de eis mōrian teleuta;] Prudence tempered with simplicity produces something divine, that is, a virtue complete in every respect. But if the one is separated from the other, the former falls into perversity, while the latter ends in folly. Faustus, On Free Will, book 2, last chapter: Let us make man simple, let us make him astute: simple, so that being crafty he may not inflict evil; astute, so that being incautious he may not fall into it. Gregory on Job, book 1, ch. 2: He necessarily joined both in the admonition, so that the cunning of the serpent might equip the simplicity of the dove, and in turn the simplicity of the dove might temper the cunning of the serpent. Sidonius, book 7, Epist. 13, on Lupus, bishop of Troyes: In the church he keeps the simplicity of the dove, in the forum the cunning of the serpent. To the good he is judged prudent, to the wicked wary, to neither crafty. St Bernard [=Bernard of Clairvaux], Epist. 327, to Pope Innocent: in the church, then, simplicity must be kept, in the forum cunning; here, lest you be deceived, there, lest you deceive. See more on this subject in Caesarius, Dial. 4, Quaest. 190. Further, the simple are here called not ἁπλοί [haploi] but ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Yet it comes to the same thing. For ἀκέραιος [akeraios], formed from κεράω [keraō], misceo [I mix], properly signifies that which has nothing external and foreign mixed into it. Some take ἀκέραιος [akeraios] to be the same as ἀκερᾶς [akeras] or ἀκέρατος [akeratos], that which has no horns, and hence is ἀβλαβής [ablabēs] and harmless, a metaphor taken from animals that strike with the horn. So the Arabic and Ethiopic translators seem to have taken it: in the former ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] are ودعا [wudaʿā], in the latter የዋሃን፡ [yawāhān], that is, mild and gentle. But the first etymology seems more regular. Nor is it quite fitting that hornless should be said for harmless, since eagles, lions and many other wild beasts that have no horns possess many ways of doing harm, which they employ to destroy other animals. Moreover, the simple are opposed to the prudent, but the mild and gentle are not. So if you render mild, the grace of the opposition will be lost, which is evident here between the serpent's prudence and the dove's simplicity. Of the same kind is that of Paul, Rom 16:19: I would have you σοφούς [sophous] wise in what is good, ἀκεραίους δέ [akeraious de], but simple in what is evil. The illustrious Beza had rendered innocent in his first editions, but in later ones he rightly changed it to simple, so that the opposition might stand . To the same effect is the fact that in that very ancient manuscript of Beza ἁπλούστατοι [haploustatoi], most simple, was read for ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi]. Nor is it a slight point that, just as the serpent's being called prudent is taken from Moses, so the dove's being called simple is taken from Hosea. But no passage of the Prophets occurs where it is called mild. Thus the Christian Arabs seem to have understood less well what ἀκέραιοι [akeraioi] means here than the Muslim doctors, who render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, that is, simple. So in the book of the priest Achmed entitled الزهد [al-zuhd], that is, abstinence, Iazid, son of Malzara, says that Jesus commanded his disciples ان يكون بلها في الله مشل الحمام [an yakūna bulhan fī Allāh mashl al-ḥamām] that they should be bulhan (that is, simple) in God like doves. Thus we render بلها [bulhan] bulhan, with the most learned of the Arabs, from the singular ابله [ablah] ablaho, to which كيس [kayyis] chaison is opposed, that is, cunning and crafty. And that it is to be so taken is shown by what follows in the same place: ليس شي ابله من الحمام وذلك انك تاخذ فرخيه من تحته فتذبحهما ثم يعود الي مكانه فيفرخ فيه [laysa shay ablah min al-ḥamām wa-dhālika annaka taʾkhudh farkhayhi min taḥtihi fa-tadhbaḥuhumā thumma yaʿūd ilā makānihi fa-yufarrikh fīhi] Nothing is simpler than the dove. For even if you kill the young taken from under it, it nevertheless soon returns to its place and hatches young in it. The very same thing the Fathers write on the passage of Hosea we have cited. Theodoret: Ἐκείνη τῶν ἰδίων νεοττῶν ἀφαιρουμένη οὐκ ἀφίπταται, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς προστρέχει χωρίοις. [Ekeinē tōn idiōn neottōn aphairoumenē ouk aphiptatai, alla tois autois prostrechei chōriois.] And following him Theophylact: When its young are taken away it does not fly off, but remains in the same places. Somewhat differently Jerome: Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own life, and when they see a hawk, a snake, a raven or a crow approach their nest, they flutter this way and that, throw themselves at it, tear it with beak and claws, and bear witness to a parent's grief with plaintive cry. The dove alone does not grieve for its young when they are taken away, nor seek them. But how truly, I do not quite know, since a kind of dove or wood-pigeon, الورشان [al-warashān] alvvarsen, is described by the Arabs بالحنو علي اولاده حتي انه ربما قتل نفسه اذا راها في يد القانص [bi-l-ḥunuww ʿalā awlādihi ḥattā annahu rubbamā qatala nafsahu idhā rāhā fī yad al-qāniṣ] as burning with such affection for its young that it sometimes kills itself when it sees them in the fowler's hand. So it is found in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]. And in general writers commend the dove for its love of its offspring. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34, on the male and female dove: Both have equal love for their offspring; often for this reason there is chastisement, when the female is slow in going in to the young. On which more in Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7; Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 45; again Aelian, Var. book 1, ch. 15; Athenaeus, book 9, ch. 11; Porphyry, Περὶ ἀποχῆς [Peri apochēs], etc., book 3; which there is no room to copy out here. Others assert that the dove's simplicity is evident in the fact that it does not avoid nets, nor the snares laid for it, when it comes down to feed. And with this stupidity of the dove they would have Hosea compare the sloth of the Israelites, who took no precaution against dangers and threw themselves into the power of their enemies. However that may be, this simplicity of the dove was recognized also by οἱ ἔξωθεν [hoi exōthen]. Thus on that line of Juvenal,

the old Scholiast says: He referred "doves" to simplicity. And in the Suda ἡμένη πελειὰς [hēmenē peleias], a sitting dove, is used as a proverb ἐπὶ τῶν ἁπλουστάτων [epi tōn haploustatōn], of the most simple-minded. This is, of course, διὰ τὸ εὔηθες τοῦ ζώου [dia to euēthes tou zōou], because of the creature's stupidity, as Eustathius has it on Iliad ψ΄ [psi]. The proverb, however, is not used of every dove, but of those that sit beside the decoy dove. As the Suda says, it is κατὰ ἀντιπαρεξέτασιν τῆς παλευτρίας [kata antiparexetasin tēs paleutrias], by contrast with the decoy dove, that is, the dove that fowlers misuse to lure the others. Aristophanes in the Birds:
Τὰς περιστερὰς θ᾽ ὁμοίως ξυλλαβὼν εἵρξας ἔχει Κἀπαναγκάζει παλεύειν δεδεμένας ἐν δικτύῳ· [Tas peristeras th' homoiōs xyllabōn heirxas echei / Kapanankazei paleuein dedemenas en diktyō]

And likewise he seizes the doves, keeps them confined, and forces them, bound in a net, to lure others. And there the Scholiast says: Εἰώθασιν ἐκτυφλοῦντές τινα τῶν ὀρνέων ἱστάναι ἐν δικτύῳ, ὅπως τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖτο τὰ ὁμοιογενῆ· [Eiōthasin ektyphlountes tina tōn orneōn histanai en diktyō, hopōs tē phōnē proskaleito ta homoiogenē] They are accustomed to keep a blinded bird in a snare, so that by its voice it may call others of its kind. That doves were used for this purpose is asserted not only by Aristophanes but also by the Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Αἱ περισταὶ, he says, ζῶσι καὶ ὀκτὼ ἔτη, αἱ τετυφλωμέναι ὑπὸ τῶν παλευτρίας τρεφόντων αὐτάς· [Hai peristerai … zōsi kai oktō etē, hai tetyphlōmenai hypo tōn paleutrias trephontōn autas] Doves that are blinded and kept as decoys live as long as eight years. Now, if you consult more recent writers, what has been said about the simplicity of doves and the ease of catching them will be considerably confirmed by what Cadamosto [=Alvise Cadamosto, Navigazioni (1455-56)] relates happened to him, Navigat. ch. 40, when he first landed on the Canary Islands. The doves, he says, were caught at will by a man's hand. For they were not frightened at the sight of a man. And in chapter 6, on the island of Madeira: I remember hearing from the inhabitants that when the island was first settled there was a very great abundance of doves there. To catch them the fowlers used no other device than a hook tied to a pole, so that they might be drawn to them from the trees on which they perch there; the birds were not frightened but full of wonder, as at something never seen before.

Meanwhile, those who take ἀκεραίους [akeraious] in Christ's saying to mean mild and gentle have followed a good many Grammarians, for whom ἀκέραιον [akeraion], said of an animal, means hornless, as well as kindly and harmless. Beyond this, they have had regard to the nature of the dove, which is in truth a most mild and gentle animal. Accordingly Ovid calls it placid, Metam. book 7, Fable 12. And Cyril says that the dove πρὸς ἄκρον ἥκειν πρᾳότητος [pros akron hēkein praotētos], reaches the highest summit of gentleness, in book 15 On Adoration. Indeed, many think it entirely lacks gall. Hence Clement calls it ἄχολον [acholon], Paedag. book 1, ch. 5; and Isidore, Orig. book 12, calls doves gentle birds without gall. Of the same kind is what Tertullian writes, On Baptism ch. 8, that the dove, even bodily, lacks gall itself. And Sedulius, book 2 of the Carmen, on the Baptism of Christ:
And it befits the Gentle One, the greatly Mild, to come forth through the bird that lacks gall. — —

And Horapollo, Hieroglyph. book 1, ch. 54: Ἱστορεῖται δὲ ὅτι οὐ χολὴν ἔχει τοῦτο τὸ ζῶον [Historeitai de hoti ou cholēn echei touto to zōon], It is also reported that this animal lacks gall. Yet he himself refutes this in book 2, ch. 45, saying that the dove ἐν ὀπισθίοις τὴν χολὴν ἔχειν [en opisthiois tēn cholēn echein], has its gall at the back. And Galen, in the book On Black Bile, says those people are ridiculous who think the dove lacks gall because it does not have τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ ἤπατι κύστιν [tēn epi tō hēpati kystin], the gall bladder next to the liver. Nor did this escape the Philosopher, whose words are, Hist. book 2, ch. 15: Ἔνιοι πρὸς τῇ κοιλίᾳ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ πρὸς τοῖς ἐντέροις τὴν χολὴν, οἷον περιστερά [Enioi pros tē koilia echousin, hoi de pros tois enterois tēn cholēn, hoion peristera]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: In some the gall is attached only to the intestine, as in doves.

Another point to be noted here in doves is their conjugal chastity, which the ancients praise remarkably. Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 7: Οὔτε γὰρ συν- δυάζεσθαι θέλουσι πλείοσιν, οὔτε προσλείπουσι τὴν κοινωνίαν, πλὴν ἐὰν χῆρος, ἢ χήρα γένηται· [Oute gar syndyazesthai thelousi pleiosin, oute proleipousi tēn koinōnian, plēn ean chēros ē chēra genētai] For they will not pair with more than one, nor do they ever abandon their partnership, except through widowhood. Pliny, book 10, ch. 34: Chastity is foremost with them, and adultery is known to neither. They do not violate conjugal fidelity, and they keep a common home. Unless unmated or widowed, a dove does not leave its nest. Propertius, book 2, Eleg. 12:
So let doves joined in love be my example, male and female, a whole marriage.

Of the turtledove and the wood pigeon the same Philosopher writes: Ἔχει δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα ἡ τρυγὼν τὸν αὐτὸν καὶ φάττα, καὶ ἄλλον οὐ προσίενται [Echei de ton arrhena hē trygōn ton auton kai phatta, kai allon ou prosientai], The turtledove too, and the wood pigeon, have one male, and do not admit another. Indeed, Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food book 3, and Phile, On Animals ch. 19, report that wood pigeons punish adultery with death. Both take this from Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 44, where he adds that turtledoves keep the same law scrupulously, but that white doves kill only the males caught in adultery, taking pity on the females. Clement, too, in the second book of the Stromata, reports that there are certain animals ἃ τὴν ἐπιμιξίαν οὐ ποιεῖται πρὸς πολλὰ καὶ ἀναίδην, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἓν, καὶ ὁμόφυλον· οἷαι αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ αἱ φάσσαι, καὶ τὸ τρυγόνων γένος, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις παραπλήσια [ha tēn epimixian ou poieitai pros polla kai anaidēn, alla pros hen, kai homophylon; hoiai hai peleiades, kai hai phassai, kai to trygonōn genos, kai hosa toutois paraplēsia], which do not mate with many and shamelessly, but with one, and that of the same kind, as are doves, and wood pigeons, and the turtledove kind, and those that are like them. What is more, they say that the black dove remains a widow after the death of its mate, and that for this reason among the Egyptians it was the symbol of a woman who shrinks from a second marriage. Horus book 2, ch. 30: Γυναῖκα χήραν ἐπιμείνασαν ἄχρι θανάτου θέλοντες σημῆναι, περιστερὰν μέλαιναν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ οὐ συμμίγνυται ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ ἕως οὗ χηρεύει [Gynaika chēran epimeinasan achri thanatou thelontes sēmēnai, peristeran melainan zōgraphousin; hautē gar ou symmignytai heterō andri heōs hou chēreuei] When they wish to signify a woman who remains a widow until death, they paint a black dove: for this bird, as long as it is widowed, does not join with another male. Accordingly Tertullian tries to establish his monogamy by the example of the dove: A bird, he says, not only harmless but also chaste, which one male alone knows. But the later Fathers, with great unanimity, transferred this very thing to turtledoves, for what reason I do not know. Origen on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: They say that the nature of turtledoves is such that the male does not approach any female besides one, nor does the female accept more than one male; so that, if it happens that one is taken away and the other survives, the love of mating is extinguished together with the mate. Basil in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τὴν τρυγόνα φασὶ διαζευχθεῖσάν ποτε τοῦ ὁμόζυγος, μηκέτι τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον καταδέχεσθαι κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ μένειν ἀσυνδύαστον, μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτε συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνημένην· [Tēn trygona phasi diazeuchtheisan pote tou homozygos, mēketi tēn pros heteron katadechesthai koinōnian, alla menein asyndyaston, mnēmē tou pote syzeuchthentos tēn pros heteron koinōnian aparnēmenēn] They say that the turtledove, once separated from its mate, never enters into union with another, but remains single without a mate, refusing marriage with another in remembrance of the partner it has lost. Gregory of Nazianzus in the Precepts to Virgins, Poem 3:

Πυνθάνομ᾽ ὡς πτερόεσσα τρυγὼν τρυγόνος φιλίοιο Χηρωθεῖσ᾽ ὁμόλεκτρον ἑὸν ποθέουσα σαόφρων, Οὐ δέχεται πόσιν ἄλλον ἑῆς καθύπερθε καλιῆς· [Pynthanom᾽ hōs pteroessa trygōn trygonos philioio Chērōtheis᾽ homolektron heon potheousa saophrōn, Ou dechetai posin allon heēs kathyperthe kaliēs]

I hear that the female of the turtledove, once widowed of her mate, restrains herself out of longing for her spouse and admits no other mate into her nest. Chrysostom, Homily On the Turtledove, English edition, vol. 7, p. 264: Φασί τινες τὴν τρυγόνα φίλανδρον εἶναι, καὶ φίλαγνον· ὥς τε κἂν συμβῇ τὸν ταύτης ἄῤῥενα ὑπὸ ἀετοῦ ἀναλωθῆναι, ἢ ὑπὸ ἰξευτοῦ θηρευθῆναι, ταύτην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μὴ ἐπιμίγνυσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸν ποθεῖν, αὐτὸν ἀναμένειν, καὶ τῇ τούτου μνήμῃ συναποθνήσκειν. [Phasi tines tēn trygona philandron einai, kai philagnon; hōs te kan symbē ton tautēs arrena hypo aetou analōthēnai, ē hypo ixeutou thēreuthēnai, tautēn heterō andri mē epimignysthai, all᾽ auton pothein, auton anamenein, kai tē toutou mnēmē synapothnēskein.] Some say that the female turtledove is held by love for her mate and is so devoted to chastity that, if her male happens to be taken by an eagle or by a fowler, she does not mate with another, but longs for and awaits him alone, and even dies together with the memory of him. So also Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 3 on the Song; Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 10; Philo of Carpasia on Cant. 1.; Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 19, and on Psalm. CXVIII.; Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 1, ch. 17; Justus of Urgel, Theodoret, Aponius and Gregory the Great on Song 1:10; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron; Ildefonsus of Toledo, Sermon on the Purification of St Mary, if it is really his; Theophylact on Luke, ch. 2; Pisides, On the Creation of the World, line 998; Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, Sermon 7; Michael Glycas, Annals, section 1; Bernard on the Song, Sermons 40 and 59, and the Sermon on the Nativity of St Mary, On the Aqueduct; the Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] on Lev 12:6; R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Ps 74:19; Damir in the chapter On شفنين [shifnīn] siphnin, that is, the turtledove. All these, I say, attribute to the turtledove what the older writers had written of the dove alone: that she is so devoted to one mate that, when he dies, she does not admit another. As a result, those who have commented on the Song of Solomon have not sufficiently understood why Solomon so often designates the bride by the name of his dove. Thus Song 2:14: My dove, in the clefts of the rock, etc. And Song 5:2: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove. And Song 6:8: My dove, my perfect one, is but one, etc. By this, clearly, he wished to signify that she was loved by him alone, and that he in turn was uniquely dear to her, just as among doves there is a remarkable love between mates and a very firm law of marriage. If this was less true in the type, that is, in Solomon, who had wives by the ἑκατοντάδας [hekatontadas], it is nevertheless most true ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντι [en tō typōthenti], that is, in Christ: just as we acknowledge him alone as bridegroom, so he has one church, which he has betrothed to himself for ever in righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness and mercy, Hos 2:19. Hence the Apostle, 2 Cor 11:2: I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.

Although המה properly means to make a noise and to be in tumult, nevertheless the Hebrew מעי המו in Song 5:4 the Greeks render ἡ κοιλία μου ἐθροήθη [hē koilia mou ethroēthē], and Jerome, My belly trembled. So too in Ezek 7:16, where the same Jerome has, They shall be on the mountains like doves, all trembling, and Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], They shall be on the mountains themselves like doves of the valleys, all trembling: the words all trembling correspond to the Hebrew כלם המות. And in Hos 11:11, for ויחרדו you may read in Junius, they shall come running in trepidation, etc., like a dove from the land of Assyria. In others: they shall tremble, or they shall fear, or they tremble like a dove, etc. These expressions exactly capture the dove's nature. For the dove is a most fearful animal. Hence Varro on doves, On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 7: Because of their natural fear they seek the highest places on roofs. And a little later: For nothing is more timid than a dove. And in Ovid, Metam. book 5, Fable 10, the nymph Arethusa says of herself and of Alpheus pursuing her:
So I ran, so that wild one pressed upon me, As the dove flees the hawk on trembling wing, And as the hawk is wont to harry trembling doves.
The dove, once wounded by your talons, hawk, is terrified by the slightest whirring of a wing.
And Valerius Flaccus, in the eighth book of the Argonautica, of Medea:

But lo! the maiden, after the manner of a frightened dove, When, encompassed by the huge shadow of a bird of prey, She falls trembling upon whatever man she meets. Just so she, Struck with heavy fear, threw herself into the midst, etc.
As the Chorus in Sophocles' Ajax, line 139:
— — — πεφόβημαι Πτηνῆς ὡς ὄμμα πελειάς. [pephobēmai / Ptēnēs hōs omma peleias.]
I fear, like the eye of the winged dove. And another poet in the Suda, under Πελειάδες [Peleiades]:
Δειλαί τοι δείλοισιν ἐφεδρεύουσι πέλειαι, [Deilai toi deiloisin ephedreuousi peleiai,]

Timid doves sit upon timid [eggs]. To this belongs the fact that the dove is so often called τρήρων [trērōn] by Homer, ἐπεὶ διὰ τὴν ἀθένειαν εὐλαβὴς ἡ ὄρνις αὕτη, τρεῖν δ' ἐστὶ τὸ εὐλαβεῖσθαι [epei dia tēn atheneian eulabēs hē ornis hautē, trein d' esti to eulabeisthai], because on account of its weakness this bird is fearful, for τρεῖν [trein] means to fear. So Athenaeus in book 9.
