Nor otherwise the old Scholiast on Homer, Eustathius on Odyssey μ' [mu], Hesychius, Suidas, the Etymologicum, etc. And Apollonius imitates Homer thus, in book 3 of the Argonautica, verse 541:
Τρήρων μὲν φεύγουσα βίην κίρκοιο πελειὰς, Ὑψόθεν Αἰσονίδεω πεφοβημένη ἔμπεσε κόλποις· [Trērōn men pheugousa biēn kirkoio peleias, Hypsothen Aisonideō pephobēmenē empese kolpois]
A timid dove, fleeing the violence of a hawk, fell terrified from on high into the bosom of Aeson's son.

Perhaps the word ἀκέραιος [akeraios] is more correctly referred, with Eustathius on Iliad 2, 855, to κεραΐζειν [keraizein], to harm, to injure, so that it denotes one who harms no one; from which it is transferred to anyone free from guile and deceit. Whoever wishes to know the opinions of others should consult SUICER, Thesaur. Ecclesiast. vol. 1, p. 155.
On the sacrifices of doves and turtledoves.

The Jews sought doves not only for eating but also for sacrifices, which were of many kinds. Thus Lev 1:14 deals with a voluntary burnt offering of turtledoves or young doves. In Levit. V, 7. one who had not rebuked another who blasphemed, or had himself sworn rashly, or had defiled himself by touching an unclean thing, is commanded to offer a pair of turtledoves or doves, one for a sin offering, the other for a burnt offering. In Lev 12:6. God requires of a woman after childbirth, once the days of her purification are completed, a yearling lamb for a burnt offering and a young dove or a turtledove for a sin offering; or, if she cannot offer a lamb, two turtledoves or two young doves. You may see the same offerings prescribed also for one who has been healed of leprosy, Levit. XIV, 22; likewise for one who has suffered from a discharge, when he has been cleansed of his flux, Levit. XV, 13. 14; and ἐν τῷ τῆς αἱμοῤῥοούσης καθαρισμῷ [en tō tēs haimorrhoousēs katharismō], Levit. XV, 28. 29; and in the purification of the Nazirite who has defiled himself by contact with a dead body, Num. VI, 10.

In these sacrifices note, first, that God preferred doves and turtledoves to other birds because of the purity, chastity, simplicity, gentleness and the other shadows of virtues that have been observed in them. 2. That adult turtledoves, but only young doves, were offered on the altar, because turtledoves are best at a mature age, doves at a tender age. 3. That most of these sacrifices were only those of the poorer people, as is expressly noted in Levit. V, 7. and XII, 6. So gather even from this how poor the holy Virgin, the mother of Christ, was, who after her purification offered not a lamb but turtledoves or young doves, Luc. II, 24. 4. That sacrifices of this kind were already in use before the Law is clear from the example of Abraham, who was commanded to offer to God, together with a three-year-old heifer, she-goat and ram, a turtledove and a גוזל gozal, that is, a young bird of the dove kind: namely, so that this sacrifice might embrace all the kinds of victims that were afterwards established in the Law. This I think the simplest explanation, although many seek various mysteries here. Some would have these five animals signify the gifts of Christ; others, those for whom God had destined the land of Canaan, and the virtues required in them; others, finally, what the condition of Abraham's descendants would be. For by the ox, the goat and the lamb, which are land animals and accustomed to live under the yoke of men, they say is signified the time when they would live abased and humble and in servitude to the Egyptians; by the turtledove, which is solitary, the sojourn of the Jews in the desert; and by the dove, which is gregarious and lives in cultivated places, their dwelling in Canaan. 5. That the gentiles too, through a certain perverse κακοζηλίᾳ [kakozēlia], adopted sacrifices of doves. Propertius, book 4, in the Elegy to the Procuress: “But take, o queen Venus, the throat of a ringed dove, cut before your hearths for its desert.”
“Therefore often the white dove, a wife taken from her husband, is burned on the hot hearths.”
Yet the eating of doves seems to have been forbidden to the initiates of Venus, as may be gathered from these lines of Martial, book 13, Epigr. 66:
“Do not violate tender doves with too hard a tooth, if the rites of the Cnidian Goddess have been handed down to you.”

The rite by which the Jews slaughtered turtledoves and doves is taught briefly by Moses in Levit. I, 15. 16. 17. and V, 8., and at greater length by the Talmudists in Zebachim ch. 6, fol. 64, and by Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 6, §§ 20, 21, 22, 23, and ch. 7, §§ 6, 7, 8. Much could be drawn from these that is not altogether commonplace, if that were our present business. But here it will suffice to have noted that the Hebrews slaughtered other victims with a blade, but birds with the fingernail alone, by which, with the head bent back, their throat was torn open. In Hebrew this is מלק, which the Greeks render ἀποκνίζειν [apoknizein], that is, to tear with the nail, or to cut off, Lev 1:15 and V, 8., the only places where it occurs. The Jerusalem Targum has עום, and Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] חום, which is the same, ח and ע being interchanged. In Arabic the same is حذم [ḥadhama] or خذم [khadhama], which they render to cut and to tear apart. Thus خذمت الصقر [khadhamat al-ṣaqr], the hawk tore with its talons, in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], in his Lexicon under the word מלק, describes the rite of tearing the bird thus: ואר״זל כיצד מולקין חטאת העוף נותן שתי גפיה בין שתי אצבעותיו ושתי רגליה בין שתי אצבעותיו והיה מותח צוארה על שתי אצבעותיו והיה מולק בצפורן ממול עורף עד שמגיע לסימנים וקוצץ אותן או רובן ואינו מבדיל שנאמר ולא יבדיל אבל בעולה העוף שאמר ומלק את ראשו ולא אמר ולא יבדיל הוא מולק ומבדיל הראש בעצמו הגוף בעצמו Our masters of blessed memory said: How was the sin offering of a bird torn? He (the priest) placed its wings between two fingers and its feet between two fingers, and stretched its neck over his two fingers, and cut with his nail opposite the nape until he reached the signs (in the throat), which he severed, or the greater part of them, yet so that he did not divide it, because it is said Lev 5:8 „And he shall not divide it“. But in the burnt offering of a bird, because it is said, „He shall wring off its head“, and it is not added, „And he shall not divide it“, Lev 1:15, he cut so that the head was separated from the trunk of the body. So he, from the passage of the Talmud we have cited. See also Maimonides, who asserts that this was מעבודות קשות שבמקדש, one of the most laborious services of the Sanctuary, in the book On the offering of sacrifices ch. 7, § 8 .

So that victims should not be lacking, in the first part of the temple, which was called פרבר parbar, 1 Chr 26:18, oxen, sheep and doves were sold, John 2:14. Accordingly in Maimonides' treatise On the vessels of the Sanctuary ch. 7, § 9 (among the officers of the temple, whom the Hebrews called ממוני המקדש and the Greeks στρατηγοὺς τοῦ ἱεροῦ [stratēgous tou hierou], Luke 22:52) there is listed הממונה שעל הקינים, the officer over the nests, that is, over the birds. And he is described thus: הדא שפוסקין עמו שימכור הקנים לקורבנות כך וכך בסלע וכל מי שהוא חייב תורים או שני בני יונה יביא דמיהם למקדשי וזה הממונה נותן הקנים לבעלי הקורבנות ועושה חשבון עם הגוברים ונותנין לו משלושים יום לשלושים יום, He is the one with whom they contract that he provide birds for the offerings, so many or so many for a shekel. And whoever was obliged to offer either turtledoves or young doves brought the price to the sanctuary. And this officer gave the birds to those whose duty it was to offer, and valued them with the treasurers; and, once he had agreed on the price, they paid him within three days. And a little later: וכן קן שנמצא פסול או שנפסל קודם שיקרוב נותן אחר תחתיו, And if any bird was found unfit, or became unfit (through ceremonial defilement) before it was offered, he gave another in its place. That these arrangements were devised for gain by greedy and avaricious priests, Jerome teaches in these words on Matthew ch. 21: According to the commandments of the Law, in the temple of the Lord, the most confined in the whole world, with the people flocking there from almost all the regions of the Jews, innumerable victims were sacrificed, especially on feast days: bulls, rams and he-goats, while the poor, so as not to be without a sacrifice, offered young doves and turtledoves. It often happened that those who had come from afar had no victims. The priests therefore devised a way to make a prey of the people: they sold all the animals needed for the sacrifices, so that they might both sell to those who had none and themselves receive back again what had been bought. Hence Christ, rightly and justly angered against these profiteers, overturned the seats of those who sold doves, Matth. XXI, 12. and Marc. XI, 15. And to those who sold doves he said, Take these things hence. Do not make my father's house a house of trade, John 2:16.

Much on this rite has been collected from the writings of the Hebrew masters by THEODOR. DASSOVIUS in a dissertation to which he gave the title Avis, ungue secta, inque sacrificium oblata, ad illustranda commata Lev 1:14 ff. et V, 7. ff. Wittenberg 1697.
On Noah's Dove, and on the Form of a Dove which appeared at the Baptism of Christ.

Noah, shut up in the ark, since he had not learned from the raven what he longed to know, namely how far the waters of the flood had decreased, also sent out the dove, a docile bird and friendly to man, which flies long and far, Ps. V, 7. and gladly feeds on the ground, because it is one of the ἐκ τῶν σπερμολόγων [ek tōn spermologōn], and has this implanted in it by its nature, that it returns to its nest from anywhere, even from the most remote places. For these reasons, then, the dove was sent out by Noah; but it returned not long after, because it found no place of rest: for although the tops of the mountains had long since appeared, yet on an earth still λιμναζομένῃ [limnazomenē], as Josephus says, that is, either still standing under water, or at least full of pools and marshy, nothing was then firm. But the same dove, sent out again seven days later, returned toward evening, carrying an olive branch in its mouth. There are some among the Hebrews who will have it that this branch was plucked on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem, or elsewhere in Judaea, which was untouched by the waters of the flood. Bereshit Rabbah ch. 33: מהיכן הביאה אותו רבי אבא בר כהנא אמר משבשושין שבארץ ישראל הביאה אותו רבי לוי אמר מהר המשחה הביאה אותו דלא טפת ארעה דישראל במבולא והוא שהקבה אומר ליחזקיאל ארץ לא מטוהרה היא ולא גושמה ביום זעם, Whence did it (the dove) bring it (the branch)? Rabbi Abba, son of Cahana (the priest), said: It brought it from the shrubs of the land of Israel. R. Levi said: It brought it from the Mount of Olives, because the land of Israel was not submerged by the flood. As God, the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Ezekiel in chapter 22, verse 24: That land is not cleansed, nor rained upon in the day of indignation. These things are utterly absurd, since we read that even the highest mountains under the whole heaven were covered by the waters of the flood, Gen 7:19. Moreover, to what end would God have kept the land of Canaan, not yet holy, free from the inundation? To what end would he have ordered Noah to build the ark with such great labour? Why was he not rather ordered to withdraw there with the beasts, wild animals and birds? And if the waters of the flood spared the land of Canaan, what became of the inhabitants of that land? Did they too escape the common destruction, and do their descendants, forsooth, acknowledge another ancestor besides Noah, from whom Moses derived the whole human race? And how did God allow the survivors of so great a destruction to be driven out by the accursed Canaan, who not long after the time of the flood seized their dwelling place? Finally, since the waters rose so many cubits above the neighbouring mountains, what prevented them from overwhelming the land of Canaan? They will say this was done by the power of God, and I grant that it could have been done. But although we believe miracles when they are written, still no one is permitted to invent them for himself on his own authority, which these men openly do. For they cite Ezekiel in vain, who has not one γρῦ [gry] about the flood. He only, while reproaching the Israelites with various crimes and recounting the various punishments inflicted, or to be inflicted, on them, denies among other things that their land was, or would be, rained upon in the day of indignation. That is, in keeping with the threats of the Law, Deuter. XI, 17. Lest the Lord, his wrath kindled against you, shut up the heavens, so that there be no rain, and the land yield not its produce. And of the prophet Amos 4:7, where God speaks thus: I also withheld the rain from you, etc. And I caused it to rain upon one city, and upon another I caused it not to rain: one part was rained upon, and the part on which it did not rain withered. This was shown by a famous example when, at Elijah's word, the heaven was shut, and neither dew nor rain came down upon Judaea for three years and more, 1 Reg. XVII. and XVIII. But we argue in vain, since the very words of Moses amply show that the olive branch was plucked from those places that the flood had inundated. For thus Moses says of Noah, Genes. VIII, 8. He sent forth the dove from him, to see whether the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. And in verse 11: And the dove came to him in the evening; and behold, a plucked olive leaf in her mouth. And so Noah knew that the surface of the earth was relieved of the waters. This would be falsely said if that leaf had been brought from a land that the flood had not touched. For it could have been brought from there even at the time when the waters elsewhere were at their very highest. From this it also follows that this leaf was not plucked in the earthly Paradise, as others of the Jews assert. Bereshit Rabbah, in the place cited above: רב ביבי אמר נפתחו לה שערי גן עדן והביאה אותו משם, R. Bibi said: The gates of the garden of Eden were opened to it, and from there it brought this leaf. The same opinion is attributed to a certain Berechiah in Vayikra Rabbah at the end of ch. 31. That is, if we believe the Hebrews, the garden of Eden was raised above the highest summits of the mountains, so that the waters of the flood did not reach that far. Many of the ancients incline to the same view. Among them is Lactantius, or rather Venantius, who speaks thus of the earthly Paradise in the poem On the Phoenix,
And when the deluge had drowned the world in its waves, it rose above the Deucalionian waters.

This is also the view of most of the Scholastics on book 2 of the Sentences, Dist. 17; of Tostatus and Cajetan on Genesis; of Bellarmine in the book De gratia primi hominis, ch. 14; and of Malvenda, De Paradiso, ch. 84. But we raise many objections to this view in a separate work, De Paradiso terrestri. From where, then, shall we say this olive leaf was brought? From Assyria, it seems, which in 2 Reg. XVII, 32. is said to be ארץ זית יצהר, or, as the Chaldee has it, ארע דזיתהא עבדין משחא, a land whose olive trees make oil, that is, a land abounding in olive trees, and very fruitful ones. For Noah's ark had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat, or of the Gordyaeans, to which Assyria lies adjacent toward the south. I would suppose that the dove, on leaving the ark, flew off toward that quarter of the sky, drawn by the warmth of the south and also driven by the wind. For it is probable that the wind which God had raised to dry up the waters, Gen. VIII, 1., blew from the north toward the south. So in Ovid, in the flood of Deucalion, Jupiter, appeased,
Scattered the clouds, and, the rain-clouds removed by the North Wind, Showed the lands to the sky, and the heavens to the lands.
This dove, then, flying south into Assyria, could have plucked an olive leaf from some mountain, part of which the receding waters had laid bare.

If it is asked how an olive branch with green leaves could have lasted so long under the waters, I shall have two things to answer. First, although in Jerome's version Noah's dove is read to have carried in her mouth a branch with green leaves, yet in the Hebrew we read only that she had in her mouth עלה זית טרף, an olive leaf plucked off. Second, the ancients report that certain species not only of the olive but of other trees too live and stay green under water. Theophrastus, Hist. Plant. book 4, chapter 8: Ἐν δὲ τῇ θαλάττῃ ἐρυθρᾷ δενδρά τινα φύεται· καὶ καλοῦσιν αὐτὰ δάφνην, καὶ ἐλαίαν. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν δάφνη ὅμοια τῇ ἀρίᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐλαία τῷ φύλλῳ· καρπὸν δὲ ἔχει ἡ ἐλαία παραπλήσιον δὲ ταῖς ἐλαίαις [En de tē thalattē erythra dendra tina phyetai; kai kalousin auta daphnēn, kai elaian. Esti de hē men daphnē homoia tē aria, hē de elaia tō phyllō; karpon de echei hē elaia paraplēsion de tais elaiais]. Pliny condenses this in book 13, ch. 25: But in the Red Sea (it is a marvel) woods live, chiefly the laurel and the olive, bearing berries. And Theophrastus again: Ἐν δὲ ταῖς νήσοις ταῖς ὑπὸ τῆς πλυμμυρίδος καταλαμβανομέναις, δένδρα μεγάλα πεφυκέναι ἡλίκα πλάτανοι· συμβαίνειν δὲ ὅθ᾽ ἡ πλημμυρὶς ἐπέλθοι, τὰ μὲν ἄλλα κατακρύπτεσθαι ὅλα, τῶν δὲ μεγίστων ὑπερέχειν τοὺς κλάδους [En de tais nēsois tais hypo tēs plymmyridos katalambanomenais, dendra megala pephykenai hēlika platanoi; symbainein de hoth᾽ hē plēmmyris epelthoi, ta men alla katakryptesthai hola, tōn de megistōn hyperechein tous kladous], etc. ἔχειν δὲ τὰ δένδρα φύλλον μὲν ὅμοιον τῇ δάφνῃ, ἄνθος δὲ τοῖς οἴσοις [echein de ta dendra phyllon men homoion tē daphnē, anthos de tois oisois] (read with Pliny τοῖς ἴοις [tois iois]) καὶ τῷ χρώματι, καὶ τῇ ὀσμῇ, καρπὸν δ᾽ ἡλίκον ἐλαίᾳ, καὶ τοῦτον εὐώδη σφόδρα, καὶ τὰ μὲν φύλλα οὐκ ἀποβάλλειν, τὸ δὲ ἄνθος, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν ἅμα τῷ φθινοπώρῳ γίνεσθαι· τοῦ δὲ ἔαρος ἀποῤῥεῖν [kai tō chrōmati, kai tē osmē, karpon d᾽ hēlikon elaia, kai touton euōdē sphodra, kai ta men phylla ouk apoballein, to de anthos, kai ton karpon hama tō phthinopōrō ginesthai; tou de earos aporrhein]. Pliny rendered this as follows, with the order somewhat changed: In the same region the tide covers woods of islands, although they are taller than plane trees and the tallest poplars. Their leaves are those of the laurel, the flower is that of the violet in scent and colour, the berries are like olives, and they too have a pleasant scent; they grow in autumn, and the leaves never fall. The sea covers the smaller of these entirely; the tops of the largest stand out. Theophrastus adds: Ἀλλὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ θαλάττῃ πεφυκέναι, ἀείφυλλα μὲν, τὸν δὲ καρπὸν ὅμοιον ἔχειν τοῖς θέρμοις [Alla de en autē tē thalattē pephykenai, aeiphylla men, ton de karpon homoion echein tois thermois]. Hence Pliny: Other trees too have been seen in the deep, etc. in the same sea, always retaining their leaves, their fruit like the lupine. Plutarch too, in the book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: Τῆς δὲ Γεδρωσίας καὶ Τρωγλοδύτιδος ἡ καθήκει πρὸς τὸν ὠκεανὸν, ἀφόρου διὰ ξηρότητα, καὶ ἀδένδρου παντάπασιν οὔσης, ἐν τῇ παρακειμένῃ καὶ παρακεχυμένῃ θαλάττῃ θαυμαστὰ μεγέθη φυτῶν τρέφεται, καὶ κατὰ βυθοῦ τέθηλεν· ὧν τὰ μὲν ἐλαίας, τὰ δὲ δάφνας, τὰ Ἴσιδος τρίχας καλοῦσιν [Tēs de Gedrōsias kai Trōglodytidos hē kathēkei pros ton ōkeanon, aphorou dia xērotēta, kai adendrou pantapasin ousēs, en tē parakeimenē kai parakechymenē thalattē thaumasta megethē phytōn trephetai, kai kata bythou tethēlen; hōn ta men elaias, ta de daphnas, ta Isidos trichas kalousin]. But that part of the Gedrosian and Troglodytic region which reaches to the ocean, although it is wholly barren through dryness and lacks trees, yet in the neighbouring sea that washes it plants of unusual size grow and sprout from the depths; some of them they call olives, others laurels, others hairs of Isis. I think Plutarch has this from Agatharchides, in whom some things are read, book 5, chapter 53, about olives in the sea and the hairs of Isis, but interpolated by Photius. The tree in the sea like a plane tree, of which Theophrastus and Pliny speak, is called in Arabic قرم [qurm] Karam. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: القرم نبت كالدلب غلظا وبياضا ينبت في البحر جوف [al-qurm nabt ka-l-dulb ghilaẓan wa-bayāḍan yanbut fī al-baḥr jawf] The alkaram grows like a plane tree, a large and white tree. It comes up in the middle of the sea . Since it is clear from these passages that true trees live in the sea itself, and among them a tree most like the olive, which therefore not only Pliny but also the inhabitants of those places simply call an olive: why should not an olive, whose leaves never fall (whence the Poet,
— — a branch of the ever-leafy olive)

have kept its leaves under the waters for several months, or at least some one of them, which was plucked by the dove? All the more so, since it may be gathered that olive leaves long withstand water and rain from the fact that the Ichthyophagi cover their huts with them. Strabo, book 16, speaks of μάνδρας στεγαστὰς ἀπὸ φυλλάδος ἐλαίνης [mandras stegastas apo phyllados elainēs], huts roofed with olive leaf. And Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 17: Οἱ δὲ τὰς τῶν ἐλαιῶν κορυφὰς ἀλλήλαις συνάπτοντες εἶτα χρῶνται σκηνώμασι [Hoi de tas tōn elaiōn koryphas allēlais synaptontes eita chrōntai skēnōmasi]; Others use the tops of olives, joined to one another, as tents. And Diodorus, book 3, p. 109: Ἐλαίαι φύονται πάνυ πολλαὶ περὶ τοὺς τόπους τούτους, τὰ μὲν πρὸς τὴν ῥίζαν ἔχουσαι προσκλυζόμενα τῇ θαλάττη, πυκναὶ δὲ τοῖς φυλλώμασι [Elaiai phyontai pany pollai peri tous topous toutous, ta men pros tēn rhizan echousai prosklyzomena tē thalattē, pyknai de tois phyllōmasi], etc. ταύτας ἀλλήλαις συμπλέκοντες, καὶ συνεχῆ σκιὰν ποιοῦντες, ἰδιαζούσαις σκηναῖς ἐμβιοῦσιν [tautas allēlais symplekontes, kai synechē skian poiountes, idiazousais skēnais embiousin]. Very many olives grow around those places, with their roots immersed in the sea and with very dense foliage. Weaving these together and making a continuous shade, they live in them privately as in tents. For ἐλαίαι [elaiai], that is, olives, our editions wrongly have ἐλάται [elatai], firs, whose leaves are too narrow to make a continuous shade. Diodorus must therefore be corrected from Agatharchides and Strabo.

There is now no need to say how pleased Noah was to see the dove returning with an olive leaf in its mouth. From this he inferred two things. 1. What the Prophet observes: that the land had been relieved of the waters, that is, not only the highest mountains, whose summits had appeared long before (Gen 8:5), but also the level places, or at least the hills, in which olives most delight. Columella, book 6, chapter 6: But it (the olive) loves neither low-lying places nor steep ones, but rather moderate slopes, such as we see in Italy among the Sabines, or in the whole province of Baetica. Palladius, book 3, chapter 18: In hot places it delights in a northern hill, in cold places in a southern one. It takes pleasure in middling slopes. It tolerates neither the lowest place nor a steep one, rather moderate slopes, such as the Sabine region or Baetica (read it rather loves moderate slopes). Florentinus, book 9 of the Geoponica, in the chapter Περὶ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδείου ἐλαίας καὶ γῆς σχημάτιον [Peri aeros epitēdeiou elaias kai gēs schēmation], On the air suitable for the olive and on the shapes of the ground: Συναίρεται δὲ τῇ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπιτηδειότητι καὶ τὰ τῆς γῆς σχήματα προσκλινῆ καὶ ὑψηλά. Αἱ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις τόποις, διὰ τὸ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων καταψύχεσθαι· τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τοῦ ἡλίου πυρῶδες, κάλλιστον ἔλαιον ποιοῦσι. [Synairetai de tē tou aeros epitēdeiotēti kai ta tēs gēs schēmata prosklinē kai hypsēla. Hai gar en tois toioutois topois, dia to hypo tōn anemōn katapsychesthai; to hyperballon tou hēliou pyrōdes, kalliston elaion poiousi.] Sloping and elevated shapes of ground also contribute to the suitability of the air. For those that are in such a situation, because the excessive heat of the sun is cooled by the winds, produce the finest oil. Perdicca, in the Themes of Jerusalem, p. 71:
Ὄρος μικρὸν ἀνεστηκώς ἐστι τοῦ Ἐλαιῶνος, [Oros mikron anestēkōs esti tou Elaiōnos,]
The small mount of Olivet rises up. And a little later,
Πρὸς δέ γε τὸ μεσαίτατον μέρος τοῦ ὄρους τούτου Ὁ Ἐλαιῶν κατάκαρπος ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν ὄντως. [Pros de ge to mesaitaton meros tou orous toutou Ho Elaiōn katakarpos hyper tēn physin ontōs.]

Toward the middle part of that mount the olive grove is fruitful wholly beyond nature. A small mount, that is, a hill, in the middle of which olives grow. This is just what Palladius had said, that they take pleasure in middling slopes. Second, Noah learned from this that the earth had not been so devastated by the waters of the flood that some fruit-bearing trees did not still survive, on which men and beasts might feed after the flood. For from the olive a judgement could be made about the rest. Indeed, the fact that the dove had returned not at once, as before, but only toward evening, suggested that it had found places where it could rest. For it was not credible that it had flown the whole day. Yet in the evening it flew back to the ark, either because resting on the branches of trees did not seem comfortable enough, or for lack of food, or from longing for its mate and its young, if it had any, or finally because God so provided, that by its return it might refresh Noah's anxious mind and rouse him to hope of an imminent deliverance. But when it was sent out a third time after seven days, it did not return to the ark any more, because then, as the waters receded more and more, it lacked neither food nor a nest in which to hide. From this it was perceived that the waters had ceased.

See the traces of this story in the Chaldaica of Abydenus, cited by Eusebius, book 9 of the Praeparatio, and by Cyril in the first book against Julian: Τρίτη δὲ ἡμέρᾳ ἔπειτα ὑὼν ἐκόπασε, μεθίει τῶν ὀρνίθων πείρην ποιούμενος, εἴπου γῆν ἴδοι, τοῦ ὕδατος ἐκδῦσαν. αἱ δὲ ἐκδεχομένου σφέας πελάγεος ἀχανέος, ἀπορέουσαι ὅπη καθορμίσονται, παρὰ τὸν Ξίσουθρον ὀπίσω κομίζονται, καὶ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῇσιν ἕτεραι, ὡς δὲ τῇσι τρίτησιν εὐτύχεεν· ἀφίκατο γὰρ δὴ πηλοῦ κατάπλεοι τοὺς ταρσοὺς, θεοί μιν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀφανίζουσιν [Tritē de hēmera epeita hyōn ekopase, methiei tōn ornithōn peirēn poioumenos, eipou gēn idoi, tou hydatos ekdysan. hai de ekdechomenou spheas pelageos achaneos, aporeousai hopē kathormisontai, para ton Xisouthron opisō komizontai, kai ep᾽ autēsin heterai, hōs de tēsi tritēsin eutycheen; aphikato gar dē pēlou katapleoi tous tarsous, theoi min ex anthrōpōn aphanizousin], On the third day after it had stopped raining, he (Xisuthrus, as he calls Noah) sent out some birds to make a trial, whether he might see land emerging from the water. But since the boundless sea everywhere received them, and they were uncertain where to land, they came back to him; and after these, others. When he succeeded with the third ones sent out, for they had returned with muddy feet, the gods removed him from among men. He says birds in the plural, because Noah sent out a raven and a dove. And that they returned muddy, just as Eutychius also says of the dove, p. 40: رجعت رجلتها مبلولة بالماء [rajaʿat rijlatuhā mablūla bi-l-māʾ] It returned with its feet wet with water. And before him Josephus: ὑπανελθούσης δὲ πεπηλομένης [hypanelthousēs de pepēlomenēs], but when it had returned muddy. For in Hebrew we have ותבא אליו היונה, and the dove came back to him. And יון, which means mud, alludes to the name of the dove, יונה. Finally, what was said of the birds, or at least of the dove, that it flew away and did not return, Abydenus ineptly transferred to Xisuthrus, or Noah, as if he had then been removed from the midst. But the Greeks report this very thing in such a way that you would hardly find anything lacking in them, except that they substitute their own Deucalion for Noah. Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Οἱ μὲν οὖν μυθολόγοι τῷ Δευκαλίωνί φασι περιστερὰν ἐκ τῆς λάρνακος ἀφιεμένην δήλωμα γενέσθαι, χειμῶνος μὲν εἴσω πάλιν ἐνδυομένην, εὐδίας δὲ ἀποπτᾶσαν [Hoi men oun mythologoi tō Deukalioni phasi peristeran ek tēs larnakos aphiemenēn dēlōma genesthai, cheimōnos men eisō palin endyomenēn, eudias de apoptasan]. The mythographers say that a dove, sent out of the ark, signalled a storm to Deucalion when it came back inside, and fair weather when it flew away. The Arab dream-interpreters attribute to the ورشان [warashān] vvarsen, that is, the wood pigeon, what Moses attributes to the dove. For thus they say of the wood pigeon in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter الورشان [al-warashān] Alvvarsen: وهو في المنام رجل غريب يدل علي اخبار ورسل لانه اخبر توحا عليه السلام تنقص الما لما كان في السفينة [wa-huwa fī l-manām rajul gharīb yadullu ʿalā akhbār wa-rusul li-annahu akhbara Tūḥan ʿalayhi al-salām tanaqquṣ al-mā lammā kāna fī l-safīna] Seen in sleep by a stranger, it signifies messengers and couriers, because it announced to Noah, peace be upon him, when he was in the ark, the decrease of the waters. The Arabs, namely, prefer the wood pigeon to the dove because God is believed to have appeared to Muhammad in the form of a wood pigeon and to have inspired many things. Ludovico di Varthema, Navigation, book 1, ch. 18: While we were on our way (towards Mecca) countless wood pigeons darkened the sky. They say that birds of this kind descend from that bird which spoke into the ear of Muhammad under the guise of the Holy Spirit. See the rest there.

So much for the literal sense of the story of the dove which Noah sent out of the ark. As for the mystical sense, many hold that the olive leaf, or twig, was a symbol of the peace and covenant which God was shortly to make with Noah. Tertullian, On Baptism, book 8: After the baptism (so to speak) of the world, the dove, herald of heaven's wrath appeased, announced peace to the earth, sent out of the ark and returning with the olive, a sign which is held out for peace among the nations too. Jerome, Epist. 83 to Oceanus, ch. 3: With a branch of refreshment and light it announces peace to the world. And in the Dialogue against Lucifer: The dove announces peace to the earth. Chrysostom on Matthew, Homily 12: Κλάδον φέρον ἐλαίας, τὴν κοινὴν τῆς οἰκουμένης γαλήνην εὐηγγελίσατο [Kladon pheron elaias, tēn koinēn tēs oikoumenēs galēnēn euēngelisato]; Bearing an olive branch, it proclaimed the common calm of the world. Amoenus in the Enchiridion of the Old and New Testament:

Messenger of the flood now abating, the dove brings back to the ark in its beak a branch of the green olive: for the raven, caught by gluttony among foul carcasses, had stayed; she brings back the new joys of peace granted.
Claudius Marius Victor on Genesis, book 2:
— — — sent out again, she brings back a small offering of the peace-bearing fruit of the olive.
And seeing the peace-bearing branch of the green olive, she plucks it and carries it back in her gentle beak to those shut in.
For the olive is a sign of peace. Virgil, book 2 of the Georgics:
— — cultivate the olive, gentle to peace.
He orders a hundred envoys to go to the king's narrow walls, all veiled with branches of Pallas.
And in his hand he holds out a branch of the peace-bearing olive,
Veiled with olive branches, and begging for pardon.

Livy, book 29: Ten envoys of the Locrians, covered in squalor and rags, while the consuls were sitting in the comitium, holding out the suppliants' emblems, olive branches, as is the custom of the Greeks, prostrated themselves on the ground before the tribunal with tearful cries. Polybius, book 3, on Hannibal crossing the Alps: Οἱ περὶ τὴν δίοδον οἰκοῦντες, συμφρονήσαντες ἐπὶ δόλῳ συνήντων αὐτῷ, θάλλους ἔχοντες, καὶ στεφάνους· τοῦτο γὰρ σχεδὸν πᾶσι τοῖς Βαρβάροις ἐπὶ σύνθημα φιλίας, καθάπερ τὸ κηρύκειον τοῖς Ἕλλησιν. [Hoi peri tēn diodon oikountes, symphronēsantes epi dolō synēntōn autō, thallous echontes, kai stephanous; touto gar schedon pasi tois Barbarois epi synthēma philias, kathaper to kērykeion tois Hellēsin.] The inhabitants along the route, having secretly conspired, come to meet him with branches of green olive and with garlands. For almost everywhere among the barbarians this is a sign of peace and friendship, as the caduceus is among the Greeks. Hence Ovid, Fasti book 1:
With your tresses bound with Actian leaves, come, Peace, and gently visit all the world.

With Actian leaves, that is, of the olive, from whose leaves a crown is woven for Peace. In the same way they hold that Minerva made peace with Neptune crowned with this tree, as Tertullian has it in De corona militis, chapter 13. So all interpret it. But why the olive's leaves are called Actian is not yet clear, and what the commentators offer does not satisfy me. I would therefore rather read frondibus Actaeis, that is, Attic leaves: because the olive is believed to have originated in Attica, which in Greek is called Ἀκτὴ [Aktē], whence the gentile adjective Ἀκταῖος [Aktaios]. Stephanus: Ἀκτὴ, οὕτως ἡ Ἀττικὴ ἐκαλεῖτο [Aktē, houtōs hē Attikē ekaleito]. And a little later: Τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀκταῖος καὶ Ἀκταῖα [To ethnikon Aktaios kai Aktaia]. Accordingly, just as Actaean honey is Attic honey in Columella on the garden,
Of Narycian pitch, or the honey of Actaean Hymettus:
so an Actaean olive is an Attic olive. Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 27, line 287:
Ἀκταίης τε γέραιρε φερέπτολιν ὄζον ἐλαίης, [Aktaiēs te geraire pheréptolin ozon elaiēs,]
And honour the city-bearing branch of the Actaean olive. Ausonius, in the Mosella, on the sheatfish:
Whom, as if his back were smeared with Actaean olive oil, I take for a river-dwelling dolphin. — —
Note in passing that in Lucian's Tragopodagra φύλλα ἀκτέας [phylla akteas] is something else, when he says:
Τίνες γὰρ οἵδε βάκτρα νωμᾶντες χεροῖν, Κάρηνα φύλλοις ἀκτέας καταστεφεῖς; [Tines gar hoide baktra nōmantes cheroin, Karēna phyllois akteas katastepheis?]
What crowd is this, who hold staves in their hands, their heads bound with garlands of Actaean leaf?

For there ἀκτέα [aktea] is ἀκτὴ [aktē], that is, sambucus [elder]: the gouty are depicted as binding their heads with its leaves, because elder leaves ποδαγρικοῖς βοηθεῖ μετὰ στέατος ταυρείου, ἢ τραγείου [podagrikois boēthei meta steatos taureiou, ē trageiou]. So Dioscorides; and Pliny not very differently. And Samonicus, in the chapter On driving away gout:

Likewise dwarf elder smeared with goat's tallow. Of the olive I add only this: that even in America the custom had long prevailed that olive branches were held to be a sign of peace. Columbus, Navigat. ch. 103, on a certain American island not far from Hispaniola: On our first arrival thirty young girls came to meet us, who, etc. carried olive branches in their hands, and when they approached the commander, they held out the branches to him as a sign of alliance and peace .

At the baptism of Christ there are some of the Fathers who hold that a real dove descended. Thus Tertullian, in the book On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 3, writes of the Spirit descending upon Christ: It was as truly a dove as it was also spirit; nor had it destroyed its own substance by assuming a foreign substance. And Augustine, On the Christian Combat, ch. 22, comparing the body of Christ with this dove, says: Nor do we say this in such a way as to say that the Lord Jesus alone had a true body, while the Holy Spirit appeared deceptively to the eyes of men; rather, we believe both those bodies to be true bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not becoming that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. But for almighty God, who made the whole creation out of nothing, it was not difficult to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves, just as it was not difficult for him to make a true body in the womb of Mary without male seed. Yet the four Evangelists do not say that a dove descended upon Christ, but ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [hōsei peristeran], as a dove. And Luke more explicitly says that the Holy Spirit descended σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [sōmatikō eidei hōsei peristeran], in bodily form as a dove. There the Syriac has ܒܕܡܘܬܐ ܓܘܫܡܐ ܕܝܘܢܐ [בדמותא גושמא דיונא], after the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Arabic, شبه جسد حمامة [shibh jasad ḥamāma] in the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Ethiopic, በሥጋ፡ ከመ፡ ርእየተ፡ ርግብ፡ [baśəgā kama rəʾəyata rəgəb] In a body as in the appearance of a dove. From this one may conclude that, in the Ethiopic translator's mind, what appeared was a body, but not the body of a real dove. St Augustine is followed by Thomas in the Summa, part 3, question 39, article 7. Indeed Sixtus of Siena, Biblioth. book 6, annotation 13, writes that almost all the Scholastic theologians hold the same view. Most of the more recent writers, however, think otherwise, namely that the Spirit descended not in a real dove but in the appearance of a dove. Caring little about Tertullian, they evade Augustine's authority in two ways. Some, like Pamelius, deny that the book On the Christian Combat is really Augustine's. Others, like Maldonatus, accept it as genuine, but contend that Augustine asserts only that a true body appeared, not however a real dove. But neither party is convincing.

Not the first, since it is established that the book On the Combat is Augustine's, both from its style and from Possidius' Indiculus and from Augustine himself, who acknowledges that book as his own in book 2 of the Retractations, ch. 3. Not the second, because Augustine calls that dove not only a true body but also a true body of a dove. It was not difficult for God, he says, to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves. In his opinion this was necessary so that the Holy Spirit should not deceive men, if that dove had not been what it seemed to be. He holds, therefore, that this dove was as truly a dove as Christ was truly a man. Accordingly I would say of both, that is, of Augustine as well as of Tertullian, that in arguing against those who held that Christ's body was as imaginary as that dove was, they erred, as often happens, τῇ τῆς ἀνθόλκης ἀμετρίᾳ [tē tēs anthol kēs ametria]. For although it would have sufficed to assert the reality of Christ's body, they wanted even this φάσμα ὄρνιθος [phasma ornithos], as Origen rightly calls it, to be taken for a real dove. But four things are to be noted here. First, outside the heat of controversy the same writers define it otherwise. For in Tertullian, book On Baptism, ch. 8, we read that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the figure of a dove. And in Augustine's Letter 102 to Evodius this dove is said to have been presented to the eyes in bodily appearance only, not expressed in the nature of a living animal. And in On the Trinity, book 2, ch. 5: Upon the Lord himself (the Holy Spirit) descended in bodily form, like a dove. Second, other Fathers regarded this dove as imaginary. Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho the Jew: Τοῦ ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνεύματος [tou epelthontos en eidei peristeras pneumatos]. Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 19: They said that the Spirit of God descended upon him like a dove. Origen on Luke, Homily 27: The Holy Spirit descended upon the Saviour in the appearance of a dove. Epiphanius against the Sabellians, Heresy 62: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς σχηματίζεται [en eidei peristeras schēmatizetai]. And the translator: He conformed himself to the likeness of a dove. Hilary on Matthew, Canon 2: The Holy Spirit is sent forth, and is recognized as visible in the appearance of a dove. Nonnus in the Paraphrase of St John calls it Ἀντίτυπον μίμημα πελειάδος [antitypon mimēma peleiados]. Juvencus, Evang. Hist. book 1:
And bearing bodily form, the Spirit descended from on high, imitating from the cloud an airy dove.
At once the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit in the appearance of a dove clothed Christ with honour.

Chrysostom on Matth., Homil. 12: Ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦμα ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς [Ēlthe to pneuma en eidei peristeras]. Isidore of Pelusium, Epist. 106: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς τὸ θεῖον ἐπεφάνη πνεῦμα [En eidei peristeras to theion epephanē pneuma]. Cyril on John: Περιστερᾶς ἐν σχήματι [Peristeras en schēmati]. And: ἐν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς σχηματισμῷ [en tō tēs peristeras schēmatismō]. The author of the book On the Wonders of Scripture, under Augustine's name, book 3, ch. 5: “But although the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the Lord in bodily form, there is not the least doubt that he did not take the dove from among the birds, but from the air.” The author of the book On the Sacraments, under Ambrose's name, book 1, ch. 5: “And behold! the Spirit descended as a dove: not a dove descended, but as it were a dove.” And a little later: “He descended from heaven not in the reality of a dove, but in the appearance of a dove.” Procopius of Gaza on Gen. XVIII: “The Holy Spirit came into our sight in the appearance of a dove; yet it was not a dove, because it did not have the nature that a dove has.” Third, it must be noted that Tertullian errs very gravely. For he says things of the Holy Spirit that cannot be true unless one imagines that the Holy Spirit took a dove to himself in hypostatic union. “The Spirit,” he says, “was as truly a dove as he was Spirit, and he had not destroyed his own substance by assuming a foreign one.” From this another error arose, namely that the Holy Spirit is as far below Christ as a dove is below a man. So Martial, comparing Stella's dove with Catullus's sparrow, maintains that Stella is a better poet than Catullus by as much
As a dove is greater than a sparrow.

But Chrysostom refutes this error as follows in Homily 12 on Matthew: Ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ φύσει, τὸ δὲ ἐν ὄψει περιστερᾶς ἐφάνη· [Ho men en tē hēmetera physei, to de en opsei peristeras ephanē] Christ appeared in our nature, but the Spirit in the form of a dove. Again: Ὁ μὲν υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ φύσιν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέλαβε· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα οὐ φύσιν ἀνέλαβε περιστερᾶς. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Εὐαγγελιστὴς οὐκ εἶπεν, ὅτι ἐν φύσει περιστερᾶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς· οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ μετὰ ταῦτα ὤφθη ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ τότε μόνον. [Ho men huios tou Theou physin anthrōpou anelabe; to de pneuma ou physin anelabe peristeras. Dia touto kai ho Euangelistēs ouk eipen, hoti en physei peristeras, all' en eidei peristeras; oukoun oude meta tauta ōphthē en toutō tō schēmati, alla tote monon.] The Son of God took on the nature of a man, but the Spirit did not take on the nature of a dove. Therefore the Evangelist did not say that he (descended) in the nature of a dove, but in the form of a dove. Nor did he appear in that form afterwards, but only then. Augustine, however, who was wholly free of this error, believed only that a real dove, created by God for this purpose, was the symbol of the presence of the Holy Spirit. This is a much lighter error. For although this opinion cannot be reconciled with the words of the Evangelists, it differs from the former in that it contains nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Holy Spirit; for, without detriment to his dignity, he could be signified as well by a real dove as by the image of a dove. Fourth, it should be noted that Augustine's argument, by which he tries to prove that this was a real dove, has little force. We believe, he says, that both those bodies, namely those of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, were real bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not proper that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. I grant this. But I deny that anyone saw this form of a dove except Christ himself, Matt 3:16 and Mark 1:10, and John, John 1:32 Christ was indeed baptized in the midst of the crowds, Luke 3:21, but no one has written that the dove appeared to them. And that it was seen by no one apart from Christ except John is plainly taught by John 1:32: John bore witness to him, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and he remained upon him. For what need would there have been of the testimony of so great a man to prove what others too had seen, indeed all the crowds that then stood around Christ and John? Moreover, this form of a dove did not deceive Christ, who was free from error; nor John, who had been forewarned by God that his Spirit would descend in visible form and remain upon his Son, and so, when he saw this form of a dove descend and settle upon Christ, he knew for certain that this was taking place in a vision, as God had foretold. Accordingly he does not say that he saw a dove, but as it were a dove. Yet even supposing, without conceding it, that this φάσμα [phasma] of a dove was seen by all and was believed by most to have been a real dove, not even so would the Holy Spirit have deceived them. For he does not truly deceive who places an image before the eyes with the intention not of deceiving but of teaching. Such was this vision, in which the form of a dove was set before the eyes, not so that it should be believed to be a real dove, but so that through it the presence of the Holy Spirit, and what his powers are, might be signified. If this is held to be falsehood, the use of all visions will be abolished, in which one thing is shown to the eyes and another to the mind. And the Holy Spirit would then have deceived not only in the vision of the dove but also in that of the fiery tongues. For those tongues were not real tongues, nor was it real fire. Accordingly, just as here he is said to have descended ὡσεὶ περιστερὰ [hōsei peristera], so there the tongues are said to have been seen ὡσεὶ πυρὸς [hōsei pyros], Acts 2:3. And a little before, a sound is said to have been heard, not of wind, but as of wind, ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας [hōsper pheromenēs pnoēs biaias], so that we may know that all these things happened in a vision.

I cannot refrain from adding that the Hebrews too, in Song 2:12, understand the Holy Spirit by the name of the turtledove, a bird of the dove kind. Hence the words of the sacred text, The voice of the turtledove is heard in our land, are paraphrased by the Chaldee thus: וקול רוחא דקודשא דפורקנא דאמרית לאברהם אביכון כבר שמעתון And the voice of the Holy Spirit, that is, the deliverance which I foretold to Abraham, your father, Gen 15:14 16., you have already heard. Origen too refers these very words to the Holy Spirit, who, he holds, is signified by the turtledove when he reveals more hidden things, and by the dove when he teaches things better suited to the understanding of the common people. The Holy Spirit, he says, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot grasp, is designated by the name of the turtledove, that is, of that bird which always dwells on mountain ridges and in the tops of trees. But in the valleys, and in those things which reach down to men, the dove is taken. So he writes on the words of the Canticle: The voice of the turtledove, etc.

An accurate description of this tree was given by Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in the Flora Aegyptiaco-Arabica p. 37, under this name: "Sceura marina, with lanceolate, entire leaves and tawny flowers. Arab. Schura, شورة [shūra], among the people of Muscat Germ, قرم [qurm]. Frequent on the islands and shores of the Red Sea; it grows in dense woods, like the alder groves of the northern world." And Forsskål's description confirms that Bochart rightly takes this tree to be the same one of which Theophrastus, Pliny and Plutarch speak in the passages adduced above; the plan of our work, however, does not permit us to add it here.
What follows from here on, on the typological significance of Noah's dove, we have thought best to omit.
It is proved that חריונים, or דביונים, 2 Reg. VI, 25, is a kind of chickpea, not dove's dung, as has hitherto been believed.

It is related in 2 Reg. VI, 25 that in the time of the famine at Samaria רובע הקב חריונים, the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung, was sold for five pieces of silver. Understand by these silver coins half-ounce pieces, each worth about thirty-six Tours sous, so that the total came to roughly nine livres of our money. Further, all the Hebrews with complete agreement report that the cab held only twenty-four eggs. So the fourth part of a cab would be a log, that is, a measure of six eggs. I shall not undertake to prove these things, lest I seem to do what has already been done. I shall only try to answer a most difficult question, which no one has solved so far: why so tiny a measure of so worthless a thing, namely dove's dung, was valued so highly, and for what use it was bought.

I. There are those who say that the Samaritans, pressed by hunger, used this dung as food. Among them is Eutychius, patriarch of Alexandria, in his Annals, where he speaks of the famine of Samaria, p. 213: واكلوا زبل الحمام [wa-akalū zibl al-ḥamām] And they ate dove's dung. In the same way Rabshakeh, about to besiege Jerusalem, threatened that he would make the inhabitants eat their own dung and drink their own urine, 2 Reg. XVIII, 27, and Es. XXXVI, 12. But these words of Rabshakeh are nothing but the empty taunt of a boastful Thraso, by which he meant that the people of Jerusalem would be oppressed by the utmost want of all things. And the Hebrews rightly interpret the saying על דרך גוזמא, by way of hyperbole; for it is a thing without precedent that anyone should, like swine, have swallowed the dung of others, let alone his own. Nature utterly recoils from so monstrous a food. Or if, when famine struck, necessity bound with iron spikes drove someone to it, he would still do it in vain, because nothing remains in excrement that can be digested. This is far more true of dove's dung than of human dung, because it is much hotter. This is taught both by experience itself and by the books of the physicians and of all who have written on manuring. Varro, De re rust. book 1, ch. 38: Cassius writes that the best dung (for manuring fields) is that of birds, etc. Of these, that of doves is the best, because it is the hottest. Columella book 2, ch. 15: There are, then, three chief kinds of dung: that from birds, that from men, and that from cattle. Of birds' dung the first is held to be that which is cleared out of dovecotes. Pliny book 17, ch. 9: Marcus Varro gives first place to the dung of thrushes from aviaries. Columella puts that from dovecotes next, then that from henhouses. Some prefer that from dovecotes. Palladius book 2, ch. 33: That of doves (dung) is the most fiery, and that of other birds is quite useful. Quintilius book 2 of the Geopon.: Ἔστι δὲ κόπρος μὲν καλὴ ἡ τῶν πτηνῶν ἁπάντων, πλὴν τῶν χηνῶν, καὶ τῶν ἐνύδρων ὀρνέων, διὰ τὴν ὑγρότητα [esti de kopros men kalē hē tōn ptēnōn hapantōn, plēn tōn chēnōn, kai tōn enydrōn orneōn, dia tēn hygrotēta], etc. Πολὺ δὲ καλλίων ἡ τῶν περιστερῶν, πολὺ τὸ θερμὸν ἔχουσα [poly de kalliōn hē tōn peristerōn, poly to thermon echousa]· The dung of all birds is good, except that of geese and water-birds, because of its moisture, etc. but that of doves is far superior, because it is the most fiery. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter زبل [zibl], or On dung: زبل الحمام اسخان الازبال المستعمل [zibl al-ḥamām askhan al-azbāl al-mustaʿmal] Dove's dung is the hottest of all those that have any use. The cause is clear from Aristotle, who lists the dove first among those that have θερμὴν κοιλίαν [thermēn koilian], a hotter stomach, De part. anim. book 2, ch. 7. Accordingly some of the moderns write that the dove, like the ostrich, swallows and digests small stones. And the Arabic name of the dove, حمام [ḥamām] himam, is formed from heat. These things, I think, show abundantly that nothing remains in dove's dung that a human being could digest .

II. Driven from this position, R. Jonah [=Jonah ibn Janāḥ, Sefer ha-Shorashim] and R. David devise something else, namely that the Israelites used the dung in place of wood, since during the siege of Samaria they could not go out to gather firewood. This is a little less absurd, since dove's dung can serve in place of wood. For Galen reports as an established fact that dove's dung catches fire so easily that somewhere in Mysia a neighbouring house burned down because dove's dung had ignited spontaneously from the sun's rays. Near that house, namely, κόπρος ἀπέκειτο περιστερῶν, ἤδη σεσηπυῖα, καὶ τεθερμαμένη, καὶ ἀτμὸν ἀναπέμπουσα, καὶ ἁπτομένοις ἱκανῶς θερμή. ταύτης δὲ πλησίον ἦν, ὡς καὶ ψαύειν ἤδη θυρὶς ἔχουσα ξύλα νεωστὶ καταληλιμμένα ῥητίνῃ πολλῇ, θέρους οὖν μέσου λαῦρος ἥλιος προσβαλὼν ἐξῆψε τὴν ῥητίνην τε, καὶ τὰ ξύλα [kopros apekeito peristerōn, ēdē sesēpuia, kai tethermamenē, kai atmon anapempousa, kai haptomenois hikanōs thermē. tautēs de plēsion ēn, hōs kai psauein ēdē thyris echousa xyla neōsti katalēlimmena rhētinē pollē, therous oun mesou lauros hēlios prosbalōn exēpse tēn rhētinēn te, kai ta xyla], there lay dove's dung, already putrid and hot, giving off steam, and quite hot to the touch, and so close to that house, that it touched a window, whose wood had recently been smeared with much resin: so in midsummer the blazing sun, striking from above, set the wood and the resin alight. So Galen, book 3 De temperam. Similar is what one reads in the same author, book 1 De different. febr. and in the book De morborum causis: that the dung of wild doves catches fire more slowly but holds it longer. So no one should think this material wholly unfit for feeding a fire. But truly, who would believe that in the city of Samaria, which, being the royal seat, we may fairly suppose was very far removed from rustic ways, there was so much dove's dung that fires could be built from it? Or that there was anyone who would not rather go without fire for a time than buy so tiny a quantity of a substance most foul-smelling in the flames at so great a price? Moreover, these things do not hang together: that there was a great famine in Samaria because there was nothing to feed a fire with except dove's dung, bought at a high price.

III. The third opinion is that of those who hold that the Israelites bought this dung in order to manure better the fields enclosed within the city, and so provide against famine in the coming year. As if it were very likely that in a most populous city there was so much farmland; or that those who lacked the means to live from day to day had the means to sow; or that the citizens of Samaria were so anxious about the future when they had nothing for the present; or so fastidious in choosing dung that, when other dung, only a little less useful, was available in great abundance, they bought dove's dung at so high a price.

IV. The fourth opinion, equally absurd, is that of Josephus: that dove's dung served them ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. For although I grant that it does not lack salt, yet if they had to use salt from excrement, everyone knows that there is much more salt in urine, and that it is extracted more easily and with less disgust. So there would have been no need to buy at so high a price what everyone had at home. Besides, what would be the point of that salt in so great a famine? If one cared to play the rhetorician, I know that much could be gathered in praise of salt, and that after bread hardly anything is more useful for life: without it a great part of foods is flat and tasteless, can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? Job 6:6. Thus, under the Law no sacrifice was without salt, Lev 2:13 and Mark 9:49. And even among the heathen, on the authority of Pliny, no rites were performed without salted meal. So too there is hardly any table of some refinement that lacks salt. But salt also seems to have been the food of the poor. For people of slender means used πρὸς ἅλα δειπνεῖν, καὶ κύμινον [pros hala deipnein, kai kyminon], to dine on salt and cumin, as can be gathered from Plutarch. Hence Diogenes, in Laertius book 6, answered Craterus when he invited him: Ἀλλὰ βούλομαι ἐν Ἀθήναις ἅλα λείχειν, ἢ παρὰ Κρατερῷ τῆς πολυτελοῦς τραπέζης ἀπολαύειν [Alla boulomai en Athēnais hala leichein, ē para Kraterō tēs polytelous trapezēs apolauein]· But I would rather lick salt at Athens than enjoy a sumptuous table at the house of Craterus. And Persius, Satire 5,
You will live content to bore with your finger into a salt-cellar tasted again and again, if you strive to live with Jove.

that is, you will be extremely poor if you are pious. And in Horace, book 1, Satire 3, Tigellius, of whom Seneca speaks in Epistle 126, in order to seem a frugal man, says: I care nothing for the luxuries of the rich,
— — — let me only have a three-legged table, and a shell of pure salt. — — — —

Varro also reports that the ancients used (salt) as a relish: for they ate salt with bread and cheese, as the proverb shows. So Pliny, book 31, ch. 7, where shortly before the same author says: It is also involved in honours and in military service: hence salaries are so called, with great authority among the ancients. Likewise, Ancus Martius, the king, gave the people six thousand modii of salt as a largess. The kings of Assyria also gave salt as pay. Accordingly, in Ezra 4:14 the governors of Samaria write this to King Artaxerxes: Because די־מלח היכלא מלחנא, we are salted with the salt of the palace. That is the literal rendering; that is, as Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] rightly puts it, we receive a salary from the king's palace. But no one praises salt more fully than Plutarch, Sympos. book 5, Probl. 10, where, on the question why Homer calls salt divine, he asserts among other things that salt is τῶν ἄλλων ὄψων ὄψον εἶναι, καὶ ἥδυσμα [tōn allōn opsōn opson einai, kai hēdysma], the relish and seasoning of all other relishes. Likewise, Θρίγκωμα τῆς τροφῆς γινόμενον εἰς τὸ σῶμα, καὶ παρέχον ἐναρμοσίαν αὐτῇ προς τὴν ὄρεξιν [thrinkōma tēs trophēs ginomenon eis to sōma, kai parechon enarmosian autē pros tēn orexin], that which becomes a safeguard of food in the body, making it agreeable and suited to our palate. Hence in Sir 39:31 certain things are praised as ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου [archē pasēs chreias eis zōēn anthrōpou], the beginning (that is, the chief) of all things necessary for life. And among these salt comes before all food. But whatever may be said of salt, this much is certain: salt is nothing but a seasoning, and seasonings are not usually bought at a great price in a severe famine, when food is lacking. For hunger itself is the best seasoning, and one does not then seek what stimulates the palate, but what satisfies.

V. The fifth opinion is that of the Talmudists. To understand it, the reader must first be told that there is this Talmudic axiom in the tractate Megilla, ch. 3: כל המקראות הכתובין בתורה לגנאי קורין אותן לשבח, All words written indecently in the Law are read decently. Therefore, wherever words occur in Scripture that are less decent in common usage, the teachers of the Hebrews, out of regard for decency, wanted them read otherwise than they are written. So in place of the word found in the text they substitute in the margin another, more decent one, which it is still the custom today to read in its place in the synagogues. Hence for שגל, to have intercourse, they read שכב, to lie with; for עפולים, diseases of the anus, טחורים, haemorrhoids; for טחוראות, latrines, properly places of dung, מוצאות, privies; for חורים and שינים, dung and urine, צואה and מימי רגלים, excrement and water of the feet. In the same way, in this passage, for חריונים, dove's dung, they want דביונים to be read, the flux of doves, a word compounded of דב, flux, and יונים, doves. But the Talmudists interpret דביונים differently, as if it were compounded of the Chaldee pronoun ד, which corresponds to the Hebrew אשר, who, which, that, the preposition ב, in, and the noun יונים, doves. For them, then, דביונים means that which (supply: is or was) in the doves. For they hold that at Samaria doves had been trained to go out foraging in the fields, so to speak; and that when they returned stuffed and swollen, their owners shook out their crops, extracted the grain and sold it at a high price. So, in their view, the words of the sacred text run thus: The famine in Samaria was so great that a quarter of a kab of the grains that were in the doves, and were extracted from their crops, sold for five shekels. Hence Comestor in the Historia Scholastica, book 4 of Kings, ch. 10: Some relate that by the word dung is meant the little bladder of the dove, in which were found grains brought from outside. I do not think anything more absurd than this fiction could have been devised. Not that I deny that doves, through love of their young, can be so trained that, released from a besieged city, they return home; for we have shown in the immediately preceding chapter that ancient and more recent people often used such messengers. But who would believe that at Samaria there were so many such docile doves? Or that in fields laid waste far and wide by the enemy they found crops everywhere at hand? Or that, returning with full crops, they so easily disgorged whatever they had swallowed in the field? And that by such arts even one kab of grain could have been gathered in the whole time of the siege? Or, if God had sustained this people for some time in so miraculous a way, that Scripture would have passed over so unheard-of a thing so lightly? But we argue in vain, since the word חריונים, which is in the text, can in no way be drawn to this sense. Indeed, hardly, or not even hardly, can the marginal word דביונים be rendered that which is in the doves, unless we suppose that a Chaldee pronoun was prefixed to a Hebrew noun, and so a hybrid, half-barbarous word was formed.

VI. Junius, thinking he could avoid these Symplegades by a new interpretation, rendered this passage as follows: There arose a great famine in Samaria, etc. so that the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, was of five shekels of silver. But at first reading it is immediately apparent that this exceedingly learned man would not have rendered it thus, almost, I would say, without any sense, had he not felt himself to be in great straits. For what would the fourth part, the belly itself of doves be? And what point was there in specifying that the belly is in the hollow? Although the hollow is rather in the belly than the belly in the hollow. Again, how could it have entered the mind of that man, who was most perspicacious, that the belly of doves was sold separately? Nor can what is found in his version, the fourth part, the belly itself, which is in the hollow of doves, be extracted by any torture from the Hebrew words רובע הקב חריונים. For if רבע, the fourth part, and הקב, the belly, as the distinguished Junius renders it, were in apposition, each noun would have the He hajedia, or article, prefixed, as one would say in Greek τὸ τέταρτον, ἡ κοιλία [to tetarton, hē koilia]. I add that in this version קב kab is wrongly confused with קבה keba. Of these, קבה keba means belly or crop; but קב kab is something quite different, namely κάβος [kabos], cabus, a kind of measure. So it is explained among the Hebrews by the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] in their Lexicons, by Mardochaeus in his Concordance, by Alphes in the tractate On Passover, ch. 5, fol. 176, and by the Gloss on the Talmud passim. Hence the compound תרקב tharkab means to some two cabs, as if contracted from תרי קבין there kabin, two cabs; to others, more correctly, three cabs, as if it were תרי וקב, two and a cab, one more. So R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] in various places of the Talmud. And κάβος [kabos] is also a measure in Hesychius, Philoxenus, the Suda, the Etymologicum, Phavorinus and others. Finally, none of the ancients renders חריונים otherwise than as dove's dung. Let Josephus and the Greek, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Latin translators be consulted, and, among the Hebrews, Iarchius, Kimchi and R. Levi on this passage. Among them a remarkable agreement will be found, which rarely happens in the interpretation of an obscure passage. Indeed, of the more recent writers no one dissents except Junius and Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], about whom now a few words.

VII. He (in the Sacred Miscellanies, book 6, ch. 11) understands both by דביונים and by חריונים (the former is written in the margin, the latter in the text) the crop of doves, their belly and entrails. It is as if they were called דביונים, that is, the flux of doves, because those who cut up and gut doves let these flow down, or slip, to the ground; and חריונים, that is, κοιλία [koilia], or the belly of doves. For he tries to prove that חריונים are the belly and entrails of doves as follows: "The Hebrew חור first "means white; 2. a hole, from the brightness of the light that is usually seen through it; 3. "τρώγλην [trōglēn], a cavity, which is a kind of hole; 4. the belly, in Greek κοιλίαν [koilian], "which is the chief cavity of the human body; whence alvus [belly] is named as if alveus [hollow], and κοιλία [koilia] "from κοῖλον [koilon]; 5. the excrement enclosed in the belly, by a metonymy of the content "for the container. Since we may choose the most "suitable of these meanings of the word, why should we not take it here to mean the belly and entrails of doves, which, "though usually thrown away, in a time of most severe famine were not only kept, "but were even sold off and disposed of at a high price." This is the opinion of Fuller, in which (if I may say so with the leave of a most careful writer) I seem to have found a good many things that have not even the appearance of truth. Thus, that the entrails of doves should be called דביונים in Hebrew never occurred to anyone even in a dream. Rather, all explain it as dung, so called from flowing, just as in Greek ῥεῦμα γαστρὸς [rheuma gastros] and διάῤῥοια [diarrhoia], and in Latin alvi profluvium [flux of the belly], are said of such a flux. And in Celsus febres fluentes [flowing fevers], in Greek ῥοώδεις πυρετοὶ [rhoōdeis pyretoi], are those that loosen the bowels. Again, in what the same Fuller asserts, that the word חור means 1. white, 2. a hole, 3. a cavity, 4. the belly, crop, entrails, 5. dung, most of it is invented. חור for white is not so much Hebrew as Chaldee and Arabic. But for a hole or a cavity it is Hebrew, and from a different root. For the former is from חור chavar, to grow white; the latter from the geminate חרר charar, to perforate. Accordingly in the Talmud, tractate Succa, fol. 20b, you may read חור שחררוהו מים, a hole which the waters have bored. And for the same Talmudists חריר is the eye of a needle, as ܚܪܘܪܐ [חרורא] is for the Syrians in Matt 19:24. Further, that this חור also means belly, or crop, or entrails is a pure invention, for which no authority is cited, nor indeed can be, since no one has ever used it so. Finally, חר, or rather חרי or חרא, for dung is an entirely different word, whose root is neither חור nor חרר, but חרה or חרא. Hence the Talmudists consistently write חרי or חריא. And in Arabic خري [khriy] charia, with hamza at the end, is to void excrement, خرء [khurʾ] is dung, مخرأة [makhraʾa] a latrine. Indeed the Hebrews too, when they write plene, insert an Aleph, as in Isa 36:12. לאכול את חראיהם, to eat their own dung. And 2 Reg. X, 27. They destroyed the house of Baal and made it למחראות, into latrines. Nor is the Aleph there adventitious, as they think, but radical, and to be supplied where it is missing, as is clear from Arabic usage. With these observations made, it is evident that the distinguished Fuller did not know the etymology of the word or its true spelling, and indiscriminately took three words of different origin, which led him astray. For since everything he adduces rests solely on the etymologies of words, if these etymologies are false, whatever is built upon them must also be false. And indeed it is most frivolous, what he attributes to the sacred author, that a cab of the bellies and entrails of doves sold at Samaria for five shekels. For it has never been heard tell that the crop and entrails of doves were sold separately. I admit that I have read this of hens, and that in Arabic تبودك [tbwdk] thabudach is said of one who sells the entrails of a hen, namely the heart, crop, etc. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] explains it as من يبيع ما في بطون الدجاج من القلب والقانصة [man yabīʿu mā fī buṭūn al-dajāj min al-qalb wa-l-qāniṣa]. But of those of doves nothing of the kind occurs anywhere, so far as I know. Nor is it fitting that the intestines of doves should have been measured by cabs. For the cab is a measure not of entrails but of grain, like the seah, the ephah and the cor. Namely, six cabs make a seah, three seahs an ephah, ten ephahs a cor, the largest dry measure. Accordingly in the Talmud and in the Aruch you may read everywhere קב חטין, a cab of wheat. And it is defined by Elias as מדת היובש, a measure of dry things; by Pomarius as מדת של חטים, a measure of grain; by Aquinas as מדת למדות דבר היבש, a measure for measuring a dry thing. So in Pollux: Κάβασον δὲ ἐκάλουν τὸν περὶ τὴν τροφὴν ἄπληστον, etc. Κάβος γὰρ σίτου μέτρον. [Kabason de ekaloun ton peri tēn trophēn aplēston, etc. Kabos gar sitou metron.] And they called a man insatiable for food a cabasus, etc. For the cab is a measure of grain. And in Hesychius: Κάβαισος· ἄπληστος· κάβος γὰρ μέτρον σιτικόν· [Kabaisos; aplēstos; kabos gar metron sitikon;] Cabasus, insatiable; for the cab is a measure of grain. From this correct Suidas, who has κάβαιστος [kabaistos] for κάβαισος [kabaisos]; and the Etymologicon, which has μετασιτικὸν [metasitikon], a word of no meaning, for μέτρον σιτικὸν [metron sitikon]. But in Hesychius what follows a little below is corrupt: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ οἰνικὸν [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai oinikon], Cab, a measure of grain and of wine. For that the cab is a measure of wine, or of liquids, you will read nowhere else. So I emend thus: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ κάδος οἰνικόν· [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai kados oinikon;] The cab is a measure of grain, and the cadus of wine. He compares two words close to each other in sound as well as in meaning. For both mean a measure, but the latter of wine, the former of grain. Indeed, that the cab is a measure of grain, as the cadus is of wine, there is no one who does not know. Thus Herodotus, book 3, chapter 20, says Φοινικηΐου οἴνου κάδον [Phoinikēiou oinou kadon], a cadus of palm wine. And in book 11 of Athenaeus, Anacreon:
Οἴνου δ᾽ ἐξέπιον κάδον, [Oinou d' exepion kadon,]
I drained a cadus of wine. And in the same place Hedylus in an Epigram,
Ἀλλὰ κάδοις Χίου με κατάβρεχε, [Alla kadois Chiou me katabreche,]
Here the translator ridiculously has But water by pouring wine from casks, instead of But drench me with casks of Chian wine : as in Tibullus, book 2, Elegy 1:
— — — loosen the bonds of the Chian cask.
At what price shall we buy a cask of Chian? — — —

And like cabus, so cadus is of Hebrew origin. Just as קב kab is cabus, so כד cad is cadus, although the Hebrew כד has a wider range. For Moses, Solomon and Elijah use it for a water jar. See Gen. XXIV, 14. Eccles. XII, 8. and 1 Reg. XVIII, 34.

Having thus weighed the opinions of others, it now remains for us to put forward our own as well. To establish it, we must first lay down as most certain that by dove's dung some kind of food is meant. Otherwise there would be no coherence in this sentence: There was a great famine in Samaria: for an ass's head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver. Further, since it has been proved that dove's dung, as these words are commonly understood, is in no way a food, something else must necessarily be meant by them. When I consulted the Arabs on this matter, I found that two things are customarily marked with this epithet among them. One of them is what is called by another name كوز كندم [kūz kandum] kuz kendem, or جوز جندم [jawz jandum] giauz gendem, that is, a nut named after a place. For a nut is called كوز [kūz] kuz in Persian and جوز [jawz] giauz in Arabic. And Kendem or Gendem is the same word, for the Persian Caph there sounds as G because of the three dots placed over it. Of this nut Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, says: كوز كندم الماهية هو خفيف كالاشنة طيني وبالرقة يسمونه حرا الحمام وببغداد يسمي جوز جندم الاختيار اجوده المربري والذفني ضغيف [kūz kandum al-māhiyya huwa khafīf ka-l-ushna ṭīnī wa-bi-l-Raqqa yusammūnahu ḥurā al-ḥamām wa-bi-Baghdād yusammā jawz jandum al-ikhtiyār ajwaduhu al-mrbrī wa-l-dhfnī ḍghīf] Kuzkendem, what is it? It is a light thing, like tree moss, clay-like. In the city of Raqqa (on the Euphrates below Samosata in Mesopotamia) they call it dove's dung. And in Baghdad giauz Gendem. Selection: the best is the Barbaric, but the Daphnensian is weak. See the rest there. The same author elsewhere: جوز جندم الطبع قال بولس له قوة مبردة مطفية مجففة قليلا [jawz jandum al-ṭabʿ qāla Būlus lahu quwwa mubarrida muṭfiya mujaffifa qalīlan] Giauz, or the nut Gendem. Its nature. Paul said that it has the power of cooling, quenching and drying somewhat. But the definition is omitted there; in the Latin version it reads thus: What is the nut Kendem? It is a granular earth like a chickpea, white, inclining to yellow, which is exported from Barca and from Corascena, from which wine is made with honey. If this definition is true, it does not help us at all. For it is a kind of earth, and no kind of earth is edible.

But there is also another kind of dove's dung among the Arabs, entirely different from this one: namely the very thing commonly called usnen. For it is established that this is called by another name sparrows' dung, or doves' dung. Avicenna, book 2: اشنان [ushnān] الماهية هي انواع الطغها الابيض ويسمي خرو العصافير [al-māhiyya hiya anwāʿ al-ṭghhā al-abyaḍ wa-yusammā khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] What is usnen? It has several species, of which the finest is white, and it is called sparrows' dung. Sylvaticus: Sparrows' dung, usnen. Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)]: الاشنان [al-ushnān] Alusnen, a cleansing powder, which is called dove's dung. The same elsewhere: الحرض [al-ḥuruḍ] Alhord, usnen, or dove's dung. Likewise: خرو العصافير [khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] dove's dung, a certain cleansing powder. Likewise: الوشنان [al-wushnān] dove's dung, a kind of medicinal powder. But even so the matter is not settled, since it is not well enough known what usnen properly is. Most hold that it is the same as القلي [al-qilī] alkali, from which a very well-known salt is named. The Pandectarius: The salt alkali is made in this way: Take of the herb otherwise called usnen, etc. The same: Antifilos (read anthyllion) or antili (read anthyllis) in Greek, in Arabic usnen, in Latin salsola, is a herb from which alkali is made. And elsewhere: Usnen, etc. is a herb whose leaves are like those of stonecrop or of the lentil, having a salty taste, from which salt is made. Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] against Cardano, Exercitation 104, Section 18: The Arabs call Chali (better kali) the plant which we call Soda. It is a shrub in the province of Narbonne. By grinding and pressing it they produce what they call salicornum, others soda, others alumen catini, from the shape of the basin into which the juice drips, etc. In Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)] it is called usnen. Giggeius: القلي [al-qilī] alkali, etc. or usnen. Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)]: اشنان [ushnān] Usnen, the herb alkali, and the ashes made from it, the best and in great quantity in الحوران [al-Ḥawrān] Auranitis, a region of Syria. Likewise: بلس [bils] bils, the same as اشنان [ushnān] usnen. Ashes of alkali. And that Alcanzius, or Alchindus, a most celebrated Arab physician and almost a contemporary of Avicenna, held this opinion, you may gather from the fact that in the chapter On usnen he describes, almost word for word, everything that Avicenna had said about kali, as though usnen and kali did not differ at all. This is partly true, partly false. قلي [qilī] kali, for the Arabs as for the Hebrews, means roasted or fried. So usnen, roasted so that from its ash a kind of lye or soap is made, is rightly called kali. And by this name it is also known to the Hebrews, who write קליא kalia, in the Talmudic tractate Erubim, ch. 3, fol. 28b. In Pomarius קליא is defined as עשב שנשרף ומשימין אפרו בבורית, A kind of herb whose ash, when it is burnt, is put into soap. And in the Aruch: עשב שורפין ונותנין אותו בבורית ורוחצין ידיהם, A herb which they burn and put into soap, in order to wash their hands with it. The Arabs say the very same of their اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or قلي [qilī] . Thus the verb تاشن [taʾashshana], formed from the noun اشنان [ushnān] usnen, is rendered by the distinguished Golius: He cleansed his hands with ashes of alkali, or with their lye. And Alcamus: غسل يده فيه [ghasala yadahu fīhi] He washed his hand in it, because it is useful للجرب والحكك [li-l-jarab wa-l-ḥakak] for scabies and itching, as is stated in the same place. But as for the view of Sylvaticus, Scaliger, Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] on Solinus, and other more recent writers, that this usuen or kali is our soda, or solida , from which they make glass , I would not grant it, except for some single species. For the most learned of the Arabs teach that usnen, or kali, is a species in the genus of the chickpea , which has nothing in common with our soda or solida. Abuchanipha: اجناس الاشنان كثيرة وكلها من الحمص والاشنان الحرض الذي يغسل به الثياب [ajnās al-ushnān kathīra wa-kulluhā min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-ushnān al-ḥuruḍ alladhī yughsalu bihi al-thiyāb] The kinds of usnen are many, all of which are from the chickpeas (if the word may be pardoned), and usnen is alhord, with which garments are washed. In agreement with this is Serapion, chapter 257: Usnen is a very hot herb, whose species are from amoch (read from amos, من حمص [min ḥimmaṣ] from chickpeas) and usnen is haron (read hord حرض [ḥuruḍ]) and it is that with which cloths are washed. Again elsewhere Abuchanipha: القلي يتخذ من الجمص واجوده ما يتخذ من الحرض وهو قلي الصباغين وساير ذلك الزجاجين [al-qilī yuttakhadhu min al-jmṣ wa-ajwaduhu mā yuttakhadhu min al-ḥuruḍ wa-huwa qilī al-ṣabbāghīn wa-sāʾir dhālika al-zajjājīn] Alkali is taken from the chickpea; but the best is that taken from alhord, which is the kali of the dyers, as the rest is that of the glassmakers.
