Albacra: الاشنان نبات لا ورق له وله اعضان دقاق شبه العقر وهي رخصة كثيرة الما وتعظم حتي يكون له خشب غليظ يتوقد به وناره حر جدا ورايحته ودخانه كريهة وطعمة الي الملوحة وهو من الحمص [al-ushnān nabāt lā waraq lahu wa-lahu aʿḍān diqāq shibh al-ʿqr wa-hiya rakhṣa kathīrat al-māʾ wa-taʿẓumu ḥattā yakūna lahu khashab ghalīẓ yutawaqqadu bihi wa-nāruhu ḥarr jiddan wa-rāʾiḥatuhu wa-dukhānuhu karīha wa-ṭaʿmuhu ilā al-mulūḥa wa-huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ] Usnen is a plant without leaves, having slender branches like a root, tender, full of moisture, which grow until there is dense wood in them, with which fire is kindled, which is very hot. Its smell and smoke are abominable, its taste salty. And it is in the genus of chickpeas. Alcamus: القلي شي يتخذ من حريق الحمص [al-qilī shayʾ yuttakhadhu min ḥarīq al-ḥimmaṣ] Alkali, a thing obtained from the burning of chickpeas. Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], from Abuchanipha, in the chapter قاقلي [qāqulī] kakeli,: هو من الحمص والناس ياكولونه مع اللبن وهو مثل الاشنان الا ان القلام اعظم منه وورقه شبيه بورق الحرف [huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-nās yaʾkulūnahu maʿa al-laban wa-huwa mithl al-ushnān illā anna al-qlām aʿẓam minhu wa-waraquhu shabīh bi-waraq al-ḥurf] It is a species of chickpea, which is eaten with milk, and it is like usnen, except that it has a larger stalk, and a leaf like the leaf of cress. Giggeius: الغولان [al-ghawlān] Algaulano, a kind of chickpea similar to alusnen . What of the fact that in 2 Sam 17:28 the Hebrew קלי kali is rendered by Jerome fried chickpea? This will seem novel to those who know that the Hebrew kali does not mean chickpea but roasted grain, Lev 23:14. Ruth 2:14 1 Sam 17:17 and XXV, 18. etc. Yet Jerome's version is doubtless correct. For there the Ammonites and Gileadites are said to have brought to David, a fugitive in the desert, wheat, and barley, and flour, וקלי, and kali, and beans, and lentils, וקלי, and kali. So in the same verse the noun kali is repeated twice. The first, joined to wheat, barley and flour, means roasted grain. But the second, which follows beans and lentils, denotes some roasted or fried legume, namely fried chickpea. For the chickpea was customarily fried or roasted. Thus in Aristophanes' play Peace, a countryman is described

᾿Ανθρακίζων τὲρεβίνθου [anthrakizōn tērebinthou] roasting chickpeas over the coals. And on the second page of the Ecclesiazusae the Scholiast has: Ὑποπίνοντες ἔκοπτον φρυκτοὺς ἐρεβίνθους [hypopinontes ekopton phryktous erebinthous], when they had drunk rather freely, they pounded roasted chickpeas. The Roman writers, too, mention roasted chickpeas more than once. Plautus in the Bacchides, Act 4, Scene 5:
I will make him as roasted as a roasted chickpea.
Horace in the Art of Poetry:
Nor if the buyer of roasted chickpeas or of nuts approves of something.

Cassian, Collat. 8, ch. 1: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia. Τρωγάλια [trōgalia], that is, sweetmeats. And the Arabs still today call roasted chickpeas قلي [qly] kali, as we have just shown . Accordingly all the Hebrews, on the passage of Samuel we mentioned, recognize two kinds of kali: the first from grain, the second מקטניות, from legumes, or ממיני קטניות, from kinds of legumes. So Kimchi, R. Levi and R. Esaias on that passage. And R. Selomo describes the second kali thus: וקלי ממינים של קטניות מיבישין אותו בתנור כשהן לחין והם מתוקין לעולם וטוחנין אותן ועושין מהם מאכל שקורין שתית, Kali are kinds of legumes which are dried in the oven while still fresh; they always remain sweet, they are ground, and from them is made a food which they call sethith. This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 38a, where we read that Barzillai the Gileadite sent David תרי מיני שתיתאה, two kinds of sethitha, that is, two kinds of kali. And there the Gloss says: שתיתא תבשיל העשוי מקמח של קליות שייבשין בתנור ויש שעושין אותו מקמח עדשין ולפי שהן מתוקין יותר מדאי נותנים שם חומץ, Sethita is a pottage made from the flour of kali dried in the oven. There are also some who make it from lentil flour, into which, because they are very sweet (that is, insipid), vinegar is poured. And it is true that שתיתא sethitha is said to be made from lentils. For in the tractate Gittin, ch. 7, fol. 70a, in the very text of the Talmud, שתיתא דטלפחי is mentioned, sethitha from lentils. But what is added about vinegar I think is a σφάλμα [sphalma] of the Glossator, who had read somewhere that this pottage is made from lentils וחמצא, and chickpeas, and understood vinegar instead of chickpeas, because in Chaldee חמצא chimtza, chickpea, and חמצא chumtsa, vinegar, are written with the same letters. However that may be, we have amply proved that usnen, or kali, is the chickpea or a kind of chickpea. And we have shown why it is called קלי kali: namely because it is roasted or fried. But اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or rather وشنان [wshnān] vvsnen, as many write it, comes from the verb وشن [wshn], which, of earth, a camel, etc., means to swell and to stand out. Hence the chickpea is rightly called usnen, because of the uneven angles with which it swells and stands out. For it is not round like a pea, but angular and top-shaped . But why it should be called sparrows' dung or dove's dung is entirely hidden from me. I only know that it is so called. And there is no doubt that the nut Kendem or Gendem is called dove's dung for this very reason, that with its grains or little stones it imitates the form of the chickpea. For it is a granular earth, like chickpeas, as the old translator of Avicenna has it, in the place cited above.

So when we read in the Sacred text that in the famine of Samaria a quarter of a cab of dove's dung sold for five pieces of silver, why should we not understand the chickpea, or a kind of chickpea? Certainly everything will then fit nicely. 1. First, that the chickpea was very well known in Judaea is shown, besides several places of the Talmud, by the Sacred History in the passage cited above from 2 Sam 17:28, where the Gileadites and Ammonites bring David, among other things, קלי kali, that is, roasted chickpea. Accordingly חמצה, that is, Emesa, a famous city on the border of Judaea, which had its own kings, seems to have been named from the chickpea. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], in book 2, chapter 53 of his Singularia, observes that in the Egyptian city of Cairo there are many shops in which nothing is sold but roasted chickpea, which is bought in great quantity by the pilgrims who set out from there every year for Mecca. And in chapter 99 he reports the same of Damascus: In Damascus, he says, there are many shops in which all are occupied with roasting chickpeas. They call them Erevithia (ἐρεβίνθια [erebinthia]) by a Greek name. Roasted and dried in bronze pans, they are very convenient for those who undertake a long journey. 2. Further, the cab is a measure of legumes as well as of grain. For legumes, just like grain, have their seeds, which the Arabs designate by the common name حبوب [ḥubūb]. 3. That some cheap kind of food is signified by dove's dung is clear from these words of the Sacred text: An ass's head was sold for eighty shekels, and a quarter of a cab of dove's dung for five shekels. For there dove's dung is compared with the ass's head: the latter was for sale at eighty shekels, a quarter of a cab of the former at five shekels. So a whole cab, which is the measure of a day's food, cost twenty shekels, and four cabs eighty shekels, the price at which an ass's head was then sold. Therefore, whatever you understand there by dove's dung, it must plainly have been a very cheap food, since four cabs of it, that is, as much as suffices a sober man for four days' sustenance, were valued no higher than one ass's head. Now among foods in common use hardly anything is cheaper than the chickpea. Accordingly the chickpea is the food only of the frugal or the poorer sort. Thus in Aristophanes' Peace, as noted above, a certain countryman wishes to be with his companions,
Ἀνθρακίζων τοὐρεβίνθου, Τήν τε φηγὸν ἐμπυρεύων· [Anthrakizōn tourebinthou, Tēn te phēgon empyreuōn]

Toasting the chickpea over the coals, and roasting the beech-nut at the fire. In Alexis the Comic poet, in Athenaeus book 2, an old woman lamenting her poverty lists, among the common foods by which she barely sustains her wretched life, ἐρέβινθον [erebinthon] and λάθυρον [lathyron], that is, chickpea and chickling. Horace, book 1, Satire 6, to show that he is content with little and that a meagre diet suffices him:
— — — thence I take myself home to a dish of leeks and chickpeas and fritters.
And in the De Arte he thus contrasts the rich with those who live on roasted chickpeas and nuts:
For those who have a horse, a father and property take offence, nor, if the buyer of roasted chickpeas and nuts approves something, do they receive it with fair minds or bestow a crown.
Hence that line of Martial, book 5, Epigram 79:
Both hot chickpea and warm lupin, it is a small little dinner, who can deny it?
And book 1, Epigram 104, on the miser Scaevola, who cheated his own appetite:
And the thick dregs of reddish Veientan are drunk: warm chickpea costs an as, and an as buys Venus.
And Epigram 42 of the same book:
— — — — — — he who sells soaked chickpea to the idle crowd. — —

That is, he who peddles the cheapest foods, among them soaked chickpea, to the common people on holiday, at leisure for the Circus and the stage. To the same effect is the fact that at Rome, at the shows, those canvassing for office, to win the favour of the populace, scattered chickpeas along with beans and lupins among the gifts thrown to the crowd. To this allude these words of Horace, book 2, Satire 3:
May you squander your goods on chickpeas, beans and lupins, so that you may strut broad in the Circus and stand in bronze.
And these words of Persius, Satire 5.

— — — — pour out chickpeas generously to the brawling people, so that the old men may remember our sunny Floralia. — — — Thus in the Scetic desert of Egypt, where the monks professed a remarkable frugality, roasted chickpeas served them as food. Cassian, in the place cited above, on Abbot Serenus: He brought in a basket containing roasted chickpeas, which they call trogalia, of which we took only five grains each. Hence Tertullian uses cicercula [chickling] for a thing of very little value, when he writes thus against Marcion, book 1, chapter 11: The God of Marcion ought to have produced at least one chickling, so that he might be proclaimed a new Triptolemus. Among the Greeks too, ἐρεβίνθινος [erebinthinos], that is, cicernus [of chickpea], is taken for worthless. Hesychius: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· οὐδενὸς ἄξιος, παρά τινα παροιμίαν ἐρεβίνθινος ζωμός [Erebinthinos Dionysos; oudenos axios, para tina paroimian erebinthinos zōmos]; Chickpea Bacchus (chickpea wine), that is, of no value; in a certain proverb chickpea broth is so called. Likewise Suidas: Ἐρεβίνθινος Διόνυσος· ἐπὶ τῶν μηδενὸς ἀξίων [Erebinthinos Dionysos; epi tōn mēdenos axiōn]. Chickpea Bacchus, of things of no value. Plutarch, in the Rom. Quaest., chapter 95, observes that τὸν λάθυρον, καὶ τὸν ἐρέβινθον [ton lathyron, kai ton erebinthon], the chickling and the chickpea, were forbidden and detested foods for some, but for a jocular reason: namely ὡς παρωνύμους τοῦ Ἐρέβους, καὶ τῆς Λήθης [hōs parōnymous tou Erebous, kai tēs Lēthēs], as alluding to Erebus and Lethe (the river of the underworld). For as ἐρέβινθος [erebinthos] alludes to Erebus, so λάθυρος [lathyros] to Lethe. He adds that pulses were very much used πρὸς τὰ περίδειπνα, καὶ τὰς προκλήσεις τῶν νεκρῶν [pros ta perideipna, kai tas prosklēseis tōn nekrōn], at funeral meals and for the summoning of the dead. But this pertains rather to the bean or the lentil. For on the bean Pliny, book 18, ch. 12: The Pythagorean opinion (on the bean) condemned it, as others have reported, because the souls of the dead are in it. For this reason it is certainly used in rites for deceased parents. Varro also reports that for these reasons the Flamen does not eat it, since mournful letters are also found on its flower. And Festus: It is not permitted to the Flamen Dialis either to touch or to name the bean, because it is thought to pertain to the dead. For it is thrown to the ghosts at the Lemuria, and used in sacrifices to deceased parents, and the letters of mourning seem to appear on its flower. Similar is the fact that the ancients counted the lentil among τὰ πένθιμα [ta penthima], mournful things, καὶ προτίθενται τοῖς νέκυσιν [kai protithentai tois nekysin], and set it before the dead, as Plutarch notes in the Crassus and Appian in the Parthica. That the Jews were not entirely free of this superstition is attested by these words of Jerome to Paula on the death of Blaesilla: And to this day the Jews, weeping, with bare feet, rolled in the dust, lie on sackcloth; and, so that nothing may be lacking to superstition, by a most empty rite of the Pharisees they take lentils as their first food, showing, no doubt, for what kind of dish they lost the birthright. But concerning the chickpea I have found only in Pliny that religion uses it at night vigils. If, however, along with the bean and the lentil, the chickpea and the chickling also belonged to funeral meals, as Plutarch seems to hint, then, since the reasons adduced have little to do with the matter, I would believe the ancients had nothing else in view than that a time of mourning befits thin and frugal foods, such as all pulses are, which fill the body but nourish it little. Accordingly the chief of Nebuchadnezzar's eunuchs feared that if Daniel and his companions ate pulses, their faces would look sadder and leaner than those of the other youths whom the king kept in his retinue. See Dan 1:8 etc. It should be noted that there, in verses 12 and 16, pulses are not called קטניות, as elsewhere by the Hebrews, but זרעים, or זרענים. This word is more general. For זרעים or זרענים are any seeds whatever. Accordingly the Greek version, which is that of Theodotion, has σπέρματα [spermata]. And Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] defines what זרעונים, seeds, are in the treatise On Mixed Kinds, book 1, ch. 8: הזרעונים נחלקין לשלושה חלקים האחד מהם הוא הנקרא תבואה והיא חמשה מינין החטים והכוסמין והשעורין ושבולת שועל והשיפון והשני מהן הוא הנקרא קטנית והן כל זרעים הנאכל לאדם חוץ מן התבואה כגון הפול והאפונים והדוחן והאורז והשומשמין והפרגין והספיר וכיוצא בהן והשלישי מהן הוא הנקרא זרעוני גנה והן שאר זרעונין שאינן ראויין למאכל אדם והפרי של אותר הזרע מאכל אדם כגון זרע הבצלין והשומין וזרע החציר והקצח וזרע לפת וכיוצא בהן, Seeds are divided into three kinds. The first is of those called produce (grain crops, σιτώδη [sitōdē]). Of these there are five kinds: wheat, spelt, barley, fox's ear (oats, whose ear resembles a fox's tail), rye. The second is of those they call pulses, that is, all seeds eaten by man, such as beans, peas, millet, rice, sesame, poppy, chickling and the like. The third is of those called garden seeds, which are themselves not fit for eating, but what grows from them is eaten by man, such as onions, garlic, leeks, nigella, turnips and the like. Yet in Daniel זרעי is explained as ὄσπρια [ospria], pulses, by Josephus and the Greek Scholiast, Tertullian, Jerome, R. Selomo, Saadias Gaon, Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], Joseph son of Jachia, etc. And they could just as well be called זרעים, that is, seeds, in Hebrew as ὄσπρια [ospria] in Greek. For they are called ὄσπρια [ospria] for σπόρια [sporia], ἀπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς [apo tēs sporas], from sowing. So this Greek name corresponds exactly to the Hebrew. But in Greek they are also called χεδροπὰ [chedropa], as if χειρόδροπα [cheirodropa], just as in Latin legumina [pulses], because they are gathered (leguntur) by hand. Referring to this, Nicander, Theriaca, verse 752, says.

Χειροδροπὰ δ' ἵνα φῶτες ἄνευ δρεπάνοιο λέγονται Ὄσπρια, χεδροπά τ' ἄλλα, μεσοχλόου ἐντὸς ἀρούρης· [Cheirodropa d' hina phōtes aneu drepanoio legontai / Ospria, chedropa t' alla, mesochlou entos arourēs]

Where men gather by hand, without a sickle, pulses and other things of that kind, in the half-green field. Once these points are noted, it will at once be clear what Josephus means when he says that dove's dung served the Samaritans in place of salt. Theophrastus (De causis plantarum, book 4, chapter 9), inquiring into the reasons why the chickpea ripens sooner than other pulses, gives this one among others: Ἡ ἅλμη πρὸς τὴν τελείωσιν συμβάλλεται [Hē halmē pros tēn teleiōsin symballetai], The saltiness of the chickpea contributes to that quick ripening. And in book 5, chapter 11: Ὁ ἐρέβινθος ἀπόλλυται σφακελίας, ὅταν ἀνθοῦσιν ὕδωρ ἐπιγινόμενον ἐπικλύσῃ τὴν ἄλμην· τὸ γὰρ ἔφαλμα οἷον σφακελίζειν ἐστί [Ho erebinthos apollytai sphakelias, hotan anthousin hydōr epiginomenon epiklysē tēn halmēn; to gar ephalma hoion sphakelizein esti]. The chickpea perishes of blight when rain washes off its saltiness while it is in flower: for the loss of its saltiness is to it a kind of blight. Cato too says of the chickpea, in De re rustica, chapter 37: If you sow chickpea in crumbly soil, since it is pulled up, it is salty and harmful. And Columella, book 2, chapter 14, says that Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] states that the soil is harmed most by the poison of chickpea and flax: the one because it is of a salty nature, the other because it is of a hot nature. And Pliny, book 18, chapter 12: It is the nature of the chickpea to grow with saltiness; therefore it burns the soil. And in book 17: A defect common to all crops is blight, the chickpea's too, when the rain, washing off its saltiness, makes it sweeter. Galen, in book 6 of De simplic., calls this bitterness, when he says of chickpeas: Μετέχουσι δέ τι καὶ τῆς πικρότητος [Metechousi de ti kai tēs pikrotētos]; They also have something of bitterness. And of the wild chickpea: Δριμύτερός τ᾽ ἐστι, καὶ πικρότερος [Drimyteros t' esti, kai pikroteros], It is sharper and more bitter. But he put bitter for salty, as when the Poet says of the sea,
let bitter Doris not mingle her wave.

Accordingly, as we have noted, the Arabs extract from a certain kind of chickpea that very famous salt which is therefore called sal alkali, that is, salt of burnt chickpea. So, on the passage with which we are dealing, when the older Hebrews had remarked that it was dove's dung, from which salt is extracted, this was misunderstood by Josephus, who wrote that at Samaria dove's dung was used ἀντὶ ἁλῶν [anti halōn], in place of salt. Hence Theodoret on 4 Kings, Question 21: Ἡ τῆς πολιορκίας ἀνάγκη, καὶ τοῦ λίμου τὸ μέγεθος ἠνάγκασεν αὐτοὺς ἀντὶ ἁλῶν κεχρῆσθαι τῷ κόπρῳ [Hē tēs poliorkias anankē, kai tou limou to megethos ēnankasen autous anti halōn kechrēsthai tō koprō]. The necessity of the siege and the severity of the famine compelled them to use dung in place of salt .

But Ol. Celsius [=Olof Celsius, Hierobotanicon (1745-47)] in Hierobot. vol. 2, p. 82, rightly points out that there is no lack of examples of others who, in the want of a long siege, turned to food things that human nature otherwise abhors. "Wretched mortals," he says, "shudder at perishing of hunger so long as anything remains, however foul and abominable, by which they may put off the fatal moment. Hence histories everywhere record that many have yielded to necessity and in sieges have used even the excrement of animals as food and drink." Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. book 3, ch. 6, writes of the final siege of the Jews: "Necessity set everything before their teeth in place of food, and they brought themselves to eat things that would not have been fit even for the most unclean brute beasts. — For some, even the stalks of old hay served as food. Some gathered refuse." In Josephus, Jewish War book 6, last chapter, near the end, we read: προσελθῶν τινὰς εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀνάγκης, ὥστε τὰς ἀμάρας ἐρευνῶντας καὶ παλαιὸν ὄνθον βοῶν, προσφέρεσθαι τὰ ἐκ τούτων σκύβαλα, καὶ τὸ μηδὲ ὄψει φορητὸν πάλαι τότε γενέσθαι τροφήν [proselthōn tinas eis tosouton anankēs, hōste tas amaras ereunōntas kai palaion onthon boōn, prospheresthai ta ek toutōn skybala, kai to mēde opsei phorēton palai tote genesthai trophēn]. "Some were driven to such necessity that they searched the sewers and took the old dung of oxen as nourishment, and the collected filth, which before had not been bearable even to look at, became food." And in Brusonius, Memorabilia book 2, ch. 41: "The Cretans, when Metellus besieged them, quenched their thirst with the urine of beasts of burden for lack of wine and water." Cipriano de Valera, in the marginal notes to the Spanish version at 2 Reg. VI, 25: En el Epitome de las chronicas de Inglaterra se dize, que año de 1316 (que fue el año 10 del rey Eduardo 2.) huvo tanta hambre en Inglaterra, que los pobres comian sus criaturas, perros, ratas, y estiercol de palomas. That is: in the Epitome of the Chronicles of England it is said that in the year 1316 (which was the 10th year of the reign of Edward II) there was so great a famine in England that people ate their own infants, dogs, mice, and dove's dung. To these examples adduced by Celsius I add a very similar one from Abdollatif, Compendium of the Memorable Things of Egypt book 2, ch. 2, p. 119 of the octavo edition. In the great famine that raged in Egypt in the year 1200 AD 1200, اكلوا الميتات والجيف والكلاب والبعر والاروات [akalū al-maytāt wa-al-jiyaf wa-al-kilāb wa-al-baʿr wa-al-arwāt] they fed on the dead, on stinking carcasses, on camel dung and on dung. The annals of the Orientals are full of examples of this kind.
Iliad. 9, 214. Πάσσε δ' ἁλὸς θείοιο [passe d' halos theioio].
Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] described the varieties of Salsola Kali in Flora Aegypt. Arab. p. 54 ff. Compare with him Rauwolf, Travels p. 37, Augsburg edition, 1583.

Suaeda monoica in Forsskål, p. 70, who, after describing it carefully, adds: "This is the plant from which the Arabs of Yemen extract alkali salt, in a dilute solution of which clothes are washed before they are treated with soap."
Rauwolf, p. 37, confirms that Salsola Kali is used for making glass.

This itself is plainly false, and rests on a strange error of our author, by which, in the passages which he will presently adduce from Arabic writers, he reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ], i.e. saline herbs. This observation is owed to Ol. Celsius, who in Hierobot. vol. II, p. 234, treating the קלי of the Hebrews, says the following: "Bochart labours most learnedly, as is his habit, to make Kali in 2 Sam 17:28 into chickpea. But, deceived either by less correct manuscripts of the Arabs or by something else, he consistently reads حمص [ḥimmaṣ] chickpea instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in the Arabs whom he cites, and confuses different things. This I make clear from my Abu'l-Fadl. Under the heading اشنان [ushnān] he says this: اشنان معروف ويسمي الحرض وهو من الحمض وهو كل نابت فيه ملوحة [ushnān maʿrūf wa-yusmī al-ḥurḍ wa-huwa min al-ḥamḍ wa-huwa kull nābit fīhi mulūḥa] Usnen is well known, and is called Alhord, and it belongs to الحمض [al-ḥamḍ], the name by which all herbs are called in which there is saltiness. The verb itself is in Golius, Lex. Arab. p. 653: حمض [ḥamaḍa] the camel grazed on the bitter and salty plant which is called حمض [ḥamḍ]. And in the 4th conjugation: the land abounded in salty and bitter plants." Thus Celsius, and his words are confirmed by the matter itself. For since all the writers whom Bochart brings forward unanimously attribute a saline taste to the plants Usnen and Alkali, it is self-evident that these are to be classed not among chickpeas, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], but among saline herbs, حمض [ḥamḍ]. Nor am I moved by the fact that حمص [ḥimmaṣ] is read here instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] not in just one passage of a single writer, but consistently in absolutely all the passages that our author adduces from various authors. For when Bochart found, no doubt through a copyist's carelessness, حمص [ḥimmaṣ] written instead of حمض [ḥamḍ] in one of these writers, he eagerly seized upon the chickpea in favour of his preconceived opinion, and inserted it into the other passages too which he cites from other writers, silently putting حمص [ḥimmaṣ] in them instead of حمض [ḥamḍ]. That Bochart did not act faithfully enough here is certainly shown by what will be observed in the following note. Therefore in what follows, حمص [ḥimmaṣ], chickpea, must always be replaced by حمض [ḥamḍ], saline plants, except for the last passage of Ibn al-Baytar on قاقلي [qāqulī],
Rather, what is read there is: a species of saline plant, similar to اشنان [ushnān].

This would truly be so, if قلي [qilī] belonged to the حمض [ḥimmaṣ]—that is, the chickpeas. As it is, since it is among the saline herbs (حمض [ḥamḍ]), it can have nothing in common with the Hebrew קלי, which Celsius, Hierobot. vol. II, p. 231 ff., shows is rightly explained as roasted grain.
This argument, since it rests on the opinion that Usnen and Kali are a species of chickpea (حمص [ḥimmaṣ]), collapses completely once that opinion is removed (by what we observed in note 5).

It hardly seems necessary to warn the reader that all this has been argued in vain, since the thing which the Arabs call dove's dung is not of the chickpea kind (on which, as on a foundation, Bochart's whole argument rests), but a species of saline plant, as we have amply proved in note 5. Of lesser weight is what Otho Verbrugge said in support of Bochart's opinion in Observatt. Philologg. de nominum Hebraeorum plurali numero, Groningen 1730, in duodecimo, p. 7–8. He himself thinks that חרייונים means small loaves, from a singular חרייון, which he takes to be a diminutive of חרי, a kind of bread among the Chaldeans and Talmudists. This opinion will hardly win anyone's approval, since what is said of the חרייונים in the sacred text, that they were measured by kabs, in no way suits loaves. Much more absurd is what Hiller put forward in Hierophyt. vol. II, ch. 22, sect. 3, p. 129: that חריינים are dove's holes, that is, the entrails of doves, which, being perforated, draw nourishment and growth out of the body. All these things weighed, it is best to retain that interpretation of this much-vexed word which Bochart listed in first place at the beginning of this chapter, but rejected there; yet undeservedly, as we have shown in note 1.
That the bird דרור deror is not the swallow, as is held, but a kind of wild dove, namely the turtledove or the wood pigeon.

Among the birds there is one which the Hebrews call דרור deror, that is, freedom or free; מפני שדרה בבית כבשדה, because it dwells as freely in the house as in the field. So R. Ishmael determined in the Talmudic tractate Betsa, ch. 3, p. 24a. Hence the later Hebrews, and the recent lexicographers and interpreters of the Bible who have followed them, hold with the greatest unanimity that דרור deror is the swallow, because there are said to be two species of swallows,
of which one seeks the woods, the other enters under roofs. — — — —

But this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds that are partly domestic, partly wild. Among these the first place belongs to the doves, of which one kind is κατοικίδιον [katoikidion], domestic, the other νομαδικὸν [nomadikon], roaming, and feeding in the fields, as is found in Galen, book 10 On Simples. Varro also makes this distinction in On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 7, yet in such a way that he says both kinds dwell under roofs: but the wild kind in the highest part of towers, from which it flies out into the fields and returns, whereas the other, tamer kind, content with domestic food, usually feeds within the threshold of the door. For my part, I think that by the name דרור deror are meant both this wild kind of dove and whatever species of doves the Greeks list among the wild ones, but above all φάτταν [phattan], the wood pigeon, and τρυγόνα [trygona], the turtledove. I am moved to this, first, by the authority of the ancient interpreters, who explain דרור as either the turtledove or the wood pigeon. Thus in Ps. LXXXIV, 4 דרור is rendered turtledove in the Greek version, and in the Vulgate, the Chaldee, the Syriac, and both Arabic versions, and in the paraphrase of Apollinaris. But the Ethiopic has መዐንቅ፡ [maʿanəq], that is, the collared one: everyone knows that the wood pigeon is distinguished by this epithet, on account of the collar it has around its neck. Martial in the Xenia:
The collared wood pigeons slow and dull the loins.
Abdorrachman, son of Abubecr, in his poem On the Divorce of Atica, once his dearest wife,

ما ناح قمري الحمام المطوق [mā nāḥa qumrī al-ḥamām al-muṭawwaq] How the wood pigeon, the ring-necked dove, laments. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: ان بيض القماري يجعل تحت الفواخت وبيض الفواخت يجعل تحت القماري كلاهما ينغقان قماري كافورية مطوقة [inna bayḍ al-qamārī yujʿal taḥt al-fawākhit wa-bayḍ al-fawākhit yujʿal taḥt al-qamārī kilāhumā yanghaqān qamārī kāfūriyya muṭawwaqa] Whether the eggs of the wood pigeon are placed under the phabe, or the eggs of the phabe under the wood pigeon, nothing will be hatched from them but camphor-coloured, ring-necked wood pigeons. The other derivation is taken from the Arabic language, in which الحر [al-ḥurr] alhorro is the young of a dove or of a turtledove, and ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the wood pigeon. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الحر فرخ الحمامة [al-ḥurr farkh al-ḥamāma] Alhorro, the young of a dove; Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] adds, or of a turtledove. ساق حر ذكر القماري [sāq ḥurr dhakar al-qamārī] Sako horrin, the male of the wood pigeons. And elsewhere: الورشان طاير وهو ساق حر لحمه اخف من الحمام [al-warashān ṭāyir wa-huwa sāq ḥurr laḥmuhu akhaff min al-ḥamām] Alvvarsen, a bird, namely sako horrin, whose flesh is lighter than that of the dove. The Arabs say it is so called from its call. Ibn Sida: سمي القماري ساق حر لصوته فانه يقول ساق حر ساق حر [summiya al-qamārī sāq ḥurr li-ṣawtihi fa-innahu yaqūl sāq ḥurr sāq ḥurr] The wood pigeon is called sako horrin on account of its call, because it says Sako horrin, Sako horrin. In the same way another species of wood pigeon, قطا [qaṭā] kata or katta, is also thought to be named from its call. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: سميت بحكاية صوته [summiyat bi-ḥikāyat ṣawtihi] It has its name from the likeness of its call. For, they say, when it comes to its young, bringing water in its crop, صاحت قطا قطا [ṣāḥat qaṭā qaṭā] it cries Katta, Katta. But this is pure invention. For قطا [qaṭā] katta is bent from the Greek name of the wood pigeon, φάττα [phatta]. The Arabs often change Greek φ and π into Kaph, because among them ف Phe and ق Kaph have the same shape and differ only in the dots, Phe having a single one and Kaph a double. Accordingly in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] قوقي [qūqī] kauke are seals. In the Arabic Dioscorides قوطوما [qūṭūmā] is φύτευμα [phyteuma], قوقي [qūqī] keuke is πεύκη [peukē], قرقسيون [qarqasiyūn] karkesion is καρπήσιον [karpēsion], قوقس البحر [qūqas al-baḥr] kukos albahri is φύκος θαλάσσιον [phykos thalassion]. That this is not a slip of the copyists but of the authors is clear from the fact that these words are arranged in alphabetical order and are listed under the letter Kaph. Thus, then, قطا [qaṭā] Kata or katta is φάττα [phatta], that is, the wood pigeon, and it is not named from its call, as the Arabs imagine. The same judgement applies to ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin. For ساق [sāq] sako by itself is the male of the dove. And ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the male of the dove of liberty, or of the free dove, that is, of the wood pigeon, or also of the turtledove, as some hold. For like the Hebrew דרור deror, so the Arabic حر [ḥurr] horro means free. And the root حر [ḥarra], in Syriac and Chaldee חרר harar, means to be free and to grant freedom. Therefore, whenever דרור is taken in the sacred text for liberty, the Chaldee translators have חירות in its place, and the Arabic ones حرية [ḥurriyya]. Nor indeed is it obscure why among the Orientals wild and field doves are named from liberty. For Basil too, in Epistle 175 to Julitta, calls a flock of such doves αὐτόνομον ἀγέλην [autonomon agelēn], a free flock, living by its own laws. For in Greek αὐτόνομος [autonomos] is the same as ἐλεύθερος [eleutheros]. Hence Thucydides in book 2 calls the same peoples indiscriminately αὐτονόμους [autonomous] and ἐλευθέρους [eleutherous]. And in Plutarch, in the dialogue On the Daemon of Socrates, Epaminondas declares himself a citizen ἐλευθέρας καὶ αὐτονόμου πόλεως [eleutheras kai autonomou poleōs]. And Demosthenes, in the First Philippic, says of the peoples who were of Philip's party: αὐτονομούμενα καὶ ἐλεύθερα (ἔθνη) ὑπῆρχε [autonomoumena kai eleuthera (ethnē) hypērche]. Accordingly Isocrates opposes αὐτονομίαν [autonomian] to servitude, saying that under Evagoras the Greeks had ἀντὶ δουλείας αὐτονομίαν [anti douleias autonomian]. Therefore, following Basil, you would rightly render the Hebrew דרור deror as αὐτόνομον περιστεράν [autonomon peristeran].

In the two passages of Scripture in which דרור deror occurs for a bird, there is nothing that conflicts in the least with this interpretation. In Prov 26:2 the דרור seems to be commended for the swiftness of its flight, in which, as we have shown in its place , the dove can compete with any bird whatever. And in Ps 84:4 the Psalmist groans, comparing his lot with the meanest birds, namely the sparrow and the דרור deror, that is, the field dove, to which not only free access to the altar of God was granted, but also to nest and hatch their young there, while he himself was a wanderer, an exile, and far from the sacred house. In the name of the altar there must be a figure of speech. For amid so great a throng of men and sacrifices, staying on the altar itself would not have been safe for birds. Therefore altar is put for the tabernacle, or for the temple: for the tabernacle if David speaks in this Psalm; for the temple if someone else after David . For the Hebrews are in doubt, as one may learn from Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. However that may be, both the tabernacle and the temple rested on great beams of cedar and of ἀρκευθίναις [arkeuthinais], in which kind of cedar the wood pigeon likes to nest, as these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 5, teach.

Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθῳ καθελὼν, τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφείσδει. [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn, tēnei gar epheisdei.] But you, my maiden, happy one, shall be given a wood pigeon, whose nest lies hidden in the lofty timber of a juniper.

But Albertus and Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)] also assert that the livia dove nests in temples. And it is known from Herodotus what happened to Aristodicus when ἐξαῖρε τοὺς στρουθοὺς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἦν νενοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα ἐν τῷ νηῷ [exaire tous strouthous, kai alla hosa ēn nenosseumena ornithōn genea en tō nēō], he took out the sparrows and the other kinds of birds that were nesting in the temple . The Hebrews, it is true, deny that any birds settled on the temple at Jerusalem, because they were driven off by what they called כולה עורב , placed on the very top of the roof. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV.: בגג הבית עשו דבר שם כדי שלא ינוח שם עוף והיו קורין אותו כולה עורב, They made something on the roof of the temple so that birds should not rest there, and it was called chole oreb, that is, keeping off ravens. This is frequently mentioned in the Talmud. Thus in the tractate Middoth, ch. 4, fol. 71a, in the Gloss: וכולה עורב מאבד העורבים לפי שהיה מקיף ההיכל למעלה מן המעקה מארבע רוחותיו בחשק של ברזל גובה אמה חד כמו הסיף כדי שלו ישב עליו שום עוף על ההיכל מפני שנחתכים רגליו באותו הסיף, And the chole oreb destroyed ravens, because it surrounded the temple above the parapet on all four sides with an iron band a cubit high, sharp like a sword, so that no bird should settle on the temple, since its feet would be cut off by that sword. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 9, fol. 90a, on the word לכליא עורב (for so it reads there), the Glossator writes: טבלאת של אמה היו עושין והן חדין כסכין סביבותיה ומסמרין חדין בכלן ומחפין בהן גגו של היכל למנוע את העורבי׳ מלישב, They made plates a cubit in size, sharp all round like a knife and all furnished with sharp nails, with which they covered the roof of the temple to keep off the ravens, so that they would not settle on it. And in the tractate Menachoth, ch. 13, fol. 107a, the Gloss defines כולה העורב as מסמרות חדין תחובין בראש גג ההיכל לכלות העורבי׳ שלא ישבו עליו, sharp nails fixed in the top of the temple roof to prevent the ravens from sitting on it. And another Gloss in the same place: כמין טבלה חדה וקיפה על צידה וחדודה לחתוך כמו סכין, A kind of sharp plate set up on its edge, with an edge like a knife for cutting. And the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome]: עשה צורה להבריח בה העופות מגג ההיכל כדרך שעושין עכשיו שומרי זרעים, They made a μορμολύκειον [mormolykeion], with which to chase birds from the temple roof, as those who guard crops do now. And again: במקדש ראשון ששכינה שרוייה בו לא היו צורכין כלה עורב שלא היו עופות פורחין עליו אבל במקדש שני שלו היתה קדושתו כקדושת ראשון הוצרכו לכלה עורב, Because the divine majesty dwelt in the first Sanctuary, there was no need for a προβασκανίῳ [probaskaniō]. For birds did not fly over it. But it was needed in the second, because the holiness of the second was not like that of the first. Yet something of the kind is described even in Solomon's temple by Eupolemus, when he says that he made δακτυλίους δύο χαλκοῦς ἀλυσιδωτοὺς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοὺς [daktylious dyo chalkous halysidōtous, kai stēsai autous] (read δικτύας δύο χαλκᾶς ἀλυσιδωτὰς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτὰς [diktyas dyo chalkas halysidōtas, kai stēsai autas]) ἐπὶ μηχανημάτων ὑπερεχόντων τῷ ὕψει τὸν ναὸν πήχεις κ΄, καὶ σκιάζειν ἐπάνω παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ προσκρεμάσαι ἑκάστῃ δικτύϊ κώδωνας χαλκοῦς ταλαντιαίους τετρακοσίους, καὶ ποιῆσαι ὅλας τὰς δικτύας πρὸς τὸ ψοφεῖν τοὺς κώδωνας, καὶ ἀποσοβεῖν τὰ ὄρνεα, ὅπως μὴ καθίζῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, μηδὲ νοσσεύῃ ἐπὶ τοῖς φατνώμασι τῶν πυλῶν, καὶ στοῶν, καὶ μολύνῃ τοῖς ἀποπατήμασι τὸ ἱερὸν [epi mēchanēmatōn hyperechontōn tō hypsei ton naon pēcheis k', kai skiazein epanō pantos tou hierou, kai proskremasai hekastē diktyi kōdōnas chalkous talantiaious tetrakosious, kai poiēsai holas tas diktyas pros to psophein tous kōdōnas, kai aposobein ta ornea, hopōs mē kathizē epi tou hierou, mēde nosseuē epi tois phatnōmasi tōn pylōn, kai stoōn, kai molynē tois apopatēmasi to hieron], two bronze nets linked with rings, and that he set them on machines which rose twenty cubits above the temple and overshadowed the whole of it, and hung from each net four hundred bells of great weight, and fitted all those nets so that the bells would ring and drive off the birds with their sound, so that they would not settle on the temple, nor nest in the coffered ceilings of the gates or porticoes, nor pollute the temple with their droppings. But in the first book of Kings, where Solomon's temple is accurately described, you will find nothing of the sort; nor in Josephus, although he writes the same of the temple built by Herod, On the Jewish War book 6, ch. 6: Κατὰ κορυφὴν δὲ χρυσέους ὀβελοὺς ἀνεῖχε τεθηγμένους, ὡς μή τινι προσκαθεζομένῳ μολύνοιτο τῶν ὀρνέων [Kata koryphēn de chryseous obelous aneiche tethēgmenous, hōs mē tini proskathezomenō molynoito tōn orneōn], On the top it bristled with very sharp golden spits, so that it should not be polluted by birds settling on it. This agrees well enough with the description of the כלה עורב handed down by the Talmudists. Yet suppose that Solomon's temple too bristled with such spits on the ridge of the roof: this would have kept the birds off the top, but not off the whole roof or the other parts of the temple. If Christ could stand unharmed ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ [epi to pterygion tou hierou], on the pinnacle of the temple, Matt 4:5, how much more little birds ?

In that passage rash words and curses are compared with the wandering and circling sparrow and with the דרור. A. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in his Commentary on this passage, p. 345 ff., shows that the latter may not unreasonably be understood of the swallow, from a similar usage of the Arabs, who are accustomed to denote rash levity by this proverb: طارت عصافيره [ṭārat ʿaṣāfīruhu], his sparrows fly. With this agrees another: طارت خطاطيفه [ṭārat khaṭāṭīfuhu] his swallows fly, customarily used of an empty and rash babbler.

Merrick, in his notes on the passage, shows from Eustathius and Hesychius that it is not unusual among the Greeks either to put the word βωμου [bōmou], altar, sometimes for temple. Schnurrer [=C. F. Schnurrer, Dissertationes philologico-criticae (1790)], it is true, in his Animadversions on this passage (in the Dissertations Published Together, p. 162), rejects this interpretation on the ground that it cannot be demonstrated by examples that the Hebrews used the word מזבח in the same sense. To me, however, a synecdoche of this kind seems so natural to the poets of every nation that I would recognize it in our Hebrew poet even without the authority of examples.
Philo, On the Life of Moses, book 3, and 2 Chr 2:8.

The observation of ANT. DRIESSEN on this passage deserves to be added, from his Specimen of Observations in which Certain Passages of the Old Testament are Explained, Defended and Emended, with a preface by Nicol. Guil. Schroeder, Groningen 1774 (this dissertation is included in the Συλλογη [Syllogē] of Philological-Exegetical Dissertations Published by Various Authors and Defended under the Presidency of A. Schultens, I. I. Schultens and N. G. Schroeder, Leiden and Leeuwarden 1775, vol. 2, p. 1094 ff.): „It has already been observed by others that this passage refers to a custom accepted among ancient peoples, whereby animals dwelling in a sacred building, especially birds nesting in its walls or on the sides of the altars, were regarded as admitted into the protection of the Deity, so that it was sacrilege to harm them or drive them from their abode. Yet it will not be useless or unpleasant to compare an altogether similar passage from the Older Monuments of Arabia [edited by A. Schultens, Leiden 1740], Poem 1, where, just as the Psalmist celebrates the excellence of the holy place and the kindness of the Deity on the ground that even animals find a safe abode there, so Amru Ben Elharith extols the excellence of the Meccan sanctuary in a similar way: ونبكي لبيت ليس يوذي حمامة [wa-nabkī li-baytin laysa yūdhī ḥamāmatun] يظل دها امنا وفيه العصافر [yaẓallu dahā āminan wa-fīhi al-ʿaṣāfir] وفيه وحوش لا تراب انيسة [wa-fīhi wuḥūshun lā turābu anīsatun] انا خرجت منه فليست تغادم [anā kharajat minhu fa-laysat tughādim] And we weep for the sanctuary, whose dove is not harmed, which rejoices secure in its shade, and the sparrows there too; there also wild beasts that are not frightened, tame, even if they go out from it; and they inflict no harm. The reason why I thought it worthwhile to compare this poem with the sacred hymn is that the same animals occur in both, namely sparrows and doves. The celebrated Schultens dates this Arabic fragment to the age of Solomon. Moreover, the particle את in the words את מזבחותיך undoubtedly means at, beside, as often elsewhere.“ Thus Driessen. These remarks, though aptly made, contribute nothing to determining the meaning of the word דרור; for swallows could nest in the temple just as well as wood pigeons.

In this whole discussion I would think Bochart more successful in refuting the fancies of others than in establishing his own opinion. For at the beginning of this chapter he rightly objected to those who render it swallow, as if it were named from freedom, that this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds, some domestic, some wild; yet soon he himself uses the same reason to show that דרור is a species of wild dove. Indeed, our author's whole argument comes to this: the Hebrew דרור, like the Arabic حرّ [ḥurr], means free; but among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is an epithet of the wild dove; therefore the Hebrew דרור, carrying the same notion of freedom, denotes that same animal. How weak this is, anyone understands at once, since among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is not the name of the dove but an epithet of the wild dove, added to the noun ساق [sāq], which signifies the male dove. As for the two passages in which the word דרור occurs, we have seen (note 1 and 3) that the swallow fits the former (Proverb. XXVI, 2.) well enough, while for the other the swallow suits as well as the dove. — Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descript. Animalium in Itinere Orientali observatorum p. 10, mentions among the migratory birds of Alexandria one named Dururi, which comes when the dates have ripened, at the end of October, from Upper Egypt, and, when these have been consumed, leaves after three months. Since Alexandria is not much further south than Jerusalem, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] (in Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 477) suspects that this bird may be the Hebrew דרור; yet he determines nothing certain, since it is doubtful in which letters the name is written in Arabic, دُرُوري [durūrī] or ضُرُوري [ḍurūrī]. Nevertheless, toward the end he adds: “Is it the species of sparrow, of the colour of a nightingale, with a very sweet song, which Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] saw around Capsa in palm-bearing places, p. 185, Travels, German trans. 164? See also Buffons Naturgeschichte der Voegel vol. 10, p. 161, German trans. Thus I could have called it Dattelnsperling.” Although Michaelis proposed this with hesitation, Ziegler nevertheless took it as certain, in his translation of Proverbs. — Finally, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in Clavis Psalmorr. p. 209, flatly denies that any bird at all is denoted by the word דרור, because it is contrasted with τῷ [tō] צפור, that is, with the whole class of birds. Hence he himself renders the Hebrew word tiny ant, comparing the Arabic ذرّ [dharr]; see Castell [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] Lexic. Hexapl. p. 77c. But צפור signifies both any birds whatever and specifically the sparrow. An ant, moreover, would hardly fit the passage Proverb. XXVI, 2. (דרור לעוף). Nor can a nest, קן, be attributed to an ant, as is done in Ps 84:4 — I would believe that דרור is an onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικον [onomatopoiētikon]) name of the turtledove, since all the ancient translators agree on this.

The turtledove is called תור thor in Hebrew and τρυγών [trygōn] in Greek. These names, however similar, are not derived from one another but are onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικά [onomatopoiētika]). They were formed, that is, in imitation of the song of the turtledove, which in Greek is called τρυσμὸς [trysmos], from the verb τρύζειν [tryzein], that is, to moan in the manner of a turtledove. So Pollux, book 5, ch. 14, in the section On the calls of birds: Εἴποις δ' ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois d' an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. But for Suidas and the Etymologicum, too, τρύζειν [tryzein] is ψιθυρίζειν, γογγύζειν, ἀσήμως λαλεῖν παρὰ καὶ ἡ τρυγὼν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀσήμως φθέγγεται καὶ γογγυστικῶς [psithyrizein, gongyzein, asēmōs lalein para kai hē trygōn, epei kai asēmōs phthengetai kai gongystikōs], to whisper, to murmur, to speak indistinctly, like the turtledove too, because it sings indistinctly and with a murmur. Hence Clement, in the fifth book of the Stromata: Γογγύζουσα ἡ τρυγὼν, μέμψεως καταλαλιὰν ἀχάριστον ἐμφαίνουσα, εἰκότως ἐξοικίζεται [Gongyzousa hē trygōn, mempseōs katalalian acharistōn emphainousa, eikotōs exoikizetai]. The murmuring turtledove, displaying the ungrateful slander of complaint, is rightly driven from the house. For others τρύζειν [tryzein] is πολυφωνεῖν, καὶ πολυλογεῖν [polyphōnein, kai polylogein], to chatter a great deal. Because τὴν τρυγόνα ἡ παροιμία ἐπὶ σκώμματι τῶν πολυλογούντων παραλαμβάνει, λαλιστέρους τῶν τρυγόνων τοιούτους καλοῦσα [tēn trygona hē paroimia epi skōmmati tōn polylogountōn paralambanei, lalisterous tōn trygonōn toioutous kalousa], the proverb uses the turtledove to mock those who chatter a great deal, calling them more talkative than turtledoves. So Eustathius, on that line of Homer, Iliad 1, verse 31:
Ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος, [Hōs mē moi tryzēte parēmenoi allothen allos,]

So that you may not chatter at me, sitting by, one from here, another from there. Besides the paroemiographers, the proverb is mentioned by Alexis in the Thraso in Athenaeus, book 4; by Menander in the Plocium; by Demetrius in the Sicilia in Aelian, On Animals, book 12, chapter 12; and by Clement in the first book of the Stromata. To this belongs what is said of chattering women in Theocritus' Syracusan Women:
Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι πλατυάσδοισαι ἅπαντα, [Trygones ekknaiseunti platyasdoisai hapanta,]

Like turtledoves they deafen us, broadening their mouths on every word. Nor do I approve the proposal of a great man to read ἐκ Ναύσοιο [ek Nausoio], that is, from the island of Sicily, instead of ἐκκναισεῦντι [ekknaiseunti]. Ναῦσος [Nausos], he says, like Νᾶσος [Nasos], is a word of the Dorians and the Sicilians, who so called their Sicily. The poet therefore very wittily calls the Dorian-speaking women (τοὺς Δωριζούσας [tous Dōrizousas]), who pronounce everything with a broad mouth, τρυγόνας ἐκ Ναύσοιο [trygonas ek Nausoio]. This conjecture, I say, I do not approve, because there is no need to change anything, since the received reading yields a most fitting sense. Ἐκκναίειν [Ekknaiein] means to deafen the ears, like ἀποκναίειν [apoknaiein]. Pollux: Ἀποκναίων ἀηδίᾳ, κόπτων τὰ ὦτα [Apoknaiōn aēdia, koptōn ta ōta], ἀποκναίων [apoknaiōn] by his unpleasantness, or by his inanities, that is, deafening the ears. As Demosthenes wrote against Midias, p. 362: Ἀποκναίει γὰρ ἀηδίᾳ, δήπου καὶ ἀναιθησίᾳ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ταῦτα λέγων· [Apoknaiei gar aēdia, dēpou kai anaithēsia kath' hekastēn tēn ekklēsian tauta legōn;] For he deafens us with his inanities and stupidity, hammering the same things in at every assembly. Thus, then, it is said of chatterboxes, Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι [Trygones ekknaiseunti], Doric for ἐκκναίσουσι [ekknaisousi], Turtledoves (or like turtledoves) deafen the ears with their talkativeness. Among the Proverbs in Suidas there is Τρυγόνα ψάλλειν [Trygona psallein], To sing the turtledove, ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλως πραττων [epi tōn phaulōs prattōn], said of those who do something badly, because the voice of the turtledove is utterly unmusical. And perhaps this is why it is called צלצל by the Hebrews, צרצילתא by the Chaldeans, and in Arabic also صلصل [ṣalṣal], as if the name were formed from a cymbal, because it has a ringing and noisy voice. Indeed, if we believe Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], for this very reason a species of cicada, the cercope, is compared with the turtledove in these words of Athenaeus, book 4, ch. 4: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἡ κερκώπη ζῶον ὅμοιον τέττιγι, καὶ τρυγονίῳ· [Esti d' hē kerkōpē zōon homoion tettigi, kai trygoniō;] The cercope is an animal like a cicada and a turtledove. On these words he says: The cercope resembles the turtledove in nothing else than its noisy chatter. But Dale- champius conjectures that a cricket is so called from the peculiarity of the sound tri. And the great Casaubon passed over this passage unconcerned. Yet that it is corrupt is as certain as whatever is most certain, and τρυγονίῳ [trygoniō] is wrongly read for τεττιγονίῳ [tettigoniō], which is a species of cicada. Aristotle, Hist. book 5, ch. 30: Καλοῦσι δέ τινες τοὺς μὲν μεγάλους (τῶν τεττίγων) καὶ ᾄδοντας ἄχετας· τοὺς δὲ μικροὺς τεττιγόνια [Kalousi de tines tous men megalous (tōn tettigōn) kai adontas achetas; tous de mikrous tettigonia]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 26: Those that sing are called achetae, and the smaller of them tettigonia. So this passage contains nothing that can be referred to the chattering of turtledoves. That chattering, though often annoying, nevertheless has something pleasing: it signals that spring and summer have come, since turtledoves do not appear in winter. Hence it is said in Cant. II, 11. 12.: For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Flowers are seen on the earth. The time of song has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. And Ierem. VIII, 7.: The turtledove and the swallow and the crane have observed the time of their coming. For the turtledove is a migratory bird . Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3.

φάττα μὲν οὖν, καὶ περιστερὰ ἀεὶ φαίνονται· τρυγὼν δὲ τοῦ θέρους· τοῦ γὰρ χειμῶνος ἀφανίζεται· [phatta men oun, kai peristera aei phainontai; trygōn de tou therous; tou gar cheimōnos aphanizetai] The wood-pigeon and the dove are always to be seen, but the turtledove only in summer. For in winter it is not seen. And in book 8, chapter 12, denying of the wood-pigeon the very thing he had affirmed here, he writes that only doves remain all year. His words are: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ καὶ αἱ φάτται, καὶ αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες, αἱ δὲ περιστεραὶ καταμένουσιν· [Apairousi de kai hai phattai, kai hai peleiades, kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones, hai de peristerai katamenousin] But the wood-pigeons, the rock-doves, the swallows and the turtledoves depart, and do not winter (here), but the doves remain. And in chapter 16 he teaches that it is above all characteristic of the turtledove to hide in winter. Φωλεῖ γὰρ [Phōlei gar], he says, καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος. καὶ ἥ γε τρυγὼν ὁμολογουμένως μάλιστα πάντων. οὐδεὶς γὰρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, λέγεται τρυγόνα ἰδεῖν οὐδαμοῦ χειμῶνος· [kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos. kai hē ge trygōn homologoumenōs malista pantōn. oudeis gar, hōs eipein, legetai trygona idein oudamou cheimōnos] For the stork also hides, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. But of the turtledove this is agreed most of all: for no one, I might almost say, is reported to have seen a turtledove anywhere in winter. Varro too, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another season turtledoves and quails in enormous numbers. And Cicero, De Finib. book 2: Turtledoves delight in running and in travel. And Gregory of Nyssa on the Song, Homily 5: Ἐν γὰρ τῇ χειμῶνι φεύγει ἡ ἀηδὼν, ναρκᾷ ἡ χελιδὼν, ἀποξενοῦται τῆς καλίας ἡ τρυγών· [En gar tē cheimōni pheugei hē aēdōn, narka hē chelidōn, apoxenoutai tēs kalias hē trygōn] For in winter the nightingale flees, the swallow grows torpid, the turtledove goes abroad from its nest. There are some, however, who think that the turtledove does not so much go away as hide. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: More truly, the turtledove hides and loses its feathers. Others wrongly read vere [in spring]. For the turtledove does not hide in spring, but in winter. Indeed Aristotle himself, in chapter 12 cited above, does not deny that some turtledoves remain ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις [en euēliois chōriois].

In Song 1:10 it is said to the bride in the Greek version, Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos?] and in the Vulgate, How beautiful are your cheeks become, like the turtledove's! On this passage the Greek doctors, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Philo of Carpasia, Theodoret, and the Latin ones, Justus of Urgel, Gregory the Great, Bede, Aponius, Bernard [=Bernard of Clairvaux], and other men of great name, have much to say about the chastity of the turtledove and about the seat of modesty in the cheeks. But all of it is beside the point, if I may say so with their leave. For the passage is not about the turtledove there: since it has no σιαγόνες [siagones], that is, cheeks or jaws, who would believe that the bride's cheeks are compared with the cheeks of a turtledove? Ἡ δὲ ὄρνις [Hē de ornis] (says the Philosopher, De partib. animal. book 2, ch. 16)

ἀντὶ σιαγόνων ἔχει τὸ καλούμενον ῥύγχος [anti siagonōn echei to kaloumenon rhynchos], in place of jaws it has what they call a beak. In vain would you object that Ovid, at the death of his parrot, invites the other birds to tear their cheeks, in Amores book 2, Elegy 6:
Go, pious birds, and beat your breasts with your wings, and mark your tender cheeks with rigid claw.
For he is applying to birds ποιητικῶς [poiētikōs], and πρωσοποποιητικῶς [prōsopopoiētikōs], things that are proper to human beings in mourning. Accordingly the same poet, Tristia book 3, Elegy 3:
Yet forbear to tear your cheeks, and do not rend your hair.
Do not wound my shade, but spare your loosened hair, and spare, Delia, your tender cheeks,

And Artemidorus, Onirocritica book 1, ch. 30: Παρειὰς ἴσχνας ἔχειν, ἢ ἑλκομένας, λύπας, ἢ πένθος σημαίνει. ἴσχνας μὲν λύπας, ἑλκομένας δὲ πένθος. καὶ γὰρ ἐν τοῖς πένθεσι λωβῶνται τὰς παρειὰς οἱ ἄνθρωποι· [Pareias ischnas echein, ē helkomenas, lypas, ē penthos sēmainei. ischnas men lypas, helkomenas de penthos. kai gar en tois penthesi lōbōntai tas pareias hoi anthrōpoi] To have thin or ulcerated cheeks (in dreams) signifies sorrow and mourning: thin cheeks sorrow, ulcerated ones mourning. For in mourning people tear their cheeks. I admit that I have read in Horus, Hieroglyph. book 2, ch. 50, that the turtledove has teeth. To signify a nursing woman, and one who nourishes well, he says, (the Egyptians) τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν ὀδόντας, καὶ μασθοὺς ἔχει [trygona zōgraphousin; hautē gar monē tōn allōn ptēnōn odontas, kai masthous echei], paint a turtledove: for she alone among birds has teeth and breasts. If this were true, she would also have jaws and cheeks. But learned men have already observed that this belongs to the bat, to which alone it applies. So some change τρυγόνα [trygona] into τριγόνα [trigona], conjecturing that the bat is called by that name there, because τρίζειν [trizein, to squeak] is proper to it. Others more correctly change it into νυκτερίδα [nykterida]; and the reason why the words were interchanged is obvious. Immediately before it had said: Wishing to signify a weak man who attempts great things, νυκτερίδα ζωγραφοῦσιν [nykterida zōgraphousin], they paint a bat, which flies without feathers. And immediately after follows: To designate a man who is charmed by dancing and the pipe, τρυγόνα ζωγραφοῦσιν [trygona zōgraphousin], they paint a turtledove, which is caught by the pipe and dancing. I have rendered turtledove with Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs], Caussinus and others. Yet — and I am surprised this escaped them — τρυγὼν [trygōn] there is not the turtledove but the stingray, which this same writer below, in ch. 105, calls simply τρυγόνα [trygona], and others, to distinguish it, θαλαττίαν τρυγόνα [thalattian trygona], the sea turtledove. For it is not the bird, the turtledove, but ἡ θαλαττία τρυγὼν [hē thalattia trygōn], the sea turtledove, that is, the stingray, that, charmed by the pipe and dancing, is lured into the fish-trap, as Aelian relates at length, On Animals book 17, ch. 18; although Philo too refers this to the turtledove, the bird. Now, to return to where the discussion digressed: the words of the Sacred Song in Hebrew read thus: נאוו לחייך בתורים צוארך בחרוזים, Your cheeks are adorned with rows (of gems), your neck with chains. For this the Greeks have Τί ὡραιώθησαν σιαγόνες σου ὡς τρυγόνος, τραχηλός σου ὡς ὅρμισκοι; [Ti hōraiōthēsan siagones sou hōs trygonos, trachēlos sou hōs hormiskoi?] and Jerome: How beautiful have your cheeks become, like the turtledove's; your neck like a necklace. For, interchanging ב and כ, they read כתורים for בתורים, and כחרוזים for בחרוזים, and they took תורי for turtledoves, whereas there it means rows, namely of gems, or of golden studs. That it must be rendered so is shown by many things: 1. תורים and חרוזים are here nearly synonymous. Moreover, although the word חרוזים does not occur elsewhere in Scripture, it is very well known from the Arabic language, in which the verb خرز [kharaza] means to sew with an awl, and الخرز [al-kharaz] a necklace of gems strung together, and also the spine, whose vertebrae are as it were sewn and strung together. Accordingly the Greek renders חרוזים as ὁρμισκοὺς [hormiskous], and Jerome as necklaces, entirely correctly. 2. Immediately there follows תורי זהב נעשה לך, where it is plain that תורי are not turtledoves but a kind of golden ornament, namely chains or something similar. Hence there Jerome has: We will make you golden chains. And the Syriac ܕܕܗܒܐ ܥܢܩܐ [דדהבא ענקא], a golden chain. And the fifth edition στρεπτὸν χρυσίου [strepton chrysiou]; so it should be read, not στρεπτοῦ [streptou]. For στρεπτὸς [streptos] or στρεπτὸν [strepton] is used everywhere for a torque by Herodotus, Xenophon, Plutarch and others. In Symmachus, for περίβλεπτα χρυσίου [periblepta chrysiou] I would read περίπλεκτα [periplekta]. For στρέφειν [strephein], whence στρεπτὸν [strepton], and πλέκειν [plekein], whence πλεκτὸν [plekton], are nearly synonymous. Hence in Hesychius πλόκιον [plokion] is εἶδος περιδεραίου [eidos perideraiou], a kind of necklace. And the same reasoning holds for the Syriac ܥܢܩܐ [ענקא] for torque, for the verb ܥܢܩ [ענק] means to fold and to twist. But why do the Elders render ὁμοιώματα [homoiōmata]? Did they read ציורי, that is, images, for תורי? Or did they think that תורי זהב meant likenesses of turtledoves made of gold, which was the opinion of Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra]? 3. Indeed, תור with Thau here is the same as טור with Teth, a word Moses uses repeatedly for a row of gems, as in Exod. XXVIII, 17: ארבעה טורים אבן, four rows of stones. Likewise, אדם פטדת וברקת הטור האחד, sardius, topaz and emerald, the first row. 5. Nor is it obscure how cheeks are adorned with rows of gems: namely if these hang from the ears, or if they are scattered over the ribbons of the mitres, that is, the broad bands that were drawn down along the cheeks and tied under the chin. For in Syria the mitre was a woman's head-covering. Virgil in the Catalecta:
The Syrian tavern-hostess, her head bound with a Greek little mitre.
Go, you who fancy a barbarian harlot with a painted mitre.
Barbarian, that is, Syrian; for there had preceded:

Long since has the Syrian Orontes flowed down into the Tiber, and brought with it its language and its manners, the slanting strings along with the piper, and its native timbrels too, and the girls bidden to sell themselves at the Circus.

We have spoken above about the sacrifices of turtledoves. Their chastity has also been treated, and it was proved from Aristotle, Aelian and Clement that turtledoves admit only one mate. From this arose what later writers have stated with great unanimity: that when its mate has died, the turtledove remains a widow. To this they would refer these words of the Psalmist, Ps 74:19. Deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude (of the enemies), that is, they say, the Church of Israel, which, even when forsaken by you, does not cleave to another God. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)]: התור הזה משמת הזכר בן זוגה אינה מזדווגת לאחר אף ישראל לא התחליפוך באל אחר אף על פי שרחקתה מהם והיו כאלמנה, The female turtledove, once her male mate has died, does not pair with another. So too the Israelites have not exchanged you for another God, even though you have withdrawn from them, but have remained like a widow. But there is no need to go so far. For it is not sufficiently certain that the turtledove in widowhood does not pair with another, even though the writers who assert it
may be defended by their number and by phalanxes joined shield to shield.

But it is certain at least that the turtledove does not mate with another while its mate is alive. If the Church conforms itself to this example, it will never worship other gods, because the God whom it worships is ever living. The Israelites could also be compared with the turtledove לפי שהם חלושי הכח ונטרפים ואינם טורפים וכן ישראל, because turtledoves are weak in strength, and are torn as prey but do not prey, and so are the Israelites. This is Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]'s conjecture. For the turtledove is a kind of dove, and the smallest of all in the dove kind. The Philosopher, Hist. book 5, ch. 13: Ἐλάχιστον δὲ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ τρυγών [Elachiston de tōn toioutōn hē trygōn]· The smallest of these is the turtledove. To the same purpose could also be referred whatever has been said of the simplicity of the dove, since the turtledove is a kind of dove. You will wonder why none of the ancient translators, as many as are extant, mentioned the turtledove in rendering this passage. For in place of the soul of thy turtledove the Greeks have ψυχὴν ἐξομολογουμένην σοι [psychēn exomologoumenēn soi], a soul confessing to thee. The Syriac and the Ethiopic follow the same. They evidently read תודך for תורך, Daleth for Resh, which are very similar letters. The printed Arabic versions have نفسا عارفة بك [nafsan ʿārifatan bika] a soul that knows thee. And one of the manuscripts in my possession has انفس يايسيك [anfus yāysīk] souls who know thee, that is, who have known thee. As if they had read נפש תדעך, a soul that knows thee. But Jerome has A soul instructed in thy Law. And the Chaldee version of Joseph the Blind has נפשת מאלפי אוריתך, the souls of those teaching thy Law, as though תורך alluded to the word תורה, which means Law. But these renderings are far-fetched and beside the point. And, apart from the Greeks, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], older than all of these, had rightly seen that תור here is the turtledove. His version, indeed, is not extant. But that he rendered it so is shown by these words of Selomo: יונתן תירגם לשון תורים ובני יונה, Jonathan rendered it as in the passages of the Law dealing with turtledoves and young doves. The Hebrews rightly follow this, as do the more recent translators, as many as there are.

Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descriptio Animalium, p. 9, also lists the turtur [turtledove] among the migratory birds of Alexandria that arrive with the flooding of the Nile (that is, either toward the end of April or at the beginning of May). But he wrongly wrote the name of the animal as كمري [kmry] for قمري [qumrī]; see Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], Lexic. Arab. p. 1964, whose feminine is قُمْرِيَّة [qumriyya]; the male is also called ساق حرّ [sāq ḥurr], on which see Bochart, preceding Chapter, p. 52, marginal note. By a strange error Hufnagel [=W. F. Hufnagel, in Paulus's [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Repertorium für biblische und morgenländische Litteratur], V. S. V., in the Annotatt. in Cantic. in the Repertorium für biblische und morgenl. Litterat. vol. 10, p. 243 243, note b), confuses the turtur [turtledove] with the turdus [thrush], Arab. سمرمر [smrmr], which Forsskål, p. 6 of the book cited, says arrives at Aleppo in the months of July and August. But there is no one who does not know that the turdus [thrush] is of an entirely different kind from the turtur [turtledove].

With תור thor, that is, the turtledove, are joined סיס sis and עגור agor, as birds that are likewise migratory, in these words of Jer 8:7. Both thor and sis and agor have kept the time of their coming. And since the turtledove has been dealt with, it follows that we treat of sis and agor. These words occur again in the song of King Hezekiah, Isa 38:14. Like sis (he says) and agor I chirped, I moaned like a dove. But elsewhere there is no mention of them. And although in both places סוס is written in the text with Vau, yet in Jeremiah the Hebrews read סיס sis, with Iod. This reading I strongly approve, both so that סיס sis may differ from the word סוס sus, which means horse, and because סיס sis seems better to express the nature of the thing signified by this name . This very point, since it is in question, must now be examined. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Munster, Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], Schindler, Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Tremellius [=Immanuel Tremellius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], the English, the Italians, etc., and most other modern interpreters consistently render סיס sis as crane. So, of course, the most learned of the Hebrews hold, Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists], Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], following Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] in the Chaldee Paraphrase, which has כורכיא kurkeja for סיס sis. Further, that כורכיא kurkeja is the crane is clear both from the Talmud and from the Arab writers, who write كركي [kurkī] kurki. For כורכיא kurkeja you sometimes find כרוכיא krukeja, as in the tractate Kiddusim, ch. 2, fol. 44a. Very similar to this word is the word כרוכא kruka, which occurs in Jonathan at Lev 11:22 for חגב chagab, or cicada. It once also stood in the Jerusalem Paraphrase, from which it is cited by Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] in the Methurgeman. Hence arose an amusing error in Symmachus, who, taking the words כרוכא kruka and כרוכיא krukeja indiscriminately, made a cicada out of the crane in Jeremiah. Hence Jerome on Jeremiah: Symmachus translated it 'cicada', which in Hebrew is called סיס sis. And in the same place Theodoret: Τρυγὼν, καὶ τέττιξ, καὶ χελιδὼν, ἀγροῦ στρουθία, ἐφύλαξαν καιροὺς εἰσόδων αὐτῶν· [Trygōn, kai tettix, kai chelidōn, agrou strouthia, ephylaxan kairous eisodōn autōn] The turtledove, and the cicada, and the swallow, little birds of the field, have observed the time of their coming. After Chrysostom quoted these very words in the Homily On the Turtledove, as if from Jeremiah, he adds by way of commentary: Τρυγόνα λέγων τὴν πάνσεμνον ἐκκλησίαν, χελιδόνα τὸν φιλέρημον Ἰωάννην, τέττιγα τὸν εὔλαλον Παῦλον [Trygona legōn tēn pansemnon ekklēsian, chelidona ton philerēmon Iōannēn, tettiga ton eulalon Paulon]. Calling the venerable church the turtledove, the dweller in the desert, John, the swallow, and the eloquent Paul the cicada. This error arose from another error. For those who render סיס sis as crane are as mistaken as those who render it cicada: since סיס sis is neither the crane nor the cicada, but the swallow. This is proved first by the agreement of the older interpreters, which carries great weight with me when no compelling reason opposes it, and here none presents itself. As older interpreters I here name: 1. the Greek Elders, by whom סיס sis is rendered χελιδὼν [chelidōn] in both places; 2. Theodotion; 3. Jerome, who follow the same; 4. that very Symmachus for whom סיס sis in Jeremiah is the cicada. For by him Hezekiah's words כסוס עגור are rendered ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλεισθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleistheisa], like a swallow shut in. 5. Add to these the Arabic translator, for whom סיס sis is سنونوه [sunūnūh] sununua, that is, swallow. In Abi Ubid, Century 1, Proverb 32, it is written سنونية [sunūniya] senunia, and the late Erpenius ὁ μακαρίτης [ho makaritēs] had rightly explained it as swallow, but only by conjecture. That it is the name of a bird, he says, is clear enough; but of what kind I do not know. I translated it swallow, because the Chaldee סנוניתא senunitha is usually so translated. Otherwise the swallow is called خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, etc. To meet these doubts of a man by far the most learned in Arabic letters, and once most deserving of my gratitude, I wish to explain the word more precisely. خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph is the swallow in general, so called from the swiftness of its flight, like the Chaldee חטפיתא chatphitha. But of this there are several species, which the Arabs in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] define thus: الخطاطيف انواع منها نوع يالف السواحل عند البحر يحفر بيتها هناك ويعشش هناك وهو صغير الجثة دون عصغور الجنة ولونه رمادي [al-khaṭāṭīf anwāʿ minhā nawʿ yaʾlaf al-sawāḥil ʿinda al-baḥr yaḥfir baytahā hunāka wa-yuʿashshish hunāka wa-huwa ṣaghīr al-jutha dūna ʿaṣghūr al-janna wa-lawnuhu ramādī] والناس يسمونه سنونوا بضم السين المهملة ونونين ومنها نوع لخضرته علي ظهرة بعض حمرة اصغر من الدرة تسميه اهل مصر الخضري لخضرته يغتات الغراش والذباب ونحو ذلك ومنها طويل الاجنحة رقيقها يالف الجبال وياكل النمل وهذا النوع يقال له السايم مغرب سامه ومنهم من يسمي هذا النوع السنونوا الوحدة سنونوة وهو كثير في المسجد الحرام بمكة يعشش في سقف المسجد في مقام ابراهيم وباب بني شيبة وبعض الناس [wa-al-nās yusammūnahu sunūnū bi-ḍamm al-sīn al-muhmala wa-nūnayn wa-minhā nawʿ li-khuḍratihi ʿalā ẓahrih baʿḍ ḥumra aṣghar min al-durra tusammīhi ahl Miṣr al-khuḍarī li-khuḍratihi yaghtāt al-gharāsh wa-al-dhubāb wa-naḥw dhālika wa-minhā ṭawīl al-ajniḥa raqīquhā yaʾlaf al-jibāl wa-yaʾkul al-naml wa-hādhā al-nawʿ yuqāl lahu al-sāyim mughrib sāmih wa-minhum man yusammī hādhā al-nawʿ al-sunūnū al-waḥda sunūnūa wa-huwa kathīr fī al-masjid al-ḥarām bi-Makka yuʿashshish fī saqf al-masjid fī maqām Ibrāhīm wa-bāb banī Shayba wa-baʿḍ al-nās] يزعم انه الطير الابابيل الذي عذب الله به اصحاب الغيل [yazʿum annahu al-ṭayr al-abābīl alladhī ʿadhdhaba Allāh bihi aṣḥāb al-ghīl] There are various species of swallows. One of them lives on the shores of the sea, and there digs out its home and nests. It is smaller in body than the bird of Paradise, and ash-grey in colour. It is called sununu, with Sin Semol given damma and two Nun. There is also a green species with some redness on the back, smaller than a parrot, which the Egyptians on account of its colour call chadra, that is, green. It feeds on butterflies, flies and other similar small creatures. There is also another species, with long and slender wings, a dweller in the mountains, which eats ants. These they call semaim, from the singular semama. But some also call them sununu. The singular of unity is sununua. Of this species there are many in the Charam temple of the city of Mecca, which nest in the roof of the temple, at the station of Abraham and at the gate of the sons of Seiba. Some assert that these are the birds called ababil, by which God punished the companions of the elephant: namely by throwing on their heads حجارة من سجيل [ḥijāra min sijjīl] stones of siggil. So they call stones baked and hardened in the fire of hell, inscribed with the names of those on whom they fell. Their leader Abraheth, king of the Abyssinians in the interior of Arabia Felix, in the very year in which Muhammad was born, had come riding a great elephant with large forces in order to destroy the temple of Mecca. The pseudo-prophet touches on this in passing in Azoara 115, entitled الغيل [al-ghīl] The Elephant. But these matters belong elsewhere. Here it suffices to have noted that it is clear from what has been adduced that سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua properly denotes the sand martin [hirundo riparia] , of which Pliny, book 10, ch. 33: The third kind of them is those which hollow out banks and so nest within. And book 30, ch. 4: Yet by far the most efficacious are the young of the bank (swallows). So they call those that nest in hollows of riverbanks. The riparia [bank swallow] is called in Greek δρεπανὶς [drepanis], from its sickle-shaped feet. So the Philosopher calls it, Hist. book 1, ch. 1. But they add that by the same name سنونوة [sunūnūa] sununua are also signified those swallows which nest in mountains and temples. These are the rustic or field swallows of Pliny, on which see Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], p. 565 . Meanwhile it is certain that this name sometimes extends more widely and is used for any swallow. Thus the stone اليرقان [al-yaraqān] icterias, that is, by which jaundice sufferers are healed, is by another name called حجر السنونوة [ḥajar al-sunūnūa] the stone of the sununua, that is, of the swallow, because it is found in its nest. For the Arabs dye the swallow's young with saffron; and the father, suspecting that they suffer from jaundice, brings that stone from India into the nest and places it under the young. Damir describes it as small, streaked with red lines that verge on black. So too the author On the Wonders of Nature, where, as Damir notes, صنونو [ṣunūnū] sununu is wrongly read with Sad. And at Bar 6:21 the Arabic translator rendered these Greek words, Ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῶν ἐφίπτανται χελιδόνες [Epi tēn kephalēn autōn ephiptantai chelidones], thus: السنونو تلمسهم علي راسهم [al-sunūnū talmisuhum ʿalā raʾsihim] Assununu (or swallows) touch them upon their heads. Touch, that is, ἐφάπτονται [ephaptontai], as he read instead of ἐφίπτανται [ephiptantai], fly upon.

It has been proved so far that for most of the ancients סיס sis is the swallow. Against them Jonathan is cited in vain, as though he had rendered it כורכיא, that is, crane. For he correctly explained the two words סיס sis and עגור agor by כורכיא kurkeja and סנוניתא sununitha, that is, crane and swallow. For as סיס sis is the swallow, so עגור agor is the crane, as will be shown in the following chapter. But he inverted the order, and put the swallow, which comes first in the Hebrew text, in the second place. This often happens with translators. And, not to seek examples further afield, in the passage of Baruch which we cited a little earlier, for the Greek words νυκτερίδες, χελιδόνες [nykterides, chelidones], bats and swallows, the Arabic has, in inverted order, السنونو والوطاويط [al-sunūnū wa-l-waṭāwīṭ] swallows and bats. Accordingly we add the Chaldee also, whom the Syriac followed, to those of the ancients for whom סיס sis is the swallow. Thus there is now none of the early translators who does not agree with the rendering we maintain.

To this authority of the ancients is added a clear reason. The word סיס sis is ὀνοματοποιητικὴ [onomatopoiētikē], by which the Hebrew intended to imitate, after a fashion, the swallow's ψιθυρισμὸν [psithyrismon]. So with the Italians around Venice, for whom zisilla is the swallow, and zisillare means to τιτυβίζειν [titybizein] or ψιθυρίζειν [psithyrizein] in the manner of a swallow. The author of the Philomela said zinzilulare:
The wren and the bee-eater, and Procne with red breast, Know how to zinzilulare with a like measure.

As though the voice of Procne, that is, of the swallow, were zizi, from which zizilulare ought to have been said, as in Italian zisillare. But for the sake of euphony an epenthetic N was added, which is frequent in Roman words. Such are lingo from λείχω [leichō], linquo from the Aeolic λείκω [leikō] for λείπω [leipō], tango from θίγω [thigō], pango from πάγω [pagō] for πήγω [pēgō], densus from δασὺς [dasys], pinguis from παχὺς [pachys], etc. .

Nor is it of slight weight that the Egyptians relate in their fables that Isis was changed into a swallow. Plutarch in the Isis: Αὐτὴν δὲ γενομένην χελιδόνα (φασὶ) [Autēn de genomenēn chelidona (phasi)]

τῇ κίονι περιπέτεσθαι, καὶ θρηνεῖν· [tē kioni peripetesthai, kai thrēnein] And she, having become a swallow (they say), flew around the pillar and lamented. For Isis plainly alludes to sis. And the fabulous metamorphoses of the gods often rest on allusions of words. Thus Anubis was represented with a dog's head, because in Hebrew נובח nobeah means barking.
