And king Apis was worshipped in a bull, because of the allusion to אביר abir: for the Hebrews so name the bull. Hence the LXX at Ier. XLVI, 15: Διὰ τί ἔφυγεν ὁ Ἄπις [Dia ti ephygen ho Apis], for the Hebrew מדוע נסחף אבירך, as they read in place of אביריך. And in the story of the Gigantomachy the gods, having taken flight into Egypt for fear of the giants, changed themselves into various forms. Ovid, book 5 of the Metamorphoses:

Jupiter, she said, became leader of the flock, whence even now Libyan Hammon is fashioned with curved horns: The Delian hid in a raven, the offspring of Semele in a goat, The sister of Phoebus in a cat, the daughter of Saturn in a snow-white cow, Venus in a fish, the Cyllenian in the wings of an ibis.

Antoninus Liberalis, Fab. 28, from Nicander: Ἀπόλλων μὲν ἐγένετο ἱέραξ, Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἴβις, Ἄρης δὲ λεπιδωτὸς ἰχθὺς, Ἄρτεμις δὲ αἴλουρος [Apollōn men egeneto hierax, Hermēs de ibis, Arēs de lepidōtos ichthys, Artemis de ailouros] (so it must be read instead of σίλουρος [silouros], as is clear from Ovid) τράγῳ δὲ εἰκάζεται Διόνυσος, ἔλλῳ δὲ Ἡρακλῆς, βοὶ δ᾽ Ἥφαιστος, μυγάλῃ δὲ Λητώ [tragō de eikazetai Dionysos, ellō de Hēraklēs, boi d' Hēphaistos, mygalē de Lētō]: Apollo was changed into a hawk, Mercury into an ibis, Mars into a scaly fish, Diana into a cat, Bacchus into a goat, Hercules into a fawn, Vulcan into an ox, Latona into a shrew-mouse. We do not undertake to explain all of these here, but only a few, for whose invention the occasion was taken from paronomasias. Jupiter, the supreme God, was changed into a ram, because אל el, God the strong, and איל ajil, ram, are paronyms, and the plural of both is אלים elim. Bacchus, the Osiris of the Egyptians, into a he-goat, because שעיר seir, in Hebrew he-goat, alludes to Osiris. Diana into a cat, because in Egyptian ΒΟΥΒΑΣΤΟΣ was the cat, and Bubastis was Diana. The one is in Stephanus, under the word Βούβαστος [Boubastos]: Οἱ δὲ Αἰγύπτιοι βούβαστον τὴν αἴλουρόν φασι [Hoi de Aigyptioi boubaston tēn ailouron phasi]: but the Egyptians call the cat bubastos; the other in Herodotus, book 2, ch. 156: Αἰγυπτιστὶ δὲ Ἀπόλλων Ὧρος, Δημήτηρ δὲ Ἶσις, Ἄρτεμις δὲ Βούβαστις [Aigyptisti de Apollōn Hōros, Dēmētēr de Isis, Artemis de Boubastis]: in Egyptian Apollo is Horus, Ceres Isis, Diana Bubastis. Hence it is that in the Herbarium of Apuleius, ch. 10, the Egyptians call Artemisia Βουβαστέως καρδίαν [Boubasteōs kardian], the heart of Bubastis, that is, the herb dear to Diana, as its Greek name also displays. Juno took the shape of a cow. For we have observed in its place that עשתרות, from which Juno was called Astarte, signifies not only flocks of sheep but also herds of cattle, and that this is why in Sanchuniathon Astarte ἐπέθηκε τῇ ἰδίᾳ κεφαλῇ βασιλείας παράσημον κεφαλὴν ταύρου [epethēke tē idia kephalē basileias parasēmon kephalēn taurou], placed a bull's head on her own head as the insignia of royalty. That Venus hid in a fish they refer to Atargatis, as if she were Dagon, to whom דג dag, that is, fish, gave the name; but I approve this less, for reasons given elsewhere.

Hezekiah in his illness says that he chirped like a swallow [Isa 38:14], because the swallow's voice seems to have something plaintive and mournful about it. All the poets proclaim this with one voice. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 366:
Τὸν δὲ μετ' ὀρθρογόη Πανδιονὶς ὦρτο χελιδὼν, [Ton de met' orthrogoē Pandionis ōrto chelidōn,]

After him, lamenting at dawn, came forth the swallow, daughter of Pandion. Hence Suidas: Ὀρθρογόη· χελιδών [Orthrogoē: chelidōn]. Others prefer ὀρθογόη [orthogoē]. Hesychius: Ὀρθογόη· ἡ χελιδών [Orthogoē: hē chelidōn]. Accordingly, from this, Ὀρθογόν· χελιδών [Orthogon: chelidōn] must be corrected in the manuscript Lexicon of Cyril in my possession. In the Etymologicum ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] is rendered ἡ μεγάλως θρηνοῦσα [hē megalōs thrēnousa], she who laments greatly. So too in Phavorinus, who adds that it is said of the swallow. Aristophanes in the Frogs:

Δὴ χείλεσιν ἀμφιλάλοις Δεινὸν ἐπιβρέμεται Θρηΐκια χελιδὼν, Ἐπὶ βάρβαρον ἑζομένη πέταλον, Κελαδεῖ δ' ἐπίκλαυτον ἀηδόνιον νόμον, [Dē cheilesin amphilalois Deinon epibremetai Thrēikia chelidōn, Epi barbaron hezomenē petalon, Keladei d' epiklauton aēdonion nomon,]
Now with chattering lips the Thracian swallow resounds heavily, sitting upon a barbarian leaf, and sings a mournful, shrill song.
Οὐδὲ τόσον θρήνησεν ἀν' ὤρεα μακρὰ χελιδὼν, [Oude toson thrēnēsen an' ōrea makra chelidōn,]
Nor did the swallow lament so much across the great mountains. Palladas, Anthol. book 1, ch. 60:
Τίπτε πανημέριος, Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε κούρη, Μυρομένη κελαδεῖς τραυλὰ διὰ στομάτων. [Tipte panēmerios, Pandioni kammore kourē, Myromenē keladeis traula dia stomatōn.]
Why all day long, O daughter of Pandion, unhappy girl, do you sing lamenting, lisping songs from your mouth? Accordingly, on these lines of Theocritus in the Thalysia,
— — — — ἁ δ' ἐλολυγὼν Τηλόθεν ἐν πυκινῇσι βάτων τρύζεσκεν ἀκάνθαις, [ha d' elolygōn Tēlothen en pykinēsi batōn tryzesken akanthais,]

And the ololygon moaned far off in the dense thorns of the brambles, ὀλολυγὼν [ololygōn] is explained by the Scholiast as ἡ χελιδὼν ἡ τὸν Ἴτυν ὀλοφυρομένη [hē chelidōn hē ton Ityn olophyromenē], the swallow bewailing Itys. And Agathias, Anthol. book 7, Epigr. 65, addresses the swallows thus:
Ἀλλ' Ἴτυλον κλαίοιτε κατ' οὔρεα, καὶ γοάοιτε, [All' Itylon klaioite kat' ourea, kai goaoite,]

But bewail Itylus in the mountains, and lament. Nor do the Roman poets speak otherwise. Catullus to Ortalus: Such as beneath the dense shade of the branches the Daulian bird sings, moaning the fate of the lost Itylus.
The unhappy bird builds her nest, tearfully moaning Itys, etc. — — —
The Daulian bird bewails Thracian Itys.
It is something to relieve a fatal ill by words; this makes Procne and the halcyons plaintive.
— — — as the Daulian bird is wont to weep for her son beneath the Ismarian shade. — —
Not the Bistonian bird that sits on the rooftops, chattering bewails the impious thefts of her dread husband.
And the Thracian concubine longs to give her wings to the new sun among her plaintive nests. — —
And in the Octavia, near the beginning:
— — — — now take up again your accustomed laments, and outdo the halcyons of the sea, outdo too the Pandionian birds. For your fortune is heavier than theirs. — — —
The Attic concubine weeps for Ismarian Itys.

Thus, when the Pandionian birds return to their faithful lodgings and the home they left when winter drove them out, they stand upon their nests and recount to the roofs the beginnings of their old fate; and that broken and tearful murmur men take for words, and yet that voice is not unlike words.
— — — the Getic birds do not complain more to the hospitable roofs in broken speech.

Against these, however, it is objected that Plato, refuting those who say that swans θρηνοῦντας τὸν θάνατον ὑπὸ λύπης ἐξάδειν [thrēnountas ton thanaton hypo lypēs exadein], sing for grief as they bewail their death, says: Οὐδὲν ὄρνεον ᾄδει ὅταν πεινῇ, ἢ ῥιγοῖ, ἤ τινα ἄλλην λύπην λυπεῖται· οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἥ τε ἀηδὼν, καὶ χελιδὼν, καὶ ὁ ἔποψ, ὃν δή φασι διὰ λύπην θρηνοῦντα ᾄδειν [Ouden orneon adei hotan peinē, ē rhigoi, ē tina allēn lypēn lypeitai; oude autē hē te aēdōn, kai chelidōn, kai ho epops, hon dē phasi dia lypēn thrēnounta adein] (read οὓς δὴ φ. δ. λ. θρηνοῦντας ᾄδειν [hous dē ph. d. l. thrēnountas adein]), No bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or sad for any other reason; not even the nightingale, the swallow and the hoopoe, which they say sing mournfully for grief. Accordingly Proclus cannot bear that the swallow should be called ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] by Hesiod, and wants to read ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē], crying in the morning, so that the Poet may not seem to disagree with Plato. But Tzetzes answers otherwise: Ὑμεῖς δ' ἴσμεν καὶ δίχα μάρτυρος Πλάτωνος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὄρνεον λυπούμενον ᾄδει· ἀλλὰ δεινῶς, καὶ ῥητορικῶς ὁ ποιητὴς τὴν λαλιὰν τῆς χελιδόνος θρῆνον εἶναι λέγει κατὰ τὸν μῦθον τῆς τοῦ Πανδίονος ἐκείνης θυγατρός [Hymeis d' ismen kai dicha martyros Platōnos, hoti ouden orneon lypoumenon adei; alla deinōs, kai rhētorikōs ho poiētēs tēn lalian tēs chelidonos thrēnon einai legei kata ton mython tēs tou Pandionos ekeinēs thygatros]. We know even without Plato as witness that no bird sings in grief. But the Poet skilfully and rhetorically calls the swallow's song a lament, in keeping with the fable of Pandion's daughter. So he, as though the swallow were said to mourn only because of the fable. Indeed, as Pausanias says in the Attica, σφίσι τὴν ἐς ἀηδόνα, καὶ χελιδόνα, μεταβολὴν ἐπεφήμισαν, ὅτι οἶμαι, καὶ αὗται αἱ ὄρνιθες ἐλεεινὸν, καὶ θρήνῳ ὅμοιον ᾄδουσιν [sphisi tēn es aēdona, kai chelidona, metabolēn epephēmisan, hoti oimai, kai hautai hai ornithes eleeinon, kai thrēnō homoion adousin], I think the common fable about Pandion's daughters, that one of them was changed into a nightingale and the other into a swallow, arose from the fact that each bird utters pitiful and mournful songs. Therefore nothing is to be changed in Hesiod. And the swallow would absurdly be called ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē] or ὀρθροβόη [orthroboē], since it is not a clamorous bird but one that twitters softly and ψιθυρίζουσα [psithyrizousa]. Hence Sidonius, book 2, letter 2, spoke of Procne twittering among the rafters. Likewise an unknown Poet in the Anthology,
Τραυλὰ μινυρομένη Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε φωνᾷ, [Traula minyromenē Pandioni kammore phōna,]

O wretched daughter of Pandion, twittering songs with lisping voice. Similar is what Pollux says in the chapter On the voices of birds, χελιδόνας ψιθυρίζειν [chelidonas psithyrizein], that swallows whisper. And that ψιθυρισμὸς [psithyrismos], or that twittering if you prefer, seems to have something in common with the complaints and murmurs that escape us in grief or for any other cause. Hence some of the ancients in Plutarch's Table Talk hold that by the swallow Pythagoras meant ψιθύρους [psithyrous], that is, whisperers or informers who secretly whisper into the ear. Still, what Plato says is true: swallows do not sing thus for grief. For a bird's song, however mournful it may seem, is the effect not of grief but of nature.

Now a few words on the migration of swallows in Ierem. VIII, 7. That they are migratory birds is known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers, and it has been observed in every age. Homer in the Εἰρεσιώνη [Eiresiōnē], quoted by Herodotus in his life,
Νεῦμαι σοι, νεῦμαι ἐνιαύσιος, ὥστε χελιδὼν, [Neumai soi, neumai eniausios, hōste chelidōn,]
I return to you every year, like the swallow. Anacreon, Ode 33,

Σὺ μὲν, φίλη χελιδὼν [Sy men, philē chelidōn] You, dear swallow, Ἐτησίη μολοῦσα [Etēsiē molousa], coming every year, Θέρει πλέκεις καλίην [Therei plekeis kaliēn], weave your nest in summer, Χειμῶσι δ' εἶς ἄφαντος [Cheimōsi d' eis aphantos]. And in winter you do not appear.

Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ, etc. καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες [Apairousi de, etc. kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones]; Both swallows and turtledoves depart, and do not winter among us. The author To Herennius: Swallows are at hand in summertime; driven off by winter, they withdraw. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: Swallows too depart in the winter months. Damir: وهو من الطيور القواطع [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ] It is one of the migratory birds. Columella, in his prose On the Cultivation of Gardens, book 12, chapter 3: Soon, when the winter solstice is over, after an interval of forty days, around the arrival of the swallow, when Favonius is already rising. And book 10, chapter 14: While the rising of Arcturus and the arrival of the swallow promise more favourable weather. In Pliny, book 2, chapter 47: Some call Favonius, on the 7th day before the Calends of March, Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. Favonius, that is, Zephyr. Hence Horace, book 1, Epistle 7, to Maecenas:
If you will allow me, with the Zephyrs and the first swallow.
And Oppian on the swallow, book 3 of the Halieutica, line 244:
— — εἰαρινὴ Ζεφύρου πρωτάγγελος ὄρνις, [eiarinē Zephyrou prōtangelos ornis,]
The spring bird, first messenger of Zephyr. And Nonnus, book 2 of the Dionysiaca:
— — εἰαρινοῖο φίλη Ζεφύροιο χελιδὼν, [eiarinoio philē Zephyroio chelidōn,]
The swallow, friend of the spring Zephyr. And in book 47:
Καὶ Ζεφύρου καλὸς ὄρνις ὑπωροφίην χέε μολπὴν, [Kai Zephyrou kalos ornis hypōrophiēn chee molpēn,]

And the beautiful bird of Zephyr poured out its song beneath the roof. As if alluding to the Greek proverb Νέα χελιδὼν [Nea chelidōn], A new swallow, which Suidas, by a lapse of memory, cites from the Birds of Aristophanes, although it is read nowhere but in the Knights, Act 1, in these words: Σκέψασθε παῖδες, οὐχ' ὁρᾶθ'; ὥρα, νέα χελιδὼν, [Skepsasthe paides, ouch' horath'; hōra, nea chelidōn,]

Look, boys, don't you see? It is spring, a new swallow. On which the Scholiast: Ἔστιν ἔαρος ἀρχή· δοκεῖ γάρ πως ἅμα τῷ ἔαρι φαίνεσθαι χελιδών. [Estin earos archē; dokei gar pōs hama tō eari phainesthai chelidōn.] It is the beginning of spring, for the swallow seems to appear together with the spring. So in the Birds (which may have misled Suidas) the appearing swallow teaches
Ὅτε χρὴ χλαῖναν πωλεῖν ἤδη, καὶ ληϊδάριόν τι πρίασθαι, [Hote chrē chlainan pōlein ēdē, kai lēidarion ti priasthai,]
When the cloak is to be sold, so that a summer garment may be bought. And in the Peace the Chorus sings:
— — ὅταν ἠρινᾷ μὲν [hotan ērina men] — — when indeed with spring Φωνῇ χελιδὼν [Phōnē chelidōn] voice the swallow Ἑζομένη κελαδῇ. [Hezomenē keladē.] sitting resounds.

Similar to which are these words of Stesichorus, as the Scholiast notes: Ὅταν ἦρος ὥρᾳ κελαδῇ χελιδών· [Hotan ēros hōra keladē chelidōn;] When the swallow shall resound in springtime. Nor are these words of Simonides in Athenaeus far off: Ἄγγελε κλυτὰ ἔαρος ἁδυόδμου κυανέα χελιδὼν [Angele klyta earos hadyodmou kyanea chelidōn], O famed messenger of sweet-scented spring, dark-blue swallow. And in Theognis, book 3, on the sacrifices of the Rhodians, the song which οἱ χελιδονίζοντες [hoi chelidonizontes] sang from door to door, that is, the beggar-minstrels who announced that the swallow had come (in Hesychius χελιδονισταὶ [chelidonistai]), begins thus: Ἦλθ', ἦλθε χελιδὼν καλὰς ὥρας ἄγουσα, καὶ καλοὺς ἐνιαυτοὺς, ἐπὶ γαστέρα λευκὰ κἀπὶ νῶτα μέλαινα· [Ēlth', ēlthe chelidōn kalas hōras agousa, kai kalous eniautous, epi gastera leuka kapi nōta melaina;] The swallow has come, has come, with white belly and black back, bringing fair seasons and fair years. See the rest there. Accordingly, as Theon writes on Aratus, the ancients painted the northern Fish with a swallow's head and called it ἰχθὺν χελιδόνιαν [ichthyn chelidonian], because by its rising it signified the prelude of spring. To the same point belong these words of Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 52: Χελιδὼν δ' ἄρα τῆς ὥρας τῆς ἀρίστης ὑποσημαίνει τὴν ἐπιδημίαν· [Chelidōn d' ara tēs hōras tēs aristēs hyposēmainei tēn epidēmian;] The swallow signals the arrival of the most beautiful season of the year. And Ovid, almost at the end of book 2 of the Fasti:
Am I deceived, or has the swallow, harbinger of spring, come?
And the swallow will have sung of spring's arrival from her nest.
— — in early spring, when the birds are already beginning to twitter, and the returning swallow plasters her nests with mud.
And an unknown poet among the Epigrams of the ancients, book 4:
The frisky kid and the chattering swallow announce springtime, and the bowl of milk, and the green grass. And in book 5, Avienus:
For when in early spring the hard earth loosens itself, and the swallow, winged one, chirps sweetly in the hollow rooftops.

But if only one or two swallows appear, the proverb of the Greeks is known from Aristotle, Ethics book 1, chapter 6: Μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ [mia chelidōn ear ou poiei], One swallow does not make a spring. Among us the swallow's stay is usually six months. Pliny, book 10, chapter 25: Birds differ greatly in their seasons. Some are perennial, like doves; some stay six months, like swallows; some three months, like thrushes and turtledoves. That is, swallows come at the beginning of spring and depart at the end of summer. Pliny on Arcturus, book 18, chapter 31: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows. Arcturus, moreover, rises in the month of September. Galen: Ἔστι μὲν ὡραιότατον τῆς ἐλάτης τὸ σπέρμα περὶ τὴν ἐπιτολὴν τοῦ Ἀρκτούρου, ὅστις καιρὸς ἐν Ῥώμῃ ὁ καλούμενος μὲν Σεπτέμβριός ἐστι [esti men hōraiotaton tēs elatēs to sperma peri tēn epitolēn tou Arktourou, hostis kairos en Rhōmē ho kaloumenos men Septembrios esti]. It is also around the autumn equinox. Theophrastus on the carob, History of Plants book 4, chapter 2: Ἀνθεῖ περὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ ἰσημερίαν [anthei peri Arktouron, kai isēmerian]; or (as Pliny says more explicitly, book 2, chapter 47) Arcturus rises eleven days before the equinox. So when swallows migrate is well enough established, but where they migrate is not likewise. Isidore says in general: (the swallow) flies across the seas and stays there. Anacreon, in the place cited above:
Χειμῶνι δ' εἷς ἄφαντος, Ἢ Νεῖλον, ἢ 'πὶ Μέμφιν. [cheimōni d' heis aphantos, ē Neilon, ē 'pi Memphin.] But in winter you are not seen, Whether you make for the Nile or Memphis.

Herodotus, book 2, chapter 22, on Ethiopia below Egypt: Ἰκτῖνοι δὲ, καὶ χελιδόνες δι' ἔτεος ἐόντες οὐκ ἀπολείπουσι [iktinoi de, kai chelidones di' eteos eontes ouk apoleipousi]; Kites and swallows are there the whole year round, and do not depart in winter. However that may be, among them it is a grave crime to desert the departing flock, if these lines of Martial, book 5, Epigram 68, are true:

When the Attic birds sought their winter retreats in their accustomed manner, one bird stayed behind in the nests: the crime was detected when they returned in springtime, and her own kind tore the deserter to pieces.

But those that remain also face no slight danger from the cold. Pliny, in the passage already cited on the star Arcturus: Let the sign of the rising of that star be observed in the departure of the swallows; for those caught behind perish. Yet it is certain that some remain in sunny places; not all of these die, but they are stripped bare and lose their feathers. Accordingly the Philosopher, History of Animals book 8, chapter 16, after teaching that kites and swallows betake themselves in winter to warmer places when these are not too far away, says: Οἱ δὲ ποῤῥοτέρω ὄντες τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἐκτοπίζουσι, ἀλλὰ κρύπτουσιν ἑαυτούς· ἤδη γὰρ ὠμμέναι εἰσὶ πολλαὶ χελιδόνες ἐν ἀγγείοις [hoi de porrhoterō ontes tōn toioutōn ouk ektopizousi, alla kryptousin heautous; ēdē gar ōmmenai eisi pollai chelidones en angeiois] (read ἐν ἄγκεσι [en ankesi], or ἐν ἀγκείαις [en ankeiais]) ἐψιλωμέναι πάμπαν [epsilōmenai pampan]; But the birds that are farther from such places do not migrate from there, but hide themselves: for many swallows have already been seen in valleys, completely featherless. And following him Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: (swallows) go off into neighbouring places, seeking the sunny recesses of the mountains, and have already been found there naked and featherless. To such a swallow Claudian compares the hairless, moth-eaten head of Eutropius, an already worn-out eunuch, in these words, book 1 Against Eutropius:
Or like the winter swallow that, its feathers falling in the icy frosts, dies upon the trunk of a tree.

But when the Prophet says that swallows know the time of their coming or their departure, it need not be understood of all of them without exception. It suffices that it holds for most, so that by this example we may be reminded how rightly Hesiod said:
— — καιρὸς δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος [kairos d' epi pasin aristos],
and one of the Seven Sages whom Greece celebrated: Καιρὸν γνῶθι [kairon gnōthi], Know the time. These are the very words of the sacred prophet.

I add one point: in the Greek copy of Tobit, chapter 2, verse 11, we read that τὰ στρουθία [ta strouthia], little birds, dropped dung into his eyes. Jerome rightly saw that this refers to swallows, and renders it thus: It happened that, as he slept, warm dung fell from a nest of swallows onto his eyes. For this is peculiar to the swallow: the mother herself either throws the droppings of the chicks out of the nest while they are small, or teaches them to void outside the nest when they are somewhat bigger. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 7: Καὶ κόπρον τὸ πρῶτον αὐταὶ ἐκβάλλουσιν· ὅταν δὲ αὐξηθῶσι μεταστρέφοντας ἔξω διδάσκουσι τοὺς νεοττοὺς προΐεσθαι [Kai kopron to prōton autai ekballousin; hotan de auxēthōsi metastrephontas exō didaskousi tous neottous proiesthai]. This is rendered by Pliny, book 10, chapter 33, as follows: With remarkable cleanliness they carry out the excrement of the chicks; and when these are older they teach them to turn round and discharge their fullness outside. Nor is this statement of the Arabs in Damir unlike it: ولا يلقي في عشه زبلا بل يلقيه الي خارج فانا اكبر فراخه علمها ذلك [wa-lā yulqī fī ʿushshihi ziblan bal yulqīhi ilā khārij fa-anā akbar firākhihi ʿallamahā dhālik] It does not void its dung into the nest but outside, and it teaches this very thing to its chicks when they have grown up. Something similar is recorded to have happened to Gorgias, for a swallow dropped dung on him. Plutarch, Table Talk, book 8, chapter 7: Γοργίας δὲ ὁ Σοφιστὴς, χελιδόνος ἀφείσης ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀπόπατον, ἀναβλέψας πρὸς αὐτὴν, Οὐ καλὰ ταῦτα (εἶπεν) ὦ Φιλομῆλα [Gorgias de ho Sophistēs, chelidonos apheisēs ep᾽ auton apopaton, anablepsas pros autēn, Ou kala tauta (eipen) ō Philomēla]· Gorgias the Sophist, when a swallow had let fall its dung on him, turned his eyes towards it and said, "This is not becoming , Philomela." The Philosopher praises this as an apt saying in the Rhetoric, book 3, chapter 3, because ὄρνιθι μὲν, εἰ ἐποίησεν, οὐκ αἰσχρὸν, παρθένῳ δὲ αἰσχρόν· εὖ οὖν ἐλοιδόρησεν, εἰπὼν ὃ ἦν ἀλλ᾽ οὐχ᾽ ὅ ἐστιν [ornithi men, ei epoiēsen, ouk aischron, parthenō de aischron; eu oun eloidorēsen, eipōn ho ēn all᾽ ouch ho estin], for a bird, if it had done it, it is not shameful, but for a maiden it is shameful. So he rebuked her well, saying what she had been, not what she then was. Nor should anyone be surprised that the swallow is given the name Philomela, although it is very commonly believed that Philomela is the nightingale. For the matter is uncertain, and many of the ancients state explicitly that Procne was changed into a nightingale and Philomela into a swallow. I could prove this without any trouble, if that were the subject at hand. But we now hasten to other matters.

Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses] (Beytrag zur Aufklär. des Dankliedes Hiskiae, in den Beyträgen zur Beförderung theologischer Kenntnisse, edited by J. A. Cramer, vol. 1, p. 60. 61. note) thinks that this difference in spelling arose because the ancient Hebrews lacked any fixed sign by which to express the sound mixed from u and i (ü), which is heard in Ssüs, סוס, and so used now the letter י, now ו.
Linn. Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 1019, 13th ed.

But because the swallow is called by the name סוס neither in the Arabic dialect nor in the Syriac, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in his Clavis in Iesaj., p. 216, denies that this word was used by the Hebrews to signify the swallow, and holds that it was used only of the horse. As if there were not many words peculiar to only one dialect or another! Cf. Velthusen on the Song of Hezekiah in the Symbolae Kilonienses, vol. 2, p. 325, note 51. Moreover, by what right the horse should be counted among the migratory birds in Jer 8:7, I can scarcely understand.
See Athenaeus, book 8, ch. 15, and Eustathius on the Odyssey, φ' [phi].

In the anatomy of the crane, Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes in book 4, chapter 1 of De Avibus that he observed something peculiar: namely, that the windpipe is arranged otherwise than in other birds. For, adhering to the breastbone, he says, it penetrates the flesh on both sides. And so it is no wonder that its voice is heard so far away. For no bird is as vocal as the crane. Hence Hezekiah, in his song of thanksgiving after he recovered from his illness , Es. XXXVIII, 14: כסיס עגור כן אצפצף, like sis and agor I chirped, that is, like the swallow and the crane; of these birds the one has a plaintive voice, the other a very strained one. Between sis and agor the copulative Vau is missing, as in Hab 3:11. שמש ירח עמד זבלה, sun, moon (that is, sun and moon) stood still in their place. And 1 Chr 2:1. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, for Reuben, and Simeon, and Levi. Thus Hezekiah's meaning is this: afflicted by grave illness, he not only moaned with a gentle murmur like a swallow, but also wailed with a strained voice like a crane. So the Talmudists in the tractate Kiddushin, ch. 2, fol. 44a: וצווח ר״ל ככורכיא, And Resh Lakish cried out like a crane. And Quintus of Smyrna, in book 3, on the lament of the Nereids at the death of Achilles,
— — — — ταί δ᾽ ἐφέροντο [tai d’ epheronto] Κλαγγηδὸν κραιπνῇσιν ἐειδόμεναι γεράνοισιν [klangēdon kraipnēsin eeidomenai geranoisin], Ὀσσόμεναι μέγα χεῖμα [Ossomenai mega cheima], — —
But they were borne along with clangor, like swift cranes that sense a great storm in advance. And in book 13, on the destruction of Troy,

— — στοναχὴ δὲ δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν [stonachē de daiktamenōn aizēōn] Ἔπλετο λευγαλέη, περὶ δ᾽ ἴαχε πάντα μέλαθρα [Epleto leugaleē, peri d’ iache panta melathra] Ἄσπετον· οἰμωγὴ δὲ πέλεν στονόεσσα γυναίκων [Aspeton; oimōgē de pelen stonoessa gynaikōn] Εἰδομένων γεράνοισιν, ὅτ᾽ αἰετὸν ἀθρήσωσιν [Eidomenōn geranoisin, hot’ aieton athrēsōsin]. Ὑψόθεν αἴσσοντα δι᾽ αἰθέρος, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τῇσι [Hypsothen aissonta di’ aitheros, oud’ ara tēsi] Θαρσαλέον στέρνοισι πέλει μένος, ἀλλὰ ἑ μοῦνον [Tharsaleon sternoisi pelei menos, alla he mounon] Μακρὸν ἀνατρύζουσι, φοβούμεναι ἱερὸν ὄρνιν [Makron anatryzousi, phoboumenai hieron ornin].

And the groaning of the slain young men was pitiful, and all the houses resounded dreadfully. And most mournful was the wailing of the women, like cranes when they see an eagle swooping from on high through the air. Nor does any brave strength remain in their breasts; they only shriek long, dreading the sacred bird of Jove. Homer too, comparing the battle cry of soldiers with the clangor of cranes at the beginning of book 3 of the Iliad,
Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ᾽ ἐνοπῇ τ᾽ ἴσαν ὄρνιθες ὥς [Trōes men klangē t’ enopē t’ isan ornithes hōs], Ἠΰτε περ κλαγγὴ γεράνων πέλει οὐρανόθι πρό [Ēute per klangē geranōn pelei ouranothi pro].
The Trojans went with clangor and clamor like birds, like the clangor of cranes up to the sky. Which Virgil imitated in book 10 of the Aeneid,

— — the Dardanians raise a shout to the stars from the walls, as beneath black clouds Strymonian cranes give their signals and swim through the air with noise, and flee the South Winds with favoring clamor.
And Martial, to indicate that the old woman Philaenis was not only talkative but also loud-voiced and Stentorian, in book 9, Epigram 30:

Alas, what a tongue is silent! A thousand slave-auction platforms could not outdo it, nor the throng that loves Serapis, nor the curly-haired troop of the morning schoolmaster, nor the bank that resounds with the Strymonian flock.
The following also pertain to the cry of cranes. Homer again, in the place cited above,
Κλαγγῇ ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων [Klangē tai ge petontai ep’ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn],
With clangor they fly toward the streams of Ocean. Hesiod in the Works,
Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖτ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης [Phrazesthai d’ eut’ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs], Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκλαγυίης [Hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklagyiēs],
Take heed when you hear the voice of the crane clangoring yearly from the clouds on high. Lucretius, book 4, verse 18:
As the small song of the swan is better than the clamor of cranes scattered among the ethereal clouds of the South Wind.
With great clamor the cranes leave their summer Thrace, when they exchange the Strymon for the warm Nile.

Accordingly Eustathius says the crane is a φωνητικὴν [phōnētikēn], vocal, bird. And it should be noted that most languages, in the very name of the bird, imitate its voice in some way. Thus the Hebrew עגור agor, the Chaldee כורכיא kurkeja, the Arabic كركي [kurkī] kurki and غرنوق [gharnūq] gurnuk , the Greek γέρανος [geranos], the Cambro-British garan, the German cran, the Roman grus are so many onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικαί [onomatopoiētikai]) words. Hence Isidore, Cranes took their name from their own voice. For they whisper with such a sound. And gruere is to clangor in the manner of cranes. Festus: Cranes are said gruere, as swine grunnire. The little poem On the Song of Philomela:
The crane cries gru, and the swans in flocks drensant near the rivers.

An old Glossary: Gruunt, γερανίζουσι [geranizousi]. Meanwhile, lest anyone think that cranes always clangor with a resounding voice, Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] says this of the crane that keeps watch while the rest sleep: والذي يحرس يهتف خافي كانه ينذر بانه جارس [wa-lladhī yaḥrus yahtif khāfī ka-annahu yundhir bi-annahu jāris] And the one on guard murmurs only in a low voice, as if it knew that it was on guard. This very thing might not absurdly be referred to the passage of Hezekiah, as though he joined this gentle murmur of the crane with the twittering of the swallow.

Now we shall treat the migration of cranes, with reference to Jer 8:7. The turtledove, and the swallow, and the crane have kept the time of their coming. In general it is agreed that the crane not only migrates elsewhere, but also travels to the most remote places to escape the cold. Symeon Seth [=Symeon Seth (11th c.), Syntagma de alimentorum facultatibus]: Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον πτηνὸν διέρχεται τὴν οἰκουμένην ἅπασαν, μὴ μένον ἐν ἑνὶ κλίματι [To de toiouton ptēnon dierchetai tēn oikoumenēn hapasan, mē menon en heni klimati]; This bird traverses the whole world, by no means staying in one region. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Ἐκτοπίζουσιν εἰς τὰ ἔσχατα ἐκ τῶν ἐσχάτων [Ektopizousin eis ta eschata ek tōn eschatōn]; They (the cranes) migrate from the farthest regions to the farthest. That is, as he himself explains, ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ [ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei], from the Scythian shores to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. He followed Herodotus, who, treating the sources of the Nile and the neighbouring Ocean in book 2, chapter 22, says: Γέρανοι δὲ φεύγουσαι τὸν χειμῶνα, τὸν ἐν τῇ Σκυθικῇ χώρῃ γενόμενον, φοιτῶσι εἰς χειμαδίην ἐς τοὺς τόπους τούτους [Geranoi de pheugousai ton cheimōna, ton en tē Skythikē chōrē genomenon, phoitōsi eis cheimadiēn es tous topous toutous]; Cranes, fleeing the winter of the Scythian region, betake themselves to those places to spend the winter. Aelian too, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 13: Εἰς Αἴγυπτόν τε, καὶ Λιβύην ἀπαίρουσι, καὶ Αἰθιόπιαν, ὥσπερ γὰρ οὖν γῆς περίοδον εἰδυῖαι, καὶ φύσεις ἀέρων, καὶ ὡρῶν διαφορὰς στέλλονται αἱ πᾶσαι [Eis Aigypton te, kai Libyēn apairousi, kai Aithiopian, hōsper gar oun gēs periodon eiduiai, kai physeis aerōn, kai hōrōn diaphoras stellontai hai pasai]; As though they knew the circuit of the earth, the nature of the sky and the variation of the seasons, they depart for Egypt, Libya and Ethiopia, and all set out. And Homer long before:
— — — ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων [tai ge petontai ep᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn],

These fly to the streams of Ocean, namely the southern Ocean, where the Pygmies are, as what follows shows. Hence Lucullus to Pompey in Plutarch: Εἶτά σοι δοκῶ ἐλάττονα τῶν γεράνων νοῦν ἔχειν, καὶ τῶν πελαργῶν, ὥς τε ταῖς ὥραις μὴ συμμεταβάλλειν τὰς διαίτας [Eita soi dokō elattona tōn geranōn noun echein, kai tōn pelargōn, hōs te tais hōrais mē symmetaballein tas diaitas]; Do I seem to you to have less sense than cranes and storks, so as not to change my abode with the seasons of the year?

The ancients believed that most of them are born in Thrace. Aelian, in the place cited above: Αἱ γέρανοι γίνονται μὲν ἐν Θράκῃ [Hai geranoi ginontai men en Thrakē]; Cranes are born in Thrace. And shortly after: Οὐκοῦν φιλοῦσι τὴν χώραν, ἐν ᾗ γεγόνασι [Oukoun philousi tēn chōran, en hē gegonasi]; They therefore love the region in which they were born. Hence they are called birds of Thrace, and Strymonian and Bistonian, from the Strymon, a river, and the Biston, a lake of Thrace, from which they are believed to set out. Virgil, Aeneid, book 10:
— — — as beneath the high clouds Strymonian cranes give their signals. — —
The Strymon is deserted, which is wont to commit the Bistonian birds to the warm Nile. — — — And book 5, line 711:
So, when winter drives them out, the cranes leave the icy Strymon, to drink of you, O Nile. — — — —
— — — you who are wont to exchange Thracian winters for the Nile. — — — —
Nor the bank that resounds with the Strymonian flock.
Not so many birds, fleeing the threats of the icy Strymon, exchange their winters, and, cleaving the sky, offset the Arctic snows with the warm Nile.
— — — — they leave Thrace in summer, when they exchange the Strymon for the warm Nile.
Antipater of Sidon, Anthology, book 3, chapter 16:
— — — — καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστονίαν γέρανον [kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]· — —

And warding off the high-flying Bistonian crane, plunderer of seed. When about to leave Thrace, they are said to gather at the river Hebrus. Aelian, book 2, chapter 1: Ὅταν τὰ ἤθη τὰ τῶν Θρακῶν καὶ τοὺς κρυμοὺς ἀπολείπωσι τοὺς Θρακίους αἱ γέρανοι, ἀθροίζονται μὲν ἐς τὸν Ἕβρον [Hotan ta ēthē ta tōn Thrakōn kai tous krymous apoleipōsi tous Thrakious hai geranoi, athroizontai men es ton Hebron]; When the cranes leave the abodes and the cold of the Thracians, they gather at the Hebrus. Tzetzes, Chiliad 4, Hist. 120:

Ὅταν γοῦν πρὸς τὸν Αἴγυπτον μέλλουσιν ἀποτρέχειν, Ὡς πρὸς τὸν Ἕβρον ποταμὸν τὸν Θρακικὸν ἐλθοῦσαι [Hotan goun pros ton Aigypton mellousin apotrechein, Hōs pros ton Hebron potamon ton Thrakikon elthousai]·
When they are about to fly off to Egypt, having come to the Hebrus, a river of Thrace.
But the Scythian cranes take another route, namely across the Pontus, which they fly over. Hence Virgil, Aeneid, book 6:
— — — as when many birds flock to land from the deep sea, when the cold season drives them across the Pontus and sends them to sunny lands.

And it is certain, says Pliny, that when they are about to fly across the Pontus, they first of all make for the narrows between the two promontories Criu-metopon and Carambis. These are only 170,000 paces apart, as he likewise asserts in book 4, chapter 12. Others indeed judge differently, namely that these two promontories are three days' sailing apart, or, what is nearly the same, 2,500 stadia. Dionysius Periegetes, line 155:
Αἵτ' ἄμφω ξυνίασιν ἐναντίαι, οὐ μὲν ἐοῦσαι Ἐγγύθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὅσον ὁλκὰς ἐπὶ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἀνύσσῃ [Hait' amphō xyniasin enantiai, ou men eousai Engythen, all᾽ hoson holkas epi triton ēmar anyssē].
So they come together facing each other, across so great a gulf Separated, as far as a ship could cross in three days. — — —

And Ammianus, book 22: Not far from there rises Carambis etc. Opposite which lies Criu-metopon, a promontory of the Taurica, separated from it by two thousand five hundred stadia. Strabo too, in book 2: Τὸ μὲν οὖν τῆς Εὐρώπης ἀκρωτήριον καλεῖται Κριοῦ μέτωπον, τὸ δὲ τῆς Ἀσίας Κάραμβις, διέχοντα ἀλλήλων περὶ δισχιλίους σαδίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους [To men oun tēs Eurōpēs akrōtērion kaleitai Kriou metōpon, to de tēs Asias Karambis, diechonta allēlōn peri dischilious sadious, kai pentakosious]· The promontory of Europe is called Criu-metopon (ram's forehead), and that of Asia Carambis, distant from each other about 2,500 stadia. These statements, however, are utterly false, and are openly refuted by Strabo's own words in book 3: Διέσηκε δὲ ἡ Κάραμβις τῆς μὲν τῶν Χερσονησιτῶν πόλεως σταδίους δισχιλίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους, τοῦ δὲ Κριοῦ μετώπου πολὺ ἐλάττους τὸν ἀριθμόν [Diesēke de hē Karambis tēs men tōn Chersonēsitōn poleōs stadious dischilious, kai pentakosious, tou de Kriou metōpou poly elattous ton arithmon]· Carambis is distant from the city of the Chersonesites by two thousand five hundred stadia, but from Criu-metopon by far less. Quite rightly: for Chersonesus the city is one thing, and Chersonesus the region, in which that city lies, another. The city, which is in the northern part of the Chersonese, is indeed 2,500 stadia distant from Carambis. But on the opposite side of the Chersonese, Criu-metopon is much nearer to Carambis. Yet these have been confused: what some had written about the city of Chersonesus, that it is 2,500 stadia from Carambis, was taken as if said of the whole Chersonese, and of its most southern part, namely Criu-metopon. The emptiness of this invention is especially apparent from what Strabo adds in the same place: Συχνοὶ γοῦν τῶν διαπλευσάντων τὸν πορθμὸν, ἅμα φασὶν ἀμφοτέρας ἰδεῖν τὰς ἄκρας ἑκατέρωθεν [Sychnoi goun tōn diapleusantōn ton porthmon, hama phasin amphoteras idein tas akras hekaterōthen]· Many of those who have sailed through this strait say that they saw both promontories at once, that is, when placed in the middle of the passage; which would not happen if the strait were 2,500 stadia wide. For the sight of the human eye is too weak to reach 1,250 stadia, which make more than 52 hourly leagues.

However that may be, the ancients relate that both in crossing this strait and on the rest of their journey the remarkable ingenuity of cranes shines forth. Pliny asserts that when about to fly across the Pontus they are steadied with ballast, and that when they have passed the middle, the pebbles are dropped from their feet, and when they have reached the mainland, the sand from their throat. That is, only then do they disgorge not pebbles but sand too. Solinus puts this more explicitly: Lest the force of the winds should resist them as they proceed to their destination, they swallow sand, and taking up little pebbles they ballast themselves to a moderate weight. And shortly after: When they know that they have come to the middle (of the Pontus), they free their feet of the load of stones. So sailors have reported, who have often been rained on by a shower of stones from this cause. The sand they do not disgorge until they are secure of their abode. Cassiodorus also mentions these pebbles, in Variae book 4, Letter 47: Cranes, when about to cross the sea, clasp small pebbles in their hooked feet, so that their lightness may not be carried off by too strong a wind, nor their native speed be weighed down by unequal burdens. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds, and Suidas following him, think that these pebbles are carried and thrown down by cranes for an entirely different reason: namely, so that from the sound of the falling stone they may perceive πότερον ἐπὶ γῆς, ἢ ἐπὶ θαλάσσης φέρωνται· καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ θαλάσσης ἥκοι ὁ λίθος ἀνύουσι τὴν ὁδόν· εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς, ἀναπαύονται [poteron epi gēs, ē epi thalassēs pherōntai; kai ei men epi thalassēs hēkoi ho lithos anyousi tēn hodon; ei de epi gēs, anapauontai], whether they are borne over land or over sea; if the stone falls into the sea, they continue on; but if onto land, they rest. But Maximus of Tyre, Oration 40, asserts that cranes carry this stone in their mouth as ballast. Οὐ πρότερον, he says, ἀνίπταται, πρὶν ξυλλάβῃ λίθον τῷ στόματι, ἕρμα μὲν εἶναι αὐτῇ πρὸς τὴν πτῆσιν, φυλακὴν δὲ πρὸς σωτηρίαν [Ou proteron … anuptatai, prin xyllabē lithon tō stomati, herma men einai autē pros tēn ptēsin, phylakēn de pros sōtērian]· It does not fly before it has taken up a stone in its beak, to be a support for its flight and a safeguard for its safety. Nor otherwise Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 40, line 521:

Αἱ στομάτων ἔκτοσθεν ἀοσσητῆρα κελεύθου Λᾶαν ἐλαφρίζουσι καταχθέα, μήποτε κείνων Ἱπταμένων πτερὰ κοῦφα παρακλάγξειεν ἀήτης. [Hai stomatōn ektosthen aossētēra keleuthou / Laan elaphrizousi katachthea, mēpote keinōn / Hiptamenōn ptera koupha paraklangxeien aētēs.]

Which carry in their mouth a heavy stone as a helper on their way, lest the wind should ever make the light wings of them as they fly go astray. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 10:

Τίς ἕρμα ποιεῖ τῇσι γεράνοις τὰς λίθους, Ἃς ἐγκαθειργνύουσι τοῖς παρισθμίοις, Πρὸς τὰς ὑπὲρ γῆς ἐμβολὰς τῶν πνευμάτων; [Tis herma poiei tēsi geranois tas lithous, / Has enkatheirgnyousi tois paristhmiois, / Pros tas hyper gēs embolas tōn pneumatōn?]

Who has made the cranes carry stones as ballast, which they hold in their throats against the onslaughts of the winds that are upon the earth? They wrongly read ἀμβολάς [ambolas]. For this is taken from these words of Aelian: Λίθον δὲ ἑκάστη καταπιοῦσα, ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα, πειρῶνται τοῦ μετοικισμοῦ· [Lithon de hekastē katapiousa, hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma, peirōntai tou metoikismou] Each one, having swallowed a stone to serve both as a meal and as ballast against the onslaughts of the winds, sets out on its migration. Others keep saying that this stone is a touchstone for gold. The same Aelian, book 3, chapter 13: Γέρανος δὲ λίθον ὅνπερ οὖν καταπίνει πετομένη ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἔχειν ἕρμα, χρυσοῦ βάσανός ἐστιν· [Geranos de lithon honper oun katapinei petomenē hyper tou echein herma, chrysou basanos estin] The stone which the crane swallows as ballast when about to fly is a touchstone for gold. Accordingly Philes calls them

Λίθους κριτικὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ τοῖς ἐμπόροις [Lithous kritikas tou chrysou tois emporois], stones that test gold for merchants. But Aristotle refutes this fiction as follows, History of Animals, book 8, chapter 12: Τὸ δὲ περὶ τοῦ λίθου ψεῦδός ἐστι· λέγεται γὰρ ὡς ἔχουσιν ἕρμα λίθον, ὃς γίνεται χρήσιμος πρὸς τὰς τοῦ χρυσοῦ βασάνους, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ. [To de peri tou lithou pseudos esti; legetai gar hōs echousin herma lithon, hos ginetai chrēsimos pros tas tou chrysou basanous, hotan ekpesē.] What they tell about the stone is false: namely, that they carry a stone as ballast which, when it has fallen out, is useful for testing gold. But if this is a fiction, perhaps what follows now will be truer.

There is among them a wonderful harmony and agreement, a wonderful concord of minds. Pliny: When they set out, they agree together. Solinus: All share a common care for the weary, so that, if any have failed, they all gather together and lift up the exhausted ones, until their strength is recovered by rest. Note here the verb congruere [to come together], taken from cranes: it is properly used of cranes, and from them transferred to other things. Festus: Congruere is said from cranes, which do not separate from one another, whether they are flying or feeding. So also ingruere means to rush upon in a great host like cranes. From this it was transferred to soldiers, to rain, to hail and to other things. And in Solinus we read fluctus ingrui [waves rushing in].
Not without reason does Oppian speak of
the high-flying chorus of cranes; and Antipater of Sidon
spoke of the high-flying Bistonian crane. And Virgil:
that is, as Servius explains, flying on high. And Ausonius in the Monosyllables:
When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was the informer.
And the crane says of itself in Avienus, Fable 15:
— — — Lofty on my wing into the air I am borne, next to the stars and the gods.

For cranes fly on high, attentive to every change of the air, so as not to be overwhelmed by a storm. Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, ch. 10: Εἰς ὕψος πέτονται πρὸς τὸ καθορᾶν τὰ πόῤῥω, καὶ ἐὰν ἴδωσι νέφη, καὶ χειμέρια [Eis hypsos petontai pros to kathoran ta porrhō, kai ean idōsi nephē, kai cheimeria] (Antigonus has καὶ συστροφὴν [kai systrophēn]) καταπτᾶσαι ἡσυχάζουσιν· [kataptasai hēsychazousin] They fly on high in order to see far ahead; and if they see clouds and stormy weather (or a whirlwind), they fly down and stay quiet. Accordingly it is among the signs of a coming storm when a sailor in mid-sea sees γεράνους ὑποστρεφούσας, καὶ τὴν ἔμπαλιν πετομένας [geranous hypostrephousas, kai tēn empalin petomenas], cranes turning back and flying in the opposite direction. So Aelian, History, book 3, chapter 14. You may see similar statements in Aratus, Virgil, Pliny, Theon and Avienus. But cranes also strive toward the greatest heights, so that from a loftier watchtower they may survey the lands they are heading for. So Solinus and Isidore. They also seem to strive for the heights because the air is calmer there, as Horus attests in these words, book 2, ch. 93: Ὑψηλῶς πάνυ ἵπτάται (γέρανος) ἵνα θεάσηται τὰ νέφη, μὴ ἄρα χειμάζῃ, ἵνα ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ διαμένῃ· [Hypsēlōs pany hiptatai (geranos) hina theasētai ta nephē, mē ara cheimazē, hina en hēsychia diamenē] The crane flies very high in order to observe the clouds, so that it may not be tossed by a storm but remain at rest. Finally, Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] gives this fourth reason: فاذا طارت ترفعت في الهوا جدا كي لا يعرض لها شي من السباع الطير [fa-idhā ṭārat taraffaʿat fī al-hawā jiddan kay lā yaʿriḍ lahā shay min al-sibāʿ al-ṭayr] And when it flies aloft, it rises very high, so that none of the birds of prey may meet it.

In flight itself the flock has the form of a triangle, which, driven at its base by the winds, cuts the air with its apex. Cicero, book 2 On the Nature of the Gods: "This too was observed by Aristotle: that cranes, when they cross the seas seeking warmer regions, form the shape of a triangle. With its apex the air in front of them is pushed aside. Then gradually, on either side, the course of the birds is borne up by their wings as by oars. And the base of the triangle which the cranes form is helped by the winds, as if from the stern." Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Εἰς τρίγωνον συνάγουσαι σχίζουσι τῇ κορυφῇ τὸ πνεῦμα περιῤῥέον, ὥστε μὴ διασπᾶσθαι τὴν τάξιν· [Eis trigōnon synagousai schizousi tē koryphē to pneuma perirrheon, hōste mē diaspasthai tēn taxin] "Gathered into a triangle, they cut with its apex the wind flowing around them, so that their line is not broken up." Aelian, book 13, ch. 13: Τρίγωνον ὀξύγονον τὸ σχῆμα τῆς πτήσεως ἀποφαίνουσι, ἵνα ἐμπίπτουσαι τῷ ἀέρι διακόπτωσιν αὐτόν· [Trigōnon oxygonon to schēma tēs ptēseōs apophainousi, hina empiptousai tō aeri diakoptōsin auton] "They shape their flight into an acute-angled triangle, so that, striking into the air, they may cut it more easily." Philes also asserts that they fly
Εἰς ὀρμαθὸν τρίστοιχον ὀξυγωνίου, [Eis hormathon tristoichon oxygōniou]
"in a three-sided formation with acute angles." And Tzetzes:
Τρίγωνον ὀξυγώνιον ποιοῦνται τούτων πτῆσιν, [Trigōnon oxygōnion poiountai toutōn ptēsin] Ὡς τὸν ἀέρα τέμνωσιν οὕτως εὐμαρεστέρως, [Hōs ton aera temnōsin houtōs eumaresterōs]

"They make their flight an acute-angled triangle, so that they may thus divide the air more easily." Indeed, by this triangular figure they are thought to imitate certain letters, namely A, V, Δ, Λ, Υ. Hence Jerome, Epist. 4 to Rusticus: "Cranes follow one leader in a lettered order." So too Isidore. This sheds light on these lines of Lucan on cranes, book 5, line 712:

— — — and in their first flight they form various figures, as chance directs; soon, when Notus strikes their outstretched wings from higher up, they are heedlessly mingled and massed into confused circles, and the letter, thrown into disorder, perishes as their feathers scatter.
You will throw the lines into disorder, and the letter will not fly whole, if you lose a single bird of Palamedes.
And on the name of Earinus, book 9, Epigram 14:
Which cranes, with writing wing, raise to the stars.
And Symphosius, Riddle 36, where the crane says:
I am a letter of the sky, written out by a flying wing.
I would prefer perscripta volante [written out by (me) flying]. And Claudian, in The Gildonic War, where he speaks of cranes:
In varied ranks a huge letter is woven across the clouds, and the air is inscribed with the marks of their wings.

And Cassiodorus, Variae book 8, Epistle 12: "For even today cranes, which form a fleet together, trace the shapes of the alphabet, nature instructing them." And in Philostratus' Heroicus, Ulysses, seeing cranes flying in their usual manner, looked at Palamedes and said: Αἱ γέρανοι, ἔφη, μαρτύρονται τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς, ὅτι αὗται γράμματα εὗρον, οὐχὶ σύ· [Hai geranoi, ephē, martyrontai tous Achaious, hoti hautai grammata heuron, ouchi sy] "The cranes," he said, "testify to the Greeks that they, not you, invented letters." I would read τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς [tois Achaiois], not τοὺς Ἀχαιούς [tous Achaious]. And Nazianzen, Oration 34: Τίνος Παλαμήδους τακτικὰ, κινήματά τε, καὶ σχήματα γεράνων, ὡς πᾶσι, καὶ ταῦτα παιδεύματα, κινουμένων ἐν τάξει, καὶ μετὰ ποικίλης τῆς πτήσεως; [Tinos Palamēdous taktika, kinēmata te, kai schēmata geranōn, hōs pasi, kai tauta paideumata, kinoumenōn en taxei, kai meta poikilēs tēs ptēseōs] "Of what Palamedes are the ordered movements, figures and precepts of the cranes, by which, as they say, they move in battle line with varied flight?" The same birds, when an eagle is sighted, κολπωσάμεναι, μηνοειδὲς τὸ μέσον ἀποφήνασαι, ἀπειλοῦσιν ὡς ἀντιταξόμεναι, [kolpōsamenai, mēnoeides to meson apophēnasai, apeilousin hōs antitaxomenai] "opening a hollow so that they imitate the appearance of the crescent moon, threaten as if about to resist"; and the eagle retreats and checks its flight.

They have leaders at the head of the column and οὐραγοὺς [ouragous] at the rear, whom the Philosopher describes as ἐπισυρίττοντας ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις, ὥστε ἀκούεσθαι τὴν φωνὴν [episyrittontas en tois eschatois, hōste akouesthai tēn phōnēn], whistling among the hindmost, so that their voice can be heard. Hence Pliny: They choose a leader to follow. At the rear of the column they have birds posted to call out in turn and to keep the flock together with their voice. And Solinus: Confident of its course, it goes before the flocks and rebukes sluggishness in flight with its voice, which keeps the column together. When that voice has grown hoarse, another takes its place. Aelian asserts that the older birds, experienced in the routes, are ἡγεμόνας τῆς πτήσεως [hēgemonas tēs ptēseōs], leaders of the flight, and that they οὐραγεῖν [ouragein], that is, command the rear of the column, while the younger ones are in the middle. Especially remarkable is the way they help one another in flight. Cicero: They rest their necks and heads on the backs of those flying in front. Because the leader himself cannot do this, since he has nothing to lean on, he flies back so that he too may rest. His place is taken by the nearest of those that have been resting, and this alternation is kept up throughout the whole journey. Basil, Hexaëmeron, Homily 8: Ἄλλό τε γὰρ ἄλλη τὴν ὁδηγίαν ἐκδέχεται, καὶ τακτόν τινα χρόνον προκαθηγησαμένη τῆς πτήσεως, εἰς τὸ κατόπιν περιελθοῦσα, τῇ μεθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν τὴν ἡγεμονίαν τῆς ὁδοῦ παραδίδωσι [Allo te gar allē tēn hodēgian ekdechetai, kai takton tina chronon prokathēgēsamenē tēs ptēseōs, eis to katopin perielthousa, tē meth᾽ heautēn tēn hēgemonian tēs hodou paradidōsi]. Hence Ambrose, Hexaëmeron, book 5, chapter 15: One goes before the rest for a set time and, as it were, runs ahead of the standards; then it turns back and yields the office of leading the column to the one following. Cassiodorus, book 9, Letter 2: Their flight, too, is arranged by an equal alternation: the last becomes first, and the one that held first place does not refuse to be behind. Damir the Arab: يقدمها واحد منها كالرايس لها وهي [yuqaddimuhā wāḥid minhā ka-l-rāyis lahā wa-hiya] تتبعه ويكون ذلك حينا ثم يخلفه اخر منها مقدما حتي يصير الذي كان مقدما موخرا [tatbaʿuhu wa-yakūnu dhālika ḥīnan thumma yakhlufuhu ākhar minhā muqaddaman ḥattā yaṣīra alladhī kāna muqaddaman muʾakhkharan] One of them goes ahead, acting as leader, and the others follow, and this for a time. Then another from their number takes its place, until the one that had been first becomes last.

The same alternation is observed in keeping watch. For when, tired from flying, they come down to the ground to rest and sleep, while the rest sleep, one or two, or a few out of the whole number, keep watch in turn over the entire flock. Aristotle, book 9, ch. 10: Ὅταν δὲ καθίζωνται, αἱ μὲν ἄλλαι, ὑπὸ τῇ πτέρυγι τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχουσαι, καθεύδουσιν ἐπὶ ἑνὸς ποδὸς ἐναλλάξ, ὁ δὲ ἡγεμὼν γυμνὴν ἔχων τὴν κεφαλὴν προορᾷ, καὶ ὅταν αἴσθηταί τι, σημαίνει βοῶν [Hotan de kathizōntai, hai men allai, hypo tē pterygi tēn kephalēn echousai, katheudousin epi henos podos enallax, ho de hēgemōn gymnēn echōn tēn kephalēn proora, kai hotan aisthētai ti, sēmainei boōn], When they settle, the others sleep with the head hidden under the wing, standing on one foot and then the other. But the leader (that is, the watchman) looks out with his head uncovered, and signals by his voice what he has perceived. Antigonus follows the same in the Mirabilia, ch. 46, and so does Alkazuinius with the Auctarium: واذا ارادت النوم ادخل كل واحد راسه تحت جناحها لعلمها ان الجناح احمل للصدمة من الراس لما فيه من العين التي هي اشرف الاعضا والدماغ الذي هو ملاك البدن ونام كل واحد منها قايما علي احدي رجليه حتي لا يكون نومها ثقيل واما قايدها وحارسها فلا ينام ولا يدخل راسه في جناحه ولا يزال ينظر من جميع الجوانب فان احس باحد صاح باعلا صوته فاخبر اصحابه بالعدو [wa-idhā arādat al-nawm adkhala kull wāḥid raʾsahu taḥt janāḥihā li-ʿilmihā anna al-janāḥ aḥmal li-l-ṣadma min al-raʾs li-mā fīhi min al-ʿayn allatī hiya ashraf al-aʿḍā wa-l-dimāgh alladhī huwa milāk al-badan wa-nāma kull wāḥid minhā qāyiman ʿalā iḥdā rijlayhi ḥattā lā yakūn nawmuhā thaqīl wa-ammā qāyiduhā wa-ḥārisuhā fa-lā yanām wa-lā yudkhil raʾsahu fī janāḥihi wa-lā yazāl yanẓur min jamīʿ al-jawānib fa-in aḥassa bi-aḥad ṣāḥa bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi fa-akhbara aṣḥābahu bi-l-ʿaduww] When they wish to sleep, they put their heads under their wings, because they know that the wings bear a blow better than the head, in which is the eye, the noblest of the parts, and the brain, on which the rest of the body depends. They sleep, moreover, standing on one foot, so that their sleep may not be heavy. But the one who is leader and guard abstains from sleep and does not hide his head under his wings. Rather, he continually looks out on every side. And if he perceives anyone, he cries out with a loud voice to signal to his companions that an enemy is near. Others add two further points. The first is that cranes keep watch in turn. Horus, book 2, ch. 90: Αὗται γὰρ ἑαυτὰς φυλάττουσι γρηγοροῦσαι κατ᾽ ὄρδινον ἐν πάσῃ τῇ νυκτί [Hautai gar heautas phylattousi grēgorousai kat᾽ ordinon en pasē tē nykti]. They guard themselves, keeping watch in order through the whole night. Solinus: They divide the night watches, so that every tenth one is sleepless. Isidore: At night they divide the watches, and keep the order of the vigils by turns. Cassiodorus: They watch in turn, and guard themselves by common caution. Basil: Τοῦ καιροῦ τῆς φυλακῆς πληρομένου, ἡ μὲν βοήσασα πρὸς ὕπνον ἐτράπετο. ἡ δὲ τὴν διαδοχὴν ὑποδεξαμένη, ἧς ἔτυχεν ἀσφαλείας, ἀντέδωκεν ἐν τῷ μέρει [Tou kairou tēs phylakēs plēromenou, hē men boēsasa pros hypnon etrapeto. hē de tēn diadochēn hypodexamenē, hēs etychen asphaleias, antedōken en tō merei]. Ambrose expands this as follows: When the time of the watch has been completed, having discharged its duty it settles down to sleep after first giving a cry, so as to wake the sleeper to whom it is to hand over its turn of duty. And that one willingly takes up its lot, and does not, as is our habit, renounce sleep unwillingly and sluggishly. Rather, it briskly shakes itself from its bed, performs its turn, and repays the favour it received with equal care and service. And Damir: في طبعه الخوف والتحارس بالنوبة فاذا قضي نوبتة قام الذي كان نايما يحرس مكانه حتي تقضي كله ما يلزمها من الحراسة [fī ṭabʿihi al-khawf wa-l-taḥārus bi-l-nawba fa-idhā qaḍā nawbatahu qāma alladhī kāna nāyiman yaḥrus makānahu ḥattā taqḍī kulluhu mā yalzamuhā min al-ḥirāsa] It is in its nature to be fearful and to keep guard by turns. And when one has completed its turn, one of those that were sleeping rises to keep watch in its place, until all have kept the watches incumbent on them. The second is that the watchmen carry a stone in the foot, which by its fall wakes them when asleep or about to fall asleep. Pliny: They keep watches at night, holding a pebble in the foot, which, loosened by sleep and falling, betrays their negligence. Solinus: The watchmen grasp small weights in their toes, which, if they should happen to fall, betray sleep. Plutarch: Αἱ προφυλακὴν ἔχουσαι νυκτὸς, ἐπὶ θατέρου σκέλους ὀχοῦνται τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δ᾽ ἑτέρῳ ποδὶ λίθον περιλαβοῦσαι κρατοῦσι· συνέχει γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἀφῆς τόνος ἐν τῷ μὴ καθεύδειν πολὺν χρόνον. Ὅταν δὲ ἀνῶσιν, ἐκπεσὼν ὁ λίθος ταχὺ διήγειρε τὴν προεμένην [Hai prophylakēn echousai nyktos, epi thaterou skelous ochountai to sōma, tō d᾽ heterō podi lithon perilabousai kratousi; synechei gar ho tēs haphēs tonos en tō mē katheudein polyn chronon. Hotan de anōsin, ekpesōn ho lithos tachy diēgeire tēn proemenēn]. Those that keep watch at night support the body on one of their legs, and hold a pebble grasped in the other foot. The effort of gripping holds off sleep for some time. But as soon as they relax, the falling stone at once wakes the negligent one. Aelian [III, 13.]: Ἑστᾶσι μὲν ἀσκωλιάζουσαι, τῷ γε μὲν μετεώρῳ ποδὶ λίθον κατέχουσι τοῖς ὄνυξι μάλα ἐγκρατῶς τε καὶ εὐλαβῶς· ἵνα ἐάν ποτε λάθωσιν ἑαυτὰς εἰς ὕπνον ὑπολισθαίνουσαι, πεσὼν καὶ ὑποκτυπήσας ὁ λίθος, ἀποδαρθάνειν καταναγκάσῃ [Hestasi men askōliazousai, tō ge men meteōrō podi lithon katechousi tois onyxi mala enkratōs te kai eulabōs; hina ean pote lathōsin heautas eis hypnon hypolisthainousai, pesōn kai hypoktypēsas ho lithos, apodarthanein katanankasē]. They rest on one foot only, and in the other, which is raised, they hold a pebble with their claws very firmly and with the greatest care, so that, if sleep should ever steal upon them, the falling pebble may wake them with its noise. Philes and Tzetzes say the same. Accordingly, when Aelian says that cranes swallow pebbles ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα [hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma], so as to have them both for a meal and as ballast against the onslaught of the winds, one should consider whether instead of δεῖπνον [deipnon] we ought to read δι᾽ ὕπνον [di᾽ hypnon], on account of sleep. For that pebbles should serve cranes as a meal is quite absurd. But perhaps Aelian meant that stones are swallowed by cranes not only to serve as ballast when they are about to fly across the Pontus, but also so that, once the sea has been crossed, they may be vomited up and serve to ward off sleep in the manner we have described.

The battles of the cranes with the Pygmies near the southern Ocean and the sources of the Nile, about which many writers since Homer have spun many tales, we gladly pass over. Yet the Philosopher asserts that in that fable at least this much is true, that very small men live in those places, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Μεταβάλλουσιν, he says, αἱ γέρανοι ἐκ τῶν Σκυθικῶν εἰς τὰ ἕλη τὰ ἄνω τῆς Αἰγύπτου, ὅθεν ὁ Νεῖλος ῥεῖ. Ἔστι δὲ ὁ τόπος οὗτος, περὶ ὃν οἱ Πυγμαῖοι κατοικοῦσιν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι τοῦτο μῦθος, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν γένος μικρὸν μὲν, ὥσπερ λέγεται, καὶ αὐτοὶ, καὶ οἱ ἵπποι. Τρωγλοδύται δ᾽ εἰσὶ τὸν βίον. [Metaballousin hai geranoi ek tōn Skythikōn eis ta helē ta anō tēs Aigyptou, hothen ho Neilos rhei. Esti de ho topos houtos, peri hon hoi Pygmaioi katoikousin. Ou gar esti touto mythos, all᾽ esti kata tēn alētheian genos mikron men, hōsper legetai, kai autoi, kai hoi hippoi. Trōglodytai d᾽ eisi ton bion.] From the Scythian regions the cranes migrate to the marshes that lie above Egypt, whence the Nile flows. Around this place the Pygmies live. For this is no fable; in truth, as they say, there is a small race there, both of men and of horses. They lead a Troglodyte life, that is, they live in caves under the earth. Everyone knows that the true sources of the Nile were entirely unknown to the ancients. Here, therefore, by the name Nile is meant the Astaboras, which the ancients believed to be a branch of the Nile, as we have shown elsewhere. The Astaboras rises in places nearest to the Avalites gulf and the trading-post of Mosylon. That is why Aethicus places the sources of the Nile there: And the river Nile, he says, which seems to emerge from the shore of the beginning of the Red Sea, in the place called the Mossylon trading-post. And indeed Nonnosus, sailing about these places on his way from the Homerites to the Axumites, Ἐνέτυχέ τισι μορφὴν μὲν καὶ ἰδέαν ἔχουσιν ἀνθρωπίνην, βραχυτάτοις δὲ τὸ μέγεθος, καὶ μέλασι τὴν χρόαν· ὑπὸ δὲ τριχῶν δεδασυμμένοις διὰ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος· εἵποντο δὲ τοῖς ἀνδράσι καὶ γυναῖκες παραπλήσιαι, καὶ παιδάρια ἔτι βραχύτερα. [Enetyche tisi morphēn men kai idean echousin anthrōpinēn, brachytatois de to megethos, kai melasi tēn chroan; hypo de trichōn dedasymmenois dia pantos tou sōmatos; heiponto de tois andrasi kai gynaikes paraplēsiai, kai paidaria eti brachytera.] came upon certain people, human indeed in form and shape, but very short in stature, black in colour, and hairy over the whole body. The men were followed by women of nearly the same size, and by children still shorter. So Photius in the Excerpts from the history of Nonnosus, who lived under Justinian. Moreover, in Hesychius Νῶβαι [Nōbai] are Πυγμαῖοι [Pygmaioi]: the Nobae, that is, the Nubae, who live in those places. And Strabo, book 17, on the Ethiopians below Egypt: τά τε βοσκήματα αὐτοῖς ἐστι μικρὰ πρόβατα, καὶ αἶγες, καὶ βόες, καὶ κύνες μικροί· τραχεῖς δὲ καὶ μάχιμοι οἰκοῦντες μικροὶ ὄντες. Τάχα δὲ τοὺς Πυγμαίους ἀπὸ τῆς τούτων μικροφυΐας ἐπενόησαν καὶ ἀνέπλασαν· ἑωρακὼς μὲν γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐξηγεῖται τῶν πίστεως ἀξίων ἀνδρῶν. [ta te boskēmata autois esti mikra probata, kai aiges, kai boes, kai kynes mikroi; tracheis de kai machimoi oikountes mikroi ontes. Tacha de tous Pygmaious apo tēs toutōn mikrophyias epenoēsan kai aneplasan; heōrakōs men gar oudeis exēgeitai tōn pisteōs axiōn andrōn.] Their livestock are small sheep and goats, oxen too, and small dogs. The inhabitants themselves are also tiny, yet rough and warlike. And perhaps on account of their natural smallness (the ancients of those parts) invented the Pygmies. For no one worthy of credit has seen them. That is, Pygmies such as they are imagined to be, three spans tall, such as not even Homer had described. But this invention has as its authors the most fabulous of writers, Megasthenes and Daimachus, of whom Strabo says in book 2: Ἐνεκαίνισαν δὲ καὶ τὴν Ὁμηρικὴν τῶν Πυγμαίων γερανομαχίαν τρισπιθάμους εἴποντες· [Enekainisan de kai tēn Homērikēn tōn Pygmaiōn geranomachian trispithamous eipontes;] They embellished the Homeric battle of the Pygmies with the cranes, saying that they were three spans tall. The Arabs too report the same on the word of a certain little Greek, who is said to have told it thus to Jacob, son of Isaac, of Siraf: ركبت في بحر الزنج والقتني الريح الي بعض الجزاير فوصلت منها الي مدينة اهلها ناس قاماتهم قدم نراع واكثرهم عور فاجتمع علي منهم جمع وانتهوا بي الي ملكهم فامر بحبسي فحبست في شبه قفص ثم رايتهم في بعض الايام يستعدون القتال وقالوا لنا عدو ياتينا في هذا الاوان فلم يلبث الي ان طلعت عليهم عصابة من الغرانيق وكان عورهم من نقرها اعينهم فاخذت عصي وشددت عليها وهربت واكرموني لذلك [rakibtu fī baḥr al-Zanj wa-alqatnī al-rīḥ ilā baʿḍ al-jazāyir fa-waṣaltu minhā ilā madīna ahluhā nās qāmātuhum qadm nrāʿ wa-aktharuhum ʿūr fa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayya minhum jamʿ wa-intahaw bī ilā malikihim fa-amara bi-ḥabsī fa-ḥubistu fī shibh qafaṣ thumma raʾaytuhum fī baʿḍ al-ayyām yastaʿiddūn al-qitāl wa-qālū lanā ʿaduww yaʾtīnā fī hādhā al-awān fa-lam yalbath ilā an ṭalaʿat ʿalayhim ʿiṣāba min al-gharānīq wa-kāna ʿawaruhum min naqrihā aʿyunahum fa-akhadhtu ʿaṣā wa-shadadtu ʿalayhā wa-harabat wa-akramūnī li-dhālik] I was once sailing on the Zanj sea, and the wind drove me to a certain island. When I reached its town, I found the inhabitants to be a cubit tall, and most of them one-eyed. A crowd of them gathered around me and led me to their king. He ordered that I be held captive, and I was thrown into a kind of cage. When one day I saw them preparing for war, they said that an enemy was threatening and would soon fall upon them. Not long after, an army of cranes rose up against them. And they were one-eyed because the cranes had pecked out their eyes. But I took a stick and charged at them, and they flew off and fled. For this deed I was held in honour among them.

The Philosopher (Hist. book 8, ch. 12) writes that cranes migrate from Thrace τοῦ Μαιμακτηριῶνος [tou Maimaktēriōnos], in the month Maemacterion; and Aelian, book 3, ch. 13, Φθινοπώρου ἤδη μεσοῦντος [Phthinopōrou ēdē mesountos], in mid-autumn. This strongly confirms what Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] maintained against Gaza, and Samuel Petit against Petavius in his Eclogae chronologicae, book 4: that among the Attic months Maemacterion is not the first but the second of the autumn months. Aelian defines the time of their return thus: Ὅταν ὑπεύδια ἄρξηται, καὶ εἰρηναῖα τοῦ ἀέρος ὑποστρέφουσιν ὀπίσω [Hotan hypeudia arxētai, kai eirēnaia tou aeros hypostrephousin opisō]; when the fair weather begins and the calm of the air returns, they come back. And Maximus of Tyre: Αἱ γέρανοι ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ὥραθέρους ἀφισάμεναι, οὐκ ἀνεχόμεναι τὸ θάλπος, τείνασαι πτέρυγας ὥσπερ ἱςία, φέρονται διὰ τοῦ ἀέρος εὐθὺ τῶν Σκυθῶν γῆς [Hai geranoi ex Aigyptou hōratherous aphisamenai, ouk anechomenai to thalpos, teinasai pterygas hōsper histia, pherontai dia tou aeros euthy tōn Skythōn gēs]; The cranes, departing from Egypt in summer because they cannot endure the heat, spread their wings like sails and are carried straight through the air to the Scythian region. Accordingly Pliny calls them summer visitors. I take this in such a way that under the name of summer I also understand spring. On these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 10,
Ἁ αἶξ τὸν κύτισον, ὁ λύκος τὰν αἶγα διώκει, Ἁ γέρανος τ᾽ ὤροτρον, — — — [Ha aix ton kytison, ho lykos tan aiga diōkei, Ha geranos t᾽ ōrotron]

The goat follows the clover, the wolf the goat, the crane the plough, the Scholiast says: Ἀρχομένου γὰρ σπόρου αἱ γέρανοι φαίνονται [Archomenou gar sporou hai geranoi phainontai], For cranes appear at the beginning of sowing. This I do not understand, since cranes do not arrive at sowing time but depart. For the migration of cranes falls in autumn, which is the customary time of sowing. Virgil, Georgics book 1:
When Libra has made the hours of day and sleep equal, and now divides the globe in the middle between light and shade, work your bulls, men, sow barley in the fields.

On these words Servius says: He says that grain is to be sown in the autumn season. So the Greekling who wrote these Scholia is talking nonsense. Aristophanes is therefore διαῤῥήδην [diarrhēdēn] opposed to him. For in the Birds he bids us
Σπείρειν μὲν ὅταν γέρανος κρώζουσ᾽ ἐς τὴν Λιβύην μεταχωρῇ, [Speirein men hotan geranos krōzous᾽ es tēn Libyēn metachōrē]
Sow when the crane migrates, crying, to Libya. The Scholiast notes that this is taken from Hesiod's Works, line 446:

Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖ τ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης, Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκληγυίης, Ἡτ᾽ ἀρότοιό τε σῆμα φέρει, καὶ χείματος ὥρην Δεικνύει ὀμβρηροῦ· — — — [Phrazesthai d᾽ eu t᾽ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs, Hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklēgyiēs, Hēt᾽ arotoio te sēma pherei, kai cheimatos hōrēn Deiknyei ombrērou]
Take heed when you hear the voice of the migrating crane, crying every year from on high in the clouds, which gives the signal for ploughing and shows the season of rainy winter.

From what has been said about the migration of cranes it is clear that the Prophet not without reason sets them forth as an example of natural prudence. The swallow, he says, and the crane have kept the time of their coming; but my people has not known the judgment of the Lord. Accordingly the Philosopher (Hist. book 9, ch. 10) begins his account of the migration of cranes thus: Φρόνιμα δὲ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ τὰς γεράνους δοκεῖ συμβαίνειν [Phronima de polla kai peri tas geranous dokei symbainein]; Many things also seem to be done prudently by cranes. And Aelian, History book 3, chapter 14, maintains that men learned τὸ κυβερνητικὸν [to kybernētikon], the art of steering, from them. And Cassiodorus holds that Mercury, Philostratus that Palamedes, had cranes as teachers. Accordingly among the Egyptians, as Horus reports, a watchful crane signified a cautious man, and a flying crane ἄνθρωπον εἰδότα τὰ μετέωρα [anthrōpon eidota ta meteōra], a man skilled in lofty matters. And among the Arabs one who is very cautious is called, in a common proverb, احرس من الكركي [aḥras min al-kurkī], more cautious than a crane.

Nor should anyone wonder that the crane is among the clean birds rather than the stork, a bird very like it, since the stork feeds on serpents, the crane on crops and seeds. An old author in Suidas: Γέρανοι γεωργοῦ κατενέμοντο χώραν ἐσπαρμένην νεωστὶ πυρίνῳ σίτῳ [Geranoi geōrgou katenemonto chōran esparmenēn neōsti pyrinō sitō], Cranes were grazing on a farmer's field newly sown with wheat. Aelian, book 2, ch. 1: Σπείραντας δὲ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους καταλαμβάνουσι, καὶ τράπεζαν, ὡς ἂν εἴποις, ἄφθονον τὴν ἐν ταῖς ἀρούραις εὑρόντες, εἶτα ἄκλητοι ξενίων μεταλαγχάνουσιν [Speirantas de tous Aigyptious katalambanousi, kai trapezan, hōs an eipois, aphthonon tēn en tais arourais heurontes, eita aklētoi xeniōn metalanchanousin]; They come upon the Egyptians as they are sowing, and finding in the fields a table, so to speak, abounding in food, they enjoy, uninvited, the rights of hospitality. Hence Mela writes that the Pygmies fought against the cranes for their sown crops; and Antipater of Sidon, as cited above, in the Epitaph of a Fowler:
Ὁ πρὶν ἐγὼ καὶ ψῆρα καὶ ἁρπάκτειραν ἐρύκων Σπέρματος ὑψιπετῆ Βιστόνιαν γέρανον. [Ho prin egō kai psēra kai harpakteiran erykōn Spermatos hypsipetē Bistonian geranon]

I, who formerly kept the starling and the high-flying Bistonian crane away from the seed (that is, from the grains). Cranes, then, will have been clean by the definition of Aristeas, who counts as clean τῶν πτηνῶν τὰ πυροῖς καὶ ὀσπρίοις χρώμενα πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν [tōn ptēnōn ta pyrois kai ospriois chrōmena pros tēn trophēn], those birds which are nourished on wheat and pulse. What is more, among the ancient Greeks cranes were not only eaten but even counted among the delicacies, especially around Thessaly, where the wealthier had on their estates their own γερανοβοτίας [geranobotias] or γερανοβοσίας [geranobosias], that is, crane pastures, which Pollux mentions, following Plato in the Statesman. And in the Balearic islands the vipio, as they called the smaller crane, was held in honour at table. So Pliny, book 10, ch. 49. The same author wonders why Cornelius Nepos, writing under Augustus, said that storks were preferred to cranes, since this bird is now, he says, sought after among the very first, while no one would want to touch the other. Hence Horace, in the dinner of Nasidienus, at which Maecenas was present, book 2, Satire 8:
— — — — then followed slaves carrying on a great platter the carved limbs of a crane, sprinkled with much salt, not without meal.
And Ovid, treating of the frugality of the ancients, Fasti book 6:

Nor did Latium know the bird that rich Ionia supplies, nor the one that delights in Pygmy blood. That is, the francolin and the crane were not yet among the delicacies of the Romans. And Statius too, in Hercules Vindex, censures thus the gluttons of his own time, whose palate was more learned than was fitting:
Ah, wretches! who delight to know how the bird of the Phasis differs from the wintering crane of Rhodope. — —

So much, then, for the word עגור agor, over which I see that the ancient translators stumbled. In Isaiah, for the words כסוס עגור, like a swallow and agor, that is, a crane, the Greek Elders have only ὡς χελιδὼν [hōs chelidōn], and the Arabic translator مثل سنونوة [mithl sunūnwa] like a swallow, the following word being omitted altogether; and Jerome, Like a young swallow; Aquila, ὡς ἵππος ἀγώρ [hōs hippos agōr]; and Theodotion, ὡς χελιδὼν ἀγὼρ [hōs chelidōn agōr], because they were content to transcribe an unknown word. But the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܣܢܘܢܝܬܐ ܕܡܨܦܪܐ [איך סנוניתא דמצפרא], like a swallow that chatters; and the Chaldee כסוסיא דאחיד, like a swallow that has been caught; with which Symmachus's version agrees, ὡς χελιδὼν ἐγκλειθεῖσα [hōs chelidōn enkleitheisa], like a swallow shut in; as if they had read סגור sagur instead of עגור agor. But that עגור agor is to be read is shown by Aquila, Symmachus, all the Hebrews, and the comparison of this passage with Ierem. VIII, 7. There again the same words סיס sis and עגור agor are joined, and indeed so joined that it is clear that עגור agor is the name of a bird, like תור thor and סיס sis, which precede it. Jerome renders it stork, and the Greeks ἀγροῦ στρουθία [agrou strouthia]. But ἀγροῦ [agrou] arose from ἀγὼρ [agōr], and στρουθία [strouthia] is a gloss that crept from the margin into the text. The Chaldee and the Syriac very well explain it as ܟܘܪܟܝܐ [כורכיא] kurkeja, that is, crane, although not in its proper order, as we noted above .

Although עגור agor is not used today for the crane among the Arabs, it may nevertheless once have been so used, and may derive from the fact that by the verb عجر [ʿajara] agara they mean that someone returns home by right of return, or flees away, which is most characteristic of cranes. For it is well known that out of love of their homeland they return every year to Scythia and Thrace, where they were born, and indeed τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστον καλιὰν ἀναγνωρίζειν, ὡς τὴν οἰκίαν ἀνθρώπους [tēn heautōn hekaston kalian anagnōrizein, hōs tēn oikian anthrōpous], that each recognizes its own nest, as men do their house: which Aelian sets out at length in book 3, ch. 13 and 23. And perhaps from the same source it came about that the royal couriers were called by the Syrians and Persians Ἄγγαροι [Angaroi], aggari or angari. For the angari were believed to rival cranes in speed of running. Φασί τινες θᾶττον τῶν γεράνων ταύτην τὴν πορείαν ἀνύττειν [Phasi tines thatton tōn geranōn tautēn tēn poreian anyttein] (says Xenophon in book 8 of the Cyropaedia): Some report that this journey is accomplished faster than the flight of cranes. That the running of the angari is treated there will be clear to anyone who reads the passage. Among the Cypriots, however, agor was a bird very different from the crane, namely the eagle, if we believe these words of Hesychius: Ἀγώρ· ἀετὸς, Κύπριοι [Agōr: aetos, Kyprioi]. But perhaps it had been written Ἀγώρ· γερανός [Agōr: geranos]; and, the first part of the word γερανὸς [geranos] having been omitted because of its similar ending to the preceding word, ἀετός [aetos] was made out of ἀνὸς [anos] .

Among the migratory birds of Alexandria, Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descript. Animall. p. 9 also lists the Kurki: "it is also called Vaes araki [إوز أرقي [iwazz arqī] anas vigilans [wakeful duck], which might indeed be a name of the crane, since the crane's vigilance is well known; see Bochart below]. It arrives at Constantinople in October, returns after three months, or, as is reported, passes on to India." But on p. 3 the same Forsskål gives Vaes araki as the name of the duck-goose. Hence Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses] (in Animadverss. ad Cantic. Hisk., printed in the Symbolae Kilonienses, vol. 2, p. 323 ff.) rightly concludes that one name was common to several birds. Yet that the crane too is called Kurki, كركي [kurkī], by the Arabs is clear at least from the proverb about a cautious man, which Bochart will cite further on: احرس من الكركي [aḥras min al-kurkī] more vigilant than a crane.

Forsskål has the same name among the obscure birds of Arabia, p. VIII: "Ghornak, white; it feeds on gadflies that nest on the backs of oxen." Clearly this bird is not the crane. However, since in the fable of the Pygmies, which Bochart will give us from a certain Arab below, p. 77, cranes are plainly to be understood by غرانيق [gharānīq], I would think that this same name was used of different animals in different regions. In Mauretania a certain species of vulture is called by that name; see Hoest, Descript. regni Fessani et Maroccani p. 298, German trans. Cf. Velthusen loc. cit. p. 321.
On the ancient interpretations see also Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1832.

But I can scarcely believe that Bochart has established anything certain by this whole very learned discussion. Let us weigh the force of his arguments. One will look in vain in this entire chapter for any explicit statement of them. At the very outset he assumes that עגור is the crane, but he is completely silent about the reasons that led him to it. Yet, so far as one can gather from the course of the whole discussion, he seems to have reasoned thus: "From the two passages of Isaiah and Jeremiah it is clear that עגור is a migratory bird and one using a strained voice; and we find both of these in the crane; therefore עגור is the crane." Nothing would be more certain than this, if those two features were peculiar to cranes. As it is, since there are many migratory birds that use a strained voice, you see how unsafe this argument is unless weightier ones are added. But Bochart is wholly without these, so that there is not even one of the ancients on whose authority he can safely rely. For the Syriac and the Chaldee put crane where the Hebrew text has סוס, but swallow in place of עגור; unless you say that the words have been transposed in both translators, which Bochart assumes without any adequate reason, merely in favour of his preconceived opinion. Equally weak is the other argument for the crane, drawn from the fact that the Arabic عجر [ʿjr] means he returned; for on that basis all migratory birds whatsoever could have been so named. But what chiefly restrains me from taking עגור as the name of the crane is this: that in Isaiah chirping (צפצף) is attributed to the birds סוס and עגור. — VELTHUSEN (in Symbolae Kilonienses vol. 2, p. 273—390) labours hard to show that the Hebrew עגור is the same word as نغر [nughar], the Arabic name of the nightingale, with an interchange of ن and ע (whose related sound in pronunciation once approached ng, like the French n in mon, ton), and of ג and غ, examples of whose interchange Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] gives in the Clavis Dialectorum p. 199. He further argues that the nightingale was in the minds both of the Alexandrians, when they put στρουθια [strouthia], sparrows, in Jeremiah, that bird being of their kind; and of the Chaldee and the Syriac, who in their Jeremiah by כורכיא (from the verb כָּרַךְ to cover) would indicate a bird that hides itself amid thick foliage in mourning, i.e. the nightingale, and by that word sought at the same time to express the same notion of hiding in the verb עגר that can be derived from the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], in Conjugation 5 he covered himself.
