How contrived and far-fetched all this is, anyone will easily notice for himself. — EVERARD SCHEIDIUS, in his Dissertatio ad Canticum Hiskiae p. 86 ff., taking our עגור in Isaiah as a passive participle of the verb עגר, which, on the testimony of Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] and Firuzabadi, has the notion of twisting and bending, considers it an epithet of the swallow, which, struck with fear, wheels this way and that and repeatedly turns aside in its course. — Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] too, in the Clavis to Isaiah, took the word for a participle; but since he there regards סוס as the name of the horse (cf. note 4 to the preceding Chapter), he interprets עגור as disturbed, anxious, calling to his aid the Syriac ܥܓܘܪܐ [עגורא] and also the Arabic عجر [ʿjr], to turn aside in the way, to wheel, so that the poet, tossed by the heat of fever, compares himself with an exhausted horse, panting from the depths of its chest and uttering a shrill and sharp sound, which is expressed by the verb צפצף. — To me עגור seems to be the name of a bird in Isaiah too, chiefly for this reason: that in Jer 8:7 the same words סיס and עגור are joined, and joined in such a way that it is evident that עגור is the name of a bird, like תור and סיס, which precede. But which species of bird is meant, since the other dialects are silent and the ancients disagree remarkably, no one today can say.
That the Hebrew name קורא kore does not signify the partridge, as has hitherto been believed, but a kind of woodcock (rusticula) or gallinago.

The bird called קורא kore in Hebrew is called קוראה koraa or קוריה korea in Chaldee, and قارية [qāriya] karia in Arabic. The sacred writers mention it in two places. In the first, David, a fugitive, addresses Saul thus, 1 Sam 26:20: the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea, כאשר ירדוף קורא בהרים, as if one were pursuing the bird kore in the mountains. The other passage reads thus, Jer 17:11: The kore gathered, and did not bring forth: so he who amasses riches, but not by justice, will leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end will be a fool. From these passages we learn that the קורא kore is a mountain bird, not of great value, in the catching of which the fowler spends his effort badly; and that it is one of those birds which sit on the eggs of others. For this is what these words of Jeremiah mean, קורא דגר ולא ילד, the kore gathered, and did not bring forth, that is, it gathered the eggs of others, not laid by itself, to brood them under its shadow. Hence Isa 34:15, of the serpent קפוז kippoz, that is, the acontias or dart-snake, ודגרה בצלה, and it gathered in its shadow, that is, it brooded its eggs. And at Job 39:14, for תחמם, will warm, said of the ostrich's eggs, the Chaldee has תדגר, will gather. This needed to be pointed out, because many wrongly refer the verb to gather in Jeremiah to the ἐπισύναξιν [episynaxin] of the chicks. Among them are Hippolytus, Chrysostom, Olympiodorus, and among the Hebrews R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] . So much from Scripture.

In section 64 of the book Bereshit Rabba, which is both very ancient and of great authority among the Jews, a certain R. Joshua, son of Chanina, אסכולסטקיא דאורייתא, Scholastic of the Law, that is, a doctor of Theology, tells this fable about the same bird: ארי טרף טרף ועמד עצם בגרונו אמר כל דאתי מפיק ליה אנא יהיב ליה אגריה אתא הדין קורא מיצראה דמוקריה אריך יהיב מוקריה ואפקיה אמר ליה הב לי אגרי אמר ליה זיל תהא מלגלג ואומר דעלית לפומא דאריא בשלם ונפקית בשלם, A lion had devoured its prey, and a bone stuck in its throat, and it said: Whoever comes and draws it out, I will give him a reward. Then came an Egyptian kore with a long beak, which it put into the lion's throat and drew the bone out from there, and said, Give me my reward. But the lion answered, Go, and boast that you entered the lion's mouth in peace and came out in peace. This fable is the twin of this Aesopic one: Λύκου λαιμῷ ὀστέον ἐπεπήγει. ὁ δὲ γεράνῳ μισθὸν παρέξειν εἶπεν, εἰ, τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς ἐπιβαλοῦσα, τὸ ὀστοῦν ἐκ τοῦ λαιμοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐκβάλοι. ἡ δὲ τοῦτ᾽ ἐκβαλοῦσα, δολιχόδειρος οὖσα, τὸν μισθὸν ἐπεζήτει. ὅστις γελάσας, καὶ τοὺς ὀδόντας θήξας, Ἀρκεῖ σοι μισθὸς, ἔφη. τοῦτο καὶ μόνον, ὅτι καὶ λύκου στόματος καὶ ὀδόντων ἐξῆρες κάραν σῶαν, μηδὲν παθοῦσαν. [Lykou laimō osteon epepēgei. ho de geranō misthon parexein eipen, ei, tēn kephalēn autēs epibalousa, to ostoun ek tou laimou autou ekbaloi. hē de tout᾽ ekbalousa, dolichodeiros ousa, ton misthon epezētei. hostis gelasas, kai tous odontas thēxas, Arkei soi misthos, ephē. touto kai monon, hoti kai lykou stomatos kai odontōn exēres karan sōan, mēden pathousan.] That is, in the rendering of Phaedrus, book 1, Fable 8:

When a bone he had swallowed stuck in a wolf's throat, overcome by great pain he began to entice each one with a reward to draw out that evil. At last a crane was persuaded by his oath, and, trusting the length of her neck to his gullet, performed a dangerous cure on the wolf. When she demanded a reward for this deed, "You are ungrateful," he said, "you who have carried your head away unharmed from our mouth, and you ask for payment."

Yet there is no reason for anyone to conclude, from comparing the Hebrew fable with the Greek and Roman, that the bird קורא kore is the same as the crane. For just as the Hebrews substituted the lion for the wolf, so they could substitute another bird for the crane. But at least we gather this: that the bird kore has a long beak. All the Hebrews assert the same. The Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], under קר, fifth entry: עוף הוא ופיו שמנקר בו ארוך ביותר, It is a bird whose mouth, that is, beak, is very long. So also R. Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] and David de Pomis [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587), a Hebrew-Latin-Italian dictionary]: קורא צפור שיש לו מקרא ארוך, Kore, a bird having a long beak.

But the Arabs teach us much more about the bird قارية [qāriya] karia, which Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] describes thus: القارية كسارية طاير قصير الرجلين طويل المنقار اخضر اللون تحبه الاعراب وتتيبن به ويشهبون [al-qāriya ka-sāriya ṭāyir qaṣīr al-rijlayn ṭawīl al-minqār akhḍar al-lawn tuḥibbuhu al-aʿrāb wa-tatayabbanu bihi wa-yushahbūn] به الرجل السخي [bihi al-rajul al-sakhī] Karia, a noun of the same form as saria (that is, beam, Luke 6:41), is a bird which has short feet, a long beak, a green colour (another copy has اخضر الظهر [akhḍar al-ẓahr] a green back); the Arabs love it, since they hold it a bird of good omen, and they compare a generous man to it. And Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ]: القارية طير خضر تحبها الاعراب ويشهبون بها الرجل السخي وذلك لانها تنذر بالمطر [al-qāriya ṭayr khuḍr tuḥibbuhā al-aʿrāb wa-yushahbūn bihā al-rajul al-sakhī wa-dhālika li-annahā tundhiru bi-l-maṭar] Karia, a green bird, which the Arabs love and to which they compare a generous man, because it signals rain. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: القارية طاير اذا راوه استبشروا بالمطر كانه رسول الغيث او مقدمة السحاب [al-qāriya ṭāyir idhā raʾawhu istabsharū bi-l-maṭar ka-annahu rasūl al-ghayth aw muqaddimat al-saḥāb] Karia, a bird at the sight of which people rejoice because of rain to come, as though it were the herald of the shower and the forerunner of the clouds. Again Damir, under the heading On its use: الحل لان العرب كانت تاكلها [al-ḥill li-anna al-ʿarab kānat taʾkuluhā] Eating it is permitted, because the Arabs eat it. And the book entitled الحج [al-ḥajj] Alchag, or Pilgrimage: الحمام يغدي بشاه وما دونه من القواري وغيرها يغدي بالقيمة [al-ḥamām yughdī bi-shāh wa-mā dūnahu min al-qawārī wa-ghayrihā yughdī bi-l-qīma] A dove (which one of the pilgrims has vowed to give as an offering at the tomb of the false prophet) is redeemed with a sheep; but whatever is below a dove (for example karia birds, or others like them) is redeemed by paying its price. From this Damir inferred two things: first, that the bird is edible; second, that it differs from the dove. However, Ibno Sachith, in the book On the Purity of Speech, defines القواري [al-qawārī], that is, karia birds, as طير خضر لها ترجيع [ṭayr khuḍr lahā tarjīʿ] green birds which make their voice reverberate in the throat, like a cooing dove, which is otherwise peculiar to those birds that drink water in a single draught. This is called عب [ʿabb] abba in Arabic.

These things having been thus explained, it follows that the bird קרא kore, or قارية [qāriya] karia if you prefer, as it is called in Arabic, is unknown to us, since it is clear that among us there is no bird to which all these marks apply. Yet of all the birds we know, the closest to it is Aristotle's ὁ σκολόπαξ [ho skolopax], or ἀσκολόπαξ [askolopax]. Gaza calls it gallinago; Pliny and Martial call it woodcock (rusticula) and rustica perdix [rustic partridge]; Nemesianus scolopax; the old Glosses acceia, whence the Tuscans to this day say acceiga; the Germans sneppa; and the French beccassa, from the size of its beak. To the same bird I refer the Hebrew קורא kore. For it is not formed from crying out, as people think, but from the noun קורה kora, which first means beam and timber, and then also a sharpened stake, from which fences are made. Hence the verb קרה kera, derived from it, means not only to lay beams and to floor with planks, as passim in Nehemiah, but also to fence in, or to repair a fence, as in the Talmudic tractate Moed Katon, ch. 1, fol. 7b: ומקרין את הפריצה במועד כיצד מקרין רב יוסף אמר בהוצא ודפני, One may also repair a breach in a fence on a festival day. But how is it repaired? Rabbi Joseph said: with stakes of palm and laurel. Thus, just as the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is so called in Greek because it has a long, straight beak like a σκόλοψ [skolops], that is, a stake, so in Hebrew it is called קורא kore, because for the Hebrews קורה kora is not only δόκος [dokos] but also σκόλοψ [skolops]. So the reasoning is parallel. The final Aleph stands for He, as in נקרא 2 Sam 1:6, and in the noun קראה for meeting, which comes from the verb קרה, to meet. Besides the size of the beak, the bird kore has this in common with the scolopax: both have short feet, both are edible, both live in the mountains. For just as David says that τὸν [ton] kore is hunted over the mountains, so Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes that the scolopax spends the summer in the Alps and the Pyrenees, and in the highest mountains of Switzerland, Savoy and Auvergne. Neither exceeds the bulk of a dove. For just as the قارية [qāriya] karia is defined by the Arabs as دون الحمام [dūn al-ḥamām] below a dove, so Nemesianus says of the scolopax:
— — the lovely scolopax is an easy prey: you will see it no larger in body than the Paphian birds.

to the Paphian birds, that is, to doves. Indeed, like the karia of the Arabs, the scolopax too, or woodcock (rusticula), is a harbinger of rain. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] in his Birds, p. 504: Some make the call of the lesser woodcock (the French call it beccassine), when heard, a prognostic of rain. He adds that the sound of its call is like that of a knife drawn across a saw. This seems to be what the Arabs mean when they attribute to the karia ترجيع [tarjīʿ], that is, a reciprocating call. So far, then, everything is quite similar. The colour, however, is different: in the karia it is green, at least on the back, while in the woodcock it is so mottled that it is very far from green. Moreover, although both birds are edible, David does not seem to have held the קורא kore in great esteem; and the Arabs celebrate the karia for no other reason than that it is among the prognostics of rain. Our woodcock, by contrast, is most renowned among the delicacies of the table, and yields little to the partridge. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigram 76, under the heading Rusticula: Whether I am a woodcock or a partridge, what does it matter, if the flavour is the same? The partridge is dearer; that is why it tastes better.

Finally, no one has written of the woodcock what Jeremiah wrote of the קורא kore: the kore gathered (or sat on eggs) and did not bring forth. I conclude, therefore, that the kore is a bird peculiar to those regions, distinct from the woodcock, yet not differing from it greatly . We must now state how the ancient and modern interpreters explain this word.

Kore קרא is rendered by the Greeks νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], nycticorax, 1 Sam 26:20, but they were doubtless misled by a faulty reading. They had evidently read קדא for קרא, Daleth for Resh, letters that are very similar to each other. The word קדא ceased to be in use among the Hebrews; but from it the Chaldeans formed קדיא, and the Syrians ܥܕܝܢ [עדין], with Koph and Ayin interchanged, as when they say ܥܛܪ [עטר], vapour, for קטר, and ܥܪܝܐ [עריא], cold, for קריא. That this conjecture is correct is evident from the fact that elsewhere in the Greek version νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax] corresponds to the Hebrew כוס, for which the Chaldee Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has קריא, Lev 11:17, and the Syriac translator ܒܣܢ [בסן], Ps 102:7. Therefore כוס and קרא, whence קריא and ܒܣܢ [בסן], are synonyms. So if כוס is the νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], as the Greeks render it, so too is קרא. There is a similar error in the Talmudic tractate Niddah, fol. 23a, where instead of קדיא with Daleth, קריא with Resh is written eight times, as if it were the bird kore, whereas it is a night bird. For joined to it is קפופא kiphupha, that is, the owl. And they are said to be birds דעיניהן הולכות לפניהן כשלאדם, whose eyes are not at the side, as in other birds, but in front, as in humans. And in the Gloss both are described as עוף צועק בלילה ופניו דומות לחתול ועיניו לפניו, a bird that cries at night, with a face like a cat's and eyes in front. Again in Berakhot, ch. 9, fol. 57b: כל מינין עופית יפין לחלום חוץ מן קריא וקפופא וקורפראי, All species of birds are auspicious in dreams, except the nycticorax, the owl and the bat. In these words too, I say, קריא is written with Resh, which must be changed to Daleth. So finally in the Chaldee paraphrase of Isa 34:15, for וקורידהון ינצפון בטולה read וקודידהון, And their nycticoraces shall howl in its shade. For there too Resh stands for Daleth. This is why the Latin translator of the Chaldee rendered it thus: And the partridges shall chatter, etc. This is utterly absurd. For the passage concerns the devastation of Edom, to which it is not fitting that partridges should chatter in it, but that nycticoraces and eagle-owls should howl in a horrifying manner.

The other passage on the kore, Jer 17:11. קרא דגר ולא ילך, is rendered thus in Greek: Ἐφώνησεν πέρδιξ, συνήγαγεν ἃ οὐκ ἔτεκεν [Ephōnēsen perdix, synēgagen ha ouk eteken], "The partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth." The words ἐφώνησεν πέρδιξ [ephōnēsen perdix] are a double rendering of the word קרא, which some read as kara and others as kore; the former rendered it ἐφώνησεν [ephōnēsen], the latter πέρδιξ [perdix] . The latter rendering is followed by Jerome, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Hebrews and all the more recent writers, as though these words referred to the common partridge. And this is explained in various ways. For there are those who assert that the partridge steals the eggs of others, incubates them, and claims the chicks hatched from them as its own. Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, chapter 9: Οὐκ ἀρκεῖ αὐτῇ τῆς ἰδίας γαστρὸς ὁ τόκος, ἀλλὰ κλέπτουσα τὰ ὠὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων φέρει αὐτὰ ἐπὶ τὴν νεοττίαν αὐτῆς [Ouk arkei autē tēs idias gastros ho tokos, alla kleptousa ta ōa tōn allotriōn pherei auta epi tēn neottian autēs]; "The offspring of her own womb does not suffice her, but she snatches the eggs of others and carries them to her own nest." Eustathius, on the Hexaemeron, p. 29: Ἀλλότρια δὲ κλέπτων ὠὰ νεοσσοποιεῖ [Allotria de kleptōn ōa neossopoiei]; "It steals the eggs of others and hatches them." Ambrose, in the Hexaemeron, book 6, chapter 3: "We know the partridge to be crafty, for it snatches the eggs of another, that is, of another partridge, and warms them with its own body." And in the Letter to Sabinus, where he expounds the passage of Jeremiah at length: "Some have thought that this too should be applied to the nature of the partridge, because it snatches the eggs of others and warms them with its own body, and by this fraud seeks to acquire the offspring of others." Philastrius, On Heresies, in the Preface: "We must recognize that the enemy of the human race was not undeservedly compared by the prophet Jeremiah to the partridge, which, since it suffers barrenness, often secretly sits on the young of others and then warms and claims them as its own children." Cassiodorus, Variae, book 2, Letter 14: "Partridges too have the custom of making good their lost eggs at the loss of another mother, so as to repair the hardship of their own bereavement by adopting another's brood." Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: "The partridge is so deceitful that it snatches another's eggs and warms them." Damir, in the chapter الحجل [al-ḥajal], or On the partridge: والانثي اذا اصيب بيضها قصدت عش غيرها وغلتها علي بيضها وتسرقه وتحضنه [wa-l-unthā idhā uṣība bayḍuhā qaṣadat ʿushsha ghayrihā wa-ghallathā ʿalā bayḍihā wa-tasriquhu wa-taḥḍunuhu] "And the female, when her egg has been spoiled, invades the nest of another partridge, and substitutes for her own egg one stolen by fraud, and warms it." So he writes; I confess I do not sufficiently understand it. For I do not see how a partridge could steal the eggs of others, since it cannot do this with its beak, nor does it have toes suited to the purpose. Therefore the great author on Solinus, on page 150, not undeservedly brings a charge against Pliny for having reported that partridges carry their eggs elsewhere, since their nature does not allow this, and the contrary can be established from Aristotle.

Accordingly, the Hebrews will seem to have written more cautiously. For they do not say that the partridge carries off the eggs of others, but that it sits in another's nest. R. Selomo on 1 Sam. XXVI, 20: הקורא עוף ששמו קורא ובלעז פרד״יז וכן קורא דגר ולא ילד ומרדף אחר קיני שאר עופות ויושב על ביציהם "Kore is a bird which is so called in Hebrew, and in the vernacular perdix [partridge], of which it is said in Jeremiah: „The kore gathered, and did not bring forth“; because it pursues the nests of other birds in order to sit on their eggs." And Porta coeli, fol. 29d: הוא רובץ על ביצי העוף אחר ומחמם אותם "It sits on the eggs of another bird and warms them." So too Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] on Jeremiah. But the same author, in his Lexicon, asserts that the partridge first gathers the eggs of others and afterwards sits on them as if they were its own: הוא מאסף ביצי עוף אחר ורובץ עליהם כאלו הם שלו. However that may be, this too is hardly very likely, that a partridge, however much it wished, should sit in another's nest, since the true mother of the eggs would by no means allow it. These things, then, are highly paradoxical.

Yet there follows something far more παραδοξότερον [paradoxoteron], namely that the chicks, hatched in this way by a foreign mother, leave her some time later in order to return to their true mother, whom they recognize by her voice. Eustathius, in the place cited above: Αὐξηθέντες οἱ νεοττοὶ, ἕκαστος, κατὰ γένος, πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους ἀνίπταται, καὶ ἔρημόν αὐτὴν καταλιμπάνουσι· [Auxēthentes hoi neottoi, hekastos, kata genos, pros tous oikeious aniptatai, kai erēmon autēn kataleimpanousi] When the chicks have grown up, each one, according to its kind, flies back to its own parents, and they leave her alone. Ambrose, in the Hexaëmeron: When she has brought out her chicks, she loses them; for when they have heard the voice of the one who produced the eggs, they leave her and betake themselves, by a kind of natural love and duty, to the one whom they have recognized as their true mother by the generation of the eggs, showing that this one performs the office of a nurse, that one of a parent. And in the Letter to Sabinus: When all the labour spent on nourishment has exhausted the one rearing them, and the chicks have begun to grow up, then she (the true mother) utters her voice, and calls her offspring with a kind of trumpet of devotion. The offspring, roused by a kind of natural hearing, recognizes its parent and deserts the pretender. Thus, when she wishes to gather what she did not bear, she loses those whom she thought to rear. Philastrius: and when the time of discerning age has grown upon them, then, having let go (read dimissis [having dismissed]) their false parents, remembering by their own sense the rights of parents, and seeing them openly with their eyes, they no longer delay to follow them. Cassiodorus: But as soon as the young have begun to have confidence in walking, they go out into the fields with their nurse; and once they have been prompted by the maternal voice, they seek rather the mother of their eggs, although they are reared by others as stolen offspring. Isidore: When the chicks have heard the voice of their own mother, by a kind of natural instinct they leave the one who brooded them, and return to the one who bore them. Damir: في طبع الحجل ان ياتي اعشاش نظاريه فياخذ بيضها فيحضنه فانا اطارت الفراخ لحقت بامهاتها التي باضتها [fī ṭabʿ al-ḥajal an yaʾtī aʿshāsh naẓārīh fa-yaʾkhudh bayḍahā fa-yaḥḍunuh fa-anā aṭārat al-firākh laḥiqat bi-ummahātihā allatī bāḍat-hā] It is of the nature of the partridge that it comes to the nests of birds similar to itself, takes their eggs, and broods them; but the chicks, when they fly off, attach themselves to their mothers who laid them. Porta coeli: והביצים ההם כשיבקעו ויצאו האפרוחים לא יהיו כמו בניו שילכו אחריו אלא יעזבוהו ולא יכירוהו ולא ילכו אלא אחרי מי שהוא להם, But after the eggs are hatched and the chicks have come forth, they do not behave as its chicks, so as to follow it; rather they desert it, and no longer know it, nor do they follow any other except the true mother. For שהוא להם read שהוא להם אם, as in Kimchi, who has these same things on Jeremiah. The reader sees that by these writers something scarcely credible is asserted: namely, that partridge chicks know by nature from which mother came the egg out of which they were hatched, and that they at once recognize her by her voice, though they have never before heard or seen her. Who would believe that such a sense belongs to egg-laying creatures rather than to viviparous ones, which generate more perfectly? Or that brutes excel in it rather than man, who, it is perfectly plain, has no natural knowledge of his parents? Otherwise Oedipus would not have unwittingly killed his father, nor lain with his mother. Accordingly, in the Poet, Telemachus, asked whether he was the son of Ulysses, answered thus :
Μήτηρ μέν τ᾽ ἐμέ φησι τοῦ ἔμμεναι αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε Οὐκ οἶδ᾽. οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω. [Mētēr men t' eme phēsi tou emmenai autar egōge ouk oid'. ou gar pō tis heon gonon autos anegnō.]
My mother indeed asserts that I am his; but I do not know. For no one has ever himself known his own begetter. And Menander, quoted by Eustathius on that passage:
Αὑτὸν γὰρ οὐδεὶς οἶδε τοῦ ποτ᾽ ἐγένετο, ᾽Αλλ᾽ ὑπονοοῦμεν πάντες, ἢ πιστεύομεν. [Hauton gar oudeis oide tou pot' egeneto, all' hyponooumen pantes, ē pisteuomen.]

No one knows of himself by whom he was begotten; we all suspect, or believe. And even if what they relate of partridge chicks were true, it could still hardly, if at all, have been observed. For suppose that, of the many chicks following a mother partridge, one or two desert her to go to another: who would dare to affirm for certain that this happens because they were hatched from eggs stolen from that other bird? How many things must be presupposed for this observation to be held true and established? And so nothing of the kind occurs among the ancient writers on natural history. Jerome's memory deceived him when he wrote on Jeremiah: The writers of natural history, of beasts and birds as well as of trees and plants, the chief of whom among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny Secundus, say that this is the nature of the partridge: that it steals the eggs of another partridge, that is, another's eggs, and sits on them and broods them; and when the brood has grown up, it flies away from it and leaves the foreign parent. But the pious men too who, with him, committed this fiction to writing placed more faith than was fitting τοῖς τερατολόγοις [tois teratologois], whose aim was to hold the people's attention with these prodigies of storytelling. For, as Synesius rightly says in the Encomium of Baldness, Τὸ δὲ ῥᾷστον καταγελάσεται ὁ δῆμος· δεῖται γὰρ τερατείας. [To de rhaston katagelasetai ho dēmos; deitai gar terateias.] What is easy, the common people laugh at; for it craves marvellous narration.

Some of the Greek Fathers held a different view: that a female partridge, while another partridge is away, approaches its nest and so deceives the chicks by imitating the mother's voice that they leave the nest and follow her, until the true mother returns and they regret their mistake. Chrysostom reports this only in part: Ἔθος φασὶ τοὺς πέρδικας, μετὰ τὸ ἀποτεχθῆναι τῶν ὠῶν, τοὺς νεοττοὺς τῇ φωνῇ προσκαλεῖσθαι, καὶ γυμνοῦν τὴν τεκοῦσαν [Ethos phasi tous perdikas, meta to apotechthēnai tōn ōōn, tous neottous tē phōnē proskaleisthai, kai gymnoun tēn tekousan]; They say it is the habit of partridges, after laying their eggs, to lure the chicks of others with their voice, and so rob the mother of them. But Olympiodorus says it more fully: Ὁ πέρδιξ, ὥς φασιν, ὑπερήφανος ὢν, διὰ τῆς φωνῆς τοὺς ἀλλοτρίους προσκαλεῖται νεοττοὺς, οἵτινες γνόντες ὕστερον ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν αὐτοῦ, καταλιμπάνουσιν αὐτόν [Ho perdix, hōs phasin, hyperēphanos ōn, dia tēs phōnēs tous allotrious proskaleitai neottous, hoitines gnontes hysteron hoti ouk eisin autou, katalimpanousin auton]. The partridge, as they say, being proud, entices the chicks of others with its voice; yet it is deserted by them once they have at last recognized that they are not its own. And Hippolytus most fully: Τοῦ πέρδικος κενοδόξου ζώου ὑπάρχοντος, ἐπὰν πλησίον ἴδῃ ἑτέρου πέρδικος καλιὰν νεοττοὺς ἔχουσαν, ἀποπτάντος τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὴν νομὴν, μιμούμενος τὴν τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου φωνὴν, προσκαλεῖται πρὸς ἑαυτὸν τοὺς νεοττούς· οἱ δὲ νεοσσοὶ, νομίσαντες τὸν ἴδιον αὐτῶν ὑπάρχειν πατέρα, προστρέχουσιν αὐτῷ· ὁ δὲ ἐγγαυριᾷ ἐν ἀλλοτρίοις τέκνοις ὡς ἰδίοις, ἐλθόντος δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου πατρὸς, καὶ βοήσαντος, τὴν ἰδίαν φωνὴν ἐπιγνόντες οἱ νεοσσοὶ, καταλιπόντες τὸν νόθον, πρὸς τὸν ἴδιον πατέρα πορεύονται [Tou perdikos kenodoxou zōou hyparchontos, epan plēsion idē heterou perdikos kalian neottous echousan, apoptantos tou patros autōn epi tēn nomēn, mimoumenos tēn tou allotriou phōnēn, proskaleitai pros heauton tous neottous; hoi de neossoi, nomisantes ton idion autōn hyparchein patera, prostrechousin autō; ho de engauria en allotriois teknois hōs idiois, elthontos de tou idiou patros, kai boēsantos, tēn idian phōnēn epignontes hoi neossoi, katalipontes ton nothon, pros ton idion patera poreuontai]. Since the partridge is a proud animal, if it sees nearby the nest of another partridge with chicks in it, while the father has flown off to feed, it lures the chicks to itself by imitating his voice. Taking it for their true father, they at once run to it. And it boasts of the chicks of another as if they were its own. But as soon as the true father has returned and called, the chicks recognize his voice, leave the spurious father, and go over to the genuine one. But I do not think these things truer than what preceded. For some charge partridges with lewdness, others with malice and cunning, but no one, as far as I know, with pride. Nor does it seem that the chicks of partridges could easily be deceived by an imitation of the mother's voice, unless one supposes them so blind that they recognize their mother by hearing alone and not also by sight. Yet even if this were granted, it would not bear on the passage of Jeremiah, in which דגר, as we have shown, does not mean to gather chicks, but eggs, to be brooded.

More ingenious is the view of certain Hebrews cited by Kimchi in his Lexicon: that Jeremiah was speaking only of the male partridge, which, whenever it broods eggs (and that it sometimes broods is attested by Aristotle , Plutarch and Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] ), broods eggs that it did not itself lay, but the female did. But it is not very likely that the Prophet had this in view. For the male brooding the eggs is not peculiar to the partridge; in most birds, too, male and female sit in turn. So it is stated in the Philosopher: Ἐπωάζει δὲ τὰ πολλὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων διαδεχόμενα τὸν ἄῤῥενα τοῖς θήλεσι [Epōazei de ta polla tōn ornithōn diadechomena ton arrena tois thēlesi]. Moreover, the comparison would limp on every side if Jeremiah compared the greedy man, who seizes the goods of others, which, ill gotten, are likewise ill lost, with a male partridge brooding the eggs of its mate. For although the male broods eggs that it did not itself produce, they still cannot be called another's, since the offspring belongs as much to the father as to the mother. Nor does it do this with evil intent, like the greedy man who gapes after what belongs to others, but, as Philes says, ἐξ εὐσπλαγχνίας [ex eusplanchnias], out of a certain paternal affection and devotion towards its own. And so the matter turns out well and prosperously for it, since in this way it increases and propagates its kind. There is thus no similarity at all. Not to mention that many deny that male partridges brood eggs, according to Ulysses Aldrovandus, a recent writer, but very experienced in these matters. See him, Ornithologia book 13, ch. 17.

Since a man most learned in Hebrew saw that the common interpretation was pressed by these difficulties, he thought that the words of Jeremiah could be rendered thus: The partridge gathered (or warmed eggs), but did not bring forth, that is, did not hatch the eggs. Several reasons could be given why it happens to the partridge more often than to any other bird that it warms eggs which it does not hatch. The first is that it nests neither on rocks, nor on the branches of trees, nor on the tops of towers, but on the ground, in a place most exposed not only to fowlers but also to wild beasts and reptiles. The second is that if the partridge's eggs become wet from falling dew or rain, ἐὰν μὴ πάλιν ἡ τεκοῦσα ἐπιθάλψῃ αὐτὰ ἐπελθοῦσα ταχέως, γίνεται ἄγονα [ean mē palin hē tekousa epithalpsē auta epelthousa tacheōs, ginetai agona], unless the mother at once sits on them and warms them again, they are rendered infertile. So Aelian, book 10, ch. 35 of the Hist. animal. The third lies in the males, which through unrestrained lust sometimes break the eggs, so that the females may not be detained too long by incubating. Besides Aelian , this is reported by Aristotle , Pliny , Athenaeus and Philes . But one thing stands against the interpretation we have described: the verb to bring forth in Jeremiah refers not to ἐκλέπισιν [eklepisin], but to ὠοτοκίαν [ōotokian], which everyone knows to be very different from hatching. The matter is perfectly plain in the passage of Isaiah we have cited about the serpent acontias: There the acontias will nest, and lay, and break, that is, hatch the eggs, which are broken in hatching. Among the Hebrews, therefore, in oviparous animals laying is one thing and hatching another. Laying is ὠοτοκία [ōotokia], and is expressed by the verbs ילד and מלט, as hatching is by the verb בקע, which means to break. Thus the passage of Jeremiah, the kore gathered, and did not bring forth, must be taken as it sounds, so that it is understood of a bird that warms eggs laid by another. This is something the naturalists nowhere ascribe to the partridge, but only the Fathers do.

R. Selomo is not consistent. For on Samuel he holds קרא kore to be the partridge, as other Hebrews do. But on Jeremiah he interprets it as the cuckoo, because many think it is peculiar to the cuckoo to sit on other birds' eggs. This opinion had long ago become established among the common people of the French (the nation among whom Selomo lived 550 years ago). Hence even today in common speech the French call cuckoo, as an insult, a man whose wife is an adulteress, because he unknowingly cherishes and rears another's children. Carried away by the same popular error, Acron, a distinguished grammarian, writes thus on the cuckoo, on Horace book 1, Sat. 7: The cuckoo bird suffers from this natural defect: forgetting where it has laid its eggs, it often warms those of others; hence rustics taunt one another with it, as if bearing the care of another's offspring. But in truth the matter is entirely otherwise. For the cuckoo does not sit on others' eggs, but lays in another's nest and hands over its eggs to other birds to be incubated and hatched. Aristotle, Hist. book 9, ch. 29: Ὁ δὲ κόκκυξ οὐ ποιεῖ νεοττίαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ἀλλοτρίαις τίκτει νεοττίαις [Ho de kokkyx ou poiei neottian, all᾽ en allotriais tiktei neottiais]. Likewise: Ἐπωάζει δὲ οὐκ αὐτὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν οὗ ἂν τέκῃ νεοττίᾳ, οὗτος ὁ ὄρνις ἐκκολάπτει καὶ τρέφει [Epōazei de ouk autos, all᾽ en hou an tekē neottia, houtos ho ornis ekkolaptei kai trephei]. Theophrastus , Antigonus of Carystus , Pliny , Aelian , Oppian , Philes and others of the ancients teach the same at greater length. Among the Hebrews too, Rabbi Gersom in Porta coeli, fol. 30, ch.: ואומר על עוף שנקרא קוג"ול שאינו מחמם ביציו אך מניח אותם בתוך קנים של שאר עופות ואותם עופות חשובים שהם ביציהם The bird which they call the cuckoo does not warm its own eggs, as they say, but places them in the nests of other birds; and those birds think these eggs are their own. And experience, the teacher of things, attests that this is so. Accordingly, in the Roman tongue a cuculus [cuckoo] is not the man who suffers the insult from his wife, but the one who inflicts it. In a word, the cuckoo is the same as the adulterer, because the adulterer, like the cuckoo, lies in a nest not his own. Hence Artemona, the woman in Plautus' Asinaria, greets her husband Demaenetus, caught in the brothel with a harlot ἐπ’ αὐτοφώρῳ [ep’ autophōrō], with this insult:
The cuckoo is even lying down.
Grey-headed cuckoo, your wife drags you home from the dens of vice.
But the man whom we French call a cuculus [cuckoo], the Romans called a curruca. Juvenal, Satire 6, of a stupid husband pitying the false tears of his adulterous wife:
You now, curruca, are pleased with yourself, and sip up her weeping with your lips. — — — — —

The curruca [warbler], in Greek ὑπολαῒς [hypolais], is a small bird in whose nest the cuckoo usually lays. The Philosopher says of the cuckoo, Hist. book 6, ch. 7: τίκτει δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ τῆς ὑπολαΐδος νεοττείᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐκλέπει, καὶ ἐκτρέφει [tiktei de epi tē tēs hypolaidos neotteia, hē de eklepei, kai ektrephei]. Hence Theophrastus (De caus. plant. book 2, ch. 24) denied that the race of cuckoos could exist εἰ μὴ ἦν ἡ ὑπολαῒς, ἡ καὶ εἰς τὴν νεοττίαν τὰ ὠὰ τίθησιν [ei mē ēn hē hypolais, hē kai eis tēn neottian ta ōa tithēsin], if there were not the warbler, in whose nest it might lay its eggs. This is not entirely true, since besides the warbler there are also other birds in whose nest the cuckoo ὠοτοκεῖ [ōotokei]. Aristotle in the Mirabilia: Τοὺς κόκκυγάς φασι μὴ ποιεῖν νεοττίαν, ἀλλ’ ἐν ταῖς τῶν φαττῶν, καὶ ταῖς τῶν τρυγόνων ἐκτίκτειν [Tous kokkygas phasi mē poiein neottian, all’ en tais tōn phattōn, kai tais tōn trygonōn ektiktein]. Likewise Hist. book 9, ch. 29: Ἐν ἀλλοτρίαις τίκτει νεοττίαις, μάλιστα μὲν ἐν ταῖς τῶν φαβῶν, καὶ ἐν ὑπολαΐδος, καὶ κορύδου χαμαὶ, ἐπὶ δένδρου ἐν τῇ τῆς χλωρίδος καλουμένης νεοττίᾳ [En allotriais tiktei neottiais, malista men en tais tōn phabōn, kai en hypolaidos, kai korydou chamai, epi dendrou en tē tēs chlōridos kaloumenēs neottia]. Antigonus, Mirab. ch. 109: Κόκκυγος δὲ νεοττοὺς οὐδένα ἑωρακέναι. Τίκτειν γὰρ αὐτὸν, οὐκ ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ νεοττίᾳ, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὰς τῶν ὀρνιθίων, ἢ εἰς τὰς τῶν φαβῶν, ἢ ὑποδυσιδέων [Kokkygos de neottous oudena heōrakenai. Tiktein gar auton, ouk en tē idia neottia, all’ eis tas tōn ornithiōn, ē eis tas tōn phabōn, ē hypodysideōn] (read ὑπολαΐδων [hypolaidōn]) εἰσπετόμενον [eispetomenon]. Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 30: Οὐ πάντων δὲ ὀρνίθων καλίαις ἐπιπηδᾷ οὗτός γε, ἀλλὰ κορύδου, καὶ φάττης, καὶ χλωρίδος, καὶ πάππου [Ou pantōn de ornithōn kaliais epipēda houtos ge, alla korydou, kai phattēs, kai chlōridos, kai pappou]. You see, reader, that besides the warbler, the wood pigeon, the turtle dove, the lark, the chloris and the pappus are also counted among the birds whose nests the cuckoo invades. Some add the sparrow. Isidore, book 12, ch. 7, on the cuckoo: It eats the sparrow's eggs found in the nest and puts its own in their place, which the sparrow takes up, incubates and rears. And Gesner adds the nightingale as well, and the wagtail, the robin and the redstart. So these are so many birds that brood what they did not lay. To them may be added from Jeremiah the bird קרא kore, different from all these and closer to the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] or woodcock (rusticula), as we have proved. This could not be observed by the Greeks and Romans, because this bird was unknown to them. And it escaped the Arabs too, because they touch on its description only briefly and lightly.

But, you will say, if קרא kore is a species of σκολόπαξ [skolopax] or woodcock, or a bird very similar to it, why do the Greek, Latin, Syriac, Arabic and Hebrew translators render it partridge with such agreement? Two answers can be given. 1. The Greeks, who preceded all these, took קרא kore, with Koph, and כרא cara, with Caph, indiscriminately; and the latter means partridge among the Arabs even today. So it is written in Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)]; others prefer كري [karī], and كروان [karawān]. Alcamus: الكروان الحجل والقبج والانثي الكروانة ويقال للذكر الكري [al-karawān al-ḥajal wa-l-qabj wa-l-unthī al-karawāna wa-yuqāl li-l-dhakar al-karī] Alcarvvan, the male partridge, and the partridge in general; and the female alcarvana. But the male is also called alcara . In Ezek 7:25. קפדה־בא, destruction comes, was rendered by the Greeks ἐξιλασμὸς ἥξει [exilasmos hēxei], propitiation will come, as if קפדה with Koph and Daleth were the same as כפרה with Caph and Resh. In the same way קרא with Koph could have been taken for כרא. 2. Moreover, some think the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is a species of partridge, because, although it differs not a little from the partridge in form and appearance, it comes close to it in taste. Hence in Martial the woodcock boasts thus:
Am I a woodcock or a partridge? What does it matter, if the taste is the same?

And this is confirmed by all who call the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] rustica or rusticula, as Pliny, book 10, ch. 38: Some (birds) run, like partridges and woodcocks. For they say rusticula or rustica for perdix rustica [wild partridge]. This is taken from the Greeks, for whom ἡ ἄγρια πέρδιξ [hē agria perdix] is the same as ὁ σκολόπαξ [ho skolopax]. So Herodian defines it. Therefore πέρδιξ [perdix] could have been put by the Greek translators for the skolopax; especially since the Greek σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is little used and occurs nowhere except in two passages of Aristotle , from which it was taken by Hesychius and Herodian. Hence, if instead of ἐφώνησε πέρδιξ [ephōnēse perdix] the Greeks had written ἐφώνησε σκολόπαξ [ephōnēse skolopax], many would have stumbled at this word, struck by its novelty .

One should also compare what Bochart says about the verb דגר below, book III, Ch. XI, p. 409 and 415. Had J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] weighed this properly, I would hardly think he would have written what we now read in the Supplemm. ad Lex. Hebr. vol. II, p. 394, and in the Animadverss. Philologg. ad Jer 17:11. There he declares that the meaning to gather has been attributed to the verb דגר wholly falsely, chiefly because agreement with the Arabic نجر [njr] is lacking; and since someone might adduce the Chaldee dialect, he says that in the passages of the Chaldee version of the O. T. which Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] gives in his Chaldee Lexicon under the word דגר, the notion of collecting was introduced from a false interpretation of the Hebrew word. But these are words, not arguments. And that the interpretation collecting is certain is proved by the Chaldee דְגוֹר, heap, plainly named from collecting, traces of which notion we find in the Arabic نغر [nghr], he snatched, seized. But on these points Michaelis is entirely silent, so that we may be all the more inclined to embrace his conjectures. He invents for himself this sequence of meanings, in the Supplemm. p. 396: "1) דגר, دجر [djr], he fled; hence 2) partridge, because of its very great speed in running [but for that very reason it could also be the ostrich]; and from this noun 3) the denominative to peep, or to cluck." Had someone else put forward such things, he would surely have been rightly and deservedly hissed off the stage by that very eminent man himself. Nor is דגר in Jer 17:11 a substantive, as Michaelis asserts. For the Pathach in the last syllable of the verb דגר is here lengthened to Cametz on account of the accent Paschta; and although this is unusual, it nevertheless happens sometimes even with the lesser accents. Buxtorf has collected examples in the Thesaurus Grammat. book II, ch. 23, p. 611.

Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], in den Vermischten Sammlungen vol. II, p. 57 ff., takes it as certain that قارية [qāriya] is merops apiaster Linn. (Syst. T. 1, p. 460, ed. 13), because some of the things the Arabs say about قارية [qāriya] are also found in the merops, such as the green colour, the shortness of the legs, and the voice drawn back in the throat. But several things keep me from agreeing with that most learned man. First, the merops has a curved and compressed bill, whereas the bill of the Karia is long. Second, the قارية [qāriya] foretells rain, which no one has observed in the merops. Oedmann, however, wrongly twists what the Arabs relate of the قارية [qāriya], that it is a harbinger of rain, to mean that the bird arrives at the season of the year when the regular rains begin to fall in those regions; evidently so that a new similarity between the merops and the قارية [qāriya] might appear. But Oedmann's opinion is wholly overthrown by the fact that the Arabs say entirely different things about the merops apiaster, which they call شُقِرّاق [shuqirrāq] or شُرِقّاق [shuriqqāq], and أَخْيَل [akhyal] (to which names must be added وَرْوَار [warwār] Varvar, from its sharp bill; see Golius' [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] Lexicon p. 2650 and Hasselquist's [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] Travels p. 302). Bochart will give the passages in full from the Arabs below, book II, ch. 25, p. 298 ff.; whoever examines them will readily see that the قارية [qāriya] and the merops are entirely different birds. To mention a few points: they write that the bird أَخْيَل [akhyal] or شُرِقّاق [shuriqqāq] hunts bees, which they do not record of the قارية [qāriya]. Further, whereas the قارية [qāriya] is a bird of good omen, the merops is of ill omen. So even after Oedmann we are no better informed than by Bochart. But it is also doubtful whether the قارية [qāriya] is the same bird as the קרא; for what we read about this bird in the books of the ancient Hebrews and in the Talmudic writers is not enough to form a sure judgement on the matter; and what Oedmann adduces to show that קרא, like قارية [qāriya], is the merops apiaster is too contrived and far-fetched, and moreover, as we have seen, it is plainly false of the قارية [qāriya].

That the Alexandrians either read קָרָא קֹרֵא, or that ἐφώνησε [ephōnēse] crept in here from another version, is an empty conjecture of Schleusner on Michaelis' Animadverss. in Ierem. Michaelis also made some remarks on the ancient versions in the Supplemm. vol. II, p. 394, under the word דגר, but such that they can be corrected from Bochart.
Franciscus Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], with whom Louis de Dieu largely agrees.
Among the birds of Eretz Yisrael and Egypt Hasselquist lists a certain species of Charadrius, related to the herons, whose Arabic name he writes as Kervan, p. 314.

That קֹרֵא is the Damascene partridge, or Linnaeus' tetrao Israelitarum, described by Hasselquist, p. 331 ff., which the Arabs call Katta, قطا [qaṭā], from the sound it utters, is maintained by J. E. FABER on Harmar's Observatt. vol. 1, p. 305, note (SCHODER follows him in Specim. Hieroz. 2, Tit. 12), but with very flimsy arguments, which I forbear to review, since they have already been sufficiently refuted by Oedmann, p. 55.
What is πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ [perdix thēreutēs en kartallō], the hunter partridge in a cage, Sir 11:31 var. 37.

Having dealt with the spurious partridge, we shall say a little about the genuine one, with reference to the well-known passage of Sirach, Sir 11:31 var. 37: Πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ, οὕτως καρδία ὑπερηφάνου, καὶ ὡς ὁ κατάσκοπος ἐπιβλέπει πτῶσιν [Perdix thēreutēs en kartallō, houtōs kardia hyperēphanou, kai hōs ho kataskopos epiblepei ptōsin]; Like a hunter partridge in a cage, so is the heart of the proud man, who like a spy watches for a fall. The sense is that a proud man, when another has been driven to ruin, exults over him in the same way as the hunter partridge in a cage exults over the birds of its own kind that it has led into the snare. For there πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a tame partridge, which by its arts lures wild partridges into the cage or the snares. Aristotle, History book 9, ch. 8: Καὶ τῶν περδίκων δ᾽ οἱ τιθασσοὶ τοὺς ἀγρίους πέρδικας ὀχεύουσι, καὶ ἐπικορίζουσι [kai tōn perdikōn d᾽ hoi tithassoi tous agrious perdikas ocheuousi, kai epikorizousi] (read ἐπικοῤῥίζουσι [epikorrizousi]) καὶ ὑβρίζουσιν. Ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρδικα ὠθεῖται τῶν ἀγρίων ὁ ἡγεμὼν, ἀντιάσας ὡς μαχούμενος, τούτου δ᾽ ἁλόντος ἐν ταῖς πηκταῖς, πάλιν προσέρχεται ἄλλος, ἀντιάσας τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον [kai hybrizousin. Epi de ton thēreutēn perdika ōtheitai tōn agriōn ho hēgemōn, antiasas hōs machoumenos, toutou d᾽ halontos en tais pēktais, palin proserchetai allos, antiasas ton auton tropon]. Tame partridges also tread the wild partridges, and beat them, and treat them with insult. And the leader of the wild ones rushes at the hunter partridge, advancing against it as if to fight. When he has been caught in the wicker cage, another in turn comes forward against it in the same way. You see in both places τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρ- δικα [ton thēreutēn perdika], the hunter partridge, and the wicker cage. For that is properly κάρταλλος [kartallos] in Sirach, as αἱ πήκται [hai pēktai] is in the Philosopher. Hesychius: Κάρταλον [Kartalon] (read Κάρταλλον [Kartallon]): τὸ πλεκτὸν ἀγγεῖον [to plekton angeion] (I would prefer πηκτὸν [pēkton], as in Aristotle) ἐν τοῖς ὀψαρτυτικοῖς κλωβός [en tois opsartytikois klōbos]. Quite correctly. For a cage of this kind is also called κλωβὸς [klōbos], as in Hebrew כלוב club, and in Syriac ܩܠܘܒܝܐ [קלוביא] klubja. Thus Ierem. V, 27: ככלוב מלא עוף, like a cluub (cage) teeming with birds. Here the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܠܘܒܝܐ [איך קלוביא], like a klubja (although the Greeks have ὡς παγὶς ἐφεσταμένη [hōs pagis ephestamenē], and the Arabic مثل فخ منصوب [mithl fakhkh manṣūb] ܡܨܝܕܬܐ [מצידתא] like a set snare, and Jerome like a trap). For the subject is a cage into which birds are lured, as is clear from the whole context. For the verse immediately preceding reads: For among my people are found those who lie in wait like fowlers, setting snares to catch men. And this verse itself: Like a club teeming with birds, so their houses are full of deceit, that is, of things gained and acquired by deceit. Thus, a point that has escaped the lexicographers: just as כלוב club occurs in the Hebrew text of Jeremiah, so also in Greek writers κλουβὸς [kloubos] or κλωβὸς [klōbos] occurs elsewhere too, either for this deceitful cage or for any cage at all. Oppian in the Ixeutica [III, 14.], on the aegithus: It is caught κλωβῷ [klōbō], in a cage, in which another bird, caught earlier, is shut up to lure it by its voice. An old poet in Suidas, under Ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Amphirrhōgas]: Κλωβοὺς τ᾽ ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Klōbous t᾽ amphirrhōgas], cages broken on all sides. Philostorgius book 10, ch. 11 (in my manuscript, which is often more correct than the printed copy), on the Egyptian dwarf: Ὁ δὲ Αἰγύπτιος οὕτω κατεβραχύνετο, ὥστε μηδ᾽ ἀχαρίστως τοὺς ἐν τοῖς κλουβοῖς πέρδικας ἐκμιμεῖσθαι, καὶ συναθύρειν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἔριν ἐκείνους [Ho de Aigyptios houtō katebrachyneto, hōste mēd᾽ acharistōs tous en tois kloubois perdikas ekmimeisthai, kai synathyrein autō pros erin ekeinous]; The Egyptian was so stunted that he imitated, not unpleasingly, the partridges shut up in clubs (or cages), which themselves contended with him in play. And Nicephorus, book 12, ch. 37, says that the same man was παραπλήσιον πέρδικι, καὶ μὴ ἀχάριστον ἐν κλωβῷ τὴν ἐκείνου προσομιλίαν [paraplēsion perdiki, kai mē acharislon en klōbō tēn ekeinou prosomilian]. And Cedrenus, Paris edition, p. 592 B: Ζῶον ἦν τι πτῆνον ἐν κλωβῷ κατὰ τὰ βασίλεια αἰωρούμενον [Zōon ēn ti ptēnon en klōbō kata ta basileia aiōroumenon]. There was a certain bird in the palace, hung up in a clobus (that is, a cage). The Glosses of Philoxenus: Κλωβὸς [Klōbos], cavea [cage]. Therefore a very learned man wishes in vain to change κλουβοῖς [klouhois] in Philostorgius to κλοιοῖς [kloiois] or κλυβοῖς [klybois]. And the translator of Nicephorus rendered the words ἐν κλωβῷ [en klōbō] quite absurdly: In a globe, namely of men. The Talmudists, in the tractate Kilaim, call a cage for catching birds פלצור paltsur, and the Romans transenna. Plautus in the Bacchides, act 4, the scene Nimio:
Now this thrush is going for the worm from the trap. He will hang there nicely today, so well have I set the snare.
And in the Persa, act 4, the scene Cui homini:
Today I shall lead this man into the trap with clever tricks.
And in the Rudens, act 4, the scene Quam mox:
O Gripus, Gripus, in men's lifetime there come to be very many traps, in which they are caught by tricks .

Moreover, others also mention the hunter partridge. Except that instead of "hunter" Athenaeus, book 9, calls it θηρεύοντα πέρδικα [thēreuonta perdika], a hunting partridge. Pliny calls it the fowler's informer, or rather his decoy [illicem], as Turnebus and Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] advise reading. Aelian , in the same sense, says τὸν παλεύοντα πέρδικα [ton paleuonta perdika]. Eustathius of Antioch says τὸν πέρδικα συμπράττοντα τοῖς θηρευταῖς πρὸς τὴν ἄγραν [ton perdika sympratonta tois thēreutais pros tēn agran]. Theodoret, in the Catena on Jeremiah, says πέρδικα θηρατικὸν [perdika thēratikon], adding that such birds are obtained from Babylon. Indeed, this kind of fowling was already in use in the East long ago. Accordingly, in Xenophon, book 1 of the Cyropaedia, Cambyses addresses his son Cyrus thus: Ὄρνιθες δὲ ἐπεπαίδευτό σοι, ὥς τέ σοι μὲν τὰ συμφέροντα ὑπερητεῖν, τὰς δὲ ὁμοφύλους ὄρνιθας ἐξαπατᾷν [Ornithes de epepaideuto soi, hōs te soi men ta sympheronta hypērētein, tas de homophylous ornithas exapatan], "You had trained birds so that they would both serve you in what was useful and deceive birds of the same kind." Whoever wants more on this subject should consult those we have cited. Also Albertus Magnus, where he treats of the cubeth , that is, the female partridge, in Arabic القبج [al-qabj], which he says, when shut in a cage, lures the males to itself. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], however, attributes this very thing to the male in these words: في طبع الذكر ان يخدع امثاله بقرقرته ولهذا اتخذه الصيادون في اشراكهم ليكثر القرقرة فيجتمع الحجل فيقعن معه [fī ṭabʿ al-dhakar an yakhdaʿa amthālahu bi-qarqaratihi wa-li-hādhā ittakhadhahu al-ṣayyādūn fī ashrākihim li-yukthira al-qarqara fa-yajtamiʿa al-ḥajal fa-yaqaʿna maʿahu] "It is the nature of the male to lure birds like itself by its call; therefore hunters take it with them, so that by its frequent calling it may gather the female partridges, which fly to it." But that both sexes are used for this, with varying success, is shown at length by the Philosopher, Aelian and Athenaeus in the places cited above. The Arabic version of Sirach, instead of القبج في القفص [al-qabj fī al-qafaṣ] a partridge in a cage, has, without any sense, الصنج في الرقص [al-ṣanj fī al-raqṣ] a sistrum, or a cymbal in the dance. That this arose through the ignorance of scribes is shown by the similarity of the letters. For Pagnino, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Camerarius, Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom] and others, πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a captured partridge, as though it were πέρδιξ θηρευθεὶς [perdix thēreutheis]. By the same error the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܩܒܢܐ ܕܨܝܕܐ [איך קקבנא דצידא] like a partridge taken in hunting; and the Vulgate, "as a partridge is led into the cage."
That a transenna is not a wicker cage, as Bochart holds, but a net enclosed by two wooden hoops and stretched along the ground, is argued by Joh. Gottl. Schneider on Oppian, Ixeutic. 3, 13, p. 435.

The various names of the quail, שלו, سلوي [salwā], سماني [sumānā], ፈርፈርት [farəfarət] and the various kinds according to the Hebrews: 1. שיכלי, Συκαλὶς [Sykalis], 2. קכלי, Κίχλη [Kichlē]. 3. פסיוני, the pheasant. 4. שליו.

Of the quails which God generously granted to the Israelites when they were perishing of hunger in the desert, Moses writes thus, Exod 16:13: And it came to pass in the evening that quails came up and covered the camp. And Num 11:31: Then a wind going forth from the Lord swept quails from the sea and scattered them over the camp, about a day's journey on this side and about a day's journey on that side, round about the camp, and that to two cubits above the face of the earth. 32. And the people rose up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and gathered the quails. He who gathered least gathered ten cors, and they spread them out widely round about the camp. 33. But while the flesh was still between their teeth, not yet chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled against the people, and the Lord smote the people with a very great plague. 34. Therefore they called the name of that place kibroth thaava (that is, graves of craving), because there they had buried the people of those who had craved. David also, Ps 78:26: He drove the east wind into the heavens, and by his power he brought in the south wind. 27. And he rained flesh upon them as dust, and winged fowl as the sand of the sea. 28. These he cast into the midst of their camp, round about their tents. 29. And they ate until they were filled, having received from him what they had craved. 30. They had not yet put away their craving, and the food was still in their mouth, 31. when the wrath of God came upon them and slew the fattest of them, and laid low the choicest of Israel. And Ps 105:40: When they asked, he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.

The Hebrew name of the quail is שלו selau; the Chaldee is likewise סליו selau; the Syriac ܣܠܘܝ [סלוי] salvai; and the Arabic سلوي [salwā] in the same letters, although they pronounce it selvva. Hence the Qur'an, Azoara 17, entitled اعراف [Aʿrāf] or The Limbo: انزلنا عليهم المن والسلوي [anzalnā ʿalayhim al-manna wa-l-salwā] We sent down upon them manna and quails. Some explain it as honey, because the Arabic word سلوي [salwā] selvva signifies honey as well as quails. Taken in that way, من [mann] manna and سلوي [salwā] selvva would be synonyms. For manna is aerial honey. That is why it is called ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] by the sons of the physicians, and by Amyntas in book 1 of τῶν τῆς Ἀσίας σταθμῶν [tōn tēs Asias stathmōn], cited by Athenaeus, book 11. But Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] and Ibnobitar do better, who assert انه السماني [annahu al-sumānā] that it is the quail. And Alachphas: هو طاير الذي انزله الله تعالي علي بني اسرايل علي القول المشهور وغلط [huwa ṭāʾir alladhī anzalahu Allāh taʿālā ʿalā banī Isrāʾīl ʿalā al-qawl al-mashhūr wa-ghalaṭa] الهزلي فظنه الغسل [al-Hudhalī fa-ẓannahu al-ghasl] It is the bird which God Most High sent down upon the children of Israel, according to the received opinion. So Alhazelius erred, who thought it was honey. There are some among the Arabs who write that the quail is called سلوي [salwā] لانه يسلي الانسان عن ساير الادام [li-annahu yuslī al-insān ʿan sāʾir al-idām] because it makes a man forget other foods. But the Hebrew is שלו selau, which I think should be referred to the verb שלה sala, although the Masoretes wrote the latter with right-hand Sin and the former with left-hand, διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs]. Properly שלה means to live in peace, and then also to abound. Hence it is often rendered by the Greeks εὐθηνεῖν [euthēnein], and שליה εὐθηνία [euthēnia]. It is therefore most likely that quails are named from abundance, since in warm regions scarcely any bird is more prolific, as will appear from what follows . Another name of the quail among the Arabs, سماني [sumānā] sumana, is agreed to be derived from fatness, because it is a very fat bird. Hence R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Exod. XVI.: השלו מין עוף ושמן מאד, The quail, a species of bird which is very fat. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon: הוא שמן מאד, it is very fat. In the Ethiopic Psalter, Ps 104:38, ፈርፈርት፡ [farəfarət] phorphorath is the quail, the name of the genus having been transferred, as it seems, to the species . For among the Talmudists פרפרות parperoth or pharpheroth, ἀρχαϊκῶς [archaikōs], are any delicacies made of small and dainty things, such as used to be served either right at the beginning or at the end of a banquet. Hence in the tractate Berachoth, ch. 6, fol. 42a: ברך על הפרפרות שלפני המזון פטר את הפרפרות שלאחר המזון, He who says the blessing over the pharpheroth (that is, delicacies) that are served before the meal exempts (from the blessing) the pharpheroth that are served after the meal. For one blessing suffices for both. And there the Gloss: ומביאין לפני הם פרפרות להמשיך אכילה כגון פרגיות ודגים ואח״כ מביאין השלחן And they served them pharpheroth (or delicacies) to whet the appetite, such as small birds and fish; then they brought the table, that is, the usual foods.

By the Greek translators שלו selau is rendered not ὄρτυξ [ortyx] coturnix [quail], but ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] ortygometra. Thus Exod 16:13 Ἀνέβη ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē ortygomētra]. And Num 11:31 Ἐξεπέρασεν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Exeperasen ortygomētran]. And in the following verse, Καὶ συνέλεγον τὴν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Kai synelegon tēn ortygomētran]. And Ps 104:40 Ἤιτησαν, καὶ ἦλθεν ὀρτυγομήτρα [Ētēsan, kai ēlthen ortygomētra]. And Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Ἦλθε μάλ᾽ αἰτίζουσιν ἀπείριτος ὀρτυγομήτρα. [Ēlthe mal' aitizousin apeiritos ortygomētra.]

And Sap. XVI, 2. Τροφὴν ἡτοίμασας ὀρτυγομήτραν [Trophēn hētoimasas ortygomētran]. And Sap. XIX, 12. Ἀνέβη αὐτοῖς ἐκ θαλάσσης ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē autois ek thalassēs ortygomētra]. And Philo, book 1 On the Life of Moses, Ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος συνεχὲς ἐκ θαλάττης ἐπιφερόμενον πᾶν τὸ στρατόπεδον ἐπεσκίαζε [Ortygomētrōn nephos syneches ek thalattēs epipheromenon pan to stratopedon epeskiaze]. Nor are there lacking those to whom the ortygometra seems to be a bird different from the quail. Augustine on Exodus, Question 62: To them the ortygometra was given, that is, birds which many Latin translators have rendered quails, although the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. And long before, the Philosopher, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ὅταν δ' ἐντεῦθεν ἀπάρωσιν (οἱ ὄρτυγες) ἥ τε γλωττὶς συναπαίρει, καὶ ἡ ὀρτυγομήτρα, καὶ ὁ ὠτὸς, καὶ ὁ κύγχραμος [Hotan d' enteuthen aparōsin (hoi ortyges) hē te glōttis synapairei, kai hē ortygomētra, kai ho ōtos, kai ho kynchramos]· When they (the quails) depart from here, the lingulaca departs together with them, and the ortygometra, and the otus, and the cynchramus. From these words it is evident that the ortygometra, like the lingulaca, the otus and the cynchramus, is distinguished from the quail. Accordingly, further on in the same place there follows: Ἡ δὲ ὀρτυγομήτρα παραπλήσιος τὴν μορφὴν τοῖς λιμναίοις ἐστὶ [Hē de ortygomētra paraplēsios tēn morphēn tois limnaiois esti]· The ortygometra is similar in form to the marsh birds. And in Athenaeus, book 9, the same bird is described by Alexander of Myndus as τὸ μέγεθος ἡ λίκη τρυγὼν, σκέλη δὲ μακρὰ, δυσθαλπὴς καὶ δειλὴ [to megethos hē likē trygōn, skelē de makra, dysthalpēs kai deilē], of the size of a turtle-dove, with long legs, sensitive to cold and timid. Δυσθαλὴς [Dysthalēs], that is, ill-flourishing, is written there without any sense; but I have emended it to δυσθαλπής [dysthalpēs]. In the opinion of these authors, then, it is plain that the ortygometra differs in species from the quail . For Hesychius, however, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] is nothing other than ὄρτυξ ὑπερμεγέθης [ortyx hypermegethēs], a very large quail, as if the mother or matrix of the others. So among cicadas there is the τεττιγομήτρα [tettigomētra], among sea-urchins the ἐχινομήτρα [echinomētra], among worms the ἰουλομήτρα [ioulomētra] (in Hesychius written ἰουλυμήτρα [ioulymētra]), among the species of lotus Pliny's λωτομήτρα [lōtomētra], and among cities and villages μητρόπολις [mētropolis] and μητροκωμία [mētrokōmia]. For Jansenius [=Cornelius Jansen of Ghent (d. 1576), commentary on Wisdom], on the book of Wisdom, ch. 16, gravely errs in holding that the ortygometra is so called as if μέτρον τῆς ὄρτυγος [metron tēs ortygos], as though it were the measure and regulator of the other quails. For the word is not written with ε, ὀρτυγόμετρα [ortygometra], but with η, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra], so that it plainly means what we said: mother or matrix of quails. And even from this you may infer that the ortygometra differs from the common quail only in size. Therefore many use ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] and coturnix [quail] indiscriminately. Among them is Josephus, who instead of ortygometras has simply ὀρτύγων πλῆθος [ortygōn plēthos], an abundance of quails, book 3, ch. 1. And again in ch. 12: Πίμπλαται τὸ στρατόπεδον ὀρτύγων ἅπαν [Pimplatai to stratopedon ortygōn hapan], The whole camp is filled with quails. Jerome too, who for the word ortygometra, which he retained in the Psalms and in the book of Wisdom, has coturnices [quails] in the Law. And the author of the Mirabilia, among the works of Augustine, book 1, ch. 27, plainly treats these as synonyms when he writes of this miracle: A wind, going forth from the Lord, seized quails across the sea and carried them to the places of the camp. And a little later: Around the places of the camp it set down the ortygometra. Nor was the intention of Aristophanes any different in the Birds, where he would have vows made

to Latona the ortygometra, that is, the quail. For Latona, when about to give birth, is fabled to have come to Delos changed into a quail, and the island was therefore called Ortygia, as if the quail's island. Jupiter too is fabled to have lain with her ὄρτυγι εἰκασθείς [ortygi eikastheis]. So the Scholiast on Pindar has it, in the argument of the Pythians. That Pliny and Solinus also counted the ortygometra among the kind of quails is proved by a great man in the Plinianae Exercitationes, p. 182. Nor do I doubt that the same was the view of the Greek translators, of the author of the book of Wisdom, of Philo and of Apollinaris, for whom שלו selau is ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra]. They preferred this word, however, to the simple ὄρτυξ [ortyx], lest it be thought that God had sent the Israelites common quails, rather than the noblest of them.

This is tolerable, and not to be compared with the absurdities of the masters in the Talmudic tractate Ioma, ch. 8, fol. 75b, where, by the definition of Rabbi Chanina Barabba, ד׳ מיני סליו הן ואלו הן שיכלי וקיכלי ופסיוני ושליו מעליא דכולהו שיכלי גריעי דכולהו שליו, There are four kinds of quails, namely sicli (that is, συκαλὶς [sykalis], ficedula [fig-pecker]), and kichli (that is, κίχλη [kichlē], turdus [thrush]), and phisioni (φασιανὸς [phasianos], phasianus [pheasant]), and selau (the quail properly so called); of which the most excellent is sicli (the fig-pecker), and the meanest of all selau (the quail properly so called). Hence it is that some interpreters render שלו or שלוים as פסיונין, that is, pheasants. So Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] on Exod. XVI, 13: וסליקו פסיינין וחפו ית משריתא, And pheasants came up and covered the camp. And R. Joseph the Blind on Ps 105:40: שאלו בסרא ואיתי פסיונין, They asked for meat, and he brought pheasants: evidently, for men born for the belly and the gullet it is not enough that God granted quails to the fathers with a liberal hand; so they chose to add those birds that most delight the palate: fig-peckers, thrushes and pheasants. Among these the fig-pecker leads the line,
The waxen fig-pecker that gleams with its broad loin
in Martial, book 5. Hence Juvenal, Satire 14:
— — — who, from a spendthrift father, learned to scrape truffles, to season a mushroom, and to drown fig-peckers swimming in the same sauce.

It was peculiar to the fig-pecker that gluttons liked the whole of it, not, as with other birds, the rump alone. Gellius, book 15, ch. 8, from Favorinus: The masters of the cookshop and of luxury, etc., deny that any bird except the fig-pecker ought to be eaten whole. Of other birds and fattened fowls, unless so much is served that the guests are filled from the rump and the lower part, they think the banquet mean through scarcity; and that those who eat the upper part of birds and fowls have no palate. Hence Martial, book 3, Epigram 59:
A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump.
And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his concubine.

After the fig-pecker follows קיכלי, κίχλη [kichlē], the thrush; these birds are often joined as equal, or nearly equal, delicacies. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, ch. 18: Of the birds that rely on flight, the larger give firmer nourishment than the small, such as fig-peckers and the thrush. Suetonius, Tiberius, ch. 42: He gave Asellius Sabinus two hundred thousand sesterces for a dialogue in which he had staged a contest of the mushroom, the fig-pecker, the oyster and the thrush. Plautus in the Captivi, alluding to both birds:
There is need of the Turdetani, need of the Ficedulenses,

But, contrary to the opinion of the Hebrews, those who measure everything by the delights of the palate give first place to the fat thrush. The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Peace: Αἱ κίχλαι εἶδος στρουθῶν, δοκοῦσι δὲ πρὸς τρυφὴν ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν περισπούδαστοι εἶναι μᾶλλον· [Hai kichlai eidos strouthōn, dokousi de pros tryphēn ek tōn allōn ptēnōn perispoudastoi einai mallon] Thrushes are a kind of small bird which are sought out above others for delicacies. Horace, book 1, Epist. 15:
He used to say that those who devour their goods are right, since nothing is better than a fat thrush. — — — —
Among birds the thrush, if anyone contends with me as judge, among quadrupeds the hare holds the first glory.
Perhaps you like a crown woven of roses or rich nard, but I like a crown made of thrushes.
There a crown heavy with fat thrushes.
Nor skilled to know the delicate savour of thrushes.

That is, not a gourmand, a λίχνος [lichnos], who knows well what flavour thrushes have. So formerly at Athens, when discipline was stricter, the young were not permitted ὀψοφαγεῖν [opsophagein], οὐδὲ κιχλίζειν [oude kichlizein], to eat fish, nor thrushes, that is, to dine delicately. And Pompey, when ill, refused to have a thrush sought from Lucullus, although the physician ordered it, using this famous saying: Οὐκοῦν, εἰ μὴ Λούκουλλος ἐτρύφα, Πομπήϊος οὐκ ἂν ἔζησεν; [Oukoun, ei mē Loukoullos etrypha, Pompēios ouk an ezēsen?] Would Pompey then not live without the luxury of Lucullus? This so pleased Plutarch that he related it at least four times: in the Lucullus, in the Pompey, in the Apophthegmata, and in the book Whether an old man should engage in public affairs.

There remains the pheasant, which in former times seems to have been the very summit of delicacies. Thus, according to Athenaeus, book 14, Ptolemy Physcon, although he kept pheasants in great numbers in Egypt, οὐδὲ φασιανικοῦ ὄρνιθός ποτε γεύσασθαι ὡμολόγησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ τι κειμήλιον ἀνακείμενον εἶχε τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας [oude phasianikou ornithos pote geusasthai hōmologēsen, all᾽ hōsper ti keimēlion anakeimenon eiche tous de tous ornithas], declared that he had never tasted a pheasant, but kept these birds as a stored-up treasure. So in Capitolinus Pertinax never ate a pheasant (fasianus, for there it is written with f) at a private banquet, nor sent one to anyone. In Lampridius, Alexander Severus served pheasant at his table only on the Kalends of January, at the Hilaria of the Mother of the Gods, at the Apollinarian games, at the feast of Jupiter, at the Saturnalia, and on festival days of that kind. In Vopiscus, the emperor Tacitus served the pheasant bird only on his own birthday and those of his family, and on the most festive days. And, as Ammianus attests in book 2, Julian forbade a pheasant to be demanded or brought in at the banquet of the Caesar. Evidently rarity added value to a bird that was excellent in itself. Petronius in the Satyricon:
The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, And African fowl please the palate, Because they are not easy to get. — — —

The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, that is, the pheasant, fetched from the Phasis, a river of Colchis. For it was brought from there, as the name itself shows. Agatharchides on the Phasis, in Athenaeus, book 9: Πλῆθος δὲ ὀρνίθων τῶν καλουμένων φασιανῶν φοιτᾷ τροφῆς χάριν πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν στομάτων [Plēthos de ornithōn tōn kaloumenōn phasianōn phoita trophēs charin pros tas embolas tōn stomatōn]; A great multitude of the birds they call pheasants resorts to the mouths of the river for the sake of food. Petronius likewise elsewhere:
— — — — Now the Phasis' wave Is bereft of its birds. — — — —
I was first carried over in the Argive keel: Before that nothing was known to me but the Phasis.
Statius in The Parrot of Melior, book 2 of the Silvae:

Whom neither the Junonian bird with jewelled tail Could surpass in beauty, nor the bird of the icy Phasis. Clement in the Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται ἀπὸ Φάσιδος [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai apo Phasidos]; Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis. Apollonius in Philostratus, book 8, ch. 3: Οὐ κρίνω τοὺς τρυφῶντας ὑπὲρ τοῦ φοινικέου ὄρνιθος, οὐδ' ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐκ Φάσιδος, ἢ Παιόνων [Ou krinō tous tryphōntas hyper tou phoinikeou ornithos, oud' hyper tou ek Phasidos, ē Paionōn]; I do not bring to judgement those given to luxury on account of the crimson bird (the flamingo), nor on account of the bird from the Phasis or from the Paeonians, that is, the pheasant or the crane. Jordanes, On the Affairs of the Goths, ch. 21: To the river Phasis, from which the Phasian birds have come forth that abound throughout the whole world at the banquets of the powerful. Eustathius on Dionysius: Οἱ φασιανοὶ δὲ τὸ ὄρνεον ἐκεῖθεν παρονομασθῆναι δοκοῦσιν ὡς αὐτόθι πλεονάσαντες [Hoi phasianoi de to orneon ekeithen paronomasthēnai dokousin hōs autothi pleonasantes]; The pheasants, a species of bird, seem to have had their name from there, as having abounded in that place. These things, however commonplace, nevertheless escaped the Talmudists and the Chaldee paraphrasts. For they would not have taken for pheasants the birds that the south wind had brought into the camp of the Israelites, had they known that pheasants are brought from the north. I admit, indeed, that pheasants are not sought from Colchis alone. For to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, ἐκ Μηδείας μετεπέμποντο [ek Mēdeias metepempontō], they were fetched from Media, as Athenaeus testifies in the place cited above. And in the province of Ergimul, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] Venetus [=Marco Polo], book 1, ch. 62, describes very large pheasants, having tails ten or eight palms long. But like Colchis and Media, Ergimul too faces the north, for it is part of Tartary. It seems to be the جرمق [jrmq] giormok of the Arabs, because the name is close and in both places there is musk. See the Nubian Geographer, section 9, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 3. The pheasant is called by another name τατύρας [tatyras] tatyras. So testify Hesychius, and Athenaeus in book 9, following Pamphilus of Alexandria in his Glossary and Epaenetus in his Opsartyticus. I have thought this worth noting because the Persian name of the pheasant, تذرو [tadhrū] tazeru, and the Arabic تدرج [tadruj] tadrug, allude to it.

Since the other name of quails, سماني [sumānā], has plainly been given them from their fatness, as Bochart presently notes, ALB. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in Originib. Hebr. book 1, ch. 3, §39, p. 231, believes that these birds were also called שלו, سلوي [salwā], from that same quality; there he shows that the root سلي [s-l-y], שלה, also contains the notion of rich and fat. — HIOB Ludolf [=Hiob Ludolf, Historia Aethiopica (1681) and its Commentarius (1691)] (in Commentar. ad Histor. Aethiop. on book 1, ch. 13, no. 96, p. 172, and in Adpend. ad Histor. Aethiop.), having come upon a passage of Porphyry, περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψυχῶν [peri apochēs empsychōn] book 1, §2, where he says that an army in Africa suffering from famine was saved by the arrival of locusts, contends that the שלוים are locusts. For it is well known that locusts are a very common food in almost the whole of the East. The Jews living in Arabia today also think that the שלוים are locusts, and Niebuhr [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] himself agrees with them, Beschreib. von Arab. p. 172. But the strongest objection is that in the Arabic, Syriac and Chaldee dialects this word without any doubt means quails. Nor is שלו found among the names of locusts in Lev 11:22. More has been noted by I. E. Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)], ad Harmar. 2, p. 427, and Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] in the Vermischten Sammlungen vol. 4, ch. 6, p. 58. — That the שלוים are flying fish, met with in the Red Sea, which the inhabitants of those lands are also accustomed to eat (cf. Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] p. 255; Niebuhr Beschreib. von Arab. p. 176; Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] Descriptt. Animal. p. 16), was formerly the conjecture of OL. RUDBECK (Ichthyol. Bibl. Specim. I.), which I. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] elaborated further in his Commentat. super lege Mosaica Deut 22:6–7. §9, and in the Addition to §9, in Syntagm. Commentatt. vol. 2, p. 104 and 115; afterwards, however, he himself rejected it, and rightly so, since in the Red Sea there is no such abundance of flying fish that many thousands of people could be fed with them daily. Nor can these fish rise more than three or four feet above the sea. In addition, flying fish are not an ordinary food; rather, dried, they serve as a medicine for strengthening the stomach. Cf. Niebuhr p. 177. For other points see Faber and Oedmann, loc. cit. — The Seleucid birds [Turdus Seleucis Forsskål vol. 6 a, p. 5, no. 16, Arabic سمرمر [samarmar], Turdus roseus Linnaeus 2, p. 819, no. 15, 13th ed.; Oedmann 2, ch. 6, p. 103], whose coming (as Pliny reports, Hist. Nat. 10, ch. 26, sect. 39) the inhabitants of Mount Casius obtain by prayer from Jupiter when locusts are ravaging their crops; it has not been discovered where they come from or where they go, and they are never seen except when their protection is needed, were suspected by HERMANN VON DER HARDT to be the same as the שלוים; RATHLEF also fought for this opinion in his Append. Acridotheol., but with futile arguments, which I. D. Michaelis long ago refuted in the commentary cited, p. 104 ff. — There is a bird, common in Syria, Arabia and Egypt, of the size of a partridge or turtle-dove, of the grouse family, with hard and dry flesh, which the Arabs, from the call it utters, call قَطًّا [qaṭṭan] Katta (as Hasselquist and Russell [=Alexander Russell, The Natural History of Aleppo (1756)] write it) (see Golius's [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)] Lexic. p. 1934, where a description of this bird is also found); in Linnaeus it is Tetrao supra varius; rectricibus duabus intermediis duplo longioribus subulatis, see Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 754, no. 11, under the heading Alchata, where the synonyms and those who have treated of it are also listed. That this bird is the שלו of the Hebrews is so certain to Hasselquist that in his Travels p. 333, after describing it fairly accurately under the name Tetrao Israelitarum, he uses these words: this, if any, is the bird taken as food by the Israelites in the desert, since it is common in the places through which they wandered. But this very point holds also of the quail, and what is read of the שלוים in Moses does not fit any other bird, as we shall see in the following Chapter. — I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 442, thinks the Arabs' Katta is the same as the quail, though these birds are carefully distinguished by all who have written on the natural history of birds.
The Arabs' فُرْفُر [furfur] and فُرْفُور [furfūr] seem to agree with the Ethiopic word; Golius, in his Lexicon p. 1773, on the authority of Firuzabadi, says it is the name of some bird.

The ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] of Aristotle and Athenaeus is the Rallus alis rufo-ferrugineis of Linnaeus, or Crex (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 711), in French Roi de cailles, in German Wiesenschnarre or Wachtelkönig. At Alexandria this bird is today called سلوى [salwā], according to Niebuhr, p. 176, Descr. Arab. But I think that the Greek translators understood by ὀρτυγομήτραις [ortygomētrais] rather very large quails, which Bochart considers probable; read what follows from him.

Five questions about the quails of Moses are resolved. I. How many times did God give quails to the Israelites? II. Are they wholesome food? III. From where did these quails come? IV. In what quantity did they come? V. What was the punishment of those who ate the quails?

Concerning the quails of Moses five questions above all are asked. 1. How many times did God send them to the Israelites? 2. Were they wholesome food? 3. From where did they come? 4. In what quantity? 5. Why did the Israelites provoke God against themselves by eating them?

I. To the first question many, without having examined the matter sufficiently, answer that they were sent only once. Yet many things not only suggest but plainly prove that this miracle was repeated.
