For in Exod 16:13 quails are given together with the manna in the desert of Sin, shortly after the exodus from Egypt, on the fifteenth day of the second month, before they had come to Mount Sinai, as is clear from the beginning of the chapter. But in Num 11:6, when the people had murmured because they saw nothing but manna, God, in verse 31 of the same chapter, grants them quails at Kibroth-thaava, where they finally arrived after leaving the desert of Sinai, Num 33:16, and that on the third day, Num 10:33. They had departed from Sinai, moreover, in the second year, on the twentieth day of the second month, Num 10:11. So this miracle must have happened a year later than the former. Furthermore, the first quails were granted by God for only one day, the later ones for a whole month. Accordingly the former covered only the camp; the latter were also outside the camp, scattered on this side and that for a day's journey. And it was at the eating of these, not of the former, that God, gravely angered, struck the people with a great plague. Therefore Josephus relates the two stories in different places: the former in chapter 1, the latter in chapter 13 of book 3 of the Antiquities. So also Jerome, Epistle 127 to Fabiola, at stations 10 and 13. Their objection, that there is no reason why God should have been angry at these rather than at the former, is refuted at the end of the chapter. Now, if you ask how Moses in Num 11:21 could doubt whether flesh could be found sufficient for so many thousands, if he had already seen a similar miracle, Exod 16:13, I answer that the earlier miracle was not in every respect like the later. For in the earlier one, as we have already observed, God had fed this people with flesh for only one day. But here he promises to do the same for a whole month, which seemed to Moses far greater. Therefore he raises this very point against God: The people, he says, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and you say that you will give them flesh for a whole month. Besides, who does not know that Moses, although at Raphidim he had drawn water from the struck rock, Exod 17:1 etc., nevertheless doubted when he was ordered to repeat the same miracle in the desert of Sin and at Kades, Num 10:1 etc.? So let no one be surprised that the same happened to him when God promised the people flesh which he had already given before elsewhere.

II. On the second question, writers observe that quails feed on hellebore, or, what is the same, veratrum. Aristotle, On Plants, book 1, chapter 5: Ὁ ἐλλέβορος ἀνθρώποις μὲν δηλητήριον, τροφὴ δὲ τοῖς ὄρτυξι· [Ho elleboros anthrōpois men dēlētērion, trophē de tois ortyxi]; Hellebore is poison to men, but food to quails. Galen, to Piso: Ὁ ἐλλέβορος τῶν ὀρτυγίων ἐστὶ τροφή· [Ho elleboros tōn ortygiōn esti trophē]; Hellebore is the food of quails. And On Foods, book 2, ch. 6: Καὶ μὲν τὸν ἐλλέβορον οἱ ὄρτυγες, καὶ οἱ ψᾶρες τὸ κώνειον ἐσθίοντες οὐδὲν βλάπτονται· [Kai men ton elleboron hoi ortyges, kai hoi psares to kōneion esthiontes ouden blaptontai]; Quails are not harmed at all by eating hellebore, nor starlings by eating hemlock. And On Temperaments, book 3, ch. 4: Τοῖς μὲν ὄρτυξιν ἐλλέβορος τροφὴ, τοῖς δὲ ἀνθρώποις φάρμακον· [Tois men ortyxin elleboros trophē, tois de anthrōpois pharmakon]; To quails hellebore is food, but to men poison. So also Alexander of Aphrodisias in the Preface to book 1 of the Problems, and Basil, Ambrose and Eustathius on the Hexaemeron. To the same point belong these lines of Lucretius, book 4, verse 641:
Moreover, veratrum is a sharp poison to us, but it fattens goats and quails.

But Sextus Empiricus, book 1, says otherwise: Τὸ γοῦν κώνειον πιαίνει τοὺς ὄρτυγας [to goun kōneion piainei tous ortygas]. Hemlock fattens quails. Others report this of the starling. And the Arabs, again, say otherwise. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt], under The Quail: يغتدي بالبيش والبيش [yaghtadī bi-l-bīsh wa-l-bīsh] هو سم قاتل [huwa samm qātil] It feeds on napellus, which is a deadly poison. Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], in the chapter بيش [bīsh], that is On napellus: والسماني يغتدي به ولا يموت منه [wa-l-summānā yaghtadī bihi wa-lā yamūtu minhu] Quails feed on it, and yet do not die from it. The same is in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]. Napellus, however, is neither hellebore nor hemlock, but aconite, λυκοκτόνον [lykoktonon]. However that may be, all agree that quails feed on poisons. And for that very reason not a few forbid them as unwholesome. Pliny, book 10, ch. 23: To quails the seed of poison is the most welcome food; for which reason they have banished them from the table. And following him Solinus: Their most welcome food is the seeds of poisonous plants; for which reason the tables of the prudent have banished them. Didymus in the Geoponica, book 14: Οἱ ὄρτυγες, ἐλλέβορον ἐπινεμόμενοι, τοὺς ἐσθίοντας εἰς κίνδυνον ἐμβάλλουσι, κατατεινομένους, καὶ ἰλιγγιῶντας· [Hoi ortyges, elleboron epinemomenoi, tous esthiontas eis kindynon emballousi, katateinomenous, kai ilingiōntas] Quails that feed on hellebore bring those who eat them into such danger that they are distended and convulsed, as if seized by vertigo . Avicenna, however, attributes this not so much to their eating hellebore as to a bad quality inherent in them. His words are in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter سماني [summānī], that is On the quail: اكل لحمه يخاف منه التمدد والتشنج لا لانه ياكل الخربق فقط بل لان في جوهره هذه القوة واظن ان اغتداه بالخربق هو والمشاكلة المزاج [akl laḥmihi yukhāfu minhu al-tamaddud wa-l-tashannuj lā li-annahu yaʾkulu al-kharbaq faqaṭ bal li-anna fī jawharihi hādhihi al-quwwa wa-aẓunnu anna ightidāʾahu bi-l-kharbaq huwa wa-l-mushākala al-mizāj] From eating its flesh tetanus and spasm are to be feared, not only because it eats hellebore, but also because this property is inherent in its substance; indeed I think it feeds on hellebore precisely because this food suits its temperament. From Pliny and Solinus it is added that it is customary to spit at it on account of the falling sickness, which alone of animals, apart from man, they fear. Rasis, however, says something very different in his book to Almansor, in the chapter On the flesh of birds, which is the tenth of the third treatise: The flesh of the starna (the partridge) is found to be lighter than the flesh of any other bird, and so more suitable for those who wish to be kept on a delicate regimen. After it the flesh of the quail stands second in goodness. And a little later: The flesh of chickens likewise is placed after it. The flesh of the quail, however, is more productive of good blood, and increases semen. And Ibnozohar, in the book On Foods, chapter On quails: وامزاجها فكانها وسط بين مزاج الدجاج والحجل وهي الي مزاج الدجاج اميل وهي الطف جوهرا واميل الي حر قليلا وهي جيدة الكيموص طيبة الطعم نافعه للاصحا والناقهين ولحومها تفتت الحصا وتدر البول [wa-amzājuhā fa-ka-annahā wasaṭ bayna mizāj al-dajāj wa-l-ḥajal wa-hiya ilā mizāj al-dajāj amyal wa-hiya alṭaf jawharan wa-amyal ilā ḥarr qalīlan wa-hiya jayyidat al-kaymūs ṭayyibat al-ṭaʿm nāfiʿa li-l-aṣiḥḥāʾ wa-l-nāqihīn wa-luḥūmuhā tufattitu al-ḥaṣā wa-tudirru al-bawl] It has a temperament roughly midway between the hen and the partridge, yet so that it comes closer to the temperament of the hen. But its substance is finer, and inclines a little more to the hot. It also yields good chyme and has an excellent flavour, and is beneficial to the healthy and strong. And its flesh breaks up the stone and promotes urine. And in the last century Nicolaus Massa [=Niccolò Massa, physician of Venice (d. 1569), Epistolae medicinales], in his Medical Letters, cited by Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: Quails, that is, qualeae, are of the same temperament as partridges, but drier. They nourish well. And Aloysius Mundella [=Luigi Mondella, physician of Brescia (16th c.), Epistolae medicinales]: Aristotle treats of quails and partridges in the same chapter, as if the two did not differ much in nature. Therefore, since they seem to be of the same kind, it remains clear that the quail is not, as is commonly said, of bad juice, nor to be banished from the table, except perhaps that of the poor, who are accustomed to eat cheaper foods. Nor would I judge that one should abstain from eating it because it is seized by the falling sickness, or because it feeds on poison. For we know some animals which, although they are sometimes nourished by poisons, nevertheless produce good and harmless juice. For example, starlings feed on hemlock, as the same Galen attests; who does not eat them without harm? nourished, are nevertheless of good juice, like starlings, which feed on hemlock. And if the quail does feed on hellebore, which is not yet established for us, it is more probable that it is helped by that food than harmed. Therefore I judge that the nourishment of the quail, which is also of no unpleasant flavour, is to be praised rather than condemned. For Averroes too praises the flesh of quails wonderfully, as producing good juice. And although they sometimes feed on poison, and are sometimes afflicted with the falling sickness, I think this is not always so, nor true of all, but perhaps of those that are caught and kept in aviaries. For on this reasoning cocks too would have to be rejected, because some of them are sometimes seized by the falling sickness. Nor would I pass over this: that the Lord our God would not have fed the people of Israel, whom he loved most ardently, with quails to the point of satiety while they passed through those desert places, had they not been an approved and wholesome food. So Mundella, and more, which the reader may see there. And if one wishes to go further back, it will appear that the makers of myths thought highly of the quail, since they relate that Hercules, slain by Typhon, was recalled to life by the smell of a quail brought to him by Iolaus, and that this is why the Phoenicians sacrificed quails to him. Athenaeus, book 9: Εὔδοξος δὲ ὁ Κνίδιος ἐν πρώτῳ γῆς περιόδου τοὺς Φοίνικας λέγει θύειν τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ ὄρτυγας, διὰ τὸ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, τὸν Ἀστερίας καὶ Διὸς, πορευόμενον εἰς Λιβύην, ἀναιρεθῆναι μὲν ὑπὸ Τυφῶνος. Ἰολάου δ᾽ αὐτῷ προσενέγκαντος ὄρτυγα, καὶ προσαγάγοντος, ὀσφρανθέντα ἀναβιῶναι. [Eudoxos de ho Knidios en prōtō gēs periodou tous Phoinikas legei thyein tō Hēraklei ortygas, dia to ton Hērakléa, ton Asterias kai Dios, poreuomenon eis Libyēn, anairethēnai men hypo Typhōnos. Iolaou d᾽ autō prosenenkantos ortyga, kai prosagagontos, osphranthenta anabiōnai.] This gave rise to a proverb current among the Greeks,
Ὄρτυξ ἔσωσεν Ἡρακλῆν τὸν καρτερὸν [Ortyx esōsen Hēraklēn ton karteron], The quail rescued mighty Hercules.

If there is any truth in this fable, I would suppose that Hercules, seized by the falling sickness (which, they say, is called Herculean because Hercules was subject to it), lay as if dead, and, revived and refreshed by the smell of a quail brought to him, recovered. At any rate, among the remedies most effective against the falling sickness, the brain of quails is prescribed: ground in myrtle ointment and stored in a tin vessel, if it is smeared on the patient's face, he will at once rise up healthy. Galen, On Easily Prepared Remedies, book 3, chapter 155: A very effective remedy for the falling sickness. Store the brain of quails, ground in myrtle ointment, in a tin vessel; and when you see someone who has collapsed from the falling sickness, smear his face with it. You will marvel at the efficacy of this natural remedy, for the patient will rise up at once. And Assariph [=al-Sharif (probably al-Idrisi), a source that Ibn al-Baytar quotes], in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], on the quail: اذا لعقت مرارته نفعت من الصرع [idhā luʿiqat marāratuhu nafaʿat min al-ṣarʿ] If its gall is licked, it is beneficial for epilepsy. Thus, with regard to epilepsy, the quail is like the elk, which is believed to be especially subject to this disease; yet there is a constant tradition among physicians that epileptics are cured by its hooves. So the quail not only does not infect people with the contagion of the disease it suffers from, but is even a powerful amulet against it . Yet even granting, though not conceding, that frequent eating of quail is less wholesome for the body, it would not follow that God provided badly for the Israelites in the desert when He fed them with quails. 1. Because it was not their ordinary food. 2. Because He who granted quails to His people by a miracle could also remove whatever was harmful in them, and by this very fact bear witness to His goodness and power, that He kept them healthy and unharmed whatever food they used.

III. To the third question, from where these quails came, Moses answers in Num 11:31 that a wind, proceeding from the Lord, brought them מן הים, from the sea. And the author of the book of Wisdom, chapter 19, verse 12: For their comfort the ortygometra came up to them from the sea. Some have taken this as though they had been born in the sea itself. I see that some of the Arabs hold this opinion. The same Assariph as above: سماني هو طاير يخرج من البحر [samānī huwa ṭāyir yakhruj min al-baḥr] The quail is a bird that comes out of the sea. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وهو من الطيور القواطع لا يدري من اين يابي حتي ان بعض الناس يقول انه يخرج من البحر المالح فانه يري طاير عليه واحد جناحية فيه منغمس والاخر منشور كالقلع والاهل مصر به عنايه ويتغالون في ثمنه [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ lā yudrā min ayna yābī ḥattā anna baʿḍ al-nās yaqūl annahu yakhruj min al-baḥr al-māliḥ fa-innahu yurā ṭāyir ʿalayhi wāḥid janāḥiyya fīhi munghamis wa-al-ākhar manshūr ka-al-qilʿ wa-al-ahl miṣr bihi ʿināya wa-yataghālūn fī thamanihi] It is one of the migratory birds, and it is so unknown where it comes from that some assert that it comes out of the salt sea and is seen flying over it, with one of its wings immersed and the other spread out like a sail. The Egyptians are very keen on it, and therefore hold this bird to be precious. Nor does Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] seem to have meant anything else when, on the words of Moses in Exod 16:13, And the quail came up and covered the camp, he added this little note: אולי עלתה מפאת ים, Perhaps it had come up from the region of the sea. And among the Greeks, Phanodemus is thought to have held the same view, when he wrote in his Atthis that Delos was called Ortygia by the ancients, that is, the island of quails, παρὰ τὰς ἀγέλας τῶν ζώων τούτων, φερομένας ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους, ἱζάνειν εἰς τὴν νῆσον διὰ τὸ εὔορμον εἶναι [para tas agelas tōn zōōn toutōn, pheromenas ek tou pelagous, hizanein eis tēn nēson dia to euormon einai], because many flocks of these creatures, borne from the sea, settle on that island, since it is a convenient resting place. And Kiranides, in book 1, talks nonsense: that from tunnies cast up on the shore of Libya, as they rot, worms are born which have first the form and size of flies, then of locusts, and finally of quails. But whatever they thought, it is certain that quails are born and feed on bare ground. The Sacred Writer therefore writes that they came from the sea in the sense in which Pliny, book 10, ch. 29, said: A great number of wood pigeons flies every year from the sea into the territory of Volaterrae. Not that they are produced in it, but that, having crossed it, they betake themselves to the area around Volaterrae. So, then, the wind is said to have brought the quails from the sea because, having crossed the Arabian sea, it had carried them from Egypt into the camp of the Israelites. To this belong these words of Josephus, Antiqu. book 3, ch. 1: Καὶ μετ᾽ ὀλίγον ὀρτύγων πλῆθος· τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος, ἐπίπταται τὴν μεταξὺ θάλασσαν ὑπερελθόν [Kai met' oligon ortygōn plēthos; trephei de touto to orneon, hōs ouden heteron, ho Arabios kolpos, epiptatai tēn metaxy thalassan hyperelthon]. And shortly afterwards a great number of quails flew in, having crossed the intervening sea; for the Arabian gulf nourishes this kind of bird more than any other. Not far from there is Rhinocolura, where, as Diodorus reports in book 1, page 38, a great number of quails flying in from the sea is caught, in these words: Καλάμην γὰρ κείροντες ἐκ τῆς ὁμόρου χώρας, καὶ ταύτην σχίζοντες λίνα παραμήκη κατασκεύαζον. ταῦτα δὲ παρὰ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν ἐπὶ πολλοὺς σταδίους ἱστάντες τὰς θήρας τῶν ὀρτύγων ἐποιοῦντο (φέρονται γὰρ οὗτοι κατ᾽ ἀγέλας μείζους ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους) οὓς θηρεύοντες ἤθροιζον πλῆθος ἱκανὸν εἰς διατροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς· [Kalamēn gar keirontes ek tēs homorou chōras, kai tautēn schizontes lina paramēkē kateskeuazon. tauta de para ton aigialon epi pollous stadious histantes tas thēras tōn ortygōn epoiounto (pherontai gar houtoi kat' agelas meizous ek tou pelagous) hous thēreuontes ēthroizon plēthos hikanon eis diatrophēn heautois] Cutting reeds from the neighbouring region and splitting them, they made long nets; setting these up near the shore over many stadia, they caught the quails, which betake themselves there in great flocks from the sea, and gathered as many of them as sufficed for their sustenance. Here it should be noted that he says the quails φέρεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους [pheresthai ek tou pelagous], just as Moses above.

These things, indeed, are obvious enough. But no one could easily say how they are to be reconciled with these words of David on the same miracle, Ps 78:26–27. He stirred up the east wind in the heaven, and by his power drove on the south wind, and rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. For what need was there for the east wind to be stirred up so that quails might be carried from Egypt into Arabia across the Arabian gulf, when this would rather be the task of Favonius and the western winds? For with respect to Egypt and Africa, the east wind does not blow into Arabia but blows out of Arabia, according to the line of the Poet:
The east wind withdrew to the Dawn and the Nabataean realms.

To the Nabataean realms, that is, into Arabia, where the Nabataean Arabs live, descended from Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael, Gen 25:13. The Israelites were in those places at that time. Thus in Exod 10:19 it is not the east wind that drives the locusts from Egypt into the Red Sea, but another wind, contrary to it, namely the west wind. For Moses says: The Lord sent a very strong west wind, which carried off those locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. This same wind, then, ought to have carried the quails from Egypt across the Red Sea into Arabia, not the east wind, as the Psalm has it. This objection seems easy to meet from Jerome's version, which reads: He took away the east wind from heaven, and brought in by his strength the south-west wind (Africus). As if, when the one was removed, the other was brought in. The version of the Greeks and of the Vulgate translator is the same, except that instead of the east wind they have Νότον [Noton], the south wind. For the Greeks read: Ἀπῆρεν Νότον ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν ἐν τῇ δυναστείᾳ αὐτοῦ Λίβα [Apēren Noton ex ouranou, kai epēgagen en tē dynasteia autou Liba]. And the Vulgate translator: He removed the south wind from heaven, and brought in by his power the south-west wind. Thus in their view the Hebrew word יסע should be rendered ἀπῆρεν [apēren], he removed or he took away. If this version is accepted, there will be no objection left. Nor will it seem easy to reject, both because it has weighty authorities and because the verb הסיע, from which יסע comes, frequently occurs in the sense of removing and taking away. For it is the Hiphil of the verb נסע, which means to set out, whether from a place or to a place. So in the Hiphil הסיע is to cause someone to set out either from a place or to a place. And said of a wind, it can mean that the wind is taken away as well as that it is sent in. Yet there are, as I at least think, compelling reasons why יסע cannot be taken in this passage in the sense of taking away. First, the Psalmist borrows this יסע from Moses, whose words are, Num 11:31. And a wind from the Lord נסע went forth, and brought quails across from the sea. Thus, just as in Moses נסע does not mean that the wind withdrew but that it advanced to bring the quails, so in the Psalmist יסע, which is the Hiphil of the same verb, does not mean that the wind was removed but that it was sent in to bring the quails. Second, ἀπῆρεν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ [apēren ex ouranou], he took away from heaven, would in Hebrew be יסע מן השמים. But the text has בשמים, which means in heaven or into heaven, not from heaven. Accordingly יסע there is not to take away but to bring in and to send in. For as a thing is taken away from a place, so it is brought into a place. Third, to what purpose would it be said, as in Jerome, He took away the east wind and brought in the south-west wind, and in the Greek version, Ἀπῆρεν Νότον, καὶ ἐπήγαγεν Λίβα [Apēren Noton, kai epēgagen Liba], He took away the south wind, and brought in the south-west wind, since these winds are not contrary and can stand and blow at the same time? Hence the greatest Poet:
Together rush Eurus and Notus, and, thick with storms, Africus. — — — — — —
And long before, Homer, Iliad 16, line 765:
Ὡς δ᾽ Εὖρός τε Νότος τ᾽ ἐριδαίνετον ἀλλήλοιϊν· [Hōs d' Euros te Notos t' eridaineton allēloiin]

Fourth, in this whole Psalm, as often elsewhere in the poetic books of the Hebrews, the two hemistichs are generally parallel and explain each other. From this it follows that יסע here is roughly the same as וינהג, and he brought in, in the second hemistich, in which we read that God by his power brought in the south wind. Fifth, if the matter is decided by authority, against the Greeks and Jerome we set the Chaldee and the Syriac, and both Arabic versions , and the Hebrews, as many as there are, and the more recent interpreters, as many as I have been able to see. For not one of them occurs for whom יסע here means to take away. Rather, all understand that the east wind was stirred up and sent in by God. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae]: He stirred up the east wind in the heaven; Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot]: He made the east wind set out in the heavens; Felix Pratensis [=Felix of Prato, Latin Psalter from the Hebrew (1515)]: He moved the east wind in the heavens; Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)]: The east wind having been driven through the heaven. Add to these all the vernacular versions. Let this therefore stand: that God, according to David's meaning, moved this wind, not removed it; brought it in, not took it away. But for the matter to be understood, it must be noted that the Israelites were then in the desert of Paran, having already advanced a three days' journey beyond Mount Sinai, Num 10:12 33., and had the farthest gulf of the Arabian sea to the south; and therefore the wind that carried the quails from the Red Sea to their camp is rightly called by David תימן Theman, that is, southern. But why is the same wind called קדים kadim, that is, eastern? Aben Ezra and Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] answer that it is called by both names because it was מזרחי דרומי, that is, partly eastern, partly southern, which you might call in one word Euro-Notus . This is utterly false. For that wind was in no way eastern, as those acquainted with the region know. Yet it is called קדים Kadim, and I shall now say why. Although four cardinal winds are established, which are in turn subdivided into many more, nevertheless the learned observe that in the ancient books of the philosophers and physicians, and especially in Aristotle and Theophrastus, to designate the conditions of weather and air produced by the winds, only τὰ βόρεια [ta boreia] and τὰ νότια [ta notia] are named, never τὰ ἑσπέρια [ta hesperia] or τὰ ἑῷα [ta heōa]. Hence Aristotle, Meteorol. book 2, ch. 6, after naming eight principal winds with their side-winds, says: Ὅλως δὲ τὰ μὲν βόρεια τούτων καλεῖται, τὰ δὲ νότια [Holōs de ta men boreia toutōn kaleitai, ta de notia]. In general, of these some are called northern, others southern. That is, the western winds, as colder, are assigned to the north wind, and the eastern ones to the south wind, because they are warmer. He adds this in these words: Προστίθηται δὲ τὰ μὲν ζεφυρικὰ τῷ βορέᾳ, ψυχρότερα γὰρ, διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ δυσμῶν πνεῖν· τῷ δὲ νότῳ ἀπηλιωτικὰ, θερμότερα γὰρ, τῷ (read διὰ τὸ) ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς πνεῖν [Prostithētai de ta men zephyrika tō borea, psychrotera gar, dia to apo dysmōn pnein; tō de notō apēliōtika, thermotera gar, tō (dia to) apo anatolēs pnein]. The eastern wind is warmer than the western for this reason, ὅτι πλείω χρόνον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιόν ἐστι [hoti pleiō chronon hypo ton hēlion esti], because it is longer under the sun. That is why in Greek it is called ἀπηλιώτης [apēliōtēs], and in Latin Subsolanus. Accordingly, in the Politics, book 4, ch. 3, the same Aristotle contends that all forms of commonwealth are to be referred either to democracy or to oligarchy, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν πνευμάτων λέγεται τὰ μὲν βόρεια, τὰ δὲ νότια, τάδ' ἄλλα τούτων παρεκβάσεις [kathaper epi tōn pneumatōn legetai ta men boreia, ta de notia, tad' alla toutōn parekbaseis], just as among the winds some are called northern, others southern, and the rest are deviations from these. Hence it is, he says, that they say τὸν μὲν ζέφυρον τοῦ βορέου, τοῦ δὲ νότου τὸν εὖρον [ton men zephyron tou boreou, tou de notou ton euron], that the zephyr belongs to the north wind, and the east wind to the south wind. To this belong the verses of Lucilius in the book on Cotys, king of the Thracians, which, badly corrupted in Nonius under the word Demagis, Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] restores thus:
King Cotys used to say that he knew only two winds, the south wind and the north wind, and moreover, that those little south winds from the storm-cloud he neither knew nor thought existed.

Since it is clear from this that the east wind is related to the south wind, in David קדים Kadim and תימן Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, could be taken as synonyms, so that in this passage Kadim is nothing other than the following Theman. And not only here but frequently elsewhere the sacred writers attribute to the wind Kadim things that seem rather to be proper to the south wind. For it scorches the crops, Gen 41:6. It also scorches vines and the fruits of trees, Ezek 17:10 and XIX, 12. It dries up the waters of the sea and of springs, Exod 14:21 and Hos 13:15. By its force it shatters ships, Ps 48:8 and Ezek 27:26. Finally, it overturns and scatters everything, Job 27:21 and Jer 18:17. Accordingly it is called a harsh wind, Isa 27:8 and חרשית, making people deaf with its roar, Jonah 4:8. Nor is it anywhere called Εὖρος [Euros] by the Greeks, but Νότος [Notos] or Καύσων [Kausōn], that is, the south wind and the burning wind. And God's words in Deut 32:22. A fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn to the lowest hell, and shall consume the earth and its produce, Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] refer to this same wind by this paraphrase of theirs, קדום תקיף כאשא, An east wind, strong as fire, has gone out from me in anger, etc. Finally, Theodoret compares the east wind and the south wind as similar winds, almost the same, when he writes in Question 8 on Genesis, Εὔρου ἢ Νότου πνέοντος, τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ διαλύεσθαι [Eurou ē Notou pneontos, to pepēgos hydōr dialyesthai], When the east wind or the south wind blows, frozen water is dissolved. Therefore, although רוח הקדים, properly and strictly speaking, means the east wind (as both the origin of the word shows and the passage Ezek 42:16 etc., where the north, south and west winds are distinguished from the wind Kadim), nevertheless, because the winds Kadim and Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, have certain things in common, I think the Hebrews used these words interchangeably. And hence it is that קדים Kadim is frequently rendered Νότος [Notos] by the Greeks: as in Exod 10:13 and XIV, 21. Num 34:15. Job 38:24. Ezek 27:26 and in that very passage of the Psalm with which we are dealing, where they render Kadim and Theman as Νότον καὶ Λίβα [Noton kai Liba]. Therefore the same wind seems to be meant by both words , namely the south wind or the south-west wind , which brought the quails to the Israelites from the interior of Egypt .

But one objection can be raised: namely, that quails do not fly when the south wind blows. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Οἱ δὲ ὄρτυγες, ὅταν πέσωσιν, ἐὰν μὲν εὐδία ᾖ βόρειον ᾖ, συνδυάζονταί τε, καὶ ἠρεμοῦσιν. ἐὰν δὲ νότος, χαλεπῶς ἔχουσι, διὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι πτητικοί· ὑγρὸς γὰρ καὶ βαρὺς ὁ ἄνεμος· διὸ καὶ οἱ θηρεύοντες ἐπιχειροῦσι τοῖς νοτίοις· [Hoi de ortyges, hotan pesōsin, ean men eudia ē boreion ē, syndyazontai te, kai ēremousin. ean de notos, chalepōs echousi, dia to mē einai ptētikoi; hygros gar kai barys ho anemos; dio kai hoi thēreuontes epicheirousi tois notiois] "When quails fall (rather, ὅταν πέτονται [hotan petontai], when they fly), if the sky is clear and the wind is from the north, they pair and stay quiet. But if the south wind blows, they fare badly, because they do not fly easily; for that wind is moist and heavy. That is why fowlers go after them when the winds are southerly." And Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: "They do not fly with the south wind, that is, a moist and heavy wind. Yet they want to be carried by a breeze, because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength," etc. "Thus they fly most with the north wind." And Solinus: "They never set out with the south wind, for they fear the force of its swollen blast. They entrust themselves mostly to the north winds, so that a drier and stronger breath may more easily carry forward their rather fat and therefore sluggish bodies." To the same effect is the fact that the winds called Ornithiae, as if they brought birds, are described as blowing from the north, or at least from the west. Aristotle, in the book De mundo: Οἱ δὲ ὀρνιθίαι καλούμενοι, ἐαρινοί τινες ὄντες ἄνεμοι, βόρειοί εἰσι τῷ γένει [Hoi de ornithiai kaloumenoi, earinoi tines ontes anemoi, boreioi eisi tō genei]. Budaeus rendered this: "Certain winds of the northern kind, gaining strength in springtime, are called Ornithiae, as it were 'bird-winds'." But Apuleius quite differently: "The spring Ornithiae (others read winds) are a kind of north wind, issuing from the air with lesser force and not maintaining their blowing with continuous persistence." These words, indeed, are taken not so much from this passage as from the Meteorologica, book 2, chapter 5, where the Ornithiae are said to be Ἐτησίαι ἀσθενεῖς· ἐλάττους δὲ, καὶ ὀψιαίτεροι τῶν Ἐτησίων πνέοντες [Etēsiai astheneis; elattous de, kai opsiaiteroi tōn Etēsiōn pneontes], "weak Etesians, but smaller and later than the true Etesians." In these words the Ornithiae are assigned to the Etesians. The Etesians, however, blow either from the western quarter or from the northern region. Diodorus, book 1: Τοὺς Ἐτησίας ἰδεῖν ἐστιν οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον ἀπὸ τῆς ἄρκτου πνέοντας, ἤπερ τῆς ἑσπέρας· οὐ βορέαι γὰρ, οὐδ᾽ ἀπαρκτίαι μόνοι, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ πνέοντες ἀπὸ τῆς θηρινῆς δύσεως ἀργέσαι κοινωνοῦσι τῆς τῶν Ἐτησίων προσηγορίας [Tous Etēsias idein estin ouden ti mallon apo tēs arktou pneontas, ēper tēs hesperas; ou boreai gar, oud' aparktiai monoi, alla kai hoi pneontes apo tēs thērinēs dyseōs argesai koinōnousi tēs tōn Etēsiōn prosēgorias]. So the Ornithiae arise from the same quarter. And Pliny, book 2, chapter 47, relates them now to the Favonius, now to the Etesians. "Some," he says, "call the Favonius around the 7th day before the Kalends of March Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. Some, however, call it Ornithias, blowing on the 71st day after the winter solstice, from the arrival of the birds, for nine days." And further on, concerning the Etesians: "There also blow after the winter solstice those called Ornithiae, but gentler, and for a few days." In Aristophanes' Acharnians χειμὼν ὀρνιθίας [cheimōn ornithias] is taken otherwise, namely for a most bitterly cold winter, in which τὰ ὄρνεα διαφθείρεται [ta ornea diaphtheiretai], birds perish from the cold, as the Scholiast and Suidas under the word Ὀρνιθίας [Ornithias] hold. Accordingly, for them the ὀρνιθίας [ornithias] wind is ὁ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν τὰ ὄρνεα στρωννὺς ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχρᾶς πνοῆς [ho epi tēn gēn ta ornea strōnnys hypo tēs psychras pnoēs], "the one that lays birds low on the ground with its cold blast." But for the philosophers the Ornithias wind is nothing other than what we have said, namely a wind bringing birds from the north or the west. It might therefore seem that it happened contrary to nature that the south wind carried the quails to the Israelites. And from this very point some argue that the miracle was greater. But there is no need to resort to this. For although Pliny and Solinus flatly deny that they fly with the south wind, from the Philosopher you can draw only this: that they then fly with more difficulty and are more easily caught . And this very point carries weight here:

because Moses (Num 11:31) and David (Ps 78:28) write that they were not only carried by the south wind but also thrown down onto the ground. And indeed it is utterly false that they never fly with the south wind. For they are migratory birds: just as the north winds carry them away from us in autumn, so the south winds bring them back to us in spring. Aristotle, in the place cited above: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ ὄρτυγες (ἀπαίρουσι)· ἐὰν μή τινες ὑπολειφθῶσι ἐν εὐηλίοις χωρίοις· [Homoiōs de kai hoi ortyges (apairousi)· ean mē tines hypoleiphthōsi en euēliois chōriois·] Likewise the quails also (depart), unless a few have remained in sunny places. Varro, Rustic. book 3, ch. 5: Thrushes fly every year across the sea into Italy around the autumn equinox, and fly back to the same place at the spring equinox. And at another time turtledoves and quails, in enormous numbers. Pliny: Quails also always arrive before the cranes. Solinus: They have their times of arrival when summer has been driven off; or rather winter, as the great commentator on Solinus shows at length. Aloysius Mundella in his Letters: To the coastal region around Pesaro a huge number of quails usually arrives, and they are caught with a thousand snares; but their arrival has been observed chiefly toward the end of spring. Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], Observat. book 2, ch. 17, on the voyage from Rhodes to Alexandria: Very many quails, flying from the north toward the south, were caught on our ship. From this I am firmly convinced that quails are migratory birds. For earlier, when I was sailing in spring from Zacynthus to Euboea, I had observed others flying in the opposite direction, from the south to the north. Gesner: Quails come to us, as I hear, at about the middle of April, and leave when the first frost sets in. From these it is clear not only that quails change their country, but also that in mid-spring they migrate from the south to the north. I note this here because at precisely that time the south wind brought quails into the camp of the Israelites, namely on the 24th day of the second month. For on the twentieth they had departed from the wilderness of Sinai; and after a three days' journey, when they had demanded meat with much murmuring, God promised that on the next day he would give it for a whole month, and he sent quails. See Num 10:11–12. 33. and XI, 18.

IV. As to the quantity, the Psalmist says that God rained quails like dust and like the sand of the sea, Ps 78:27, that is, sent them down in great quantity and abundance. Thus in Athenaeus, book 8, Phaenias relates ἐν Χεῤῥονήσῳ ἐπὶ τρισὶν ἡμέραις ὗσαι τὸν Θεὸν ἰχθύας [en Cherrhonēsō epi trisin hēmerais hysai ton Theon ichthyas], that in the Chersonese God rained fish for three days. And Phylarchus in the same place: ἑωρακέναι τινὰς πολλαχοῦ τὸν Θεὸν ὕσαντα ἰχθῦσιν, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ πυροῖς [heōrakenai tinas pollachou ton Theon hysanta ichthysin, pollakis de kai pyrois], that some have observed God raining fish in many places, and often wheat too. And Heraclides Lembus: Περὶ τὴν Παιονίαν καὶ Δαρδανίαν βατράχους, φησὶν, ὕσεν ὁ Θεὸς καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτῶν ἐγένετο τὸ πλῆθος, ὡς τὰς οἰκίας καὶ τὰς ὁδοὺς πλήρεις εἶναι· [Peri tēn Paionian kai Dardanian batrachous, phēsin, hysen ho Theos kai tosouton autōn egeneto to plēthos, hōs tas oikias kai tas hodous plēreis einai·] Around Paeonia and Dardania, he says, God rained such a mass of frogs that they filled the houses and the roads. See the rest there, and the note on Exodi VIII, 3. In the same way God rained quails in such quantity that they were like dust,
— — — and of the sand that has no number.

That they were immense in number, Moses proves by two arguments. The first is that they were scattered not only through the camp but on every side, for a day's journey, and stood two cubits high above the ground. The second is that so many myriads of men laboured for two whole days in catching and gathering them that he who had gathered the least of them heaped up ten cors [Numer. XI, 31. 32.]. This cloud of quails, then, extended on every side at least forty miles (for a day's journey is at least twenty miles), and rose two cubits above the ground. This can be understood in three ways. 1. That it means the quails were so heaped up over that whole space that everywhere they rose to two cubits. 2. That it signifies heaps of quails two cubits high, scattered here and there in such a way that empty spaces were left between them, through which the people might make their way to gather the food offered by God. 3. That it signifies that in their very flight they came down so low that they were no more than two cubits from the ground, as though offering themselves of their own accord to the hands of those catching them. Following this, Jerome rendered the sacred words thus: And they flew in the air at a height of two cubits above the ground. And Jonathan: וכרום תרתין אמין הוה פרח על אנפי ארעא והוו מהלכין בהון עד פרתהון מטול דלא ילעון בזמן מכנשהון יתהון, And they flew at a height of two cubits over the face of the ground, and (the Israelites) walked among them up to the navel, so that they might not toil in gathering them. And R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] in his Notes: פורחות בגובה עד שהן כנגד לבו של אדם כדי שלא יהא טורח באסיפתן לא להגביה ולא לשחות, They flew at the height of a man's breast, so that no one in gathering them should tire himself by stretching up or bending down. Nor do I doubt that Philo had this very thing in mind when he describes ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος τὰς πτήσεις προσγειοτάτας ποιούμενον εἰς τὸ εὔθηρον [ortygomētrōn nephos tas ptēseis prosgeiotatas poioumenon eis to euthēron], a cloud of quails flying very close to the ground, so that catching them was easy. This fits the nature of the quail not badly, which, when it comes to us, says Pliny, is a ground bird rather than a high-flying one. I am therefore not averse to this interpretation, although I prefer the second, because David says expressly that the quails fell in the midst of the camp, and Moses that they were spread out upon the ground. These words seem to describe birds lying flat on the ground rather than fluttering in the lowest air. The word raining points the same way, for only things that fall all the way to the ground are said to rain. Moreover, had they been flying, hardly so many could have been caught in two days that each man had ten cors . For the cor was the largest measure of the Hebrews, containing ten baths, as the bath contained three seahs, the seah six kabs, the kab four logs, the log six eggs. In Hebrew it is called חומר chomer, which some of the Hebrews derive from חמור chamor, that is, ass, as though it had been an ass's load. But others more correctly contend that the cor was twice as heavy, and so would have loaded a camel. It is therefore most probable that in the space Moses defines, that is, a day's journey around the camp, heaps of quails lay not everywhere but here and there , in places rising two cubits above the ground. These, wearied by their long flight, either divine power, or angels sent by God, or rather violent winds had scattered hither and thither, to serve this people as food.

Meanwhile I confess that I do not rely much on that last argument, taken from the ten cors which each of that people is believed to have gathered. For there was no need for each person to gather ten cors of quails. God had promised this people meat for a month, and he would have fulfilled this promise if, instead of ten cors, he had given each person only a third of a cor. This is easy to prove. To each of the Israelites an omer of manna is assigned as daily food, Exod 16:16, that is, the tenth part of an ephah, in the same place, verse 36 [var. 35]. And an ephah is the tenth part of a cor, Ezech. XLV, 11. Therefore a cor contains a hundred omer measures. And if an omer suffices for a day, a cor suffices for a hundred days, that is, for three months and more. Accordingly, if each of the Israelites gathered ten cors of quails, they gathered more than thirty times what God had promised. But when Moses says that even he who had gathered least gathered ten cors, perhaps this is to be referred only to the heads of families; and wives, children and slaves are not counted in that census. Or, what I think truer, in that place עשרה חמרים are not ten cors but ten heaps. For חמר chomer also means heap. Thus in Hab 3:15. חמר מים רבים is a heap of many waters. And in the same sense it is said of the frogs in Exod 8:10. ויצברו אותם חמרים חמרים, And they gathered them into heaps, heaps, that is, into many heaps. And in Judg 15:17 [var. 16.] חמרתים in the dual is two heaps. But also in this very passage עשרה חמרים, Onkelos renders עשרא דגורים, and the Arabic edited at Paris عشرة انابير [ʿashrat anābīr], and Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] عشرة اجداس [ʿashrat ajdās], ten heaps. If you take it this way, Moses will not have defined precisely what measure of quails each person gathered, but will only have said that ten heaps were gathered by him who gathered least. Ten heaps, that is, very many, by a phrase familiar to the Hebrews, who everywhere use ten for many. Thus Gen. XXXI, 7: He has changed my wages ten times. Num 14:22: They have tempted me now ten times. Neh 4:6: They have told us now ten times. Job 19:3: These ten times you have reproached me, that is, many times. Lev 26:26: Ten women shall bake your bread, that is, many. 1 Sam 1:8: Am I not better to you than ten sons? Eccl 7:19: Wisdom gives strength to the wise more than ten rulers who are in the same city. Zech 8:23: Ten men shall take hold of the skirt of a Jew, that is, very many. So, then, Moses will have said ten heaps of quails for many . And that it should be translated thus rather than ten cors is suggested, besides what we have already said, also by this reason: that כור, cor, or חומר chomer, is a measure of grain, not of meat . This observation is not worthless. For if each of the Israelites is said to have gathered ten cors of quails, their number will be enormous and will exceed all belief. Cornelius a Lapide, who tried to compute it in his Commentaries on this passage, reckons the figures so as to prove that the Israelites gathered about twelve thousand million quails. But we, instead of ten cors, maintain that each did not gather or consume even a third part of a cor. We do this not to diminish God's power, but so as not to do violence to faith by extorting from it more than God has revealed to us in his word .

But, you will say, this at least is certain: Moses asserts that God fed all the Israelites with quails for a month, among whom there were six hundred thousand footmen. I admit too that this bird is less frequent in our regions than that such a thing could happen without a new creation. But in hot regions the matter is quite otherwise, for there the abundance of quails is far greater. Thus that in Greece nothing was more common than the quail may be gathered from these lines of the comic poet Aristophon on peacocks in Athenaeus, book 14.

Τὸν ταὼν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον, [Ton taōn men hōs hapax tis zeugos ēgagen monon,] Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ’ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων· [Spanion on to chrēma; pleious d’ eisi nyn tōn ortygōn;]

Of peacocks someone had once brought only a single pair, a rare thing in that age; but now there are more of them than quails. And that at Rome too they were cheap is shown by these lines of Juvenal against legacy-hunters, Satire 12.
He has three heirs; I should like to see who would spend a sick hen, closing its eyes, on so barren a friend: but this is too great an expense; no quail will ever fall for a father. — —

He says that no one offers a hen for the health of a friend who is already a father and has heirs, however sick and dying he may be ; not even a quail, which is the cheapest of birds and costs much less. Nor is this surprising, if what Gesner relates from Flavius Blondus is true: on the shore of Antium, when in early spring the swallows and quails cross the Tyrrhenian Sea and return to Italy, within five thousand paces sometimes a hundred thousand little birds of this kind are caught daily, and this fowling continues for about a month. The ancients report similar things . Thus Varro, after writing that thrushes fly away from Italy across the sea, and fly back again about the equinoxes, says: And at another time turtledoves and quails, in enormous numbers. Hence, exhausted by flying, they sometimes fall upon ships in such numbers that they sink them by their weight. Pliny: These (quails) also fly in in a similar way, not without danger to sailors, when they have come near land. For they settle on the sails, and always at night, and sink the vessels. Solinus: When they perceive land, they gather in flocks. Then, massed together, they hasten more vehemently; and this haste generally brings destruction to sailors. For it happens at night that they settle on the sails and, weighing down the edges, overturn the hulls, elsewhere tilt, or sink, as in Pliny. To the same effect is the fact that from the abundance of quails the name Ortygia was once common to several places. Thus Delos was called Ortygia, and the island of Syracuse, and the city of Ephesus, and the grove nearest to it, and another near Miletus. What of the fact that for this very reason the ancients gave the name Ortygia to the whole of Libya? The witness is Stephanus under Λιβύῃ [Libyē].

But nowhere is the abundance of quails greater than in Egypt and the neighbouring places, whether the warmth of the air attracts them or the richness and fertility of the soil. Hence Josephus: Τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος· [Trephei de touto to orneon, hōs ouden heteron, ho Arabios kolpos] The Arabian Gulf nourishes this bird above all others. We have also already heard Diodorus on the immense abundance of quails around Rhinocolura. And the ancients say much about the chennia, a kind of quail peculiar to Egypt, with which at a certain season of the year the Egyptians so abounded that, since they could not consume them all, they were forced to preserve them in salt for later. This is especially noteworthy in a region so populous that Theocritus reckons more than thirty thousand towns in it, and Josephus seven hundred and fifty myriads of people, apart from the inhabitants of Alexandria. What we have said about the chennia is proved by these passages: Athenaeus book 9, ch. 11, at the end of the treatise On quails: Τῶν δὲ καλουμένων χεννίων, μικρὸν δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὀρτύγιον, μνημονεύει Κλεομένης ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἀλέξανδρον ἐπιστολῇ γράφων οὕτως· Φαληρίδας ταριχηρὰς μυρίας, τυλάδας πεντακισχιλίας, χέννια ταριχηρὰ μύρια. [Tōn de kaloumenōn chenniōn, mikron d᾽ estin ortygion, mnēmoneuei Kleomenēs en tē pros Alexandron epistolē graphōn houtōs· Phalēridas tarichēras myrias, tyladas pentakischilias, chennia tarichēra myria.] Cleomenes mentions the so-called chennia, which are small quails, in his letter to Alexander, writing thus: ten thousand salted phalarides, five thousand tylades, ten thousand salted chennia. The phalaris is a kind of diver, the tylas a kind of thrush, and the chennium a kind of quail, as Athenaeus himself states. In the same place Hipparchus in the Egyptian Iliad:
Οὔ μοι Αἰγυπτίων βίος ἤρεσεν, οἷον ἔχουσιν Χέννια τίλλοντες· — — — — [Ou moi Aigyptiōn bios ēresen, hoion echousin Chennia tillontes]
I do not like the life which the Egyptians lead, plucking chennia. An old poet, against a stingy host who served his guests everything cheap and salted, Anthology book 2, ch. 47:
Ἡμεῖς δ᾽ ἐσθίομεν κεκλημένοι ἅλμυρα πάντα, Χέννια, καὶ τυροὺς, χηνὸς ἁλιστὰ λίπη. [Hēmeis d᾽ esthiomen keklēmenoi halmyra panta, Chennia, kai tyrous, chēnos halista lipē.]

But we, having been invited, ate all the salted things, chennia, and cheeses, and salted goose fat. Hesychius: Χέννιον· ὀρνιθάριόν τι κατ᾽ Αἴγυπτον ταριχευόμενον [Chennion· ornitharion ti kat᾽ Aigypton taricheuomenon]; Chennium, a certain small bird in Egypt, preserved in salt. Since, then, there was so great an abundance of chennia and quails in Egypt and in all Africa, from where were they carried on the wings of the winds into the camp of the Israelites? There is no need here, as some do, to invent new miracles for ourselves, and to say that God created or multiplied the quails, as Christ multiplied the loaves in the hands of the Apostles. It is our part to hold fast to the sacred text, in which we do not read that the quails were created or multiplied by the power of God, but that they were brought by the winds from regions beyond the sea. I am not unaware that in the Vulgate version, Wis 19:10, they are called a new creature of birds, and that many infer from this that God created them anew. But, to say nothing of the author of the book, to whom we have not bound our faith, the Greek copy does not have κτίσιν [ktisin], creature, but γένεσιν νέαν ὀρνέων [genesin nean orneōn], a new generation of birds; the Syriac likewise has ܡܘܠܕܐ ܚܕܬܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ [מולדא חדתא דפרחתא], and the Arabic توالد طيور جديدة [tawālud ṭuyūr jadīda]. And it is called new not in itself, but to the Israelites, who had experienced nothing of the kind. Similar is the fact that the same author attributes to this very food ξένην γεῦσιν [xenēn geusin], a new taste, Wis 16:2, that is, one unaccustomed and unknown to those who ate it. Here, therefore, we recognize no creation of quails. But this was miraculous: that they were brought in such great abundance, and at precisely the time that God had appointed, and that they all fell down around the camp of the Israelites, so as to serve them as food divinely provided.

V. There remains the fifth question, concerning the punishment that God inflicted on the Jews who ate the quails. The sin was this: weary of their condition, they had murmured against God as follows: Who will give us meat to eat! We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic: but now our soul is dried up, and nothing is before our eyes except the Manna, Num 11:4–5. 6. Hence the Psalmist, Ps 78:19: Speaking against God they said, Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Behold! he struck the rock so that waters flowed and streams overflowed. Can he also give food? Will he provide meat for his people? In these words, 1. they show themselves remarkably ungrateful, since they prefer their former condition, that is, the Egyptian servitude, from which God had rescued them with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, to the liberty they now enjoyed. Who, hearing this, would not have thought that they had lived sumptuously in Egypt and in great prosperity? Yet there they had lived wretchedly, pressed and nearly crushed under Pharaoh's yoke. But it is customary for the ungrateful, even when raised to greater things, to extol the past and disdain the present, lest they acknowledge that they owe thanks to anyone for the improvement of their state. 2. They reveal a remarkable ἀῤῥωστίαν τῆς διανοίας [arrhōstian tēs dianoias] in that they prefer little fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic, in short carnal things, to spiritual goods and to the glorious presence of God, which he had attested by so many signs and miracles. 3. Not content with the Manna, from which the necessary sustenance was abundantly supplied to them, they had demanded meat besides, and had limited God, as it says in Ps 78:41, that is, they had defined his power by their own judgement, asking not only to be delivered, but to be delivered in this or that way. 4. After having experienced God's power so many times, these are nevertheless words of distrust: Can God furnish a table in this wilderness? Can he also give food? God therefore, justly provoked to anger, promises that he will give meat, not only for one or two days but for a whole month, so that, having eaten it not only to satiety but even to nausea and loathing, they would at last spit it out and reject it. These are the words of one whose mind is stirred, and who had heard the people's prayers only in his anger. So when the month was over, while they still had in their mouths the food with which they had gorged themselves, God, blazing against them, struck the people with a great plague. Aben Ezra takes this to be pestilence. There are some who infer from Ps 106:15 that רזון, that is, leanness or consumption, is meant. Others explain it otherwise. But I side with those for whom this plague is fire, by which some of this people were consumed. For so David has it, Psal. LXXVIII, 21: Therefore the Lord heard and was enraged (hearing, that is, what is reported in the preceding verse, Can God furnish a table, etc.) and a fire was kindled in Jacob. Understand the fire spoken of in Num 11:1: And when the people complained, it was evil in the ears of the Lord. So the Lord heard and was enraged, and the fire of the Lord, blazing up, consumed the outermost parts of the camp, etc., up to the fourth verse, where the things that are afterwards explained more fully in the rest of the chapter seem to be narrated briefly by πρόληψιν [prolēpsin]. And the same place was given a double name: one, Tabera, from the burning, Num 11:3; the other, Kibrot-taava, because those who had craved meat were buried there, Num 11:34 . There is also another example of similar obstinacy in this same people.

For in Exod 16:2 we read that the congregation murmured and said to Moses and Aaron: Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! But you have brought us into this wilderness, so that this whole assembly may be destroyed by hunger. But in what seems a like case, the judgement was unlike. For to these murmurers God granted quails that very evening and Manna the next day, exacting no punishment from them, Exod 16:12–13. Indeed, God can either punish the same sins in justice or pardon and remit them in mercy. Yet many reasons can be given why he punished the latter severely for what he had kindly remitted to the former. First, if anyone falls again into sins which God has once remitted, he sins more gravely, because besides God's justice he also spurns his mercy, and so he is evil because God was good. Moreover, the former had murmured because they were pressed by hunger and the want of everything. But the latter had Manna for food, which satisfied them, so that their so greedily desiring meat and demanding it so importunately was a cry wrung not by necessity but by wicked lust. Finally, the former were still untaught, and the Law had not yet been given, immediately after the departure from Egypt; the latter murmur when already instructed, and after receiving the Law, so that the sin is graver. So it is not surprising that God, who had spared the former, dealt so severely with these.

If we believe the Jews, the gods of the Sepharvites, Adrammelech and Anammelech, mentioned in 2 Reg. XVII, 31., were worshipped in the form of peacocks and pheasants, or of quails. Kimchi on that passage: ובירושלמי אדרמלך וענמלך זה טווס ופסיוני וטווס הוא הנקרא בלשון לע״ז פאון וידוע הוא ופסיוני הוא שלו והרגים שאלו ויבא שלו שאלו בסרא ואייתי פסיונין, In the Jerusalem Talmud (in the tractate On Idolatry), Adrammelech and Anammelech, that is, ταὼς [taōs] and pheasant. And ταὼς [taōs] is the same as peacock, the name of an idol, which is well known. And the pheasant, that is, the quail. For at Ps 105:40, for the words „They asked, and he brought quails,“ „the Targum has, They asked for meat, and he brought pheasants“. But in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin ch. 7, fol. 63b, Adrammelech and Anammelech are rendered הפרד והסוס, the mule and the horse. Both are false, or uncertain. For it is customary with these men to blurt out whatever comes into their mouths, and to smear their dreams onto paper.
Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. II, p. 171, declares this utterly false. Against this, he says, stand certain other animals which, although they feed on poisons,
See Aristot. Problem. sect. 30, at the beginning.

"If quails were banished from the tables of the ancients, as Pliny asserts, because they suffer from epilepsy, then oxen, goats, rams and capons too will have to be banished, since all these animals have also been observed to suffer from the same disease." Aldrovandi, loc. cit.
Compare v. 52 of the same Ps. LXXVIII.

Here our author suffered a human lapse. Both Arabic versions have من السما [min al-samā] like the Greeks, as Schnurrer [=C. F. Schnurrer, Dissertationes philologico-criticae (1790)] rightly points out in his Dissertat. in Ps. LXXVIII. p. 18. no
I. E. Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)], on Harmar II, p. 445, holds the same view, without adequate reason.

"The noun קדים seems rather to be said generally of wind, and of a more violent wind, as in Ps 48:8. For there is a kind of parallelism, not indeed noted by Lowth, On the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews, lecture 19, yet not very infrequent, in which something is first said universally and generally, and then designated more specifically, as in v. 43: when he performed his miracles in Egypt, and his wonders in the region of Tanis. And the Syriac translator too seems to have understood the passage thus, rendering: ܐܫܒ ܪܘܚܐ ܒܫܡܝܐ [אשב רוחא בשמיא], he stirred up the winds in the heaven, unless you prefer to pronounce ܪܘܚܐ [רוחא] as wind." Thus Schnurrer, loc. cit.
Rather, from Arabia Felix or Yemen, as Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] rightly observes, Fasc. 4, p. 65, where the opinions of others are also assessed.

That is, at the time when, leaving Europe at the beginning of autumn, they make for southern lands; the matter itself shows that a south wind is contrary to them. Nor are the words of Aristotle, book 8, ch. 12, quoted above, to be understood otherwise; Pliny wrongly interpreted them to mean that quails never fly when the south wind blows, and for this he is also criticized by our author in what immediately follows. Aldrovandi, Ornithol. II, p. 156, therefore rightly, after quoting the words of Belon which Bochart himself presently cites, continues thus: "For if in flying they use the north wind, and refrain from flight in a south wind, as we have said from Pliny and Aristotle, it must be declared that they fly with a contrary wind when they come to us; which plainly appears to conflict with reason and with our senses. For the north wind, which takes its name [aquilo] from the very swift flight of the eagle [aquila], is a very fast wind and also very violent; quails, by contrast, have a very weak flight because of the excessive heaviness of their body. How, then, they could come to us while this wind blows, I cannot at all persuade myself, nor would anyone else easily persuade me. Therefore I think that when leaving us they use the help of the wind, but by no means when coming to us; indeed, unless a north wind is granted for their departure, they reach the desired places with difficulty." Buffon holds the same opinion on those words of Aristotle, Hist. Nat. des Oiseaux [=Buffon, Histoire naturelle des oiseaux] vol. 2, p. 461: I believe indeed that it is the wind that helps quails make their journey, not the north wind but a favourable wind; just as it is not the south wind that delays their course but a contrary wind; and this is true in all countries where these birds have a considerable crossing to make over the seas. The Commander Godeheu has very well remarked that in spring quails land on Malta only with the north-west wind, which is contrary to them for reaching Provence, and that on their return it is the south-east wind that brings them to this island, because with that wind they cannot land in Barbary: we even see that the Author of Nature used this means, as the most consistent with the general laws he had established, to send numerous flocks of quails to the Israelites in the desert.
That is, חמר, which is in the text, where it is the name of a measure, is the same as כר. See Ezek 45:11 14. Esr. VII, 22.

But then, I should think, חמרים חמרים would have been added. You will say it is incredible that the quails over that whole space (of a day's journey around the camp (v. 31)) were heaped up so that everywhere they stood two cubits high. But the one who wrote this book about the wanderings of the Israelites through the Arabian desert, the fourth of those that bear Moses' name, meant to relate incredible things. That it was by no means written by Moses, however, we shall prove at another time.

Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in the Supplemm. vol. III, p. 833, thinks the meaning heap hardly suits this passage. "Where birds are spoken of," he says, "what kind of measure is a heap? For one could make heaps larger or smaller." But what if the writer, as Bochart holds, did not want to define the number precisely? Michaelis adds: "Nor did he remember that, had the quails been gathered into heaps, it would have followed that they grew hot, decayed and stank." But Michaelis did not remember that the quails, as soon as they fell, were gathered by the Israelites and spread out through the camp (v. 32), namely so that they might be dried, just as in the East even today people usually dry fish and meat in the heat of the sun, as Maillet reports, Lettres sur l' Egypte 10, p. 21; 11, p. 110. Michaelis himself would prefer to understand by the word חמרים a certain number of birds joined by a thread passed through them (einen Bund Voegel), from חבר, he joined, which the Arabs would have interchanged with أحمر [aḥmar]. This meaning is unsatisfactory because it lacks support in the usage of the language. Nor can Bochart's suggestion hold, that עשרה, ten, is put for many. For the whole sequence of the words in v. 32 plainly shows that the writer wanted to define precisely the number of quails gathered: there were gathered by him הממעיט, WHO [gathered] LEAST, עשרה חמרים; here, if you put many, there will be no sound sense. And for this very reason, that the writer manifestly wished to give a definite number, I am more inclined to the view of those who think that חמרים is here the name of a measure, namely the cor.
But what prevents us from believing that the quails were gathered in bushels?
But cf. above, note 10, and what Bochart reports below, p. 107, from Gesner, and our note 14.

To these may be added what Aldrovandi, Ornithol. T. II, L. XIII, p. 164, reports in confirmation of this account, from a letter of Franc. Arrivabene of Mantua, chamberlain of Cardinal Paleotti, to Camillo, senator of the city of Bologna, brother of the said Cardinal: I shall gladly tell you what I saw at Nettuno, where we spent three nights. When the most illustrious Cardinal, your brother, set out from here to visit Astura (this is, if I am not mistaken, the name of another town), we had scarcely left the town when we came upon a quail hunt. The nets stretched over four miles, and a very great number of birds was being caught. The fowlers said that they are carried there from Barbary and cross the sea in a single flight, leaving there toward evening and landing here at early morning; that they had sometimes sown in the ground basil seed taken from the birds' crops, and it had germinated successfully, which is certainly proof of a most famous journey. The governor of the place, asked how many had been caught that morning, answered, on the fowlers' reported word, ten thousand and more. Other testimonies from more recent writers have been collected by Oedmann, IV, p. 69, and V, 80.

In this way the most divergent things can be reconciled. But whoever reads will notice that what is read from v. 4 onward happened at another place and time. In the first place (vv. 1, 2, 3) a fire, which arose, it seems, through carelessness, burned part of the camp; superstitious people took this as a punishment for their complaints. Yet it is not reported that anyone perished in that fire. In the other place, however (dealt with from v. 4 onward), a huge multitude of people perished from immoderate eating of quails, which is not obscurely hinted at in these words (v. 20) עד אשר־יצא מאפכם והיה לכם לזרא, and (v. 33) הבשר עודנו בין שניהם. Excessive eating of meat is much more harmful to health in the hot regions of the East than in our lands. This is attested by many who have visited those shores, and Niebuhr [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] too confirms it from his own and his companions' experience in the Praefat. ad Descript. Arab. p. VIII. Moreover, quails, as Aldrovandi asserts, Ornithol. vol. II, p. 171, when eaten rather often and in larger quantity, produce thick, phlegmatic and viscid humors. Others' thoughts on this matter have been presented by Oedmann, Fasc. IV, p. 71 ff., and Fasc. V, p. 79.

Twelve passages of the Prophets which some interpreters refer to the gallinaceous kind. I. Lev 14:4. II. 1 Reg. IV, 23. var. V, 3. III. 2 Reg. XVII, 30. IV. Job 3:7. V. Job 38:32. VI. Job 38:36. VII. Job 39:13. VIII. Ps 50:11. IX. Ps 80:14. X. Prov 30:31. XI. Eccl 12:4 var. 6. XII. Esaj. XXII, 17.

The cock is called ديك [dīk] dic in Arabic, and ܬܪܢܓܠ [תרנגל] tarnegol in Syriac; both names, if I am not mistaken, are very old. For traces of the former appear in the Hebrew דוכיפת dukiphat, by which Moses names the hoopoe; a word, as it seems, compounded of דוך and כיפה, so that it means cock of the rocks, or rock-dwelling cock, as we shall show elsewhere. And from the Syriac ܬܪܢܓܠ [תרנגל] tarnegol, I think, the Phoenicians who had come with Cadmus into Boeotia gave its name to Tanagra, a very ancient city of Boeotia, home of the Tanagraean cocks. These are praised as most pugnacious by Varro, Columella, Pliny, Pausanias, Hesychius, Suidas and others, whose passages we have cited in our Chanaan, book 1, ch. 16. That is, the city itself was called Tarnegol or Tarnegal by the Phoenicians after those cocks. And the Greeks, dropping the final l, as in Ἀννίβα [Anniba] and Ἀσδρούβα [Asdrouba], made from Tarnegal first Tarnegam, then Tanagram, by the transposition of a single letter. Thus the city of Tanagra is the city of the cock, or of cocks. Their renown was so great that among the ancients cock and Ταναγραῖος [Tanagraios] are almost interchangeable, as if all cocks must have originated from Tanagra. Hence in Lucian's Cock, Micyllus says to Pythagoras, who has been transformed into a cock: Εἰπὲ δὲ ὅμως, ὦ Μνησάρχου παῖ, ὅπως ἡμῖν ἀντὶ μὲν ἀνθρώπου ὄρνις, ἀντὶ δὲ Σαμίου Ταναγραῖος ἀναπέφηνας· [Eipe de homōs, ō Mnēsarchou pai, hopōs hēmin anti men anthrōpou ornis, anti de Samiou Tanagraios anapephēnas] Yet explain, son of Mnesarchus, how it has come about that you have appeared to us as a bird instead of a man, and as a Tanagraean instead of a Samian. Tanagraean, that is, cock, תרנגול. Meanwhile, neither name for the cock appears in the Prophetic books. Nor is it sufficiently known what the ancient Hebrews called the cock; although interpreters refer many passages of the Prophets to the gallinaceous kind, but on conjectures that are not certain enough, as will be clear to anyone who runs through them, as what follows will make plain.

I. The first passage, as far as I recall, is Lev 14:4, where the leper who has been cleansed is commanded to offer to God δύο ὀρνίθια ζῶντα καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia zōnta kathara], that is, as some would have it, two living clean little hens. Origen, Homily 8 on Leviticus: He commands that two living hens be taken for him who is cleansed. And a little later: These two hens also seem to me here to bear a certain likeness to the two goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent out into the wilderness: for so here too, of the two hens one is sacrificed and the other is released into the field. And again: He who is purged of leprosy and offers hens. Likewise: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding, through which the purification of the sinner is effected, of which it is written, “How often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen,” etc. Since these words are ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], they seem to need reading thus: Because the Lawgiver commands that on the same day on which he is purged two hens be taken, let there be a hidden understanding of the hen, through which, etc. That is, by those hens he wants Christ to be signified, who in the Gospel compares himself to a hen. Hence the addition: The hen shall be killed in an earthen vessel into which running water has been put, so that water too may be taken for the purification, and the fullness of the mystery may be fulfilled in the water and the blood which is said to have come forth from the side of the Saviour. And much more about this same hen can be read in what follows. In the ninth volume of the Works of Jerome, the author of the thirty-ninth Epistle, On the various kinds of leprosies, following the same view, says: But why are two hens commanded to be offered for the cleansing of leprosies? The two hens seem to indicate the soul and the flesh: but one hen, he says, you shall kill, the other you shall wash and release, etc. Yet in the Hebrew text nothing is said of hens: God merely commands that in the purification of leprosy שתי צפורים be taken, two birds (or two little birds, or two sparrows), which the Greeks rendered not badly as δύο ὀρνίθια [dyo ornithia], but with an ambiguous word, which in the age of the Fathers meant only hens, or for the most part hens. Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 4, where he treats of the gallinaceous kind: Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ὄρνιθας, καὶ ὀρνίθια νῦν μόνον ἡ συνήθεια καλεῖ τὰς θηλείας· [alla mēn kai ornithas, kai ornithia nyn monon hē synētheia kalei tas thēleias] Now indeed the custom has prevailed that only the females of cocks (that is, hens) are called ὄρνιθες [ornithes] and ὀρνίθια [ornithia]. This gave occasion to the error. Yet Plutarch, nearly contemporary with Athenaeus, says in the Artaxerxes that the rhyndax is μικρὸν ἐν Πέρσαις ὀρνίθιον [mikron en Persais ornithion], that is, a small little bird among the Persians. And that in the Law δύο ὀρνίθια καθαρὰ [dyo ornithia kathara] are two clean little birds ought to have been clear enough even to those ignorant of the Hebrew language. For the lawgiver would not have said two clean hens. That epithet would have been pointless, since every hen is clean.

II. The second passage is 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.], where among Solomon's provisions are reckoned ברבורים אבוסים, that is, תרנגולין פטומין, fattened cocks, as it is found in Selomo, whom Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] follows. Likewise for Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)] ברבור barbur is תרנגול סריס, a castrated cock, that is, a capon. Nor do the Greek translators depart far from this; here they have ἐκτὸς ὀρνίθων ἐκλεκτῶν νομάδων [ektos ornithōn eklektōn nomadōn], besides choice pasture-fed hens. I prefer this to rendering it, as others do, besides birds, etc. For although ὄρνιθες [ornithes] are often birds in general, yet for the Greek translators, as for the Evangelists, a bird is ὄρνεον [orneon], and a hen is ὄρνις [ornis]. Moreover, ὄρνις νομὰς [ornis nomas] is nothing other than a fattened or pasture-fed hen. In Nicander's Alexipharmaca, line 295, there is βοσκὰς ὀρταλὶς [boskas ortalis], where the Scholiast has νομὰς ὄρνις [nomas ornis], the very words of the Greek translators. And in Artemidorus's Ὀψαρτυτικά [Opsartytika], as cited by Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 23: Νομάδα παχεῖαν ἕψε, καὶ νεοσσοὺς τῶν ἤδη κοκκυζόντων [Nomada pacheian hepse, kai neossous tōn ēdē kokkyzontōn]; Boil a fat pasture-fed hen, and, of the chicks, those that already crow. So it must be rendered, not, as the translator most ineptly has it, a fat dove, etc., and of the chicks those that still peep. For the subject is a mattya to be made from a hen. Accordingly it is immediately added: Εἶτ᾽ ἐξελὼν τὰ λάχανα εἰς τρυβλίον, καὶ τῆς ὄρνιθος τῶν κρεῶν ἐπιθεὶς [Eit᾽ exelōn ta lachana eis trublion, kai tēs ornithos tōn kreōn epitheis]; Then taking out the vegetables, put them into a dish, and placing the hen's meat on them. And ἤδη [ēdē] does not mean still, but already. Nor is κοκκύζειν [kokkyzein] proper to doves, but to cocks, as is clear from Aristophanes, Aristotle, Theocritus, Aelian and Lucian. For it is an onomatopoeic word, like the vernacular coq for the cock, which we name thus from its crowing. Finally, νομὰς [nomas] is a hen, yet not a Numidian one, as the most learned commentator would have it, but a pasture-fed one. Others call them σιτιστὰς [sitistas] or σιτευτὰς [siteutas]. Athenaeus, book 14, chapter 21: Σιτιστῶν δὲ ὀρνίθων μὲν μνημονεύει Μάτρων ἐν ταῖς Παρῳδίαις οὕτως [Sitistōn de ornithōn men mnēmoneuei Matrōn en tais Parōdiais houtōs],
Ὣς ἔφαθ᾽, οἱ δ᾽ ἐγέλασσαν, ἐπήνεγκάν τ᾽ ἐπὶ τούτῳ Σιτευτὰς ὄρνιθας ἐπ᾽ ἀργυρέοισι πίναξι· [Hōs ephath᾽, hoi d᾽ egelassan, epēnenkan t᾽ epi toutō Siteutas ornithas ep᾽ argyreoisi pinaxi]

Matron mentions fattened hens thus in his Parodies: When he had said this, they laughed, and then brought in fattened hens on silver platters. I say fattened hens with Metellus, the Pontifex Maximus, whose words are in the description of the pontifical dinner in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 3, chapter 13: Before the dinner, sea urchins, raw oysters, as many as they wished, giant clams, spondyli, a thrush, asparagus, and beneath it a fattened hen. Nor did Pliny mean anything else by the term altilia when he said of the seed of the tamarisk, book 24, chapter 9: Applied with the fat of fattened fowls to boils. Cato had said pascales; whence Festus: Both sheep and hens are called pascales, because they graze about everywhere. Pascales, that is, νομάδες [nomades], as altiles are σιτισταὶ [sitistai] or σιτευταί [siteutai]. Thus in the view of the Greeks ברבורים אבוסים are pasture-fed or fattened hens. And that some of the older Hebrews held the same view is found in Selomo. This, however, can by no means be held as certain and established, since there is no word whose meaning is more disputed, as we shall show below in a chapter devoted to that word.

III. The third passage about the cock is 2 Reg. XVII, 30., where, of the peoples transferred by Shalmaneser from Assyria into Judaea, the Babylonians are said to have worshipped סכות־בנות Succoth-Benoth, and the Cuthaeans Nergal. Succoth-Benoth, that is, the hen with her chicks; and Nergal, that is, the cock, as the Hebrews would have it. For so the Talmudists in Sanhedrin, chapter 7, folio 63b: אנשי בבל עשו את סכות־בנות ומאי ניהו תרנגולת אנשי כותה עשו נרגל ומאי ניהו תרנגול, The men of Babel made Succoth-Benoth. What (idol) was this? A hen. The men of Cutha made Nergal. What was that? A cock. Solomon Jarchi [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac), called Jarchi by the Christian Hebraists]: סכות־בנות דמות תרנגולת עם אפרוחיה נרגל דמות תרנגול, Succoth-Benoth was the image of a hen with her chicks, and Nergal the image of a cock. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]: ובדברי רז״ל סכות־בנות זה תרנגולת היו עובדים והיה שמה סכות בנות וכמו שקורין לתרנגול סכוי כן היו קורין לתרנגולת סכות ובנות פירוש עם אפרוחיה נרגל זה תרנגולת הבר, In the words of our masters of blessed memory, Succoth-benoth is the hen, which they worshipped under this name. For just as they called the cock שכוי secui, so they called the hen סכות succoth. And the added benoth signifies that she was with her chicks. And nergal is the wild hen. The most trifling of trifles. Literally, סכות בנות Succoth-benoth are tents of daughters, or of girls. So when the Babylonians are said to have made Succoth-benoth, I understand that they built a shrine of goddesses who were called בנות benoth, that is, girls, just as the Greeks called Proserpina κόρην [korēn], that is, girl. So in Amos V, 26. סכות מלככם, the tabernacle of your king, that is, the shrine of your idol . And what נרגל Nergal is, I do not know, except that almost the same name as this idol belongs to a species of palm called even today by the Persians, Arabs and Indians نارجيل [nārjīl] nergil, of which they tell wonders. It must therefore be considered whether the idol of the Persians could have been named from this palm, as in Syria ܪܡܘܢ [רמון] Rimmon was from pomegranates, 2 Reg. V, 18.

IV. The fourth passage is Job 3:7. There, for the words of Job in which he curses the night in which he was born, Let no רננה, song, come in it, the Chaldee has: לא תעול רננא דתרנגול ברא למקלסה בה, Let not the song of the wild cock come to give praise in it. This does not concern the cock in general, but a fabulous cock of prodigious size, which we shall treat in the treatise On the Ostrich. And the same translator says more about it in the passages that follow, taken from Job and the Psalms.

V. The fifth passage is Job 38:32, where the Chaldee in the Venetian and Basel editions has וזגתא על אפרחהא תדברנון, And will you lead the hen with her chicks? Literally, over her chicks. But over the chicks means with the chicks. So Deuter. XXII, 6. You shall not take the mother over the young, i.e. with the young. The hen is זגתא, as in the Talmudic tractate Bechoroth ch. 1, fol. 8. 2: אייתו לה תרי ביעי אמר ליה הי דוגתא אוכמתי והי דוגתא חיוורתי, When two eggs were brought, he said to him: That egg is of a black hen, and this one of a white hen. Nor is זגתא pronounced Zagtha, as some think, but Zaggatha. For it belongs to the verbs that double the second radical, like the Arabic name of the hen, دجاجة [dajāja] degiagia, which they derive from the verb دج [dajja] daggia, that is, to walk gently. I think it is formed from the bird's call, which different people render differently. Or from the Chaldee זגג, with Zain and Daleth interchanged, which is customary in those languages. For the rest, beware of understanding an ordinary hen in the paraphrase of Job. For it is a matter of the celestial one, which in the vernacular is called pullicenaria [hen with chicks], by the Greeks Πλειὰς [Pleias] or Πλειάδες [Pleiades], and by the Latins Vergiliae .
