But the Hebrew has ועיש על בניה תנחם, and will you lead עיש with its sons? And in that passage עיש is plainly something other than the Pleiades. Namely, עיש is the same as עש in Job 9:9. And עש as is formed by ἀφαίρεσιν [aphairesin] from the Arabic نعش [naʿsh] nas, as an initial N often drops out. Thus גיא gia, splendour, from נגה naga, to shine; גר gar, river, from נגר nagar, to flow; שיא si, or שאת seeth, elevation, from נשה nasa, to lift up; שיג sig, pursuit, from נשג nasag, to pursue or overtake. Further, for the Arabs نعش [naʿsh] nas is first a bier: as in Luke 7:14 and in Eutychius of Alexandria p. 277; then the constellation of the bear. Thus for the astrologers النعش الكبري [al-naʿsh al-kubrī] is the greater bier, that is, the Great Bear; النعش الصغري [al-naʿsh al-ṣughrī] the lesser bier, that is, the Little Bear. Namely, four stars arranged in a square are regarded by them as a bier, or coffin, on which a corpse is carried out. And the three following (for us the bear's tail) are for them the daughters, or sons, who accompany the funeral. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: بنات نعش الكبري سبعة كواكب اربعة منها نعش وثلاث بنات [banāt naʿsh al-kubrī sabʿat kawākib arbaʿa minhā naʿsh wa-thalāth banāt] The daughters of the greater bier: of which four are the bier, and three are the daughters. And elsewhere: الحية كواكب ما بين الغرقدين وبنات نعش [al-ḥayya kawākib mā bayn al-gharqadayn wa-banāt naʿsh] The Serpent (or Dragon): the stars that are between alpharkadin (the polar stars) and the daughters of the bier. Again elsewhere: الصبا ريح مهبها من مطلع الثريا الي بنات نعش [al-ṣabā rīḥ mahabbuhā min maṭlaʿ al-thurayyā ilā banāt naʿsh] Saba, a wind blowing from the rising of the Pleiades to the daughters of the bier, that is, Caecias. Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] notes that in the poets one sometimes reads بنى نعش [banī naʿsh] sons of the bier, and of individual stars in the singular ابن نعش [ibn naʿsh] son of the bier . Hence clear light falls on the passage of Job we are dealing with: Will you lead עיש, the bier, with its sons? And although the reason for this expression escaped the interpreters, Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] nevertheless rightly saw that it concerns the sign of seven stars in the north. This sign some call the Bear, others the Wagon, others Helice, others the Septentriones. Nor do I pay heed to the Talmudists, for some of whom עש is זנב טלה, the tail of the Ram; for others רישא דעגלא, the head of the Bull, in the tractate Berachoth fol. 58b The Glossator tries to reconcile these opinions, because ראש השור סמוך לזנב טלה שכן הסדר טלה שור תאומים, The head of the Bull is joined to the tail of the Ram, since this is the order of the signs: Ram, Bull, Twins, etc. Nor am I unaware why the Chaldee wanted עיש to be the Pleiades. ערש in Hebrew means to come together and to be gathered, Ioel IV, 11. So it seemed to him that this sign was called עיש as if from coming together. Just as in Greek it is called Πλειὰς [Pleias], ὡς ἐκ πλειόνων ἀςέρων οὖσα [hōs ek pleionōn asterōn ousa]. And in Arabic ثري [thurayy] from the same notion, for ثرا [tharā] means to be multiplied. But why do the Greek translators render Καὶ ἕσπερον ἐπὶ κόμης αὐτοῦ ἄξεις αὐτὸν [Kai hesperon epi komēs autou axeis auton], And the evening star, will you lead him by his hair? For בניה, its sons, they read בנית, hair. And they derived עיש, or עש, from עשי, the word by which the Arabs call evening. In the Vulgate the old editions have And do you make the evening star rise over the ends of the earth? And the new ones over the sons of the earth. But I think both are corrupt. For one should read And do you make the evening star rise over its sons then? That tune [then], though otherwise rare in that version, is nevertheless found at 2 Reg. II, 20. and 3 Reg. XIII, 13. 14. and XVIII, 17. The scribes corrupted the passage because they did not understand what the sons of the evening star were. But the corruption is very ancient, for it had already taken root in the age of Gregory the Great, who evidently read sons of the earth, in book 29 on Job, chapter 17.

VI. The sixth passage, Job 38:36, reads thus in Hebrew: Who has put בטחות wisdom in the reins, or given לשכוי understanding to the heart? In Scripture, namely, heart and reins are frequently joined, as being, in the mind of the Hebrews, the proper seat of thoughts. For examples see Ps 7:10 and XXVI, 2. and LXXIII, 21., Proverb. XXIII, 15. 26. Jer 11:20 and XVII, 10. and XX, 12. So also in this passage. But whereas the reins are commonly called כליות and the heart לב, here each is given another name, and a more poetic one. The reins are called טוחות tuchoth here and in Ps 51:8, from the verb טוח, which means to smear and to coat, because the reins are smeared and coated with fat, as has already been proved elsewhere. The heart, on the other hand, is called שכוי, from the verb שכה, which means to think and to imagine. Hence also שכיות are pictures and images, Isa 2:16, and אבן משכית is a painted stone, Lev 26:1; and משכיות לבב, imaginations of the heart, Ps 73:7; and במשכיתו, in his imagination, Prov 18:11. Although these things are clear and plain, and confirmed in explicit words by the most learned of the Hebrews, namely Kimchi, Aben Ezra and R. Levi, others have nevertheless chosen to interpret the words of Job just cited thus: Who has put wisdom in the reins, or given understanding to the cock? As if שכוי in that place meant cock. The first author of this fiction was a certain R. Simeon, son of Lakis, whose words are cited as follows in the Talmudic tractate On the beginning of the year, fol. 26a: כשהלכתי לתחום קן נשריא הוו קורין לכלה נינפי ולתרנגול שכוי, When I was travelling through the territory of Kennasaria, there they called a bride nympha, and a cock secui. In the same place others trifle that a bride is called nympha because Mount Zion is called beautiful in נוף noph, that is, in situation, Ps 48:3 (For the Greek word νύμφη [nymphē] escaped these circumcised doctors.) They add that the cock is called שכוי secui from the passage of Job we have mentioned. From so impure a source the error at once spread more widely and found many defenders. Among them the Chaldee translator gives a twofold interpretation of this passage: one sound and true, מן יהב ללבא בינתא, Who gave understanding to the heart?; the other Talmudic, מן יהב לתרנגולא ברא בינתא למקלסא למרה, Who gave the wild cock understanding, to praise his Lord? And R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] asserts both thus: למכוי זה תרנגול לשון חכמים וי״א הלב, Secui in the language of the sages means cock, although others explain it as heart. And Aquinas, after quoting the passage of Job: יש מפרשים תרנגול והוא שגור מאד במשנה, There are some who interpret it as cock, which is very common in the Mishnah. Kimchi proves this at some length, although he is of the other opinion. Accordingly, in the Prayer Book, printed and reprinted so many times, this prayer is found among the morning prayers: בא״י אמ״ה אשר נתן לשכוי בינה להבין בין יום ובין לילה, Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, who hast given τῷ [tō] secui (that is, the cock) understanding to distinguish day from night. In this prayer the allusion to the passage of Job is evident. And Jerome, no doubt persuaded by that Jew whom he had as his teacher, rendered the same passage thus: Who has put wisdom in the inward parts of man? or who has given understanding to the cock? He thus joins in the same verse two ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], namely the wisdom of man with the natural instinct of the cock, by which it is prompted to crow at fixed hours. And this in a book in which the two hemistichs of a verse are almost always ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]. I shall note in passing the origin of the version of the Greeks, which might seem entirely foreign: Τίς δὲ ἔδωκεν γυναιξὶν ὑφάσματος σοφίαν, ἢ ποικιλτικὴν ἐπιστήμην; [Tis de edōken gynaixin hyphasmatos sophian, ē poikiltikēn epistēmēn?] And who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in embroidery? For בטחות, in the reins, they read בטוות, in spinning women; and לשכות, for painting or variegating, for לשכוי, to the heart. Written that way, the Hebrew is rendered word for word: Who has put wisdom in spinning women? Or who has given them understanding for painting, or variegating? But the Greek translators turned the skill of spinning into ὑφάσματος σοφίαν [hyphasmatos sophian], because νῆμα [nēma] and ὕφασμα [hyphasma] are often used interchangeably, as it would be easy to prove from Homer, Hesychius and Eustathius.

VII. The seventh passage, Job 39:13 (var. 16.), כנף רננים נעלסה, is rendered thus by the Chaldee: גדפא דתרנגולא דמשבחא ומקלסא, The wing of the cock, which praises and celebrates. They refer this to the cock discussed above. But in the chapter On the Ostrich we have proved at length that these words must be rendered thus: The wing of the ostriches exults. Accordingly this passage too is beside the point.

VIII. The eighth is Ps 50:11, where the Hebrew has I know every bird of the mountains, וזיז שדי עמדי, and the ziz of the field is with me. And the Chaldee: Before me are open all the kinds of birds that fly in the air of the heavens, ותרנגול ברא דקרצולי שרין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא, and the wild cock, whose legs stand on the ground, and whose head reaches the heavens.

IX. And the ninth is Ps 80:14, where for the Hebrew וזיז שדה ירענה, And the ziz of the field has grazed upon it, the Chaldee again has ותרנגולא ברא יתפרנס מנה, And the wild cock shall feed on it. It is as if the Hebrew זיז ziz meant cock, and indeed that cock of which so much is said. But in the chapter On the Boar we have shown that זיז ziz in Hebrew is a wild beast, and is so called from its motion, as in Greek κνώδαλα [knōdala] and κινώπετα [kinōpeta]. So neither of these passages contains anything about the cock.

X. The tenth passage is Prov 30:31, where Solomon calls some animal that walks with a stately gait, by periphrasis (περιφραστικῶς [periphrastikōs]), זרזיר מתנים, girded in the loins. For verses 29, 30, 31 read thus: There are three things of comely gait, indeed four that step finely: the lion, strongest of animals, who turns back before none; the one girded in the loins; and the he-goat; and the king, against whom no one rises up. And there the words זרזיר מתנים, that is, girded in the loins, are rendered by the Greeks with remarkable freedom ἀλεκτὼρ ἐμπεριπατῶν θηλείαις εὐψύχως [alektōr emperipatōn thēleiais eupsychōs], a cock walking briskly among the females. And by the Arabic translator الديك اذا تمشا بين الاناث من الدجاج بطيبة النفس [al-dīk idhā tamashshā bayna al-ināth min al-dajāj bi-ṭībat al-nafs], The cock, when he walks among the female hens with briskness of spirit. And also by the Syriac ܐܒܟܐ ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ ܒܝܢܬ ܬܪܢܓܠܬܐ [אבכא דמזדרכל בינת תרנגלתא], A cock walking proudly among the hens. If you compare these with the Chaldee version, from which they were drawn, you will find that a threefold error has crept into it. For the Chaldee version reads אכבא דמזדרז בינת תרנגולי, for which one should write אבכא דמזדרכל בינת תרנגולן. By the Chaldeans and Syrians the cock is called ܬܪܢܓܘܠ [תרנגול] tarnegol. Nowhere otherwise, so far as I remember, except in this one passage, where for cock the Syriac has ܐܒܟܐ [אבכא] abacha, and the Chaldee אכבא achaba. Hence Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] quietly passed over the word אכבא achaba. And Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] confesses that he does not understand it. Others explain it as cock. I prefer to write it with the Syriac ܐܒܟܐ [אבכא] abacha rather than with the Chaldee אכבא achaba, because if it is written אכבא achaba, it will be of unknown origin. But ܐܒܟܐ [אבכא] abacha comes from the verb אבך abach, whose Hithphael התאבך hithabach means to be lifted up and to be raised aloft, Isa 9:18. Hence the cock seems to be called ܐܒܟܐ [אבכא] abacha by a most fitting name, one that expresses the nature of this bird exactly. For, if you except the peacock, no bird is prouder than the cock. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 21, after treating the pride of the peacock, says: Next, these night-watchmen of ours also have a sense of glory, whom nature produced to rouse mortals to their work and to break their sleep. And a little later: But if victory (in combat) falls to them, they at once crow in triumph and proclaim themselves rulers. The vanquished hides in silence and bears servitude ill. And yet the common sort struts just as proudly, with neck held high and lofty comb, and alone of birds often looks up at the sky, also raising its sickle-shaped tail aloft. These are so many signs of pride. And Aelian, Hist. book 4, ch. 29: Κρατήσας δὲ γαῦρός ἐστι, καὶ ὑψαυχενεῖν, καὶ κυδρουμένῳ ἔοικεν [Kratēsas de gauros esti, kai hypsauchenein, kai kydroumenō eoiken] (read ὑψαυχενῶν, καὶ κυδρουμένῳ ἐοικὼς [hypsauchenōn, kai kydroumenō eoikōs]), When he has won he is proud, with neck erect, and like one who glories. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 12:

Ἀλεκτρυὼν μέν τοι γε νικῶν τὴν μάχην Σφριγᾷ τε καθαρῶς, καὶ σοβεῖ, καὶ τέρπεται· [Alektryōn men toi ge nikōn tēn machēn / Sphriga te katharōs, kai sobei, kai terpetai] The cock, when he prevails in the fight, swells outright, and struts with pomp and exults. And Basil, in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Γαῦρον ὁ ἀλεκτρυὼν, Φιλόκαλον ὁ ταὼς, λάγναι αἱ περιστεραί· [Gauron ho alektryōn, Philokalon ho taōs, lagnai hai peristerai] The cock is a proud thing, the peacock fond of elegance, doves lustful. Lucilius, book 8 of the Satires:
When the barnyard cock, victorious, has proudly raised himself onto his toes and lifts up his foremost claws.

To this, then, belongs the Chaldee and Syriac ܐܒܟܐ [אבכא] abacha, by which I would think not just any cock is meant, but a cock that carries itself thus; and there is added by way of explanation (ἐπεξηγητικῶς [epexēgētikōs]) ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ ܒܝܢܬ ܬܪܢܓܘܠܬܐ [דמזדרכל בינת תרנגולתא], which struts proudly among the hens. To strut proudly is in Arabic درقل [darqala] darkala, and in Syriac ܕܪܟܠ [דרכל], whence that ܕܡܙܕܪܟܠ [דמזדרכל] in the Syriac version, which was without doubt taken from the Chaldee. For Elias cites it thus in the Methurgeman: ואכבא דמזדרכיל. But in our editions it is wrongly read דמזרז, which is girded. Those, that is, who supervised the edition corrupted a word they did not understand, substituting another that was closer to the Hebrew. But one must restore דמזדרכל, which struts proudly. For in this place the Targum follows not the Hebrews but the Greek translators, and that דמזדרכל corresponds exactly to the Greek words ἐμπεριπατῶν εὐψύχως [emperipatōn eupsychōs]. There were also others among the ancients who thought a cock is treated here. Among them are Aquila and Theodotion, who had ἀλεκτρυὼν νώτῳ [alektryōn nōtō], a cock with the back, with no sense, or an obscure one. And Jerome, in whom we read a cock girded about the loins. Yet among the Hebrews there is scarcely anyone who refers this place to the cock. And others understand the Gallic dog, or greyhound, which
— — tightly girds the flanks of its belly;

as we have it in the Cynegeticon of Grattius. Others prefer the leopard, which is itself slender about the flanks, as though girded, and walks magnificently. Others the bee, because of the incisions of its abdomen. Others the starling, which in Arabic is called زرزور [zarzūr] zarzur, and in the Talmud זרזיר zarzir. But no one is wiser than Solomon [Jarchi], who admits that he does not know what it is; and Aben Ezra, who says only that it is the name of a beast. As for me, although I defer greatly to so many ancients who would have the cock described here, I see no reason that drove them to that opinion. Nor could the Greeks, who led the way for the others in this rendering, interpret it of the cock except by substituting for the Hebrew words that have nothing in common with it. For the Hebrew means literally girded in the loins, but the Greek something quite different, namely a cock strutting briskly among the females; and these are as far apart as two octaves (δὶς διὰ πασῶν [dis dia pasōn]). Accordingly Symmachus, bidding that cock fly away, rendered περιεσφιγμένον τὴν ὀσφὺν [periesphigmenon tēn osphyn] (for so it should be read, not περιεσφραγισμένον [periesphragismenon]). And Jerome, to reconcile both versions in some fashion, a cock girded about the loins. But what else was this (be it said with all respect to so great a man) than κλώθειν τὰ ἀσύγκλωστα, καὶ τὰ ἀσύστατα συνάπτειν [klōthein ta asynklōsta, kai ta asystata synaptein]? For it does not belong to the description of the cock to say that it has girded loins. And their claim that the cock is so contrasted with the capon is beside the point. For just as a capon is not said to have ungirded loins, so no one would say a cock has girded loins. Granted, though not conceded, that girded in the loins in Hebrew idiom is opposed to castrated: it will not follow that a cock is meant by that name rather than any other animal equally whole and uncastrated. Moreover, since Solomon places the one girded in the loins between the lion and the he-goat, it is very likely that a quadruped, not a bird, is designated by that name. I therefore more willingly side with those who understand the horse here, an animal of proud gait and whose loins are customarily girded, as was said in its place [vol. 1, book 2, ch. 6, p. 103, ss. 40. 41 of this edition]. However that may be, this at least is certain: here too there is nothing that can with certainty be referred to the cock.

XI. The eleventh passage is Eccles. XII, 4. (var. 6.), where it is said of the old man, He shall rise up at the voice of the bird. The Greeks understand the song of sparrows, others of little birds, others finally of cocks. These last would have it mean that the old man is woken at cockcrow, that is, very early in the morning. But the former, that he sleeps so lightly that his sleep is broken at the slightest noise, say at the voice of a sparrow or some other little bird. And they deny that the cock can be meant, because the Hebrew הצפור means only sparrows, or the smallest little birds. That this is utterly false I shall show in its place. So, as far as I am concerned, it may be interpreted either way.

XII. The twelfth passage is Es. XXII, 17, where the Prophet says to Shebna, יהוה מטלטלך טלטלה גבר, The Lord will carry you away with a carrying away, O man. Others render with the carrying away of a man, that is, they say, a manly, strong, vehement one. But this version has two drawbacks. The first is that no example of this expression is adduced. For when we read elsewhere of the way of a man, the sorrow of a man, the redemption of a man, the teaching of a man, no one understands vehemence. We only infer from it that these things either are in a man or proceed from a man. Thus the carrying away of a man would be nothing but that by which a man carries away or is carried away, which would be very weak. Besides, the carrying away of a man would be expressed in Hebrew as טלטלת גבר, not טלטלה. For who would grant what some assert here, that the final He in טלטלה is epenthetic and not the mark of the feminine, since this too is without example? Finally, the accent tiphcha on טלטלה suspends the voice and prevents it from being joined with the following גבר. Clearly, then, גבר is in the vocative case, as if it read אתה הגבר, O you man. This Aben Ezra and Kimchi rightly observed. And long before them the Syriac translator, who has: ܡܪܝܐ ܡܛܠܛܠ ܠܟ ܛܘܠܛܠܐ ܓܒܪܐ [מריא מטלטל לך טולטלא גברא], The Lord will surely cast you out, O man. Yet there are some among the Hebrews who render, The Lord will carry you away with the carrying away of a man, or even with the carrying away of a cock. For although the word גבר, very frequent in Scripture, everywhere else means man, here they chose to do violence to the sacred text and interpret it as cock, compelled by no necessity but only by an itch and bad habit of καινοτομία [kainotomia]. Hence on the words טלטלה גבר R. Selomo has כהדין תרנגולא דמטלטל מאתר לאתר, Like a cock that is carried from place to place. This is taken from the Midrash on the Psalms, as Kimchi observes. Accordingly Jerome here has: The Lord will make you be carried off, as a cock is carried off. This, of course, follows the view of that Jew from whom he had learned Hebrew letters, as he himself notes in his Notes, where he paraphrases (παραφράζει [paraphrazei]) this passage thus: And I say this, that you should not labour at hewing out a sepulchre, because the Lord will transfer your priesthood, as גבר is wont to be transferred, which all have interpreted as man. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament translated it cock. “As (he says) a cock is transferred from one place to another on the shoulder of a carrier, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place”. Accordingly in the Talmud גבר is sometimes used for cock, as when they say קריאת הגבר for cockcrow. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, p. 67b, גברית is the same as תרנגלת, hen. Indeed, among the paraphrasts Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] calls Ezion-geber כרך תרנגולא, the fortress of the cock, Num 33:35–36. and Deut 2:8, as if Ezion-geber were named from a cock, whereas עציון גבר is the spine of a man. That Ezion-geber was called by this name we have shown in our Phaleg, p. 764, because it is situated in a place inaccessible because of reefs and rocks (ῥαχίαις καὶ σπίλοις ἀπροσίτῳ [rhachiais kai spilois aprositō]), like Dyrrachium in Macedonia. And what is read of Balaam in Num 24:3, נאם הגבר, The man said, Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] takes as if it read The cock said, and taking occasion from this he draws a ridiculous comparison of Balaam with a cock in these words: קרא גבר שדומה בלעם לתרנגול כמו שהתרנגול הוא נואף מכל כן בלעם רבע אתונו וכמו שהתרנגול יודע בעתים כן בלעם יודע לכוין השעה שהקב״ה כועס וכמו שהתרנגול דרכו לעמוד על רגל אחד כן בלעם חגר באחד רגליו, He calls him גבר, because Balaam was like a cock. As the cock is lecherous above all, so Balaam lay with his she-ass; as the cock knows the times, so Balaam knew how to find out the hour at which God, the Holy One, blessed be He, is angry; as the cock is wont to stand on one foot, so Balaam was lame in one foot. Most absurd of all is this: although the other sacrifices which God had prescribed in his Law have now been abolished, yet on the day preceding the feast of Atonement there is no one among the Jews who does not offer a cock for himself, repeating these words while he strikes it against his head three times: זה חליפתי זה תחתי זה כפרתי זה התרנגול ילך למיתה ואני אלך לחיים טובים עם ירשאל אמן, Let this cock be an exchange for me; let this be in my place; let this be an atonement for me; let this cock go to death, but I, with all Israel, to a happy life. Amen. For the rest, consult the distinguished Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum]'s Synagoga, chapter 20. Here it suffices to add that the occasion of the error was the ambiguous word גבר, by which they hold that both man and cock are signified. It is fitting, therefore, they say, that since גבר has sinned, גבר should bear the penalty of the sin. As if a cock and a man could be held as one before God's tribunal because, through an abuse of the word, they are called by the same name. I deliberately pass over what is found about the cock in the second Targum of Esther, because these are not paraphrases but the author's mere fabrications.

More probable is the view of SELDEN (de Diis Syris, Syntagma 2, ch. 7), that these were the huts of the daughters, in which daughters prostituted their virginity at the temple of Venus Mylitta; see Herodotus, book 1, §. 199; Strabo, book 16, p. 1081, ed. Almeloveen.

But since in none of the other dialects is the hen called by the name זגתא, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1902, can hardly persuade himself that it was so called in Chaldee. In Arabic زجّ [zujj] is the extremity of a thing, the iron at the lower end of a spear, and then the pole, or the pivot around which a millstone turns. Hence Michaelis thinks it probable that זגתא is the pole star. But that most learned man did not consider that in the very passage of the Chaldee version with which we are dealing, a meaning other than hen can hardly have a place, since אפרחתא is immediately added to זגתא. If, then, you take זגתא here in the sense Michaelis devised, this charming rendering will result: and will you lead the pole star with her chicks? Moreover, Michaelis wrongly disregards the use of the word זגתא in the Talmud, confusing the Talmudic writers, who write fairly pure Chaldee, with the later Rabbis. To the authority of the latter, indeed, no one will attribute anything in establishing meanings; but the usage of the Chaldee dialect was certainly well known to those older writers.

Niebuhr [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] also testifies that not only the Jews of Sanaa and Baghdad, but also the Arabs living on the Persian Gulf call the Great Bear Asch. In the Descript. Arab. p. 114 he relates that a Jew of Sanaa, an astrologer but unskilled in knowledge of the stars, when questioned by him, answered after consulting other Jews that Asch is Om ennäsch, the Great Bear. P. 115: Näsch, or Benäth Näsch, which constellation the Jews at Sanaa and Baghdad, as well as the Arabs on the Persian Gulf, also call Asch, is the Great Bear.

Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], in his Commentary on this passage of Job, holds that the Hebrew עיש should be referred to the Arabic عوس [ʿws] and عسّ [ʿass] to go round by night, whence عاسّ [ʿāss] a night watchman walking through cities. For both Bears, never setting and wandering about in the sky through the whole night, could be excellently compared to such a night watchman. Although Michaelis follows this in the Supplemm. p. 1907, it displeases me, chiefly because it smacks of etymological subtleties, whereas we see that in naming celestial signs it was not so much etymological reasons that were considered as resemblances to other things whose forms and shapes they most nearly approached. Nor am I moved by what Schultens and Michaelis object to Bochart's view, that Hebrew ש usually corresponds not to Arabic ش but to س, since not a few words exist in which ש and ش correspond to each other; Schultens himself collected several in the Clavis Dialector. p. 300, 301.
On the Crowing of the Cock.

It has so far been clearly established that, of the many places in the Old Testament in which some claim that the fowl kind is treated, none is sufficiently certain. But the matter stands otherwise with the New, where Christ speaks openly of the crowing of the cock and of the hen's affection for her chicks, which she gathers under her wings. To the crowing of the cock belongs Mark 13:35 "Watch therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or at the crowing of the cock, or in the morning." The Evangelist calls the crowing of the cock by a single word, ἀλεκτοροφωνία [alektorophōnia], as others say ἀλεκτρυοφωνία [alektryophōnia], and the Romans gallicinium [cockcrow]. The Glosses of Philoxenus: Ἀλεκτρυοφωνία [Alektryophōnia], gallicinium, galli cantus [cockcrow, the crowing of the cock]. The Hebrews call this very time קריאת הגבר, the cry, or crowing of the cock. Thus in the Talmudic tractate Yoma, ch. 1, fol. 20a: בכל יום תורמים את המזבח בקריאת הגבר או סמוך לו בין לפניו בין לאחריו, "Every day they remove the ashes from the altar at the crowing of the cock, or at the time nearest to it, whether before or after." And fol. 21a: היוצא לדרך קודם קריאת הגבר דמו בראשו, "Whoever sets out on a journey before the crowing of the cock, his blood is upon his own head": that is, he is answerable for his own death if anything goes wrong. And in Shemot Rabbah, chapter 1, concerning the servitude of the Israelites in Egypt: והיו הנוגשים הולכים לבתי השוטרים בהשכמה להוציאן למלאכתן לקריאת הגבר, "And the taskmasters went to the houses of the officers very early in the morning, to bring them out to their work at the crowing of the cock." And a little later: עמד לשעת קריאת הגבר והוציאו מביתו, "He stood by at the hour of the crowing of the cock, to bring him out of his house." The crowing of the cock is properly the time midway between μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion] and morning, as the Evangelist defines it: "At midnight," he says, "or at cockcrow, or in the morning." Hence Censorinus, in chapter 19, enumerates the parts of the day thus: "There are also several times of night and day marked out and distinguished by their own names, which are found written here and there in the old poets. I shall set them all out in order. I begin from midnight, which is the beginning and the end of the Roman day. The time next to this is called 'after midnight'. Then follows cockcrow, when the cocks begin to crow; then conticinium, when they have fallen silent; then 'before light', and so it is called diluculum [dawn]. Morning, when the light of the sun is seen," etc. Nor otherwise Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1, ch. 3: "The first time of the day is called the declining of midnight, then cockcrow, then conticinium, when both the cocks fall silent and men too are still at rest; then diluculum, that is, when the day begins to be discerned; then morning, when the day is bright," etc. And the old Glosses: Conticinium, ὁ μεταξὺ ἀλεκτρυοφωνίας χρόνος [ho metaxy alektryophōnias chronos], "the time which is between the cockcrows." This makes no sense; rather one should read ὁ μετὰ τὰς ἀλεκτρυοφωνίας χρόνος [ho meta tas alektryophōnias chronos], "the time which is after the cockcrows." These are spoken of in the plural because there are several. For the cock begins to crow from midnight. Then, in the space midway between μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion] and dawn, it crows again. Therefore many call this crowing the second. Aristophanes in the Ἐκκλησιάζουσαι [Ekklēsiazousai], page 735:
Οὐδ᾽ εἰ μὰ Δία τοτ᾽ ἦλθες, ὅτε τὸ δεύτερον Ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο. — — — [Oud᾽ ei ma Dia tot᾽ ēlthes, hote to deuteron Alektryōn ephthengeto.]

"Not even, by Jove, if you had come when the cock was crowing for the second time." Heliodorus, book 5: Ἀλεκτρυόνες ἤδη τὸ δεύτερον ᾖδον [Alektryones ēdē to deuteron ēdon], "The cocks were already crowing for the second time." Hence the old proverb among the Paroemiographers, on which Erasmus [=Desiderius Erasmus, Adagia] says much: Πρὶν ἢ τὸ δεύτερον ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο [Prin ē to deuteron alektryōn ephthengeto], "Before the cock crows a second time," that is, very early in the morning. Synesius, Epist. 4: Ἧς (νυκτὸς) ἤδη περὶ δευτέραν οὔσης ὀρνίθων ᾠδήν [Hēs (nyktos) ēdē peri deuteran ousēs ornithōn ōdēn]; "When the night was already about the second crowing of the cocks." Juvenal, Satire 9, line 106:
"Yet what he does at the crowing of the second cock, the nearest innkeeper will know before daybreak." — —

Ammianus, book 22: He climbed Mount Casius, from which at the second cockcrow the first rising of the sun is seen. Others write that the sun is seen from Mount Casius at the fourth watch. Mela, book 1, ch. 10: So that from its highest summit it shows the rising of the sun from the fourth watch. Pliny, book 10, ch. 22: Casius, whose lofty height beholds the sun rising through the darkness at the fourth watch. Solinus: From whose summit the orb of the sun is seen while it is still the fourth watch. Martianus Capella, book 6: Casius, whose height sees the sun through the darkness at the fourth watch. Thus that second cockcrow and the fourth watch are the same. For cocks, on the authority of Pliny, go to bed with the sun, and at the fourth military watch call men back to their cares and labour. But although cocks crow twice in the depth of night, nevertheless, when something is read to have been done at the time of cockcrow without the addition of a number, the later one is always understood. It is so called κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [kat᾽ exochēn], either because the cocks then crow more keenly and briskly; or because that later crowing is more useful to men, since it rouses them to the labours of the day; or finally because the time of the first cockcrow is designated by another name: for it is called μεσονύκτιον [mesonyktion], midnight, mid-night. Therefore not only Mark the Evangelist, but also Censorinus and Macrobius place cockcrow midway between midnight and morning, as has already appeared above. And Isidore (Orig. book 5, ch. 31) writes that cockcrow is so called on account of the cocks, the heralds of the light. Hence it is clear that only the later one is meant by him. In the words of Heliodorus too, book 1 of the Aethiopica, καθ᾽ ὃν καιρὸν ἀλεκτρυόνες ᾄδουσιν [kath᾽ hon kairon alektryones adousin], at the time when the cocks crow, the words that immediately follow show that the same thing is meant: that they crow αἰσθήσει φυσικῇ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς περιστροφῆς ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόσρησιν κινουμένους [aisthēsei physikē tēs tou hēliou kath᾽ hēmas peristrophēs epi tēn tou Theou prosrēsin kinoumenous], stirred by a natural sense of the sun's turning towards us to salute God. And in Pollux too, among the last parts of the night is reckoned the time περὶ ἀλεκτρυόνων ᾠδὰς [peri alektryonōn ōdas] and ἀλεκτρυόνων ᾀδόντων [alektryonōn adontōn]. And Horace, Satire 1:
The man skilled in law and statutes praises the farmer's lot, when towards cockcrow a client knocks at his door.

That is, at earliest dawn. Nor does the cockcrow of the night mean anything else in these words of Apuleius at the beginning of book 8: At the cockcrow of the night a certain young man came from the nearest city. And in the Vulgate, Tob 8:11: About the crowing of the cocks Raguel ordered his servants to be summoned; and they went with him to dig a grave. About the crowing of the cocks, that is, at the time when the domestic cocks crow. That the time before daybreak is meant is shown by what is found in verses 13 and 14: And when they had prepared the pit, Raguel returned to his wife and said to her, Send one of your maidservants, and let her see whether he (Tobias) is dead, so that I may bury him before the day grows light. The Hebrew has נקברהו טרם אור הבוקר ואיש לא ידע, We shall bury him before the morning light, so that no one may know. Since, therefore, the same time is sometimes called simply cockcrow, and sometimes more explicitly the second cockcrow, men learned in every field rightly think that by this observation Mark can easily be reconciled with the other Evangelists in specifying the time at which Peter was to deny Christ three times. For according to Mark, Christ foretold to Peter that he would deny him three times πρὶν ἢ δὶς ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι [prin ē dis alektora phōnēsai], before the cock had crowed twice. And indeed, after it had crowed following the first denial, after the third ἐκ δευτέρου ἀλέκτωρ ἐφώνησε [ek deuterou alektōr ephōnēse], the cock crowed again. So Mark has it in ch. 14, verses 30, 68, 69, 70, 71. But in the others the cock does not crow before the third denial. For thus Christ says in Matt 26:34 Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ, πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι, τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ με· [En tautē tē nykti, prin alektora phōnēsai, tris aparnēsē me] This night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And Luke 22:34 Οὐ μὴ φωνήσει σήμερον ἀλέκτωρ, πρὶν ἢ τρὶς ἀπαρνήσῃ μὴ εἰδέναι με· [Ou mē phōnēsei sēmeron alektōr, prin ē tris aparnēsē mē eidenai me] Today the cock will not crow before you deny three times that you know me. And John 13:38 Οὐ μὴ ἀλέκτωρ φωνήσει, ἕως οὗ ἀπαρνήσῃ με τρίς· [Ou mē alektōr phōnēsei, heōs hou aparnēsē me tris] The cock will not crow before you deny me three times. These seem ἀσύστατα [asystata]. But, they say, they are reconciled without any difficulty if you suppose that Peter first denied about midnight, and that the cock then crowed for the first time; and that he denied the third time about the fourth watch, or about the time usually called cockcrow, and that the cock then crowed again. On this assumption, these words of Christ, The cock will not crow, or Before the cock crows, will be the same as if he had said, Before the time of cockcrow, or The cock will not crow that customary crowing from which the time at which it crows is called ἀλεκτοροφωνία [alektorophōnia], before you have denied me three times. Meanwhile I have no doubt that Mark, who had been a disciple of Peter, reported the very words of Christ, just as he had learned them from Peter. But it sufficed for the others to record what was most important, namely that Christ had not only foreseen and foretold that threefold denial of Peter, but had also specified the time, and that Peter would deny Christ three times before cockcrow. Although it is plain that this is to be understood of the second cockcrow, since this alone is called simply cockcrow, Mark nevertheless expressed it explicitly, and added moreover that Peter's first denial preceded the first cockcrow. But, you will say, between the first and second cockcrow a fourth part of the night usually intervenes; and that span would then have been nearly three hours (for in Judaea, at the season of the year when Christ was delivered to death, the nights are more than eleven hours long); whereas between Peter's first and last denial scarcely half of this span can have elapsed. This is clear from Lucae XXII, 56. 57. 58. For there, when Peter had denied to the maidservant that he knew Christ, which was the first denial, μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy], a little later, another, seeing him, said, You too are one of them: but Peter said, Man, I am not; which was the second denial. Καὶ διαστάσης ὡσεὶ ὥϱας μιᾶς [Kai diastasēs hōsei hōras mias], And after about one hour had passed, when another asserted the same thing, Peter denied a third time, and immediately the cock crowed. I answer: 1. The Evangelists reported most things summarily; and while Peter, being accused, tried to clear himself, the matter could have been drawn out at greater length, and, with many words exchanged back and forth, much time could have been spent in the dispute itself. 2. From Luke's words μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy] it does not follow that there was no interval of time, or a very short one, between Peter's first and second denial. For John, in chapter 18, from verse 17 to 25, inserts many things as having taken place in that interval. And the third denial, which Luke separates from the second by an interval of about an hour, is nevertheless said in Matthew and Mark to have occurred μετὰ μικρὸν [meta mikron], a little later. Therefore that μετὰ μικρὸν [meta mikron], or, what is the same, μετὰ βραχὺ [meta brachy], can be extended more widely than is thought. 3. Something may be added to Luke's hour, since he did not say precisely that one hour intervened, but ὡσεὶ ὥρας μιᾶς [hōsei hōras mias], about one hour. 4. Although a fourth part of the night usually intervenes between the first and second cockcrow, this is not invariable. For it often happens that cocks crow at random, and not at fixed hours. Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)] writes in Exercitatio 239 against Cardano that he experienced this both formerly on night watch and later in his nocturnal studies. A cock, therefore, could have anticipated the usual time of cockcrow by one hour after Peter's third denial. Another objection may be raised: when Peter denied Christ, the scribes, priests and elders were in Caiaphas's house to inquire into Christ's life; and Peter meanwhile, having entered the courtyard, waited to see how the matter would finally turn out and what would be decided about Christ. But it is not likely that that assembly lasted so far into the night. For who would believe that so many men from among the leaders of the Jewish people spent almost the whole night without sleep in order to decide this case, when the matter could just as conveniently have been put off to another time? But this objection is raised in vain. For it is certain that it happened so. This will be clear to those who consider how many things were done that night before Peter's third denial. Ὀψίας γενομένης [Opsias genomenēs] , When evening had already come, that is, at the very setting of the sun, Christ celebrated the Passover with the Apostles. He washed their feet . He preached on the occasion . He instituted the eucharistic supper . He restrained with the gravest words the disciples, who were contending among themselves over the primacy . He sang a hymn, which consisted of several Psalms, if the Talmudists are to be believed . He went to the Mount of Olives ; and came to an estate named Gethsemane . He withdrew to pray , and after an hour's prayer returned to the disciples; finding them asleep, he rebuked them because they could not keep watch one hour . The same happened a second and a third time . Meanwhile the officers sent with Judas seize Christ . And they lead him first to Annas . And from there to Caiaphas . There the scribes, priests and elders assemble. And Peter, admitted with difficulty into the courtyard and recognized, denies Christ . Christ is questioned by Caiaphas . After this he is denied by Peter a second time , and, after an hour had passed, a third time . No fair judge of the facts will fail to recognize at once that all these things could not have taken place before the dead of night. And it was indeed altogether extraordinary that a man's life should be dealt with at those hours. But, besides the feast that was close at hand, they were driven to it by their savage rage against Christ and by a more than Vatinian hatred with which they were borne against him. Closest to the interpretation we have given comes that of Theophylact on Mark: Ὅπερ δὲ εἶπεν ἀσαφῶς ὁ Ματθαῖος, ὅτι πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι ἡρμήνευσεν ὁ Μάρκος, ὅτι πρὶν φωνῆσαι δίς. Εἰώθασι γὰρ οἱ ἀλέκτορες κατὰ μίαν ἀγωγὴν πολλάκις φωνεῖν, εἶτα οἷον ὑπνώττειν, καὶ πάλιν μετά τινα καιρὸν ἑτέραν ἀρχὴν ποιεῖσθαι τοῦ φωνεῖν· ὃ οὖν εἶπεν ὁ Ματθαῖος, τοῦτό ἐστιν, ὅτι, πρὶν ἀλέκτορα φωνῆσαι, τουτέστι, πληρῶσαι τὰς κραυγὰς τῆς πρώτης ἀγωγῆς, ἀπαρνήσῃ με τρίς. [Hoper de eipen asaphōs ho Matthaios, hoti prin alektora phōnēsai hērmēneusen ho Markos, hoti prin phōnēsai dis. Eiōthasi gar hoi alektores kata mian agōgēn pollakis phōnein, eita hoion hypnōttein, kai palin meta tina kairon heteran archēn poieisthai tou phōnein; ho oun eipen ho Matthaios, touto estin, hoti, prin alektora phōnēsai, toutesti, plērōsai tas kraugas tēs prōtēs agōgēs, aparnēsē me tris.] What Matthew says obscurely, „Before the cock crows“, Mark has explained as before it crows twice. For cocks are accustomed often to crow in one stretch, then, as it were, to sleep, and after some time to begin crowing again. What Matthew said, then, namely, before the cock crows, means: before it completes the cry of the first crowing, you will deny me three times .

In the crowing of the cock there are two marvels. One is that so small an animal crows with so strained a voice that it is heard from very far away. The other is that it crows at fixed hours, and at the very time when the other birds give themselves to sleep. The former is wonderfully extolled by the Talmudists in the tractate Yoma, fol. 20b, where someone says of the sacred cock at Jerusalem: והיה קולו נשמע משלוש פרסאות מעשה באגריפס המלך שהיה בא בדרך ושמע קולו בשלוש פרסאות וכשבא לביתו שיגר לו מתנות, Its voice was heard from three parasangs. Let King Agrippa serve as an example: while he was on a journey, he heard it from three parasangs, and when he had come home, he sent it gifts. This is slight compared with what another says in the same place: ונשמע קולו ביריחו, its voice was heard as far as Jericho. For, as Rabbi Yochanan asserts, מירושלם ליריחו עשרה פרסי, From the city of Jerusalem to Jericho there are ten parasangs. These things are indeed fabulous; but truer is what Cardano says, De subtilitate book 10: The cock, if it were a rare animal, would be worthy of admiration not only for its form but for its crowing. It exults with its voice, and it is heard far off: at night even a thousand paces and more. Of its nocturnal crowing at fixed hours Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] says: ومن عجايب معرفته ساعات الليل فان الليل اذا كان خمسة عشر ساعه يقسط اصواته عليها كما كان يقسطه عليها وهو تسع ساعات وذلك بالهام من الله [wa-min ʿajāyib maʿrifatuhu sāʿāt al-layl fa-inna al-layl idhā kāna khamsata ʿashar sāʿa yuqassiṭ aṣwātahu ʿalayhā kamā kāna yuqassiṭuhu ʿalayhā wa-huwa tisʿ sāʿāt wa-dhālika bi-ilhām min Allāh] Among the marvels (of its nature is this), that it knows the hours of the night: so that, when the night is of fifteen hours, it apportions its crowings in proportion to it; just as it also apportions them when it is of only nine hours, and this by the inspiration of God. And Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: واعظم ما فيه من العجايب معرفه الاوقات الليلية فيقسط اصواته عليها تقسيطا لا يكاد يغادر منه شيا سوا طال او قصر ويوالي صياحه قبل الفجر وبعده فسبحان من هداه لذلك [wa-aʿẓam mā fīhi min al-ʿajāyib maʿrifat al-awqāt al-layliyya fa-yuqassiṭ aṣwātahu ʿalayhā taqsīṭan lā yakādu yughādir minhu shayʾan sawāʾ ṭāla aw qaṣura wa-yuwālī ṣiyāḥahu qabl al-fajr wa-baʿdahu fa-subḥān man hadāhu li-dhālika] The most marvellous thing in it is that it knows the times of the night, and according to them distributes its crowings with so even a balance that it omits hardly anything of them, whether they be longer or shorter. And its crowing continually precedes and follows the dawn. Praise be to Him who taught it this. From the Chronicles of Isfahan we shall show in its place that Muhammad, seeking the causes of so great a thing, took refuge in fables. For he imagines that God has a white cock whose wings are adorned with emeralds, jacinths and pearls and spread from east to west, whose head is beneath the throne of glory and whose feet are in the highest air; and that it thus announces the time of prayer every morning and is heard by all the inhabitants of heaven and earth except men and demons. And therefore, he says, يجيبه ديوك الارض [yujībuhu duyūk al-arḍ] the cocks of the earth answer it. We have shown that this was partly taken from the Hebrews. But among the Greeks too Callisthenes recognizes something divine in the crowing of the cock. Hence Cicero, De Divinatione book 2: What came into Callisthenes' mind, to say that the gods gave cocks the signal to crow? Yet in the same author Democritus explains in excellent words the cause why cocks crow before daylight. For when the food has been driven out of the breast, distributed through the whole body and assimilated, they utter their crowings, satisfied with rest. And in our own age a very learned man writes: It crows chiefly about the midnight, or just before sunrise. That is, partly when the sun has completed half of its nocturnal course, partly from the time when it has reached, or nearly reached, our horizon, the cock's senses are released. For this animal, by a force of nature, or from a property of its temperament, is so affected by the sun that it then wakes up. Rejoicing, therefore, both in the rest it has sweetly enjoyed and because it feels that its breast or stomach is not weighed down by food as before (since this has now been digested through the whole body), it attests its joy by crowing and by clapping its wings. At the same time also, because the cock's warm and thin blood, through the nocturnal condition of the air, has raised exhalations and vapours in the muscles, it therefore claps its wings and, singing with its throat, strives to dispel the vapours together with the phlegm gathered by the cold of the night, just as other animals expel wind by stretching or yawning. Of this I approve only the statement that this animal is affected by the sun. But why it is affected by the sun is the very thing in question, and indeed sought in vain, since it depends on a hidden property of nature. For as to what is alleged about joy felt from the digestion of food: if it were true, then, since in a healthy cock digestion is as quick or even quicker in winter than in summer, because the heat of the stomach by which food is digested is then more intense, the winter cockcrow would not be later than the summer one. But the matter is quite otherwise. For the morning crowing of the cock here takes place in winter three or four hours later than in summer. And the same reasoning applies to the other things they add here. So the question must be investigated further.
John 13:12 etc. up to ch. XVIII.

It is recorded in the Talmudic tractate Bava Kama, ch. 7, last section, that it was forbidden by law to raise cocks in Jerusalem: אין מגדלין תרנגולין בירושלם מפני קדושים, They do not raise cocks in Jerusalem on account of the holy things, nor do the priests raise them anywhere in the land of Israel. The Gloss gives the reason: Israelites too are forbidden to raise cocks in Jerusalem on account of the holy things; for the Israelites ate there the flesh of the peace offerings and thank offerings, and it is the habit of cocks to turn over dunghills, and from them they might perhaps bring out the flesh of creeping things, by which those holy things that were to be eaten could be defiled. Hence some interpreters have come to doubt the cockcrow mentioned by the writers of the Gospels. For my part, I would count that Talmudic rule among the fictitious prohibitions which the petty subtlety of the Jewish masters drew out of the simple laws of Moses, but which no one heeded outside the shade of the schools. Certainly, if one wishes to argue the matter from the Talmud, many more passages from the same Talmud can be set against that passage of Bava Kama in which cocks and cockcrow are mentioned, some of which Bochart has cited above. And in the tractate Berachoth we read of a cock that, because it had pierced an infant's skull at the spot where it is most tender and killed the infant, was punished by stoning by sentence of the Sanhedrin. See Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], Lexic. Chald. p. 2654. But if anyone is unwilling to accept this, let him follow the opinion of Reland [=Adriaan Reland, Dissertationes miscellaneae (1706–08)] (in the oration de Galli cantu Hierosolymis audito, Rotterdam 1709, 8vo), that Pilate, or the other Romans living in the city, being either wholly indifferent to or ignorant of Jewish institutions, kept cocks or hens, either for food or for the sake of auspices. For the opinions of others, listed and assessed, see Wolf, Curae Philologg. on Matt 26:34, vol. 1, p. 378 ff. One may also compare Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], Einleit. in das N. T. vol. 1, p. 71. 72.
On the hen's love for her chicks.

It remains for us to say something about the hen's love for her chicks, in connection with the notable passage of Christ, Matt 23:37 and Luke 13:34: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" Hen in Greek is ὄρνις [ornis], a word which among the older Greeks signified bird in general. Yet in Plato, Laws book 7, ὀρνίθων θρέμματα [ornithōn thremmata] are thought to be the chicks of hens. And in Aristophanes, in the Wasps, ὀρνίθων γάλα [ornithōn gala] is hens' milk. And in Aristotle οἱ ὄρνιθες [hoi ornithes] are cocks, when he writes in Hist. book 9, ch. 50: Ἐκτέμνονται δὲ οἱ ὄρνιθες κατὰ τὸ ὀῤῥοπύγιον [ektemnontai de hoi ornithes kata to orrhopygion], that is, Cocks are castrated near the rump. And αἱ ὄρνιθες [hai ornithes] are hens in De generat. anim. book 1, ch. 21, where he reports that some people περὶ τὰς ὄρνιθας τὰς γενναίας σπουδάζειν [peri tas ornithas tas gennaias spoudazein], take pains to breed well-bred hens. Nor is anything else meant in these words of Theophrastus, De causis book 2, ch. 15: Τὰ ὅλως εὔτοκα βραχύβια· καὶ τὰ ὑπερτοκήσαντα πολλάκις ἀπόλλυται, καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν τε συνανθρωπευομένων αἱ ὄρνιθες [ta holōs eutoka brachybia; kai ta hypertokēsanta pollakis apollytai, kai malista epi tōn te synanthrōpeuomenōn hai ornithes]. This should certainly be rendered thus: All the most prolific animals are short-lived; and those whose breeding is excessive often perish, and hens above all among those that live with humans. Nor in these words of Chrysippus in Athenaeus, book 9, ch. 4: Καθάπερ τινὲς τὰς λευκὰς ὀρνίθας τῶν μελανῶν ἡδίους εἶναι μᾶλλον [kathaper tines tas leukas ornithas tōn melanōn hēdious einai mallon]; As some hold that white hens are tastier than black ones. And he likewise proves, by adducing examples, that the old comic poets Menander, Cratinus and Antiphanes used it for hens. And in the same author, book 1, ch. 15, Phylarchus relates that τινὰς δυνάμεις στυτικὰς [tinas dynameis stytikas] sent by Sandrocottus, king of the Indians, to Seleucus, ὁρμὰς ἐμποιεῖν ὀρνίθων δίκην [hormas empoiein ornithōn dikēn], excited sexual desire, such as is found in cocks. A very great man noted on that passage that στυπτικὰς [styptikas] is wrongly printed; and that the translator substituted Sandropyctus for Sandrocottus, Antiochus for Seleucus, and little sparrows for cocks, so that nothing sound remains in this passage. Since, then, ὄρνις [ornis] in Homer and Hesiod is nothing other than bird in general, in Plato's age it began to be used for the gallinaceous kind, and for some centuries was said of the cock as well as of the hen, until usage prevailed that it was the proper name of the hen. Hence Myrtilus in Athenaeus, book 9: Ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ ὄρνιθας καὶ ὀρνίθια νῦν μόνον ἡ συνήθεια καλεῖ τὰς θηλείας [alla mēn kai ornithas kai ornithia nyn monon hē synētheia kalei tas thēleias]; Now indeed custom has it that only the females (of cocks) are called ὄρνιθες [ornithes] and ὀρνίθια [ornithia]. Therefore in Matthew and Luke ὄρνις [ornis] is not طير [ṭayr] or طاير [ṭāyir], bird in general, as the Vulgate translator renders it in Luke, and as one of the Arabic versions renders it in Luke and the other in both places, but دجاجة [dajāja], hen, as the Vulgate translator and Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] have it in Matthew. Accordingly the Syriac too consistently renders ܬܪܢܓܘܠܬܐ [תרנגולתא], and the Ethiopic ዶርሆ፡ [dorəho], that is, hen. So also Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, and most of the ancients, except Ambrose on Luke, where this passage is rendered thus: How often would I have gathered your children, as a bird its nest under its feathers? But this is most especially proper to the hen, that she not only sits on her eggs, like the other birds, but also gathers her chicks, once hatched, under her wings, so that they may be warmed and invigorated by their mother's heat. Hence it is that in Arabic she is surnamed ام حفصة [umm ḥafṣa], mother of gathering. So the two distinguished lexicographers Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] expressly write, and, among the writers on nature, Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], often cited by us. Here is a striking example of this hen's φιλοστοργία [philostorgia] from Alpheus of Mytilene, Anthology book 1, ch. 87.

Χειμερίαις νιφάδεσσι παλυνομένα τιθὰς ὄρνις Τέκνοις εὐναίας ἀμφέχεε πτέρυγας· Μέσφά μιν οὐράνιον κρύος ὤλεσεν. ἦ γὰρ ἔμεινεν Αἰθέρος οὐρανίων ἀντίπαλος νεφέων. Πρόκνη, καὶ Μήδεια, κατ᾽ ἀΐδος αἰδέσθητε, Μητέρες, ὀρνιθίων ἔργα διδασκόμεναι. [Cheimeriais niphadessi palynomena tithas ornis teknois eunaias amphechee pterygas; mespha min ouranion kryos ōlesen. ē gar emeinen aitheros ouraniōn antipalos nepheōn. Proknē, kai Mēdeia, kat᾽ aidos aidesthēte, mēteres, ornithiōn erga didaskomenai.]

Sprinkled with the winter snows, the gentle hen spread her sleep-bringing wings over her chicks, until the cold of the sky killed her. Truly she held out as a fighter against the clouds of heaven. O mothers, Procne and Medea, blush in the underworld, as you learn the works of hens. And the excellent writer Plutarch, in the book On Affection for Offspring, sets the matter before our eyes thus: Τὰς δὲ ἀλεκτορίδας ἐν τοῖς ὄμμασι καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἔχομεν, ὃν τρόπον τὰ νεοττία περιέπουσι, τοῖς μὲν ἐνδῦναι χαλῶσαι τὰς πτέρυγας, τὰ δὲ ἐπιβαίνοντα τῶν νώτων, καὶ προσέρχονται πανταχόθεν ἀναδεχόμεναι, μετὰ τοῦ γεγηθὸς, ἢ καὶ προσφιλὲς ἐπιφθέγγεσθαι. κυνέας δὲ, καὶ δρακοντίας [Tas de alektoridas en tois ommasi kath᾽ hēmeran echomen, hon tropon ta neottia periepousi, tois men endynai chalōsai tas pterygas, ta de epibainonta tōn nōtōn, kai proserchontai pantachothen anadechomenai, meta tou gegēthos, ē kai prosphiles epiphthengesthai. kyneas de, kai drakontias] (read κύνας δὲ, καὶ δράκοντας [kynas de, kai drakontas], or δρακόντια [drakontia]) ἂν περὶ αὐτῶν φοβηθῶσι φεύγουσιν· ἂν δὲ περὶ τῶν τέκνων, ἀμύνονται, καὶ διαμάχονται παρὰ δύναμιν [an peri autōn phobēthōsi pheugousin; an de peri tōn teknōn, amynontai, kai diamachontai para dynamin]. And hens, which are before our eyes every day: with what care they protect their chicks, letting down their wings for some to creep under, while others climb onto their backs! And they come up from every side to receive them, so as to testify their joy and love with their voice. Dogs and serpents, if they fear for themselves, flee; but if they fear for their young, they drive off the attacker and fight beyond their strength. Augustine observes this very thing in these words in the Gospel Questions, book 1, question 36: What you will find with greater difficulty in other animals, protecting her young with her wings she fights against the kite. But he also often asserts that it is peculiar to the hen that she is so affected by the weakness of her chicks that she herself becomes weak and sick. Thus on Psalm 58: He (Christ) was made weak even unto death, and took on the flesh of weakness, in order to gather the chicks of Jerusalem under his wings, as the hen becomes weak with her little ones. And a little later: Surely I speak of a well-known thing, which is before our eyes every day. How her voice grows hoarse! How her whole body becomes bristly, her wings droop, her feathers loosen! And on Psalm XC.: Many birds here breed before our eyes and warm their chicks; no bird becomes weak with her chicks as the hen does. Let your charity consider swallows, sparrows and storks. We see them outside their nests, and we do not know whether they have young. But the hen we recognize by the weakness of her voice and the loosening of her feathers: she is wholly changed by affection for her chicks; because they are weak, she makes herself weak. And in On the Words of the Lord, Sermon 29: That hen is the wisdom of the Lord. But it took on flesh in order to be suited to the chicks. See the hen, bristling in her feathers, wings lowered, voice broken, shaken, weary and languid, suiting herself to her chicks. And in the Questions cited above: This kind of animal has great affection for its young, so that, affected by their weakness, it too becomes weak. Hence in Euripides, in the Madness of Heracles, Megara, greatly anxious about the children she had borne to Hercules, repeatedly says that she keeps them under her wings, like a hen brooding her chicks. The words are:

Οἵ θ᾽ Ἡράκλειοι παῖδες, οὓς ὑποπτέρους Σώζω νεοσσοὺς, ὄρνις ὡς ὑφειμένη· [Hoi th᾽ Hērakleioi paides, hous hypopterous Sōzō neossous, ornis hōs hypheimenē] And the sons of Hercules, whom under my wings I keep, as a hen is wont to brood her chicks.

I adduce these things here because they are very similar to the words of Christ, in which he compares his φιλανθρωπίαν [philanthrōpian] with the φιλοστοργίᾳ [philostorgia] of the hen, which with the greatest eagerness draws her chicks to herself, in order to keep them safe and sound under her wings from the threatening kite or hawk.
What the ברבורים אבוסים, fattened barburim, at the table of Solomon were, 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.].

As with the Roman ancilia, so in the various interpretations of the word ברבורים barburim in 1 Reg. IV, 23. [var. V, 3.], the false ones have been fashioned so closely to resemble the true that it is not easy to tell the one from the other. From an inspection of the passage itself it is clear that the ברבורי׳ barburim are listed among the animals that were consumed daily at the table of Solomon. For the sacred text reads: And the provisions of Solomon for each day were ten oxen, etc., besides harts, and roebucks, and buffaloes, ברבורים אבוסים, and fattened barburim. Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] explain this as all the choicest animals. Apuleius would have said pastus electiles [choice fare], as in book 10 of the Metamorphoses: Nor could the ass, who alone was present, be affected by such food, and yet every day the choice fare was nowhere to be found. The Greek interpreters were of the same opinion; two versions of theirs survive. One has ἐκλεκτῶν σιτευτὰ [eklektōn siteuta], the other ὀρνίθων ἐκλεκτῶν νομάδων [ornithōn eklektōn nomadōn]. But in both ἐκλεκτῶν [eklektōn] stands for ברבר׳ barburim, and in the second they supply ὀρνίθων [ornithōn] on their own. As if choice fattened birds were meant, and these of the gallinaceous kind. For that is what ὄρνιθες [ornithes] are in that passage, as we proved above . So too the Talmudists, in the tractate Bava Metsia, ch. 7, fol. 86b, understand choice oxen or choice hens, fattened in a particular way. The passage reads: מאי ברבר׳ אבוס׳ אמר רב שאובסין אותן בעל כרחן ושמואל אמר שאובסין ועומדין מאליהם ורבי יוחנן אמר מביאים תור ממרעיתו בדלא אניס ותרנגולת מאשפתו בדלא אסינא אמר רבי יוחנן מובחר שבבהמות שור מובחר שבעופות תרנגולת אמר אמימר זגתא אוכמתא בי בטניתא דמשתכחא ביני עצרי ולא מציא פסיא קניא, What are fattened barburim? Rab said: Those which they fatten by force (that is, with food forced into the mouth). But Samuel said: they are fattened as they stand by themselves (that is, left to themselves, with no force applied). And Rabbi Iochanan said: They bring an ox from its pasture which has not yet worked (in tilling the land), and a hen from its dunghill which has not yet laboured (in rearing chicks). Again Rabbi Iochanan said: The choicest of cattle is the ox, and the choicest of birds is the hen. Amimar said: A black hen, pot-bellied (var. fattened at home), which is found among the winepresses (where it grows fat on grape-pips), and cannot step over a reed, because of its fatness. Hence R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] in his Commentary on the books of Kings: וברברים אבוסים יש מרבותינו אומרים תרנגולין פתומין, Fattened barburim: there are some of our Doctors who say they are fat cocks. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] understand capons, because העוף המסורס הוא שיתפטם ביותר, a castrated bird grows fatter. On this opinion see further what we adduced above on the second passage of Chapter 16.

In the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome], Rabbi Judah explains ברבורים barburim as מיני ביברים, kinds of those animals that are kept in vivaria. This is very ambiguous. It is uncertain whether he means fish, birds or wild beasts. For although the Hebrew ביבר bibar, Greek βιβάριον [bibarion] (French vivier), is taken by the Hebrews and Greeks of a later age for a fishpond, the word vivarium once extended much more widely. Its scope, namely, embraced any enclosures in which living animals were fed. Thus Gellius, book 2, chapter 20, distinguishes three kinds of vivaria: aviaries (les volieres), hare-warrens (les garennes) and fishponds (les estangs). From the same author, however, it may be gathered that vivaria rather concerned wild beasts, like the παράδεισοι [paradeisoi] of the Greeks. “Vivaria,” he says, “as they are now called, are certain enclosed places in which wild beasts are fed alive.” Likewise: “The vivaria, as the common people now say, are what the Greeks call παραδείσους [paradeisous].” The Hebrews define exactly so what a ביבר bibar is. Aruch: ביבר הוא פרדס שמאספין שם חיות וחפירה שמאספין שם דגין ומקום מקורה ששם עופות, “A bibar is a park in which wild beasts are gathered; also a pit in which fish are collected; and finally a roofed place in which there are birds.” This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On the Sabbath, chapter 13, folio 106b, where the Gemara says: ביברין של חיות ושל עופות ושל דגין אין צדין מהם ביום טוב, “From bibarin (or vivaria) of wild beasts, birds and fish one may not hunt on a festival day.” Therefore the explanation of R. Judah, by which he defines ברבורים barburim as kinds of animals that are kept in vivaria, is far too broad. I add that it is hardly safe, because it rests entirely on a most empty play on the name. For R. Judah thought that ביבר bibar and ברבור barbur were words of the same origin, and hence that ביבר bibar was said for ברבר birbar, the letter Resh after the first being dropped, in the way Lamed has disappeared in the Chaldee or Syriac words ܓܓܘܠܬܐ [גגולתא], and ܩܝܩܘܠܬܐ [קיקולתא], and ܨܘܨܠܬܐ [צוצלתא], and ܫܘܫܠܬܐ [שושלתא]. Yet it is perfectly plain that the Hebrew ביבר bibar, the Greek βιβάριον [bibarion], the Spanish bivar and the French vivier derive from the Roman word vivarium. Nevertheless, following this view, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] rendered the passage we are dealing with thus: “His provision for each day was thirty cors of fine flour,” etc., “besides harts, roes, wild oxen and vivaria.” In this respect, however, he is more inept than the Hebrews, since he put vivaria for the animals that are kept in vivaria. That is utterly absurd. For vivaria themselves are not among foods; nor would they be called אבוסים, fattened. And so Castalio passed over this word entirely untouched. Note in passing that in the Aruch the passage of R. Judah in which he explains the Hebrew ברברים as מיני ביברים is cited from Vayikra Rabbah, the chapter וכי ימוך אחיך, which is the thirty-fourth. Yet it appears nowhere there in the Venice edition of 1545, the only one I have been able to see. So either the Aruch is mistaken, or this edition is defective.

The third interpretation is that of those for whom ברברים barburim are birds in general, as if אברברים abarburim, from אבר eber, that is, from wing. This seems to be followed by Josephus, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Vulgate, R. Levi and Mordecai. So in their opinion ברבור barbur would stand for אברבר abarbur, of the pattern of אספסף asapsuph. But it is almost without precedent for the first radical to drop out of nouns formed from quiescent Pe Aleph verbs.

Baal Aruch [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] gives the fourth interpretation from the book Vajekra Rabba, already cited, as follows: רבנן אמרו עוף טהור הוא ומעולא הוא והיה בא מברבריאה והיה עולה על שולחן שלמה בכל יום, Our teachers said that it is a clean and excellent bird, which was brought from Barbaria and was served daily at the table of Solomon. And Kimchi on the books of Kings: ובדברי רז״ל עוף הבא מברבריא ונקראים ברבורים על שם מקומם, In the words of our teachers of blessed memory, it was a bird brought from Barbaria, called barbur (or barbar) after the name of its place. And in the Lexicon he cites the very same words as Baal Aruch. Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] too, in the Thisbi: אומרין שהוא עוף שמן מברבריאה, They say it is a fat bird from Barbaria, and the rest, as in the others. This interpretation ought not to have been met with such hissing by the learned, as though the name Barbaria for a particular region had been born only today or yesterday. For it is supposed that the Arabs not long ago gave the name Barbaria to Numidia, or, as some hold, to the whole part of Africa that lies along the Mediterranean Sea from Egypt as far as Gades. Anyone curious about such matters will find the reasons for this name in Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], Exercitation 51 against Cardano, in Leo Africanus, book 1, chapter 2, and in Marmol, Africa, book 1, chapter 6. And indeed the name Barbaria for the part of Africa we have mentioned is not to be found in Strabo, nor in Mela, nor in Pliny, nor in Marcianus, nor in Ptolemy, nor in any geographer of antiquity. Yet it is utterly false that it was given by the Arabs, since it was already current in the age of Justinian, long before the Arabs went there. Hence Anastasius Sinaita, a contemporary of Justinian, in his Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron: Ἐν τοῖς πλησιοχώροις Αἰγύπτου τοῖς ἐν Πενταπόλει τῇ Βαρβαρικῇ λεγομένοις ἀδύτοις [En tois plēsiochōrois Aigyptou tois en Pentapolei tē Barbarikē legomenois adytois]. In these words the Cyrenaic Pentapolis is placed in the Barbaria of Africa. And those whom the Vandals around that time transferred from Mount Aurasius in Mauretania to Sardinia were called Barbaricini. So testify Procopius in book 2 of the Vandal War, and Gregory, Epistles 25 and 27 of book 3. But I also find in the writings of the ancients another Barbaria, whose name is much older: namely the Ethiopian Barbaria, which is in turn twofold. One is Barbaria properly so called, the other the Troglodytic. Both lie along the sea: the latter along the Arabian, Adulic and Avalite gulfs, the former along the Barbaric gulf. By the name Barbaria Ptolemy and Marcianus of Heraclea understand only the former. But others also count among the Barbarians the dwellers by the Arabian Sea and the Troglodytes. Thus Arrian in the Periplus places the Barbarians and Barbaria around Berenice, Orine, the island of Diodorus, Ptolemais Theron, and the emporium of Avalites, which are places of the Troglodytica. And Stephanus, in his book On Cities, writes that Barbaria is παρὰ τὸν Ἀράβιον κόλπον [para ton Arabion kolpon], where the Troglodytica is. The Arab geographer likewise describes ارض بربرة [arḍ barbara], the Barbaran land, or land of Barbaria, الي البحر اليماني [ilā al-baḥr al-yamānī] towards the Yemenite sea, that is, the Arabian, Clim. [=climate (section) of al-Idrīsī's geography, in the Latin Geographia Nubiensis] 1, section 6. And in the preceding chapter he describes مدن الحبشة الساحلية [mudun al-ḥabasha al-sāḥiliyya] the coastal towns of the Abyssinians الي ما اتصل بها من عمارات البربرة [ilā mā ittaṣala bihā min ʿimārāt al-barbara] until one reaches the inhabited places of Barbaria. And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] on the word بربر [barbar] Barbar: بربر جيل البرابرة وهم بالغرب وامة اخري بين الحبوش والزنج يقطعون مذاكير الرجال ويجعلونها مهور نسايهم وكلهم ولد كيس غيلان او هم بطنان من حمير صنهاجة وكتامة صاروا الي البربر ايام فتح افريقيس الملك افريقية [barbar jīl al-barābira wa-hum bi-l-gharb wa-umma ukhrā bayna al-ḥubūsh wa-l-zanj yaqṭaʿūna madhākīr al-rijāl wa-yajʿalūnahā muhūr nisāyihim wa-kulluhum walad kays ghaylān aw hum baṭnān min ḥimyar ṣanhāja wa-kutāma ṣārū ilā al-barbar ayyām fatḥ ifrīqīs al-malik ifrīqiya] Barbar, the nation of the Barbarians, who are in the west. There is also another nation between the Abyssinians and the Zinj, which cuts off men's genitals and assigns them as dowry to their wives (just as David acquired a wife for himself with a dowry of two hundred foreskins, 1 Sam 18:25 27. and 2 Sam 3:14). All of them are sons of Cais Gailan, or of the stock of Humeir (from whom the Homerites are named). But Sunhagia and Cutama went into Barbaria when the African king opened up Africa. And more recent geographers too describe, in the Avalite gulf, a part of the Troglodytica, a city Barbara, or Barbora, and an island of the same name next to the city, at which Varthema says he landed after setting sail from Zeila, Navigat. book 2, ch. 16. And Duarte Barbosa has much about the same in his India, in the chapter On Barbora. From this Galen is easily reconciled with Dioscorides: the former reports that ginger is brought ἀπὸ τῆς Βαρβαρίας [apo tēs Barbarias], from Barbaria; the latter, from the Troglodytica. For Barbaria and Troglodytis are the same region. Not knowing this, Pliny misunderstood what he had read in the Greeks, that Troglodytic myrrh is also called Barbaran, as if they meant that this kind of myrrh was squalid and barbarous in appearance. For so he interprets it in book 12, chapter 16. Whereas, on the contrary, in Dioscorides it is said to be διαυγὴς [diaugēs], shining or translucent. Hence in Isidore, book 17, ch. 8, it is commended for its purity: Myrrh, he says, Troglodyte, from an island of Arabia, where a better and purer kind is gathered. Accordingly it is praised in these words in the old Hymn On the Epiphany of the Lord: Incense to God, myrrh Troglodyte for burial. For that is how it should be read, not, as commonly, trocletem, as Cassander rightly pointed out long ago. Troglodytic myrrh was therefore called Barbaran, not as squalid in appearance, but by reason of its native soil. Nor is there any other reason why at Gen 10:3 the Jerusalem translator renders Thogarma as ברבריא Barbaria than a deceptive play on the names Thogarma and τρώγλην [trōglēn], whence Troglitis or Troglodytis. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the name Barbaria comprises the whole seacoast of Eastern Ethiopia, from the borders of Egypt as far as the promontory of Rhapta. It seems to have received this name because of its uncivilized customs. Arrian: Ἀτακτότεροι δὲ οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὸν τόπον Βάρβα- ροι [Ataktoteroi de hoi katoikountes ton topon Barbaroi]. Or because of its barbarous and uncouth speech, if one can call speech what is more truly the squeaking of bats. Herodotus, Muse 4: Οἱ Τρωγλοδύται Αἰθίοπες γλῶσσαν οὐδεμίῃ ἄλλῃ παρομοίην νενομίκασι, ἀλλὰ τετρύγασι καθάπερ αἱ νυκτερίδες [Hoi Trōglodytai Aithiopes glōssan oudemiē allē paromoiēn nenomikasi, alla tetrygasi kathaper hai nykterides]. Pliny, book 5, ch. 8: Their (food) is the flesh of serpents, and they have a squeak, not a voice: so wholly do they lack the exchange of speech. Martianus Capella, book 6: They squeak rather than speak. As Solinus: Ignorant of speech, they squeak rather than speak. Rightly, then, were they called Barbarians. For properly so are called οἱ δυσεκφόρως, καὶ σκληρῶς, καὶ τραχέως λαλοῦντες [hoi dysekphorōs, kai sklērōs, kai tracheōs lalountes], as Strabo shows at length on that verse of Homer in which he calls the Carians Βαρβαροφώνους [Barbarophōnous]. In this very sense the Greek, Chaldee, Arabic and Latin translators at Ps 114:1 call barbarous the people which the Hebrews call עם לועז. For to the Hebrews לועז is one who speaks a foreign tongue, and that absurd and uncouth. Nor do the lexicographers of the Arabs explain بربار [barbār] barbar otherwise. Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)]: بربار [barbār] (barbar) garrulous, making a din, clamouring. بربرة [barbara] (barbara) the bleating of goats, triviality, the speech of an angry man, which is usually abrupt with ill-articulated words, as it is in Seneca. Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)]: بربر [barbara] (barbara, verb) he grumbled as angry men do: which is taken from Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ]. But Alcamus preceded Giggeius; his words are: البربرة صوت المعز وكثرة الكلام والجلبة والصياح [al-barbara ṣawt al-maʿz wa-kathrat al-kalām wa-l-jalaba wa-l-ṣiyāḥ] (Albarbara) the voice of the goat, much talking, clamour and shouting. Therefore the name Barbaria was as much Chaldee and Arabic as Greek, and so was very well known to the Jews and Syrians, in whose books it occurs everywhere. Examples from the Talmud and the paraphrasts are found in Baal Aruch; from the Ielammedenu in Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum]; from Semoth Rabba and Esther Rabba in David Cohen de Lara. To these I add from Gorionides, on Aretas, king of the Arabs, about to fight against Herod, book 5, ch. 18 and 19: He gathers all his army, the army, that is, of Arabia, וצבא ברבר, and the army of barbaria. And shortly after, the Jews bring back much spoil from the Arabs, ומן ברבר, and from the Barbarians. In that age, of course, part of Barbaria was subject to the rule of the Arabs. Indeed even the more remote Barbarians as far as Rhapta acknowledged the kings of Arabia Felix as their lords. Hence Arrian on Rhapta and the region around Rhapta: Νέμεται δὲ αὐτὴν κατά τι δίκαιον ἀρχαῖον, ὑποπίπτουσαν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῆς πρώτης γινομένης Ἀραβίας, ὁ Μωφαρίτης τύραννος [Nemetai de autēn kata ti dikaion archaion, hypopiptousan tē basileia tēs prōtēs ginomenēs Arabias, ho Mōpharitēs tyrannos]· The Mopharite tyrant possesses it, subject by some ancient right to the kingdom of the first Arabia. I think the same Barbarians are meant by the Talmudists when, in the tractate Iebamoth, fol. 63b, they say that the foolish people of whom Moses speaks in Deut 32:21 are אנשי ברבריא שמהלכין ערומין בשוק, the men of Barbaria, who walk naked through the streets. For they were either naked or half-covered with a hide. Dionysius on the Erembi, or Troglodytes, verse 965.
Γυμνοὶ, καὶ κτεάνων ἐπιδεύεες· [Gymnoi, kai kteanōn epideuees] — —
Naked, and lacking possessions. And Festus:
And with limbs uncovered, they ever creep up the steep roofs of their dwellings. — — —

And Strabo, in book 16: Γυμνῆται δὲ, καὶ δερματοφόροι, καὶ σκυταληφόροι διατελοῦσιν· [Gymnētai de, kai dermatophoroi, kai skytalēphoroi diatelousin] They live naked, or clad in skins and carrying clubs. In Africa, therefore, there was a twofold Barbaria: one western, extending as far as Gades; the other eastern, extending to the Arabian Gulf and the eastern Ocean, as far as Rhapta. It is certain, moreover, that the Hebrews were speaking of the latter, not the former, when they held that the ברברים barburim, or barbarim, were named after Barbaria, from which they had been brought to Solomon. For this interpretation is taken from the book Vajekra Rabba, whose author, Rabba, son of Nachmoni, flourished around the three hundredth year of Christ. In that age there is no mention of a Barbaria in the west. Nor does he speak on his own authority; rather, he cites his predecessors, Judah and Berechiah. Besides, by whatever name those Barbarians who live in the west of Africa may be called, Solomon had no trade with them. For Solomon fitted out his fleet not on the Mediterranean but on the Red Sea, at Aelana and Ezion-geber. From there the route led not to the western but to the eastern Barbarians; and from there guinea fowl could have been brought and called ברברים barburim, or barbarim, that is, Barbarian or Barbaric birds. For at a time when these birds were very rare and scarce, a certain island of the Red Sea belonging to the Barbaria of the Troglodytes was extremely productive of them. This is recorded by reliable authors: besides Agatharchides, by Diodorus and by Artemidorus as cited in Strabo.
