Strabo's words in book 16 run thus: Φησὶ δ᾽ Ἀρτεμίδωρος ἀπὸ Ἡρώων πόλεως πλέουσι κατὰ τὴν Τρωγλοδυτικὴν πόλιν εἶναι Φιλοτέραν, etc. Εἶτα Μύος ὅρμον, καὶ Ἀφροδίτης ὅρμον καλεῖσθαι λιμένα μέγαν, τὸν εἴσπλουν ἔχοντα σκολιόν· προκεῖσθαι δὲ νήσους τρεῖς, δύο μὲν ἐλαίαις κατασκίους, μίαν δ᾽ ἧττον κατάσκιον, μελεαγρίδων μεστήν· [Phēsi d' Artemidōros apo Hērōōn poleōs pleousi kata tēn Trōglodytikēn polin einai Philoteran, etc. Eita Myos hormon, kai Aphroditēs hormon kaleisthai limena megan, ton eisploun echonta skolion; prokeisthai de nēsous treis, dyo men elaiais kataskious, mian d' hētton kataskion, meleagridōn mestēn] Artemidorus says that for those sailing from the City of the Heroes there is, near the Troglodytic city, Philotera, etc. Then a large harbour with a winding entrance, which is called the Mouse's Anchorage, and the Anchorage of Venus. Before it lie three islands, two shaded with olive trees, the third less shaded, full of guinea fowl. And Diodorus, book 2, p. 120: Ὑπέρκεινται δὲ τούτου νῆσοι τρεῖς, ὧν δύο μὲν πλήρεις εἰσὶν ἐλαιῶν, καὶ σύκων· μία δὲ λειπομένη τῷ πλήθει τῶν προειρημένων δένδρων· πλῆθος δ᾽ ἔχουσα τῶν ὀνομαζομένων μελεαγρίδων. [Hyperkeintai de toutou nēsoi treis, hōn dyo men plēreis eisin elaiōn, kai sykōn; mia de leipomenē tō plēthei tōn proeirēmenōn dendrōn; plēthos d' echousa tōn onomazomenōn meleagridōn] Beside it lie three islands, two of which abound in olives and figs; but one, less fertile in these trees, is filled with the birds called guinea fowl. And, older than both, Agatharchides, On the Red Sea, book 5, ch. 42: Ἐν οἷς καὶ νῆσοι τρεῖς εἰσι προσκειμέναι· ὧν αἱ μὲν ἐλαίαις πεπύκνωνται, μία δὲ ἧττον μὲν δασεῖα, τῶν δὲ καλουμένων μελεαγρίδων ἐκτρέφουσα πλῆθος. [En hois kai nēsoi treis eisi proskeimenai; hōn hai men elaiais pepyknōntai, mia de hētton men daseia, tōn de kaloumenōn meleagridōn ektrephousa plēthos] Where three islands lie nearby: two of them are thick with olives; one is indeed less wooded, but it nourishes an abundance of the birds they call guinea fowl. So it appears that this island was most famous for its yield of these birds.

What exactly meleagrides are is not sufficiently established. Some think they are the same bird as the African or Numidian hens. Varro, Rei Rust. book 3, ch. 9: "The African hens are large, speckled, humpbacked; the Greeks call them μελεαγρίδας [meleagridas]." Pliny, book 10, ch. 26, after relating that the Memnonides birds fight at the tomb of Memnon, says: "In like manner the meleagrides fight in Boeotia" (namely at the tomb of Meleager). "This is a humpbacked kind of hen of Africa, sprinkled with speckled feathers," etc. Columella, however, distinguishes them thus in book 9, chapter 2: "The African hen, which most call the Numidian, is like the meleagris, except that it bears a red helmet and crest on its head, both of which are blue in the meleagris." But they also differ in their place of origin. For the African is found nowhere else, whereas the meleagris is a Greek bird, known already in the heroic age. And in the fables of the Greeks a twofold origin of it is handed down. Some write that the sisters of Meleager, others that the companions of the maiden Iocallis, worshipped on the island of Leros, were changed into these birds. Suidas: Λέγουσι δὲ οἱ μὲν τὰς ἀδελφὰς τοῦ Μελεάγρου μεταβαλεῖν εἰς τὰς μελεαγρίδας ὄρνιθας· οἱ δὲ τὰς συνήθεις Ἰοκάλλιδος τῆς ἐν Λέρνῃ παρθένου, ἣν τιμῶσι δαιμονίως [Legousi de hoi men tas adelphas tou Meleagrou metabalein eis tas meleagridas ornithas; hoi de tas synētheis Iokallidos tēs en Lernē parthenou, hēn timōsi daimoniōs]. For ἐν Λέρνῃ [en Lernē] read, at my own risk, ἐν Λέρῳ [en Lerō]. For that Iocallis is the very one of whom Clytus speaks in Athenaeus, book 14: Περὶ δὲ τὸ ἱερὸν τῆς παρθένου ἐν Λέρῳ εἰσὶν οἱ καλούμενοι ὄρνιθες μελεαγρίδες [Peri de to hieron tēs parthenou en Lerō eisin hoi kaloumenoi ornithes meleagrides]; "Around the temple of the maiden in Leros there are birds called meleagrides." Nor should Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] be heeded, who, in order to refer it to Pallas, reads ἐν Ὠλέρῳ [en Ōlerō], because in the city of Crete, Olerus, there was a temple of Pallas, from which come Ὠλερία Ἀθηνᾶ [Ōleria Athēna] and Ὠλερία [Ōleria], a festival sacred to Pallas, in Stephanus, De urbibus. For the meleagrides were not in the city of Olerus but on the island of Leros. Hence Aelian, Hist. book 4, ch. 42: Ἴσασι, he says, οἱ τὴν νῆσον οἰκοῦντες τὴν Λέρον [Isasi hoi tēn nēson oikountes tēn Leron]; "Those who inhabit the island of Leros know", namely why those who worship Diana abstain from eating meleagrides. And book 5, ch. 27: Τὰς δὲ ἐν Λέρῳ μελεαγρίδας ὑπὸ μηδενὸς ἀδικεῖσθαι τῶν γαμψωνύχων ὀρνέων λέγει Ἴστρος [Tas de en Lerō meleagridas hypo mēdenos adikeisthai tōn gampsōnychōn orneōn legei Istros]; "Ister related that the meleagrides on Leros are harmed by none of the birds of prey." And Antoninus Liberalis, Metamorphosis 2, on the sisters of Meleager: Αὐτὰς Ἄρτεμις ἁψαμένη ῥάβδῳ μετεμόρφωσεν εἰς ὄρνιθας, καὶ ἀπῴκισεν εἰς Λέρον τὴν νῆσον ὀνομάσασα μελεαγρίδας [Autas Artemis hapsamenē rhabdō metemorphōsen eis ornithas, kai apōkisen eis Leron tēn nēson onomasasa meleagridas]; "Diana touched them with a rod and changed them into birds, and removed them to the island of Leros, giving them the name meleagrides." But writers wrongly confuse the Lerian meleagrides with the Aetolian. For the Lerian ones were kept in honour of Iocallis, who was worshipped on Leros, and the Aetolian ones around Calydon and Pleuron in honour of Meleager. Hence Statius, Thebaid, book 4, line 103:
"And Meleagrian Pleuron, bewailed by kindred birds."

And Menodotus of Samos in Athenaeus, book 14, relates that peacocks were first produced on Samos and carried from there elsewhere, ὡς καὶ οἱ ἀλεκτρυόνες ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ αἱ καλουμέναι μελεαγρίδες ἐν τῇ Αἰτωλίᾳ [hōs kai hoi alektryones en tē Perside, kai hai kaloumenai meleagrides en tē Aitōlia], "as the cocks in Persia, and in Aetolia those called meleagrides." So I cannot at all understand why Pliny, in the place cited above, set the meleagrides and the tomb of Meleager in Boeotia. For Meleager, leader of Aetolia, had nothing in common with the Boeotians, who lived far from there. From Clytus, Athenaeus has a long description of the meleagrides, yet so ambiguous that one cannot tell whether he describes the African or Numidian hen (today the Barbary hen), or the turkey (which our people call the Indian cock), or a third kind of bird unlike either. Indeed, it suits neither that ὁ τόπος ἑλώδης [ho topos helōdēs], a marshy place, is assigned for rearing the meleagris. Nor does what we read, that the bird is ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖν τῶν νεωτέρων, ὥς τε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν [astorgon pros ta ekgona to orneon, kai oligōrein tōn neōterōn, hōs te anankē tois hiereusin epimeleisthai autōn], "a bird without any affection for its offspring, which neglects its chicks so much that the priests must take care of them." As for flavour, the poets extol the African hen above all among the delicacies of the ancients. Horace, Epode 2:
"May no African bird go down into my belly, nor Ionian attagen, more pleasing than," etc.
"For your palate the peacock is fed in confinement, for you the Numidian hen, etc."
"Our little apprentice does not know how to filch a morsel of roe, nor the wing of an African bird." — —

Statius, book 1 of the Silvae, on the Saturnalia of Domitian: "Among which there suddenly fall in flight immense clouds of birds through the stars, those which the sacred Nile and the rugged Phasis, those which the Numidians gather under the damp South Wind."
And the painted partridge, and the speckled Numidian hens.
Neither Libya nor Phasis sends you birds.
If we had birds of Libya and of Phasis, you would receive them: but as it is, receive birds of the farmyard.

Yet of these Varro says: These were the latest to come from the kitchen into the gluttons' dining-room, owing to the fastidiousness of men. And Pliny: They are the most recent of foreign birds to be admitted to the table, on account of their unpleasant smell. So rarity alone seems to have raised their price. Varro teaches us this in these words: They sell at a high price because of their scarcity. Likewise Petronius:
The bird sought from Phasian Colchis and the African fowl please the palate because they are not easy to get. — —

So much for the various interpretations of the word ברבורים barburim. Of these, although the third and fourth may be tolerated, the first pleases me most. I mean that most ancient one, according to which ברבורים אבוסים are all the choicest fattened fowl. For, to say nothing of the agreement of the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint] with the Talmudists in asserting it, analogy requires it. Just as from חרר charar, to burn, comes חרחור charchur, extreme burning, Deut 28:22, so from ברר barar, to choose, comes ברבור barbur, a most choice thing; the first radical is doubled so that the meaning is intensified. This is customary in these languages. Thus, since קלל means to be light or to be worthless, קלקל is a most worthless, most light, most despised thing. And the Jews, murmuring, call the manna so in contempt, Numer. XXXI, 5. And from צלל, to overshadow, comes צלצל, a denser shadow. And from רבב, to make great, come רברבים , the magnates, who stand out most among the people. And from כידור, spark, comes כרכר, the Carchedonian stone, a gem that sparkles exceedingly. Publilius Syrus in Petronius Arbiter:
Why do you desire Carchedonian stony fires, except that they may sparkle? — — —

And from דקק, to make thin, comes דקדוק, a subtle disquisition. Hence Grammar is so called by the Hebrews, because it is a subtle and precise examination of speech. Moreover, this explanation yields a most fitting sense. Solomon's provisions for each day were thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred sheep, besides harts, roebucks, and bubali, and all the choicest fattened fowl, that is, those animals which were selected from among the rest to be fattened in a special way and set on the royal table. The ancients understood this chiefly of birds, both because small birds hold the first place in the delicacy market, and in order to distinguish them from those already mentioned, namely oxen, sheep, harts, roebucks and bubali. Yet this is not necessary, since the very method of fattening sufficiently distinguishes these from the rest; from it they are called אבוסים abusim, that is, fattened at the stall, not, like the others, in the pastures. For אבוס ebus is a stall (manger), Iob. XXXIX, 12. Prov. XIV, 14. and Es. I, 3. Hence אבס abas means to fatten livestock, not in any way whatever, but tied at the stall, and indeed with food put and thrust into the mouth, if we believe the Talmudists. Aquila renders it φατνιάζεσθαι [phatniazesthai], and Theodotion φατνεύεσθαι [phatneuesthai]. But there was no need to coin new words, since σιτεύειν [siteuein] means this. For σιτευτὰ [siteuta] is said of animals that are fattened in confinement. Hence Plutarch, Sympos. 4, Question 1: Ὅσα δὲ σιτεύουσι καθείρξαντες [hosa de siteuousi katheirxantes], Whatever they fatten shut up. So the same Theodotion renders שור אבוס as βοῦν σιτευτὸν [boun siteuton], quite rightly. And in Luc. XV, 23. the prodigal's father orders τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτὸν [ton moschon ton siteuton] to be killed, that is, השור האבוס: out of many oxen or calves, the one that had been fattened in this way. For the article placed before it is not idle. And Matth. XXII, 4. τὰ σιτιστὰ τεθυμένα [ta sitista tethymena], that is, האבוסות. Accordingly, one of the Greeks renders ברבורים אבוסים as ἐκλεκτῶν σιτευτά [eklektōn siteuta]. Somewhat parallel to the passage under discussion is another, Nehem. V, 18., in which for Nehemiah's daily food are prepared one ox, six choice sheep, and birds. Choice in Hebrew is בררות, which with the first letter doubled could have been called ברברות. For בררות and ברברות are the same, except that in ברברות the meaning is more intense because of the doubled letter. So if ברורות means choice, ברברות would mean most choice .

I shall now say why I think that ברברים אבוסים are neither fattened hens, nor guinea fowl, nor birds in general. 1. Although among the later Hebrews אבס abas is said also of birds that are fattened, yet in Scripture אבוס ebus is the manger of cattle or beasts of burden, not a fattening coop for birds. And אבס abas, derived from it, is applied only to cattle. Hence, when those who had come with Cadmus occupied the island of Euboea, as is found in Strabo, their leader was called אבס Abas, that is, fattener of cattle. From this, with a Greek inflection, the inhabitants themselves were called Abantes . For the greatest Poet calls them by no other name. So too the island was called Εὔβοια [Euboia] from oxen, and Ἀργιβόειος [Argiboeios] in Aelian, book 12, chapter 36. For that this island was long ago famous for its ox pastures is shown by the oxen driven off from Euboea by Autolycus, of which Apollodorus speaks in book 2 of the Bibliotheca, and Tzetzes, Chil. 8. Accordingly, at the beginning of the Peloponnesian War the Athenians πρόβατα, καὶ ὑποζύγια εἰς τὴν Εὔβοιαν διεπέμψαντο [probata, kai hypozygia eis tēn Euboian diepempsanto], sent their sheep and beasts of burden to Euboea, as Thucydides has it in book 2; and on the coinage of the Euboeans an ox's head was engraved. So Antonius Augustinus testifies in Dialogue 3 On Coins. But on Euboea see more in our Chanaan. 2. If by ברברים אבוסים the Sacred Writer meant to signify birds, of which there had been no mention before, there appears no reason why, content with epithets alone, he did not expressly name צפורים, that is, birds, so that there would be no room for doubt. 3. The same objection can be raised regarding the gallinaceous kind. For no one would say that ברברים are cocks or hens. 4. If the ברבורים had their name from Barbary, they would not be called barburim, but barbarim. 5. And although the eastern coast of Africa long ago bore the name of Barbary, yet that this was already in use in the age of Solomon cannot be proved by any argument. 6. Finally, who would believe that guinea fowl, or birds of Barbary, whatever they may have been, came into the reckoning of Solomon's provisions rather than so many others native to Judaea and the neighbouring regions, which were set daily on the royal table? 7. But there was no need to descend so far. Otherwise fish too, and vegetables, and the fruits of trees, and every kind of delicacy ought to have been listed together. Josephus saw this in part. And so he added fish to the birds on his own account. Ταῦτα πάντα, he says, πάρεξ τῶν ἐπ᾽ ἄγρας ἐλάφων λέγω, καὶ βουβάλων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν, καὶ ἰχθύων, ἐκομίζετο καθ᾽ ἡμέραν τῷ βασιλεῖ· [Tauta panta, parex tōn ep᾽ agras elaphōn legō, kai boubalōn, kai tōn ptēnōn, kai ichthyōn, ekomizeto kath᾽ hēmeran tō basilei] All these, besides wild animals taken in the hunt, I mean deer and bubali, and birds, and fish, were brought daily to the king, book 8, ch. 2 Antiqu.
Tzetzes, Chil. 8, Hist. 173. Scholia on Oppian and on Nicander's Ther.

On the meleagrides [guinea fowl] compare what SCHNEIDER said on Aelian's History of Animals IV, 42, to which he added some things in the Appendix to the Commentaries on the Remains of the Books of Frederick II and the chapters of Albertus Magnus on the art of hunting with birds, Leipzig 1789, p. 163. That the meleagrides are the Numidae of Linnaeus (Syst. Nat. vol. I, part II, p. 744, 13th ed.), Perlhühner [guinea fowl], was shown, following Perrault, by PALLAS in Spicil. Zoolog. III, p. 13 ff.

Yet the opinion of J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in the Supplements, vol. I, p. 228, does not seem to be dismissed: that ברברים, or, as it is written in 14 of Kennicott's codices, ברבורים, are animals of the fields, forests and deserts which we usually catch by hunting, as opposed to domestic ones, from the Chaldee בָּרָא, Syriac ܒܪܐ [ברא], Arabic بَرّ [barr], field, desert. What he added to commend this opinion should be read in his own work.

There is nothing about Cadmus in that passage of Strabo, as Michaelis observed, loc. cit. p. 227, who quoted the Greek words themselves; and he should certainly be compared on what Bochart adduces here.

There is a notable passage on the peacock in 1 Reg. X, 22. and 2 Chr 9:21: Once every three years the fleet (of Solomon) went to Tarshish, and brought gold and silver, elephants' teeth, apes and peacocks. The Hebrew name of the peacocks, תכיים thoucijim, or תוכיים thuccijim, the Greek translators left ἀνεϱμήνευτον [anermēneuton] [untranslated], because they did not understand it. But the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Latin translators explain it as peacocks, and so do all the Hebrews of any repute: R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], R. Levi, Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]. For those who, in Kimchi's Lexicon, render it גאטו מימון gato maimon, that is, long-tailed monkey, are obscure and unknown. So too are those who render it parrot, as Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] notes in the margin . Therefore I cannot at all understand why the late Diodati preferred to follow them. It is hardly safe to depart from the received version unless there are weighty reasons, and I see none here. On the origin of the word, Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] says in his Thesaurus: The word seems foreign, for its etymology is unknown. Perhaps it is from striking, by onomatopoeia. The French, to be sure, express onomatopoeically the sound of someone knocking at a door with the words toc, toc; hence toquer means to strike, as does toccare in Italian. But since such things are largely arbitrary: among the Hebrews תוך תוך thoc thoc is said of the sound of a boiling pot. Thus in Berachoth ch. 6, fol. 39a: דיתיב אבי תפי ועביד תוך תוך, That which is placed in the place of setting (of pots on the fire), and makes thoc thoc. But however you understand it, this has nothing to do with the peacock. Nor can any reason be devised why it should be named from striking. I therefore hold a different view: namely, that peacocks are called תוכיים thuccijim by an inversion of the word, for כותיים cuthijim, as if you were to say Cuthaeans, or Persians. For Cuth (var. Chuth) is in Persia. Josephus, Antiquities, book 9, near the end: Οἱ δὲ μετοικισθέντες εἰς Σαμάρειαν Χουθαῖοι (ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐχρῶντο μέχρι δεῦρο τῇ προσηγορίᾳ, διὰ τὸ ἐκ τῆς Χουθᾶς καλουμένης χώρας μεταχθῆναι, αὕτη δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Περσίδι, καὶ ποταμὸς τοῦ τ᾽ ἔχων ὄνομα) [Hoi de metoikisthentes eis Samareian Chouthaioi (tautē gar echrōnto mechri deuro tē prosēgoria, dia to ek tēs Chouthas kaloumenēs chōras metachthēnai, hautē d᾽ estin en tē Persidi, kai potamos tou t᾽ echōn onoma)]. The Cuthaeans deported into Samaria (for so they were then called, because they had been transferred from the region of Chutha, which is in Persia, where there is also a river of the same name). Nor is it anything new for birds to be named after places. Thus the pheasant is named from the Phasis; African and Numidian birds from Numidia and Africa; Seleucides from Seleucia; Garamantides from the Garamantes. And, not to seek examples further afield, the very peacock we are discussing is often called the Median or Persian bird by the ancients. Aristophanes in the Birds:
Ὁ μὲν ὄρτυγα δοὺς, ὁ δὲ πορφυρίων᾽, ὁ δὲ χῆν᾽, ὁ δὲ Περσικὸν ὄρνιν᾽ [Ho men ortyga dous, ho de porphyriōn᾽, ho de chēn᾽, ho de Persikon ornin᾽]

One giving a quail, another a porphyrion, another a goose, another a Persian bird. And there the Scholiast: Τὰ πολυτελῆ πάντα, οἷς μόνος βασιλεὺς ἐχρῆτο, ἐκαλεῖτο Περσικά· καὶ νῦν οὐκ ἰδίως τις ὄρνις Περσικός. τινὲς δὲ τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα, οἱ δὲ τὸν ταῶ [Ta polytelē panta, hois monos basileus echrēto, ekaleito Persika; kai nyn ouk idiōs tis ornis Persikos. tines de ton alektryona, hoi de ton taō]. All costly things, which the king alone used, were called Persian. Some, however, understand the cock, and others the peacock. And in the Acharnians, of the Persian envoys:
Ἥκοντες ἀπὸ Περσίδος ταὼν ἔχοντες ἐληλύθασιν, [Hēkontes apo Persidos taōn echontes elēlythasin,]

when they had set out from Persia, they had come bringing a peacock. Suidas: Μηδικὸς ὄρνις· ὁ ταώς [Mēdikos ornis; ho taōs]· The Median bird, the peacock. Likewise: Ταὼς εὐπήληξ· ὁ Μηδικὸς καὶ χρυσόπτερος, καὶ ἀλαζονικὸς ὄρνις [Taōs eupēlēx; ho Mēdikos kai chrysopteros, kai alazonikos ornis]. The well-helmeted peacock, the Median bird, furnished with golden wings, and proud. Hence Clement, Paedag. book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται τοὺς ἀπὸ Φάσιδος, ἀτταγὰς Αἰγυπτίας, Μῆδον ταῶνα [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai tous apo Phasidos, attagas Aigyptias, Mēdon taōna] · Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis, Egyptian francolins, the Median peacock. And book 3, ch. 4: Ὄρνεις Ἰνδικοὺς, καὶ ταῶνας Μηδικοὺς ἐκτρέφουσι [Orneis Indikous, kai taōnas Mēdikous ektrephousi]· They rear Indian birds and Median peacocks. And Diodorus, book 2: Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Βαβυλωνία ταώνων ἐκτρέφει πλῆθος παντοίαις χρόαις ἐπηνθισμένων [Hē men gar Babylōnia taōnōn ektrephei plēthos pantoiais chroais epēnthismenōn]. For Babylonia rears a great many peacocks, variegated with colours of every kind. For although the true homeland of peacocks was India, as we prove elsewhere, they were nevertheless called Median and Persian because they were first carried from India into Persia and Media, and from there gradually dispersed into Judaea, Egypt, Greece, Latium and other regions of the world. Indeed, the very peacocks which Solomon's fleet brought into Judaea may have been obtained from Persia. For it is not likely that on that three-year voyage, by which they made their way to Taprobane (as we show in its place), they always kept a straight course. Rather, by various detours they sought out whatever served their purpose: also in the Persian Gulf, where lay the most celebrated islands of the Phoenicians, Tyrus or Tylus, and Aradus, not far distant from Persia. The name תוכיים thuccijim could also have been given to peacocks after Solomon's time, once they began to be brought overland from Persia and Babylon into Judaea.

Now, that they were called תוכיים with the letters inverted, instead of כותיים, is not without precedent, whether this happened through the carelessness of copyists or, as I believe more likely, was done by deliberate design, so that the name of the bird might be distinguished from the name of the people. Thus you may see the same wood called אלמוגים almugin, 1 Reg. X, 11. and אלגומים algumim, 2 Chr 2:7. The same city in which Joshua was buried is called תמנת־סרח Thimnath-Serach, Josh 24:30 and תמנת־חרס Thimnath-Cheres, Judg 2:9. The same son of Dan is called חושים Chusim, Gen 46:23 and שוחם Sucham, Num 26:42. The same man is רחום Rechum, Neh 12:3 and חרם Charim, in the same place, verse 15. Another is שמלי Samlai, Esd. II, 46. and שלמי Salmai, Neh 7:48. So the sheep is called now כבס chebes, now כשב cheseb. And the Ethiopians sometimes invert Hebrew words entirely. Thus רחם, to have pity, is for them ምሕረ፡ [məḥəra]; קלס, to mock, for them ሰለቀ፡ [salaqa]; זנק, to leap, for them ቀነጸ፡ [qanaṣa]. Therefore, on the same pattern, peacocks could have been called תוכיים instead of כותיים. However, I propose this, I do not decide it, and I leave everyone free to judge for himself.

If the peacock were unknown, we would ask what moved Solomon to fetch from so far away, along with treasures of gold and silver, birds of no great use. Or why the sacred writers thought it worth recording? But these doubts are resolved by the appearance of this exceptional bird, which seems made for the very purpose of feasting the eyes of beholders with a delightful spectacle. Accordingly Varro asserts that nature gave it the prize for beauty among birds. And after the Greeks, who vied with one another in describing it, Tertullian paints it thus, De Pallio ch. 3: And yet the peacock too has a garment of feathers, and indeed one of the finest: deeper than any purple where the neck blooms, more gilded than any border where the back gleams, more flowing than any trailing robe where the tail lies. Many-coloured, and diverse-coloured, and changing-coloured. Never itself, always other; and yet always itself when other. In short, changed as often as it is moved. The Arabs too have toiled in the same arena, among them Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: تري في وسط كل ريش دايرة من الذهب مخلطة بالزرقة والصفرة والخضرة وغيرها من الاوان التي [tarī fī wasaṭ kull rīsh dāyira min al-dhahab mukhallaṭa bi-l-zurqa wa-l-ṣufra wa-l-khuḍra wa-ghayrihā min al-awān allatī] تلايم بعضها بعضا لينشا من تركيبها [talāyam baʿḍuhā baʿḍan li-yansha min tarkībihā] You will see in the middle of all its feathers a golden circle, mixed with blue, yellow and green, and other colours which harmonize with one another, so that from their combination the highest beauty arises. He adds that gold, laid over any colours whatever, is nothing compared with this splendour, although it is scarcely dug out of the earth and only refined with much labour; whereas so beautiful a bird emerges from the egg of its own accord, without human effort. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] has much more, which I have preferred to pass over, lest I weary the reader on a subject most hackneyed of all. So for the present it will suffice to add a few verses from an anonymous Arabic poet: سبحان من خلق الطاوس [subḥān man khalaqa al-ṭāwūs] * طير علي اشكاله رييس [ṭayr ʿalā ashkālihi rayīs] * كانه من نقشه عروس [ka-annahu min naqshihi ʿarūs] * في الريش منه ركبت فلوس [fī al-rīsh minhu rukkibat fulūs] * تشرق في داراته شموس [tushriqu fī dārātihi shumūs] * في راس منه شجرة مغروس [fī raʾs minhu shajara maghrūs] * كانه ببنفسج يميس [ka-annahu bi-banafsaj yamīs] *

Glory be to him who created the peacock, a bird of exceptional beauty, which in the variety of its colours resembles a bride. Scales are set into its feathers. In its dwelling many suns rise. On its crown a little tree is planted. It struts in pomp as though in a violet garment. In Arabic, as though in a violet. But there violet is taken for a garment of violet, or purple colour, which stands out most among the other colours in the neck and tail of the peacock. Hence Tertullian above: Deeper than any purple dye, where the neck blooms. And Achilles Tatius, book 1: Ὁ δὲ τοῦ ταῶ λειμὼν εὐανθέστερος· πεφύτευται γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ χρυσὸς ἐν τοῖς πτεροῖς, κύκλῳ δὲ τὸ ἁλουργὲς τὸν χρυσὸν περιθέει τὸν ἴσον κύκλον [Ho de tou taō leimōn euanthesteros; pephyteutai gar autō kai chrysos en tois pterois, kyklō de to halourges ton chryson peritheei ton ison kyklon]. The meadow of the peacock (than any meadow) is more flowery: for in its feathers gold also is set, and purple surrounds the gold in an equal circle. To this belongs the description of the peacock by Publilius Syrus:
Clad in a feathered golden Babylonian mantle.

As though Babylonian were the same as purple, since Arrian in the Periplus mentions purple from Apologus, a city of Babylonia, at the mouth of the Euphrates. And Philostratus, Epistle 28, to a woman, praises τὸν Βαβυλώνιον κόκκον [ton Babylōnion kokkon]. Accordingly, אדרת שנער, the mantle of Shinar, or Babylonian mantle, Josh 7:21, is for Rabbi Chanina a mantle מן פרפרא בבלאה, of Babylonian purple; and for Jerome scarlet. But by feathered Babylonian we understand variegated. For, as we have proved elsewhere from Pliny and others, to weave different colours into a picture Babylon most made famous and gave it its name. We are led to this by these words of Aelian on the peacock, book 5, ch. 21: Δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον ὑπὲρ τὴν τῶν Μήδων ἐσθῆτα, καὶ τὰ τῶν Περσῶν ποικίλματα [Deiknys philoponōs to tēs pterōseōs polymorphon hyper tēn tōn Mēdōn esthēta, kai ta tōn Persōn poikilmata]; Ostentatiously displaying the multiform appearance of its plumage, surpassing the garment of the Medes and the varied colours of the Persians. Accordingly Antiphon, in his speech On the Peacocks against Erasistratus, cited by Athenaeus, book 9, and by Aelian in the place above, nowhere calls peacocks by their proper name, that is, ταῶνας [taōnas], but only ὄρνεις ποικίλους [orneis poikilous], variegated birds; as if by this very feature they were most distinguished from others.

From this same speech, compared with the life of Pericles in Plutarch, it is gathered that around the time of Pericles peacocks began to be kept at Athens in the house of a certain Demus, son of Pyrilampes, who made great profit from it. For he exhibited them to be viewed for a fixed fee at every new moon. And to this spectacle the curious flocked from Lacedaemon and Thessaly, that is, from both extremities of Greece. He also sold a male and female of the peacock kind for a thousand drachmas. Indeed, in Greece peacocks were not yet common in the age of Alexander, who, on the testimony of Aelian, ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἰδὼν τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας ἐξεπλάγη, καὶ τοῦ κάλλους θαυμάσας, ἠπείλησε τῷ καταθύσαντι ταὼν ἀπειλὰς βαρυτάτας [en Indois idōn tous de tous ornithas exeplagē, kai tou kallous thaumasas, ēpeilēse tō katathysanti taōn apeilas barytatas], seeing those birds among the Indians was astonished, and, admiring their beauty, fixed a heavy penalty for those who should kill them. Likewise at Rome Hortensius, as the same author reports, καταθύσας ἐπὶ δείπνῳ ταὼν πρῶτος, ἐκρίθη [katathysas epi deipnō taōn prōtos, ekrithē], having been the first to slaughter a peacock for a dinner, was summoned to court: or, as others read, κατεκρίθη [katekrithē], was condemned, or fined. Yet, as luxury prevailed, many following Hortensius raised the prices of peacocks; so much so that in Varro Merula asserts that in his time their eggs sold for five denarii each, the birds themselves easily for fifty. And that M. Aufidius Lurco made an annual income of over sixty thousand sesterces from flocks of peacocks. For although the flesh of the peacock tastes no better than the flesh of a hen, the peacock was valued much more highly because of its tail and feathers: as if this concerned the palate, or as if they ate the feathers with the flesh. This folly of gluttons Horace wittily mocks in these words, book 2, Satire 2:

Yet I shall hardly keep you, when a peacock is served, from wishing to wipe your palate with it rather than with a hen, corrupted as you are by empty things: because the rare bird is sold for gold and spreads a spectacle with its painted tail. As if that mattered at all. Do you eat that plumage you praise? Once it is cooked, does the same glory remain? Yet though in flesh there is no difference, it is plain that you are deceived by the unequal appearance into preferring this to that. — —

For these dishes were valued not for their flavour but for their price; nor were they sought for any other reason than that they sold more dearly, like parrots brought from India. Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:
Who whet the belly with price, and hand over to the palate the starry birds of Juno, and any green bird skilled in speech brought from the coloured Indians.

What of the fact that in Symeon Seth [=Symeon Seth (11th c.), Syntagma de alimentorum facultatibus] the flesh of the peacock is ἰνώδης, καὶ περιττωματικὴ, καὶ δύσπεπτος, καὶ κακόχυμος [inōdēs, kai perittōmatikē, kai dyspeptos, kai kakochymos], fibrous, productive of excrements, hard to digest, and of bad juice? Just as in Galen it is σκληροτέρα, καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα, καὶ ἰνωδεστέρα [sklērotera, kai dyspeptotera, kai inōdestera].

And in Damir: لحمه عسر الهضم ردي المزاج وهي يولد كيموسا غليظا [laḥmuhu ʿasir al-haḍm radī al-mizāj wa-hiya yuwallid kaymūsan ghalīẓan], Its flesh is difficult to digest, of a bad temperament, and it produces a thick chyme. In Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)]: لحوم الطواويس صلبة [luḥūm al-ṭawāwīs ṣulba], The flesh of peacocks is hard. In Mesue: ردي المزاج [radī al-mizāj], of bad juice; whence Juvenal in his first Satire:
— — you carry the undigested peacock into the baths: hence sudden deaths, and an old age without a will.

Therefore, apart from that exceptional beauty, there was no reason why the peacock was so highly valued among the ancients. Indeed, the Arabs imagine that the peacock, however beautiful, is nonetheless a bird of ill omen, because, as they tell the tale, كان سببا لدخول ابليس الجنة وخروج ادم منها [kāna sababan li-dukhūl Iblīs al-janna wa-khurūj Ādam minhā], it was the reason why the devil entered Paradise, and why Adam went out of it. But for what reason, I have not yet found. Of the same sort is what the anonymous author of the روضة العلما [Rawḍat al-ʿulamā], Garden of the Learned, reports: that the vine was sprinkled by the devil with the blood of four animals, namely of the peacock when it was first planted, of the ape when it began to put out leaves, of the lion when it pushed out its grapes, and finally of the pig when the fruit was already ripening. And that this is why whoever drinks wine 1. becomes more handsome, like the peacock; 2. plays, dances and gesticulates in the manner of an ape; 3. rages like a lion; 4. like a pig
— — lies buried in sleep and wine.

God's words in Job 39:13, כנף רננים נעלסה, are explained by most of the more recent writers, following Kimchi and Pomarius, as The wing of the peacocks exults, as though it dealt with peacocks, which take pride in the beauty of their feathers. Yet in that passage רננים are ostriches, not peacocks, as we prove at length in the treatise On the Ostrich; and those who interpret them as peacocks rest on no reasoning, although today no explanation of this word is more widely accepted.

No more acceptable is the view of the Chaldee translator, who held that in Ezek 27:15 the Hebrew word הבנים hobnim means peacocks, although R. Selomo follows it, and the other Hebrews are in doubt, and among our own scholars Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] rendered the whole passage thus: The sons of Dedan were thy merchants. Many isles were the merchandise of thy hand. They brought horns of ivory and peacocks as thy present. The Greeks (whom the Arab follows) and the Syrian seem to have misread this same word. For the former render τοῖς εἰσαγομένοις [tois eisagomenois], to those who are brought in, that is, הובאים; the latter לבונתא, frankincense, which in Hebrew would be לבנה. Thus of the ancients only Symmachus and Jerome saw that הובנים hobnim is ebony. Many things confirm this interpretation. First, hobnim and hebenus are not dissimilar words. In the first syllable the vowels O and E have been interchanged, which everyone knows to be frequent. Priscian, book 1: O passes into E, as tutor tutela, bonus bene, γόνυ [gony] genu, ποῦς [pous] pes. The ancients said compes for compos. In this we follow the Aeolians, for they say ἐδόντα [edonta] for ὀδόντα [odonta]. Quintilian, book 1, ch. 7: What shall I say of vortices and vorsus, and the rest of the same kind, which Scipio Africanus is said to have been the first to turn into the second letter, E. Hence the same people are called Ὀσσηνοὶ [Ossēnoi] and Ἐσσηνοί [Essēnoi]. And Ptolemy speaks of the Ὁρκύνιος δρυμὸς [Horkynios drymos], which others call Ἑρκύνιος [Herkynios], that is, the Hercynian forest. Second, קרנות שן והבננים, horns of ivory and ebony, are rightly joined in the Prophet as wares in some way homogeneous, although the one is obtained from an animal, the other from a tree. For, as Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)] notes in his Miscellanea, book 6, ch. 14, each has an extreme colour in the same degree of excellence: ivory, namely, of the most beautiful whiteness, ebony of the most splendid blackness. Both are highly polished, very lustrous, and remarkable for an incomparable smoothness. Hence they are applied to almost the same uses; and from both are made bows, combs, gaming boards, knife handles, etc. Third, the words of Ezekiel could be rendered thus: horns of (elephant) tooth and of ebony, in the genitive, so that the word קרנות, horns, belongs to both. For as ivory is called horn because of its resemblance to true horn, ebony too could be called horn by the same καταχρήσει [katachrēsei], since Dioscorides describes it as ἐμφερὴς κέρατι εἰργασμένῳ τῇ λειότητι [empherēs kerati eirgasmenō tē leiotēti], like polished horn in smoothness; and Isidore as a black wood, smooth and horn-like; and Avicenna as يشبه في ملاسته قرنا محكوكا وقيل مخروطا [yushbihu fī malāsatihi qarnan maḥkūkan wa-qīla makhrūṭan] resembling in its smoothness polished horn, or, as others say, horn worked smooth. Ebony therefore could be called horn καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs]. I would not, however, call it a tooth with Jerome, who has here teeth of ivory and of ebony. Fourth, ivory and ebony originate in the same places. For just as Polybius, Pliny, Philostratus, and, in the Scholiast on Pindar, Amyntianus in his book On Elephants distinguish elephants into Indian and Ethiopian, so Dioscorides, Pliny and Isidore report that ebony grows in India and Ethiopia. And as Theophrastus, Arrian and Ennodius mention Indian ebony specifically, so Herodotus, Diodorus, Mela, Avicenna and the Nubian Geographer mention Ethiopian. Lest you object to them these words of the supreme poet in Georgics book 2,

one must know that by the name India Ethiopia is also understood. Hence Servius on that passage: By India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. That this is very true is shown by these words of the same poet on the Source of the Nile in Georgics book 4,

The river flowing down all the way from the dark-coloured Indians, that is, from innermost Ethiopia. There are some who add Egyptian ebony to the Indian and Ethiopian, as on the authority of Lucan, whose words in book 10 are:
— — — Mareotic ebony does not cover the vast doorposts. — — —

Maereotic, that is, from Mareotis, a part of Egypt near Alexandria, as they would have it. Consonant with them are these words of Servius: And yet ebony also grows in Egypt. But in both places there is an error. For in Lucan one must read Meroitica, as the distinguished Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] excellently proves in his work on Solinus; Meroë, which appears below in the same book of Lucan,
— — Meroë, fertile with black settlers, rich in the foliage of ebony. — — —

Accordingly Diodorus, book 1, where he speaks of the island of Meroe: Πρὸς δὲ τούτοις (λέγουσιν) ἔχειν πλῆθος ἐβένου [Pros de toutois (legousin) echein plēthos ebenou], Moreover they say that it has an abundance of ebony. And Pliny records that the rare tree ebony was brought to Nero (fetched) from as far as Meroe, a distance of 996 miles from Syene, the boundary of the empire. But in these words of Servius too, And yet it grows also in Egypt, there is an obvious error. For he had certainly written, And yet it grows also in Ethiopia, as what follows shows: But by India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. This would be ἀνακόλουθα [anakoloutha] if we read in Egypt. For Servius says this on the passage of Virgil discussed above,

which he maintains is true, even though ebony also grows in Ethiopia, because the name of India includes Ethiopia. But if you say that ebony grows in Egypt, this excuse will not hold. For Egypt is one thing, Ethiopia another; nor is there anyone who understands Egypt by the name of India. Fifth, ebony and ivory, together with gold, were the constant tribute of the Ethiopians. Hence in Diodorus, book 1, p. 35, when Sesoosis (var. Sesostres), the most ancient king of the Egyptians, had subdued the Ethiopians, ἠνάγκασε τὸ ἔθνος φόρους τελεῖν, ἔβενον, καὶ χρυσὸν, καὶ τῶν ἐλεφάντων τοὺς ὀδόντας [ēnankase to ethnos phorous telein, ebenon, kai chryson, kai tōn elephantōn tous odontas], he imposed on the nation as tribute ebony, and gold, and elephants' teeth. The Persians are read to have exacted the same things from the same Ethiopians. Herodotus, Muse 3, ch. 97: Ἀγινέουσι δὲ καὶ τὸ μέχρι ἐμεῦ δύο χοίνικας ἀπύρου χρυσίου, καὶ διηκοσίας φαλάγγας ἐβένου, καὶ ἐλέφαντος ὀδόντας μεγάλους εἴκοσι· [Agineousi de kai to mechri emeu dyo choinikas apyrou chrysiou, kai diēkosias phalangas ebenou, kai elephantos odontas megalous eikosi] Down to my own time (the Ethiopians, as a triennial tribute to the Persians) bring two choenixes of apyrous gold (that is, not yet tried by fire), and two hundred logs of ebony, and twenty large elephant tusks. For the region is rich in these three things, as the same author writes in ch. 114: Αὕτη δὲ χρυσόν τε φέρει πολλὸν, καὶ ἐλέφαντας ἀμφιλαφέας, καὶ δένδρεα πάντα ἄγρια, καὶ ἔβενον· [Hautē de chryson te pherei pollon, kai elephantas amphilapheas, kai dendrea panta agria, kai ebenon] This land produces much gold, and very large elephants, and wild trees of every kind, and ebony. Pliny too, book 12, ch. 4, where he states of ebony that by way of tribute the Ethiopians paid to the kings of Persia every third year a hundred logs of its wood, together with gold and ivory. And in the procession of Ptolemy Philadelphus, according to Callixenus of Rhodes, Ethiopians are reported to have carried these same things. Ἐχόμενοι τούτων ἦσαν (he says) Αἰθίοπες δωροφόροι, ὧν οἱ μὲν ἔφερον ὀδόντας ἑξακοσίους, ἕτεροι δὲ ἐβένου κορμοὺς δισχιλίους, ἄλλοι χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργυρίου κρατῆρας ἑξήκοντα, καὶ ψήγματα χρυσίου [Echomenoi toutōn ēsan … Aithiopes dōrophoroi, hōn hoi men epheron odontas hexakosious, heteroi de ebenou kormous dischilious, alloi chrysou kai argyriou kratēras hexēkonta, kai psēgmata chrysiou]. Next to these came Ethiopians bearing gifts, some of whom carried six hundred (elephants') tusks, others two thousand logs of ebony, others sixty bowls of gold and silver, and gold dust. Accordingly, at the festival of Adonis celebrated with great pomp at Alexandria under the same king, the Syracusan women, on seeing the ebony and the gold and the abundant ivory, burst out in these words, Idyll 15, line 123:
Ὦ ἔβενος, ὢ χρυσὸς, ὢ ἐκ λευκῶ ἐλέφαντος Αἰετώ! [Ō ebenos, ō chrysos, ō ek leukō elephantos Aietō!]

O ebony, O gold, O eagles of white ivory! Moreover, at Rome, as Pliny teaches, ebony held the third place in the esteem of tributes. Sixthly, although the Hebrews defer greatly to the Chaldee paraphrast, for whom הבנים hobnim are peacocks, they nevertheless acknowledge that some interpret it as ebony, and they waver between the two opinions. Hence Kimchi in his Commentaries: הובנים פירשו בו העץ הנקרא בערבי אבנוס, They interpret hobnim as the wood which is called ebony in Arabic. This is better than in his Lexicon, where it is יבנים jabnim, or jebenim. And Abarbanel [=Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508), commentary on the Bible]: פירשו בו שהוא העץ הנקרא בערבי אוינוס שמביאין גם כן מארצות המזרח, They explain it as the wood which in Arabic is called evenus, which they also (like ivory) bring from the eastern lands. Mardochaeus and Aquinas: עצם חיה מה או מין עץ, The bone of some animal, or a kind of wood. Their repeated claim that it is the bone of an animal is a third opinion, which Kimchi explains in his Lexicon thus: הבנים הם חיות שעושין מלאכה מהעצם שלהן או מהקרנות כמו שעושין מעצם הפיל שהוא השן, Hobnim are animals from whose bones or horns certain works are made, as they are made from the bone of the elephant, which is ivory. But he reduces this third opinion to the first, which explains hobnim as peacocks, adding that it may be שיעשו מלאכה מעצם שלהם, that some work is made from their bones, namely as from ivory, with which הבנים hobnim is joined here. This is a monstrous opinion. For who has ever heard tell of peacock bones being carved or engraved, or used for any work in the manner of ivory? Thus the very fact that those who would have הבנים hobnim be peacocks slide into such absurd fictions shows how much more soundly those judge who understand ebony here; in that rendering there is nothing that does not fit exactly.

Yet one objection can be raised, namely that the Hebrew הבנים hobnim is a plural, whereas the word for ebony is only singular. It is indeed inflected and spelled in various ways. For one says haec ebenus, or evenus, or hebenus, and hoc ebenum, or evenum, or hebenum. And in Greek ἡ ἔβενος [hē ebenos], or ἔβελος [ebelos], as in the Suda; or ἐβένη [ebenē], as in Theophrastus. But in the plural, ἐβένους [ebenous] in Greek was said only by Symmachus; and in Latin ebenos or ebena only, as far as I remember, by Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] and Mercerus in their rendering of this passage. Junius answers that it is named in the plural by the Hebrews because there are two kinds of ebony. That is indeed what Theophrastus teaches, Hist. book 4, ch. 5, where he treats the trees of India: Ἴδιον δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐβένη τῆς χώρας ταύτης. Ταύτης δὲ δύο γένη τὸ μὲν εὔξυλον, καὶ καλόν· τὸ δὲ φαῦλον. σπάνιον δὲ τὸ καλὸν, θάτερον δὲ πολύ. Τὴν δὲ χρόαν οὐ θησαυριζομένη λαμβάνει τὴν εὔχρουν, ἀλλ᾽ εὐθὺς τῇ φύσει ἐστὶ δὲ τὸ δένδρον θαμνῶδες, ὥσπερ ὁ κύτισος [Idion de kai hē ebenē tēs chōras tautēs. Tautēs de dyo genē to men euxylon, kai kalon; to de phaulon. spanion de to kalon, thateron de poly. Tēn de chroan ou thēsaurizomenē lambanei tēn euchroun, all᾽ euthys tē physei estin de to dendron thamnōdes, hōsper ho kytisos]. Ebony too is peculiar to this region. Of it there are two kinds: one of excellent wood, and good; the other bad. The good one is rare, but the other common. Nor does ebony acquire its fine colour by being stored away, but has it at once from nature. Moreover it is like a shrub, as the cytisus is. That this is the true meaning of Theophrastus Salmasius proves at length in his Exercitations on Solinus, and not the one that Pliny, book 12, chapter 4, ascribes to him in these words: There are two kinds of it. The rarer is the better one, tree-like, with a trunk free of knots, its wood of a black lustre, and pleasing at once even without craftsmanship. The other is shrubby, like the cytisus, and spread over all India. Good ebony is not called εὔξυλος [euxylos] because it is tree-like, that is, large like a tree, but from the excellence of its wood. Nor is being θαμνώδης [thamnōdēs] peculiar to the bad kind; it is common to both. And there θαμνῶδες [thamnōdes] does not mean fruticosum [shrubby], that is, dense with many twigs, but behaving like a shrub, as all bushes do. Dioscorides also makes two kinds of ebony, but distinguishes them by place: Ἔβενος κρατίστη ἡ Αἰθιοπικὴ, καὶ μέλαινα, καὶ μὴ ἔχουσα κτηδόνας [Ebenos kratistē hē Aithiopikē, kai melaina, kai mē echousa ktēdonas]; The best ebony is the Ethiopian, black, and without veins running through it like the teeth of a comb. The Arabic translator calls them طبقات [ṭabaqāt]. And a little later: Ἔστι δέ τις καὶ Ἰνδικὴ, ἔχουσα διαφύσεις λευκὰς, καὶ κιῤῥὰς, καὶ σπίλους ὁμοίως πυκνούς· πλὴν βελτίων ἡ πρώτη [Esti de tis kai Indikē, echousa diaphyseis leukas, kai kirrhas, kai spilous homoiōs pyknous; plēn beltiōn hē prōtē]. There is also another, Indian, with white and reddish lines running through it, and frequent spots as well. But the former is better. So also Isidore: Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia; when cut it hardens into stone; its wood is black, and its bark smooth like that of the laurel. But the Indian is spotted, with small white and tawny markings. The Ethiopian, however, which is held to be superior, is spotted nowhere, but black, smooth and horn-like. And Serapion [=Serapion, Liber de simplicibus medicinis (the Arabic-Latin pharmacopoeia)]: It has two species, namely Absi and Inda. And Absi is a black wood, without lines, etc. In the Indian, however, there are white lines, and of a reddish colour, etc. This is taken from Dioscorides. Absi is حبشي [ḥabashī] Habasi, that is, Ethiopian. Common to all of these is that they recognize only two species of ebony. To which the Hebrew הבנים hobnim does not correspond, because it is a plural, not a dual noun. For the dual would be hobnajim. So something else must be sought. Fuller indeed refers this plural to the palangae of ebony, which were brought from India and Ethiopia in great numbers. Herodotus and Arrian in the Periplus call them φάλαγγας [phalangas]; Pliny palangae or phalangae, the spelling varying; that is, round poles, such as are placed under ships, or on which several men carry the same load. Pollux, book 7, ch. 33, §. 9: Τὰ δὲ τῶν νεῶν ξύλα, οἷς ὑποβληθεῖσιν ἐφέλκονται αἱ νῆες, φάλαγγες, καὶ φαλάγγια [Ta de tōn neōn xyla, hois hypoblētheisin ephelkontai hai nēes, phalanges, kai phalangia]. Hesychius: Φαλάγγια· στρόγγυλα ξύλα, καὶ σύμμετρα [Phalangia; strongyla xyla, kai symmetra]. Nonius: Palangae is the name for round poles which are put under ships when they are drawn down to the sea, or when they are hauled up onto the shore. The Glosses: Phalangarii, Οἱ τοῖς δοκοῖς ἀποκρεμῶντες βάρη, καὶ πλείονες ἅμα βαστάζοντες [Hoi tois dokois apokremōntes barē, kai pleiones hama bastazontes]. Again Nonius: We call palangarii those who carry some load on poles. The origin of the word seems to be Hebrew. For in Hebrew פלך pelec, or in archaic form phelec, is baculus [staff], 2 Sam 3:29. And in Arabic فلك [falaka] phalaca means to be round. Hence the round ebony staves which the Tyrian merchants called פלכין pelakin or phelakin could have been called φάλαγγες [phalanges], phalanges, or palanges. Callixenus, in book 5 of Athenaeus, names ἐβένου κορμοὺς [ebenou kormous], logs of ebony. Apuleius, in the first Apology, staves of ebony, though some prefer to read loculos [little boxes] there. These, then, whether staves or κορμοὺς [kormous], or these palangae of ebony, Fuller thinks are signified by the plural הבנים hobnim. But learned men seem to weary themselves here in vain, since the Hebrews scarcely name precious woods of this kind otherwise than with a plural word. Thus the tree from which the ark was made is called once in the singular שטה sitta, Isa 41:19. But in the plural שטים sittim more than twenty times in Exodus. And another tree, from which the beams and supports in the temple of Solomon were made, and the harps and lutes of the singers, is called only by a plural word, אלגומים algumim or אלמוגים almugim, 1 Reg. X, 11. 12. and 2 Chr 9:10–11. And in the Chaldee paraphrases of Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and Jerusalem, Gen 50:1: Joseph laid his father בערס דסנדפין, on a couch of sindaphin, that is, as they hold, on a bed made of the most excellent kind of wood, so called with a plural word. And I once suspected that it was so named after two villages of Egypt called سندف [Sndf] Sendapha. Yet in the treatise On the Elephant above, a truer explanation of this word is given.

It should be noted in passing that the books of the Arabs mention certain woods so similar to ebony that some take them for ebony. Among these is the wood شيز [shīz] Siz, or شيزي [shīzī] Siza, so called from a place; and the wood ساسم [sāsam] sasem, or سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim, called by the same name as sesame, although it is entirely different from sesame. To this belong these words in Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الشيز والشيزي خشب اسود للقصاع وهو الابنوس والساسم او خشب الجوز وناحية بارض بادر بيجان [al-shīz wa-l-shīzī khashab aswad li-l-qiṣāʿ wa-huwa al-abanūs wa-l-sāsam aw khashab al-jawz wa-nāḥiya bi-arḍ bādr bījān] Siz, or Siza, a black wood for making dishes. It is either ebony, or sasim, or the wood of the walnut; and also a certain region in the land of Adarbigian (that is, the Atropatia of Strabo and the Atropatena of Ptolemy), from which, namely, this wood is brought and takes its name. The same author elsewhere: الساسم شجر اسود او الابنوس او الشيز او شجر يعمل منه القسي [al-sāsam shajar aswad aw al-abanūs aw al-shīz aw shajar yuʿmal minhu al-qisī] Sasim: a black tree, or ebony, or siz, or a tree from which bows are made. Damir, in the chapter On سمسمة [simsima] simsima, which is a kind of red ant, like שומשמנא among the Chaldeans, says that this same wood is called سمسم [simsim] semsem, in the plural سماسم [samāsim] semasim. He proves this from these words of the pseudo-prophet about الجهنميين [al-jahannamiyyīn], that is, about those who are tormented in Gehenna: تخرجون من النار بعد ان يكونوا فيها فيخرجون كانها عيدان السماسم [takhrujūn min al-nār baʿd an yakūnū fīhā fa-yakhrujūn ka-annahā ʿīdān al-samāsim] They will come out of the fire after some stay in it; they will come out, I say, like the woods semasim, that is, equally black from being scorched by the fire. On these words the commentators offer many quite absurd things. But the more learned recognize that the semasim woods are ebony woods, or woods resembling ebony in blackness, so that they seem burnt. This throws light on these words of Dioscorides in the chapter On ebony: Ἔνιοι δὲ τὰ σησάμινα, ἢ ἀκάνθινα ξύλα ἐμφερῆ ὄντα, ἀντὶ ἐβένου πωλοῦσι· [Enioi de ta sēsamina, ē akanthina xyla empherē onta, anti ebenou pōlousi]. Marcellus Virgilius rendered this as follows: Some sell in place of ebony the timber of the Indian thorn, or of the mulberry, the resemblance deceiving. He thinks, namely, that σησάμινα [sēsamina] should be read συκάμινα [sykamina], because sesame has nothing in common with ebony. But neither has the sycamine or sycomore, except that both are wood. Beware, therefore, of changing anything. For sesamina here means something other than in common usage: namely, the wood of that tree which is called sasim and semsem in Arabic, and in the plural semasim. Accordingly the Arabic translator of Dioscorides rightly has here: ومن الناس من ياخذ اعضان خشب بعض اصناف الشوك والخشب الذي يقال له سيساما فيبيعه بدل الابنوس لانه شبيه به [wa-min al-nās man yaʾkhudh aʿḍān khashab baʿḍ aṣnāf al-shawk wa-l-khashab alladhī yuqāl lahu sīsāmā fa-yabīʿuhu badal al-abanūs li-annahu shabīh bihi] There are some who take the wood of a certain kind of thorn, and the wood which they call sesamum, and sell it in place of ebony, because it resembles it. What is more, besides Dioscorides, Arrian too in the Periplus mentions φαλάγγων σησαμίνων, καὶ ἐβενίνων [phalangōn sēsaminōn, kai ebeninōn], beams of sesamine and of ebony, which are brought from the Indian city of Barygaza to Persia. This reading is therefore certain and beyond doubt.

Pliny writes, Hist. Nat. book 10, ch. 42, §. 58, that the psittacus [parrot] is called Sittace in India. Reland [=Adriaan Reland, Dissertationes miscellaneae (1706–08)], in Dissertatt. Miscellann. vol. 1, p. 184, thinks this name was formed from Tedac, and this from תך: "whether," he says, "from תך others made تدك [tdk] by doubling the first letter or adding a letter of similar sound, or whether תך arose from Tedac by dropping one of the first two letters because of the similarity of sound." How slippery and uncertain this is, everyone will see for himself. I pass over the dreams of others about this word; whoever wishes to know them may consult Simonis, Lexic. under the word. For my part, I would think one should rest content with what Bochart has argued here no less acutely than learnedly.
Pliny, book 11, ch. 38: "On the head peacocks have crests of hairy little tufts like small trees."
On the word צפור tsippor, which denotes both birds of any kind and specifically the sparrow. Its kinds according to the Arabs; and on the house sparrow and its chirping.

Among the infirmities of old age which Solomon vividly depicts, this too is listed, Eccl 12:6: that one is roused and rises לקול הצפור, at the voice of the tsippor, or bird, that is, of the cock, as many think. The most learned Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] refutes them thus: Those who understand the cock, at whose voice one is roused, do not understand the force of the Hebrew word צפור (tsippor), which means a little bird, etc., and is not said of larger birds. And the same author in his Thesaurus: צפור (tsippor) means smaller birds, etc.; עוף (oph), however, is a bird or winged creature in general. And Schindler: צפור (tsippor) is a little bird flying about, or one that circles in the air. It comprises the smaller birds, and among them the sparrow, the one most frequently found among men, a very common bird. So too most other recent lexicographers. And in Philo's book Who is the Heir of Divine Things, Sepphora is ὀρνίθιον [ornithion], a little bird. Yet among the Hebrews עוף oph and צפור tsippor are equally general, and both names embrace absolutely all winged creatures. Hence Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] in their Lexicons, under the word צפור tsippor: שם כלל לכל עוף, it is a name common to every bird. And Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)]: שם כולל לכל מיני עוף שיעופף, This name comprises every species of bird that flies. That this is entirely true will be clear to anyone who compares the passages of Scripture. For in Deut 4:17, when God forbids the worship of תבנית כל צפור כנף אשר תעוף בשמים, the likeness of any winged tsippor that flies through the heavens, who would say that only the worship of little birds is forbidden, and not that of larger birds as well? And in Deut 14:11, when the same God permits the eating of כל צפור טהורה, every clean tsippor, will he be said to have permitted only little birds, and not hens, guinea fowl and pheasants? Or who ever restricted to little birds the law found in Deut 22:6: If there come before you קן צפור, a nest of a tsippor, in any tree or on the ground, a nest of young or of eggs, where the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs, do not take the mother with the young? Again, who would deny that all birds are meant when we read that God subjected to man the beasts of the field, צפור שמים, the tsippor of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, Ps 8:9? Or when wild beasts, and all cattle, creeping things, וצפור כנף, and the winged tsippor are invited to praise God, Ps 148:10? Or when we read that in the branches of the mystical tree dwell כל צפור כל כנף, every tsippor, everything winged, Ezek 17:23? And in the plural, צפרי שמיא, the tsippare of the heavens, Dan 4:9 18.? Finally, it is clear that birds of prey, which are generally by far the largest, are designated by this name, when in Ezek 39:4 17. God hands over the hosts of Gog and Magog to be devoured לעיט צפור, by the ravenous winged tsippor. And in Daniel IV, 20, where the nails of the Babylonian king are said to have grown כצפרין, like tsipparin, that is, like the talons of birds of prey, which from the curvature and size of their talons are called in Greek γαμψώνυχες [gampsōnyches]. It is therefore evident that the name צפור tsippor extends even to the largest birds. Rabbi Moses, son of Gershom, maintains that birds are so called שבעלות השחר מתחילות לרנן ולצפצוף, because at the rising of the dawn they begin to sing and to warble. I, for my part, hold that they are named not from singing, which is not common to all, but from צפר, that is, morning; because it is customary for birds to rise very early in the morning, whether they are songbirds or not, while wild beasts are then sound asleep, because they spend the night awake, Psal. CIV, 20.

But although the name צפור tsippor is common to all birds, the Hebrews nevertheless assert that this same name sometimes signifies the sparrow specifically. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV, 4: וצפור הוא עוף קטן וקורין לו בלעז פשרא And tsippor (in that place) is a small bird, which in the vernacular (that is, Spanish) they call paxaro (that is, sparrow). Hence Pomarius: קמחי אומר שלפעמים יוקח בעד עוף קטן שקורין לו בלעז פאסרו, Kimchi said that it is sometimes taken for a little bird, which in the vernacular (or Italian) tongue they call passaro. Aquinas: הוא שם מין עוף מה, It is the name of a certain species of bird. And a little later: והוא עוף קטן וידוע, It is a well-known little bird, namely the sparrow. Accordingly, just as Jerome renders it sparrow in Lev. XIV, 4, so too does the old translator in Psal. X, 1, and LXXXIII, 4, and CI, 8, and CIII, 16, and CXXIII, 7, following the Greeks, who render it στρουθίον [strouthion] in those same passages of the Psalms, and in Eccles. XII, 6, and Thren. III, 52. And conversely, the Greek στρουθία [strouthia], that is, sparrows, in Matth. X, 29, and Luc. XII, 6, the Syriac translator renders ܨܦܪܝܢ [צפרין] tsipparin, for which the Arabic has عصافير [ʿaṣāfīr] atsaphiro. For to them عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] otsphur is the sparrow, a word formed from צפור tsippor with a guttural prefixed. Not knowing this, Chamza, a not undistinguished Arab grammarian, thought that the sparrow is called عصفور by a compound word, because عصي وفر [ʿaṣá wa-farra] it strikes and flees. Nor is it peculiar to the Hebrews that they call the sparrow by the same word as they also call larger birds. For the Greek name of the sparrow, στρουθὸς [strouthos], is also used of the hen. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 60:
Ἠέ τι μηελόεντα χαλικρότερον ποτὸν ἴσχοις Ὄρνιθος στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — — [Ēe ti mēeloenta chalikroteron poton ischois / Ornithos strouthoio katoikados]
Or may you have some marrowy, undiluted drinkable remedy from the domestic sparrow-bird, that is, from the hen. And again, line 535:
Ἠὲ πάτον στρουθοῖο κατοικάδος, — — [Ēe paton strouthoio katoikados]

Or the dung of the domestic sparrow, that is, of the hen. Hence it came about that the great Libyan hen, by far the largest of birds, was called στρουθὸς [strouthos], in a word the ostrich. Imitating this, the Roman writers call the ostrich the sea sparrow. Plautus in the Persa, Act 2:
Fly at a run. P. That is what the sea sparrow usually does around the circus.
Cook you the egg of the sea sparrow.

Festus: The sea sparrow, which the common people call the struthiocamelus. The Roman word passer is thought to allude to the Hebrew צפור tsippor and to have arisen from it. But a great man, commenting on Solinus, observes that the sparrow was also called passa, as the female sparrow is called paisse in French. Hence the Glosses: Passa, εἶδος ὀρνέου [eidos orneou]. And passa was formed from the Aeolic πίζα [piza], for σπίζα [spiza]. For σπίζα [spiza] is the finch, a bird similar to the sparrow. Hesychius: Σπίζα· ὀρνιθάριον στρουθῷ παρεμφερές [Spiza: ornitharion strouthō paremferes]. And sometimes it is taken more broadly for a little bird in general, as in Timon, quoted by Laertius, on Arcesilaus:
Οἱ δέ μιν ἠΰ τε γλαῦκα περὶ σπίζαι τερατοῦντο, [Hoi de min ēy te glauka peri spizai teratounto]

But they will marvel at him like little birds that surround an owl. Accordingly Hesychius: Σπίζια· ὄρνεα ἅπαντα [Spizia; ornea hapanta]. Rightly, provided that his ὄρνεα [ornea] are ὀρνίθια [ornithia] or ὀρνιθάρια [ornitharia], that is, little birds, not birds. Thus the Arabic عصفور [ʿuṣfūr], although properly it means sparrow, nevertheless embraces many species of little birds. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: وهى انواع منها ما هو مطرب بصوته ومنها ما يعجب بصورته وحسنه والعصفور الصوار هو الذي يجيب اذا ادعي من الصرورة وعصفور الجنة وهو الخطاف والعصفور البيوت فان في طباعه اختلافا [wa-hiya anwāʿ minhā mā huwa muṭrib bi-ṣawtihi wa-minhā mā yuʿjib bi-ṣūratihi wa-ḥusnihi wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-ṣawwār huwa alladhī yujību idhā duʿiya min al-ṣarūra wa-ʿuṣfūr al-janna wa-huwa al-khuṭṭāf wa-l-ʿuṣfūr al-buyūt fa-inna fī ṭibāʿihi ikhtilāfan] There are various species of sparrows: some please by the modulation of their voice; others are admirable for their appearance and form. And the sparrow called suar is the one that, when called, answers by chirping. And the sparrow of paradise is the swallow. And the house sparrow is the one that is quarrelsome by nature, etc. And further on: ومن انواعه عصفور الشوك واكثر ماواه السياج وزعم ارسطو ان بينه وبين الحمار عداوة [wa-min anwāʿihi ʿuṣfūr al-shawk wa-akthar maʾwāhu al-siyāj wa-zaʿama Arisṭū anna baynahu wa-bayna al-ḥimār ʿadāwa] Among its species is the sparrow of thorns, which mostly lives in thickets. Aristotle reports that there is mutual hatred between it and the ass. It is plain that the acanthis is meant, which some explain as the goldfinch, others as the siskin, others as the ligurinus. For of it the Philosopher writes in Hist. book 8, chapter 3: Τὰ δὲ τοιάδε ἀκανθοφάγα, ἀκανθὶς, θραυπίς· ἔτι ἡ καλουμένη χρυσομήτρις. Ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκανθῶν νέμεται [Ta de toiade akanthophaga, akanthis, thraupis; eti hē kaloumenē chrysomētris. Tauta gar panta epi tōn akanthōn nemetai]. Gaza rendered this as follows: These seek thorns: the siskin or ligurinus, the goldfinch, and also the one called aurivittis. For all these live on thorns. And in book 9, chapter 1: Ὄνος δὲ, καὶ ἀκανθίδες πολέμιοι· αἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν βοητεύουσιν [Onos de, kai akanthides polemioi; hai men gar apo tōn akanthōn boēteuousin] (read βιοτεύουσιν [bioteuousin]), ὁ δὲ ἁπαλὰς οὔσας ἐσθίει τὰς ἀκάνθας [ho de hapalas ousas esthiei tas akanthas]: The ass and the acanthides are enemies: for they get their living from thorns, which the ass eats while they are still tender. And the Arabs rightly assign this bird to the sparrow kind. For the acanthis is the same as the acanthyllis, of which Hesychius says: Ἀκανθυλλίς· στρουθοῦ γένος [Akanthyllis; strouthou genos], Acanthyllis, a kind of sparrow. In French it is called serin; whether from the song of the Sirens, as Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] holds in the Ornithology, book 7, chapter 14. There follows in Damir: ومن انواعه القبرة والحسون والبلبل والصعوة والحمرة والعندليب والمكاكي والصافر والتنوط والوصع والابوبراقش والقبعة [wa-min anwāʿihi al-qubbara wa-l-ḥassūn wa-l-bulbul wa-l-ṣaʿwa wa-l-ḥumra wa-l-ʿandalīb wa-l-makākī wa-l-ṣāfir wa-l-tanawwuṭ wa-l-waṣaʿ wa-l-abū barāqish wa-l-qubaʿa] Also among its species are the kubbara (the crested lark), and the hassun (I do not find it elsewhere; it seems to be named from its beauty) , and the bulbul (the nightingale), and the savva (a little bird with a red crown), and the hamra (a red species of lark), and the andalib (a species of bird similar to the nightingale), and the mechachi (plural of the singular مكا [mukkā] maccha, a bird named from its whistling), and the saphir (which also whistles all night long with its head bent down and its feet fastened to the tree), and the thenavvut (a little bird not unlike this one, named from the nest that it hangs from a tree), and the vvasa (the wren), and the abubarakis (a songbird with long neck and legs, and red, yellow, green and blue feathers, which repeatedly change their colours), and the kubaa (a variegated little bird that draws in its neck when afraid, whence its name). These are the birds that the Arabs assign to the sparrow kind. So too among the Hebrews, according to Kimchi in his Lexicon: הוא רב המין לפיכך כלל כל עוף בזה השם, The sparrow has many species: hence this name is applied to all birds.

He describes the البيوتي [al-buyūtī] domestic sparrow as follows: في طباعه اختلاف وذلك فيه من الطباعه ما يشبه السباع وهو اكله اللحم ولا يزق فراخه ومن البهايم انه ليس بذي مخلب ولا منسر وياكل الحب والبقول وهو اذا سقط علي العود قدم اصابعه الثلاث واخر الدايرة وساير الطير تقدم اصبعين وتوخر اصبعين وتميز الذكر منها بلحيه سودا كما الرجل والتيس والديك وليس في الارض طاير ولا سبع ولا بهيمة احني من العصفور علي ولده ولا اشد له عشقا وذلك مشاهد عند اخذ فراخه ووكره في الغمران تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح واذا حلت مدينة من اهلها ذهبت العصافير منها فاذا عاد واعادت العصافير والعصفور لا يعرف المشي وانما يثب وثبا وهو كثير السفاد فربما سفد في الساعة الواحدة ماية مرة ولذلك قصر عمره فانه لا يعيش في الغالب اكثر من سنة والفرخه تدرب علي الطيران حتي انه يدعي فيجيب قال الجاحظ انه رجع من فرسخ It is of a pugnacious nature. For something wild has been implanted in it by nature. Accordingly it feeds on flesh, and does not feed its young by inserting its beak into their mouths. But it has this in common with non-raptorial birds, that it has no talons with which to tear, nor a hooked beak, and it eats grain and vegetables. When it alights on a tree, of its four toes it stretches three forward and one backward, whereas in other birds two toes are in front and as many behind. The male is distinguished from the female by a black beard, which it has like a man, a he-goat, or a cock. Nowhere is there a bird, wild beast, or beast of burden more devoted to its offspring or loving it more ardently. Hence it places its young and its nest in inhabited places and under the roofs of houses, for fear of birds of prey. When a city is deserted, the sparrows leave it, and return together with the inhabitants. The sparrow does not know how to walk, and moves only by hopping. It is a bird of such frequent coition that it sometimes mates a hundred times in an hour, and consequently it is short-lived, and generally does not live beyond a year. Its young are more teachable than the common run of birds, so that when called they answer. Algiahid testifies that a sparrow returns from a parasang away. One could add more from Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt], but these things apply to the whole sparrow genus, not to the domestic sparrow alone.

In Hebrew צפצף tsiphseph means to murmur and to mutter, Isa 8:19 and XXIX, 4. This is taken from the twittering of birds. R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Es. XXIX.: ציפצוף הוא לשון קול לחש כקול עופות דקין, tsiphtsuph signifies a muttering voice, like the voice of little birds. This is evident from Isa 38:14, where it is applied to the swallow. Yet more properly צפצוף is the chirping of sparrows. Pomarius: צפצף עשה קול צפורים, tsiphseph, he chirped in the manner of sparrows. That this is true is clear from the Arabs, for whom صفصف [ṣafṣaf] tsophtsoph is عصفور [ʿuṣfūr] sparrow, and صفصفة [ṣafṣafa] tsaphtsapha is صوته [ṣawtuhu] its voice. So it is given in the Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]. Hence in Es. X, 14. the Hebrew words ופצה פה ומצפצף, And opening the mouth, and chirping, are rendered in Greek thus: Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn]. On which Theodoret says: Ἀπὸ τῆς κρατούσης συνηθείας παρὰ ἀνθρώποις εἴρηται τῇ γραφῇ. εἰώθαμεν γὰρ λέγειν περὶ τῶν λίαν ἀγωνιώντων, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε γρύξαι· οἱ δὲ λοιποί φασιν, Οὐκ ἐτόλμησε τρύσαι. τὸ οὖν Ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων, ἀντὶ τοῦ Οὐ μόνον οὐδεὶς ἀντιπαρατάξασθαί μοι τολμήσει, ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲ γρύζειν στρουθοῖς παραπλησίως ἐπιχειρήσει [Apo tēs kratousēs synētheias para anthrōpois eirētai tē graphē. eiōthamen gar legein peri tōn lian agōniōntōn, Ouk etolmēse gryxai; hoi de loipoi phasin, Ouk etolmēse trysai. to oun Anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn, anti tou Ou monon oudeis antiparataxasthai moi tolmēsei, all' oude gryzein strouthois paraplēsiōs epicheirēsei]. Scripture has taken this from human usage. For we are accustomed to say of those who are in great distress, He did not dare to mutter. Others, however, say, He did not dare to squeak. Thus "opening the mouth and chirping" (there will be no one) is the same as if he said, Not only will no one dare to oppose me, but no one will even attempt to chirp in the manner of sparrows. From the same source is taken that gloss of Suidas: Στρουθίζων· τρίζων [Strouthizōn; trizōn]. For τρίζειν [trizein], to squeak, is also said of sparrows, as is clear from Iliad 2, line 314, where the serpent devoured eight little sparrows together with their mother

devoured, miserably shrieking: not τιτίζοντας [titizontas], as Zenodotus wanted it read. Nor should anyone be surprised that Isaiah describes men chirping like birds. For it is a continuation of the metaphor. There the Prophet speaks in the words of the king of Assyria, who boasts like a Thraso and compares the peoples he has conquered with a nest of birds which fear of the fowler so dismays that they do not even dare to chirp. So the whole verse reads thus: And my hand has reached the wealth of the peoples as (birds') nest. And as one gathers abandoned eggs, I have gathered the whole earth; and there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps. The words Καὶ ἀνοίγων στόμα, καὶ στρουθίζων [Kai anoigōn stoma, kai strouthizōn] are missing in most editions, and were read neither by Basil nor by Cyril. Yet the Complutensian edition and the recent Paris edition present them so. Theodoret also read them, and so did the Arabic translator, who made his version from the Greek. And in Procopius they are found in the margin with an asterisk. The version of the Elders [=the translators of the Septuagint], namely, is often rather free: provided they express the sense in some way, they are often little concerned about the words. Thus the Hebrew, And there is none who moves a wing, or opens the mouth, or chirps, they had rendered thus: Καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς διαφεύξεταί με, ἢ ἀντείπῃ μοί [Kai ouk estin hos diapheuxetai me, ē anteipē moi]: And there is none who escapes me, or contradicts me. But someone supplied the rest from another translator. Was it Aquila, who was most skilled in the Hebrew language and accustomed to render word for word?
The Arabic مصع [maṣʿ] matsaon for the male sparrow echoes the Dutch name of the sparrow, mosche, and the Norman moisson. Alcamus: المصع العصفور الذكرة [al-maṣʿ al-ʿuṣfūr al-dhakara].

Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descript. Animal. p. 10: "Hassun comes from Natolia and Smyrna with the cold, that is, at the beginning of November; it leaves when the heat sets in, 1 month before the harvest. In French and Italian Calderine."

Nine passages of the Prophets which some interpreters refer to sparrows, for the most part rather uncertain. I. Levit. XIV. passim. II. Job 40:24. III. Ps 10:1. IV. Ps 84:4. V. Ps 102:8. VI. Ps 104:16. VII. Ps 124:7. VIII. Eccl 12:4. IX. Lam 3:52.
Interpreters do not sufficiently agree in which passages of Scripture צפור tsippor is taken for the sparrow. For of the nine passages that are adduced, most are very doubtful.

I. The first is Levit. XIV., at the beginning of the chapter and at the end, where it treats of two צפורים tsipporim, by which, one being killed and the other released, the leper was purified, and also a house infected with leprosy. Most hold that the tsipporim there are sparrows, as Jerome, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], the Genevans and others render it. But that birds in general are meant will be clear to anyone who reads attentively verse four: And let him that is to be cleansed take שתי צפורים חיות טהרות, two living clean tsipporim. This does not fit the sparrow, whether it is held to have been clean or unclean. For it could not be called clean if by the Law it was unclean. Conversely, if it was clean, the Law would have commanded in vain that clean sparrows be taken, since there were no unclean ones. Nowhere is it commanded that clean doves or turtledoves be offered, because all were clean. It appears, therefore, that צפורים tsipporim there are birds in general; and since some of these were clean and others unclean, God commands that clean ones be taken, for instance doves or turtledoves, which are called הצפור in Gen 15:10, or any others, provided they are clean and permitted as food according to the law of Deut 14:11. כל צפור טהרה תאכלו, Every clean tsippor you shall eat. Thus, as we showed above, some understand hens here too, and the Greek ὀρνίθια [ornithia] can be referred to this. Nor do the Hebrews specify a species, provided they are צפרים דרור טהורות, free and clean birds. On the rite of this purification Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] has much that is notable in the treatise On Leprosy, chapter 11, which does not belong here.

II. The second passage is in the description of the Leviathan, Job 40:24 (var. 29.), and in Hebrew it reads thus: Will you play with him כצפור, as with a tsippor? And will you bind him for your girls? And in the Greek version: Παίξῃ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ ὥσπερ ὀρνέῳ; ἢ δήσεις αὐτὸν ὥσπερ στρουθίον παιδίῳ; [Paixē de en autō hōsper orneō; ē dēseis auton hōsper strouthion paidiō?] Will you play with him as with a bird? and will you bind him like a sparrow for a child? And in the Arabic: هل تضحك عليه مثل العصفور [hal taḍḥaku ʿalayhi mithla al-ʿuṣfūr] Will you play with him as with a sparrow, etc. Those who pursue mysteries refer this to the devil, as though through baptism and conversion he were handed over to us bound, like a little sparrow to a child. Origen, of the faithful man: Ὅ γε δράκων αὐτῷ ὥσπερ στρουθίον παραδέδοται παιδίῳ· [Ho ge drakōn autō hōsper strouthion paradedotai paidiō] The dragon has been handed over to him as a sparrow to a child. And shortly after: Τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Κυρίου, ὡς στρουθίον ὑποχείριον, ὁ Σατανᾶς δεδεμένος γεγένηται τοῖς νηπίοις, καὶ θηλάζουσιν, ὧν ἐκ στόματος κατηρτίσατο αἶνον ὁ Θεός· [Tē chariti tou Kyriou, hōs strouthion hypocheirion, ho Satanas dedemenos gegenētai tois nēpiois, kai thēlazousin, hōn ek stomatos katērtisato ainon ho Theos] By the grace of the Lord, like a tame sparrow, Satan has been bound for children and sucklings, out of whose mouth God has perfected his praise. Chrysostom: Δήσας τὸν ἐχθρὸν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν δέδωκε καταπαίζειν αὐτοῦ, ὡς στρουθίου, τοῖς στραφεῖσι, καὶ γενομένοις ὡς τὰ παιδία. [Dēsas ton echthron ho Kyrios hēmōn dedōke katapaizein autou, hōs strouthiou, tois strapheisi, kai genomenois hōs ta paidia.] To those who have been converted and have become as infants, our Lord has handed over the adversary, bound, to be mocked like a sparrow. Alluding to this, the author of the life of Pachomius, chapter 49, attributes these words to the devils: Since the wonderful incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we have begun to exist wholly without strength; so that we are mocked like sparrows by those who believe in his name. Leaving these aside, we ask only whether the Hebrew is well rendered: Will you play with him as with a sparrow? and will you bind him for your young ones? That a mention of the sparrow is fitting here is suggested by that very well-known line of Catullus,
Sparrow, darling of my girl, with whom she is wont to play, whom to hold in her lap, to whom, as it seeks it, to give her fingertip and to provoke its sharp bites.

Hence Arnobius, book 7: as little boys (to spare their feelings and keep from crying) are given little sparrows, poplar toys, loaves, with which they can divert themselves. And an Arab poet, whom Ibno Rasik cites in the book entitled غرايب [gharāyib] garaibo, that is, Curiosities:
كعصفورة في كف طفل يسوخها * حياض الردي والطفل يلهو ويلعب * [ka-ʿuṣfūratin fī kaffi ṭiflin yasūkhuhā * ḥiyāḍa al-radī wa-l-ṭiflu yalhū wa-yalʿabu *]

Like a hen sparrow in a boy's hand, which he plunges into the evil troughs while he jests and plays. Yet in Job there is no need to understand the sparrow precisely, since there is no lack of other birds with which boys and girls are equally amused. Plautus in the Captivi, Act 5:
— — as jackdaws, or ducks, or quails are given to patrician boys to play with.

Pliny, writing to Clemens about the son of Regulus in Letter 2 of book 4: "The boy had many ponies, both harnessed and unharnessed; he had dogs large and small; he had nightingales, parrots, blackbirds." Julius Capitolinus in Clodius Albinus: "Seven small eagles were brought from the nest and placed, as if in play, around the boy's cradle."
