Pausanias in the Corinthiaca: Κόκκυγα δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ σκήπτρῳ καθῆσθαί φασι, λέγοντες τὸν Δία, ὅτε ἤρα παρθένου τῆς Ἥρας ἐς τοῦτον τὸν ὄρνιθα ἀλλαγῆναι· τὴν δὲ ἅτε παίγνιον θηρᾶσαι· [Kokkyga de epi tō skēptrō kathēsthai phasi, legontes ton Dia, hote ēra parthenou tēs Hēras es touton ton ornitha allagēnai; tēn de hate paignion thērasai] "They say the cuckoo sits on the sceptre of Jove because Jupiter, seized with love for the maiden Juno, turned himself into that bird, which the girl caught as a plaything." Hence Jupiter Coccygius, whom the same author mentions further on. Accordingly Jerome explains the passage of Job we mentioned thus: "Will you play with him as with a bird? Or will you bind him for your maidservants?", making no mention of a sparrow. And most of the more recent interpreters follow the same.

III. The third passage is Ps 10:1 (in the Hebrew XI, 1.), where the Greek version has Μεταναστεύου ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη ὡς στρουθίον· [Metanasteuou epi ta orē hōs strouthion], and the Vulgate, "Flee to the mountain like a sparrow." The Arabic also has مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr], like a sparrow. And Apollinaris in his Metaphrase:
Στρουθὸν ὀρεσσιβότοισιν ὅπως θρώσκοντα νομῆσι, [Strouthon oressibotoisin hopōs thrōskonta nomēsi]

"Like a sparrow leaping in mountain pastures." And Theodoret in his Commentary: Τί δή ποτέ φησι παραινεῖτέ μοι φυγεῖν, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περινοστεῖν στρουθίου δίκην ἐπτοημένου; [Ti dē pote phēsi paraineite moi phygein, kai ta orē perinostein strouthiou dikēn eptoēmenou?] "Why," he says, "do you urge me to flee and wander over the mountains like a frightened sparrow?" But Jerome does better, as I at least think, with "Fly over to the mountain like a bird", as do most of the more recent interpreters. For the sparrow is not a mountain bird. And David, who is the subject here, says that Saul is pursuing him as one would hunt, not a sparrow, but the bird Kore in the mountains, 1 Sam 26:20, that is, the woodcock, as we have shown. It would be vain to object that near Lake Larius in Italy there is a bird which they call the mountain sparrow. For that bird is not truly a sparrow, but of the blackbird kind, as Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] proves at length, p. 608. Nor is this passage of Galen, De ingenio sanitatis ch. 2, more to the point: "Among birds, partridges are praised, together with all mountain sparrows." For there not sparrows properly so called are meant, which are very hot and incite lust, but those small birds in general that live in the mountains. For it is agreed that small birds are sometimes called στρουθία [strouthia]. Moschopulus, Περὶ σχεδῶν [Peri schedōn] p. 178: Τρώγλη· ἡ τρύπα, ἀφ᾽ οὗ τρωγλίτης, ὃς καὶ στρουθὸς λέγεται· στρουθία δὲ οὐδετέρως πάντα τὰ μικρὰ τῶν ὀρνίθων. [Trōglē; hē trypa, aph᾽ hou trōglitēs, hos kai strouthos legetai; strouthia de oudeterōs panta ta mikra tōn ornithōn.] So also Phavorinus under Στρουθία [Strouthia].

IV. The fourth passage is Ps. LXXXIV, 4. גם צפור מצאה בית, for which the Greeks have Καὶ γὰρ στρουθίον εὗρεν ἑαυτῷ οἰκίαν [Kai gar strouthion heuren heautō oikian]. And the Arabic in the same sense: لان العصفور وجد له مسكنا [li-anna al-ʿuṣfūr wajada lahu maskanan]. And the Vulgate translator: "For the sparrow has found itself a home." And Jerome: "Since the sparrow has found a home." And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon proves from this passage that צפור tsippor is not a general name for all birds but proper to a certain species, because in the following hemistich דרור deror is the swallow, as he at least asserts. "Therefore," he says, אחר שאחרון פרט הראשון גם כן פרט, "since the latter (that is, דרור deror) is the name of a particular bird, so also is the former (namely צפור tsippor)." Accordingly in his Commentaries he likewise holds that צפור there is the little bird which the Spaniards call פשׂרא paxaro, that is, the sparrow. So this verse is to be rendered according to Kimchi's mind: "Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, namely your altars, O God of hosts." We agree with this view, except that we have interpreted דרור deror as the wood pigeon instead of the swallow. And by the name altars, by synecdoche of part for whole, we have understood the tabernacle, on whose beams both sparrows and wood pigeons nested, as has already been said elsewhere.

V. The fifth passage is Ps 102:8 "I have kept watch, and I have become כצפור בודד על גג", where the Greeks have ὡσεὶ στρουθίον μονάζων ἐπὶ δώματι· [hōsei strouthion monazōn epi dōmati], and the Vulgate translator, "like a solitary sparrow on the roof"; and one of the Arabic versions, "I was in my solitude كالعصفور [ka-l-ʿuṣfūr] like a sparrow upon the roof"; and the other, "I have become like a sparrow that stays alone upon the roof." And Apollinaris:
Ἢ στρουθόν τιν᾽ ἄϋπνον ἐόντ᾽ ἐν δώματι μοῦνον, [Ē strouthon tin᾽ aypnon eont᾽ en dōmati mounon]

Or some sparrow, which is sleepless, alone on the roof. For Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] said above that the sparrow nests تحت السقوف خوف من الجوارح [taḥta al-suqūf khawf min al-jawāriḥ] under the roof, for fear of birds of prey. And Suidas, under Νυκτικόραξ [Nyktikorax], describes the sparrow as δειλὸν ὄρνεον [deilon orneon], a timid bird, and one that ὑπὸ ἀγωνίας ἐλαύνει τὸν ὕπνον [hypo agōnias elaunei ton hypnon], drives away sleep out of anxiety. These things will seem to bear most closely on this passage, in which David, as some would have it, says that he kept watch like a sparrow that is alone on the roof. The same point is thought to be supported by the fact that, instead of passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], Augustine reads passer singularis [single sparrow]. In Greek this would be στρουθὸς μόνιος [strouthos monios], or στρουθίον μόνιον [strouthion monion]. And the vernacular word moineau for the sparrow will seem to have been formed from μόνιος [monios]. Finally, around Trent there is a bird which the common people call the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow], which wanders alone and usually stays on roofs. Accordingly, like many of the ancients, nearly all the more recent interpreters, Latin, French, Italian, German, Dutch and English, understand the sparrow here. Jerome, however, renders it otherwise: I was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Nor is there any of the Hebrews who points out that the sparrow is meant here, as in the preceding passage. And indeed I think nothing is further from the Prophet's mind. For these words belong entirely to the description of a nocturnal bird. I am surprised that this has not yet occurred to the interpreters, since all the circumstances of the passage openly proclaim it. For whoever speaks in this Psalm, since, worn out by heavy grief, he was fleeing the company of men and pouring out continual groans from the depths of his breast, compares himself with funereal birds, which are both solitary and have something mournful and ominous in their voice. By reason of the voice of my groaning, he says, my bones cleave to my flesh. I am become like a pelican of the wilderness. I was like an owl (or a horned owl) of the desert places. So he speaks in the two verses immediately preceding. Then, continuing the comparison he has begun, he says: I kept watch, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. I kept watch, that is, I spent a sleepless night. Accordingly the Chaldee has there שקדת כל ליליא, I kept watch all night. That is, like the light-shunning nocturnal birds, which, because they hate the light, after hiding by day come out of their hiding places at night to watch for prey. The Philosopher, Hist. book 9, ch. 34: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ νυκτικόρακες, καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ, ὅσα τῆς ἡμέρας ἀδυνατεῖ βλέπειν, τῆς νυκτὸς μὲν θηρεύοντα τὴν τροφὴν αὐτοῖς πορίζεται· [Glaukes de, kai nyktikorakes, kai ta loipa, hosa tēs hēmeras adynatei blepein, tēs nyktos men thēreuonta tēn trophēn autois porizetai] Owls and nycticoraces, and the other birds that cannot see by day, obtain their food by hunting at night. Hence Athenaeus must be corrected, who condenses these words thus, book 8, ch. 12: Γλαῦκες δὲ, καὶ κόρακες ἡμέρας ἀδυνατοῦσι βλέπειν, διὸ νύκτωρ τὴν τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς θηρεύουσιν· [Glaukes de, kai korakes hēmeras adynatousi blepein, dio nyktōr tēn trophēn heautois thēreuousin]; and instead of κόρακες [korakes] one must write νυκτικόρακες [nyktikorakes]. Accordingly all writers attribute almost continual wakefulness to nocturnal birds. And in Aristophanes' Lysistrata a certain woman speaks thus:
Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπὸ τῶν γλαυκῶν γε τάλαιν᾽ ἀπόλλυμαι, Ταῖς ἀγρυπνίαισι κακκαβιζουσῶν ἀεί. [Egō d' hypo tōn glaukōn ge talain' apollymai, Tais agrypniaisi kakkabizousōn aei.]

But I, wretched woman, have perished because of the owls, which were always hooting in the night watches. And Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 29, on the owl: Νύκτωρ μὲν ἀγρυπνεῖ· [Nyktōr men agrypnei] By night it keeps awake. And of the same bird Varro, De ling. Lat. book 4: By night it sings and keeps awake. With this in view, then, the Psalmist says: I have watched, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Some, however, refer this to the sparrow, as though it kept awake for fear, which Suidas has from Theodoret. But you will read nothing of the kind in those who have written on the nature of birds. And those who keep sparrows at home know that they sleep at night, like all birds except the nocturnal ones. Otherwise, since they are awake by day, they would never sleep at all. Moreover, צפור בודד, a solitary bird, is rightly said of the eagle-owl or the owl, because it lives in desert places, as was said in the preceding verse. Hence Damir: وكنية الانثي ام الخراب [wa-kunyat al-unthī umm al-kharāb] And the female (owl) is surnamed mother of desolation. And further on: البوم اصناف وكلها تهب الخلوة بانفسها والتفرد [al-būm aṣnāf wa-kulluhā thb al-khalwa bi-anfusihā wa-l-tafarrud] There are several species of owls, all of which love seclusion and solitude. Therefore, just as the wild ass is called בודד boded, that is, solitary, in Hos 8:9, because it dwells in the wilderness, by the same reasoning the eagle-owl or owl is here rightly called צפור בודד, bird boded, that is, solitary, since it nests in places very far removed from human traffic. Accordingly Pliny, book 29, ch. 4, mocking the magi who prescribe remedies for the hair from the egg of the eagle-owl, says: Who, I ask, could ever have seen an eagle-owl's egg, when to have seen the bird itself is a por- tent? And Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] on الصدي [al-ṣadā], that is, the eagle-owl: طاير يصر بالليل يقفر قفرانا [ṭāyir yaṣirr bi-l-layl yaqfur qafrānan] It is a bird that shrieks at night and lives in desert places. Indeed, to this point belongs the fact that in Arabic it is called صدي tsada, as in Chaldee צדיא tsadja. For צדו tsadu or צדות tsaduth means to the Chaldeans waste, desolation; and the verb צדה tseda means to be laid waste, to be made desolate. In this sense it is used in the Niphal by Zephaniah, ch. 3, v. 6. Thus from the very name which the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs gave the eagle-owl, you may infer that it is a solitary bird, living in desolate places. But the eagle-owl is also called a solitary bird because it is not a gregarious animal but one that wanders alone. Hence the Poet, in book 4 of the Aeneid:
And the eagle-owl alone on the rooftops with funereal song was seen to lament, and to draw out its long notes into weeping.

But why should the sparrow be called solitary, since it is a gregarious bird and nests under the roofs of houses? I admit that within the sparrow kind some are wild. Hence Alexander of Myndus teaches, in Athenaeus book 9, δύο γένη εἶναι τῶν στρουθῶν, τὸ μὲν ἥμερον, τὸ δὲ ἄγριον [dyo genē einai tōn strouthōn, to men hēmeron, to de agrion], that there are two kinds of sparrows, one domestic, the other wild. But wild sparrows do not betake themselves to the roofs of houses, as does the bird of which the Psalmist speaks, whom he describes upon the roof. Therefore, if a sparrow is meant, it cannot be the wild sparrow but only the domestic one. They answer that the domestic sparrow is called solitary because it has been bereaved of its mate. This might be tolerable if the sparrow, like the turtledove or the dove, remained widowed after losing its spouse. But sparrows live by other customs: it is a most lustful animal, so given to Venus that it covers the female, if not a hundred times, as the Arabs report, at least seven times in an hour. Hence the poets yoke it to the chariot of Venus. Bound by no law, then, it rushes into promiscuous love and has no fixed spouse. So, as it was never a husband, neither does it become a widower. That is why the books of the Philosophers say nothing of a solitary sparrow. And those err by the whole breadth of heaven who derive the French name of the sparrow from the Greek μόνιος [monios]. For μόνιος [monios] is an epithet of the boar, not of the sparrow. And to us moineau is something quite different, namely μοναχίσκος [monachiskos], monachulus [little monk]. By this name the male is called, because, like monks, it seems to be hooded. Something else again is the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow] of the people of Trent. For it belongs not to the sparrows but to the blackbird kind, which the Philosopher describes as βαιὸς [baios], dusky, and ἐπὶ τῶν πετρῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων τὰς διατριβὰς ποιῶν [epi tōn petrōn, kai epi tōn keramōn tas diatribas poiōn], living on rocks and roof-tiles. So this is nothing to the point. Now if you ask why the Psalmist describes a nocturnal bird, say the eagle-owl or the owl, upon the roof, the answer is ready. For although eagle-owls and owls nest in desert places, yet at night they are accustomed sometimes to come to towns and cultivated places and to sound their funereal song from the roofs and gables of houses. There is no one who has not heard this at some time. So nothing is more frequent in the poets. Ovid, Metam. book 6, Fable 7:
— — — — and on the roof the unholy eagle-owl brooded, and sat on the gable of the bridal chamber.
The nocturnal eagle-owl sat on the opposite gable.
— — — let the violent screech-owl sing from the roofs.
Propertius, book 4, in the Letter of Arethusa to Lycotas:
Or whether the owl moaned, perched on the neighbouring beam.
And the greatest Poet, book 1 of the Georgics:
— — — — from the highest rooftop the owl plies her late songs in vain.
And in the passage cited a little earlier:
And alone on the rooftops the eagle-owl with funereal song.

But examples of this kind also occur everywhere in the Historians. Lampridius, on the death of the emperor Commodus: An eagle-owl was also caught above his bedchamber, both at Rome and at Lavinium. Above the bedchamber, that is, above the roof of the bedchamber. Dio also, in his Commodus: Ὁ βύας ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔβυξεν [Ho byas ep᾽ autou ebyxen], the eagle-owl hooted upon it (that is, upon the roof of the Capitol). For so some read instead of ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ [ap᾽ autou], from it. And in his Augustus an eagle-owl portended the war of Actium, flying into the temple of Concord, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἐπικαθήμενος [kai epi tous allous epikathēmenos], and perching on the others (that is, on the roofs of other buildings). Finally Ammianus, book 30, on the death of Valentinian: While he was still staying at Sabaria, an eagle-owl perched on the rooftops of the royal bath and hooted funereal notes, etc. We conclude, therefore, that the Psalmist's solitary bird, which keeps watch at night and perches on roofs, is not the sparrow, as they would have it, but the eagle-owl or the owl. The sparrow does indeed nest under the roof, but not על גג, upon the roof, as the Psalmist says.

VI. The sixth passage is Ps 104:16: The trees of God shall be satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted, where צפורים tsipporim make their nests. Trees of God, that is, very lofty trees. So also cedars of God, Ps 80:11; mountains of God, Ps 36:7; flame of God, Song 8:6, that is, a most vehement flame; wrestlings of God, Gen 30:5, that is, most severe wrestlings. Thus trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are put forward as synonyms, since cedars are among the tallest of trees. And the trees of God and cedars of Lebanon are said to be satisfied, namely with rain, of which verse 13 speaks. And God is said to have planted them, like the aloe trees in Num 24:6, because they grow of their own accord, by God's will alone, without human labour and care. It is added that צפורים tsipporim nest in them, that is, sparrows, as many think. For so the LXX: Ἐκεῖ στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσουσι [Ekei strouthia ennosseusousi]. And Symmachus: Ὅπου στρουθία ἐννοσσεύσει [Hopou strouthia ennosseusei]. And the Vulgate translator: There the sparrows shall make their nests. And Apollinaris:
Κεῖσε νεηγενέων πέλεται στρουθῶν ἀλεωρὴ [Keise neēgeneōn peletai strouthōn aleōrē],

There is the refuge of newly hatched sparrows. And both Arabic versions: هناك عششت العصافير [hunāka ʿashshashat al-ʿaṣāfīr] There the sparrows nest. But Aquila, it seems, does better: Ἐκεῖ ὄρνεα νοσσεύσουσιν [Ekei ornea nosseusousin]. And Jerome: There the birds shall make their nests. For the summit of Lebanon, where the cedars are, is inaccessible to sparrows, which, as we have already shown, are not mountain birds.

VII. The seventh passage is Psal. CXXIV, 7: Our soul has escaped כצפור, like a tsippor, from the snare of the fowlers. The Greeks: ὡς στρυθίον [hōs strythion]; the Vulgate: like a sparrow; the Arabic likewise: مثل العصفور [mithl al-ʿuṣfūr] like the sparrow; Apollinaris: στρουθοῦ πανομοίϊος [strouthou panomoiios], entirely like a sparrow; but Jerome: as a bird. This I approve more, because sparrows and similar little birds are caught with birdlime rather than with a snare. This is taught by Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] on the word שפשף, which signifies a pole smeared with birdlime for catching little birds.

VIII. The eighth is Eccles. XII, 4 (var. 6), where the Greeks say of the old man: Καὶ ἀναστήσεται εἰς φωνὴν τοῦ στρουθίου [Kai anastēsetai eis phōnēn tou strouthiou], And he shall rise up at the voice of the sparrow. But Jerome: And he shall rise up at the voice of the bird. And the Chaldee: And you shall be roused from your sleep על עסק קול דעופא, because of the voice of the bird, that is, at the song of a bird, which some take to be the cock, and cockcrow to be meant. Just as the cock, which wakes people with its morning song, is simply called ales [the bird] in these lines of the Poet of the Amores, book 1, Eleg. 6:
And now Lucifer drives forth his frosty axles, and the bird rouses wretched men to their work.

Others prefer to understand the song of the sparrow or of a little bird, by which, however faint, the old man is woken from sleep, while the young sleep so deeply that they do not hear even the crash of thunder. Nor is it easy to decide which version is sounder. For we have amply refuted those who deny that the cock, or any of the larger birds, is signified by the word צפור. It can also be taken of the morning chatter of birds, which in Arabic is called by a most proper word, زقزقة [zaqzaqa] zakzaka. Alcamus: الزقزقة صوت طير عند الصبح [al-zaqzaqa ṣawt ṭayr ʿinda al-ṣubḥ] the chatter of birds about dawn.

IX. The ninth passage reads thus, Thren. III, 32: My enemies hunt me כצפור, like a tsippor, deservedly [sic]. Here the Greeks: ὡς στρουθίον [hōs strouthion]; but Jerome: like a bird. This I would rather take of the larger birds, on the catching of which effort is more willingly spent, and with greater profit.

In Tobit the Latin copy disagrees with the Greek on this word, Tob 2:9 (var. 11.). For in the Greek Tobit says, Καὶ οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι στρουθία ἐν τῷ τοίχῳ ἐστί· καὶ, τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν μου ἀνεωγότων, ἀφώδευσαν τὰ στρουθία θερμὸν εἰς τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου [Kai ouk ēdein hoti strouthia en tō toichō esti; kai, tōn ophthalmōn mou aneōgotōn, aphōdeusan ta strouthia thermon eis tous ophthalmous mou]; And I did not know that there were sparrows in the wall; and, my eyes being open, the sparrows voided warm dung into my eyes. But the Latin relates that it happened one day that, when Tobit had fallen asleep beside a wall, warm dung fell upon him as he slept from a swallows' nest. I do not see how these can be reconciled otherwise than by saying that στρουθία [strouthia] in the Greek there are not sparrows but little birds, just as Moschopulus and Phavorinus asserted above that every kind of little bird is called στρουθία [strouthia] in Greek. Or else that by the name of sparrows swallows are meant, after the manner of the Arabs, who call the swallow عصفور الجنة [ʿuṣfūr al-janna] the sparrow of Paradise. Similar is the case of Prov 26:2, where some render the Hebrew דרור deror as swallow, but the Greek interpreters as στρουθοὺς [strouthous], sparrows.
On the providence of God concerning sparrows and little birds, in Matt 10:29 and Luke 12:6.

Christ, in Matt 10:29, says that two sparrows are sold for an assarion, and yet not one of them falls to the ground without God. And in Luke 12:6 he says that five sparrows are sold for two assaria, and yet not one of them is forgotten before God. Thus individual sparrows were sold for half an as, or a little less. For those are mistaken who hold that the assarion is half an as. Rather, the assarion is the same as the as. The Latin-Greek Glosses: Asse, Ἀσσάριον [assarion]; read Ἀσσαρίου [assariou]. And elsewhere: Sesquas, Ἓι ἥμισυ ἀσσάριον [hei hēmisy assarion]. Read Ἓν ἥμισυ καὶ ἀσσάριον [hen hēmisy kai assarion]. The Greek-Latin Glosses of Philoxenus: Ἀσσάριον [assarion], Hic as.; Ἀσσαρίου ἥμισυ [assariou hēmisy], Sesquas; read Ἓν ἀσσάριον καὶ ἥμισυ [hen assarion kai hēmisy]. The as, by Budé's reckoning, was worth four of our little deniers and a trifle more. The Syriac translator has ܐܣܪ [אסר] assar, a word which the Hebrews also often use for the assarion. David Cohen de Lara, in his book De convenientia Rabbinismi cum Graeco, defines אסר assar in Spanish as moneda de tres maravedis, which comes very close to Budé's λογισμὸν [logismon]. In Maimonides' [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] treatise On Shekels, ch. 1. 3.: הסלע ארבעה דינרין והדינר שש מעין ומעה היא היקראת בימי משה רבינו גרה ומאה היא שני פונדיונין ופונדיון שני אסרין ופרוטה אחת משמונה באסר נמצא משקל המעה והיא הגרה שש עשרה שעורות ומשקל האסר ארבע שעורות ומשקל פרוטה חצי שעורה, The shekel is worth four denarii. The denarius six obols. The obol was called a gerah in the days of Moses our master. The obol is worth two pondia, and the pondion two assaria. And the perutah is the eighth part of an assarion. The weight of the obol, which is called a gerah, is sixteen barley grains. The weight of the assarion four grains, of the perutah half a grain. Drusius cites a similar passage from the Book of Commandments. For assarion the Arabic translator has فلس [fals] follis, and for two assaria فلسين [falsayn] two folles; and Jerome has dipondium. But in Matt 5:26 the same Arabic version has follis for quadrans. And in Mark 14:42 فلسين [falsayn] two folles stands for two mites, that is, two פרוטות perutoth, which together make one quadrans. It is evident, therefore, that this translator, caring little about the true value of the coins, was content to put one cheap coin for another cheap coin, though of different value. And indeed, to be sold for an assarion or an as means nothing other than to be sold off at a low price. For whatever is sold or valued at an as must be cheap. Hence Catullus to his Lesbia:
And the gossip of stern old men, let us value it all at a single as.
Son, you cannot sell it for an as.
You think it not worth an as? O filth, O brothel!

And Cicero, for Quinctius: He says he will not pay an as unless he has first settled all the affairs and accounts of the partnership. And for Roscius the Comedian: Say he gave LLS. CCCIↃↃↃ, he who gave not a single as. And Juvenal, Satire 10:
Whoever still worships Minerva, acquired for a single as.

And the Mishnah at the end of the tractate Chullin, concerning the precept by which the Israelites are commanded to let the mother go when they take eggs and young from a nest, that it may be well with them and their days be prolonged, Deut 22:6–7.: אם מצוה קלה שהיא באסר אמרה תורה למען ייטב לך והארכת ימים קל וחומר על מצות חמורות שבתורה, If concerning a lighter precept, about a thing that is scarcely worth an assarion, the Law says, “That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days,” how much more (is the same to be hoped) for the weightier precepts that are in the Law? For assarion the older Greeks would have said obol. Thus in the Birds of Aristophanes the birds complain bitterly of a certain Philocrates, who,
— συνείρων τοὺς σπίνους, πωλεῖ καθ᾽ ἑπτὰ ὀβολοῦ, [syneirōn tous spinous, pōlei kath᾽ hepta obolou,]

Tying finches together, he sells seven for one obol. For an obol, that is, for two assaria, or asses. This is shown by these words of Polybius, Histories book 2: Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἐπιτοπολὺ παρίενται τοὺς καταλύτας οἱ πανδοχεῖς ἡμιασσαρίου, τοῦτο δ᾽ ἐστὶ τέταρτον μέρος ὀβολοῦ [Hōs men oun epitopoly parieнтai tous katalytas hoi pandocheis hēmiassariou, touto d᾽ esti tetarton meros obolou]. Innkeepers generally receive their guests for half an as, or half an assarion, which is a quarter of an obol. So when Christ says that five sparrows are sold for two assaria, it is the same as if he had said they are sold for an obol. From this you may infer that at Athens in the time of Aristophanes provisions were somewhat cheaper than in Judaea in the time of Christ. For at the price for which the Athenians bought seven finches, the Jews bought only five sparrows. Further, the Latin translator of Aristophanes has passeres [sparrows] for fringilli [finches], because the sparrow and the finch are very similar birds. Hence the Glosses of Philoxenus: Σπίνος· ὁ στρουθὸς [Spinos; ho strouthos], Frincillus, fringillus, as if σπίνος [spinos] were the same as στρουθὸς [strouthos], or passer [sparrow]. Fringillus is in French pinson, formerly perhaps pintion, like σπίνθιον [spinthion] in Hesychius. So too chanson from cantione, maison from mansione, raison from ratione, etc. But whether five or seven such little birds are sold for an obol, and whether the author of the Mishnah valued the mother alone, or the mother with her young, at an as, they must be very cheap animals, since they are on sale for so slight a price. Yet here Christ teaches us that even these little creatures are such a concern to God that none of them falls to the ground without him, that is, perishes without his permission. With this agrees Luke: Ἓν ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπιλελησμένον ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ [Hen ex autōn ouk estin epilelēsmenon enōpion tou Theou]; Not one of them is forgotten before God. The phrase is taken from Ps 9:19, where it is said of the poor man: Οὐκ εἰς τέλος ἐπιλησθήσεται [Ouk eis telos epilēsthēsetai], He shall not be forgotten for ever; in Hebrew לא לנצח ישכח. Hence the royal Psalmist, of small and great animals alike, Ps 104:27: These all wait upon you, that you may give them their food in due season. Yet, to say nothing for the present of the Jews, most of whom hold a different opinion, Jerome on Habakkuk ch. 1 says this: It is absurd to lower the majesty of God to this, that he should know at every moment how many gnats are born and how many die; how great is the multitude of bugs, fleas and flies on the earth; how many fish swim in the water; and which of the smaller must fall prey to the larger. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we drag his power down to the lowest things, we do injury to ourselves, saying that the providence over rational and irrational creatures is the same. These words might seem rather harsh unless softened by a kindly interpretation, so that we understand them to be said comparatively (as he hints toward the end): lest God be thought to have the same regard for brutes as for men, whom he created in his own image, since he preserves the brutes chiefly for the sake of men, for whose use they were created. We therefore recognize different degrees of divine providence, and that God does not care for oxen in the same way as for men, as Paul teaches, 1 Cor 9:9. Yet it is certain that oxen as well as men, and even the meanest creatures, are subject to God. Nor does he disdain to govern and preserve what he deigned to create. And we must beware of inventing limits to that providence, which, as the greatest things do not burden it, so the smallest do not escape it or go neglected by it. Who would believe that God did not know the number of the quails with which he fed the Israelites in the desert, or of the fish that swam in the lake of Gennesaret when Peter cast his nets at Christ's command? Or that he did not know how many frogs or lice he would use against the Egyptians; or that those locusts which are called God's army, Joel 2:11, were of no concern to him, and that this supreme commander did not know how many soldiers he had enlisted in his army? Finally, what could be plainer than Christ's words, that none of the sparrows falls to the ground without God, or is forgotten before him? On this passage note what the most learned Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum] cites from the Jerusalem Talmud in his Lexicon Talmudicum, p. 553: Rabbi Simeon ben Yochai was hiding in a cave. One day, sitting at the mouth of the cave and seeing a fowler catching birds and spreading his net, he heard a daughter of the voice (an oracle); when it said דימוס dimos (that is, release), the bird escaped. But when the daughter of the voice said ספיקולא, spicula (that is, sentence of death), the bird was caught. Then the oracle said, צפור מבלברי שמיא לא יבדא כל שכן בר נשא, A little bird does not perish without heaven (that is, without God's will and providence): how much less a man! For לא יבדא read לא יאבד. The pagans too write things not unlike these. Thus Plutarch somewhere proves from Homer that the ancients held the opinion that by the divine power are cared for οὐ μόνον βόας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ζῶα [ou monon boas, alla kai panta ta alla zōa], not only oxen, but all other animals too. And Aelian, Hist. book 11, ch. 31: Ἴδιον δὲ ἄρα τῶν ζώων καὶ ἐκεῖνο ἀγαθὸν, πρόνοιαν αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ Θεοὶ ποιοῦνται, καὶ οὔτε αὐτῶν καταφρονοῦσιν, οὐδὲ μὴν ὀλιγώρως ἔχουσιν [Idion de ara tōn zōōn kai ekeino agathon, pronoian autōn kai hoi Theoi poiountai, kai oute autōn kataphronousin, oude mēn oligōrōs echousin]; The brutes too have this good, that the gods provide for them, and neither despise them nor treat them with indifference.
ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE PART TWO BOOK TWO ON ON THE UNCLEAN BIRDS.
The eagle, king of the birds; its name, beak, talons, plumage, baldness, renewal, colour.

In this book we shall set out the unclean birds in the same order as Moses in Lev 11:13 and Deut 14:2. First of all is the eagle. To this pertains what Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] has here: פתח בנשר שהוא מלך בעופות, He began with the eagle, because it is king of the birds. That is, in the list of those birds whose eating God forbade the Jews, he holds that the eagle rightly leads the line, since the consensus of nations has given it kingship over the other birds because of the outstanding gifts by which it surpasses them. As to the Greeks the matter is plain. For Pindar, Olymp. 13, calls the eagle
king of the birds. And Pyth. 1:
Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν [Dios aieton, archon oiōnōn],
the eagle of Jupiter, leader of the birds. And Isthm. 6:
— — — ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν μέγαν αἰετὸν [archon oiōnōn megan aieton],
the prince of the birds, the great eagle. And the oracle about the Athenians in the Knights of Aristophanes, Act 3:
Αἰετὸς ὡς γίνει, καὶ πάσης γῆς βασιλεύσεις [Aietos hōs ginei, kai pasēs gēs basileuseis],
Be like an eagle, and you will rule the whole world. Nicander too, where he speaks of the fight of the eagle and the serpent, Theriaca, line 448:
Τῷ μέν τ᾽ ἔκπαγλον κοτέων βασιλήϊος ὄρνις Αἰετὸς, — — — — — — [Tō men t᾽ ekpaglon koteōn basilēios ornis Aietos]

But against him the royal bird, the eagle, raging in monstrous fashion. And Boeus, in book 1 of the Ornithogonia, on Periphas, changed by Jupiter into an eagle: Ποιεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὄρνισι βασιλέα [Poiei gar auton en pasi tois ornisi basilea]. For he makes him king among all the birds. And Dionysius in the Bassarica, cited by Stephanus under Κάσπειρος [Kaspeiros]:
Αἰετὸς εἰν ὄρνισι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένοισιν [Aietos ein ornisi metaprepei agromenoisin],
The eagle excels among the wild birds. And Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 3, line 353:
The eagle, most excellent of birds. And Oppian, Halieutica, book 2, line 539:
Ὅσσον γὰρ κέφοισι μετ᾽ οἰωνοῖσιν ἄνακτες Αἰετοί. — — — — — — [Hosson gar kephoisi met᾽ oiōnoisin anaktes Aietoi]

As much as among the light birds the eagles, their kings (excel). And Aelian, Hist. book 9, ch. 2: Τὸν ἀετὸν, τὸν τῶν ὀρνίθων βασιλέα, οὐ μόνον παρόντα, καὶ ζῶντα δέδοικε τὰ ὄρνεα [Ton aeton, ton tōn ornithōn basilea, ou monon paronta, kai zōnta dedoike ta ornea]; The birds fear the eagle, king of the birds, not only when it is alive and present. Finally Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] calls it πτηνοκράτορα [ptēnokratora], that is, prince of the birds. And Tzetzes, Chiliad. 5, Hist. 9, denies that either eagles or lions touch carrion, since they are kings, the former of birds, the latter of wild beasts. And among the Roman writers, Horace, book 4, Ode 4:
Like the winged minister of the thunderbolt, to whom the king of the gods granted kingship over the wandering birds, etc.
Tell me whom you carry, queen of the birds.
Apuleius, The Ass, book 6: that royal bird of supreme Jupiter. Claudian, Preface to the Third Consulship of Honorius:
— — both mighty over the birds and heir of the thunderbolt.

That the Egyptians too held the same view is shown by these words of Diodorus in book 1: Τὸν δ᾽ ἀετὸν Θηβαῖοι τιμῶσι, διὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν εἶναι δοκεῖν τοῦτο ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἄξιον [Ton d᾽ aeton Thēbaioi timōsi, dia to basilikon einai dokein touto zōon, kai tou Dios axion]· The Thebans worship the eagle, because they think this animal is royal and worthy of Jupiter. From there the cult of the eagle had also spread to the Arabs. The Talmudists, in the treatise On Idolatry, ch. 1, fol. 11b: בתי ע״ז קבועין אלו הן בית בל בבבל בית נבו בכורסי תרעתא שבמפג צריפא שבאשקלון נשרא שבערביא, These are the fixed idolatrous temples: the temple of Bel at Babylon, the temple of Nebo at Borsippa, Atergatis at Hierapolis, Venus Urania at Ascalon, and the Eagle in Arabia. Those temples are called fixed whose idols are worshipped on every day of the year, as the Gloss explains. Thus Bel was worshipped at Babylon and Nebo at Borsippa (for instead of בכורסי read בבורסיף). And at Hierapolis Derceto, or Atergatis, whose worship at Hierapolis Lucian describes at length in his book On the Syrian Goddess. Derceto, or Atergatis, is in Hebrew תרעתא Tirgata. And Hierapolis is ממבג Mambeg, as in Arabic منبج [Manbij] Manbeg. In Pliny too the text once read Bambyca and Mambeg, which was altered into Magog. Accordingly in the Talmud one should read שבממבג instead of שבמפג. Further, we know from Herodotus that Venus Urania was held in the highest worship at Ascalon. Hence she seems to be the צריפא שבאשקלון, Tseripha, which is at Ascalon. Why she is called צריפא Tseripha, however, is not quite clear. Unless you think she was named from casting [metal]; for among the Hebrews צרף tsaraph means to cast. Hence the Talmudists' בית נצרפי, house of molten images, that is, a temple of idols. Or from lust, over which she presides. For in Arabic صرف [ṣarafa] tsarapha means to burn with lust, and صارفة [ṣārifa] tsaripha is said of a female dog when she is in heat and burns with lust for the male. It remains for us to speak of the eagle of the Arabs. It was the idol of the Dulkelaites among the Homerites, a very well-known people of Arabia Felix. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: النسر الصنم كان لذي الكلا بارض حمير [al-nasr al-ṣanam kāna li-Dhī al-Kalāʿ bi-arḍ Ḥimyar] The Eagle was the idol of Dulkela in the land of Humeir, that is, of the Homerites. Evidently among the Arabs too this opinion had prevailed, that the eagle is the chief of the birds. So Muaphius, in the book entitled نفحات الازهار [Nafaḥāt al-azhār] Fragrances of Flowers, attributes this to the impure Muhammad: هبط علي جبرييل فقال يا محمد ان لكل شي سيد فسيد البشر ادم وسيد ولد ادم انت وسيد الروم صحيب وسيد فارس سليمان وسيد الحبش بلال وسيد الشجر السدر وسيد الطير النسر [habaṭa ʿalayya Jabrīl fa-qāla yā Muḥammad inna li-kull shayʾ sayyid fa-sayyid al-bashar Ādam wa-sayyid walad Ādam anta wa-sayyid al-Rūm Ṣuhayb wa-sayyid Fāris Salmān wa-sayyid al-Ḥabash Bilāl wa-sayyid al-shajar al-sidr wa-sayyid al-ṭayr al-nasr] Gabriel came down to me and said: O Muhammad, every thing has its lord. The lord of men was Adam; but you are the lord of the sons of Adam. And the lord of the Greeks is Sahib, and of the Persians Soliman, and of the Abyssinians Bilal. And of trees the connarus, a species of lotus, and of birds the eagle, etc. Now, if one wishes to hear the Hebrews: Josephus, On the Jewish War, book 3, chapter 5, writes that the Romans had the eagle as the standard in the first cohort of the legion because the ἀετὸς [aetos] is βασιλεύς τε οἰωνῶν ἁπάντων, καὶ ἀλκιμώτατος [basileus te oiōnōn hapantōn, kai alkimōtatos], king of all birds, and the strongest. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] on Ezek 17:3: הנשר הוא משל לנבוכדנצר מלך בבל כי הנשר מלך העופות וכן נבוכדנצר היה מלך על כל מלכי הארץ, The eagle there is a figure of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because, as the eagle is king of the birds, so Nebuchadnezzar was king over all the kings of the earth. Hence in the Masal Kadmoni the thirty-eighth Fable bears this title:
צורת הנשר על מושבו : וסנהדרי׳ העוף יושבים סביבו :

The figure of the eagle upon its throne, and the council of birds sitting around it. That is, in the council of the birds the eagle is depicted, distinguished by a crown and raised high on a throne, and the other birds stand by it. And of the eagle Baal Hatturim says, right at the beginning of this chapter, הוא מלך העופות, It holds kingship over the birds. Finally, the Fathers define the very same thing. Thus Ambrose, Hexaëm. book 5, ch. 18, calls the eagle a royal bird and attributes to it royal eminence. Jerome on Mich. 1: The eagle, which is queen of the birds. And on Dan. VII.: As the lion holds kingship among the beasts, so the eagle among the birds. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 6: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· [Esti gar ho aetos basileus tōn orneōn] For the eagle is king of the birds, or queen, if you prefer. Theodoret, in the Preface to the Song, on the passage Ezek 17:3: Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· [Aeton men ton basilea (enoēsen), epeidan kai to zōon basilikon] By the name of eagle he meant the king, because it is a royal animal. Theodore of Heraclea on Psal. CII.: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασιλεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· [Epeidē ho aetos dokei basileuein tōn peteinōn hapantōn] Because the eagle seems to rule over all the birds. And a little later: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται, [Dia gar tou ornithos tou aetou tēn basileian ainittetai] For by the eagle he signifies the kingdom. What of the fact that it was commonly believed that the eagle is at war with the wren because the latter καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς [kaleitai presbys, kai basileus], is called senator and king, as though it begrudged it this name? So the Philosopher attests, Hist. book 9, ch. 11. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 74: The eagle and the wren are at odds, if we believe it, because the latter is called king of the birds.

Whence the eagle, in Hebrew נשר neser, gets its name has so far escaped the masters. For absurd is the fancy of Rabbi Bechai on Gen. II. that it derives from the Chaldee נשר nesar, which means to fall down, because, after it has risen in flight to the element of fire, as they indeed would have it, it then falls headlong into the sea. Nor do I agree with those who assert that it is named from the shedding of its feathers, because נשר among the Rabbis means to fall off; or from sight, because נשר neser seems to allude to the verb שור sur, which means to see. Rather, I most approve of the Arabs, for whom نسر [nasara] nasara means to pluck with the beak, and منسر [minsar] minsar means beak, and properly that of a bird of prey. From this, then, they hold that the eagle is called نسر [nasr] nesr, لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه [li-annahu yansiru al-shay wa-yaqtaliʿuhu] because it tears and plucks a thing with its beak. So Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and Alcamus. Other birds of prey also pluck with the beak; yet this is ascribed by special right to the prince of the birds of prey, the eagle, because its beak is more hooked and it tears more forcefully with it. Likewise, swooping upon prey is common to all, which in Hebrew is העיט. Hence עיט ajit is in general a bird of prey. Yet usage among the Greeks made ἀετόν [aeton] or αἰετόν [aieton], derived from it, the proper name of the eagle .

The eagle is remarkable not only for its beak but also for its talons, which it has not straight, like a man, but curved and hooked like a lion's. For of the animals that have claws, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς [ta men eisin euthyonycha, hōsper anthrōpos; ta de gampsōnycha, hōsper kai tōn pezōn leōn, kai tōn ptēnōn aietos], some have straight claws, like man; others hooked, like the lion among land animals and the eagle among birds. So the Philosopher, Hist. book 3, ch. 9. In birds, that is, the talons imitate the shape of the beak. Suidas: Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γένυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· [Gampsōnycha hosa tōn zōōn tēn epirynchida gegampsōken hypo tēn genyn, hoia estin aetos] Those animals have hooked claws which have a beak curved beneath the jaws, to which kind the eagle belongs. The Grammarians are uncertain to which of the two it refers that the eagle which the sleepless Penelope saw is called

For to some ἀγκυλοχείλης [ankylocheilēs] is ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος [ho echōn ankyla cheilē, ētoi to rhamphos], one that has curved lips, that is, a curved beak; to others ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων [epikampeis tas chēlas echōn], one that has bent talons. In this sense, in Aristophanes' Knights, Cleon is called
because like an eagle he had hooked or rapacious claws, as not only the Scholiast but also Aristophanes himself explains. And in Plautus' Pseudolus the cook says,
Do you expect to find any cook who has not a kite's or an eagle's talons?

But many of the ancients also believed that in Ezek 17:3 7. the eagle is called מלא הנוצה and רב הנוצה on account of its talons. For this is rendered by the Greeks ὁ ἀετὸς πλήρης ὀνύχων [ho aetos plērēs onychōn], the eagle full of talons, and πολὺς ὄνυξι [polys onyxi], great in talons, or having many talons. The Arabic follows the same. Nor does the Syriac differ much in verse 3, ܡܠܝܢ ܛܦܪ̈ܘܗܝ [מלין טפרוהי], its talons are full, and in verse 7, ܣܓܝܐܢ ܛܦܪܘܗܝ [סגיאן טפרוהי] its talons are many. For them, that is, נוצה is talon. But the Chaldee, Jerome and all the Hebrews more correctly explain it as feather or plumage. Indeed the Greeks themselves in Lev 1:16 have σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς [syn tois pterois] for בנצתא, and Theodotion σὺν τοῖς πτίλοις [syn tois ptilois]. For נצה means to fly, whence נצו they flew, or flew away, Lam 4:15, and נוצה feather or plumage, which lifts birds up to flight. This suits this passage better. For I, at least, cannot understand what an eagle full of talons, or with many talons, would be, since all eagles have the same number of talons. But an eagle is rightly said to be full of feathers, or to have many feathers, in contrast to the bald one , of which Mic 1:16 speaks: Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle. For at the onset of spring birds of prey are subject to the shedding of their feathers. This we call muer, that is, to change feathers. For so those speak who write on this subject. And this is precisely μουτεύειν [mouteuein] among the Greeks of a later age. Demetrius, Orneosophion, book 2, chapter 53: Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνῃ εἰς τὸ μουτεῦσαι [Ean de bradynē eis to mouteusai]. Though proper words are not lacking, such as μαδίζεσθαι [madizesthai], πτεροῤῥυῆσαι [pterorrhyēsai], and ἀποβάλλειν τὰ πτερὰ [apoballein ta ptera], which the same writer uses. In Arabic you would say كرز [kariza] curiza. Alcamus: كرز البازي سقط ريشه [kariza al-bāzī saqaṭa rīshuhu] curiza albazi, that is, of the hawk, its plumage fell out. Whence كرز [kurraz] corraz, a hawk, or any bird of prey whose feathers are falling out. Thus in Micah the baldness of the eagle is the time when most of its feathers have dropped out. For although baldness is properly attributed to man, birds too are called bald. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: Some animals are naturally bald, such as ostriches and water ravens, which among the Greeks take their name from this, that is, οἱ φαλακροκόρακες [hoi phalakrokorakes]. Thus both the Greeks and the Hebrews attribute baldness to birds, differing only in this, that whereas among the Greeks the baldness of birds concerns the head alone, the Hebrews extend it to the whole body; and they call a bird bald which is smooth and stripped of feathers .

But when others have gradually grown in place of the feathers that fell out, then at last the eagle (in Hebrew נשר) is called מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, teeming with plumage. And Scripture indicates in more than one place that feathers grow again in eagles. So in the famous passage of David, Psal. CIII, 5. תתחדש כנשר נעוריכי, You will renew your youth like the eagle. I prefer to render it so with the Chaldee rather than with others, Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's, because the verb תתחדש, of the third person, since it is singular and feminine, agrees neither in gender nor in number with נעוריכי, which is plural and masculine. However that may be, youth is renewed in the eagle in no other way than when new feathers succeed the old, just as a serpent is said to shed its old age when it lays aside its old skin. Hence the Greeks call the slough of a serpent γήρας [gēras], the Romans senium [old age] and senectus [old age]. Thus the words of the Psalmist have the same sense as these of Isaiah, chapter 40, verse 31: Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength. They shall mount up (grow) feathers like eagles. Where the Seventy elegantly have Πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί [Pterophyēsousin hōs aetoi]. But by a strange metamorphosis the Syriac has transformed the eagles into doves in this version of his, ܢܦܩܘܢ ܓܦܐ ܐܝܟ ܕܝܘܢܐ [נפקון גפא איך דיונא], They will put forth wings like those of doves. And by no smaller error eagles have been made lions in these words of Theodotion about king Nebuchadnezzar, Dan 4:30 var. 33. Αἱ τρίχες αὐτοῦ ὡς λεόντων ἐμεγαλύνθησαν [Hai triches autou hōs leontōn emegalynthēsan]. His hairs grew like those of lions. For in the original it is כנשרין, like those of eagles. But this is an error of the scribes, not of the translator. For no doubt the translator had written ἀετῶν [aetōn], which ignorant scribes changed to λεόντων [leontōn] because αἱ τρίχες [hai triches], that is hairs, did not seem able to fit eagles. So they substituted for eagles the name of a hairy animal, but from a pointless scruple. For in the Prophet's words an analogous word could be supplied: His hairs grew like those of eagles, supply feathers, which are in birds what hairs are in men. Moreover, hairs and locks are sometimes attributed even to birds. By this catachresis Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, says of the hen that sees a hawk gaping after her chicks,
bristled with its hair. And Matron, in the Parodies quoted by Athenaeus in book 14, describes hens served at a banquet,
Ἄτριχας, οἰετέας, λαγάνοις κατὰ νῶτον ἐΐσας, [Atrichas, oieteas, laganois kata nōton eïsas,]

Hairless, equal in age, like flat cakes on the back. Hairless, that is, featherless. Nor is there any need to restore ὄτριχας [otrichas] with Casaubon, because that is the reading in the verse of Homer to which he alludes, Iliad 2, line 765. For the parody [παρῳδία, parōdia] consists precisely in this, that a similar word, not the same one, is substituted. Many examples make this plain. So, just as the feathers of hens are called hairs, so too are those of eagles. Hence Tertullian, near the end of his book On Penitence, speaking of King Nebuchadnezzar: his hair, through neglect, displaying an eagle-like shagginess. For this Pamelius substituted leoninum [lion-like], as if an eagle could not be said to bristle with hair. This is refuted by what we have already shown, that the feathers of birds too are reckoned under the name of hairs. And indeed, since Micah (ch. 1, v. 16) says that eagles grow bald, why could not the Prophet Daniel have attributed hairs to them? Certainly the same catachresis [κατάχρησις, katachrēsis] occurs in both places. For baldness is properly the falling out of the hair of the head. Meanwhile the corruption of the passage of Daniel is not recent, since besides the Arabic translator it is followed by Theodoret on Daniel, by the author of the Questions attributed to Justin, Question 44, and by those who wrote the Lives of the Prophets under the names of Epiphanius and Dorotheus, who, though spurious and pseudonymous [ψευδώνυμοι, pseudōnymoi] writers, are nevertheless fairly ancient. Now, if you compare these three passages, first that of the Psalmist, you will renew your youth like the eagle; second that of Isaiah, For those who hope in the Lord their strength will be restored, their wings will grow again like eagles'; third that of Daniel, His hairs grew like those of eagles : you will see that all of them concern the feathers of eagles, which are restored after moulting [ψίλωσιν, psilōsin]. Hence the eagle comes to seem more vigorous, and so even younger. Nor would it be absurd to join to these the passage of Job about the hawk, chapter 39, verse 26: Is it by your understanding that יאבר נץ, the hawk grows its feathers, spreading its wings toward the south? That is, so that during that moulting [ψιλώσει, psilōsei] it may be revived by the gentle warmth of the sun, and new feathers may more easily grow back in place of those it has lost.

Because many ancient writers did not pay sufficient attention to these points, they invented a great deal about the ἀνακαίνωσις [anakainōsis] and ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of eagles, which it is tedious to report here . Well known is the fiction of Saadia, cited by Kimchi on Psal. CIII. and Es. XL.: הנשר יעוף על כל העופות ויעלה מאד על פני רקיע השמים ויקרוב לחום האש היסודי ויפול עצמו בים מרוב חום ויתחדש ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו כן כל עשר עד מאה וכשיגיע למאה יעלה כמנהגו ויפול בים וימות שם, The eagle flies higher than any of the birds and is carried far up towards the firmament, until it comes near the elemental fire. Then, burning with the heat, it throws itself headlong into the sea, and is renewed; its feathers grow again, and it returns to the days of its youth. And this happens every ten years up to the hundredth year; when it has reached that, it is carried upward as usual, falls headlong into the sea, and dies there. Similar is what we read in Porta coeli fol. 22, col. 2: ויש אומרים כי הנשר טבעו לעלות קרוב לגבול האש ומתלהב בסוף עשר שנים לעשר שנים ומרוב חמומו מפיל עצמו בים לקרר חומו ושם ימרט נוצתו ויתחדש נוצה אחרת ויתחדש כחו עד ק׳ שנה שיעלה שם ויפול בים ויטבע, There are some who say that it is natural to the eagle to ascend close to the boundary of fire and to be set ablaze every ten years, and, burning with the heat, to cast itself into the sea to cool that heat; and that there its feathers fall out and others grow in their place, and its strength is restored, up to the hundredth year, when, carried up to the same place, it falls headlong and is drowned in the sea. Others say it is plunged not into the sea but into a spring, and, washed in it, grows young again. Damir, on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, that is, περὶ τοῦ μελαναιέτου [peri tou melanaietou] [on the black eagle], which is a kind of eagle especially common in Arabia Felix: متي ثقلت عن النهوض او عميت حملتها الفراخ ونقلتها من مكان الي مكان تلتمس لها عينا صافيتا بارض الهند علي راس جبل فيتغمسها فيها ثم تضعها في شعاع الشمس فيذهب ريشها وينبت لها ريش جديد ويذهب ظلمة بصرها ثم تعوص في تلك العين [matā thaqulat ʿan al-nuhūḍ aw ʿamiyat ḥamalathā al-firākh wa-naqalathā min makān ilā makān taltamisu lahā ʿaynan ṣāfiyatan bi-arḍ al-Hind ʿalā raʾs jabal fa-yataghammasuhā fīhā thumma taḍaʿuhā fī shuʿāʿ al-shams fa-yadhhabu rīshuhā wa-yanbutu lahā rīsh jadīd wa-yadhhabu ẓulmat baṣarihā thumma taʿūṣu fī tilka al-ʿayn] فاذا هي قد عادت شابة [fa-idhā hiya qad ʿādat shābba] And when it becomes slow in flight and goes blind, its chicks carry it and move it from place to place, and in India they seek for it a pure spring on the summit of a mountain; they plunge it into this and set it facing the rays of the sun. Then its feathers fall out and new ones grow for it, and the dimness of its eyes is dispelled; and it is plunged again into the same spring, when its grey age has returned. The author of the Letter to Praesidius, which is attributed to Jerome: When the eagle has grown old, its feathers and eyes become heavy; it seeks a spring, raises its feathers, and gathers heat into itself, and so its eyes are healed; and it plunges itself three times into the spring, and thus returns to youth. Eustathius, on the Hexaëmeron, p. 27: Φασὶ γηράσαντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ εἰς πηγὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα ἀνιπτάμενον, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τὰς πτέρυγας καταφλέγεσθαι, καὶ ἀναβλέπειν· εἶθ᾽ εὐθὺς ἐπὶ τὴν πηγὴν καταβάντα τρίτον βαπτίζεσθαι, καὶ ἀνανεοῦσθαι. Διὸ καὶ τὸν Ψαλμὸν φάσκειν φησὶν, Ἀνακαινισθήσεται ὡς ἀετοῦ ἡ νεότης σου. [Phasi gērasanta ton aeton amaurousthai tas opseis, kai bareisthai autou tas pterygas, kai eis pēgēn aphikneisthai, kai eis ton aithera aniptamenon, hypo tou hēliou tas pterygas kataphlegesthai, kai anablepein; eith᾽ euthys epi tēn pēgēn katabanta triton baptizesthai, kai ananeousthai. Dio kai ton Psalmon phaskein phēsin, Anakainisthēsetai hōs aetou hē neotēs sou.] They say that the eagle, worn out by old age, has the sharpness of its eyes dulled and its wings grow heavy, and it makes for a spring; and while it is carried up in flight into the air, its wings are scorched by the sun and it recovers its sight; then, when it comes down into the spring, it is plunged into it three times and renewed. And therefore the Psalm said, „Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's“. An Anonymous writer on the Psalms: Ὁ ἀετὸς κατὰ φ´ ἔτη ἀνακαινίζεται. καιόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται. [Ho aetos kata ph´ etē anakainizetai. kaiomenos hypo tou hēliou, kai katadyomenos eis pēgēn hydatos, palin neos heurisketai.] The eagle is renewed every five hundredth year. Scorched by the sun and plunged into a spring of water, it is found young again. Some write ϱ´ [r´], that is, hundredth, instead of φ´ [ph´], that is, five hundredth, so that this writer may agree with Epiphanius, whose words are: Ἀετὸς δὲ καλεῖται διὰ τὴν πολυετίαν αὐτοῦ. οὗτος μὲν ζῇ ἔτη ἑκατὸν, καὶ γηράσαντος γρυποῦται ὁ προμυκτὴρ, καὶ ἀμβλυώττουσιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ μὴ ὁρᾷν, καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύει φαγεῖν. ἀνέρχεται δὲ εἰς ὕψος λίαν, καὶ ῥίπτει ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ ἀκροτόμου πέτρας, προσκρούσας αὐτῇ τὸ ῥάμφος, καὶ λούεται ἐπὶ τὴν ψυγρὰν λίμνην, καὶ κάθηται κατὰ τὸ ἡλιακὸν θερμὸν, πίπτουσι δὲ λεπίδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ πάλιν εἰς νέους τελεῖν ἄρχεται. [Aetos de kaleitai dia tēn polyetian autou. houtos men zē etē hekaton, kai gērasantos gryproutai ho promyktēr, kai amblyōttousin hoi ophthalmoi autou, tou mē horan, kai ouk ischyei phagein. anerchetai de eis hypsos lian, kai rhiptei heauton epi akrotomou petras, proskrousas autē to rhamphos, kai louetai epi tēn psygran limnēn, kai kathētai kata to hēliakon thermon, piptousi de lepides apo tōn ophthalmōn, kai palin eis neous telein archetai.] The eagle is called ἀετὸς [aetos] on account of its long life. For it lives a hundred years. But when it grows old, its beak becomes hooked and its eyes grow dim, so that it can neither see nor eat. So it rises on high and hurls itself against a sheer rock, against which it strikes its beak; and it washes itself in a cold lake and sits in the heat of the sun; and scales fall from its eyes, and it grows young again. Augustine too, on Psalm 102, writes that the upper beak of an ageing eagle grows so much that the passage for eating is closed. This very thing Aristotle , Pliny and Horapollo expressly teach. But whereas they add that with its beak growing in this way it dies of hunger, Augustine asserts that, having worn down its beak against a rock, it restores its failing strength by eating. Yet lest anyone think this is handed down by him as certain, here are the holy man's words on Psalm LXVI.: Our youth shall be renewed like the eagle, provided only that we wear down our old age against the rock. Whether those things are true, etc., which are said about the eagle, or whether it is rather a report of men than the truth, yet the truth is in the Scriptures, and not without reason have the Scriptures said this. Let us do whatever it signifies, and not trouble ourselves how true it is. Indeed, since the things that the writers we have cited relate about the ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of the eagle are either false or uncertain, let us embrace only what all acknowledge as true and certain: namely, that the eagle at a fixed time casts off its old feathers and then takes on others, and is renewed in this way. Hence the genuine Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 40: We have often said that the old age of eagles grows young again by the changing of their feathers. And Euthymius on Psalm CII.: You will lay aside the feeble old age which diseases and sins had brought on, ὡς ἐκεῖνος τὸ γῆρας τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos to gēras tōn heautou pterōn], as it does the old age of its feathers. You will be renewed through repentance, ὡς ἐκεῖνος διὰ τῆς παλιφυΐας πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos dia tēs paliphyias pterōn], as it is through the regrowth of its feathers.

Among the kinds of eagles, many take their name from their colour. Thus the πύγαργος [pygargos] is so called from its whitish tail, the μορφνὸς [morphnos] from its dusky colour, the μελαναίετος [melanaietos] from its black colour, the περκνόπτερος [perknopteros] from the markings of its wings, and the χρυσαίετος [chrysaietos], also called ἀστερίας [asterias], from its golden gleam and from the spots sprinkled over it like stars. To this last I refer these words of Ezek 17:3: A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of plumage, in which was רקמה rekama, that is, Phrygian work. For that this eagle, the ἀστερίας [asterias] or starry eagle, is the largest of the eagles, we learn from these words of Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 39: Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος ἀετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀστερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν καλοῦσιν· ὁρᾶται δὲ οὐ πολλάκις, etc. μέγιστος δὲ ἀετῶν εἶναι πεπίστευται. [Akouō de ti kai genos aetōn, kai onoma autōn chrysaieton ethento; alloi de asterian ton auton kalousin; horatai de ou pollakis, etc. megistos de aetōn einai pepisteutai.] I hear that there is also a certain kind of eagle which some call Chrysaetos, others Asterias or the starry eagle. It is not often seen, etc. It is believed to be the largest of the eagles . But I know of no kind of eagle with a blood-red tail, such as the Syriac translator describes in these words at Rev 8:13: And I saw, and heard one eagle flying in the midst, ܕܢܫܪܐ ܕܕܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ [דנשרא דדמא אית לה], which had a blood-red tail. So the matter would be stuck here, were the sources of the error not plain. The Greek has μεσουρανήματι [mesouranēmati], that is, in mid-heaven. The translator took this as if he had read ἐν μέσῳ οὐρὰν αἵματι [en mesō ouran haimati], supplying βεβαμμένην ἔχοντος [bebammenēn echontos]: an eagle in the midst, having its tail (supply dyed) with blood, than which nothing more absurd could be devised. On this passage see the Notes of Edward Pococke [=Edward Pococke, Commentary on Hosea (1685)], a man by far the most learned in these studies.

That نِسْر [nisr] is today the Arabic name of eagles is also confirmed by Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descriptt. Animall. p. 12. But just as the Arabs often take eagles, نِسْر [nisr], and vultures, رخم [rakham], indiscriminately, and attribute to the eagle many things that are proper to the vulture, as Bochart will show at length below in Chapter XXVII, so it is likely that the Hebrews too sometimes confused birds of both kinds and took one for the other. Medieval writers also confuse vultures with eagles, as Jo. Gottl. Schneider observes on Frederick II, De arte venandi cum avibus, p. 52. "Of eagles," says Leo Africanus, Descript. Afr. book 9, ch. 56, "there are various species, differing in their properties, size and colour: the larger are called Nesir in the Arabic idiom." And in ch. 57: Nesir "is the largest of the birds of Africa; in body it exceeds the crane, yet it is shorter in beak, neck and legs." These marks are rather uncertain and fit more than one bird of the eagle kind. This one thing seems certain: the word نسر [nsr] comprehends birds similar to one another but different in species. Alb. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] rightly says in his Commentary on Job XXXIX, p. 1136: "See Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, where six kinds of eagles are indicated. The name common to all is נשר, نسر [nsr]. The species noted in Scripture are פרס, the ossifrage, and עזניה, the Melanaetos or Valeria." Therefore I cannot agree with Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] [Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 1, ch. 5; fasc. 3, p. 164; and fasc. 5, p. 73], who assigns the name נשר to the bearded vulture alone, although I do not think it should be excluded altogether. But most of what is recorded of the נשר in the sacred books fits the whole kind of eagles and vultures. — Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. p. 1695, which should be read, inclines more to the eagle; with him may be compared what a certain learned man notes in the Sylloge of observations on Bruce's [=James Bruce, Travels to discover the source of the Nile (1790)] travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 161.

For my part I would think that these words refer rather to the fact that birds of the eagle and vulture kind bear a denser covering of feathers than other birds of prey. There is no adequate reason for referring them specifically to the bearded vulture, with Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73.

Oedmann's opinion, vol. 1, p. 64, is that Micah's words allude to the bald back of the head of the bearded vulture, which the head of one who has shorn his hair in mourning resembles. To the objections raised by J. D. Michaelis in the Bibl. Orient. Nova vol. 3, p. 45 ff., he replied in vol. 3, p. 168 ff. The head of the bearded vulture is seen in an illustration at the end of Part 3 of Oedmann's book.

To Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73, this passage seems to hint at the shaggy appearance of the bearded vulture, caused by the projecting hair-like feathers on the neck, breast and upper back. I can hardly persuade myself that any particular species of eagle was in the writer's mind.

This fable perhaps originated from what Leo Africanus relates of the Nesir, book 9, ch. 57, p. 511: "It lives a very long life, and we have seen very many featherless from old age: therefore, when their feathers fall out, they return to the nest, as if newly hatched, and are fed by the younger ones."
Arist. Hist. book 9, ch. 32. Plin. book 10, ch. 3.

This very eagle, which he had carefully observed, was described most accurately by Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 1, book 2, p. 112. There, among other things, he says: "The colour of the wings and tail was dusky, the more so the larger the feathers. That of the other, smaller feathers of the whole body was a rusty or chestnut brown," with white spots scattered here and there, few on the back, more on the belly, the roots everywhere white. "The flight feathers of the wings were six on each side, two spans and a palm long, with very firm and hard quills." You see that Bochart, with every right, refers Ezekiel's words to the ἀστερίας [asterias], which is also the χρυσάετος [chrysaetos], the largest of the eagles. But here too Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 74, sees his bearded vulture.
The eagle's wings, flight, nest, sight and food.

Scripture commends the eagle's wings for their size, Ezechielis XVII, 3. A great eagle with great wings, long-winged, etc. And there the Greeks have Ὁ ἀετὸς ὁ μέγας, ὁ μεγάλου πτέρυγος, ὁ μακρὸς τῇ ἐκτάσει [Ho aetos ho megas, ho megalou pterygos, ho makros tē ektasei]. For the eagle both has great wings and spreads them as widely as possible in flight. Hence the poets call it τανύπτερος [tanypteros], as if one were to say with outstretched wings. Hesiod, Theogony line 523:
Καὶ οἱ ἐπ᾽ αἰετὸν ὦρσε τανύπτερον, [Kai hoi ep᾽ aieton ōrse tanypteron,]
And he roused against him an eagle with outstretched wings. And Pindar, Pyth. 5:
Τανύπτερος ἐν ὄρνιξιν αἰετὸς, [Tanypteros en ornixin aietos,]
The eagle, among birds the one with the most outstretched wings. This the greatest of poets describes thus in the last book of the Iliad, line 317:

Ὅσση δ᾽ ὑψορόφοιο θύρη θαλάμοιο τέτυκται Ἀνέρος ἀφνειοῖο εὐκληῒς ἀραρυῖα, Τόσσ᾽ ἄρα τοῦ ἑκάτερθεν ἔσαν πτερά. [Hossē d᾽ hypsorophoio thyrē thalamoio tetyktai Aneros aphneioio euklēis araryia, Toss᾽ ara tou hekaterthen esan ptera.]

As great as is the door of a rich man's lofty chamber, well bolted and skilfully wrought, so great were its wings on either side. And in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], p. 206, Georg Fabricius mentions an eagle's nest found in the year 1500 between Meissen and Bresa, towns of Germany, with three chicks in it, the wings of one of which, stretched out crosswise, measured seven ells.

With these wings the eagle is borne along most swiftly and with the greatest force, especially when it swoops on its prey. Hence Apuleius, Florida book 1, says the eagle hurls itself down from above upon its prey like a thunderbolt. And in Cicero, On Divination book 2, when a runner reported to an interpreter that he had dreamed he had become an eagle, the latter said: You have won, for no bird flies more vehemently than that one. Accordingly the ancients relate that the serpent, otherwise a bold and fearless animal, is put to flight by the mere rushing sound of the eagle's wings. Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 26: Καὶ τόν γε τῶν πτερῶν αὐτοῦ ῥοῖζον, καὶ τὸ τῶν θηρίων ἀτρεπτότατον, ὅμως κατέπτηξεν ὁ δράκων ἀκούσας μόνον καὶ παραχρῆμα κατέδυ, καὶ ἀσμένως ἠφανίσθη [Kai ton ge tōn pterōn autou rhoizon, kai to tōn thēriōn atreptotaton, homōs kateptēxen ho drakōn akousas monon kai parachrēma katedy, kai asmenōs ēphanisthē]. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], ch. 1:

Τούτου δὲ καὶ τὸν ῥοῖζον ἀκούσας δράκων, Ἔπτηξέ τε παραχρῆμα, καὶ συνεστάλη, Καὶ τοὺς μυχοὺς ὑπῆλθε τοὺς ἀποκρύφους. [Toutou de kai ton rhoizon akousas drakōn, Eptēxe te parachrēma, kai synestalē, Kai tous mychous hypēlthe tous apokryphous.]

Hence Festus holds that the wind aquilo [north wind] is so called from its most vehement flight, like that of an eagle. And most think that the eagle itself is called ἀετός [aetos] in Greek from ἀΐσσειν [aïssein], that is, to rush with force and to swoop. We have derived it from עיט ajit, the name by which the Hebrews call a bird of prey. But it comes to much the same thing, for עיט is formed from העיט, that is, from flying at and swooping. All this serves to show that it is not without reason that Scripture so often compares the speed and force of those who rush into battle with eagles, and indeed with eagles swooping on their prey. Thus Deut 28:49. The Lord will raise against thee a nation from afar, from the farthest ends of the earth, כאשר ידאה הנשר, as the eagle flies. The Greeks: ὡσεὶ ὅρμημα ἀετοῦ [hōsei hormēma aetou]; and Jerome: like an eagle flying with force. So in Iliad 21, line 252, Achilles, rushing upon the Trojans, is described by the Poet as αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou oimat᾽ echōn], having the onrush of an eagle. For to the Scholiast οἴματα [oimata] are ὁρμήματα [hormēmata]; to Hesychius, Οἴματα· ἀετοῦ ὁρμήματα [Oimata: aetou hormēmata]. Likewise the same poet of Hector, Iliad 22, line 308:
Οἴμησεν δὲ ἀλεὶς, ὥς τ᾽ αἰετὸς ὑψιπετήεις, [Oimēsen de aleis, hōs t᾽ aietos hypsipetēeis,]

Gathering himself, he swooped with force, like a high-flying eagle. Wrongly, therefore, did Philetas want to read αἰετοῦ ὄμματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou ommat᾽ echōn], having the eyes of an eagle, instead of αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou oimat᾽ echōn]. For the subject here is not the eagle's eyes but the force of its swoop. To the same point belongs David's statement that Saul and Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan], most warlike men, were swifter than eagles, 2 Sam 1:23. And what Jeremiah writes of the Chaldeans, IV, 13. Their horses are swifter than eagles. And of their king, Ier. XLVIII, 40. He shall fly as an eagle, and shall spread his wings over Moab. And again Ier. XLIX, 22. He shall come up as an eagle, and fly, and spread his wings over Bozrah. And Lam 4:19. Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven.

Job uses the same simile, but in a different context, Job 9:26. They have passed by (my days) like ships אבה ebe, as the eagle flies to its food. In these words, to say this in passing, I suspect with Selomo and others that Ebe is the name of a river, because even today there are two rivers named ابى [Abī] Ebe or Ebbe in those regions: one of them is near Kufa, the other in the district of Babylonia called Wasit, which is the Mesene of the Greeks. See the Lexicon of the distinguished Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)], p. 2. Something else could also be adduced. In Arabic ابى [abā] aba is a verb meaning to gird oneself for a journey. So אניות אבה, ships ebe, could be called swift ships, girded for a journey, or actuariae [light vessels], if you prefer, which are the more nimble . Thus the spans of our swiftly running life are compared both with ships of this kind and with the birds we have mentioned, that is, with eagles hastening to their food. This is not only because the speed is equal in both cases, but also because nothing remains of time once it has slipped away, just as the eagle in the air and the ship in the sea leave no trace of themselves, as Solomon observes, Prov 30:19. Hence in Wis 5:10–11. 12. the author of the book, whoever he is, elegantly uses both similes to teach that we, scarcely born, at once so fail that nothing is left of the life we have lived.

Now another point must be observed in the flight of eagles: it is not only swift but also sustained. For the eagle does not tire quickly, but, when the situation demands, flies for a very long time and travels to quite distant places. Hence the poets imagine that two eagles, sent out by Jupiter, one from the farthest east and the other from the farthest west, did not cease from flight until they met at Delphi, or on neighbouring Parnassus. See Pindar, Pyth. 4, and the Scholiast there, Strabo, book 9, Plutarch, De Orac., and Claudian's Prologue to the Panegyric of Manlius Theodorus. Of the same kind is the fiction of the Arabs in Damiri: وهو اشد الطير طيرانا واقوي جناحا حتي انه ليطير ما بين المشرق والمغرب في يوم واحد [wa-huwa ashadd al-ṭayr ṭayarānan wa-aqwā janāḥan ḥattā annahu la-yaṭīru mā bayna al-mashriq wa-al-maghrib fī yawm wāḥid] It is of all birds the most vigorous in flight and has the strongest wings, so that it flies across all that lies between east and west in a single day. Accordingly Scripture applies eagle's wings to those who are carried far away. Thus in Rev 12:14 the woman, who is the church, is given two wings of a great eagle, with which to fly into the desert out of the serpent's sight. And in Ps 139:9 the Syriac translator has: If I raise my wings ܐܝܟ ܕܢܫܪܐ [איך דנשרא], like an eagle, and dwell in the uttermost sea. And the Arabic: If I were lifted up on two wings كالنسر [ka-al-nasr] like an eagle, so as to come to the ends of the sea. The Ethiopic also: If I take my wings ከመ [kama] ፡ ንስር [nəsər] ፡ like an eagle, etc. Yet the Hebrew does not have כנפי נשר, wings of an eagle, but כנפי שחר, wings of the dawn. This is followed by the Greeks, the Chaldee, the Vulgate translator, Jerome and all the Hebrews. Here also belongs the statement in Proverb. XXIII, 5. that fleeting riches take on the wings of an eagle, with which they fly off into heaven, that is, they slip away very swiftly and are removed far from you, so that they are no longer in your possession. Hence in Lucian's Timon Plutus, the god of riches, says that he limps and advances only slowly when he is sent by Jupiter to someone to increase his wealth. Ὁπόταν δὲ ἀπαλλάττεσθαι δέῃ [Hopotan de apallattesthai deē], he says, πτηνὸν ὄψει πολὺ τῶν ὀρνέων ὠκύτερον [ptēnon opsei poly tōn orneōn ōkyteron]· But when I must depart, you will see me winged, far swifter than birds. So, since God says in Exod 19:4 that he carried the Israelites, as they went out of Egypt, as on eagles' wings, the Jews infer from this that they covered 120 miles in one hour from Rameses to Succoth. So R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] on Exod 12:37: מרעמסס סכתה מאה ועשרים מיל היו ובאו שם לפי שעה שנ״ ואשא אתכם על כנפי נשרים, From Rameses to Succoth is a journey of one hundred and twenty miles, which they covered in the space of one hour, as it is said: “And I will carry them on eagles' wings”.
Nor should this be omitted: there is no bird that rises higher than the eagle . Hence in the oracle given concerning the Athenians,
Αἰετὸς ἐν νεφέλῃσι γενήσεαι, — — [Aietos en nephelēsi genēseai, — —]

You will be an eagle in the clouds: the Scholiast on Aristophanes, Birds, says this means that they τοσοῦτον αὐξηθήσεσθαι, ὅσον αἰετὸς τῶν ἄλλων ὀρνέων ἐν ταῖς νεφέλαις προὔχει [tosouton auxēthēsesthai, hoson aietos tōn allōn orneōn en tais nephelais prouchei], will be increased as much as the eagle in the clouds stands out above the other birds. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] too, on Job 29:30: אין עוף שיגבה יותר ממנו, There is no bird that rises higher. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], on Jer 49:16, asserts that it flies גבוה מכל העופות, higher than all birds. And Apuleius, Florida book 1: For the eagle, when it has raised itself most high, up to the clouds, borne on its wings, beyond that whole space where it rains and snows, beyond which summit there is no place for thunderbolt or lightning, in the very floor, so to speak, of the aether and the topmost height of winter. And Horus, book 2, ch. 53: ὑψηλότερον πάντων τῶν πετεινῶν ἵπταται [hypsēloteron pantōn tōn peteinōn hiptatai], it flies highest of all birds. Hence the poets call it ὑψιπετὴς [hypsipetēs] and ὑψιπετήεις [hypsipetēeis] , high-flying. Indeed, for this very reason, that it flies on high, if we believe Aristotle, Histor. book 9, ch. 32, θεῖον οἱ ἄνθρωποί φασιν εἶναι μόνον τῶν ὀρνέων [theion hoi anthrōpoi phasin einai monon tōn orneōn], men say it alone among birds is divine. At least from this arose the fables of the eagle in the bosom of Jupiter, and as the minister of his thunderbolts; and that some dreamed its feathers were scorched by the elemental fire, others by the rays of the nearby sun. Not to mention the eagle that used to be released from the pyre of the Caesars, as though to carry the emperor's soul to heaven. For so it was believed. Dio, book 56, on the funeral of Augustus: Καὶ ἡ πύρα μὲν ἀναλίσκετο· ἀετὸς δέ τις ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀφεθεὶς ἀπίπτατο, ὃ καὶ δὲ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἐς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀναφέρων [Kai hē pyra men anaKisketo; aetos de tis ex autēs aphetheis apeptato, ho kai de tēn psychēn autou es ton ouranon anapherōn]. And the pyre was consumed, and from it flew an eagle, bearing his soul to heaven. Herodian, book 4: Ἀετὸς ἀφίεται σὺν τῷ πυρὶ ἀνελευσόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα, ὃς φέρειν ἀπὸ γῆς ἐς οὐρανὸν τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως ψυχὴν πιστεύεται ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων [Aetos aphietai syn tō pyri aneleusomenos eis ton aithera, hos pherein apo gēs es ouranon tēn tou basileōs psychēn pisteuetai hypo Rhōmaiōn]: Together with the (kindled) fire an eagle is released to ascend into the aether, which the Romans believe carries the emperor's soul from earth to heaven. Accordingly on ancient coins one may see on one side the emperor's portrait, on the other an eagle on which the emperor sits, with this inscription: CONSECRATIO S. C. And if a king or prince dreams that he is carried by an eagle, this portends death for them, writes Artemidorus, book 2,

ch. 20, because there was an old custom πλάσσειν τε, καὶ γράφειν ἐπὶ ἀετῶν ὀχουμένους [plassein te, kai graphein epi aetōn ochoumenous], to sculpt and paint them seated on eagles. What of the fact that from Scripture itself it seems one can gather that the eagle flies right up to heaven and has its nest among the stars? For so Solomon, Proverb. XXIII, 5.: Like an eagle it will fly to heaven. And Obadiah, vers. 4., addressing the Edomites, proud of the height of their strongholds: Though you exalt yourself like the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, thence I will bring you down, says the Lord. But even boys know that heaven is taken by the Hebrews for the air. And the nest set among the stars is said with the same hyperbole with which the king of Babylon boasts, Isa 14:13. I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God. Not unlike this is the boast of Xerxes in Herodotus, book 7, ch. 10: Γῆν τε τὴν Περσίδα ἀποδέξομεν τῷ Διὸς αἰθέρι ὁμουρέουσαν [Gēn te tēn Persida apodexomen tō Dios aitheri homoureousan], We shall make the Persian land border on the aether of Jupiter. That is, just as exalting one's throne above the stars and making one's land border on the aether of Jupiter means raising it to the highest summit of loftiness, so one who nests in the loftiest places is said to set his nest among the stars. That the eagle does this, besides Obadiah, Jeremiah also teaches in a passage parallel to this, addressed to the same Edomites, Ier. XLIX, 16.: O you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who hold the summit of the hill. Though you should make your nest as high as the eagle, thence I would bring you down. And there the Chaldee paraphrast: You are like the eagle, which lives בשני כיפא, on the crags of the rock: its dwelling is בתקוף רומא, in a lofty stronghold.

To these must be added the famous passage on the eagle in Job 39:27 var. 30., in which God addresses his servant thus: Will the eagle rise up at your command, and set her nest on high? She dwells on the rock, and on the sheer crag as in a citadel she abides. From there she searches out food, her eyes gazing far off; and her chicks suck up blood; and where the slain are, there is she. Since all of this pertains to the nature of the eagle, it must be expounded carefully. Will the eagle, he says, rise up at your command? namely in lofty flight.
