Man did not give the eagle this nature, that she should rise up to the very clouds; nor can you steer her in flight and bend her to your will, since at times she is so high in the air that she wholly escapes the sight of men. At your command, etc. will she set her nest on high in places that are often impassable and inaccessible to us? This the following words explain thus: She dwells on the rock, and on the sheer crag as in a citadel she abides. The Septuagint: Ἐπ᾽ ἐξοχῇ πέτρας, καὶ ἀποκρύφῳ [Ep᾽ exochē petras, kai apokryphō]. Had they not rather written καὶ ἀποκρήμνῳ [kai apokrēmnō]? So Jerome: She remains on the rocks, she lingers on sheer flints and on inaccessible cliffs. Not very differently the Philosopher, on the nests of eagles, Histor. book 9, ch. 32: Ποιοῦνται δὲ αὐτὰς οὐκ ἐν πεδινοῖς τόποις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς μάλιστα μὲν, καὶ ἐν πέτραις ἀποκρήμνοις· [Poiountai de autas ouk en pedinois topois, all᾽ en hypsēlois malista men, kai en petrais apokrēmnois] They make them not in level places but in lofty ones, and chiefly on sheer cliffs. And Pliny, book 10, ch. 3: They nest on rocks. And Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On النسر [al-nasr] or the Eagle: تبيض في الاماكن [tabīḍu fī al-amākin] العالية [al-ʿāliya] She lays her eggs in lofty places . And in the chapter On العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, or the Melanaeetus: ولا تقعد الا علي الاماكن المرتفعة [wa-lā taqʿudu illā ʿalī al-amākin al-murtafiʿa] She dwells only in elevated places. As Pliny says of the same bird: It keeps to the mountains. And Albertus of the herodius, the name by which barbarous writers call the larger eagle: It is always found sitting and nesting on sheer flints.

There are, moreover, two reasons why she betakes herself to these steep places, which the sacred writer touches on here in passing. The first, that they may serve her as מצודה, that is, as ὀχυρώματος [ochyrōmatos], or a stronghold, as Aquila rightly rendered it; and that the chicks, which she is forced to leave in the nest in order to provide food for them, may be safe by the very nature of the place. For such lofty crags are not open to just anyone. To this pertains what the Arabs relate in Damir: قيل لبشار بن يزد الاعمي الشاعر لو خيرك الله أن تكون حيوانا ماذا كنت تختار قال العقاب لانها تلبث حيث لا يبلغها سبع ولا ذواريع وتحيد عنها سباع الطير [qīla li-Bashshār ibn Yazd al-aʿmī al-shāʿir law khayyaraka Allāh an takūna ḥayawānan mādhā kunta takhtār qāla al-ʿuqāb li-annahā talbathu ḥaythu lā yablughuhā sabʿ wa-lā dhawārīʿ wa-taḥīdu ʿanhā sibāʿ al-ṭayr] Besar, son of Iazid, the blind poet, when asked what he would choose if God gave him the option of becoming any animal, answered: Alokab (that is, that he would choose the melanaeetus), because it dwells in places inaccessible to all wild beasts and animals, and even the birds of prey flee from meeting it.

The second reason why the eagle prefers to dwell in a lofty place is expressed thus in Job: From there she searches out food, her eyes gazing far off. Nor did this escape the Philosopher, who says of the eagle in the place cited above: Ὑψοῦ δὲ πέτεται, ὅπως ἐπὶ πλεῖστον τόπον καθορᾷ [Hypsou de petetai, hopōs epi pleiston topon kathora], She flies high, so as to look down upon more places. And Apuleius: When therefore the eagle has borne herself up there, etc. looking down upon everything from there, etc. she gazes around and seeks where above all she should swoop down from on high upon her prey. These things agree with the words of Job: From there she searches out food, her eyes looking down from afar. Searches out is in Hebrew חפר, a verb which properly means to dig, but here to search out with the eyes. The same kind of metaphor is found in the verb rimari [to search out]. For properly rimari is rimas agere [to make cracks], and almost the same as fodere [to dig]. Hence the Poet in book 3 of the Georgics:

So with difficulty they scratch the earth with hoes, and with their very nails dig in the grain. — — — Nor is it added in vain that the eagle gazes far off with her eyes. For no animal is more sharp-sighted than the eagle. Homer, Iliad ρ΄ [17], line 674:
— — — ὥς τ᾽ αἰετὸς, ὅν ῥά τέ φασιν Ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι ὑπουρανίων πετεηνῶν. [hōs t᾽ aietos, hon rha te phasin Oxytaton derkesthai hypouraniōn peteēnōn]

Like the eagle, which they say sees most keenly of the birds of the air. Where the Scholiast says: Αἰετός· ὄρνις δορατικὸς (an legendum διορατικὸς) καὶ ὀξὺς ἐν τῷ ὁρᾷν, καὶ ἵπτασθαι [Aietos· ornis doratikos (or should we read dioratikos) kai oxys en tō horan, kai hiptasthai]. Aelian likewise, Hist. book 1, ch. 42: Αἰετὸς δὲ ὀρνίθων ὀξυωπήστερος [Aietos de ornithōn oxyōpēsteros]. Horace, Serm. 1, Sat. 3:
— — — — you see as sharply as either the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent.

Seneca, De Beneficiis book 2, ch. 29: They complain that dogs surpass us in keenness of scent, and eagles in sharpness of sight. Apuleius, Florida book 1: If they were stronger in the judgement of the eyes than of the mind, then surely wisdom would have to be conceded to the eagle. Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: It is said to have such power of vision that, when it is borne over the seas on motionless wing and is not visible to human eyes, it sees little fish swimming from so great a height. Sidonius, book 7, Letter 14: But perhaps they prefer the power of seeing: as though the sight of eagles were not more eminent. Philes, ch. 1:
Πλὴν ὀξυδερκής ἐστιν ὁ πτηνοκράτωρ, Καὶ μέχρι σητὸς ἐκ νεφῶν πάντα βλέπει· [Plēn oxyderkēs estin ho ptēnokratōr, Kai mechri sētos ek nephōn panta blepei]

But the prince of birds is sharp-sighted (that is, the eagle), and from the clouds sees everything, down to a moth. Apostolius, Adage 62: Ὀξύτατα ὁρᾷ ἐκ πολλοῦ τοῦ αἰθέρος [Oxytata hora ek pollou tou aitheros]. And among the Arabs, Damir, though not without hyperbole: وهو حاد البصر يري الجيفة من اربع ماية فرسخ [wa-huwa ḥādd al-baṣar yarī al-jīfa min arbaʿ māya farsakh] It is of the keenest sight, so that it sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. To this many refer the name aquila, as if it were said from the sharpness [acumen] of sight. Accordingly it alone of animals is said to gaze at the sun with unblinking eyes, and not to regard its chicks as genuine unless they endure the light of the sun.

There follows in Job: And its chicks suck up blood, namely from the prey which the mother carries to the nest. They suck up is in Hebrew יעלעו, by metathesis for ילועו. Since this is without parallel, some interpreters have stumbled over this word. The Greeks have φύρονται ἐν αἵματι [phyrontai en haimati], as if they had read יתגללו בדם, as in 2 Sam 20:12 πεφυρμένος ἐν τῷ αἵματι [pephyrmenos en tō haimati] stands for the Hebrew מתגלל בדם. This is plainly foreign to the sense. Nor do I understand what ἐστυμισμένοι [estymismenoi] in Aquila means. Be that as it may, Jerome, the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic and most of the Hebrews render it very well, and according to the mind of the sacred writer, they lick or suck up blood. You will say that the eagle is πάμπαν ἄποτον [pampan apoton], wholly without drink. For so the Philosopher asserts, History book 8, ch. 3 and 18,

where he charges Herodotus with ignorance, because in the siege of Nineveh he makes an eagle, presiding over an augury, drink. In the Assyrian History, that is, which is no longer extant; for in those works of Herodotus that are extant nothing of the kind is found. Hence Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 26: Οὐδέποτε αἰετὸς οὔτε πηγῆς δεῖται, οὔτε γλίχεται κονίστρας, ἀλλὰ δί- ψους ἀμείνων ἐστί· [Oudepote aietos oute pēgēs deitai, oute glichetai konistras, alla dipsous ameinōn esti] The eagle never needs a spring, nor does it seek to roll in the dust, but it is superior to thirst. Likewise: Ὑπερφρονῶν δὲ καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων, καὶ τῆς ἀναπαύσεως· [Hyperphronōn de kai tōn hydatōn, kai tēs anapauseōs] And it scorns both waters and rest. And Gregory of Nyssa in the book On the Soul: Πολλὰ τῶν ζώων ἐστὶ μὴ πίνοντα, ὡς ἐπί τινων ἀετῶν ἱστόρηται· [Polla tōn zōōn esti mē pinonta, hōs epi tinōn aetōn historētai] There are many animals that abstain from drink, as is related of certain eagles. Pisides in Suidas:
Ἀλλ᾽ εἰσι δίψης καὶ κρύους ἀνώτεροι, [All' eisi dipsēs kai kryous anōteroi] And they know not the force of thirst and cold.

And Suidas himself, under Γαμψώνυχος [Gampsōnychos], has this: Οἷός ἐστιν ἀετὸς, ἱέραξ, κεγχρηΐς, ἄλλα τε τὰ μὴ πίνοντα· [Hoios estin aetos, hierax, kenchrēis, alla te ta mē pinonta] Such as the eagle, the hawk, the kestrel, and other animals that do not drink. And Apostolius, Adage 62: Οὐ γὰρ ἁλίσκεται ἐν νεφέλαις ὁ ἀετὸς, καὶ δίψους ἀμείνων ἐστί. [Ou gar haliksetai en nephelais ho aetos, kai dipsous ameinōn esti] For the eagle is not caught in the clouds, nor is it overcome by thirst. But there is nothing contrary to these in Job. For he does not write that eagles drink water, but that they suck up blood; which the very authors who deny the eagle drink themselves write. Thus, on the authority of Oppian in the Ixeutica, cited by Gesner: The blood of the animals they have caught suffices them, but water they do not taste at all. As Horapollo says of the hawk: Ὕδωρ οὐ πίνει τὸ καθόλου, ἀλλ᾽ αἷμα· [Hydōr ou pinei to katholou, all' haima] It does not drink water at all, but blood. And Demetrius in the Hieracosophion: Πρῶτον μὲν τὸν φάρυγγα τοῦ ἁλόντος ὄρνιθος τέμνε, καὶ δίδου πίειν τῷ ἱέρακι θερμοῦ ἀναβλύζοντος αἵματος· [Prōton men ton pharynga tou halontos ornithos temne, kai didou piein tō hieraki thermou anablyzontos haimatos] First cut the throat of the captured bird, and give the hawk the warm, gushing blood to drink. And Aelian, History book 10, ch. 14: Σαρκῶν δὲ ἥδεται βορᾷ, καὶ πίνει αἷμα, καὶ τὰ νεόττια ἐκτρέφει· [Sarkōn de hēdetai bora, kai pinei haima, kai ta neottia ektrephei] It delights in eating flesh, and drinks blood, and with these it rears its chicks. Hesychius also, of the vulture, under Τόργιον [Torgion]: Τόργος· εἶδος γυπὸς αἱματοῤῥόφους· [Torgos; eidos gypos haimatorrophous] Torgos, a kind of vulture that sucks blood.

One thing about the eagle remains in Job: Where the slain are, there is she. The slain, that is, the bodies of the slain or of the killed. Accordingly, the words of Christ in Matt 24:28 and Luke 17:37 plainly allude to this passage: Wheresoever the carcass is, there the eagles are gathered together. The Arabs assert the same. Damir, above, on the eagle: It sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. Again: واذا وقع علي جيفة وعليها عقبان تاخرت ولم تاكل ما دام تاكل منها [wa-idhā waqaʿa ʿalī jīfa wa-ʿalayhā ʿiqbān taʾakhkharat wa-lam taʾkul mā dām taʾkul minhā] And when it comes upon a carcass on which there are ossifrages, it withdraws and does not eat their leavings. Again: اذا وقع علي جيفة وامتلا منها لم يستطع الطيران حتي يثب وثبات يرفع بها نفسها طبقة بعد طبقة في الهوا [idhā waqaʿa ʿalī jīfa wa-imtalā minhā lam yastaṭiʿ al-ṭayarān ḥattā yathib wathabāt yarfaʿ bihā nafsahā ṭabaqa baʿd ṭabaqa fī al-hawā] And when it comes upon a carcass and has filled itself with it, it cannot fly until, advancing by leaps, it has raised itself into the air by degrees. But this properly belongs to the percnopterus, or gypaeetus, a degenerate kind of eagle of vulturine appearance, which alone of the eagles carries off dead bodies, as Pliny has it from Aristotle . That the percnos, which is also the morphnos, differs greatly from the percnopterus is clear from the same Pliny. For in him the percnos, or morphnos, is the eagle of the third kind, and the percnopterus of the fourth. And the descriptions of the two differ considerably from each other. But Suidas, not knowing this, attributed to the percnos, or morphnos (which is the same), what is proper to the percnopterus. His words are: Μόρφνος· εἶδος ἀετοῦ· μόνοι δὲ οὗτοι τῶν ἀετῶν οὐ κυνηγητοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ νεκροῖς σώμασι τρέφονται· [Morphnos; eidos aetou; monoi de houtoi tōn aetōn ou kynēgētousin, alla nekrois sōmasi trephontai] Morphnos, a species of eagle; of the eagles these alone do not hunt, but feed on carcasses. By a like error Theophylact took the eagles of which Christ speaks for vultures. Ὥσπερ, he says, ἐπὶ νεκρὸν σῶμα συνάγονται ὀξέως οἱ ἀετοὶ, οἱ γῦπες δηλαδή· [Hōsper epi nekron sōma synagontai oxeōs hoi aetoi, hoi gypes dēladē] As the eagles, that is, the vultures, gather at once to a carcass. And Tzetzes, Chil. 5, ch. 9, denies that the eagle kind touches carcasses in any way; his words are:
Λέοντες θῆρες, σὺν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀετῶν τὸ γένος, Νεκρῶν οὐκ ἀπογεύονται τὸ σύνολον σωμάτων· [Leontes thēres, syn autois kai aetōn to genos, Nekrōn ouk apogeuontai to synolon sōmatōn]

Lions, the beasts, and with them the eagle kind, do not taste dead bodies at all. Unless exceptions are added to so general a statement, its truth will not stand, as what has already been adduced amply proves. These are further confirmed by the words of Solomon, Proverb. XXX, 17: The eye that mocks his father and despises the instruction of his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it. For rebellion against parents was then a capital crime, as is clear from Exod 21:15 17. Lev 20:9 and Deuter. XXI, 18. And the bodies of the condemned remained unburied, exposed to wild beasts and carnivorous birds. Nor is it without reason that Solomon mentions the eye, since in the whole body no part is so exposed to the attacks of birds of prey. Hence Epictetus, explaining the sense of the old adage Κρεῖττον εἶναι ἐς κόρακας ἀπελθεῖν, ἢ ἐς κόλακας· [Kreitton einai es korakas apelthein, ē es kolakas] It is better to go to the ravens than to flatterers, says: Οἱ μὲν κόρακες τῶν τελευτηκότων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς λυμαίνονται, ὅταν αὐτῶν οὐδέν ἐστι χρεία· οἱ δὲ κόλακες τῶν ζώντων τὰς ψυχὰς διαφθείρουσι, καὶ τὰ τούτων ὄμματα τυφλώττουσι· [Hoi men korakes tōn teleutēkotōn tous ophthalmous lymainontai, hotan autōn ouden esti chreia; hoi de kolakes tōn zōntōn tas psychas diaphtheirousi, kai ta toutōn ommata typhlōttousi] Ravens ravage the eyes of the dead only when they are of no further use; but flatterers corrupt the souls of the living and blind their eyes .

Cf. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], Supplemm. vol. 1, p. 3, where the view of Alb. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)], who understands boats made of papyrus or of reed, comparing إباء [ibāʾ], is also weighed, and Bochart's is defended. Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde], fasc. 3, ch. 12, renders אניות אבה as ships of skins (as if אוב and אבה were the same word), and understands light rafts set on inflated goatskins so that they may run the faster, such as the river Tigris carries to this day.
See Iliad 12. 206. 219. Iliad 13. 822. Iliad 22. 308. Odyssey 20. 243 and 24. 537. Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 40, etc.
Leo Africanus on the Nesir, ch. 57: In flight it rises so high into the air that it cannot be seen.

Leo Africanus, as above, on the Nesir: they live on the highest rocks and the summits of wild mountains. Schultens cites some passages from the Arabic poets in his Commentary on the passage, p. 1134–35.

Chiefly from the fact that the eating of carcasses is ascribed to the נשר in Job 39:29 and Prov 30:17, Oedmann concludes that in those places the χρυσαιετον [chrysaieton] is not meant, since it never touches a carcass. This itself is not so certain as to be placed beyond all doubt. For concerning the golden eagle (dem Steinadler, Goldadler), which is the χρυσαίετος [chrysaietos] of the Greeks, Taube in his Descript. Slavon. vol. 1, p. 25, relates that it eats dead horses and oxen; and Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], a great expert in natural history, who always uses the Linnaean names of animals, has this in Descript. Animal. p. 12: The eagle, Nisr, lives on flesh and carcasses. Yet if anyone wishes some vulturine species of eagle to be meant in those places, he will not find me much opposed, since I think נשר should not be restricted to some particular bird of the eagle kind, but extended to that whole kind. See above, note 1. Leo Africanus on his Nisr: when it sees a dead animal, it suddenly swoops down. This is confirmed by Hoest, Beschreibung von Fes und Marocco p. 298, whose words are these: Ich habe auch einen hellgrauen Vogel gesehen, zweymal so gross, als ein Welscher Hahn, der bey einem Aase stand. Die Mohren sagten, dass er wohl mit einem grossen Lamme davon fliegen könne, und dass er viele Schaafe umbringe. Einige nannten den Vogel Ensir, نسر [nsr], andere Gernuk, غرنوق [ghurnūq]. Also worth reading is what J. D. Michaelis said on this matter in Bibl. Orient. vol. 9, p. 37 ff., in his review of Forsskål's book.
On the eagle's love for its young, from Deut 32:11.

Now we must speak of the eagle's love for its young. That it is most tender is shown by these words of Moses, Deuter. XXXII, 11: As the eagle stirs up its nest, and hovers over its young, with wings spread out, and taking them carries them upon its feathers. Its nest, that is, its brood: the container for the contained. This manner of speaking is frequent among the Romans. Virgil, in book 4 of the Georgics, says of the bee-eater and the swallow,
They carry in their beaks sweet food to the pitiless nests:

that is, to the cruel chicks, as Servius explains there. Hence Nonius: On the authority of Virgil we may call nidi not only the dwellings of birds but also their offspring. And Columella followed this in his Garden:
And the swallow will have sung the coming of spring to its nests.

So too Solinus on the ibis: It feeds on the eggs of serpents, and brings from them a most welcome food to its nests. And Ammianus, book 22, of the same bird: supplying the eggs of serpents as food to its little nests. Hence the Glosses: Νεοσσὸς [neossos], nidus, chick. And Juvenal, Satire 5, uses it also of children: But now, though your Mygale should give birth, and pour three boys at once into their father's lap, he himself will delight in the chattering nest. — — — —

R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] explains the verb to stir up thus: הזה רחמני על בניו ואינו נכנס לקנו פתאם עד שהוא מקשקש ומטרף על בניו בכנפיו בין אילן לאילן בין שוכה לחברתה כדי שיעורו בניו ויהא בהן כח לקבלו, The eagle, being compassionate towards its young, does not enter its nest abruptly; rather it first makes a noise over them and claps, striking its wings against two trees or against two branches, so that the chicks, thus roused, may have enough strength (that is, may be better prepared) to receive it. To this belongs what follows: על גוזליו ירחף אינו מכביד עצמו עליהם אלא מחופף נוגע ואינו נוגע, It broods over its young (for so he takes the Hebrew ירחף), that is, it does not press its weight on them, but holds itself up so that it touches them as if not touching. Thus he. But Jerome's version, though freer, nevertheless renders the Prophet's meaning much more faithfully: As the eagle, provoking its young to fly, and hovering over them, etc. For the eagle is certainly said to stir up its nest, or its brood, when it provokes it to fly. And the Hebrew רחף means to move oneself, as in Jer 23:9. רחפו, All my bones have trembled. So at the creation the Spirit of God מרחפת, was moving to and fro over the face of the waters. From there, transferred to birds, רחף means to move the wings to and fro, as birds do when hovering. From this the Talmudists derived a verb of the same meaning, רפרף, with the guttural elided and the other letters doubled. Hence in the tractate Cholin, fol. 38b: והעוף אפילו לא רפרף אלא גפו ולא כשכש אלא זנבו הרי זה פירכוס, And a bird, if it only moves its wing, or only wags its tail, this is a convulsive movement. Accordingly in Beresith Rabba the Spirit מרחפת of Gen 1:3 is said to be כעוף הזה שהוא מרפרף בכנפיו, like that bird which moves its wings to and fro. The Arabs too use the same verb in this way. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] renders it بسط جناحها [basaṭa janāḥahā] It spread out its wings. And the verbal noun الرفرفة [al-rafrafa] is for him الصوت وتحريك الظليم جناحيها حول الشي الذي يريد ان يقع عليه [al-ṣawt wa-taḥrīk al-ẓalīm janāḥayhā ḥawla al-shay al-ladhī yurīdu an yaqaʿa ʿalayhi] The noise and movement of the wings of the ostrich around the thing on which it wishes to alight. Since this is habitual to the ostrich, the bird itself is called رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph. So too another bird, very different from the ostrich, whose other name is خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi], that is, σκιάρπαξ [skiarpax], snatcher of its own shadow: because, when it sees its image in the water, it flies at it, moving its wings, as if to seize it. Moreover the verb رف [raffa] in the fourth conjugation, that is, ارف [arafa] arappha, is attributed to birds that spread their wings to brood. The same Alcamus: ارفت الدجاجة علي بياضها بسطت الجناح [arafat al-dajāja ʿalā bayāḍihā basaṭat al-janāḥ] Arapphath the hen over her eggs, that is, she spread out her wings, namely in order to brood on them. Yet what we have said is true, that this verb properly signifies a spreading of the wings accompanied by moving them to and fro. This is especially fitting for the eagle, or for any other bird that teaches its still tender chicks their first πτερυγισμοὺς [pterygismous] and ὀρταλισμούς [ortalismous]. Accordingly the Prophet, after ירחף, adds by way of explanation (ἐπεξηγητικῶς [epexēgētikōs]) יפרש כנפיו, it spreads its wings; because the eagle does not move its wings to and fro unless they are spread. Indeed, the movement of the wings is so natural to the eagle that even the chicks constantly flap their wings while eating. So the Arabs report in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: ومن عادة هذا الطاير ان يزق كل فرخ ضايع [wa-min ʿādat hādhā al-ṭāyir an yuzaqqa kull farkh ḍāyiʿ] It is also of the nature of this bird that every chick flaps its wings while it is being fed: namely by its mother, beak inserted into beak. For that is properly زق [zaqq].

Further, the eagle's chicks are called in Prov 30:17. בני נשר, sons of the eagle, and in Job 39:33 (var. 30.) אפרוחיו, its chicks, a general word applied to the chicks of all birds. But here they are called גוזליו, καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs]. For גוזל gozel is the chick of a dove, or of a related bird, as we have shown in its place . Likewise in Lampridius pipiones [squabs] are the chicks of doves. Yet for others pipiunculus is a hawk. The Glosses of Isidore: Pipiunculus, accipiter, acceptor [pipiunculus, hawk]. Something else is to be noted here, namely that both Job and Moses, in the passage we are dealing with, attribute several chicks to a single eagle, although eagles for the most part rear only one each. Albertus reports that this was observed by fowlers in eagles' nests in Germany, in one place for six, in another for eight successive years. He also gives this reason: although the mother hatches two or three, she is nevertheless not equal to rearing more chicks, because they need much food on account of the heat of their temperament. The ancients say much the same. To this belongs the old verse of Musaeus about the eagle in the Philosopher, Hist. book 6, ch. 6.
Ὃς τρία μὲν τίκτει, δύο δ᾽ ἐκλέπει, ἓν δ᾽ ἀλεγίζει, [Hos tria men tiktei, dyo d᾽ eklepei, hen d᾽ alegizei,]

Which lays three, hatches two, and cares for one: or ἓν δ᾽ ἀλυβάζει [hen d᾽ alybazei], rears one, as Plutarch quotes it in the Marius. And the Philosopher admits that this is mostly what happens. Yet, as he also adds, ἤδη καὶ τρεῖς νεοττοὶ ὠμμένοι εἰσὶν [ēdē kai treis neottoi ōmmenoi eisin], sometimes even three eagle chicks have been seen. Pliny also: They lay three eggs and hatch two chicks; three have sometimes been seen as well. Indeed, in Plutarch, Marius relates that once, when very young, he ὑποδέξασθαι τῷ ἱματίῳ καταφερομένην ἀετοῦ νεοττίαν ἑπτὰ νεοττοὺς ἔχουσαν [hypodexasthai tō himatiō katapheromenēn aetou neottian hepta neottous echousan], caught in his toga an eagle's nest that had fallen down, with seven chicks. Of the same kind is what Julius Capitolinus reports of Clodius Albinus: Seven little eagles were brought from a nest and set, as if in play, around the boy's cradle. The Arabs write that the melanaeetus, of the three it hatches, mostly rears two. So Damir from Ibnozohar: العقاب تبيض ثلاث بيضات في [al-ʿuqāb tabīḍu thalāth bayḍāt fī] الغالب وتحضنها ثلاثين يوما وما عداها من الجوارح تبيض بيضتين وتحضن عشرين يوما [al-ghālib wa-taḥḍunuhā thalāthīn yawman wa-mā ʿadāhā min al-jawāriḥ tabīḍu bayḍatayn wa-taḥḍunu ʿishrīn yawman] فاذا خرجت فراخ العقاب القت واحدا منها لانه يثقل عليها طعم الثلاث [fa-idhā kharajat firākh al-ʿuqāb alqat wāḥidan minhā li-annahu yathqulu ʿalayhā ṭuʿm al-thalāth] Alokab (that is, the melanaeetus) mostly lays three eggs, which it incubates for thirty days, whereas other birds of prey lay only two eggs, which they incubate for twenty days. And when the chicks of alokab are hatched, it throws out one of them, because it is burdensome for it to feed three. So two remain, which it undertakes to rear.

There follows in the Prophet: Taking them up, it carries them on its wings. Literally, it takes him up, it carries him. But him means any one of them. Or him means them, by an enallage of number. Or it refers to the more remote noun, that is, to nest, a word which we have said means the brood. Upon its feathers, or upon its wings. In Hebrew, על אברתו. The Greeks: ἐπὶ τῶν μεταφρένων αὐτοῦ [epi tōn metaphrenōn autou]. Hence Jerome: on its shoulders. For the eagle is thought to carry not only with its beak or talons, but also with its shoulders and wings. Thus in Plutarch, On Civil Instruction: Αἰσώπου βασίλισκος ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων τοῦ ἀετοῦ κομισθεὶς [Aisōpou basiliskos epi tōn ōmōn tou aetou komistheis], Aesop's wren, carried on the shoulders of the eagle, etc. In Aelian, Hist. book 12, ch. 21, when Tilgamus, a Babylonian boy, was falling headlong from the top of the citadel, ὁ αἰετὸς, πρὶν ἢ τῇ γῇ προσαῤῥαχθῆναι τὸ βρέφος, ὑπῆλθεν αὐτὸ, καὶ τὰ νῶτα ὑπέβαλεν [ho aietos, prin ē tē gē prosarrhachthēnai to brephos, hypēlthen auto, kai ta nōta hypebalen] (or κατὰ νῶτα ὑπέλαβεν [kata nōta hypelaben], as it reads in Apostolius, Proverb 1793), before he was dashed against the ground, the eagle came beneath him and caught him on its back. Aristomenes too, in Pausanias' Messeniaca, when he had been thrown by the Lacedaemonians into the Caeadas: ὄρνιθα τὸν ἀετὸν ὑποπέτεσθαί (φασι) καὶ ἀνέχειν ταῖς πτέρυξιν, ἐς ὃ κατήνεγκεν αὐτὸν ἐς τὸ πέρας, οὔτε πηρωθέντα οὐδὲν τοῦ σώματος, οὔτε τραῦμα ἐπιλαβόντα [ornitha ton aeton hypopetesthai (phasi) kai anechein tais pteryxin, es ho katēnenken auton es to peras, oute pērōthenta ouden tou sōmatos, oute trauma epilabonta], they say that an eagle flew beneath him and held him up with its wings until it had brought him down to the bottom neither maimed nor injured in any part. I do not offer these as true, but as fables invented by people who were convinced that it is not foreign to the eagle's nature to carry something on its shoulders and wings in flight itself. Yet I by no means think that the chicks are carried by eagles in continuous transport. It is only likely that those eager to fly, and failing in the very attempt, are caught and held up by their parents' wings until, having regained courage, they dare to commit themselves to the air again. R. Selomo offers something else, more subtle than solid: כשבא ליטלן ממקום למקום אינו נוטלן ברגליו כשאר עופות לפי ששאר עופות יראים מן הנשר שהוא מגביה לעוף ופורח עליהם לפיכך נושאין ברגליו מפני הנשר אבל הנשר אינו ירא אלא מן החץ לפיכך נושאן על כנפיו אומר מוטב שיכנס החץ בי ולא יכנס בבני, When the eagle moves its chicks from place to place, it does not carry them in its feet as other birds do, because these fear the eagle, which soars aloft in flight and flies higher than they; and therefore they carry their chicks in their feet, so as not to expose them to the eagle. But the eagle fears nothing except the arrow; that is why it carries its chicks on its wings, as if saying to itself: Better that the arrow strike me than my chicks. But this invention does not please me, because neither does the eagle on its back, nor do other birds in their feet, usually move their chicks from place to place by deliberate design. And if they did, they would do it by the sole guidance of nature, not for the reasons alleged, about which no one will persuade me that birds reflect. In Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: The tuci (as he calls cuckoos with an old Spanish word) have a set time of coming, carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and small flights, lest, exhausted over long stretches of air, they should fail. If this were reported by a reliable writer, it would shed no little light on what has been said about the eagle carrying its chicks. But apart from Isidore, a writer hardly skilled in natural history, none of the older authors is found asserting the same. Yet, if we believe Aelian, Hist. book 7, ch. 17, their mates the ceryli, worn out by old age, αἱ ἀλκυόνες περιάγουσιν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῶν τῶν καλουμένων μετοπτερυγίων [hai alkyones periagousin ep᾽ autōn tōn kaloumenōn metopterygiōn], the halcyons carry about upon what are called the interscapulars. Hence Plutarch on the halcyon in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals: Ὅταν δὲ διὰ γῆρας ἀσθενὴς ὁ ἄῤῥην γένηται, συνέπεσθαι καὶ βαρὺς, ὑπολαβοῦσα γηροφορεῖ, καὶ γηροτροφεῖ [Hotan de dia gēras asthenēs ho arrhēn genētai, synepesthai kai barys, hypolabousa gērophorei, kai gērotrophei]; taking up the male, now heavy with years and following with difficulty, she carries and feeds him. And long before, Antigonus had taught the same, Hist. 27: Τῶν δὲ ἀλκυόνων οἱ ἄρσενες κήρυλοι καλοῦνται. ὅτ᾽ ἂν οὖν ὑπὸ τοῦ γήρως ἀσθενήσωσι, καὶ μηκέτι δύνωνται πέτεσθαι, φέρουσιν αὐτοὺς αἱ θήλειαι, ἐπὶ τῶν πτερῶν λαβοῦσαι [Tōn de alkyonōn hoi arsenes kēryloi kalountai. hot᾽ an oun hypo tou gērōs asthenēsōsi, kai mēketi dynōntai petesthai, pherousin autous hai thēleiai, epi tōn pterōn labousai]; The males of the halcyons are called ceryli. When they are weak from old age and can no longer fly, the females take them up on their wings and carry them. Hence that well-known saying of Alcman, quoted in the same place: Οὔ μ᾽ ἔτι παρθενικαὶ [Ou m᾽ eti parthenikai], etc. The same is also told of storks. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, on the Birds: Οἱ γὰρ πελαργοὶ, δικαιοπραγεῖς ὄντες, ἐπὶ πτερῶν βαδίζουσι τοὺς πατέρας γεγηρακότας βαστάζοντες [Hoi gar pelargoi, dikaioprageis ontes, epi pterōn badizousi tous pateras gegērakotas bastazontes]; Storks, since they observe justice, migrate carrying on their wings their fathers, worn out with age. So also Suidas under Ἀντιπελαργεῖν [Antipelargein]. And Basil, Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τὴν δυνατὴν καὶ ἐν τῇ πτήσει παρέχονται βοήθειαν, ἠρέμα τῷ πτερῷ κουφίζοντες ἑκατέρωθεν [Tēn dynatēn kai en tē ptēsei parechontai boētheian, ērema tō pterō kouphizontes hekaterōthen]. And Eustathius of Antioch: Εἰ δὲ τῇ πτήσει ὑποκάτωθεν αὐτὸν ὑποβαστάζουσιν, καὶ τοῖς ἰδίοις πτεροῖς ἠρέμα αὐτὸν ὑποκουφίζουσιν ἑκατέρωθεν [Ei de tē ptēsei hypokatōthen auton hypobastazousin, kai tois idiois pterois ērema auton hypokouphizousin hekaterōthen]. From the same source Ambrose, Hexaemeron book 5, ch. 16: so that, lifting up the old one from this side and that with the prop of their wings, they exercise him in flying. Tacitus also tells the fable that the phoenix takes up its father's body. That is why Artemidorus declares that whoever sees a phoenix in his dreams will be reduced to such poverty that he will be forced, after the manner of the phoenix, to carry out his parent's corpse on his own shoulders. See the distinguished Vossius on Mela, p. 297.

After pulling out so many thorns, and to refresh the reader somewhat, who has long been detained by these trifles and quibbles, I should like to render the passage of Moses that we have explained in the words of a most celebrated poet , who in the last century wrote an excellent paraphrase of the Song of Moses:

And as the prince of birds, the tawny armour-bearer of the Thunderer, cherishes with anxious care his featherless and still feeble young, and indulges them with feasts of rich game; then, when the clothed-headed chicks have grown in strength of wing, if a gentler breeze calls, he invites them with spread plumage, takes the lingering ones upon his back and raises them on his shoulders, and with favourable beat is borne over the fields, fearing for his burden, and yet with checked impetus slowing the oarage of his wings, and gathering the curved sails of his pinions, he swims through the low regions beneath the clouds. Thence he gradually seeks the heights above: and now beneath the stars he rises, and swiftly presses his light course into the air, flying far and wide over all places, and in varied formation carries his offspring to and fro, and teaches them the manner of flying. And they, taught by long habit, little by little begin to entrust themselves on their wings to the sky, fearless. So much does care from tender years avail.

While Moses so highly commends the φιλοστοργίαν [philostorgian] of eagles, he will perhaps seem to agree little with the writers on nature, who hold quite the opposite. For they describe the eagle as a bird wholly ἄστοργον [astorgon] and pitiless. Aristotle, book 9, chapter 34: Ἐκβάλλει (τὰ τέκνα) ὁ ἀετὸς πρὸ ὥρας, ἔτι βίου δεόμενα, καὶ οὔπω δυνάμενα πέτεσθαι· ἐκβάλλειν δὲ δοκεῖ τοὺς νεοττοὺς ὁ ἀετὸς διὰ φθόνον· φύσει γάρ ἐστι φθονερὸς, καὶ ὀξύπεινος [Ekballei (ta tekna) ho aetos pro hōras, eti biou deomena, kai oupō dynamena petesthai; ekballein de dokei tous neottous ho aetos dia phthonon; physei gar esti phthoneros, kai oxypeinos]. The eagle casts out its chicks before it is time, while they still need feeding and have not yet acquired the power of flight; and it seems to cast them out from envy. For by nature it is envious and ravenous. And a little later: Φθονεῖ οὖν τοῖς νεοττοῖς ἁδρυνομένοις, ὅτι φαγεῖν ἀγαθοὶ γίνονται, καὶ σπᾷ τοῖς ὄνυξι [Phthonei oun tois neottois hadrynomenois, hoti phagein agathoi ginontai, kai spa tois onyxi]; It envies its chicks, then, as they grow up, because they are very voracious, and it plucks at them with its talons. Likewise: Ὁ δὲ ἐκβάλλει, καὶ κόπτει αὐτοὺς· οἱ δὲ ἐκβαλλόμενοι βοῶσι, καὶ οὕτως ὑπολαμβάνει αὐτοὺς ἡ φήνη [Ho de ekballei, kai koptei autous; hoi de ekballomenoi boōsi, kai houtōs hypolambanei autous hē phēnē]. It casts them out and beats them; the ejected ones cry out, and so the ossifrage takes them up. Accordingly Basil, in the eighth Homily on the Hexaemeron: Ἀδικώτατος περὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκγόνων ἐκτροφὴν ὁ ἀετός [Adikōtatos peri tēn tōn ekgonōn ektrophēn ho aetos]. So too Eustathius, Hexaem. p. 26. But I am not without a reply to these. In Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 40, you may read a whole chapter Περὶ τῆς τῶν αἰετῶν στοργῆς [Peri tēs tōn aietōn storgēs], On the love of eagles for their chicks, in which among other things this is found: Ζηλοτυπώτατον δέ ἐστι ζῶον ἀετὸς περὶ τὰ νεόττια. ἐὰν γοῦν θεάσηταί τινα προσιόντα, ἀπελθεῖν ἀτιμώρητον οὐκ ἐπιτρέπει· παίει γὰρ τοῖς πτεροῖς αὐτὸν, καὶ τοῖς ὄνυξι λυμαίνεται [Zēlotypōtaton de esti zōon aetos peri ta neottia. ean goun theasētai tina prosionta, apelthein atimōrēton ouk epitrepei; paiei gar tois pterois auton, kai tois onyxi lymainetai]. Of all animals it shows the greatest devotion to its young. Therefore it fiercely pursues anyone it sees to have invaded its nest, and does not let him go unpunished: for it beats him with its wings and tears him with its talons. Almost the same is related by Apostolius, Cent. 2, Prov. 6. Oppian too, On Hunting, book 3, line 115, in his list of birds that cherish their little ones with constant love, places eagles in these words:

Πῶς δ᾽ ἄρ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι ποθὴν ἀλίαστον ἔχουσιν ῟Ων τεκέων φῆναί τε, βαρύφθογγοί τε πέλειαι, Αἰετόεντά τε φῦλα· — — — — [Pōs d᾽ ar en oiōnoisi pothēn aliaston echousin / Hōn tekeōn phēnai te, baryphthongoi te peleiai, / Aietoenta te phyla]

Just as among birds, too, both the ossifrage and the deep-voiced doves and the races of eagles have a constant love for their offspring. Truly, then, does Jerome say on Isaiah, chapter 66: Those who have written on the nature of animals say that an affection for their offspring and young is inborn in all beasts, beasts of burden, cattle and birds, but that the greatest love is that of eagles. But, what is most to the point, Suidas, under the word Εὔξενος [Euxenos], has this about the eagle's chicks, without naming his author: Οἱ νέοι τῶν ἀετῶν ἐν ἁπαλῷ μὲν τῷ πτερῷ παραπέτονται τοῖς γειναμένοις, μελετώμενοι ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν τὴν πτῆσιν· [Hoi neoi tōn aetōn en hapalō men tō pterō parapetontai tois geinamenois, meletōmenoi hyp᾽ autōn tēn ptēsin] The chicks of eagles, while their feathers are still weak, fly about their parents, learning flight from them. These words are so similar to those of Moses that they could seem to have been copied either from Moses himself or from some translator of Moses. In fact he took them from Philostratus, Apollonius, book 1, chapter 5, where they are read word for word. Yet Philostratus had not read Moses; rather, both described the nature of eagles in this respect. Not unlike this is what Albertus reports he saw: a goshawk, that is, a larger hawk, which threw live birds it had caught to its chicks so that they might pursue, catch and kill them, and thus gradually accustom themselves to hunting. Against this it is objected in vain that Aristotle says the eagle throws its chicks out of the nest when they grow up. Nor is that true without qualification. Rather, out of two or three it throws out one, because it is not able to rear more, just as the ancient Romans exposed those of their children whom they were unable to bring up. The Philosopher himself teaches this, Hist. book 6, ch. 6: Ἐκβάλλει δ᾽ αὐξανομένων τὸν ἕτερον τῶν νεοττῶν, ἀχθόμενος τῇ ἐδωδῇ· [Ekballei d᾽ auxanomenōn ton heteron tōn neottōn, achthomenos tē edōdē] When the chicks grow up, it throws one out, weary of feeding it. For during the time of rearing the mother is often burdened, and almost overwhelmed, by very severe hardships, as follows in the Philosopher: Λέγεται ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ τούτῳ ἄπαστος γίνεσθαι, ὅπως μὴ ἁρπάζῃ τοὺς τῶν θηρίων σκύμνους. οἵ τε οὖν ὄνυχες αὐτοῦ διαστρέφονται ὀλίγας ἡμέρας, καὶ τὰ πτερὰ λευκαίνεται. [Legetai en tō chronō toutō apastos ginesthai, hopōs mē harpazē tous tōn thēriōn skymnous. hoi te oun onyches autou diastrephontai oligas hēmeras, kai ta ptera leukainetai.] Pliny imitates this as follows: For at that time nature has denied them food, taking care that the young of all wild beasts should not be carried off. Their talons too are turned back during those days, and their feathers turn white from want of food. If, then, in these straits the mother throws out one of the chicks, she is forced to it by sheer necessity, as when for fear of shipwreck the cargo is thrown into the sea, as in Jonah 1:5 and Acts 27:19 Ambrose, in the place cited above, gives another answer: namely, that the eagle casts out only those which, when exposed to the rays of the sun, turn their eyes away as degenerate; and so it becomes harsh not from stinginess in feeding but from the test of judgment; nor does it, as it were, disown its own chick when it expels it from the nest, but rejects it as a stranger's.
Mystical eagles: God, the angels, the faithful, great kings, above all the Assyrian king and the forces of the Assyrians.

Because of the wonderful endowments we have noted in the eagle, whatever is lofty in heaven or most excellent on earth (God, that is, the angels, the faithful, empires and the greatest kings) is compared with the eagle by the sacred writers. Thus God says to the Israelites, whom he had led out of Egypt, Exod 19:4. You have seen what I have done to the Egyptians, and how I bore you up on eagles' wings, i.e. ὡσεὶ ἐπὶ πτερύγων ἀετοῦ [hōsei epi pterygōn aetou], as upon eagles' wings, as the Greeks rightly render it, and the three Chaldees, and the Syriac, and one of the Arabic versions, adding the mark of comparison, which must necessarily be supplied in this place. Yet the divine writer did not suppress it without reason. That is, so that the comparison might be more vivid and strike the mind more, he attributes to God eagle's wings, with which he carried the Israelites from Egypt into Arabia. So that we may know that he behaved toward his people in the same way as the eagle usually does toward its brood. For Scripture is accustomed to give the thing signified the name of the sign, and in turn to give the sign the name of the thing signified. Further, the reason for the figure is explained in various ways. Some refer it to the eagle's swiftness, because God had led so many myriads of people out of Egypt in a single day. Others to the ease of its flight, because this was done without any effort, and Israel had escaped from so monstrous a servitude as easily as the eagle flies. Others to the eagle's lofty flight, by which it carries both itself and its chicks beyond all range of missiles. For so God had preserved his own with a mighty hand, and had set them, as it were, on high, so that the weapons of the enemy might not reach them. Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrases (παραφράζει [paraphrazei]) the words of the sacred text thus: טעית יתכון על עננין היך על גדפי נשרין מן פילוסין, I carried you upon clouds, as upon eagles' wings, from the city of Pelusium. Not much differently the Jerusalem translator. That is, they invent for themselves this miracle, about which Scripture is entirely silent: that God carried the Israelites upon clouds from the region of Pelusium all the way to Mount Sinai. Nor are there lacking those who observe that of two chicks the eagle feeds and rears only one, casting out the other, so as to refer this to God, who loved Jacob and hated Esau, content to choose one of two peoples and acknowledge it as his own. But no one is a better interpreter of the words of Moses than Moses himself, in these words of his Song, Deut 32:11. As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young with outspread wings, and takes them and carries them on its pinions, so the Lord alone led him, etc. He made him ride on the heights of the earth etc. Since what is said there of the eagle has already been explained, it remains for us to show how these things apply to God. Nor is the matter obscure. The eagle rouses with its cry the chicks lying sluggish in the filth of the nest, to provoke them to flight. So God, by his word, stirred up the Israelites, so oppressed by wretched servitude that they did not aspire to liberation, to obey the champions of liberty raised up for them by God. The eagle hovers over its chicks with outspread wings. So the Spirit moves over those in whom he works effectually. For Moses uses the same word when he says at the creation that the Spirit of God moved upon the waters. And that power of the divine Spirit bent the Israelites, otherwise intractable, to obedience. Moreover, he spread over them the wings of his providence, of which Scripture speaks so often. As when in Ruth 2:12 she is said to have come under the wings of God to shelter herself. And when the godly are said to be hidden, to take refuge, to sing, and to be protected under the shadow or in the covert of his wings, Ps 17:8 and XXXVI, 8. and LVII, 2. and LXI, 5. and LXIII, 8. and XCI, 4. etc. This was signified by the cloud that covered the Israelites, Num 14:14. Finally, with the same wings he carried them on this journey, as the eagle carries its chicks, whenever he kept them from falling or from stumbling on a slippery and rough road exposed to many dangers. Accordingly you read elsewhere that God carried them in his arms, like παῖδας ὑπαγκαλίους [paidas hypankalious]. Thus Deut 1:31. The Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his little son, all the way that you went until you came to this place. And Hos 11:1 3. When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son, etc. Where the Chaldee paraphrase has: And I, through an angel sent from my presence, led Israel by a fitting way: ונטלתנון כר על דרעין, and I carried them as upon arms. Indeed, it is said to the godly man in Ps 91:11. He has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone. It should be noted that, as in the Law, so also in the Gospel the church is compared to chicks which the mother warms and protects under her wings. But in the Law that mother is an eagle, and in the Gospel a hen; and thus, as they would have it, the different dispensation under each Testament is foreshadowed. The one of power, which God displayed when he led his people out of Egypt with a strong right hand and an outstretched arm and brought them into the promised land. The other of grace, when Christ came lowly, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself even to the death of the cross. Yet in such a way that in both God's supreme love shines forth, and the care he takes of his own. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that in the New Testament too God sometimes delivers his own with power. Accordingly, as the Jewish church, when on the point of being crushed by Pharaoh, was borne up on eagles' wings and carried into the desert, so in Rev 22:14 the Christian church too is given two great wings, with which to fly into the desert from the sight of the dragon. Of him Pharaoh, king of Egypt, was a figure, who himself is also called a dragon in Ezek 29:3.

Second, that angels are signified by eagles is shown by the description of the four living creatures in Ezekiel and the Apocalypse , which we have explained elsewhere. Hence in Rev 8:13, where the common reading is Καὶ εἶδον, καὶ ἤκουσα ἑνὸς ἀγγέλου πετωμένου ἐν μεσουρανήματι [Kai eidon, kai ēkousa henos angelou petōmenou en mesouranēmati], instead of ἑνὸς ἀγγέλου [henos angelou] a Spanish manuscript of the highest quality, and following it the Complutensian and Plantin editions, have ἑνὸς ἀετοῦ [henos aetou]. So also Arethas in his Commentary on the Apocalypse, chapter 25. Nor did the Syriac and the Ethiopic read otherwise. Finally the old version has: I heard the voice of one eagle, flying through the midst of heaven, saying, etc. Both readings seem admissible: the one teaches that an angel appeared to John; the other, that this angel had the form of an eagle, which suits an angel exceedingly well because of its swiftness, strength and longevity, its τὸ ὀξυδερκὲς [to oxyderkes], its τὸ ὑψιπετὲς [to hypsipetes], and whatever else the eagle has in common with the angelic nature.

Third, the faithful seem to be signified by the name of eagles in the words of Christ, Matt 24:28. For wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together. Of the many interpretations of this passage, the one I like best is that of Beza, by which this verse and the preceding one are connected with verse 26 as follows. If any should whisper that Christ is to be sought here or there, as though he were in hiding, do not believe it; for Christ will show himself openly, like lightning flashing from the east to the west and illuminating the whole world. And just as eagles fly at once to a carcass with wonderful keenness of scent, so in the end all the godly will likewise have to run together when they perceive the life-giving savour of the death of Christ. And not without reason are those who gather to Christ called eagles, since no one is united with him except one who feeds on his flesh and blood. Accordingly Jerome takes πτῶμα [ptōma], or carcass, to mean the passion of Christ. And Chrysostom, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, Homily 28, says that the body of Christ is called πτῶμα [ptōma] on account of his death. Applying this to the eucharistic communion of Christ, he adds that the faithful are called eagles, to show that he who approaches this body must strive towards the heights, and must have nothing in common with the earth, nor be drawn down to lower things and creep; but must always fly to higher things, gaze upon the sun of righteousness, and have the eye of the mind most sharp. Ἀετῶν γὰρ, οὐ κολοιῶν αὕτη ἡ τράπεζα [Aetōn gar, ou koloiōn hautē hē trapeza]· For this table is for eagles, not for jackdaws. In Luke 17:37, where the Evangelist repeats the same saying of Christ, he has τὸ σῶμα [to sōma] instead of τὸ πτῶμα [to ptōma]. But it comes to the same thing. For Homer, Xenophon, Plutarch, Porphyry and other Greek writers commonly use τὸ σῶμα [to sōma] for a carcass.

Fourth, eagles in Scripture are sometimes great kings. Thus in Ezek 17:3 A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of feathers, of various colours, is the king of Babylon, as the same prophet explains in verse twelve. Again, in verse seven, A great eagle, with great wings and many feathers is the king of Egypt, on the interpretation of the same prophet in verse fifteen. And the reason for the likeness is obvious to everyone. For the eagle is powerful in strength, excels in swiftness, is keen of sight and fearless of spirit, and in the whole bearing of its body displays a certain royal majesty. Hence it is believed to hold dominion over the birds, as was proved at length at the beginning of this book . And the Persian kings had a golden eagle with outspread wings as their royal standard, as we have shown elsewhere from Xenophon, Curtius and Philostratus. Nor is it unlikely that the ancient kings of Assyria had this same standard, and that Scripture alludes to it whenever it designates them by the name of eagles: as in the words of Ezekiel just cited, A great eagle, etc.; and Dan 7:4, where it is said of the first beast, which foreshadowed the Babylonian empire, And it had the wings of an eagle; and Hos 8:1 The trumpet to your throat (say, set it there), As an eagle (he swoops) upon the house of the Lord. Here the Chaldee paraphrast has: O prophet, cry out with your throat as with a trumpet, and say, Behold! like an eagle that moves itself to and fro, so shall the king (of Assyria, Nebuchadnezzar) go up with his army, and encamp against the house of the sanctuary of the Lord. And Jer 48:40 As an eagle he has swooped, and he shall spread out his wings over the Moabites. And Jer 49:22 He shall go up as an eagle, and swoop, and spread out his wings over Botsra. That is, like an eagle he rushed with force upon the prey before him, and brought his wars to an end with marvellous speed. And Ezekiel rightly calls that eagle great, because Nebuchadnezzar was a most powerful king; and he assigns him great wings, that is, great armies. As in Isa 8:8 His wings shall fill the breadth of your land. Wings, that is, forces. These things, indeed, the Egyptian king had in common with the Assyrian. So the Egyptian too is called a great eagle and with great wings. But the Assyrian had longer pinions and of more colours, that is, a greater dominion, extending over more peoples. And accordingly Ezekiel ascribes the length and variety of the pinions to him as his own. Note in passing that, like the Persian and Roman commanders of old, the Greeks also had the eagle as a military standard, if we believe Seneca in the Thebaid, where he says of the seven commanders at Thebes, in verse 389:

— — — now the bronze trumpets stir up war, and the eagle, as standard-bearer, set in motion, calls to battle. Fifth, the Chaldeans and Assyrians who, under the leadership of Nebuchadnezzar, laid waste all Judaea, levelled Jerusalem to the ground and consumed the temple with fire, are often compared by the Prophets to eagles hastening to their food and swooping upon their prey. See Ier. IV, 13. Lam 4:19. Hab 1:8. Therefore these threats of the law also refer to them, Deut 28:49 The Lord will raise up against you a distant nation, which will swoop like an eagle from the furthest ends of the earth. And Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] is mistaken in referring this to Alexander, relying on a futile reason, namely that the Prophet's words ידאה הנשר, that is, the eagle will swoop, are ἰσόψηφοι [isopsēphoi] with the word עשרה, that is, ten; and Alexander completed a ten days' march in one day. But after the death of Nebuchadnezzar those eagle's wings of the Assyrians were gradually plucked off, as Daniel VII, 4. had foretold, and their empire was utterly overthrown by the Persians.
It is proved that פרס peres is the ossifrage.

In the list of unclean birds פרס peres is second in order. The Greeks render it τὸν γρύπα [ton grypa]. Hence Jerome, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] and Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] have "griffin". So too, among the Hebrews, Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], who holds that Perusia, a town of the Etruscans, took its name from it, and therefore has the פרס peres, or griffin, in its arms. Yet Origen, book 4 Against Celsus, rightly observes that the griffin has never ὑποχείριον ἀνθρώπων γεγονέναι [hypocheirion anthrōpōn gegonenai]. And whatever those most frivolous writers Ctesias and Aristeas of Proconnesus relate about griffins, Pliny, Arrian and Pausanias quite rightly reject as fabulous, as we show elsewhere. This rendering, therefore, cannot stand, unless by the name gryps [griffin] something other than the common meaning is understood, namely γρυπαίετος [grypaietos], that is, an eagle with a remarkably hooked beak. For that is properly γρυπότης [grypotēs]. The beak, of course, usually has the same hookedness as the talons. Further, I think those ancient interpreters conjectured that the name פרס peres signifies a bird with especially large talons because the Hebrew פרסה parsa, "hoof", is written with almost the same letters. But this conjecture pleases me less, because פרסה parsa is only the hoof of quadrupeds, while that of birds is צפרן tsipporen, in Chaldee טפר tephar, Dan 4:30.

For the Samaritan, פרס peres is ࠁࠆࠀࠄ [בזאה] bezaa, the hawk; so too for Münster and Schindler. But for Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] it is עוזא uza, of which in the next chapter. For the Arabs it is عقاب [ʿuqāb] okab, the melanaeetus. For the Jews in Germany it is בלאבֿוז blafus, as if you were to say "blue-foot". So they call a kind of falcon from its blue feet, of which Albertus says: The ninth kind of falcons, already falling short of the excellence of the noble falcons, is the one whose feet are hyacinthine or azure, etc. By the Italians, according to Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], it is called zafiro from the sapphire colour of its feet. Following this, Diodati rendered it "falcon" in his Italian version, and "gerfalcon" in the French. The first origin of this rendering will now be explained. The old French word pers, derived from prasinus [leek-green], first meant a green, then also a blue colour. When the Jews, who once lived in large numbers in France, noticed this, those witless men inferred that the bird פרס peres is at least partly blue in colour, as if our pers for blue were formed from the Hebrew. This is utterly absurd. But raving is customary with those men. And by no less ridiculous an error David de Pomis [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587), a Hebrew-Latin-Italian dictionary] recently asserted that this very word פרס peres produced the name of Perusia (an old town of the Etruscans, mentioned besides Ptolemy by Silius, Appian, Eutropius, Stephanus and others).

From the same flock, someone cited by Münster decided that the פרס peres is a bird found only in Persia, as if פרס peres alluded to the Hebrew word for Persia, פרס paras. But this conjecture too is empty, for two reasons. 1. Because the name of Persia is about nine hundred years more recent than Moses: it arose in the time of Cyrus, who first taught his countrymen to ride. Hence those who were formerly Cuthaeans, or Cissians, Susians and Elamites began to be called פרסין or פרשין, Persians or horsemen, as we proved in our Phaleg. 2. Because Moses would not have forbidden the Jews a bird peculiar to Persia, which is immensely distant from Judaea. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that a certain bird had its name from Persia, which Aristophanes in the Birds calls Περσικὸν ὄρνιν [Persikon ornin]. But the Scholiast writes that some understand τὸν ἀλεκτρυόνα [ton alektryona], others τὸν ταῶ [ton taō], the peacock; both of these birds are clean, whereas the peres is unclean.

Now it is worth knowing why Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] renders פרס, peres, "ossifrage", and Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] anataria [duck-eagle], which are species of eagles. The verb פרס paras, from which פרס peres comes, first means to divide and to distribute, then also to break, because things are divided by breaking. Castalio had this in view, because Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, writes of the duck-eagle: It has the habit of breaking tortoises it has seized by dropping them from on high, a fate which killed the poet Aeschylus. But Junius, as if פרס peres were named from distributing, gives this reason for his rendering in his Notes: The ossifrage has its name from distributing, because Pliny attributes this to the creature: The related kind, the ossifrages, take in the young cast out by the eagles and rear them with their own. Yet in these words of Pliny there is not even a γρῦ [gry] about distribution, except καθ᾽ ἀκολούθησιν [kath᾽ akolouthēsin]; for since the ossifrage feeds strange young with its own, it must divide the food between both. Nor is the name of the ossifrage from distributing, but from the breaking of bones, as everyone knows.

Having thus set out the opinions of others, we shall here also present our own and try to support it with suitable arguments. First, I side with those who hold that פרס peres is a species of eagle. Among them are the Greeks, Jerome, the Chaldeans, the Arabs and most of the more recent writers. In favour of this is the fact that among the Macedonians, who enriched from the spoils of the East not only their wealth but also their language, the eagle was called παραὸς [paraos], in manifest allusion to the Hebrew פרס peres. Hesychius: Παραός· ἀετὸς ὑπὸ Μακεδόνων· [Paraos; aetos hypo Makedonōn;] Paraos, the eagle among the Macedonians. Moreover, just as by universal agreement נשר denotes the true eagle, so it is very probable that the words immediately following in Moses, namely פרס and עזניה, designate other species of eagles known to the Jews. Nor is it safe to oppose so many interpreters who hold this view. Let it stand firm, then, that פרס is among the species of eagles. But now we must inquire into the species, which can be extracted from nothing else than the origin of the word, since apart from the bare name we have nothing whatever about it. And Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] rightly notes that the origin is to be taken from these words of Es. LVIII, 7: פרוס לרעב לחמך Break your bread for the hungry. By this note he meant to indicate that it is a kind of eagle so called from breaking. But to make the matter clearer, consider, reader, these words of Mic 3:3, which it is surprising have not yet been cited in this discussion: ואת עצמותיהם פצחו ופרשו כאשר בסיר וכבשר בתוך קלחת, And they broke their bones and shattered them as in a pot, and as flesh in the midst of a cauldron. From this it is evident that the verb פרס (or פרש with Sin Semol, which is the same) is also used of the breaking of bones. From this, then, there is no one who would not conclude that פרס peres is the ossifrage, that is, that species of eagle which from breaking bones is called in the Roman tongue ossifraga or ossifragus [bone-breaker], and in Arabic either simply كاسر [kāsir], that is, breaker, or كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones . Thus Junius rightly rendered it ossifrage, although the true reason for this rendering escaped him. And perhaps it bears on the same point that for פרס Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] and the Jerusalem Targum have ער or עריא. For the words ער and עריא, with the radicals inverted, could have been derived from the verbs רעע or רעה, which mean to break and to crush. Of the ossifrage Lucretius writes thus, book 5, line 1077:
Lastly the race of winged things, and the various birds, hawks and ossifrages — — —

And Pliny uses it throughout, as in book 10, ch. 3, where he speaks of the haliaeetus: That which is born from them has its kind among the ossifrages. And a little later: Some add a kind of eagle which they call the bearded eagle; the Tuscans, however, call it the ossifrage. And again, where he speaks of the chicks that eagles throw out because they are weary of feeding them: When they have been thrown out by these, the related kind of the ossifrage takes them up and rears them with its own. And in ch. 7: Some think that the immussulus is the chick of the vulture, and the sanqualis that of the ossifrage. Likewise Massurius says that the sanqualis is the ossifrage. And in book 30, ch. 7: The ossifrage has a single intestine of wonderful nature, which digests everything it has swallowed. And a little before: The stomach of the ossifrage, dried and taken in drink, is very useful to those who do not digest their food. And in the chapter immediately following he prescribes that the same be taken to expel stones. Isidore too, book 12, ch. 7: The bird that drops bones from on high and breaks them is commonly called ossifrangus (read ossifragus), and hence it received its name from breaking bones. See also Festus under the words immussulus and sanqualis. Ossifragus is rendered in Greek in one Glossary as ὀστοκόπος [ostokopos], ὀστοκλάστης [ostoklastēs], ὀστοκατεάκτης [ostokateaktēs]; in another, but wrongly, as ὀστοκόραξ [ostokorax]; in Dioscorides as φίνις [phinis]. Φίνις [Phinis], he says, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον [to orneon, ho Rhōmaisti kalousin ossiphragon]. And among older writers it is φήνη [phēnē], a word very well known from Homer and Aristotle, and one which the Arabs also use. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], from Ibnosaida [=Ibn Sīda (d. 1066), lexicographer, as cited by al-Damīrī]: الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فاذا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن [al-fīna ṭāyir yushbih al-ʿuqāb fa-idhā khāfa al-bard inḥadara ilā al-Yaman] Phena, a bird resembling the eagle, which, when it fears the cold, goes off to Ieman, that is, to Arabia Felix. But it is commonly called, as we have said, كاسر [kāsir] breaker, and كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām] breaker of bones. Also مكلفة [mukallafa] mechalapha, from its black colour mixed with reddish or yellowish. Damir: الكاسر العقاب [al-kāsir al-ʿuqāb] Alchasir (or breaker) is a kind of eagle. The same elsewhere: كاسر العظام المكلفة [kāsir al-ʿiẓām al-mukallafa] The breaker of bones, that is, the mechalepha. And in the chapter On the mechalepha: الفرخ الذي ترمي به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه [al-farkh alladhī tarmī bihi al-ʿuqāb min al-thalatha yaḥḍunuhu ṭāyir yuqāl lahu al-mukallafa wa-yuqāl lahu kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-turabbīhi] The chick which the eagle has thrown out of the three is warmed and fed by a bird which is called mechalepha and breaker of bones. And in the chapter العقاب [al-ʿuqāb], or On the eagle: والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر [wa-al-ʿarab yusammī al-ʿuqāb al-kāsir] The Arabs also call the eagle (that is, a species of eagle) the breaker. And below: والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه [wa-al-farkh alladhī tulqīhi yaʿṭifu ʿalayhi ṭāyir yusammā kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-yusammā al-mukallafa ayḍan fa-yurabbīhi] And on the chick thrown out by the eagle a bird takes pity, which is named ossifrage and mechalepha, so that it rears it. It is evident that the French orfraye is derived from ossifraga, although among us it denotes something else, namely the haliaeetus or sea eagle. This was observed long ago by Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], On Birds, book 2, ch. 7.
Falcon with yellow cere and half-feathered feet, rust-coloured body, the tail feathers white on the inner side: LINNAEUS, Syst. vol. 1, part 1, p. 255, no. 4, 13th edition.
It is proved that עזניה oznija is not the haliaeetus, as most hold, but the melanaeetus, or Valerian eagle.

Third among the unclean birds is עזניא oznija. The Greeks render it Ἁλιαίετον [Haliaieton], whence Jerome, Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Diodati have haliaeetus or sea eagle; the English have ospray, which is the same; the Genevans have falcon, for what reason I do not well know, unless because some take the sea eagle for a falcon, whom, however, Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] refutes. In the word עזניה oznija the Hebrews note that the Nun is נוסף, that is, epenthetic, and that עזניה oznija is said for עזיה ozja. Accordingly Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] here has עזיה ozja. And it is agreed that this species of eagle is so named from עוז oz, that is, strength. Hence I infer on very probable grounds that it is rather the μελαναίετον [melanaieton], that is, the black eagle, which, though the smallest of eagles, is nevertheless the strongest. For this reason the Romans call it Valeria, as being most powerful (valeat) in strength. Pliny, in the place cited above: "Called melanaeetos by the Greeks, and also Valeria, smallest in size, outstanding in strength, blackish in colour", etc. And before Pliny, the Philosopher, book 9, ch. 32: Ἕτερος δὲ μέλας τὴν χρόαν, καὶ μέγεθος ἐλάχιστος, καὶ κράτιστος τούτων. οὗτος οἰκεῖ ὄρη, καὶ ὕλας· καλεῖται δὲ μελαναίετος, καὶ λαγωφόνος. [Heteros de melas tēn chroan, kai megethos elachistos, kai kratistos toutōn. houtos oikei orē, kai hylas; kaleitai de melanaietos, kai lagōphonos.] "But there is another eagle, black in colour, smallest in size, but most excellent in strength. It inhabits mountains and forests, and is called melanaeetus" (that is, black eagle) "and hare-killer." And before the Philosopher, the greatest Poet, of Achilles, Iliad 21, line 252:
Αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων μέλανος, τοῦ θηρητῆρος· Ὅς θ᾽ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε, καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν· [Aietou oimat' echōn melanos, tou thērētēros; Hos th' hama kartistos te, kai ōkistos peteēnōn;]

"Having the onset of the black eagle, the hunter, which is at once the strongest and swiftest of birds." On this passage Eustathius: Αἰετοῦ μέλανος τῆς θηρητῆρος, ὃν καὶ μελαναίετόν τινες συνθέτως φασὶ, τὸν καὶ φασσοφόνον [Aietou melanos tēs thērētēros, hon kai melanaieton tines synthetōs phasi, ton kai phassophonon] (perhaps one should read λαγωφόνον [lagōphonon]) μικρὸν μέν φασιν ὄντα, τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἰσχυρότερον· [mikron men phasin onta, tōn allōn de ischyroteron;] "Of the black hunting eagle, which some call by a compound word melanaeetus, and dove-killer; small indeed, as they say, but stronger than the others." The old Scholiast of Homer writes that Aristotle, instead of μέλανος τοῦ [melanos tou], read with the words joined μελανόστου [melanostou], meaning that the eagle has black bones, and others μελανόσσου [melanossou], as if with black eyes. But in the extant books of Aristotle nothing similar occurs. And the Poet's reading is tampered with in vain, for it is apt and learned, and brings him into agreement with Aristotle and Pliny in describing the black eagle. Since, then, by their consensus the black eagle is the strongest of all, why should it not have been called עזניה osnija by the Hebrews from its strength, as valeria by the Romans? Moreover, it is not at all likely that this species was omitted by Moses among the eagles, since after that greater and genuine eagle, properly called נשר, this is the most noteworthy (ἀξιομνημονεύτατος [axiomnēmoneutatos]) of all eagles. For besides its exceptional strength it has very many qualities that especially commend it. The Philosopher describes them thus in the place cited: Ἐκτρέφει δὲ μόνος οὗτος τὰ τέκνα, καὶ ἐξάγει· ἔστι δὲ ὠκυβόλος, καὶ εὐθήμων, καὶ ἄφθονος, καὶ ἄφοβος, καὶ μάχιμος, καὶ εὔφημος· οὐ γὰρ μινυρίζει, οὐδὲ λέληκεν. [Ektrephei de monos houtos ta tekna, kai exagei; esti de ōkybolos, kai euthēmōn, kai aphthonos, kai aphobos, kai machimos, kai euphēmos; ou gar minyrizei, oude lelēken.] "This one alone rears and brings out its young. It is also swift, elegant, without envy, without fear, vigorous, of good omen; it neither screams nor murmurs." Accordingly the most distinguished Thuanus, book 1 De re accipitraria, compares it with the chrysaetus thus:

"Excellent, she too equals that one in mighty spirit, though she is inferior in bulk of body, and not so strong in talon, beak or toes; but, not belying her birth nor forgetful of a manly spirit, she makes hawks look bastard by comparison. Her too our people call Valeria, the Greeks μελαναίετον [melanaieton], because in beak, feathers and talon she shows a dark colour" .

It should be noted that both עזניה oznija and פרס peres are taken by some for the griffin, and that accordingly both are rendered עוז uz or עוזא uza, a word that among the paraphrasts and the Talmudists means griffin. Thus in Jonathan's [=Targum Jonathan] paraphrase עוזא uza stands for פרס peres, while in the Samaritan ࠏࠅࠆࠀ [עוזא] uza stands for ࠏࠆࠍࠉࠄ [עזניה] oznija. And in the Talmudic tractate Kelim, ch. 17, § 14, where vessels made מכנף העוז, from the wing of the uz, that is, of the griffin, are discussed, the Glossator has this: עוף הוא ששמו עזניה ורגילים היו לעשות כלים מכנף אותו העוז, It is a bird which (in the sacred text) is called oznija, from whose wings vessels used to be made. Here perhaps instead of מכנף miccanaph (from the wing) we should read מכף miccaph (from the sole). And shortly after, כף העוז מכל הכפים, The sole (of the bird) uz surpasses every other, instead of כנף העוז מכל הכנפים, The wing of the bird uz surpasses every wing. Sole, that is, foot and talon; for that is what כף caph means in birds. So Gen 8:9. The dove found no rest לכף רגלה: and Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] has لكف رجلها [li-kaff rijlihā] for the sole of her foot, that is, τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῆς [tois posin autēs], for her feet, as the Greeks have there. Moreover, they commonly say that vessels are made from the griffin's feet or talons, not from its wings. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], in the chapter On عنقا [ʿanqā] anka, or the Griffin: فيصنع من مخاليبها اقداح عظام للشرب [fa-yuṣnaʿ min makhālībihā aqdāḥ ʿiẓām li-l-shurb] And from its talons large drinking vessels are made. Gesner, on the griffin: John Mandeville writes that its talons are like the horns of an ox, from which cups of great value are made. And shortly after: I remember seeing at a goldsmith's in our city a smooth black horn, hooked at the top, almost as in chamois, perhaps three times as thick, whose rim the goldsmith was about to mount in silver, so that it might be used as a cup at table. It was perhaps the horn of some foreign ox, such as the one they call Indian, or of a buffalo. But he had received it as a griffin's talon. I shall adduce another testimony showing that עזניה oznija is the griffin in the opinion of the Hebrews. In the book בעל החיים, or On the Natures of Animals, which Calonymus translated from the Arabic of Abulsapha into Hebrew, the עזניה oznija, ruling far and wide over the birds of prey, summons them from every side and speaks thus in their council: הנה אני עם גודל גופי ואומץ כוחי ומהירות עופפותי עזבתי בתיהם וברחתי מהם אל האיים הרחוקים ואל ההרים הרמים והנשואים, I indeed, though vast in body, outstanding in strength and swift of wing, have left their (men's) dwellings and fled from them to remote islands and to steep and lofty mountains. Not very differently Maimonides [=Moses Maimonides (Rambam), Mishneh Torah] on the peres and the oznija, in the tractate On Forbidden Foods, ch. 1, § 17: פרס ועזניה אינן מצויין בישוב אלא במדברות איי הים הרחוקות עד מאד שהן סוף הישוב, The Perez and the oznija are not found in the inhabited world (ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ [en tē oikoumenē]), but in the most remote islands of the sea at the farthest edge of the world. It is obvious that this refers to the anca of the Arabs, or griffin, which they fable once lived among men in Arabia and fed on beasts and birds; but when it had once carried off children and even a bride, it was banished at the prayers of the Prophet Handala to an island most remote from human intercourse, from which it is forbidden to come out to betake itself to more cultivated places. Accordingly, for the Hebrew עזניה oznija one reads in the Arabic paraphrases, of Saadia as of others, العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka. And for this reason Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] is angry with Saadia for holding that God forbade הדבר שלא היה, a thing that does not exist. The Arabs themselves admit this. Among them is Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author], by whom العنقا [al-ʿanqā] alanka is defined with an elegant paronomasia as طاير معروف الاسم ومجهول الجسم [ṭāʾir maʿrūf al-ism wa-majhūl al-jism], a bird of known alism, that is, name, but unknown algism, that is, body. And the poet who says الجود والغول والعنقا ثلاثة اسما اشيا لم توجد ولم تكن [al-jūd wa-l-ghūl wa-l-ʿanqā thalātha asmā ashyā lam tūjad wa-lam takun] Liberality, and algol (or empusa) and alanca (or griffin) are three names of things that are not found and exist nowhere. But elsewhere I show that Saadia and the other paraphrasts who use this word can be excused, because, although anca is mostly the name of a fictitious bird, as griffins are for us, yet it sometimes also occurs for a real bird. But whatever they had in mind, this is certain: עזניה oznija in Moses signifies a real bird, and very probably it is the black eagle, which the Greeks call by the compound word μελαναίετον [melanaieton].

You will find the synonyms of the Valerian eagle in Linn. Syst. T. I. vol. I. p. 254, no. 2, under this name: Falco cera lutea pedibusque semilanatis, corpore e ferrugineo nigricante, striis flavis [falcon with yellow cere and half-woolly feet, body blackish from rust-colour, with yellow streaks]. Other conjectures, but less probable, in my opinion, were put forward by Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in the Supplemm. vol. 5, p. 1880. These too rest on etymologies alone,
That the kite is named from flying, דאה daa, as in Leviticus, rather than from sight, ראה raa, as in Deuteronomy.

Next comes דאה daa, or ראה raa. For it is not certain which way it should be written, since the same bird is called דאה in Leviticus and ראה raa in Deuteronomy; of these, one is taken from flying, the other from sight. For דאה daa is the verb to fly, and ראה raa to see. The letters Daleth and Resh, being very similar, are often confused by scribes. Thus דודנים Dodanim, Gen 10:4 and רודנים Rodanim, 1 Chr 1:7 are the same; so are ריפת Riphath, Gen 10:3 and דיפת Diphath, 1 Chr 1:6; הדר Hadar, Gen 36:39 and הדד Hadad, 1 Chr 1:46; הדד־עזר Hadad-ezer, 2 Sam 8:3 and הדר־עזר Hadar-ezer, 1 Chr 18:3; ההרודי Harodites, 2 Sam 23:25 and ההרורי Harorites, 1 Chr 11:27; חמדן Hamdan, Gen 36:26 and חמרן Hamran, 1 Chr 1:39 (var. 41.); דעואל Daguel, Num 1:14 and VII, 42. and רעואל Raguel, Num 2:14. And of God it is said in 2 Sam 22:11. וירא vajera, and he appeared, instead of וידא vajeda, and he flew, Ps 18:11. In exactly the same way the same bird is called דאה daa in one place and ראה raa in another. But if that bird is truly the kite, as most of the ancient and more recent interpreters hold, among them Jerome, the Arabs, Munster, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible], Diodati, Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], Schindler, etc., I would rather have it written דאה daa than ראה raa, with the name derived from flying rather than from sight. For while writers on natural history observe nothing peculiar in the kite's sight, in its flight it has this first distinctive feature: with its wings almost motionless it hovers in the air longer than any other bird. Munster: רחף, It moved, namely as the kite moves in the air without moving its wings, etc. Budaeus: We have watched kites for a whole hour or more catching prey without beating their wings, etc. This the Italian fowlers call tendere, the French planare. For by raising the wing a little they take the movement of the air into the rest of the body as well, and are thus held up. Moreover, there is scarcely any bird that flies higher than the kite. Martial, book 9, Epigram 55:
Hence the rapacious kite flies almost to the highest stars.

Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)], De Avibus book 2, ch. 26: When a hawk is let loose at a kite, both are carried up into the highest air, so that they escape human sight. Budaeus in his Philologia: Neither herons nor kites, though hidden within the clouds, can escape human hands. Finally, the kite does not easily tire in flying. Hence Persius on Vectidius, Satire 4:
— he ploughs at Cures more than a kite could fly over.
Where Cornutus comments: As is commonly said in the proverb, "As far as kites do not fly", because kites fly a great deal. And Juvenal, Satire 9:
— — for whom are you keeping so many mountains, so many Apulian estates, so many kites wearied within your pastures?

And there the old Scholiast says: The poet wishes to show the size of the estates, how widely they extend in fields, so that not even kites can fly across them. This, then, suits the nature of the kite better: that it was called דאה daa from the excellence of its flight rather than ראה raa from its sight. You may object these words of Apuleius, Metamorphoses book 6: Yet I could not escape the kite's eyes of the crafty little old woman, in which remarkable keenness of sight seems to be attributed to the kite. I shall reply, 1. that the same is attributed to all birds of prey; 2. that this passage of Apuleius is unique. This the illustrious commentator Philippus Beroaldus acknowledges in these words: No writer, so far as I know, celebrates the eyes of the kite as excelling in keenness of sight. I add that in the Samaritan copy, both in Deuteronomy and in Leviticus, ࠃࠀࠄ [דאה] is read with Daleth, nowhere ࠓࠀࠄ [ראה] with Resh. And from the Hebrew דאה daa the Arabic حدا [ḥdā] hida seems to have been formed, with a guttural prefixed, as in the Hebrew name of the Tigris, חדקל Hiddekel, formed from the Chaldee דגלה Digla. At least this is certain: among the Arabs the kite is called حداة [ḥidāh] hida . This is clear from Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], in the chapter قاطاننقي [qāṭānanqī] Catananke, in which these Greek words of Dioscorides on the dried seed of the herb catananke, Ἰκτίνου ὄνυξιν ὁμοιοῦται νεκροῦ [Iktinou onyxin homoioutai nekrou], It resembles the claws of a dead kite, are rendered thus in the Arabic paraphrase: وكان شكلها شبيها شكل مخالب الحداة الميتة [wa-kāna shakluhā shabīhan shakla makhālib al-ḥidāh al-mayyita] And its shape is similar to the shape of the claws of a dead hida. Hida, that is, kite. To say nothing of Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], who in the chapter On حداة [ḥidāh] hida attributes to it whatever the Philosopher has about the kite, Hist. book 6, ch. 6. Nor of Andrea Bellunensis, whose words are: Alhada is a bird which is called the kite. Correct, except that alhida should be written, not alhada.
