For الحداة [al-ḥadāh] alhada with Fatha is a double axe, as Damir and Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author] note; but alhida with Kasra is the name of the bird. There are some who interpret both דאה daa and ראה raa quite differently; but I pass over their versions because they do not seem in any way probable .

Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], p. 1, describes a falcon with yellow cere and feet, ash-grey above, rust-coloured below, the wings dusky above, the tail forked, banded with dusky brown, of the length of the body. He renders the Arabic name of this bird in Latin letters as Haddai; perhaps the man from whose mouth Forsskål took down this name pronounced our حِداة [ḥidāh], plural حِداء [ḥidāʾ], with that sound. In an observation Forsskål adds the following: "Is it Falco Milvus Linn.? But it is neither wholly rust-coloured, nor is the head whitish. Is it Falco forficatus? But below it is not whitish, but rust-coloured." Hence in the newest edition of the Linnaean System, vol. 1, part 1, p. 261, this falcon forms a distinct species under the heading Aegyptius.

Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] has set out conjectures on the guesses of the ancients about this word in den Fragen an eine Gesellschaft von Gelehrten, die nach Arabien reisen, p. 303 ff.
It is proved that איה aja is a species of hawk, which the ancients call the aesalon, the Germans Smirle, and we esmerillon [merlin].

After the treatise On the Eagle we tried to explain three names of birds, namely פרס peres, עזניה oznija, and דאה daa, or ראה raa, which are found nowhere outside the catalogue of unclean birds. Since in interpreting these the ancient and modern interpreters disagree greatly, their true meaning could be extracted from no other source than the origin of the words alone. Now four follow, namely איה aja, דיה daja, עורב oreb, and בת־יענה bath-jaana; since these are found elsewhere, more light will shine on their explanation. Yet there is much doubt about the first. The Greeks explain it sometimes as vulture, sometimes as kite. The former is followed by Jerome, Munster, Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], and the English and Italian versions; the latter by the Arabic translator in Job, Schindler, and the Genevans. Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] renders it דייתא אוכמתא, black vulture; the Jerusalem Targum, אבו ibbu, which I think is the same. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] has טרפיתא, bird of prey, a generic name, because he did not know the species. The Arabs in Moses have الصدا [al-ṣadā] owl. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] has יגא״וא, magpie. Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] and Buxtorf [=Johannes Buxtorf the Elder, Synagoga Judaica and Lexicon Chaldaicum Talmudicum et Rabbinicum], magpie or crow. Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot], variegated bird. Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)], vulture or hawk. Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra], island bird, as if the name were formed from אי, that is, from island. Other Hebrews, such as R. Levi, Mordecai, and Aquinas [=Philippe d'Aquin, Dictionarium hebraeo-chaldaeo-talmudico-rabbinicum (Paris 1629)], more prudent than the rest, say only that it is שם עוף, the name of a bird.

In our view the Hebrew האיה haaja is the same bird as the Arabic اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju. The bird is so called from its cry. For just as eagles are said to clangere, kites jugere or lipire, hawks pipare, and ravens crocitare, so the proper sound of this bird, according to the Arabs, is يايا [yāyā] jaja, and the cry itself is called اليايا [al-yāyā] aljajao. From this, then, the bird itself seems to have been called in Hebrew איה aja, as in Arabic يويو [yūyū] juju, and in the plural يايي [yāyī] jaji. Nor should it seem strange that a bird's name is taken from its voice, if Varro is right in book 4 of On the Latin Language: Most (birds) are named from their own calls, such as these: upupa, cuculus, corvus, hirundo, ulula, bubo; likewise these: pavo, anser, gallina, columba. Further, اليويو [al-yūyū] aljuju is among the species of hawks; and as Aristotle reckons ten kinds of them and Pliny sixteen, so the Arabs too count many. Among these is the صقر [ṣaqr] sacer, in the vernacular sacre, which is again subdivided into three species, namely the saker properly so called , the كونج [kawnaj] chauneg, and the يويو [yūyū] juju, of which Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] says: الصنف الثالث من الصغور اليويو وتسميه اهل مصر والشام الجلم لخغة جناحه وسرعته ولان الجلم هو الذي منجز به وهو المقص وهو طاير صغير قصير الذنب ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الباشق بارد رطب لانه اصبر منه نغسا واثغل حركة ويشرب الما شربا ضروريا كما يشربه الباسق الا انه ابخر ومزاجه بالنسبة الي الصغر حار يابس واذلك هو اشجع منه ويغال ان اول من ضراه واصطاد به بهرام جور وذلك انه شاهد يويو يطارد قبرة ويراوغها ويترفع وينخغض معها وما تركها الي ان صادها فاعجبه ذلك وامر به فادب وصاد به [al-ṣinf al-thālith min al-ṣughūr al-yūyū wa-tusammīhi ahl Miṣr wa-l-Shām al-jalam li-khiffat janāḥihi wa-surʿatihi wa-li-anna al-jalam huwa alladhī munjaz bihi wa-huwa al-miqaṣṣ wa-huwa ṭāyir ṣaghīr qaṣīr al-dhanab wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-bāshiq bārid raṭb li-annahu aṣbar minhu nafasan wa-athqal ḥarakatan wa-yashrab al-mā shurban ḍarūriyyan kamā yashrabuhu al-bāsiq illā annahu abkhar wa-mizājuhu bi-l-nisba ilā al-ṣaqr ḥārr yābis wa-li-dhālika huwa ashjaʿ minhu wa-yuqāl anna awwal man ḍarrāhu wa-iṣṭāda bihi Bahrām Jūr wa-dhālika annahu shāhada yūyū yuṭārid qubbara wa-yurāwighuhā wa-yatarafaʿ wa-yankhafiḍ maʿahā wa-mā tarakahā ilā an ṣādahā fa-aʿjabahu dhālika wa-amara bihi fa-uddiba wa-ṣāda bihi] The third species of SAKERS is aljuju, which the Egyptians and Syrians call algelem, because of the lightness and swiftness of its wings. For algelem means a sickle, or one furnished with a sickle (as though it cut the air with its wings as with a sickle). It is a small bird with a short tail. If you compare its temperament with that of albasik (another kind of hawk), it is cold and moist, because it holds its breath longer and is heavier in movement, and it drinks water when it must, as albasik drinks; yet it is more foul-smelling than it. But if you compare it with the saker (properly so called), it will appear to be of a hot and dry temperament, and is accordingly bolder than it. Moreover, a certain man named Behram Giur is said to have been the first to use it for hunting. For when, in his presence, a juju bird had pursued a lark and grappled with it, rising and descending with it, and not leaving it until it had caught it, he marvelled at this, ordered the bird to be trained, and afterwards used it for hunting. So far Damir. From this it is clear that the bird described is the one called in German Smirle, in Italian smerlo and smeriglio, in French esmerillon [merlin]. For it too is reckoned among the species of hawks and falcons. But in size it is the smallest (says Albertus, book 23, chapter 14), yet it yields to none in spirit and daring, in proportion to its body and strength, etc. Thus William the Falconer reports that he once caught a crane by means of these birds. Otherwise it can overcome only larks and similar birds etc. Its wings are very long in relation to its body, its tail moderate (that is, of middling size), its legs and feet flat, etc. They are very swift and crafty, and in taking their prey they ascend, and descend as they strike, etc. And Crescentiensis: The Ismerli are like falconelli, that is, little falcons, which they resemble both in shape of body and in colour of plumage, etc. They take chiefly larks, which they pursue with such eagerness and impetus that they sometimes dash even against a burning oven, or into a well, or against men's clothing. Another writer in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: The Smerillo has the form of a falcon, is smaller than the sparrowhawk, and flies faster than any other bird. It takes the same birds as the sparrowhawk, but especially small ones, such as the sparrow, the lark and the like . You see, reader, that like the Arabs' aljuju, our smirlus or smerillon belongs to the hawk species, is small in stature, short-tailed, swift in flight, remarkable for daring, and especially given to hunting larks; so that there can be no doubt at all that the same bird is designated by different names. But another point must above all be noted, because it bears most on our subject. If someone has lively and very keen eyes, the French say by a common proverb that he has the eyes of a smerillon, because this bird has such eyes. And the Arab poets too greatly praise the eyes of their juju. Among them an anonymous poet in Damir:
يويو مهذب رشيق ۞ كان عينيه لذي التحقيق ۞ فصان مخروطان من عقيق ۞ [yūyū muhadhdhab rashīq ۞ ka-anna ʿaynayhi li-dhī al-taḥqīq ۞ faṣṣān makhrūṭān min ʿaqīq ۞]

The Iuju is swift and nimble (in flight), whose eyes are truly lovely, and its pupils, as if polished on the lathe, more than sapphire. And Abu Nuwas, in his work On Fowling, entitled طريدة [Ṭarīda] Tarida, says of the same bird, among other things:
ازرق لا تكذب عيناه ۞ فلا يري القانص ما يراه ۞ [azraq lā takdhib ʿaynāhu ۞ fa-lā yarā al-qāniṣ mā yarāhu ۞]
These we have rendered in Latin words almost word for word thus:
Grey-eyed, and with eyes that never deceive, What the hunter does not see, that bird sees.

We have said that these words bear especially on our subject, because the following is read of the eye of this same bird, Iob. XXVIII, 7: The bird עיט knew not the path, nor has עין איה, the eye of the aja, seen it. He is speaking of mines, from which metals are dug out by human industry. Since these lie hidden in the innermost bowels of the earth, their path, says the sacred writer, the עיט ajit knew not, that is, not just any bird, but the bird of prey, a kind that is far more keen-sighted. This is in the first hemistich; and in the other, parallel to it: Nor has the eye of the aja, or juju if you prefer, seen it, that is, of the smerillon [merlin], although that bird is most sharp-eyed and sees as keenly as the eagle or the Epidaurian serpent. Many things prove that the smerillon is the αἰσαλών [aisalōn], the aesalon, of the ancients. 1. Aristotle (Hist. book 9, ch. 36) and Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) list the aesalon among the species of hawks. 2. By Aelian (book 2, ch. 51) it is called ὄρνις ἰσχυρός [ornis ischyros] . 3. And by Pliny (book 10, ch. 74) a small bird. 4. The same Pliny (book 10, ch. 8) writes that the aesalon appears at every season, whereas the others depart in winter. This fits the smerillon exactly, as Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)] has noted. His words are: Among the smaller hawks only the merlin, as the English call it, or smerla, as the Germans do, is always seen. Yet the most noble Lord de Grentemesnil contends that this is false. Some write aesaron instead of aesalon. Hesychius: Αἰσάρων· εἶδος ἱέρακος [Aisarōn; eidos hierakos]. Both perhaps come from αἶσα [aisa], because it is a bird αἴσιος [aisios], auspicious and of good omen, like every kind of hawk. This I could prove without any trouble, if it were worth the effort.

Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descript. Animall. p. 8, in his list of birds that stay at Alexandria, has, as received from an Arab hunter: „Vultur — Sákr“. What the medieval writers wrote about this same falcon has been carefully collected and explained by IO. GOTTL. SCHNEIDER on the Reliqua librorum Frideric. II. de arte venandi cum avibus, p. 90. 109. 185. 186.
Cf. IO. GOTTL. SCHNEIDER on the Reliqua librorum Friderici II. p. 65.
Compare Schneider on that passage; to him, however, in the place cited above, note 2, it seems doubtful whether the αἰσαλων [aisalōn] is the same bird as the smerillon.
It is proved that דיה daja is the black vulture.

After איה aja comes דיה daja, Deut 14:13. It is omitted in Leviticus, either by the Prophet himself, for a reason we do not know, or by scribes after the Prophet because of the τὸ ὁμοιόπτωτον [to homoioptōton] of the two words האיה haaja and הדיה hadaja; I think the latter is nearer the truth. What דיה daja is, is not sufficiently known. Jerome, the Arabs , and many of the more recent writers interpret it as the kite, as though it were the same as דאה daa, Lev 11:14 . This seems scarcely tenable, because, as we have proved, דאה daa and ראה raa are the same. Moreover, ראה raa and דיה daja cannot be the same, since in the same verse they are forbidden to the Jews as different animals. For the sacred text reads: These are the ones of which you shall not eat: the eagle, etc. והראה ואת האיה והדיה, and the raa, and the aja, and the daja. Here, since ראה raa is the same as דאה daa in Leviticus, namely the kite, דיה daja is certainly something else: namely the vulture, as I at least think. So render R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)], Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)], Schindler, and the English and Italian versions; also Fuller [=Nicholas Fuller, Miscellanea theologica / sacra (1612–22)], Miscellanea book 6, ch. 4. This rendering is strongly confirmed by Es. XXXIV, 15., on the desolation of Idumaea: There the דיות dajoth have gathered together. For דיות dajoth, the plural of דיה daja, cannot be kites, which are not gregarious birds and never gather or flock together . But they can be vultures, of which Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium] says, p. 785: Vultures alone among the birds with hooked talons live in flocks, so that sometimes fifty appear in a single flock, as Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] writes that he observed in Egypt. Hence the Philosopher, Hist. book 6, chapter 5: Πολλοὶ ἐξαίφνης φαίνονται ἀκολουθοῦντες τοῖς στρατεύμασι [polloi exaiphnēs phainontai akolouthountes tois strateumasi]; Many suddenly appear, following armies. And in book 9, chapter 11, he writes likewise, φαίνεσθαι ταχὺ πολλοὺς [phainesthai tachy pollous], that many suddenly appear. Basil too, in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Ἴδοις ἂν μυρίας ἀγέλας γυπῶν τοῖς στρατοπέδοις παρεπομένας [Idois an myrias agelas gypōn tois stratopedois parepomenas]; You may see countless flocks of vultures following armies. And Ambrose, imitating him, in the Hexaemeron, book 5, chapter 23: When opposing lines renew a lamentable war among themselves, the aforesaid birds follow in a great column. Pietro Bembo [=Pietro Bembo, Historia Veneta (1551)], History of Venice, book 5: It is established that in those days when war against Bajazet was being prepared in Apulia, ravens and vultures fought one another in the air with such force and in such hosts that twelve carts were filled with their carcasses. I cannot here omit the twelve vultures seen by Romulus when he founded the city of Rome, from which Vettius inferred that the Roman empire would end after as many centuries had passed. Censorinus, following Varro, wrote of this in chapter 14, about the thousandth year from the founding of the city. How many centuries, he says, are owed to the city of Rome it is not for me to say. But I will not keep silent about what I have read in Varro, who in book 18 of the Antiquities says that there was at Rome one Vettius, not undistinguished in augury for his talent, equal to any learned man in debate; and that he had heard him say that if things were as the historians reported about the auguries of Romulus at the founding of the city and the twelve vultures, then, since the Roman people had passed 120 years unharmed, it would reach a thousand two hundred. Nor did the prophecy lack fulfilment. For shortly after those twelve centuries had passed, when the strength of the state had been transferred from the West to the East, the Roman dignity was exhausted and the Western empire came to an end in Augustulus. For he laid down the purple out of fear of the Heruli, who under their leader Odoacer had burst into Italy, as Paul the Deacon writes in book 16. Likewise, when Caesar was leading his army down into the Campus Martius, six vultures appeared to him. Then, when he mounted the rostra after being made consul, six vultures were again seen and gave a sign, as though he were to found a new city under the auspices of Romulus. So Julius Obsequens reports. And in Suetonius, twelve vultures showed themselves to Octavius Augustus, as to Romulus, when he was taking the auspices in his first consulship. Dio reports this somewhat differently: Πρώτῃ τῶν ἀρχαιρεσιῶν ἐς τὸ πεδίον τὸ Ἄρειον εἰσελθὼν, γύπας ἓξ· καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα δημηγορῶν τι πρὸς τοὺς στρατειώτας, ἄλλους δώδεκα εἶδε [Prōtē tōn archairesiōn es to pedion to Areion eiselthōn, gypas hex; kai meta tauta dēmēgorōn ti pros tous strateiōtas, allous dōdeka eide]. On the first day of the elections, having entered the Campus Martius, he saw six vultures; and shortly afterwards, while addressing the soldiers, twelve others. From these it can at least be inferred that vultures often flock together, which is not written of other birds of prey. In vain would you object what we read in Matt 24:28 and Luke 17:37, that eagles too gather at a carcass. For there it is not a question of true eagles but of percnopteri, or gypaeeti, which are degenerate eagles of vulturine appearance, born, as it seems, from the mating of an eagle with a vulture, as we showed above. However that may be, whoever would have kites understood in the words of Isaiah where he writes that the דיות dajoth gather or flock together, will have to show, either from experience or from reliable writers, that kites sometimes flock together. This is as foreign to the disposition of kites as it is suited to the nature of vultures. Therefore the דיות dajoth are certainly vultures, not kites. Yet I would not think that every kind of vulture is contained under this name, but only the black ones. 1. Because in Deut 14:13 17. Moses distinguishes דיה daja and רחם racham as different animals; and that the latter signifies a kind of vulture largely white will be shown below. 2. Because דיה daja and דיו dejo, ink, are cognates. Not to mention that the Syrians and Persians call a demon ܕܝܘܐ [דיוא] dajava, or deva, from the appearance of a black colour, in which it chiefly shows itself to men, to strike greater terror into those who see it. Hence a certain species of savin is called in Persian ديودار [dīvdār] diudar, that is, demon's tree. So also that kind of vulture which is black is called דיה daja from its colour. And Elias [=Elijah Levita (1469–1549), author of the Aramaic lexicon Meturgeman and of Tishbi] rightly says: The bird that is black כדיו, like ink, is called דיה Daja. Nor without reason does Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] refer דיה and דיו to the same root. Moreover, much can be read about the black vulture in the ancients. Thus Pliny, book 10, chapter 6, says that among vultures the black ones prevail. And among the poets, one of the gravest punishments of the underworld is to be gnawed by a black vulture. Hence Juvenal, Satire 13,
— — — nor the rock, or the punishment of the black vulture. — — — — — —
And Seneca in the Thyestes, of Tityus:
With his dug-out entrails he feeds the black birds.
Black birds, that is, black vultures. Physicians, too, prefer to use the black vulture in their remedies. Thus Samonicus, in chapter 14, would have applied, to soothe pain of the eyes,
— — — — the gall of the black vulture, with which blades of celandine have been mixed.
And in chapter 34, πρὸς εὐτοκίαν [pros eutokian] [for an easy delivery]:
— — they place beneath the dung of the black vulture, so that she may scarcely feel the birth that presses close. And in chapter 58, for the falling sickness:
The gall of the black vulture is of help with old Bacchus.

Others, however, read ampli [large]; and Pliny makes an exception for remedies against serpents, in which, he writes in book 29, chapter 4, black vultures are less effective. Among birds (he says) the vulture is foremost as a help against serpents. It has also been noted that the black ones have less power. That those black vultures are properly called αἰγυπιοὺς [aigypious], that they are of both sexes, unlike other vultures, and that they stand between the eagle kind and the vulture kind, Aelian reports in book 2, chapter 46, in these words: Τοὺς δὲ αἰγυπιοὺς (λέγουσιν) ἐν μεθορίῳ γυπῶν ὄντας καὶ αἰετῶν, εἶναι καὶ ἄῤῥενας, καὶ τὴν χρόαν πεφυκέναι μέλανας [tous de aigypious (legousin) en methoriō gypōn ontas kai aietōn, einai kai arrhenas, kai tēn chroan pephykenai melanas]. And Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] hints that aegypii are so called for Aegyptii [Egyptians], when he writes in chapter 2: εἶναι δὲ καὶ τοὺς μέλανας ὡς Αἰγυπτίους [einai de kai tous melanas hōs Aigyptious], that they too are black, like Egyptians. But αἰγυπιὸς [aigypios] is one thing, Αἰγύπτιος [Aigyptios] another. The former comes from γυπός [gypos]; the latter is formed from Cophti.

To these Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] (in den Fragen an eine Gesellschaft von Gelehrten, die nach Arabien reisen, p. 305. 306.) adds the Syriac and the Alexandrian translators, about whom, however, we must look a little more carefully. That the Syriac translator puts his ܕܝܬܐ [דיתא] for דיה might indeed seem doubtful, since for the six bird names that are read in the Hebrew text of Deut 14:12–13. he gives only these two: ܢܨܐ ܘܕܝܬܐ [נצא ודיתא]. It is nevertheless clear from the fact that the same translator has that same ܕܝܬܐ [דיתא] for the Hebrew דיות in Isa 34:15. That the kite is meant by that word is believed on the authority of the Arabic translator, since in Job 28:7 he renders the Syriac ܕܝܬܐ [דיתא] by his حداة [ḥidāh] (which Bochart proved in Chapter 7 to be the kite; whether rightly, I do not dare to decide). But the matter is much more uncertain with the Alexandrians. For the three bird names found in the Hebrew of Deut 14:15 they give only these two: τον γυπα και τον ἰκτινον [ton gypa kai ton iktinon]; whether the Hebrew דיה is expressed by either of them, and if so by which, no one will say with certainty. In Isaiah (XXXIV, 15.), moreover, they translate that same Hebrew word as ἐλάφους [elaphous].

To these Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] has recently been added, in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 3, ch. 3, p. 75 ff., relying chiefly on the authority of the Alexandrian translator; how much that is worth you will understand from what was said in the preceding note. Nor does that most learned man seem to have weighed sufficiently what Bochart adds immediately afterwards about the order of the Hebrew words in both passages, Lev 11:14 and Deuter. XIV, 13.

But Oedmann, p. 81, asserts the contrary, producing Belon as witness, who writes that he saw great flocks of kites, and so dense that the crowd of birds in flight darkened the rays of the sun. But, with all respect to that most learned man, he seems to have made poor use of Belon's words. For in the passage Oedmann cites, Belon is speaking of kites changing their abode as winter approaches, and then, like absolutely all migratory birds, flying in great swarms. Here are Belon's own words (de avibus book 2, ch. 28): Once, when we were on the shore of the Euxine Sea, in the part where Thrace lies, at about the end of April, on a very lofty hill next to the column that stands at the mouth of the Bosporus, where a fowler was spreading a net to catch sparrowhawks flying in from the right-hand stretch of the sea, we observed kites arriving there in flocks on a straight course, in such numbers and so dense a column that it seemed a marvel to us. — But when summer comes on, they return to Europe to escape the excessive heat of those regions. But there is yet another thing that prevents us from taking דיות as kites. It is clear from Isa 34:15 that the דיות inhabit desolate places and wildernesses, whereas kites shun the wilderness and seek out cities and places frequented by men, as Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)] reports from his own observation and the testimony of many others, Ornithol. vol. 1, book 5, ch. 15, p. 401. Belon too, loc. cit., writes that in Egypt kites are so tame that they fly right up to the windows of houses.

Schneider, on Aelian 2, 46, suspects that the Αἰγυπιον [Aigypion] is the same bird that Belon (de avibus book 2, ch. 23) saw frequently in Egypt and called the black vulture, although it is not yet sufficiently established whether it is the same as Linnaeus' percnopterus. The same Schneider, on the Reliqua of Frederick II, p. 14, observes that the vultur ater [dark vulture] of the ancients is the Emperor's Galeranus niger (p. 28), the Avoltoio nero of Cetti [=Francesco Cetti, Storia naturale di Sardegna (1774–77)] in the Histor. Nat. Sardin. vol. 2, p. 9 ff., German trans. In the newest edition of the Linnaean System, vol. 1, part 1, p. 248, no. 9, this species of vulture appears under the heading Vultur niger, with dusky primaries and tail feathers, the feathers of the feet black. Yet Gmelin [=J. F. Gmelin, 13th edition of Linnaeus, Systema naturae (1788–93)] too doubts whether it is a mere variety of the percnopterus (which is the Hebrew and Arabic רחם). — But by what argument Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], in the Clavis in Iesaj. p. 234, was moved to take the דיות as white vultures, I for my part cannot grasp.
